10625-a-concise-dictionary-of-middle-eng:
A. L. Mayhew of Wadham College, Oxford, and Walter W. Skeat, professor of Anglo-Saxon at Cambridge, compiled this Concise Dictionary of Middle English, published by the Clarendon Press in 1888. It covers English words used from about 1150 to 1580, the age of Chaucer, Langland, and the early Tudors. Skeat's preface explains how to use its entries and marks.

Students of medieval texts use it to unlock spelling, sense, and grammar that modern English has left behind. The dictionary is compact but scholarly, built for readers working through old poems and prose. Anyone reading Chaucer or Malory in the original will find it an essential companion.
23258-journal-of-jasper-danckaerts-1679-:
The Journal of Jasper Danckaerts records a Dutch journey across America in 1679 and 1680, in an edition issued in 1913. Its editors explain their text with care. The translation is substantially Mr. Murphy's, as printed in his edition of 1867, and Murphy was an excellent Dutch scholar.

Careful checks were made between that translation and the original manuscript. The Long Island Historical Society, which owns the manuscript, allowed the editors to examine it. Readers get both a first-hand early colonial travel record and a model of how such records are edited, checked, and brought back into print.
28079-the-honest-american-voter-s-little:
Blythe Harding published The Honest American Voter's Little Catechism for 1880 in New York with John Polhemus in 1880. The preface explains that Harding, invited to stenograph a discussion on the election, heard one disputant pump his antagonist dry by the method, and decided to give the dialogue to the public.

The catechism asks what a republic is, how the people exercise power through elected senators, who the president is, and whether electors are bound to follow the majority of their states. Harding's pamphlet is a lively civics primer for the election year, teaching the machinery of American government through questions.
31756-screw-thread-cutting-by-the-master:
Edwin A. Battison's Smithsonian paper, number 37 in United States National Museum Bulletin 240, published in Washington in 1966, studies screw-thread cutting by the master screw method since 1480. It is part of the museum's Contributions from the Museum of History and Technology, a series on science and technology. It includes the bulletin front matter and index entries with the single paper.

Its subject is a workshop technique with a long history: how threads were cut true by guiding a lathe with a master screw, and how that method developed over centuries. Readers get a specialist history of technology, precise about tools and practice, that explains a humble process behind modern machinery.
32510-the-life-of-william-ewart-gladston:
John Morley's Life of William Ewart Gladstone appears here in volume two of three, covering 1859 to 1880 and published in Toronto in 1903. Book Five, 1859 to 1868, follows the Italian revolution, the great budget, the battle for economy, and the spirit of Gladstonian finance. It also covers the American Civil War, Garibaldi and Denmark, defeat at Oxford, the death of Lord Palmerston, parliamentary leadership, and reform, including household suffrage and the opening of the Irish campaign.

Book Six, 1869 to 1874, treats religious equality, agrarian revolution, education, the Franco-German War, neutrality, the Black Sea, and a day's work of a giant, with Gladstone's autumn decline in popularity. Morley, a statesman and biographer, writes with close knowledge of Victorian politics. The volume suits readers who want Gladstone's middle career in full, detailed narrative.
4832-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
This thirtieth volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1579 to 1580. Its file header numbers it as the thirty-second Gutenberg volume. Chapter two opens with Parma's feint upon Antwerp, as he invests Maestricht, while deputations and letters pass from the states-general, from Brussels, and from Parma to the Walloon provinces. Active negotiations by Orange and by Farnese run beside the siege.

Walloon envoys in Parma's camp before Maestricht, festivities, and the Treaty of Reconciliation follow, with rejoicings of the royalist party and a comedy enacted at Paris theatres. Religious tumults in Antwerp and Utrecht close the sampled scope, as reconciliation with Spain splits the provinces along lines of faith and loyalty. Parma's siege craft and Orange's diplomacy contend for the same towns, and the Walloon provinces choose. Readers get Motley's account of Maestricht, reconciliation, and religious tumult.
8428-the-afghan-wars-1839-42-and-1878-80:
Archibald Forbes, war correspondent and historian, wrote this history of Britain's two Afghan wars, with portraits and plans. Part one covers the first war: the march to Cabul, the years of occupation, the road to ruin, the catastrophe of the retreat, the siege of Jellalabad, and retribution and rescue. The second war, 1878 to 1880, follows in the same detailed style.

Forbes wrote for readers who wanted campaigns explained by a man who knew war reporting. His account stresses marches, sieges, and the politics that sent armies into Afghanistan. Readers of military history get a Victorian classic, clear on battles and unsparing about blunders, and still useful for the long shadow those wars cast.
9180-life-of-johnson-volume-3-1776-1780:
This third volume of Boswell's Life of Johnson, in the Hill edition, covers March 1776 to October 1780. Boswell and Johnson change horses at Derby and enjoy talk with Dr. Butter, a Scots physician indignant over a militia bill. The volume adds notes on George Psalmanazar, Johnson's travels, and the inmates of his house.

Readers meet Johnson in late middle age, still fierce in talk and generous in friendship. Boswell's letters on a Royal Academy post close the volume. For lovers of the Life, this stretch keeps its famous mix of wit, learning, and daily life.
a-concise-dictionary-of-middle-english-f: Anthony Lawson Mayhew compiles a concise dictionary of Middle English from 1150 to 1580. Published at the Clarendon Press, it gathers ancient words for readers of old English texts. Mayhew draws on earlier scholarship and sets his entries out for practical use. The dictionary remains a handy guide to the language of Chaucer's age and beyond.
acosta-natural-moral-history-markham-vol:
José de Acosta, a Spanish Jesuit who spent years in Peru, published his Historia natural y moral de las Indias in 1590. Volume one here is Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society edition of 1880, built on Edward Grimston's English translation of 1604. Acosta set out to describe the New World whole: its skies, lands, plants, and peoples.

His natural history reasons about winds, climates, and species with a scholar's care and a traveler's eyes. His moral history turns to the customs and beliefs of the native peoples. Acosta even framed an early theory of how humans first reached the Americas. The work became the first broad natural history and ethnography of the New World.

Volume two completes Markham's 1880 edition of José de Acosta's Natural and Moral History of the Indies. The Spanish work of 1590, in Grimston's English of 1604, joined two surveys in one: the nature of the Americas and the life of their peoples. Acosta wrote from long residence in Peru and wide reading of reports.

The second volume carries his account of native religion, government, and custom to its close. He treats the peoples of Mexico and Peru as nations with laws, rites, and histories of their own. That respect, rare in his century, gives the book lasting worth. With volume one, it forms the first systematic survey of the New World.
arxiv-2412-00080: Peter Seokhee Seong (2024) gives a new proof of a formula in knot theory. The classical Torres formula links the Alexander polynomial of a link to those of its sublinks. Morifuji had already extended the formula to the twisted setting. Seong reaches the same result through twisted Reidemeister torsion instead. The new route stays closer in shape to Torres' original argument. The paper is a short proof note for specialists in low-dimensional topology.
arxiv-2412-01280:
Houhao Wang and co-authors hunt for crystals whose sound vibrations form linked rings in momentum space, a pattern called a Hopf link. Their paper appeared in 2024. Such interlocked nodal loops are exotic and rare. The team first listed 141 symmetry groups that can host the pattern. Then they screened a phonon database of 10,034 materials. Nearly all had plain loops or chains, but only 113 could host the full Hopf link in their vibration spectra.

Eight clean examples are showcased, from lithium gallium sulfide to a rubidium thorium fluoride. Surface vibration states tied to the loops are displayed for one of them. The authors offer the 113 materials as a shopping list for experimenters who want to probe linked-loop physics in real crystals.
arxiv-2412-02480:
Yuzhi Che and co-authors show the strong force's grip can be read from B meson decays in two thousand twenty-four. That grip, the coupling alpha-s, is a core constant of particle physics. Their route uses the total rate of semileptonic B decays, where a bottom quark sheds a lepton pair.

The rate is written through the coupling, quark masses, and a mixing term, then fit to world averages for charged and neutral B mesons. The fit lands near the value from the Z boson scale after scaling, with the main error from the mixing term and theory sums. Future B and Z factories could sharpen the method to rival the best current measures, those from tau decays.
arxiv-2412-03980:
Vakada Naveen, Arvind Krishna Sridhar, Yinyi Guo, and Erik Visser built a chatbot that answers questions about sound. Their twenty twenty-four paper links many expert models in one system. A query may ask what was said, who spoke, what song played, or for new audio to be made.

A classifier first reads the intent of the query and sends it to the right expert. A context module pulls events and times from the audio, and a language model of modest size blends all outputs into one reply. On custom tests of time-based questions, the system beat large audio models. It also did well on a known sound bench, which makes it a good fit for use on a device.
arxiv-2412-05680:
Rory Conlin and co-authors compute free-boundary plasma equilibria at high order in the DESC code. The task asks what shape a hot plasma takes when its edge is not fixed by a wall. Such shapes matter for fusion devices that confine plasma with magnets. Boundary rules split into fixed and free cases, with a sheet current allowed at the edge in some.

The team reviews when that sheet current can exist at the plasma-vacuum seam. A fast, exact method scores how well a trial shape meets the rules. DESC then finds equilibria in vacuum and at set plasma pressure. Runs cover cases with and without the sheet current. The work backs design studies for stellarator fusion devices.
arxiv-2412-06780:
Yanbo Xu and co-authors present a method that makes image and 3D generation more varied, in work from 2024. A common tool guides 3D building with scores from a 2D image model trained to produce pictures from text. That tool tends to give near-identical results, even though the image model itself can produce varied pictures.

The new method borrows from how the image model samples pictures step by step. It guides building along paths set by random starting seeds, which spreads the results out. The team adjusts the idea for cases where the building steps cannot follow those paths exactly, such as 3D shapes whose views change together. Tests on 2D tasks, text-based 3D building, and rebuilding a scene from one photo show more varied results with quality kept.
arxiv-2412-08280:
Liempi and co-authors published a 2024 astronomy paper on how giant black holes may have been born. Most large galaxies hold a dense cluster of stars at their center, and many also hold a black hole millions of times heavier than the sun. The two seem to trade places: in smaller galaxies the cluster dominates, in larger ones the black hole does. That pattern hints at a shared origin.

The team added two ideas to a computer model of galaxy growth. In the model, the central cluster forms in place as gas gathers and makes stars. Inside such a crowded cluster, stars can collide and merge, planting the seed of a black hole. Tight, compact clusters proved best at making seeds. Seeds of many sizes grew, some reaching the huge masses seen in real galaxies. The model's black hole counts matched what telescopes observe at the heavy end.
arxiv-2412-10180:
Jakob Thumm, Julian Balletshofer, Leonardo Maglanoc, Luis Muschal, and Matthias Althoff gave a safety framework for robot arms near people in two thousand twenty-four. Robots could take on repetitive and hazardous work, but safe contact with humans must be guaranteed. Older methods are either too cautious for natural teamwork or assume a fixed path.

Their shield, called SARA, uses reachability analysis to sort possible contacts by type in a formally sound way. Loose contacts allow higher force than clamping contacts, where a body part is trapped. For each type they verify the robot's kinetic energy stays below pain and injury limits. Tests showed safe contact with much better speed than prior methods.
arxiv-2412-10380:
Gagan Bansal and seven co-authors catalog what makes talking with AI agents harder than talking with software. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Modern agents observe, use tools, and message other agents. Users still meet them through plain natural language. The agents' complexity hides many failure modes. Communication grounding, how partners build shared understanding, frames the analysis.

Twelve key challenges emerge from the study. Some block information flowing from agent to user. Others block the user's side of the channel. A third set spans every exchange. The authors ground each challenge in prior research. Designers of agent systems gain a checklist of conversational risks. Human-AI interaction research gets a shared agenda.
arxiv-2412-10580:
Belén Costanza, Claudia G. Scóccola, and Matías Zaldarriaga teach a neural network to clean maps of the faint glow left from the early universe. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Sharp maps of this cosmic microwave background help pin down how the universe began. A classic filter does the cleaning well but slowly.

Their network, DeepWiener, first learned the trick for heat maps and now handles polarised light too. It takes in the raw map, a noise map, and a mask of the blocked sky. A step-by-step loop splits the signal into its two modes and fixes leaks caused by the mask. The cleaned maps match the classic method but come far faster. Their error bars also beat a common shortcut method. Messy masks, the team notes, still make one mode hard to recover.
arxiv-2412-11980:
Medina-Dozal, Urzúa, and Récamier-Angelini solved this quantum optics problem in twenty twenty-four. An optomechanical system couples light in a cavity to a moving mirror-like part. The coupling can be linear or quadratic in the light field, and an outside force may drive the system. Tracking its exact change over time is a hard algebra problem.

The authors use Lie algebra methods to build the time evolution operator in closed form. For the undriven case the result is exact. For the driven case they give a close approximation. Computer simulations matched the formulas well in both cases. The work gives theorists a clean tool for a widely used quantum device model.
arxiv-2412-13880:
Shalini Saini, Anitha Chennamaneni, and Babatunde Sawyerr review how attackers and defenders duel around learning based network intrusion detectors, in work from twenty twenty-four. Deep learning guards scan huge traffic flows for odd patterns. Attackers can also bend those same tools against the guards.

The review covers poisoned training data, test time evasion, and reverse engineering of detectors. It traces how each attack works and what counters exist. The authors note the field is still young and oddly split: defenses lag attacks in real traffic settings. Gaps include scarce real attack data and weak testing of AI defenses. They frame the work as groundwork for sturdier network defense.
arxiv-2412-15080:
Nico Guth and co-authors model a small effect that could matter a lot for fusion power. Pellets of frozen fuel fired into a hot, magnetically held plasma do not just slow down and dissolve. The plasma heats the pellet's vapor cloud unevenly, and the lopsided pressure pushes back like a tiny rocket, speeding the pellet up as it flies.

Their model starts from a round, even picture of the dissolving pellet and adds a small uneven correction. It predicts speed-ups near one hundred thousand meters per second squared in today's tokamaks, matching lab estimates. For the ITER reactor's high-performance runs, the push could reach ten times that, cutting how deep pellets fly. The authors warn this could weaken a key tool for calming dangerous plasma disruptions.
arxiv-2412-16980:
Rousseeuw builds a chart to make straight line forecasts easy to explain in twenty twenty-four. Such forecasts are a basic tool, yet it is hard to see which inputs drive a given forecast up or down. His chart shows each input's push on the forecast for the case at hand. It works whether the formula was fit by hand or by machine.

The chart handles number inputs, group inputs, and inputs that act jointly. A second chart shows how the pushes link to each other across cases. Both charts are plain to read and pack a lot of facts into one view. The aim is to help users trust and explain a forecast as it stands.
arxiv-2412-17080:
Schooltink and Zennaro aligned two styles of causal abstraction in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Causal models can be zoomed out to simpler levels, but the levels must agree on cause and effect. Graphical methods zoom by clustering the diagram. Functional methods zoom by mapping variables and their values.

The authors prove the two styles match under set conditions. Cluster diagrams correspond to functional abstractions whose value maps are reversible, and to a third, constructive style. They then widen the graphical side with partial cluster diagrams. Those allow some clusters to stay unmerged. The results let theorems travel between the two frameworks, which had grown up apart.
arxiv-2412-18980:
Reza Jalayer and co-authors compare deep learning systems that diagnose faults in rotating machines while reporting their own uncertainty, in a paper from 2024. A diagnosis is safer when the model can say it is unsure. Doubt comes in two kinds: from unseen fault types and from plain noise in the data.

The team benchmarked the leading design families, including dropout sampling, Bayesian networks, and deep ensembles. Two cutoff rules decided when a reading counted as out of place. Against unseen faults, all models caught a large share of the odd data. Ensembles did best under either cutoff rule. Under noise, the picture was more mixed. The findings guide engineers who must field fault systems they can trust.
arxiv-2501-00280:
Sharing quantum keys over long distances is limited by loss in ground fiber, so Yichen Gao, Guanqun Song, and Ting Zhu look to the sky. They study how fleets of satellites should be arranged to pass quantum signals between far-apart ground stations. Their plan adds relay satellites in Molniya orbits, the tall, stretched orbits that linger long over one hemisphere.

Those relays stretch the time a satellite can serve a target region, widening coverage and cutting delay in the quantum link. The team lays out a strategy for placing the fleet and its relays. Their aim is a sturdy world-wide quantum network that beats the reach of fiber alone.
arxiv-2501-00680:
Mauro Goncalves, Monica Graf, Marek Pasciak, and Jiri Hlinka wrote this materials paper, issued in two thousand twenty-four, on tiny crystals of bismuth ferrite. This compound is ferroelectric, and at nanoparticle size its inner electric pattern depends heavily on how the surface ends.

Using atomistic simulations grounded in first-principles data, the team varied the particles' surface endings and charge patterns. Many multi-domain layouts emerged, each with its own way for the order to bend near the surface. For neutral surfaces, an unusual phase appeared: not the bulk's rhombohedral form, but a stripe-like arrangement of polarization. The authors track polarization, oxygen cage tilts, and volume change across every layout found. The work shows how much a nanoparticle's skin can rewrite its core behavior.
arxiv-2501-01680:
Prihadi, Dwiputra, Khairunnisa, and Zen wrote in twenty twenty-five about chaos inside charged black holes with scalar hair. Hair here means an extra field around the hole beyond mass and charge. They send charged shock waves in from the outer edge. Then they track special correlators that reveal how fast a small disturbance scrambles. Near the inner singularity, the space takes a Kasner form, with uneven stretching in different directions.

As the deformation grew, one chaos measure fell relative to surface gravity. At large deformation it could still beat a standard charged case. Deformation also cut the delay before scrambling began. A coupling in their model strongly shaped that delay. The results show how outer changes can reshape inner chaos.
arxiv-2501-01780:
Frank Calegari and Qiankang Chen determine over which number fields hyperbolic triangle groups can be defined. A compact hyperbolic triangle group has a canonical discrete representation into the real projective special linear group, unique up to conjugation. Its trace field is built from cosines of the triangle's angles, and the question is when the group can be realized over its own trace field, or over any totally real field.

The authors prove that exactly eleven such groups are conjugate to subgroups over their trace fields. They further prove no additional compact hyperbolic triangle groups work over any totally real field whatsoever. The result answers a question first raised by Waterman and Maclachlan. It also settles, positively, five interrelated recent conjectures of McMullen. The paper closes a classification problem at the meeting point of hyperbolic geometry and number theory.
arxiv-2501-02680:
Li and a large team reviewed in twenty twenty-five how spread models, a kind of smart art tool, can help design proteins. Design of proteins with set traits has been hard for years. Spread models have strong math roots and have done well at such tasks.

The review lays out two main kinds of spread model and how each works. It then maps their use in protein design, short chain builds, drug hunts, and drug-protein binds. A key need is to keep the model true to three-view turns and flips of space. The team ends with paths to self-run protein design.
arxiv-2501-03380:
Ignacio Garrón and Andrey Ramos present a 2025 paper on nowcasting carbon dioxide emissions for US states. Official emissions data arrive yearly and late, which slows climate policy. The authors build a panel framework that estimates current emissions growth at higher frequency.

Their model predicts per-capita energy use growth from quarterly income, monthly electricity use, and a weekly economic index, mixing data of different frequencies. A bridge equation, fitted with quantile regression, converts energy nowcasts into the full distribution of emissions growth. In a dress rehearsal over 2009 to 2018 that mimicked real release dates, the nowcasts beat a historical benchmark. The method gives policymakers an earlier, sharper read on state emissions.
arxiv-2501-04080:
Mónica Taormina and a large team of colleagues measure precise physical properties of three detached eclipsing binary systems in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Such systems anchor the extragalactic distance scale. The team modeled light and radial velocity curves, analyzed period changes, and ran detailed spectroscopic analysis for the system with O-type stars.

Component masses run from about twelve to twenty-two solar masses, with temperatures between 22,500 and 36,000 kelvin. One system appears to be at least triple; another shows a significant period decrease of unclear origin. For one system, mass and radius precision improved about sixfold over earlier work. The team also provides a new mass-luminosity relation for O and B stars in the Cloud.
arxiv-2501-04780:
Shubhayan Sarkar sets out the use of quantum far links to sync clocks in a safe way. He also uses them to back up facts of fast moves with no trust in the gear used. Plain clock sync can be hit with ease. A foe who holds a sign back by a bit can cause large flaws down the line. Those flaws hit tools from GPS to work split on more than one screen.

His fix uses a stamp of truth that needs no trust in gear and rests on quantum far links. Clocks can then be synced with no trust in any gear in the set. He then grows the plan to watch time stretch from fast moves in the same no trust way. The text is a plan in rules that links base quantum work to a real time task.
arxiv-2501-06580:
Jeong-Myeong Bae, Hammam Raihan Mohammad, Ewan Stewart, and Heeseung Zoe wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It calculates the ripples in the early universe's density that were seeded by heat jitter during a phase called thermal inflation.

In thermal inflation, the universe's temperature sets how long a burst of expansion lasts. Tiny thermal wiggles therefore stretch into lasting differences in density. Using plain thermodynamics, the authors work out the small-scale heat fluctuations and follow them as expansion carries them to large scales. They convert the resulting temperature differences into curvature ripples with a standard bookkeeping method. The paper ends with a closed formula for the ripple strength across scales. Such predictions let future sky surveys test whether a thermal inflation phase really happened.
arxiv-2501-09880: Svetlik wrote a solo math study in twenty twenty-five that proves a stronger form of a known rule for smooth wave-like functions. The rule, Harnack's rule, bounds how much such a function can vary on a round disc when it stays above zero. His stronger form holds for the same class of functions on the unit disc. The proof of that stronger bound is the full content of the study.
arxiv-2501-10480:
Roy Burson wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025. It looks at the famous P versus NP problem through two lenses: the sliding tile puzzle and finding roots of polynomials. The focus is how the shape of the solution space drives how hard a problem feels.

The core contrast is between finding a solution and checking one. Checking is often far quicker. The paper argues the gap depends on how the set of possible states is laid out, and how fast it can be crossed. By counting configurations of the tile puzzle and relating them to search time, the author shows that navigating the space well matters as much as raw solving power. The study adds to the debate on why some problems resist efficient solution, tying algorithm design to the geometry of where answers live.
arxiv-2501-10780:
George Montagnon and Elizabeth Winstanley compute the electric current of a quantum field around a charged black hole, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The field is a light, charged scalar field, and the black hole can amplify waves that carry charge away. Three standard quantum states for the field are compared.

A mode-sum method with practical shortcuts yields the cleaned-up current for each state. The team traces how the current shifts with the charges of the hole and of the field. They also work out how the current feeds back on the surrounding electric field. The study sharpens tools for quantum fields in curved space.
arxiv-2501-11880:
He Yu and Jing Liu propose CTWalks in 2025, a method for learning from graphs that change over time. Such graphs model things like message networks where links appear by the minute. Older methods often lose either time detail or community structure.

CTWalks samples walks through the graph using community labels, with no tunable parameters in the sampler. It anonymizes the walks while keeping community tags, then encodes time flow with ordinary differential equations. The design captures both within-group and between-group interactions. Theory connects the method to matrix factorization and shows it avoids locality bias. On benchmark datasets it beat established methods at predicting future links.
arxiv-2501-13180:
Maxime Van de Moortel (2025) reviews the strong cosmic censorship conjecture, an old claim about how gravity must behave. Roger Penrose proposed it in the wake of the relativity breakthroughs of the 1960s. The claim says, roughly, that singularities inside black holes must never leave the future open to arbitrary influence. If it failed, Einstein's theory would lose its power to predict what happens next. The question has driven deep work in mathematics ever since.

The review gathers recent progress made with modern methods for partial differential equations. Those tools let researchers test the conjecture in the setting where it was born: gravitational collapse. Van de Moortel traces how results on black hole interiors have sharpened both the claim and its possible exceptions. The paper is a map of where the conjecture now stands. It shows a physics idea still generating hard, fruitful mathematics sixty years on.
arxiv-2501-13580: Changjiang Du builds a bridge in p-adic number theory in a twenty twenty-five paper. He starts with a field K that is an unramified extension of the p-adic numbers. To each suitable representation of the Galois group of K, he attaches a module of a special multivariable kind. He then proves that this assignment is fully faithful and exact, so it keeps the structure of the representations intact. The construction is a p-adic analogue of recent work by Breuil and co-authors.
arxiv-2501-14580:
Mark Shiliaev studied a number puzzle in a 2025 math paper. Take a number between zero and one, and try to stay just below it using the sum of two unit fractions. The allowed bottom numbers come from Fibonacci-type lists, where each term builds on the ones before it, like the famous Fibonacci list itself.

A greedy method picks the largest allowed fraction first, then the best second one. Shiliaev finds exactly which target numbers make that greedy pair the best possible pair of all. He then gives a neat, simple form for that set when the list is the Fibonacci list or the Lucas list. The work settles a clean question in approximation.
arxiv-2501-15280:
Robin Young argues for a simple twist on cleaning the data used to train language models in a 2025 paper. Filtering harmful text from training sets is known to make models safer at no cost to skill. Young proposes doing it twice: let a model trained on filtered data filter the corpus again, then train on the cleaner set.

His analysis shows the loop settles at a point where the model approves of its own training data. Even if each pass is only as good as the last, harmful content decays round by round. A side benefit is a large set of preference labels over documents, which humans can audit even though model internals stay opaque. He calls for labs to test the loop.
arxiv-2501-15380:
Labani Mallick and colleagues published an astrophysics paper in 2025 on glowing black holes called active galactic nuclei. Gas spirals into these black holes through a hot disk. A surrounding corona shines in X-rays. Open questions include how power moves between disk and corona, and how fast the black holes spin.

The team fitted X-ray spectra from eleven nearby examples. Their data came from two space telescopes working together. A dense disk reflection model explained three sources fully. The rest still needed an extra warm gas component. That supports a mixed origin for a puzzling soft X-ray glow. The study also gives early estimates of disk-to-corona power sharing.
arxiv-2501-17580:
Stolbov, Stepanov, and Raikher study a magnetic rubber strip lying on a table that, under a vertical field, either lifts its free end or folds into an arc. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The strip is soft magnetic: it magnetizes only while the field is on. As a bending element it mimics a single cilium.

Experiments show both shapes occurring, with a wide zone where either can persist. Cycling the field produces hysteresis between the modes. Theory finds the transition resembles a first-order jump, with a twist. The flat state never loses stability, even under huge fields. So the exact field at which bending starts is in principle unpredictable. That contrasts with in-plane fields, where bending is smooth and reversible. As a cilium the strip also behaves backwards from earlier designs. The work guides soft magnetic actuators.
arxiv-2501-18380:
Hu and Kamada wrote in twenty twenty-five about gravitational waves from fading cosmic strings in the early universe. Cosmic strings are thin, dense threads predicted by some theories of cosmic history. Pulsar timing groups recently found hints of a faint nanohertz wave background. Metastable strings could explain that signal, but standard formation routes face problems. Their spectrum clashes with non-detections at higher frequencies for strong strings. A delayed scaling scenario, where strings start radiating later, eases both issues.

Dilution during inflation also thins out unwanted monopoles before strings form. The authors clarify the expected spectrum under that scenario. It fits pulsar hints while respecting higher-frequency limits. They explore signals future detectors could catch across many frequency bands. Links to inflation theory and grand unified theories are discussed. The work keeps cosmic strings a live explanation for the background.
arxiv-2502-00780:
Diogen Babuc laid out the base claims of a framework he calls the Theory of Proportions and Symbolic Allusions in twenty twenty-five. The framework joins math, language study, psychology, and game theory. Its core claim is that assigning numbers to symbols, dates, and words reveals patterns that repeat across scales and reflect deep rules of the world.

Babuc applies the scheme most fully in therapy. A patient might assign numbers to fingers, dates, or words and find links between private events and shared symbols, which can loosen rigid thinking. He suggests a similar reframing may help people with obsessive-compulsive disorder treat their fixations as codes to read rather than walls. Uses in teaching, ciphers, and language software are also proposed. The paper states the theory's aims and terms.
arxiv-2502-02380:
Shiri Alouf-Heffetz and co-authors study the cost of liquid democracy in a 2025 paper. In liquid democracy, a voter may vote directly or hand the vote to a trusted delegate, who may pass it on again. The authors use an approval-based model where voting and delegating both carry costs, and a budget caps the total. A central planner must pick the casting voters so every voter is represented.

The team studies the problem through computational complexity. They ask how hard it is to keep total cost low, delegation paths short, and voting power from piling up in few hands. They also ask a control question: can an outsider tweak parts of the election to shift some voters' power? The results map where liquid democracy stays manageable and where it turns intractable.
arxiv-2502-02780:
Songlin Xu and five co-authors built simulated students for online education in twenty twenty-five. Teachers could rehearse and refine lessons against virtual learners, but past simulators ignored how course materials shape behavior, and the long texts involved strain language models. The team first ran a six-week workshop with sixty students on a custom platform that logged fine-grained learning behavior.

On that data they built a transferable iterative reflection module that strengthens both prompted and fine-tuned language models. The enhanced models simulated student learning more accurately than classical deep learning baselines, even with few demonstrations. They captured both the grain of individual progress and correlations across a class. The authors frame the result as a step toward a digital twin of the online classroom.
arxiv-2502-03780:
Javid Naikoo, Ravindra Chhajlany, and Adam Miranowicz report a sensitivity boost for quantum sensors in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. Sensors can gain extreme sensitivity near singular points where a system's eigenvalues merge. Exceptional points and diabolic points are two different kinds of such degeneracies. The authors study a four-mode bosonic system at hybrid points that are both at once, doubly degenerate exceptional-diabolic singularities.

Near these hybrid points the response to a small linear perturbation is singular, and the pole order of that response sets how the estimation error scales. The hybrid points deliver a twofold improvement in error scaling over non-hybrid singular points. Quantum Fisher information gives the ultimate bound on the error, and the authors identify heterodyne detection as the measurement that achieves the optimal scaling. The result suggests a design principle for sensors targeting extremely weak signals.
arxiv-2502-03880:
Starovoitov and Kruglikov prove results on nonlinear Hermite-Chebyshev approximations in twenty twenty-five. Approximation theory swaps in simpler rational forms for hard functions. Hermite type forms match a function and its derivatives at once. The team studies systems of functions given by Fourier series.

They find sufficient conditions for such forms to exist at all. The results cover trigonometric versions named for Hermite and Jacobi. They also cover Chebyshev polynomial versions of the first and second kind. When they hold, explicit formulas follow from the proofs. Those formulas give the numerators and denominators of the forms. The work extends rational approximation theory for function systems.
arxiv-2502-05180:
Anas Mifrani published this mathematics note in 2025. It settles a conjecture by Richard Soland about decisions with several competing goals. In such problems, some solutions are efficient: no other option improves one goal without harming another. One might hope every efficient solution can be justified by a single scoring rule. Soland conjectured that a smooth scoring function, rising and bending the right way, could peak exactly at any chosen efficient solution's scores.

Mifrani proves that this need not hold. His argument shows that for a given efficient solution, such a well-behaved function may fail to exist. The result matters for multicriteria decision making, where analysts often justify choices by fitting a single utility function after the fact. If no suitable function exists, that justification route closes. Decision methods must then rest on the trade-offs themselves rather than on a hidden score.
arxiv-2502-05280:
Yackolley Amoussou-Guenou and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper that frames a shared model for agreements run by self-executing code on blockchains. Many blockchain problems are old distributed computing problems in new dress. The model must capture both the kinship and the difference. The focus is agreements where groups of parties act through trusted code that sits on the ledgers of more than one chain.

Such agreements can do broad work, but their main use is to track who owns coins and valuable data. So the model differs from the older ones in set ways. Some parties may behave falsely, so tasks are framed by what each side can gain. The parties name the desired moves, but the code, not the parties, makes the moves real. That reversal, since code alone controls ownership, is the core of the model.
arxiv-2502-06280:
Li and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about graph neural networks that must learn from skewed class labels. In many graphs, a few classes hold most labeled nodes. Unlabeled nodes are plentiful but often ignored by past fixes. Their framework, IceBerg, trains the model partly on its own predictions for unlabeled nodes. Two problems dog that approach: bias toward big classes and shifted label patterns. A double balancing module tackles both with only a few lines of code.

They also split message passing from feature change to spread weak signals farther. Tests on standard benchmarks beat prior imbalance methods clearly. The framework also led the field when labels were extremely scarce. The authors argue unlabeled data are the bulk of the iceberg. Small, careful changes can unlock large gains, they conclude.
arxiv-2502-08280:
Michael Neumann and Anne Leucht tackle trend estimation for time series whose noise has heavy, polynomial tails, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Data points arrive at uneven times, and rare large errors can wreck simple trend fits. The authors assume only that the trend varies in a bounded way and that the errors meet mild moment conditions.

They build an estimator from wavelets of the simple Haar type, reshaped to fit sample sizes that are not powers of two. A threshold rule, first worked out in a general sparse-signal setting with heavy-tailed noise, decides which parts of the signal to keep. The result is a trend fit designed to stay reliable when wild values appear now and then.
arxiv-2502-09380:
Kalyan Banerjee proved a case in twenty twenty-five of Beilinson's conjecture for some K3 surfaces. It links special values of L-functions to regulators. Those values code the arithmetic of a surface. The regulators are built from its algebraic cycles. K3 surfaces are a rich test class for it. The claim is known in just a few scattered cases.

Banerjee treats K3 surfaces over the algebraic closure of the rationals. Each one has an involution, a symmetry of order two. The key condition on shape is this. If you quotient by that symmetry, you get the projective plane. It branches along a sextic curve. For those cases the note verifies the claim in full. Each new family makes the claim look more sound. It sharpens the tools at hand for the general case too.
arxiv-2502-09480:
Borkovits and a large team revisit triple star systems first found by the Kepler space telescope in twenty twenty-five. In a triple, a close pair of stars is orbited by a third, farther star. Shifts in the pair's eclipse times can betray the third star's pull. The team added eclipse times from a newer telescope, TESS, and from ground follow ups.

The longer record confirmed most old finds and sharpened their orbits. It also turned up fifty new triples with long outer periods. Some old candidates could not be solved anew, as eclipses had faded or data failed. In total, two hundred forty-three triple candidates now stand in the Kepler field. Tight triples show rich dance like effects worth close study.
arxiv-2502-09580:
José Reina-Valero and co-authors cross-correlate signals from several cavities to hunt axion dark matter with direction sense. Axion searches so far ignore how the detector's motion through the field should modulate the catch. Correlating signals across cavities grows the signal-to-noise faster than summing power. Three array layouts are simulated on paper.

Sets place cavities at scattered sites, at one site with mixed aim, or six at one site in varied directions. Phase gaps above two degrees appear for the longest cavities in two layouts. The six-cavity design shows a daily swing in the correlation's imaginary part. That swing could reveal the axion wind's speed spread.
arxiv-2502-11680:
Lerner, Burgun, and Bach learn link graphs from ward time series with rough time stamps in this twenty twenty-five paper. Ward series are tracked in many sick folks with gaps and odd gaps in time. Past graph tools need neat, even time steps to read such links well.

Inside, their frame casts all series as one shared wave law with the same links. A graph is drawn as a set of one-way links with no loops in the chain. A bent-note tool then solves a chain of smooth fits to get that graph back. Mock runs got most true links back at high catch and fair truth grades. The path of shrink weights proved key to name the true graph in tests.
arxiv-2502-13980:
A large collaboration presents results in two thousand twenty-five on how momentum is shared inside two light particles, the pion and the kaon. Inside each particle, quarks and gluons each carry part of the total momentum. Measuring the split tests our picture of the strong force.

Using lattice simulations with realistic quark masses, the team computed both shares and, for the first time, extrapolated cleanly to the continuum for the physical pion. Quarks carry a bit over half the pion's momentum and about two-thirds of the kaon's. The shares add up to the required total, checking the method.
arxiv-2502-15280:
Hojoon Lee and co-authors present SimbaV2, a reinforcement learning design that scales up without the usual training wobble, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Bigger models help in supervised learning but often overfit or shake in reward learning on shifting data. Two guards anchor the design.

Weights and features are pinned to a sphere so their size cannot run away. Value reads come as spreads with reward scaling to keep gradients steady. Built on a soft actor-critic base, the system topped fifty-seven control tasks across four domains. Code is shared openly. Readers who scale reward learning get a stability recipe that holds at size.
arxiv-2502-15980:
Tian and a team including Li present SQLsynth in twenty twenty-five, a tool for building text to SQL data. Such models turn plain language questions into database queries. They drop in accuracy when moved to new, specialized database schemas. The main cause is a lack of domain specific training data.

Getting high quality data for each new schema is very costly by hand. SQLsynth pairs humans with language models in a structured workflow. That pairing streamlines the creation of accurate training sets. A user study compared it with manual annotation and with a chat model alone. SQLsynth sped up annotation and lowered mental load. Its data sets were also more accurate, natural, and diverse.
arxiv-2502-18280:
Ishan Koralege and five co-authors improve wireless networks that use smart reflecting surfaces in this two thousand twenty-five paper. These surfaces, called RIS, are panels that bounce radio waves in controlled directions. They are seen as a key part of future 6G networks. Setting their many phase shifts well needs accurate knowledge of the radio channel. Getting that knowledge is costly and often stale.

The team proposes to predict the channel instead of measuring it each time. A transformer model, the same family used in language AI, forecasts channel states. Their method unfolds a classic optimization into a learning system. The predicted channel then drives the phase settings. The work aims at stronger signals and wider coverage with less overhead.
arxiv-2502-18380:
Haodong Zhang, Fei Wang, and Britta Nestler rethink slip and friction where a fluid meets a solid, through the idea of an adsorption layer. Classic flow models assume no slip at the wall or set a slip length by fiat, neither with firm ground. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The layer is a thin zone at the wall where fluid and solid pulls govern both clinging and slip. From an energy low point rule, the authors derive balance laws that link wall friction, thick flow stress, and clinging shifts. The frame joins this zone to the bulk fluid in a self matched way. It explains why water slips more in tight carbon tubes, matching lab and model data where classic models fail.
arxiv-2502-18780:
Qian Cui and co-authors count blue straggler stars in far-off open clusters in a 2025 paper. Blue stragglers are stars that look younger and bluer than their cluster mates, likely after gaining mass. Using data from the Gaia mission, the team searched fifty-three clusters, most in the outer disk of the Milky Way.

They confirmed more than a hundred blue stragglers and flagged hundreds more as possible cases. The new finds grow the known sample for the outer disk by nearly half. The team also studied how much extra mass the most extreme stragglers carry. That peak rose with cluster mass, which fits the idea that heavier clusters make mergers more likely. Age alone showed little link to the peak.
arxiv-2502-21180:
Anca Preda, Goran Senjanović, and Michael Zantedeschi revisit a minimal SO(10) grand unified theory in two thousand twenty-five. The theory joins forces in one frame based on the SO(10) group. Three Higgs sets drive breaks at the top, middle, and weak scales. The model can be renormalized, a trait the title stresses.

Tests of the joining rules allow the left right scale to sit near LHC reach. The quark lepton scale can drop near its lowest allowed bound. Neutron to anti-neutron shifts could show at current reach in both cases. Light new scalars could also drive a rare double decay. A fine tuning worry for the light Higgs is weighed.
arxiv-2503-01080:
Chen Tong and Peter Reinhard Hansen wrote a 2025 paper on a new model for how asset returns move together. Stock returns in the same trade group often swing in linked ways. Their link also shifts over time and can spike in wild markets.

The new dynamic factor correlation model tracks these links through a few shared factors. A fresh setup for the factor weights keeps the model clean and free of clashes. It handles many assets at once and allows fat-tailed shocks. The team tests it on 12 asset returns for close checks, then on 323 returns to show scale. Banks and funds use such models to gauge joint risk.
arxiv-2503-01680:
Thibaut Delcroix and Simon Jubert built new numerical tests for special geometric metrics in a 2025 paper. On certain complex shapes, called Fano varieties, prized metrics with constant scalar curvature may or may not exist, and stability invariants predict the answer in the unweighted case. The authors work in a weighted setting, where a chosen weight function reshapes both the metrics and the solitons that generalize them.

They define a weighted delta invariant, plus a reduced version, that characterize when weighted solitons exist, and prove a sufficient condition for weighted constant-curvature metrics. Links to the best lower bound on weighted Ricci curvature are spelled out, with a general cap from moment images. Fibration examples show how to estimate the bound from base and fiber.
arxiv-2503-02380:
Michael Good and Eric Linder argue that a universe born from a vacuum blip must speed up late in its life, in a paper from 2025. Most accounts start the cosmos in a hot, dense Big Bang state. Their account starts it as a chance flicker of empty space instead. From that start, they derive a sum rule for how expansion must unfold.

The rule rests on a form of the expansion equations tied to a special math function. It forces the growth of space to cross into speeding up at late times. They note links to symmetry maps used in geometry. They also check the rule against current data on the cosmos. The data fit a past crossing of the key quantity through zero. In the standard model, that crossing would not have happened yet.
arxiv-2503-07480:
Prabhash Kumar, Anu Nath, Mahesh Panchagnula, and Anubhab Roy study how small heavy particles move in a Taylor-Green vortex flow, in a two thousand twenty-five fluid mechanics paper. A classic result says particles below a critical Stokes number get trapped by the flow's separatrices.

Earlier work treated particles as points with density effects only. Here the authors add two neglected forces: added mass and the Boussinesq-Basset history force. Linear stability analysis near stagnation points maps trapping conditions in the Stokes number and density plane. Added mass creates extra stagnation points and shifts behavior between trapped, diffusive, and ballistic regimes. With both forces included, all particles turn ballistic.
arxiv-2503-07580:
Zijun Liao, Jinbiao Chen, Debing Wang, Zizhen Zhang, and Jiahai Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It trains neural nets to solve hard routing and scheduling tasks, where reward signals are sparse and good tries often go to waste.

Their method, BOPO, learns from pairs of tries ranked by their true scores. Each pair is anchored on the best try found, and the loss scales with how far apart the pair's scores are, so no reward model or fixed guide policy is needed. Tests on job-shop scheduling, the traveling salesman problem, and a flexible job-shop variant beat top neural rivals and close much of the gap to the best known answers. BOPO can plug into most net shapes already in use.
arxiv-2503-08380: Fujita proved in twenty twenty-five a guessed rule for a class of sym-met-ric mul-tiple zeta val-ues, sums built from ones and threes in turn. Past work by Hirose, Murahara, and Saito showed some such val-ues can be writ-ten as sums of plain zeta val-ues. Their proof had left this case, start-ing with one and end-ing with three, as a con-jec-ture. Fujita's proof settles that case in full.
arxiv-2503-08880:
Shuoxue Li, Chenghan Li, Huanchen Zhai, and Garnet Chan stretch an embedding method from still states to moving spectra in tied lattices, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The method nails ground-state values cheaply, but motion reads stayed open. A single-mode kick ansatz supplies the bridge.

Embedding tools fill the matrix parts that the kick form needs. On the one-dimensional Hubbard model, results track gold-standard answers closely. Neutral kicks, single-particle spectra, and charge and spin waves all come out. The team frames the route as a cheap path to dynamics in hard lattices. Readers get motion from a still-state workhorse.
arxiv-2503-09780:
Arman Zharmagambetov and co-authors present AgentDAM, a benchmark that tests whether web agents keep private data private, in a research paper from 2025. Autonomous web agents can carry out long, multi-step tasks for users, which often means handling personal details. The rule they should follow is data minimization: use a private fact only when the task truly needs it.

AgentDAM stages realistic web tasks end to end and fits any current web agent. Agents built on GPT-4, Llama-3, and Claude all leaked, using sensitive facts they did not need. A prompting defense cut the leakage in the team's tests. The authors argue that end-to-end trials give a truer read on privacy than asking models abstract questions.
arxiv-2503-10180:
Li and a team of colleagues dissected a gravitational lens nicknamed the blue eye in twenty twenty-five. An Einstein ring forms when a massive galaxy bends light from a background source into a near-perfect circle. Spectroscopy confirmed this Kilo-Degree Survey find: an early-type lens galaxy and a background emitter at much greater distance.

Lens modeling on sharp telescope images gave an Einstein radius of about ten and a half kiloparsecs. The total density slope matched that of lower-redshift galaxies, suggesting growth through dry mergers plus mild accretion. Stellar population analysis put the lens's stellar mass near four times ten to the eleventh suns, leaving a dark matter fraction around thirty percent inside the effective radius. Fitting the dark matter halo's own slope required either halo contraction or a heavier-than-usual initial mass function.
arxiv-2503-11880:
Jieming Bian and colleagues personalized federated fine-tuning of language models in a 2025 paper called FedALT. Devices can adapt a shared model on private local data, but averaging all local versions blurs each user's gains when data differ a lot. Standard averaging-based tuning suffers exactly that cross-client interference, trading personal fit for shared knowledge.

FedALT keeps each client's own adapter training locally instead of restarting from the average. A second adapter carries knowledge from the rest of the world, and a learned mixer blends the two afresh for each input, borrowing the mixture-of-experts idea. Tests on language benchmarks beat leading personalized methods on local fit. Privacy stays intact, since raw data never leaves the device.
arxiv-2503-14380:
Sara Cabo and co-authors rethink how to shield light sensors in huge particle detectors from Earth magnetism, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The sensors lose skill when a sideways field crosses them, and past designs judged shields by how many sensors saw a high field. Coil sets cancel much of the field around the detector.

The team argues the mean leftover sideways field tracks lost skill better than the old count rule. A coil design tuned to that mean gives good results at fair cost. As detectors grow, the cheaper and truer gauge matters more. Readers who build large detectors get both a new yardstick and a workable shield plan.
arxiv-2503-15380:
Bruno França, Denis Kolegov, and Igor Konnov lead a team presenting the consensus protocol that orders transactions inside the ZKsync rollup. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Blockchains need agreement among machines that may lie or fail. This protocol blends ideas from three earlier fault-tolerant designs.

It works by committee with a single round of voting per decision. Slots finalize one at a time with modest communication growth. The tolerance threshold demands more honest nodes than classic setups, a deliberate trade. Simplicity, low latency, and reduced complexity were the design goals. Formal methods were used to analyze and test the protocol before this write-up. The audience is the ZKsync community and anyone auditing its safety. The paper is as much assurance document as research. It shows its work for a system holding real value.
arxiv-2503-17180:
M. Orte-García and co-authors measured chlorine in the glowing gas clouds where stars are born, in a 2025 study of the local universe. Amount ratios such as chlorine to oxygen trace how generations of stars have enriched their galaxies, but chlorine is rarely measured well. The authors mined a large data store of ionized region spectra, selecting over two hundred spectra of galactic and extragalactic star-forming regions where the doubly ionized chlorine amount could be determined.

All actual conditions and part amounts were recomputed uniformly for the sample, a deliberate choice for comparability. A central methodological contribution is a scheme for choosing which electron heat level indicator best shows the zone where the chlorine ions live, boosting the amount determination. The team then weighed results under two ionization correction schemes and set the nebular chlorine-to-oxygen pattern against what stars themselves show.
arxiv-2503-18380:
Gulnara Suliyeva and nine co-authors published a 2025 study of the Fan-Wang spacetime, a model of a black hole that stays regular at its centre. The model comes from a theory where electric and magnetic fields behave in a nonlinear way. The team compared its geometry with how particles actually move in it.

They worked out how light and matter bend around the object, how much it can capture, and how its gravity shifts light toward red. A magnetic charge in the model adds a small correction to the classic black hole solution. That correction changes even local predictions of Einstein’s theory. The authors argue that future instruments could test whether such an object exists.
arxiv-2503-18580:
Talal Ahmed Chowdhury, Kwangmin Yu, and Raza Sabbir Sufian measure entanglement growth in a model of quantum chaos on real quantum computers, in two thousand twenty-five. The model is a standard test bed for chaos, many-body physics, and ideas linking gravity and quantum theory. Today's machines are noisy, so checking known results on them matters.

The team tailored two measurement protocols to a commercial superconducting machine with limited links between qubits. They ran circuits in parallel to improve one protocol's results. With error reduction steps added, the machine's readings matched theory well. The authors take that as a sign that current hardware can probe chaotic quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2503-19280:
Amogh Inamdar and co-authors published this education technology paper in 2025. Propositional logic proofs are a core skill in computer science degrees, but students need guided practice to master them. Tutoring on demand is rarely available, and many students fear judgment when asking for help. The team lists what a good practice tool should do. They built LogicLearner, a web application for step-by-step proof practice.

Students work through proofs in the interface and can request guidance whenever they stall. An automatic solver generates solutions on the fly, powering that guidance. The team piloted the tool across two semesters of a discrete mathematics course. Student surveys praised its usability and teaching value. The authors say LogicLearner is, to their knowledge, the only tool offering a complete practice environment for logic proofs. Its feedback is immediate and judgment-free, which they argue is what beginners need.
arxiv-2503-19980:
Basabendu Barman, Nicolás Bernal, and Javier Rubio wrote a guide to the reheating of the young universe for particle physicists. Their review, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the shift from inflation to a hot thermal cosmos. This phase is key yet oft misread. The plain Boltzmann path, they argue, misses the wild first steps of energy hand off. Those steps are non perturbative and nonlinear by nature.

Burst like particle making, inflaton break up, turbulence, and the settle to heat all sit in that gap. The team maps the tool box, from Boltzmann math to lattice sims, and says when each fits. Readers get a clear on ramp to a phase that sets the stage for all later cosmos.
arxiv-2503-22380:
Murauer, Krishnakumar, Tornow, and Geierhos tested in twenty twenty-five a quantum tool that learns from a stream of data with loops fed back. Old quantum pool tools must restart the loop at each step, which wastes time. Pure stream tools are fast but lack the back-links that boost scores.

Their plan adds back-links that work while the quantum bits still hold their state. On a small test case it kept a trace of past inputs, as a short-term memory score showed. That score was not zero, which means the links work mid-stream. The plan may give stream tools the gains of restart tools at less cost.
arxiv-2504-00280:
Gunbir Baveja tested a diffusion-based policy for robot learning in worlds that will not sit still, in a solo paper published in 2025. Tasks in real factories and driving work shift their rules and aims over time. The policy builds actions by slowly removing noise from a rough guess, which gives smooth, fitting action chains. Vision feeds the policy in the tests.

On game-like worlds and a maze task, the policy beat two standard learners on mean and top scores. Its scores also varied less from run to run. The cost was more computing per action. The author flags sharp, fast world shifts as the weak spot that remains. The findings support diffusion policies for work where the ground rules drift, from assembly line robots to self-driving.
arxiv-2504-00380:
Yang Hai and colleagues sped up video frame interpolation in 2025 by teaching a diffusion model to imagine motion rather than pictures. Frame interpolation invents the in-between frames that make video smoother. Diffusion-based versions had lagged older methods in both accuracy and speed, partly because they denoise in a large image-like space. The new method models optical flow from both directions explicitly, in a hierarchy, which shrinks the search space.

A flow-guided synthesizer then builds the final frame from the predicted motion. The two parts train together end to end. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy while running more than ten times faster than other diffusion-based interpolators. That combination matters for practical video work, from slow-motion generation to streaming, where earlier diffusion methods were simply too slow to use.
arxiv-2504-00980:
Mitch Hamidi, Lara Ismert, and Brent Nelson study when a quantum graph algebra is simple, meaning it has no hidden two-sided parts, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Quantum graphs extend the graph idea into the quantum setting. The work links traits of the graph to traits of its algebra.

They give conditions on the graph that ensure the algebra is simple. They also build a map from one form of the algebra onto a related form. Joined, the results yield the first case where two named forms of the algebra truly differ. Set cases, such as complete and trivial quantum graphs, are settled as well.
arxiv-2504-01580:
Alexandre Wagemakers assembles a zoo of systems that can settle into several different fates, in a 2025 paper. Such multistable systems appear everywhere: ecosystems flip between states, circuits latch, and lasers choose modes. Which fate occurs depends on the starting point, and the map of starting points leading to each fate is called a basin of attraction.

The paper catalogs notable examples across scientific fields, classified for easy browsing. Companion code lets readers reproduce every basin picture themselves, turning the survey into a working tool. For researchers meeting a new multistable system, the zoo offers analogies at a glance: someone has likely mapped a cousin of your problem. It also serves teaching, since basins make abstract dynamics visible at once.
arxiv-2504-01880:
Sriram Shastry, writing alone, finds a shortcut to special zeros of quantum systems in a 2025 paper. The zeros belong to the partition function, a master quantity in statistical physics, read in the Yang-Lee picture. Locating them for lattice fermions, like the Hubbard model, is normally heavy going. Shastry proves a theorem about the single-electron self-energy in the imaginary-time formulation.

The theorem maps each zero to a virtual energy labeled by wavevector and spin. Those energies solve equations built from the self-energy at matching labels. What was a global hunt becomes a set of local solves. Shastry shows the method at work in simplified cases. The author presents the link as a new handle on phase behavior, since Yang-Lee zeros mark where phases change. The proof's core is the self-energy's hidden bookkeeping of the zeros.
arxiv-2504-04080:
Pavel Exner and David Spitzkopf wrote a mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five about rows of potential wells and what happens when a few of them shift. A potential well traps a quantum particle in a small region. An even row of wells spreads allowed energies into bands, with gaps where no extended state can live.

The authors study an array of separate wells laid along a straight line in two or more dimensions. They shift a finite number of wells along the line, keeping them apart. Under a stated limit on the shape of each well's support, they prove the shift creates bound states in the gap below the lowest band. Such localized states are the mathematical sign that a small local change can trap a particle.
arxiv-2504-04480:
Braghadeesh Lakshminarayanan, Margarita Guerrero, and Cristian Rojas improve estimators that learn from simulators, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Factories now run digital twins of real systems, but the twin's settings must be tuned to match reality. One route generates fake data at sampled settings and trains a model to read settings back from data.

Trouble comes when the true settings sit outside the sampled range. Predictions then skew, a flaw known as out-of-distribution error. The authors add a fine-tuning stage to a known two-stage estimator that corrects for this drift. Simulations confirm the fix sharpens accuracy. The work targets engineers who must calibrate twins that start far from the truth.
arxiv-2504-11380:
Mark Edison Jim and co-authors design an augmented reality coach for public speaking, called SpeakAR, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Fear of speaking is wide, yet live practice chances are few. Virtual audience members react as the user speaks, giving a safe stage.

Five users with mixed fear levels each ran six speaking tasks. Users said the tool helped practice and lifted confidence. Lively faces and small idle moves in the virtual crowd were flagged as key for realism. The work draws on past virtual training and feedback studies. Readers who build learning tools get design cues for calm, real-feeling rehearsal.
arxiv-2504-11480:
Andrea Lucchini wrote a 2025 paper on a graph built from the subgroups of a finite group. In this graph, each subgroup is a point, and joined points mark a set relation between them. A graph is regular when every point has the same number of links.

Lucchini proves a crisp rule for when this subgroup graph is regular. It happens only when the group is cyclic, meaning one element generates the whole group. The group's order must also be square-free, with no prime factor repeated. Both traits are needed, and together they are enough. Short proofs of sharp rules are prized in group theory, and this one closes the question fully.
arxiv-2504-11980:
Nicholas Fazio and nine co-authors report a new way to measure errors in a quantum computer, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their test case is a key two-qubit operation used in logic built to resist errors. The work ran on a sixteen-qubit register in a trapped-ion machine.

Their method rebuilds the error pattern of a full cycle of operations. It can spot errors that depend on context, so those errors can be eased. It also shows how single gates behave inside larger logical operations. The team says the method can predict how well error correction will work, and can tell fixable errors from those that cannot be fixed.
arxiv-2504-12480:
Srinivasan, Plenz, and Girvan improve in twenty twenty-five a lean form of neural computing that borrows ideas from the brain. Their system keeps a fixed random network, called a reservoir, and trains only the output layer. That design is cheap, but it is fussy about its settings and ignores a key brain trait: the balance between go and stop signals.

They show the system works best when stop signals match or slightly outweigh go signals. They then add a self-tuning rule that adjusts each unit's balance to hit a target firing rate. Gains were large on memory and forecast tasks. Varied targets across units cut the need for fine tuning even more, across simple and hard tasks alike.
arxiv-2504-12980:
Jiangnan Biguo and Xiaoquan Yu chart how dark solitons move inside trapped superfluids that carry spin, in a 2025 paper. A ferrodark soliton is a traveling dip in the fluid's density with a magnetic twist. The authors split the force on such a soliton into a buoyancy part and spin corrections. The corrections come from the hollow core and from the coupling between the soliton's motion and its spin mixing.

In a bowl-shaped trap, the math maps the soliton's path onto a marble rolling in a quartic valley. Near the center it swings to one side only, like a marble caught in one dip of a double well. Starting farther out brings three regimes of swing before that one-sided motion. In a hard-walled trap with a slope, the motion turns into a plain harmonic swing.
arxiv-2504-13080:
Abhishek Ghadai, Pradip Kumar Bera, and Sayantan Majumdar present a 2025 study of a rod dragged through a soap-like fluid of worm-shaped micelles. Past a speed line, the rod's path turns wild and stress swings wide. The team built a rig on a shop rheometer to log the stress on the rod live. Flow cameras mapped the speed field around it at the same time.

Past the line, stress climbed slowly, then dropped in a snap, the sign of stored stretch let go. The stretch zone's size matched the build time times the rod speed. Shear and stretch gauges at the flip shared one threshold number. At higher drives the rod churned in mixed stick-slip bursts. Such fluids fill foods, gels, and oil work.
arxiv-2504-14580:
Viet Hung Pham, Malte Wagenfeld, and Regina Bernhaupt study how virtual reality can help judge and improve walkability in city planning, in a paper from 2025. Classic planning tools, such as flat maps and fixed renders, miss how a street actually feels to walk. Fast urban growth and green goals make that gap costly.

Virtual reality lets residents and planners step inside a design, spot walking problems, and suggest fixes on the spot. Early interviews with residents of Eindhoven in the Netherlands surfaced what pedestrians value and where they struggle. Next, the team plans prototypes that fuse the virtual scenes with a live digital twin of the city. A design generator would then propose options. The goal is a decision tool that folds public views into design.
arxiv-2504-15480:
Antonin Brun, Gale Lucas, and Burçin Becerik-Gerber study stress at work through the eyes of office staff. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is based on long talks with eight workers. Stress harms health and output, yet most aids treat people as if they were all alike. The team asks what sets off stress and how workers cope day to day.

Patterns show stress is shaped by place, timing, and the person. Workers named clear triggers and their own coping tricks. They also said stress is not all bad and can sometimes push good work. The authors draw design lessons for aids that fit the moment. Help should arrive at the right time and in the right form.
arxiv-2504-15680:
Bikash Chandra Roy, Aroonkumar Beesham, and Bikash Chandra Paul built a model of the late universe in a new gravity frame. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses f(Q) gravity, where a nonmetricity term drives the action. They built models for a few forms of that function. Each model tracks how the young fast phase gave way to the late speed up of cosmic growth.

They set the model with a fixed jerk value and fit its parts to real data. The data came from Hubble rate facts and a supernova set. They traced how the slow down term, energy density, and the state term shift with time. Readers in cosmology get a test of whether this gravity frame fits the late universe.
arxiv-2504-16180:
Md Saeed Siddik, Hao Li, and Cor-Paul Bezemer wrote this review in two thousand twenty-five. It maps software engineering research on Jupyter Notebook, the tool that blends code, text, and output in one page.

The team picked well over a hundred papers from a large bibliography, through the end of two thousand twenty-four, and sorted them by topic. Top venues for this work sit in human-computer interaction, not classic software venues. Hot topics run from code reuse to readability to run settings. Yet few studies could be reused from their links, and most code packs lack lasting homes. Testing, refactoring, and group documentation stay thin, the authors say.
arxiv-2504-18480:
Li-Wei He and three co-authors probe, in a 2025 paper, a plateau in the magnetization of a frustrated magnet. The magnet sits on a kagome lattice, a weave of corner-sharing triangles that blocks spins from settling at once. In a magnetic field, its spin climbs, stalls at one third of full, then climbs again. New tests on a copper-based crystal made its cause a live question.

The team ran two computer methods, variational Monte Carlo and exact diagonalization, on the Heisenberg model of this lattice. They find three degenerate valence-bond-solid states with a David-star pattern of spin values. In them, spins take two fractional values, and the states swap into each other by shifts. Their spin links stay short-ranged, like a quantum spin liquid. Yet a measure shows no topological order. The authors tie the plateau to these states.
arxiv-2504-19280:
Xiaorong Zou solves stubborn differential equations by fitting their curvature with waves. The target is a second-order nonlinear equation whose solution must meet mixed conditions at its ends. Instead of attacking the solution directly, Zou represents its second derivative as a trigonometric polynomial. Integration then rebuilds the solution and its slope.

An optimization loop bends the polynomial until the rebuilt curves satisfy the equation itself. Fast Fourier transforms carry the gradient work, keeping the method quick. Adding grid points raises accuracy sharply. When several solutions exist, the search can be steered toward a desired one, such as a positive solution. Tests under varied boundary conditions behaved as hoped. Zou notes the scheme extends to higher-order equations, at the price of heavier implementation.
arxiv-2505-05280:
Hwasoo Shin, Marco Ferreira, and Allison Tegge wrote this statistics paper in 2025. Many data sets need two things at once: fewer dimensions to grasp, and groups to sort cases. Their frame, Bayesian clustering factor models, does both in one model. Shared factors sum up each case, and the factors themselves are drawn from a blend of bell curves, which forms the groups.

A Gibbs sampler explores the model's odds, so doubt is measured, not hidden. A set information rule picks how many groups and factors to use, and it beat a past rival rule in tests. Fake-data trials showed sound recovery of the truth. The team then sort people recovering from opioid addiction, where sound groups could shape care fitted to each person.
arxiv-2505-05880:
Bettina Fazzinga and co-authors combine two tools in a 2025 paper for reading streams of low-level process events. Firms track each step of their work as events, but the raw events often do not match the named steps of the business process. Someone must translate each event into the step it belongs to, and that mapping can be unsure.

One known approach frames the task as argumentation, weighing which readings of an event hold up against prior knowledge of the process. That route can be slow and can leave too many readings open when doubt is high. The authors add machine learning to the mix to guide the choice. The blend aims for faster, sharper readings of live event streams, with reasons kept for the cases that clash with what is known.
arxiv-2505-06580:
Dongyoon Yang, Jihu Lee, and Yongdai Kim introduce a 2025 method called TAROT for training models that must work across new settings and still resist attacks. Models often fail when the data shifts or when small, crafted changes trick them. The authors seek a way to keep accuracy steady across domains while also holding up under attack.

They first derive a new bound on risk for the target setting, using a fresh measure of the gap between domains. They then build TAROT to learn features that stay the same across domains. In tests, the method beat prior work on accuracy and on strength under attack. It did well on the hard DomainNet set, which spans many kinds of images.
arxiv-2505-07880:
Jared Hand and a large team from the Nearby Supernova Factory wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on Type Ia supernovae. These exploding stars are used as yardsticks for cosmic distances. To use them well, scientists need a model of how their light rises and fades over time and across colors.

The team built a fresh model from their own survey data, with few set views about what shape it should take. Their model uses three patterns of color change, one tied to the burst's phase and two that stay steady. The fit shows the bursts vary in color in ways dust alone cannot explain. That finding matters for fine measures of the expanding universe.
arxiv-2505-08380:
Chitradeep Saha, Sanghita Chandra, and Dibyendu Nandy asked how much magnetic flux the Sun needs to climb out of a grand minimum.
