A grand minimum is one of the decades-long lulls when sunspots nearly vanish, like the Maunder minimum. During such lulls the Sun's polar fields fade and stop reversing. Using dynamo simulations spanning thousands of years with random forcing, the team measured the polar flux at which reversals resume.

A clear threshold emerged: once enough polar flux accumulates, regular cycles restart. How long a minimum lasts did not depend on how fast it began, and recovery speed was steady. The threshold gives forecasters a target for judging when a future minimum might end. Predicting when one will start, the authors admit, remains unsolved.
arxiv-2505-09080: Marcello Lanfranchi and Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay sort all the slope-like structures, of a named kind, that the world of affine schemes can bear. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, in the math of categories. That world is a tangent world, whose slope bundle comes from a known form of calculus. The team asks how rare that is. They coin a tool, the tangentoid, for objects that breed such a structure by pairing. They prove such objects, for rings, match a class of solid rings.
arxiv-2505-10380:
Naoko Nakagawa and Shin-ichi Sasa propose a variational principle in twenty twenty-five. Consider a liquid-gas system where gravity favors one stacking and heat flow favors another. Predicting the stable arrangement is a fundamental problem. Standard equilibrium thermodynamics cannot settle it, since the state is a non-equilibrium steady one.

Their principle rests on an extended framework called global thermodynamics. Within it, gravity and heat flow merge into one parameter, effective gravity. The sign of that parameter decides the outcome. Positive effective gravity puts liquid at the bottom. Negative values let liquid float above the gas. The result is a quantitative tool for configuration prediction under competing drives. Readers get a single dial where two forces used to fight.
arxiv-2505-10780:
Trisha Das, Afrah Shafquat, Beigi Mandis, Jacob Aptekar, and Jimeng Sun wrote a 2025 paper on finding past clinical trials that resemble a new one. Trial designers learn from history: similar trials reveal pitfalls in dosing, recruiting, and safety. But trial documents are long and varied, so finding true matches by hand is slow.

Their system, called SECRET, sums up each trial protocol and searches by meaning. It learns from partly labeled data, since full labeling is costly. The authors report it beats all rival methods they tested. Better matching at the design stage could cut failed trials, which waste years and large sums and delay new treatments for patients.
arxiv-2505-11580:
Andrew Liu and six co-authors present Flash Invariant Point Attention in two thousand twenty five. Invariant Point Attention drives geometry aware protein and RNA models. Its quadratic cost caps the sequence lengths it can handle in practice. FlashIPA refactors the method around FlashAttention instead.

Memory and time now scale linearly with sequence length. Performance matches or beats standard IPA in their tests. Training reaches lengths that were out of reach before. Generative models retrained without length caps make thousand residue structures. The code is public for structural biology teams worldwide.
arxiv-2505-12480:
Maxim Kontsevich and Alexander Odesskii compute, in exact formulas, where deformed operators live in arithmetic terms. Their work came out in 2025. The start is a product operator built from simple scaling pieces. Rational shifts mark each factor in that product. A formal deformation then perturbs the operator term by term. The question is the arithmetic support of the whole series that results. It is a hard question, and exact answers of this kind are rare.

For large enough primes, monodromy data in characteristic zero decides the answer. The monodromy tracks how solutions wind around singularities as they move. A twin result covers q-difference operators, which replace derivatives with scaled shifts. The work ties arithmetic to analytic winding in a concrete way.
arxiv-2505-13680:
Siddharth Prasad, Maria-Florina Balcan, and Tuomas Sandholm design a new family of auctions for selling bundles of items, where bidders value combinations. Their paper came out in 2025. Good auctions in this space pin prices so no group of bidders, together with the seller, would rather renegotiate the deal.

Their twist is to use what the designer already knows about bidders before bidding starts, expressed as limits on plausible valuations. That information, they show, can break a known impossibility result about honest bidding in such auctions. Their new designs minimize bidders' total incentive to bid dishonestly. Computing the prices needs new constraint methods built on quadratic programming. Experiments favored the new auctions on honesty, revenue, fairness, and speed against designs used in real high-stakes sales.
arxiv-2505-13780:
Hanlun Lei and Evgeni Grishin build a sharper model for three-body orbits in a 2025 arXiv paper. Triple systems with weak hierarchy are common, from high lunar satellites to binaries near a black hole. Standard averaged models miss strong nonlinear effects in such systems.

Their extended Brown Hamiltonian adds quadrupole terms from both the inner and outer bodies. The formulas for the energy and for element conversion stay in elegant closed form. Tests on Jupiter's irregular satellites match direct simulations well over long spans. The model targets von Zeipel-Lidov-Kozai oscillations, the slow swings of tilt and stretch in triple systems.
arxiv-2505-15680:
Rivero-Acosta and four co-authors work out light-shed rates for rare heavy baryons in this twenty twenty-five paper. These short-lived bits hold one heavy bottom quark and sit in a small kin class. Light-shed paths can prove a state is real when strong paths are shut.

Inside, a quark build frame sets the rates from high shell states down to ground and bent states. The work gives first rates for a class of wave states and mixed states not yet charted. Both test error and model error are folded into each rate as a range. Such rates also help split states that share mass and width, the team notes. The set gives hunters a map for ring lab checks.
arxiv-2505-16180:
Dahal, Ghimire, Murad, and Rahimi proposed this scoring framework in twenty twenty-five for judging image captions. Captions written by AI need fair grades, yet older metrics often miss meaning or reward awkward wording. Bad scores can mislead builders about real progress. The team's Redemption Score grades a caption on both what the image shows and how the words read.

The score blends three signals into one number. One checks how well the caption's meaning lines up with the image. One rebuilds an image from the caption and compares it with the original. One compares the caption's wording with human-written references. On a standard photo test set, the score matched human rankings better than most older metrics, with no special training needed.
arxiv-2505-16480:
Akriti Garg and Ayan Chatterjee study collapsing matter in an expanding universe in a 2025 paper. Their setting is de Sitter space, a universe driven by a steady expansion like our own late-time cosmos. They follow round clouds of matter as gravity pulls them inward, for many kinds of matter, from simple dust to fluids with pressure and viscosity.

Mixing exact math with computer work, they track how trapped surfaces form and grow during the collapse. These surfaces are the seeds of horizons. The authors show that black hole horizons and the universe's own cosmological horizon can both be read as the time history of such surfaces. The framework gives a unified way to follow horizon birth in an expanding cosmos.
arxiv-2505-16780:
Zhi-Xuan Meng, Shuai-Xia Xu, and Yu-Qiu Zhao present a study from twenty twenty-five on a one dimensional gas of bosons that cannot share a spot. Links between points in space and time are the key gauge. That gauge can be written with a determinant of a sine based kernel and with answers to a set of split wave equations.

The team works out how the gauge grows at large time and span. Two zones of the space time plane get unlike forms: a space like zone and a time like zone. A phase shift marks the line between them. That shift is told by a set answer to the Painlevé IV equation, a known special equation.
arxiv-2505-16880:
Saša Ceci, Hedim Osmanović, and Branimir Zauner resolve a puzzle about a famous particle resonance in a 2025 physics paper. The resonance, called Δ(1232), is a short-lived excited state of nuclear matter. Its traits are usually read from a pole in the scattering math: the pole's place gives mass and total width, and the size of its residue gives the partial width.

That reading fails here, because it makes one part of the decay wider than the whole. The team builds a simple model that predicts residue phases for several well-known particles, light mesons among them. With those phases the anomaly dissolves. Their moral is sharp: a pole residue is not a basic trait of a resonance.
arxiv-2505-18380:
Praphul Singh, Charlotte Dzialo, and five colleagues build RedactOR, a system that scrubs private details from medical records on its own, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Health data must stay private, yet hospitals and researchers still need records that read coherently for analysis.

Older scrubbing tools miss items, fail on new kinds of records, or cost too much to run. RedactOR handles structured files, free-text notes, and even clinical audio. It mixes cheap rule-based passes with language model passes, routing each piece of data to the cheaper method that can handle it. Audio is cleaned in two steps. When a private name is swapped out, a retrieval step keeps the replacement consistent across the whole record. The design aims to protect patients without gutting the data's usefulness for AI-driven care and research.
arxiv-2505-18880:
Turning a long documentary into a short teaser takes more than cutting: the short must tell a story and still quote real clips. Weihan Xu led a team that built REGen, a system for that job. First, a fine-tuned language model drafts the teaser's script, leaving placeholders where a quote belongs. Then a retrieval model picks, for each placeholder, the clip from the source film that best fits the story.

Tests on documentary teasers showed the method weaves clips in while keeping the tale coherent. In a viewer survey it beat both cut-only and write-only rivals on coherence, fit, and realism. The team frames the work as editing by writing first and quoting second.
arxiv-2505-19180:
Lukas Exl and Sebastian Schaffer upgrade a fast method for computing the stray field a magnetized body casts around itself. That field is a core cost in micromagnetic simulation. Their tensor grid approach works on rectangular domains. It dodges the singular kernel convolution by using a super-potential formulation. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the extension represents magnetization and field in higher-order spline bases. That buys accuracy and smoothness. The field is stored as a compressed functional Tucker tensor built from separable pieces. A multilinear version of extreme learning machine training fits the representation.

Because the scheme is mesh-free, the field can be evaluated continuously anywhere, not just at grid points. Numerical tests confirmed high accuracy. The energy error fell exponentially as the expansion grew, and cost rose only linearly in the tensor rank. The method targets large, high-fidelity micromagnetics.
arxiv-2505-19580:
Murooka and six co-authors enabled whole-body contact motion for humanoid robots in twenty twenty-five. To work in tight spaces, humanoids must lean and brace with knees, elbows, and forearms, not just hands and feet. Sensing those mid-limb contacts is the challenge.

Flexible sheet sensors spread over the limbs measure contact force without changing the robot's shape much. The team extended an existing multi-contact controller, built for hands and feet, to use these mid-limb signals. Feedback from the sheet sensors steadied the motion. Simulations showed better stability against pushes and errors in the environment model. A life-sized humanoid, RHP Kaleido, then demonstrated the skills: stepping while bracing on a forearm, and balancing seated with thigh contact.
arxiv-2505-19780:
Amrita Dey studies the topology of convergence in measure on a ring of measurable functions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The setting is a probability measure space with its real-valued measurable functions. Equality between functions is understood in the almost everywhere sense. On that basis the space turns out to be completely metrizable.

Dey introduces the notion of a measure being bounded away from zero. Such a measure is exactly one that is purely atomic with at most finitely many disjoint atoms. Several topological properties hinge on this condition, including being a P-space and extremal disconnectedness. The space is shown never to be Lindelöf, hence never separable or compact. Connectedness holds exactly when the measure is non-atomic. Dey also computes the component of a point in full generality.
arxiv-2505-20080: Yulin Ye studies whether helicity stays conserved for weak solutions of the compressible Euler equations. Helicity gauges how swirled a fluid flow is. The flow sits inside a bounded box that may include vacuum regions. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Ye derives a sufficient condition for conservation. It joins inner regularity of a Besov type with vanishing mean oscillation. It also needs velocity and vorticity to stay smooth near the boundary. Extra regularity demands on the density near vacuum are added. The pressure law is left general.
arxiv-2505-20180:
Sylvain Fichet, Rodrigo Fresneda, Lucas de Souza, and Dmitri Vassilevich test a shortcut for counting how much fractional fermion charge a vortex carries. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Fermion number on a swirling field background is famously hard to compute directly. A recent proposal ties it to a heat-flow coefficient and to states at the region's edge.

The team tries the shortcut on a classic vortex that forms in a Higgs-type field. Their checks show the key invariant does not care which edge rules are picked, within a fair class. That stability backs the method's soundness. The vortex spectrum also shows a surprise twist in the Higgs phase. As a bonus, edge states on a disk-shaped vortex carry fractional charge themselves. The work firms up tools for soliton physics.
arxiv-2505-20580:
Michael Arnold Bruna proposes, in a 2025 paper, a field theory of consciousness built on resonance. His Resonance Complexity Theory holds that awareness arises when the brain's oscillatory activity locks into stable interference patterns, woven by feedback and waves reinforcing each other. Cross a threshold of organization, and the pattern is, on this account, an experience: an attractor spread across the neural field, needing no central controller and no symbols.

To make the claim measurable, Bruna defines a Complexity Index multiplying four quantities: fractal dimension, signal gain, spatial coherence, and how long an attractor dwells. He then tests the idea in a minimal simulation of radial wave sources on a flat field. Coherent, attractor-like patterns emerge from interference alone, meeting the index's thresholds. The author presents the exercise as a proof of principle, offered for others to sharpen or refute.
arxiv-2505-20680:
Haodong Lu and six colleagues tackle continual learning for CLIP, the vision-language model, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Continual learning means a network keeps learning new tasks without forgetting old ones. CLIP's rich image and text embeddings make light prompt tuning attractive for this job.

Many existing methods add complex prompt pools, routing schemes, or staged training. The authors argue these designs underuse CLIP's own stability. Their method, called TPPT, uses textual prototypes as anchors that guide visual prompt learning. The text side of CLIP stays steady while the visual prompts adapt. Experiments reported in the paper show this simpler route shapes the embedding space effectively.
arxiv-2505-20880:
Hikal, Nasreldin, and Hamdi built a fake-span spotter in twenty twenty-five for a shared task on made-up text in many tongues. Word models oft add false claims in their output, in any tongue they serve. Their plan has one model pull the suspect spans first.

Three more models then vote on each span by score odds. A fuzzy match step lines the spans up with the source text. It placed first in two tongues and near top in six more. The vote plan mimics how human marks were checked, they note.
arxiv-2505-21380:
Byungjun Kim and co-authors addressed a sneaky evasion tactic against Korean hate speech sensors in 2025. Abusive users more and more swap in words that sound alike to slip past machine-run filters. Korean is above all exposed because its writing system closely follows pronunciation. Earlier research mostly built attack data sets for other languages and rarely built a sensor-side defense.

The team contributes on both sides. Their PHISH method generates true-to-life phonetic substitutions that exploit the sound form of the Korean script, modeling what attackers do. Their MESH defense builds phonetic information into the sensor's design beside meaning, mixing semantic and sound-based traits. Tests on both attacked and clean data showed the pairing boosts finding results, giving moderators a defense shaped by the real actions of people trying to evade it.
arxiv-2506-00880:
Zhuo Chen and co-authors build a shared frame for studying how pairs of molecules interact, with help from large language models, in a paper from 2025. Such pair studies matter for drug work and basic chemistry. Many model types and input forms now exist, which makes fair tests hard to set up.

Their frame, called ModuLM, lets users swap parts in and out with ease. It offers many encoders for flat and three-dimensional molecule shapes, several layers for pair interaction, and a range of language model cores. Those parts can form tens of thousands of distinct models. The team gives broad test results to show the frame works for its target tasks. It should cut repeat coding across labs.
arxiv-2506-01180:
Padilla-Castillo and nine co-authors demonstrate a large trap of cadmium atoms fed by a cryogenic helium beam. Trapping cadmium is hard because strong photoionization drains atoms away. A cold buffer-gas beam offers a way to load the trap quickly despite those losses.

Using a deep ultraviolet transition, the team captured over ten million atoms of one cadmium isotope within ten milliseconds. Zeeman slowing happened within five centimeters of the trap, thanks to the strong scattering force. Shifting the laser frequency dynamically reduced ionization losses so several pulses could accumulate. Beyond cadmium itself, the setup benchmarks their ultraviolet laser system. It also prepares groundwork for cooling aluminum fluoride molecules.
arxiv-2506-01380:
Xinle Cheng and five colleagues present Next-Frame Diffusion, a model for generating interactive video in real time, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Autoregressive video models suit streaming and interactive content because they build frame by frame. Their weakness is speed, since diffusion sampling is expensive.

The model is a diffusion transformer with block-wise causal attention. Tokens within each frame generate in parallel. Two innovations push speed past thirty frames per second. Consistency distillation, adapted to video, cuts the needed sampling steps. Speculative sampling exploits the fact that neighboring frames often share the same action input. Frames guessed with a stale action are simply discarded. Experiments used a large-scale action dataset.
arxiv-2506-01880:
Djamel Lamouri, Iheb Aouadj, Smail Kourta, and Riyadh Baghdadi present Pearl, a system that speeds up code with reinforcement learning. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with compiler optimization: picking the right chain of code transforms to make a program run fast. Past learning methods handled only narrow loop shapes or only programs seen in training.

Pearl's agent chooses both the transform and the part of the loop nest it applies to, through a new action design. It also covers polyhedral optimizations, an advanced class. Caching and pre-training cut the slow training cost. Built into the Tiramisu compiler, Pearl beat prior methods on benchmarks and handled new programs.
arxiv-2506-02280:
Kedir Hussen and co-authors survey how well large language models serve Africa's languages, in a 2025 paper. Africa holds about 2,000 languages, most with little digital text, and the gains of modern language AI have largely passed them by. The team compares coverage across six large models, eight small models, and six specialized small models.

They count just 42 African languages with any support and 23 public datasets. Four languages, Amharic, Swahili, Afrikaans, and Malagasy, appear nearly everywhere, while over 98 percent of the continent's languages get nothing. Only three writing systems are handled, though twenty are in active use. The authors blame scarce data, token rules that short-change these languages, high computing costs, and weak test sets. They call for community-built corpora, language standards, and cheaper ways to adapt models.
arxiv-2506-02980:
Xiaoqi Liu, Dorian Baudry, Julian Zimmert, Patrick Rebeschini, and Arya Akhavan give a comprehensive study of bandit convex optimization in changing environments, in a two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. The learner picks actions from a continuous domain but sees only one loss value per round, never a gradient.

Non-stationarity is measured by comparator switches, total loss variation, and path length. Their algorithm TEWA-SE adapts sleeping experts to the bandit setting and is provably minimax-optimal for strongly convex losses. A second algorithm, cExO, handles general convex losses and improves known bounds. A bandit-over-bandit wrapper covers cases where the non-stationarity is unknown.
arxiv-2506-03380:
Zach Patterson, Emily Sologuren, and Daniela Rus built soft-rigid robots from wave-spring-like helicoids in a 2025 paper. Soft robots increasingly mix rigid links with architectured stuff whose actions comes from shapes rather than lab science. Trimmed helicoid forms, spiral ribbons that stretch and twist predictably, are a promising soft element. Yet their stiffness lacked a model for arbitrary shapes, and making them was artisanal.

The authors derive that stiffness model, then introduce injection molding with three-dimensionally printed molds. Releasing a design tool that generates molds for any shapes in the class. A finished robot built by the chain runs in closed-loop demonstrations. Hybrid design moves from craft toward engineering with reusable models and tooling.
arxiv-2506-04380:
Bence Bakó, Tenzan Araki, and Bálint Koczor present a quantum algorithm for reading properties of quantum states in a 2025 paper. Many tasks need the average of some measure in a pure energy state of a system. Early fault-tolerant quantum computers may shine here, if errors can be tamed. Their method starts from a state that overlaps mostly, but not only, with the target state.

Random time evolution on the quantum device turns the input into an averaged mixed state. A virtual cleaning step then boosts the target part, suppressing errors at an exponential rate, all from a single copy of the state. The authors prove firm performance bounds. Cost scales with the energy gap of the system and matches known top methods in precision scaling. Simulations, plus a hundred-qubit classical run, show wide use.
arxiv-2506-05480:
Daniel Wang, Patrick Rim, Tian Tian, and three colleagues present a method for predicting how dynamic 3D scenes will evolve in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Existing reconstruction methods warp scenes with time-conditioned networks, so they can only interpolate inside the recorded time window. ODE-GS instead removes timestamps from the model. It first learns an interpolation model producing accurate trajectories for the scene's Gaussian primitives within the observed window.

A transformer encoder then compresses past trajectories into a latent state, which a neural ordinary differential equation evolves forward in continuous time. Numerical integration yields smooth, physically plausible future trajectories, renderable at any future moment. On the D-NeRF, NVFi, and HyperNeRF benchmarks, the method beat leading baselines on extrapolation metrics by roughly twenty percent. The approach points toward scene models that genuinely forecast rather than merely replay motion.
arxiv-2506-05880:
Adrien Petralia, Philippe Charpentier, Youssef Kadhi, and Themis Palpanas introduced NILMFormer in twenty twenty-five, for splitting a household's total electricity use into per-appliance consumption from smart meter data. Utilities want to give customers appliance-level feedback without extra sensors. Deep learning leads this task, but real meter data drift within each analysis window, and that non-stationarity degrades models.

Their transformer adds a stationarization and de-stationarization scheme that tames drift inside each subsequence, plus a positional encoding built only from timestamps. On four real-world data sets it significantly beat leading methods. The system runs in production as the engine of the French utility EDF's consumption monitoring service, serving millions of customers.
arxiv-2506-05980:
Geonwoo Cho and co-authors present, in twenty twenty-five, a method for teaching AI agents reusable skills. Skill-based learning trains an agent on skills first, so it can adapt fast to new tasks where rewards are rare. Good skill learning needs two things at once: wide exploration and diverse skills. Those aims can clash. Their method, called AMPED, balances the two during pre-training by reshaping the learning gradients, the step signals, so they do not fight.

During fine-tuning, a selector picks the skill that suits each new task. Tests beat prior skill methods on several benchmarks. Taking the method apart showed each part helps. Theory and tests link greater skill diversity to fewer samples needed later.
arxiv-2506-06380:
Jingyi Gu, Xuan Zhang, and Guiling Wang present a survey from 2025 on fake data for rare disasters. Market crashes, pandemics, and storms are rare but ruinous, and warning models starve for examples. Making synthetic data is a promising fix, yet past surveys focus on privacy, not on extremes.

The survey gathers methods that make fake extremes ring true, from generative models to language models tuned with tail-aware training. It lists bench data sets and builds a score frame that spans stats, dependence, looks, and task value. Each score gets a close read on when it fits extreme settings. Uses span finance, fire, quakes, wind, and outbreaks. The authors flag open gaps, like behavior-driven finance and rare-event transfer.
arxiv-2506-06780:
Lennart Bastian and co-authors forecast how objects rotate, learning the motion as a smooth flow through time. Their paper appeared in 2025. Rotation tracking is core to vision and robotics, but sensors are noisy and sparse, motions are complex, and users want long forecasts. The team models rotation with neural controlled differential equations, a method that follows a guiding path, here smoothed with a classic Savitzky-Golay filter, while respecting the true geometry of three-dimensional rotations.

Unlike simpler methods that assume plain motion patterns, theirs learns a general hidden dynamical system behind the observed trajectory. On real-world data it forecast rotations more convincingly than existing approaches. The authors aim at robots and cameras that must predict where a turning object will face next.
arxiv-2506-07180:
Wenrui Zhou and a team of co-authors present VISE, a benchmark for sycophancy in video language models in two thousand twenty-five. Sycophancy means a model sides with the user even when the video says else. That trait breaks trust in grounded tasks. Past work on the flaw skipped the video domain.

VISE tests top video models across question forms and prompt biases. It sorts flattery by type with tools from language study. Two training free fixes are also tried. One picks key frames to ground the model in sight. The other steers inner states away from flattery at run time. Both show paths to cut the bias.
arxiv-2506-07280:
Pablo Acuaviva and co-authors (2025) show video generation models can learn new visual tasks from a few examples. Such models are trained to produce coherent moving scenes. The authors argue this training forces them to build an inner picture of how the visual world works. To test it, they reframe each new task as a visual change: an input clip, then the output clip. Small adapter weights learn the change while the main model stays frozen.

With a handful of training pairs, the adapted model handled tasks far from video making. Low-level jobs such as outlining objects and finding body poses worked. So did a high-level reasoning test from the ARC-AGI set. The authors say these results recast video models as flexible visual learners. They suggest such models could serve as the base for future vision systems, not just as tools for making clips.
arxiv-2506-08480:
Huixuan Zhang and Xiaojun Wan wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five questioning how image generators are graded. Text-to-image models often miss details of the prompt, so automatic scores judge how well a picture matches its text. Existing checks mostly ask whether the scores agree with human ratings.

The authors argue a trustworthy grading framework needs more than agreement. They name two further properties it should have. Then they test mainstream frameworks across many metrics and models and show the current ones fall short on those properties. The paper closes with recommendations for building alignment evaluations that deserve trust.
arxiv-2506-08580:
Yang Lv, Jinlong Lei, and Peng Yi proposed HGFormer in twenty twenty-five for two-stage Colonel Blotto games, the classic contest where rivals split resources across battlefields. Here the battlefields form a network, and play runs in two phases: an opening deployment, then rounds of dynamic reallocation. The stages interact, and graph constraints defeat traditional solvers.

HGFormer pairs an enhanced graph transformer encoder, which reads the network with structural biases, with a two-agent hierarchical decision model. A layer-by-layer feedback reinforcement learning scheme passes long-term returns from lower-level choices up to the higher-level strategy, coordinating the stages. In experiments it beat hierarchical and graph neural baselines on allocation efficiency and payoff in complex dynamic scenarios.
arxiv-2506-10280:
Samiha Shimmi, Hamed Okhravi, and Mona Rahimi published a systematic literature review in twenty twenty-five of artificial intelligence methods for finding software vulnerabilities. Traditional detectors lean on static analysis and hand-written rules; the field has swung toward learned models. The review covers studies from twenty eighteen to twenty twenty-three.

The authors build a taxonomy of techniques, feature representations, and embedding methods across the literature. Ninety-one percent of studies used AI-based approaches, with graph-based models — which read code as structured graphs — the most common. They flag weak points in data set quality, reproducibility, and interpretability. Underexplored directions like federated learning and quantum neural networks get highlighted as a research road map.
arxiv-2506-10880:
Giunzioni, Merlini, and Andriulli wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with given names shown as initials in the byline. It studies the spectra of boundary integral operators once they are split into a mesh, at high wave frequency.

Wave models often mesh a surface with cells near a tenth of the wavelength, on faith that the solve stays true as frequency climbs. By reading the spectra of the split matrices, the authors show a drift from the true operators that grows with frequency. That drift puts the faith in doubt. The work is a warning for boundary element practice in scattering and wave spread.
arxiv-2506-11280:
Francesco Sinigaglia and seven co-authors bound the count of star-forming galaxies by their cold gas mass, at a past time when the cosmos was young. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The gas count is a core tool for how galaxies' gas grew over time. The team joins two strands: the star-mass count from light surveys, and a fresh link between gas mass and star mass from stacked radio data of two scopes. They draw fake star-mass sets from a public photo set's results. Each star mass is then turned into a gas mass by that link. The path gives bounds on the gas count and on the gas share of the cosmos then.
arxiv-2506-12480:
Leo Zhao and colleagues shrank state-space sequence models for edge devices in a 2025 paper. State-space models handle long sequences efficiently, making them attractive for small hardware, but their weights still need quantization, storing numbers in fewer bits, to fit tight memory. Using the S4D design, the team found which parts suffer most under quantization: the state matrix and the internal state itself.

Simple post-training quantization crushed accuracy on a sequential digit task. Training with quantization in the loop restored nearly all of it at eight-bit precision, and even allowed going below eight bits with the right parameterization. Giving sensitive parts more bits and robust parts fewer cut total memory further. Edge AI gains a recipe for tiny sequence models.
arxiv-2506-13580:
Guang-Yao Xiao and Fabo Feng published this astronomy paper in 2025. It refines the orbit geometry of 14 Herculis, a nearby star with two giant planets that do not transit. The angle between the two planets' orbital planes, the mutual inclination, is hard to measure. A recent study combining radial velocity data with satellite and telescope astrometry found two possible values, near 32 degrees or near 145 degrees, leaving the system's true layout ambiguous.

Xiao and Feng added astrometry from an earlier Gaia data release to the mix. The extra data pinned down the orientation of the inner planet's orbit. The result is a single, unambiguous mutual inclination of about 35 degrees. The two planets' orbits are therefore strongly tilted against each other, an unusual architecture. The authors suggest the system as a benchmark for studies of how planetary systems evolve dynamically.
arxiv-2506-14980:
Ziteng Li, Malte Kuhlmann, Ilana Nisky, and Nicolas Navarro-Guerrero advance softness sensing for robots in a 2025 engineering study. Compliance, how much an object gives under pressure, matters in engineering, farming, and medicine, yet classic measurement rigs are bulky, costly, and unfit for a robot hand. Vision-based tactile sensors watch a soft gel deform under touch, and neural networks read softness from those images, though earlier attempts still fell short.

New models built for those sensors push accuracy further. A robot that can feel ripeness or tissue stiffness by touch gains a sense that cameras alone cannot give.
arxiv-2506-16280:
Jaewon Yoo, Jihye Shin, Ho Seong Hwang, and four colleagues test how well visible matter traces dark matter in galaxy clusters in this two thousand twenty-five study. They use over four hundred massive clusters from the Illustris TNG300 cosmological simulation. Four components are compared in each cluster's center: dark matter, member galaxies, gas, and intracluster light, the faint glow from stars between galaxies. A weighted overlap coefficient quantifies how similar the spatial maps are.

Intracluster light combined with the brightest cluster galaxy, and the gas distribution, both closely matched the dark matter map. The match was strongest in relaxed clusters that formed their mass earlier. The similarity itself appears to reflect a cluster's dynamical state. The findings support using cluster light as a practical dark matter tracer.
arxiv-2506-16680:
Quady, Tuckman, and Neuscamman test a fix-up method for states of stirred electrons in this twenty twenty-five paper. Common fast methods can miss the true energy of a stirred state by a wide gap. Charge-shift states are the worst case, with gaps that can span whole units.

Inside, the fix-up method takes the fast result as a start and then refines it. Starts that began far off ended near as good as starts that began at the best level. For charge-shift states, large gaps shrank to a small share of a unit. The team asks if a costly prep step is even worth it, since the fix does so much of the work itself.
arxiv-2506-16880:
Mehdi Badra, Jérémi Dardé, and Emmanuel Zongo wrote a 2025 math paper on a linked system of heat and a bending beam. The beam stands for a structure that touches a fluid, and heat flows through the fluid part. The team asked whether a control applied to part of the system can drive it to rest.

To answer, they proved a global estimate for the linked system, keeping track of how the result depends on the damping in the beam. Along the way they showed several bounds for the beam alone, covering cases with weak and strong damping. Work of this kind supports the control of real structures that mix flexible parts with flowing fluids, though the paper itself stays at the level of proof.
arxiv-2506-17680:
Zhengni Yang, Rui Yang, Weijian Han, and Qixin Liu present a deep learning method for materials tests, in two thousand twenty-five. A small punch test can probe strong steel with a tiny sample. The hard part is turning its load and movement data into a full stress and strain curve.

The team first turns the data series into images that hold both space and time patterns. A sequence model with a focus step then reads those images and predicts the curve. In tests, the errors stayed low across the steels tried. The authors offer the method as a faster, more exact stand-in for older lab routes.
arxiv-2506-18480:
Hui Liu, Chengfeng Sun, and Jie Xin chart the long-run behavior of a noisy, fractional fluid model on a three-dimensional torus. Their equations extend the Navier-Stokes system with fractional smoothing and additive white noise. Random dynamics of this kind settle onto a random attractor, a moving set that traps all futures. The paper asks how smooth that attractor is and how large.

Under a bound linking the noise's gradient to viscosity and the first Stokes eigenvalue, a tempered attractor exists in a high-regularity space. Its fractal dimension there is finite. The proof builds a bounded absorbing set indirectly, by comparing random solutions with deterministic ones. Lipschitz control over initial values then yields the needed compactness. Stronger assumptions on force and noise lift the attractor to even higher regularity spaces. The results extend random attractor theory to fractional three-dimensional flows.
arxiv-2506-19380:
Osmi Vilhu and Karri Koljonen trace where X-ray emission lines are born in the binary system Cygnus X-3, in a research paper from 2025. The system pairs a compact star with a Wolf-Rayet star whose dense wind fills the space between them. The team used Chandra grating data taken during a very soft X-ray state.

All of the lines shifted back and forth with the orbit. Lines from more highly charged ions swung wider and peaked at earlier phases. One iron line moved in step with the compact star, placing its source near the disk or corona. Most other lines pointed to the wind between the two stars, along curved equal-velocity surfaces. A few lines also had parts arising near the compact star, matching recent funnel models.
arxiv-2506-19980:
Václav Cenker, Ivan Chajda, and Helmut Länger study the symmetric difference operation beyond Boolean lattices, in a 2025 paper. In Boolean settings the operation has two classic definitions that agree. In any bounded lattice with complements, both definitions still make sense, but they can part ways. The authors examine the class of lattices where the two forms coincide and name some notable subclasses.

Using a result of Berman, they estimate the sizes of free algebras in those subclasses. The headline theorem is sharp: the symmetric difference is associative exactly when the lattice is Boolean. A single two-variable identity also captures Booleanness on its own. They further characterize lattices carrying an operation that obeys the De Morgan laws. The paper sorts out where Boolean behavior truly comes from.
arxiv-2506-21780:
Anya Osborne and five co-authors study meetings in social virtual reality in a twenty twenty-five paper. After the pandemic, many teams meet by video call, and social VR offers a more shared feel. The team asks which avatar styles and which virtual rooms help groups do creative work.

Two studies build on each other, both on the Mozilla Hubs platform. The first asked eighty-seven people what avatar and room traits they prefer for varied meeting types. The second put forty people in pairs, as avatars in headsets, to do creative tasks in distinct settings. The results guide how avatar looks and room design shape teamwork.
arxiv-2506-23080:
Fang, Tao, and Li sketch a five-stage tale of how AI has grown in this twenty twenty-five paper. They say its path mirrors the long path of human thought tools, from early marks to strict logic frames. Each stage turns on a fresh way to store and work with ideas.

Inside, the frame runs from marks and script through rules of tongue and math to formal logic. Past AI shifts, from rule-based tools to the current big nets, are mapped onto those stages. The authors say AI now nears a self-aware stage marked by step-by-step thought prompts. They close with a path to AI that can check its own work and with tips for firms that build it.
arxiv-2506-23480:
Tang, Zhou, Tan, and Grauer present a neural method to reconstruct fluid structure interaction in twenty twenty-five. Such interaction covers cases where a flow moves a solid and the solid reshapes the flow. Measurements near a moving boundary are often sparse or missing. The team aims to infer both the flow and the motion from sparse data.

Their method combines a modal model of the surface with neural fields for the fluid and solid. Physics equations and interface conditions constrain the learning. It needs only particle tracks away from the body and a moving wall condition. Tests cover a flapping plate, a flexible pipe, and flow around a swimming fish. Reconstructions stayed accurate even with very sparse data near the interface.
arxiv-2506-23880:
Matthew Cellot builds higher-dimensional path machinery for tracking how connections transport along routes, surfaces, and volumes. Holonomy classically assigns a group element to each loop, measuring a connection's twist. Building on ideas of Kohno, the framework uses formal power series connections as the transported objects. Higher holonomy functors then arise naturally.

Functors are constructed from the path groupoid, the path two-groupoid, and the path three-groupoid of a manifold, each layer remembering homotopies of the one below. The showcase application is a Gray functor on the path three-groupoid of a configuration space: the space of several distinct points moving in at least four dimensions. Such configuration spaces underlie braid-like phenomena in higher dimensions. The work extends a classical bridge between geometry and algebra into the categorical heights where modern mathematical physics increasingly lives.
arxiv-2507-01380:
Seokcheon Lee, in a solo paper from 2025, rechecks what the newest sky survey data say about rival models of the universe. The data measure baryon acoustic oscillations, a frozen sound pattern from the early universe that works as a cosmic ruler.

Lee compares three models that differ in how dark energy behaves over time. Using the ruler data alone, all three models fit well. Fancy model scores give at most a weak edge to the simplest model. Lee then fixes the ruler's true length using early universe data, instead of using the full sky microwave analysis. Under that anchor, there is no significant sign that dark energy changes over time. The choice of anchor, he argues, is what drives claims of change.
arxiv-2507-01880:
Stefano Schuppli and co-authors present a 2025 report on reshaping a supercomputer center's services for machine learning work. Their Alps machine fields over ten thousand GPUs for Swiss research. Classic supercomputer services, built for batch physics runs, fit AI training poorly. Since early access in 2023, the team logged the friction points. They propose a user space that trades some raw speed for ease, plus a quick speed-screen tool for code in growth.

Watch tools and data feeds for live training runs join the list. A node health check, a service plane for support and serving jobs, and storage shaped for AI data round out the plan. Centers worldwide face the same graft of AI onto classic frames.
arxiv-2507-03380:
Shailesh Kumar, Tieguang Zi, and Arpan Bhattacharyya present a 2025 physics paper on small objects spiraling into black holes. In these extreme mass-ratio inspirals, a compact body slowly winds around a much larger black hole and emits gravitational waves. Such signals could test whether space has extra dimensions.

The authors study orbits around a black hole from a braneworld model, where extra dimensions leave a mark called a tidal charge. They use an improved equation framework that handles the curved space more exactly than an older approximation. Both methods gave nearly the same bound on the tidal charge. The gap between them grows as orbits get more stretched. Future space detectors could use such signals to probe new physics.
arxiv-2507-04180:
Nazerian, Asllani, Tyloo, Ku, and Sorrentino study the frequency response of networks treated as open systems, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Real networks exchange signals with their surroundings through chosen nodes. Whether structure passes or blocks signals is the core question. The H-two norm quantifies amplification for any input-output choice.

Many natural networks prove organized to enhance signal passing. Food webs, signaling pathways, and gene circuits show this pattern. Power grids, by contrast, seem built to suppress propagation. The contrast separates evolved from engineered design logics. Input and output node choice matters as much as wiring.
arxiv-2507-04280:
Akihito Katsumata and Tomohiro Harada wrote this relativity paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on orbits around a stretched black hole. The Zipoy-Voorhees spacetime describes a static, axisymmetric mass that can be deformed by one parameter; at a set value it reduces to the round Schwarzschild case.

The pair derive a fresh formula for periapsis shift, the slow swing of an orbit's closest point, using a post-Newtonian expansion. The hole's quadrupole shape turns out to enter the shift at an early order. They test the formula on S2, a star that loops around the Milky Way's central giant. The data bound the deformation from below, which means the central object cannot be very prolate, or cigar-shaped. A new series form of the solution also converges fast in both weak and strong fields.
arxiv-2507-04980:
Francesco Zerman builds a Kolyvagin system for families of modular forms over quaternion algebras in two thousand twenty-five. Kolyvagin systems are rigs of cohomology classes that bound the size of Selmer groups, a core task in number theory. The starting stock here is an Euler system of big Heegner points on towers of Shimura curves.

The new system adapts that stock to a quaternionic setting and drops a classic side condition on the family's tame conductor. The route extends prior work by Buyukboduk to the wider frame. As a by-product, one side of the anticyclotomic Iwasawa main conjecture is proved for Hida families. The result links curve points to deep claims about L-values.
arxiv-2507-05280:
Andras Ferenczy, a solo author, assesses Hungary's artificial intelligence strategy in a two thousand twenty-five paper, and compares it with the strategy in Singapore. The work draws on strategy texts, public funding records, and talks with Hungarian AI leaders. Twenty-two goals from the Hungary strategy are scored on design, governance, timing, and funding.

Public spending on AI in Hungary was put at several billion euros. Yet funding data were public for just half the goals, and three projects made up nearly all the funding on record. The plan's rollout was split up after ministry reshuffles, and planned two year reviews have not taken place since two thousand twenty. The advice for the next plan is to adapt to large language models. It also urges the use of the car industry as an East West test ground for AI in cars.
arxiv-2507-06080:
Joaquim Comas and five co-authors put out CAST-Phys, a data set to know moods with no touch of the one felt. Touch tools worn as moods are called up can warp the moods that staff gauge. Their base in its place backs fetch of body signs from far. It pairs high grade face film with no squeeze with base signs for truth.

The tapes hold light pulse signs from skin, sweat gland acts, and breath. They sit next to the face film from which such signs might be read. Reads show body cues count in real scenes where faces sole are not clear. Tests of sole signs and of signs joined show the hope of far mood reads in more than one mode. The set aims at mood screen staff who need truth on the ground for no touch ways.
arxiv-2507-07180:
Innes Bigaran, Stephen Parke, and Pedro Pasquini settle a debate about telling Dirac from Majorana neutrinos in a two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. The Dirac-Majorana confusion theorem says any telling-apart vanishes as neutrino mass goes to zero.

Recent claims hinted multi-neutrino events might evade the theorem. Using spinor-helicity methods spread to massive fermions, the authors compute every helicity amplitude for a light scalar decaying into two neutrinos and two oppositely charged leptons. The calculation exposes exactly where earlier thinking could go wrong. With correct antisymmetrization and all contributions summed, the decay obeys the confusion theorem, backing a foundational result about neutrino identity.
arxiv-2507-07480: Tobias Kappé surveys when two programs count as the same if one ignores what their steps mean. His short paper, from twenty twenty-five, covers propositional equivalence. Swapping the branches of an if-test and flipping its guard gives the same program, whatever the parts are. He frames new results through a logic of guarded tests and loops, known as GKAT, and notes where the theory stands.
arxiv-2507-07780:
Mélanie Roschewitz, Raghav Mehta, Fabio de Sousa Ribeiro, and Ben Glocker run a wide work on how true chance calls stay when art sort tools face real world data shift. They weigh ways to set calls right past train and ways in train like smooth of marks. That work spans eight sort tasks and more than one art field. Base model tunes are in the set next to models trained from scratch.

A join of a push to spread picks with smooth of marks gave the best raw set right scores in shift. Tools set right past train that saw a bit of off task data proved most firm. New ways built for shift scarce beat plain past train fixes. Gains in shift scores often made in set scores worse. Groups of models lent aid, most when set right came first and models sprang from base weights.
arxiv-2507-08080:
Benjamin Sappler, Masataka Kawano, Michael P Zaletel, and Frank Pollmann introduce a new form for tensor network states in two dimensions. Their 2025 paper deals with ways to write down complex quantum states on large grids. A one-dimensional form exists, but extending it to flat grids has been hard.

Their form adds helper tensors to mark the surface where states stay properly normalized. They run a standard time-step method on this form and test it on a classic magnet model. Ground states and short-time motion came out accurately, even at the critical point, on grids of more than a thousand sites. The form also fits other grid shapes, such as honeycomb layouts. The work gives simulators a cleaner tool for flat quantum systems.
arxiv-2507-08280:
Jihye Lee, Minseo Kang, and Dongha Kim address a common data problem in twenty twenty-five. Tables used for prediction often have missing values. Those gaps reflect how data was collected, and the pattern of gaps can shift across time or place. The facts under the gaps may stay the same while the gap pattern changes. That shift can badly hurt a model at test time.

Their method, MIRRAMS, is built for the hard case where test data is unseen. They set conditions based on mutual information to steer the model toward label-relevant facts. Simple loss terms enforce those conditions during training. Readers get a way to keep tabular models steady when missingness shifts.
arxiv-2507-09480:
Guoyou Wang, Yihua Tan, and Shiqi Liu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a fresh way to read off derivatives from sampled points, and to rebuild a smooth function near them, based on Taylor's classic formula.

Taylor's form frays in high dimensions, and errors grow as derivatives are chained from discrete data. The new operator uses a Vandermonde matrix from the cut Taylor series. It gets all low-order derivatives in one pass, which curbs error growth. Even spacing gives high-order accuracy and softens the dimension curse. Tight error bounds are proved for both tasks. In tests it beats finite differences at slopes, and splines at rebuilds, and it extends to two dimensions.
arxiv-2507-10180:
Mutsumi Sugizaki, Tatehiro Mihara, Kohei Kobayashi, and six colleagues report observations of a violent X-ray transient in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. The source, MAXI J0709-159, was discovered in January two thousand twenty-two during a fast outburst. Its luminosity swung enormously within hours, and its position matches the Be star LY CMa, also identified as a B supergiant. The team analyzed data from the NICER telescope taken from three hours to six days after discovery.

Activity continued for about seven hours as sparse flares, each under one hundred seconds, with luminosity briefly reaching extreme levels. Light curve and spectral features fit accretion of a clumpy stellar wind onto a magnetized neutron star. During the brightest flare the variability spectrum showed a broad peak near one hertz, resembling a quasi-periodic oscillation. If that peak marks the Keplerian orbital frequency, it constrains where the accreting gas orbits.
arxiv-2507-11180:
Jian Li and a team of co-authors report a way to prepare and check quantum states in real time, in two thousand twenty-five. Good state preparation is central to quantum work. Full checks of a state take huge effort as systems grow, yet quick checks often rest on guesswork.

The team turn a checking method into a guide for preparation itself. The checks state which measures to take and give a clear score for quality. In a test with a three-part state, nine settings were enough to guide the work. The result matched full checks that need far more data. The plan could later feed into fast, closed-loop control.
arxiv-2507-12080:
Mrityunjoy Charan, Jaban Meher, and Siddhi Pathak settle a conjecture in analytic number theory in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Ramanujan polynomials, studied earlier by Murty, Smyth, and Wang, are a notable family of reciprocal polynomials. Maji and Sarkar proposed a two-parameter generalization and conjectured a precise statement about where its zeros lie. The zeros' location matters because it governs the polynomials' analytic behavior and their connections to related number-theoretic quantities.

The authors prove the conjecture in full. For positive integer parameters, all zeros of the generalized polynomials lie on the unit circle, with exactly two exceptions, both real. Unit-circle results of this kind echo famous phenomena like the Lee-Yang circle theorem and often signal hidden structure. The paper thus closes an open question and confirms that the two-parameter family keeps the striking zero geometry of the original Ramanujan polynomials.
arxiv-2507-12580:
Josephine Borre and co-authors probe age and language bias in speech emotion AI in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Most such systems train on adult, English, unplanned speech. How they read acted emotion from teens or older adults, or in other tongues, is little tested.

Twelve teens and twelve adults over fifty-five acted four target emotions in Danish and English, steering toward points on a mood grid. A live system scored their voices at once. Against expectations, age and language groups barely differed, though high-arousal feelings were read poorly. The authors urge a shift from raw accuracy toward models built around users, and warn of gaps between human intent and machine reads.
arxiv-2507-12980:
Kyosuke Maeda and Ken-ichi Yoshida classify special ideals on a family of singular surfaces. Their paper appeared in 2025. The surfaces are rational triple points, a standard class of two-dimensional singularities. The ideals in question, called Ulrich ideals, are tightly tied to the shape of the singularity. The authors first show that one canonical ideal, the trace of the dualizing module, is always Ulrich for these surfaces.

From that anchor they list every Ulrich ideal on a rational triple point. They also prove that for quotient singularities with multiplicity at least four, the maximal ideal is the only Ulrich ideal. Together the results complete the classification for both families. Such lists help algebraists read a singularity's structure from its ideals.
arxiv-2507-14080:
Derek Leung, Nickolai Zeldovich, and Frans Kaashoek present Shipwright in a 2025 paper, a framework for proving that a distributed system keeps making progress even when some of its members act maliciously. Systems like PBFT, which let many machines agree on a shared log, have no single operator who can restart them, so a hidden stall bug can freeze them for good. Until now, no one had verified both correctness and this forward-progress property, called liveness, for a runnable version.

Shipwright adds three techniques. One supports reasoning about dishonest participants. Another splits systems and proofs into matching modular parts. A third handles digital signatures inside messages in a sound way. The team used it to build and verify a starter version of single-entry agreement in PBFT. They turned it into a working Go program and showed it running through normal operation and failure cases.
arxiv-2507-14780:
Phillip Isaac and Mitchell Ryan analyzed the Dirac oscillator through unusual symmetry algebras in 2025. The Dirac oscillator is a relativistic model where a particle feels a spring-like pull written in Dirac's equation. Its raising and lowering operators, which step between energy levels, turn out to generate graded Lie superalgebras with a double grading, one family in each spatial dimension from one to three.

Those algebras connect to parastatistics, a generalized rule for how identical particles may share states, and to the state spaces built from them. Isaac and Ryan show the algebras organize the oscillator's energy levels neatly, with the richest payoff in full three-dimensional space. Algebra becomes a lens for the model's spectrum.
arxiv-2507-15480:
Liang Chen and four co-authors improve how vision-language models are fine-tuned in a paper from 2025. Models like CLIP join image and text features, and the final merged table of scores drives each prediction. Most tuning methods adjust the image or text side alone and ignore that merged table, where the decision is actually made.

Their method, RAda, adds one light attention layer at the very end of the model. It learns a mask that reweights each entry of the merged table during tuning. Tests across settings, including tuning on unlabeled test data, matched or beat current methods with minimal code change.
arxiv-2507-16580:
Olmo and four co-authors draw how black holes with free-form traits would look through their disk glow in this twenty twenty-five paper. The holes are set by long lists of free values, with no tie to one gravity frame. Two known free-form sets are used, each trimmed by sun-system and far-field checks.

Inside, disk-lit views are made for holes whose dark core is blown up or shrunk. Ring size and ring glow traits are weighed in depth for each view. The team says next-wave long-base scopes could tell such holes from the plain round case. Views of bare cores with no dark zone are also drawn and weighed in the mix.
arxiv-2507-17580:
Amandeep Singh Bhatia and Sabre Kais propose improving quantum federated learning with Fisher information. In federated learning, clients train a shared model without handing over sensitive data. The quantum version adds parameterized circuits, with promise for fields like health care and finance, but communication costs and uneven client data remain obstacles.

Fisher information measures how much a quantum state reveals about its parameters, capturing geometric and statistical structure. The authors use it, computed on each client's local model, to spot the parameters that matter most for performance. Those critical parameters are then protected during the shared training process. The goal is faster, safer learning across unevenly split datasets.
arxiv-2507-18080:
Makoto Nakashima studies the critical two-dimensional stochastic heat flow in a two thousand twenty-five mathematics paper. This random object arises as a scaling limit of directed polymers in random environments. It also appears as a limit of solutions to a smoothed stochastic heat equation.

Nakashima focuses on the mass the flow assigns to pairs of balls in the plane. He establishes an upper bound on the lower tail of that mass. Small values, in other words, cannot be too likely. Two consequences follow from the bound. The logarithm of the mass is integrable, and the mass itself is strictly positive. These results partly answer open questions about the flow's local behavior.
arxiv-2507-19480:
Bešlić and a large team of co-authors mapped the ionization fraction across the Orion B molecular cloud in twenty twenty-five. The ionization fraction is the share of gas particles that carry an electric charge. It shapes how clouds form stars, but it is hard to measure outside dense cores, where only a few faint lines can be seen.

The team used fresh chemical models that pick out line ratios able to trace the fraction in thin and thick gas alike. They observed many molecular lines in the three-to-four millimeter band across Orion B. The fraction ran far higher in thin, lit gas than in dense gas. In dense regions lit by ultraviolet light, it fell as density rose. The map gives star formation studies a firmer base across a whole cloud.
arxiv-2507-19780:
Zhiming Liu, Paul Hill, and Nantheera Anantrasirichai present a compact framework that both clears air turbulence from images and finds targets in them, in a paper from 2025. Turbulence warps video with ripples, blur, and flicker. That hurts both image quality and detection. Doing the two jobs in sequence wastes effort and loses accuracy.

Their framework, JDATT, joins a strong clearing model and a detector, then shrinks both by joint distillation. A large model's skill is passed to a small one at two levels: inner features and final outputs. Tests on synthetic and real turbulence data showed better restored images and detection scores. Model size and running time fell sharply, suiting live use on light gear such as remote cameras.
arxiv-2507-19880:
Croce and South show how a fake tool server can trick an AI aid into theft in this twenty twenty-five paper. A shared tongue now lets aids call out to tools from far firms with ease. That trust opens a door that had not been probed in depth till now.

Inside, a fake sky tool hides a hunt for a linked bank tool in its code. Once called, it steers the aid to pull a user's bank sums out. The whole chain needs just base code skill and free web tools to run. No costly rig or deep hack craft is part of the chain at all. The pair urges quick shields now and tongue rules that curb cross-tool trust.
arxiv-2507-20380:
Yu-Kuo Hsiao, Yan-Li Wang, and Wen-Juan Wei hunt for the elusive kappa meson in semileptonic D decays, in a two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. The kappa, also called K0 star 700, is the least settled of the light scalar resonances.

A partial-wave analysis of the decay D plus to K minus, pi plus, positron, and neutrino extracts a clear kappa signal. Its branching fraction, formerly assumed negligible, actually dominates the observed s-wave rate, meaning the evidence sat mislabeled as background. The extracted form factor is far below the quark-antiquark prediction and close to the tetraquark expectation. The authors read this as support for a compact tetraquark nature of the kappa.
arxiv-2507-22380:
Yifei Chen and four co-authors help robots that learn by copying experts stop being fooled by side details in what they see. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Copy-based training can latch onto clues that do not drive the expert's acts. When the scene shifts a little, those false clues break the robot.

Their fix learns which parts of the view truly cause the expert's moves. It does so by stepping in and changing the policy's inputs, then watching what shifts. The team shows the heavy feature-splitting step used before is not in fact needed. Their light framework plugs into modern copy-based systems. Tests with a two-armed robot in simulation show far better carry-over to new scenes. The method could make trained robots less brittle on factory and lab floors.
arxiv-2507-23580:
Bradley Keister, Saeed Najafi, Joan-Emma Shea, and Krastan Blagoev study why droplets in living cells do not merge and grow the way simple physics predicts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In a still system, big droplets tend to swallow small ones in a process called Ostwald ripening. Cells stay out of balance, though, and their droplets seem protected from that fate.

The authors ran computer models of particles that pull on each other, then pushed the system out of balance in two ways. In one, particles randomly flipped between two states; in the other, their speeds were randomly reset. In every driven case, ripening stopped, while calm systems ripened as expected. The team suggests this effect may be what keeps cell droplets stable.
arxiv-2508-00580:
Raul Castilla-Arquillo and four colleagues build a perception system, in a 2025 preprint, to help planetary rovers judge the ground ahead. A rover must sort sand, bedrock, and packed soil to travel safely. No single sensor sees all of that well. Color, depth, and heat images each carry part of the story. Heat images in particular reveal soil type through how fast ground warms and cools. The team fuses all three in one network.

Their network, OmniUnet, is built on transformer blocks. To train it, they mounted a custom sensor box on a test rover and drove it in a Spanish semi-desert that mimics Mars. Part of that data was labeled by hand. The network reached pixel accuracy above eighty percent on tests. It answered in well under a second on a small onboard computer. The team released the code and labeled data for others to use.
arxiv-2508-01780:
Guozhao Mo and co-authors benchmark AI agents on using a vast ocean of software tools, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A common protocol now links language models to over ten thousand tool servers. Past tests used one server and fed tools straight to the model, skipping the hard parts.

Their bench holds ninety-five real daily tasks and a suite of seventy servers with hundreds of tools. An automated judge checks true task outcomes. Twelve top models were graded: the best passed near four in five tasks, while most passed only a third to a half. Retrieval slips caused near half of all failures.
arxiv-2508-02880:
Pengwei Sun and four co-authors evaluate fake-but-plausible brain scans in twenty twenty-five. Counterfactual generation simulates how a scan would look under a hypothetical change. It could help explain disease and create realistic training data. For 3D brain MRI, the task is hard: data is scarce, anatomy is complex, and no standard evaluation exists.

The team converted six generative models into counterfactual ones. Each was guided by a causal graph in which regional brain volumes act as direct inputs. They judged the models on composition, reversibility, realism, effectiveness, and minimality. Scans came from a major Alzheimer's disease imaging initiative. They also tested how well each model carried to other data. Readers get a benchmark for a fast-growing medical imaging idea.
arxiv-2508-04380:
Tuan Hoang, Chuyen Nguyen, and Thanh Pham blend two access schemes for light-based wireless networks in a 2025 paper. Their users share LED light links, served in time slots. Inside each slot, up to two users can share one channel at once by power splitting, if their signal strengths differ enough for clean separation.

The pairing choice is the crux. For any pair, the authors compute the range of channel-strength ratios where sharing beats taking turns, solving two optimization problems with an approximation method. Simulations across user counts and LED powers show their adaptive scheme beats the fixed hybrid baseline on total data rate. The design aims to keep the added complexity low.
arxiv-2508-04580:
Yi and four colleagues probe how electrons localize in a near periodic lattice with mixed disorder in twenty twenty-five. In the clean case, waves spread, then pass through a middle phase, then trap as the pattern strengthens. Adding staggered or sequence based patterns changes the story. One kind merely shifts the trapping point.

Two sequence patterns trap waves at once, and the team ties that to pattern complexity. A typical fidelity measure scales cleanly at the transition, giving firm exponents. One pattern family shows fresh exponent values distinct from known models. Two unlike patterns share one exponent, though. The work unifies trapping rules across pattern types.
arxiv-2508-05280:
James M Cline writes a comment on a claimed unified field theory, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The theory, set out in a recent post, says it joins gravity with the Standard Model. It claims to be finite and unitary, and to predict all values of the model from just two inputs.

Cline points to a missed result: the photon gains mass at one loop in that model. The cause is a lack of gauge invariance in its non-local interaction points. He also clears up a point about Wick rotation that had clouded the debate. He spells out more of the gauge troubles, and he flags a domain wall problem in the model as well.
arxiv-2508-06180:
Ten Kate, Ohnmacht, and eleven colleagues listen to the bound states inside germanium Josephson junctions with microwave spectroscopy, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Germanium quantum wells, paired with superconductors, are a fresh platform for Andreev bound states, thanks to strong spin-orbit coupling and clean transport.

The team built junctions in proximitized germanium wells and read their spectra with microwaves. A short junction, three hundred fifty nanometers long, showed signs of several bound states, matched by a model with finite-length effects. A longer junction, one point two micrometers, needed a model with three bound states in two channels plus Coulomb interaction between charges. Interactions, often ignored, clearly shape the spectra. The results form a base for controlling these states in future devices. Germanium is attractive because it fits the silicon technology world.
arxiv-2508-06780:
Nizamudheen V, Riyasudheen T K, Noufal Asharaf, and Shefeeq T solve a fractional option pricing equation numerically in a 2025 study. The time-fractional Black-Scholes equation prices European options when prices move with long memory, as if through a fractal market process. Fractional derivatives look backward over history, which makes accurate solutions hard to compute.

Their algorithm combines a standard fractional time step with a spatial method based on modified cubic splines. Differential quadrature turns the spatial part into algebra a computer can solve efficiently. The hybrid scheme aims for accuracy without heavy cost. Better solvers help test whether fractional models describe real option markets.
arxiv-2508-08380:
Rohan Bali, Trevor Bailey, Michael Bullock, and Boulat Bash published this communications paper in 2025. Covert communication hides the very existence of a message, not just its content. Theory sets a strict limit, the square root law: over a channel used n times, only about the square root of n bits can pass undetected. Turning that math into hardware is hard, because ordinary link upkeep operations would give the game away. Only two prior experiments existed, both on optical channels.

The team demonstrates provably covert radio communication using software-defined radios. Their setup sends messages that a watcher cannot reliably distinguish from noise, within the proven limits. The authors say the experiment validates the theory on a radio channel for the first time. It also opens practical questions about building real covert systems and about what adversaries would need to detect them.
arxiv-2508-10080:
Jiaqiang Yan and co-authors report a change of crystal form in a lead-lanthanum oxide that may compete with superconductivity, in a paper from 2025. The compound cools through a transition point at 225 kelvin. Below that point, pairs of atoms shift along one axis and the crystal takes a new symmetry. Electric and heat measures show kinks at the change.

Under pressure, the change fades away. In its place, signs of superconductivity appear, peaking at a transition near ten kelvin. Computer models show the electron states barely shift at the change point. That hints the shift is driven by chemical bonding, not by the electron sea. The compound offers a clean stage for studying how weak structural shifts and superconductivity interact.
arxiv-2508-10480:
Grontas, Terpin, Balta, D'Andrea, and Lygeros present a paper from twenty twenty-five on neural networks that always respect hard constraints. Their added output layer projects network answers onto the allowed set. Splitting methods make those projections fast and reliable. Backpropagation runs through an implicit function result. The layer acts as a stand-in solver for families of optimization problems. Single problems solve faster than classic solvers at modest accuracy. Batches of problems solve dramatically faster still.

Training time and solution quality beat prior learning methods by wide margins. Multi-vehicle path planning tests the non-convex side. A graphics-ready package in JAX is released. Feasibility by design is the core promise.
arxiv-2508-10780:
Alessandro Adami and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on teaching robots to stack tasks in the right order on their own. Robots with spare joints must rank jobs like safety, aim, and speed. Hand built stacks take long to tune. Their frame learns the whole stack from a cost score that states the user's likes.

Genetic search with simulation tests both the rank order of tasks and their gains. A dual arm mobile robot served as the test bed. Learned stacks dropped moot tasks on their own and looked like expert work. All stacks moved from simulation to the real robot with no more tuning. They dodged blocks and tracked paths well, even near people.
arxiv-2508-13380:
Seohyeon Cha, Kevin Chan, Gustavo de Veciana, and Haris Vikalo schedule AI models across phones, edge servers, and the cloud in a 2025 study. Real services run many tasks at once, such as detection, segmentation, and depth estimation for driving or augmented reality, while older frameworks assumed one task and one model. Loading a model onto a tier costs time, and batching requests changes the math again.

Their framework decides jointly which models to load or unload at each level, with batching built into the accounting. Smart placement keeps weak devices responsive without wasting cloud capacity.
arxiv-2508-13480:
Mithra Karamchedu and Lucas Bang list a graph's spanning trees and count twin copies as one. For series-parallel graphs, they solve the task in full. Plain lists drown in twin copies from the graph's own shape flips. The paper scans the task for graphs at large, then builds tools for the two-end set.

Where each end is marked on its own, list time tracks list size. In the half-marked case, ends are a marked pair with no set roles, and the same tools bend to fit. The case with no marks at all is left to notes and open asks. One sharp point: the tools never work out the flip group as such. The loop shape of the twins' traits tracks the loop shape of the trees.
arxiv-2508-13680:
The authors introduce a Vietnamese benchmark for vision-language models in a paper from 2025. The head of the record titles it VMMU, a multitask multimodal benchmark. It holds about two and a half thousand exam-style questions in Vietnamese across seven tasks, from science problems to rule-based visual puzzles, all needing true joint use of image and text.

Top commercial and open models were tested on the full set. Despite strong scores at reading Vietnamese text in images, the best models averaged only about sixty-six percent correct. Failures came mostly from weak grounding and reasoning over the two inputs, not from misread text. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2508-13880:
Valentina Corbetta and five co-authors introduced LCRReg in twenty twenty-five, a training method that keeps medical image models honest. Deep networks often ace familiar data but fail when conditions shift, leaning on spurious cues like scanner marks instead of real anatomy. LCRReg steers a network toward features clinicians actually care about.

The method needs no concept labels in the main training set. A small side data set yields clean examples of chosen concepts, from which latent concept directions are extracted. A penalty then nudges the network to work inside those directions. On a toy task it resisted planted spurious cues, and on diabetic retinopathy screening it improved accuracy under both faked shifts and true out-of-distribution tests. It beat multitask and post-hoc rivals while staying light and architecture-free.
arxiv-2508-14180:
Gaurav Bhatt and four co-authors present RewardRank, a new way to train search ranking systems, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Old rankers learn from stand-in goals that treat users in a simple way. They miss real habits, such as favoring items near the top of a list. As a result, rankers that score well in tests often fail to lift clicks or sales in live trials.

RewardRank first learns a reward model that scores any ranking from past user clicks. It then trains the ranker to make that score as high as it can. The team also built two test suites for fair checks. One uses an open click model as a stand-in judge on a public data set. The work aims to close the gap between test scores and real gains.
arxiv-2508-14480:
