Filip Najman and Ivan Novak determined the quadratic points on a family of modular curves in twenty twenty-five. Modular curves, written X0(N), are curves whose points encode extra structure on elliptic curves. Quadratic points are those defined by square-root extensions of the rational numbers, and listing them all is a classic hard task in number theory.

The authors settle every level up to one hundred that was still open, eleven levels in all. Their tool is an improved going-down method. It uses the fact that all quadratic points are known for some smaller level dividing the target level, then lifts that knowledge upward. The result completes a case-by-case map that other researchers had built over many years.
arxiv-2508-14980:
Balykin and five co-authors built this face security method in twenty twenty-five. Face recognition can be fooled in two ways: by physical fakes, such as photos or masks, and by digital forgeries. Separate detectors for each kind add cost and leave gaps. The team trained one model to catch both.

Their method pairs each real selfie with a matched attack version during training. Contrasting the pairs teaches the model signs of liveness that work across attack types. On a major challenge benchmark, the method posted a low average error of about two percent. It beat earlier solutions while staying light and quick to train. The team released code and trained models for others to use.
arxiv-2508-15280:
Yuanchen Zhao, Li Rao, and Dong E. Liu wrote a 2025 physics paper on weak measurements in quantum systems. Weak measurements nudge a system gently instead of forcing it into one state. The authors study what happens when two kinds of weak measurement compete and do not commute, meaning the order in which they act changes the result.

Using theory and computer simulations, the team maps out the phases the system can enter. The outcome depends heavily on whether the measurement results are read out fully, partly, or not at all. Full readout can build long-range entanglement, while no readout leads to a different kind of order. The work gives experimenters a clearer guide for building stable entangled states.
arxiv-2508-16480:
Linda Hirsch, James Fey, and Katherine Isbister turn local flood actions into cards for a table game, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Work ran with a community-led learning center through field watch, expert groups, and a survey. The aim is bottom-up flood strength, not top-down drills.

Twenty-seven acts that lift or keep flood strength were found. Twenty became playing cards in a bigger interactive table game still in build. The team argues cards can teach non-experts through play. Local fit came from the joint design path itself. Readers in game design get a method for grounding serious play in place.
arxiv-2508-17180:
Pande, Yerramilli, Tamarapalli, and Grover built this benchmark in twenty twenty-five to test AI vision on math. Multimodal models describe images well but may not truly reason over them. Surface plots, the graphs of math functions, strip away everyday meaning and leave pure shape. That makes them a clean test of spatial and math reasoning.

The benchmark, MaRVL-QA, holds two task types. One asks models to count features such as peaks on a plotted surface. The other asks which geometric change was applied to a shape. The plots come from a curated function library with checks against ambiguity. Even top models scored poorly and leaned on shortcuts. The authors offer the set as a yardstick for deeper reasoning.
arxiv-2508-17780:
Lee, Ma, and Zhao build a sound way to draw facts about a new group from a model trained on an old one in twenty twenty-five. Labels are costly to gather for the new group, so only unlabeled data exist there. When the mix of labels shifts between groups, naive reuse misleads. Their method models how outcome density changes between the groups.

The estimate grows in three stages: a rough guess, then a steady estimate, then a sharp one. Each stage feeds the next, a self improving path that is new in this field. They prove the math traits of the final estimate. Tests on fake and real data beat past methods, they report.
arxiv-2508-17880:
Aditi Bhalla and three co-authors release a dataset on trust in self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Trust and comfort decide whether people accept such vehicles, yet past work studied them separately with thin data. Their dataset records drivers in a simulator running fully self-driving trips. Participants voted their trust in real time and rated comfort continuously throughout each drive.

Body signals such as heart rate, gaze, and emotion were captured alongside car and traffic data. Questionnaires before and after trips added context. Learning models trained on the body data predicted trust and comfort well, with tree-based methods on top. The authors aim at cars that adapt to their riders.
arxiv-2508-19580:
Omkar Gurjar, Agam Goyal, and Eshwar Chandrasekharan build a new benchmark for argument summarization in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Pulling key points from debates is a core summarization task. The standard data set, though, poorly matches real human conversation.

Their new set, ArgCMV, holds about twelve thousand arguments from real online debates across more than three thousand topics. Its arguments run longer, refer back to each other, and carry more subjective material than the old set. Existing extraction methods adapt badly to it. The authors benchmark classic baselines and fresh open models to show the gap. They pitch ArgCMV as the proving ground for the next wave of language model summarizers.
arxiv-2508-21380:
Elias Sandmann, Sebastian Lapuschkin, and Wojciech Samek peer inside a top chess engine and find it ignoring its own best moves. Earlier work showed the engine, Leela Chess Zero, plans ahead in its layers. The team asks whether that inner planning rules the final choice. Often, it does not.

Using a lens that reads out each layer's leaning, they tracked puzzle positions. Correct mates appeared in middle layers, then vanished by the output. The look-ahead machinery itself still worked: future moves sat encoded and causal. Late layers instead drifted toward safe, quiet play. Steering the model against that drift rescued most of the lost puzzles. The study warns that inner algorithms do not guarantee outer behavior. A network can solve a problem and still answer wrong.
arxiv-2509-00180:
Nguyen Phan and Guoning Chen evaluate neighbor search for curve-based vector field processing in 2025. Vector fields assign a direction and strength to each point in space, as in fluid flow. Integral curves trace those fields and often stand in for large simulation data. Many tasks need the neighboring curve segments near a query point or segment.

Popular search strategies can return skewed and redundant neighbors, since curves may spread unevenly and may not capture the full flow. The study tests two strategies with distinct distance metrics on field reconstruction and segment salience tasks. It shows how each search setup affects the downstream result. The findings guide analysts who must pick a search method for flow data.
arxiv-2509-00380:
Cong Yi, Xiang-Yu Wu, Jie Zhu, Shi Pu, and Guang-You Qin study how fluid motion shapes spin alignment in heavy-ion collisions in 2025. When nuclei crash, the hot fluid they form can swirl and shear. That motion can align the spins of Lambda hyperons, short-lived particles made in the crash, along the beam line.

The team uses the CLVisc code, which models the fluid's flow, for gold-on-gold and proton-on-lead crashes at distinct energies. They compute one harmonic term of the spin alignment as a function of how central each crash is. Three cases for how spins settle are compared side by side. Two flow traits drive the signal: thermal vorticity, the local swirl of the hot fluid, and the thermal-shear tensor, which tracks how flow speed changes across space. Their split roles are spelled out for each system and case.
arxiv-2509-00580:
Felipe Tejo and Ruben M Otxoa study magnetic hopfions. A hopfion is a three-dimensional swirling texture in a magnet. Its shape is protected by topology, so it resists change. Tests have now confirmed that hopfions are stable when still. How they move and vibrate is still largely unknown.

The pair uses computer models of tiny magnets plus hand analysis. They characterize the breathing mode of a hopfion. In that mode, the core and the shell swell and shrink as one. The topological charge stays fixed all the while. A model of domain wall forces explains the shell's weak response to fields. It also gives a formula for the restoring stiffness. The breathing rate that follows is below one gigahertz. It matches the computer spectra well.
arxiv-2509-00880:
Li-Ren Bao and one co-author, Wei-Hsuan Yu, construct large m-distance sets on triangular lattices. An m-distance set is a collection of points where distances between any two points take only m possible values. Finding large examples is a central problem in discrete geometry.

Bao and Yu use two different methods. One takes the first m smallest distances on the lattice and finds the largest cliques, fully connected groups, in the resulting graph. The other uses notions of hexagons, natural cells of the triangular lattice. They observe multiplicities of the distances, how often each distance occurs, to compare the two methods. The constructions add concrete large examples for testing bounds on distance sets.
arxiv-2509-01380:
Solving elliptic equations, which describe steady states such as heat or electric potential, inside complex shapes is hard when a mesh must fit the boundary. Qing Xia presents an unfitted boundary algebraic equation method that works on a regular grid instead. The grid need not conform to the shape, which gives freedom for domains with sharp corners or odd forms.

The method builds single and double layer potentials from lattice Green's functions and discrete potential theory, echoing boundary integral methods. Local basis functions on cut cells handle varied boundary conditions, and fast Fourier solvers speed the layer computations. Xia proves stability and convergence through a new interpolation framework. Tests on ellipses and diamonds with varied proportions and sharp corners confirm accuracy and robustness, with gains such as smaller problem size and conditioning that does not depend on the mesh.
arxiv-2509-01480:
Flipping a magnet's direction with light promises faster, cheaper data storage, and phonons, quantized vibrations in a crystal, offer one route. F. G. N. Fennema, C. S. Davies, A. Tsukamoto, and A. Kirilyuk study magnetization switching driven by circularly polarized phonons in a sample's substrate. A polarization-modulated transient grating excites those phonons in a controlled pattern.

The polarized phonons induced robust reversal of the magnetic layer, with the direction set by the light's helicity, its spiral sense. At frequencies matching the target phonon modes, switching quality barely changed when the light's ellipticity was varied. Slightly off resonance, by contrast, quality became highly sensitive to ellipticity. The results show when phonon-driven switching is forgiving of imperfect light and when it is not, a practical guide for optical magnetic devices.
arxiv-2509-01680:
Chuanxin Cui and Moshe Rozali test a claimed link between a gravity model and a quantum model of black holes. The gravity side uses sine-dilaton gravity, a two dimensional theory with a wavy term. The quantum side is a scaled model known by its short name DSSYK. The pair derive matter correlation functions, which track how matter fields relate across points, straight from the gravity side.

Their trick treats matter lines as special boundary sheets, letting them cut and rejoin the space in steps. The counts they get match the quantum side results drawn from chord diagrams. Along the way they find a new identity for a key symbol in quantum group math. The setup also extends past the simplest space shape to harder cases.
arxiv-2509-01780:
Parth Chavan and Christophe Vignat revisit an identity of Ramanujan about Bernoulli numbers, a famed sequence in number theory. The identity uses multisection, a trick that splits a series into parts by index pattern. They give two fresh proofs that stay elementary, meaning they use basic tools only. One proof is geometric and leans on symmetry in the complex plane.

The shape of the summation region explains why the identity holds in the geometric proof. The second proof uses generating functions, which pack a sequence into one formula. That route extends the identity to other special functions, such as Eisenstein series. The paper shows how one old trick can open several doors at once.
arxiv-2509-02080:
Riya Mehta, Bivas Rana, and Susmita Saha sum up work on spin wave flow in crystals with a near repeat pattern. Spin waves are ripples in how tiny magnets point, and patterned films can guide them. Crystals with near repeat lack strict repeat, so their wave bands split into many gaps. That split gives finer control of spin waves than strict repeat films can give.

The sum up spans flip of the magnet state and spin wave motion in many such films. Band shapes show how the near repeat form grants strong control of the waves. Films that can be reprogrammed are a prime use in view for these parts. The pair close with open paths for new work and a brief sum up. Their text helps designers pick forms for wave based logic and signal parts.
arxiv-2509-02480:
Avinash Maurya, M. Mustafa Rafique, Franck Cappello, and Bogdan Nicolae present a 2025 systems paper on training language models too large for combined GPU memory. Overflow data spills to host memory or disk, but moving it back and forth slows every training step.

Their MLP-Offload engine spreads optimiser state, the bookkeeping data of training, across several storage tiers and paths. Design choices follow three observations: update-phase transfers dominate step time, remote storage bandwidth sits idle, and competing transfers worsen congestion. Cache-aware placement plus controlled concurrency ease those bottlenecks. On models up to hundreds of billions of parameters, iterations ran about two and a half times faster than leading training runtimes, easing the memory wall for modest clusters.
arxiv-2509-02680:
Ramona Gröber, Alejo N. Rossia, and Michał Ryczkowski present a 2025 particle physics paper comparing two frameworks for describing possible deviations in Higgs boson behaviour: SMEFT and HEFT. Both extend the Standard Model, but their predictions split most clearly when several Higgs bosons are produced at once.

The authors study double and triple Higgs production through gluon fusion using bootstrapped on-shell amplitudes, a method that builds scattering results from physical pieces without field-redefinition confusion. A new technique assembles five-point amplitudes from smaller ones plus contact terms. Matching against both frameworks reveals at which order each kinematic structure first appears. Some structures in triple Higgs production only arise at very high order in one framework, giving experiments a sharp discriminator.
arxiv-2509-03180: Francesco Meazzini and Claudio Onorati proved 2025 results in algebraic geometry about deformations of twisted sheaves. A sheaf assigns algebraic data to regions of a space, and a twisted version allows a controlled mismatch between regions. Tiny deformations of such objects are governed by an algebraic structure built from their derived automorphisms, the symmetries computed in a homological sense. The authors show that structure is formal, meaning its higher operations vanish in effect, for stable twisted sheaves on certain surfaces and for a special class on hyper-Kähler manifolds.
arxiv-2509-03580:
A basic identity linking particle mass to the trace of the energy-momentum tensor is the subject of a 2025 theoretical physics paper by Long Chen and two co-authors. That trace summarises how a system's energy and pressure respond to stretching space. The identity concerns a single particle in an on-shell state, meaning it carries its physical mass.

Their proof is diagrammatic, working through Feynman diagram patterns rather than assumed renormalisation rules or Ward identities. Mass-dimensional analysis and the on-shell condition carry the argument to any loop order in gauge theories. Direct calculation through three loops checks the identity in quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics, with at most one heavy fermion. The trace anomaly seems to hold all leading renormalon effects, the stubborn ambiguities of perturbation theory. A new mass definition for heavy quarks and electrons follows from subtracting that part.
arxiv-2509-03680:
Ruofan Liang and six co-authors' 2025 research paper is about estimating how a scene is lit, working from one image or a video clip. Lighting estimation matters for graphics and vision, since inserted objects must match a scene's light to look real. Ground-truth environment maps in high dynamic range are expensive to capture, so training data stay scarce and narrow.

Their system, LuxDiT, fine-tunes a diffusion transformer for video, a generative model that builds images step by step, to output those environment maps instead. Training uses a large synthetic dataset with varied lighting, teaching the model to read indirect cues like shadows and reflections. A small collected set of real high-dynamic-range panoramas then aligns the outputs with real scenes through a low-rank fine-tuning strategy. The results carry realistic fine angular detail. Quantitative and qualitative tests place the method ahead of leading existing techniques.
arxiv-2509-03780:
Natural latents, hidden variables that stay stable when different learners describe the same world in different ways, are the subject of a 2025 research paper by John Wentworth and one co-author. Two Bayesian agents may learn generative models of one environment and agree perfectly on observable predictions. Their internal latent variables, the unobserved factors each model invents, can still differ completely.

The question is when one agent can guarantee that its latents derive from the other's, making translation between models possible. The authors give simple conditions, called the natural latent conditions, under which that guarantee holds. Absent further constraints, those conditions are also the most general ones possible, so nothing weaker can promise translatability in all cases. Importantly for real use, the theorems are robust: small approximation errors in the conditions do not destroy the guarantee. The result speaks to science and artificial intelligence alike.
arxiv-2509-03880:
Pisin Chen and one co-author follow plasma wakefield acceleration from its origins to laboratory black holes in a 2025 review paper. Written for the 2024 S. Chandrasekhar Prize, it covers the prehistory, the accelerator's birth, and the theory that followed. In such a device, a driver pulse leaves a wake in plasma that can surf later particles to extreme energies.

Conceptual evolution is the narrative thread, running through key breakthroughs to echoes in astrophysics and analog gravity. Because the acceleration is so intense, equivalence-principle reasoning turns it toward gravity experiments. One example flies relativistic plasma mirrors to imitate an evaporating black hole, targeting Hawking evaporation and the information paradox. The AnaBHEL experiment, pursuing analog black hole evaporation with lasers, is described. The outlook ends with hybrid schemes and the next collider generation. The review shows how a collider technique grew into a probe of quantum gravity.
arxiv-2509-03980:
Alessandro Mirri and three co-authors work on detecting multiple preambles in random access systems using OTFS signalling in a 2025 research paper. In random access, many devices announce themselves with short preamble signals, and the receiver must spot which preambles arrived. OTFS, orthogonal time frequency space modulation, suits fast-moving channels by working in the delay-Doppler domain.

The detection problem is cast as structured sparse recovery in the complex domain: few preambles are active, and OTFS signals are themselves sparse in delay-Doppler coordinates. Their approximate message passing algorithm enforces that double sparsity at once. Because the complex sparsity constraint does not separate, deriving it takes care, and the result is a novel denoiser inside the message passing loop. Simulations show robust detection with significant gains over leading existing techniques. The work targets future wireless systems where many devices contend for access over difficult, high-mobility channels.
arxiv-2509-04180:
Safouane El Ghazouali and one co-author, Umberto Michelucci, release an open-source tool that speeds up labeling images for computer vision in a 2025 research paper. Training vision models needs huge numbers of images tagged with boxes or outlines, and hand labeling is slow. Their web application, VisioFirm, drafts labels automatically. It mixes the CLIP image-text model with ready-made detectors for common objects, plus a zero-shot detector for custom labels requested in words.

Drafts favor catching everything, then people fix mistakes with editing tools for boxes, tilted boxes, and polygons. One-click outlining runs inside the browser through WebGPU acceleration. Exports cover the main formats used by training software. Benchmarks claim manual effort dropped by up to ninety percent.
arxiv-2509-04280:
Tobias Raichle and two co-authors adapt speech-cleaning models to new rooms and voices at test time in a 2025 research paper. Models that remove noise from recordings shine when test audio resembles training audio, then stumble when accents, languages, or noise types change. Their method, LaDen, works inside the model's latent space, the compressed internal description of sound. A simple linear reshaping turns noisy latent patterns toward clean ones, guided by strong pre-trained speech representations.

That reshaping transfers across settings, producing stand-in clean labels for the new environment. The main model then tunes itself using those labels, with no hand-labeled target data needed. A new benchmark covers many shift types. LaDen beat rival approaches, especially across speakers and languages.
arxiv-2509-04680: Rithwik Susheel Vidyarthi gives a short alternative proof of a result by Honda, Kazez, and Matic in a solo-authored 2025 topology paper. The result concerns a fibered knot with pseudo-Anosov monodromy. That is a type of surface map with strong stretching behaviour. Its fractional Dehn twist coefficient is at least one. Under those conditions, the knot supports a contact structure obtained as a perturbation of a taut foliation, a layered structure on the surrounding space.
arxiv-2509-04780:
Extreme heat and weather have renewed interest in modelling sustainability risk across the economy, environment, and society together. Yiren Wang and one co-author propose such a model in a 2025 paper. Their framework generalises the classic Lotka-Volterra equations, long used for interacting populations, to the economic-environmental-social nexus.

The authors compare their approach with the World3 model from the landmark Limits to Growth study. They claim better analytical tractability, meaning the model is easier to solve and study formally. They also argue it represents economic development from innovation more faithfully, and that its sub-dynamics suit many sustainability applications.
arxiv-2509-05280:
Labelling tree graphs so edge sums never repeat is solved for a wide class by Alp Müyesser and Alexey Pokrovskiy in a 2025 combinatorics paper. The problem traces to Graham and Sloane in 1980 and asks when tree vertices can take the labels of an abelian group, one-to-one, with all edge sums distinct.

The authors give an exact characterisation for trees of bounded degree, where each vertex has a limited number of neighbours. One consequence is that the cyclic group case always works for such trees. That settles a 1980 conjecture of Graham and Sloane, and a later one from 1987, for this class. The results also bear on the study of graph coverings.
arxiv-2509-05480: Rigidity of distance-preserving maps between certain complex shapes is proven by Anand Chavan in a solo 2025 paper in complex geometry. The shapes are two-dimensional Lempert manifolds, complex surfaces equipped with the Kobayashi distance. They are also assumed to have a finite universal set for a companion distance. Chavan shows that any Kobayashi isometry of such a manifold must be holomorphic or anti-holomorphic, meaning it either preserves or cleanly reverses the complex structure rather than bending it arbitrarily.
arxiv-2509-05580:
Neutron stars in high-mass binaries are spinning faster over decades, and Vitaliy Kim with Yerlan Aimuratov propose tides as the engine in a 2025 astrophysics paper. These X-ray pulsars also show shrinking orbits, and the energy source behind the long spin-up trend has been an open question.

The authors name the longest pattern super-global spin-up. From five well-monitored systems they take spin histories and estimate energy losses from orbital decay and spin acceleration. Their hypothesis is that orbital angular momentum passes to the neutron star through tidal interaction with its massive companion. The observed spin-up values stay below the upper limits their scenario predicts, keeping the explanation viable.
arxiv-2509-05880:
The small moon of the dwarf planet Makemake gets its first orbit estimate in a 2025 paper by Daniel Bamberger. Makemake is one of the large icy worlds beyond Neptune, and its satellite was known from discovery images only. Bamberger mines archival Hubble Space Telescope pictures taken on thirteen days between 2015 and 2019.

The moon appears on twelve of those days, enough to fit a preliminary circular orbit. The fit gives a period of about eighteen days, a separation of roughly twenty-two thousand kilometers, and a path tilted nearly edge-on to our line of sight. That geometry raises the chance of mutual events, seasons when the moon crosses in front of or behind Makemake as seen from Earth. More images will sharpen the orbit and test whether it stays circular.
arxiv-2509-06180:
Electrons in a single layer of iron selenide do not all feel magnetism alike, and their orbital matters, and Mercè Roig and eight co-authors explain why in a 2025 paper. Monolayer FeSe superconducts and shows only electron pockets. Around one corner of the Brillouin zone, antiferromagnetic fluctuations couple strongly to one orbital set and weakly to another.

Symmetry arguments trace the selectivity to how orbital and sublattice wavefunctions intertwine at that point: one orbital set can localize on iron sites, the other cannot. That coupling produces orbital-selective shifts that match their photoemission measurements. Unlike earlier Mott-transition accounts, this band-theory mechanism is required by symmetry, and it extends to other space groups with suitable screw axes.
arxiv-2509-06580:
Who benefits when AI enters the laboratory? Georgia Channing and one co-author argue in a 2025 essay that putting AI to work in research is mainly a social problem. Technical hurdles like scarce data and tight budgets for machines are real, the authors note, but social factors and workplace rules often bind harder.

Four linked challenges structure the argument: coordinating communities, research priorities that ignore upstream needs, fragmented data, and unequal infrastructure. Stories about autonomous AI scientists, they say, undervalue the data and systems work that makes new findings possible, and incentives pull domain experts and machine learning researchers apart. Their remedies mix technical and social steps: community building, cross-disciplinary education, shared benchmarks, and shared tools. The paper calls for treating AI for science as a collective project, where fair participation comes before technical gains.
arxiv-2509-06880:
Which algorithm parameters actually take small values on real graphs? Christian Komusiewicz and three co-authors answer with data in a 2025 algorithms paper. Parameterized algorithmics designs methods whose cost depends on a chosen parameter, and smaller parameters usually mean slower-growing guarantees. Theory alone cannot say whether real instances reward that trade.

The authors measured many parameters across benchmark graphs from real applications: degree-based ones like maximum degree and degeneracy, neighborhood-based ones like modular-width, modulator-based ones like vertex cover number, and treewidth. Some parameters disappoint: vertex cover numbers often sit just below half the graph size, so gains are slim. Treewidth, by contrast, is usually far below the graph size, making treewidth-based running times genuinely practical. Code and full experimental data are openly available, including first implementations of several parameters.
arxiv-2509-07080:
Raphael Baer-Way and 15 co-authors report the first radio detection of a type Ibn supernova, SN 2023fyq, in a 2025 paper. Type Ibn events happen when a star explodes into nearby material that is rich in helium and poor in hydrogen.

The team followed the blast with radio and X-ray telescopes for eighteen months. They used what they saw to rebuild the history of mass loss from the star that exploded. Early radio waves fit synchrotron radiation dimmed by free-free absorption in the surrounding material. That points to a stretch of heavier mass loss starting under a year, and ending a few years, before the explosion. The timing lines up with optical outbursts seen from the star before it blew up. Later visits found nothing, and the paper discusses those non-detections as well.
arxiv-2509-07180:
Searching for new materials usually means testing one atomic arrangement at a time. Justin Tahmassebpur, joined by 6 co-authors, introduces Effective Atom Theory in a 2025 research paper. The method places atom identities into a smooth, continuous space where gradient-based optimization, the workhorse of machine learning, can run. During a search, sites hold temporary mixtures of elements, then settle into real, single atoms.

The team runs the method inside density functional theory and machine-learned potentials, two standard tools for computing material behavior. It recovers the known ground state of table salt in a large cell. It also rebuilds the copper-palladium phase diagram and improves high-entropy oxides for oxygen evolution, a step in splitting water. The authors report speedups of orders of magnitude over older discrete searches, opening faster routes to designed materials.
arxiv-2509-07380:
Keith Promislow and 2 co-authors build a framework in 2025 for gradient flows of surface energies with active agents. A gradient flow moves a shape downhill in energy, like a soap film settling. Here the interface, the boundary between two regions, carries curvature agents, embedded elements that respond to bending and push back on the surface.

A penalty method creates families of flows that stay locally incompressible, meaning patches of surface keep their area, by coupling stretching to a flux of interfacial mass. The authors prove the penalty flows converge to a truly incompressible one, formally for a broad family of energies and rigorously for a narrower class. They also analyze an Allen-Cahn type model, a diffuse-interface approximation, for the coupled agent energy. Such models matter for membranes and active materials that reshape themselves.
arxiv-2509-07480:
Heikki Mäntysaari and 1 co-author recalculate how often a J/psi particle is produced alone in electron-proton scattering in a 2025 paper. Exclusive production, where the proton stays intact, probes the proton's gluon content. The calculation uses the QCD dipole model and pictures the dilute proton as a few gluonic hot spots, dense gluon patches whose sizes and numbers fluctuate from event to event.

The refined model adds those fluctuations in both hot spot count and local saturation scale, plus the first relativistic corrections to the J/psi wave function. A Bayesian fit constrains the parameters against HERA collider data, and agreement improves significantly. Saturation scale fluctuations matter more than count fluctuations, the authors find. The relativistic correction proves important for matching the observed power-law behavior of the incoherent cross section at large momentum transfer.
arxiv-2509-07580:
Coralia Cartis and 2 co-authors prove global convergence rates in 2025 for regularization methods that approximate high-order derivatives cheaply. Adaptive regularization is an optimization framework that models a function with polynomial terms plus a penalty, and high-order versions need derivative tensors that are expensive to compute exactly. Their framework allows inexact tensor approximations built from lower-order derivatives.

Between refreshes, a secant equation can update the tensor estimate, or it can lazily stay constant. Refreshes themselves may use an exact evaluation or a finite difference with an explicit step size. For every variant, the authors bound the iterations needed to reach an approximate second-order stationary point and count the oracle calls involved. The second-order case gives a quasi-Newton style method with a matching rate. The results guide practitioners who trade derivative accuracy against computing cost.
arxiv-2509-07680:
Sachit Menon and 5 co-authors build CAViAR in 2025, an agent system for reasoning about long videos. Video models keep improving at perceiving short clips, but benchmarks such as LVBench, Neptune, and ActivityNet-RTL show performance drops as questions grow complex and videos grow long. The authors ask whether existing perception skills can be composed, by an agent, into genuine reasoning.

A large language model agent calls video modules as tools and decides each next step from the results, rather than following a fixed script like earlier visual programming systems. A critic, inspired by textual reasoning work, learns to tell successful action sequences from unsuccessful ones. Agent plus critic achieve strong performance on the named benchmarks. The design suggests long-video understanding may advance by orchestrating tools, not only by scaling perception models.
arxiv-2509-07780:
Tsao-Hsien Chen and 2 co-authors construct part of a local Langlands correspondence for Moy-Prasad types in a 2025 paper. The Langlands program links representations of p-adic groups to Galois-side data. It is a guiding framework in modern number theory. Here the group is a tamely ramified p-adic reductive group. The representations are the irreducible smooth ones of a fixed depth. Depth measures how deeply they see the group's structure.

The authors build a partial correspondence between those representations and a set of conjugacy classes. The classes consist of continuous homomorphisms from a filtration subgroup of the inertia group into the dual group. Partial correspondences test the expected shape of the full Langlands dictionary, in concrete families. Moy-Prasad types organize representations by depth. A depth-by-depth correspondence gives the program a workable foothold.
arxiv-2509-07880:
A beam of fast ions passing through magnetized plasma can gain energy from waves rather than from any accelerator. J. T. Y. Chu, with 27 co-authors, reports such an experiment in a 2025 research paper. The experiment ran at the GSI Helmholtz Centre in Germany. Two laser-blasted plasma jets collided to form a magnetized interaction region.

A mono-energetic chromium ion beam was fired through that region. Laser measurements showed no strong large-scale turbulence. Even so, the beam ions accelerated and spread in energy, driven by wave-particle interactions. The authors suggest a kinetic instability, the lower-hybrid drift instability, as a likely mechanism. Results like these matter for understanding cosmic ray acceleration, where plasmas in space energize particles without any machine at all.
arxiv-2509-08080:
Meerzhan Kanatbekova and 2 co-authors cut the qubit cost of putting constrained problems on quantum hardware in a 2025 paper. Quantum solvers usually need problems in QUBO form, a standard binary format. Encoding limits, especially inequalities, normally takes extra variables, and each variable costs a qubit. Today's noisy quantum machines have few qubits to spare, so encodings run out of room fast.

A generalised encoding is proposed to represent constrained optimisation problems more economically. Saving qubits directly extends the size of logistics, scheduling, and design problems that near-term devices can attempt. Until fault-tolerant machines arrive, clever formulations like this are one of the few honest ways to widen quantum computing's practical reach.
arxiv-2509-08180:
Neural networks are notoriously poor at plain arithmetic, often failing to generalize beyond their training numbers. Paul Curry proposes a new arithmetic layer, the Domain Mixed Unit, in a 2025 research paper written alone. The unit learns a single gate parameter. That gate blends logarithmic and linear representations of numbers while the unit adds or subtracts.

Two starting settings are proposed: one covering addition and multiplication, another covering subtraction and division. On a standard benchmark for neural arithmetic units, the new unit solved the highest share of multiplication and division problems across random seeds. Curry plans to submit the unit to the open benchmark project, and the code is public. A single learned gate is a strikingly small fix. If it holds up, arithmetic layers could become far more reliable inside larger learning systems.
arxiv-2509-08380:
Prathamesh Vasudeo Naik and 4 co-authors build an agent team that drafts money-laundering reports in a 2025 paper. Banks must file suspicious activity reports for regulators. Each report is a clear, factual story of suspect deals. Human teams write them slowly, at high cost. Plain language models write fast but invent facts and miss crime patterns.

Their system is called Co-Investigator AI. Agents split the drafting work and check each other, in the style of recent agent designs. The aim is reports made far faster, with better accuracy than the old route. Compliance work cannot accept made-up facts. A drafting partner that stays factual could free investigators to chase the crime, not the paperwork.
arxiv-2509-08480:
Do language models, like survey respondents, tend to agree with whatever they are asked? Daniel Braun tests acquiescence bias across models, tasks, and three languages in a solo 2025 study. Humans notoriously say yes to survey statements regardless of belief. Models trained on human text and easily swayed by small prompt changes might inherit the habit.

The results cut the other way: the tested models lean toward answering no, regardless of whether agreement would mean yes or no. English, German, and Polish tasks all feed the comparison. A built-in nay-saying tilt matters wherever models grade, screen, or survey: an instrument with a default answer quietly rigs every questionnaire it touches.
arxiv-2509-08580:
Outlining organs by hand in three-dimensional medical scans is slow, expert work that radiotherapy planning cannot skip. Mathilde Monvoisin and 9 co-authors reduce that burden in a 2025 research paper. Their method learns an implicit shape prior, a statistical memory of what organs look like. A clinician then annotates only a few slices, and the system completes the volume.

The framework also picks which slices are most informative to annotate next, minimizing interactions. It generalizes from single organs to the multi-organ case. Validation covers two uses. One protects organs at risk in brain cancer patients. The other builds a database of muscle shapes for sarcopenia, age-related muscle loss. Cutting manual segmentation time matters wherever specialists are scarce. It also makes large annotated datasets, the fuel of medical AI, cheaper to create.
arxiv-2509-09380:
How strongly can two variables move together when the link is not a straight line? Luca Giuliani and 1 co-author take up that question in a 2025 paper centred on the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi measure, a broader alternative to Pearson correlation. Their concern is practical: recent differentiable estimates can be fragile when used inside constrained learning systems.

Giuliani and his co-author propose a route built on polynomial kernels that the user can configure. They argue it gives steadier, more repeatable results, with a faster restricted version that loses little. A short test inside a constrained learning setup shows the computed value can also supply a useful subgradient for regularising a loss.
arxiv-2509-10080:
Minsang Kong and 5 co-authors predict where traffic will move next without leaning on a prebuilt map in a 2025 self-driving paper. High-definition maps give forecasting models a tidy scaffold, but they cost heavily to maintain, cover only mapped ground, and age badly where roads change. Working from a bird's-eye view built directly out of sensor data promises freedom, at the price of dense, unstructured features that are slow to reason over.

Their BEVTraj system uses deformable attention to sip context only from useful spots in that dense view. A goal proposal module then names a short list of believable destinations, letting forecasts stay multimodal with no hand-written cleanup afterwards. Scores matched leading map-based systems while keeping the flexibility to drive unmapped streets.
arxiv-2509-10180:
Danni Zhang and Dongling Wang study computer simulations of the nonlocal Cahn-Hilliard equation in this 2025 numerical analysis paper. The equation models how mixed materials separate into phases, and the nonlocal version lets each point interact with neighbors across a finite distance. Proving that simulated solutions settle down over long times is unusually hard here.

The pair builds first- and second-order time-stepping schemes paired with a second-order method in space, all designed to keep the system's energy stable. Using that stability plus a classic inequality about energy landscapes, they prove the numerical solutions do approach an equilibrium as time runs on. The result supports trusting long simulations of phase separation in materials science.
arxiv-2509-10280:
Junshan Luo, Shilian Wang, and Boxiang He design defenses for drone-carried communication surfaces in this 2025 wireless engineering paper. Aerial reconfigurable intelligent surfaces ride on unmanned aerial vehicles and can reshape radio channels while linking ground users, a useful shield against jamming. The catch is scale: tuning huge numbers of these surfaces directly is too heavy, and a smart jammer adapts.

Instead of optimizing each drone, they model the fleet's layout as a smooth density and optimize that. They show the jammer faces a trade-off between moving closer and focusing its beam. Their defense jointly tunes base-station beamforming, surface reflection, and fleet placement, following what they call a spatial water-filling pattern. Simulations show clear gains, and the computing cost stays fixed as drones are added.
arxiv-2509-10680:
What is a quantum individual? Christian de Ronde and Ivan Klarreich enter a long argument over that question in this 2025 paper. It is philosophy of physics at its most basic. One camp follows Décio Krause. It says quantum theory refers to non-individual particles. Such particles lack identity altogether. The other camp follows Dennis Dieks. It keeps the classical particle notion that practicing physicists actually use.

The authors argue the supposed rivals share hidden common ground. A single methodology unites them. It entrenches the classical concepts imposed by Bohr and Dirac, within the orthodox formulation of the theory. Against both camps, the authors discuss a newer relational account. It is relativist yet objective. It is modeled on Einstein's way of working. Their claim is bold. This account opens the door to a genuinely realist view of quantum individuality. It is not a patch on classical thinking.
arxiv-2509-10780:
Ruiwei Xiao and six co-authors name a problem every global teacher using AI now meets: cultural distance. They define it in this 2025 education paper. It is the gap between a generative model's default cultural repertoire and what a local classroom demands. The repertoire comes from uneven training data. The team interviewed thirty K-12 teachers. Ten each came from the United States, Taiwan, and South Africa. All had woven AI into their teaching.

From those accounts, they build a framework of cultural distance with three levels. Six cases illustrate it, spanning low to high. Teachers bridge the distance daily, by hand. They rephrase prompts. They substitute local examples. They correct the model's assumptions. The authors turn those tactics into guidance. Designers, policymakers, and educators all get advice. The goal is AI tools that fit the classroom they enter. The average of the internet is not that classroom.
arxiv-2509-10980:
Haoming Lu, writing alone, introduces TrueSkin, a data set for fairer skin tone recognition and generation, in this 2025 paper. Skin tone matters for fairness, health tools, and image generation, yet leading multimodal and image models still read and reproduce it badly, partly for lack of good training data.

TrueSkin holds more than seven thousand images sorted into six tone classes, gathered under varied lighting, angles, and capture settings. Benchmarks on it exposed real biases: recognizers pushed mid-range tones toward lighter labels, and generators drifted when prompts mentioned unrelated details like hair. A recognizer trained on TrueSkin beat the big models by a wide margin, and fine-tuning on it improved generated tones as well.
arxiv-2509-11780:
Takashi Takahashi reworks a classic method from statistical physics for learning problems. This 2025 paper has no co-authors. The replica method studies how well fitted models can learn. Its textbook form assumes ideal data spreads. Averages over disorder can then be done in closed form. Real data rarely honor that assumption.

Takahashi swaps in a variational bell-curve fit for the replicated system. A grand canonical frame holds it. The data average is postponed, then swapped for averages of the data itself. Balance conditions adapt the trial Hamiltonian to each dataset. The approach clarifies how wobble in the data limits what can be learned. It ties the replica machinery to known tools like model-choice scores. Linear regression serves as the demo, with learning curves derived for real-world data.
arxiv-2509-12280:
Why the quantum world looks classical once someone measures it is the oldest puzzle in quantum theory. Environment-induced decoherence explains much of the appearance but leaves the observer's own quantum state unresolved. A solo 2025 study by Eyad I. B Hamid tackles the gap with computation instead of philosophy.

Hamid simulates a small closed universe with three parts, a system, an environment, and a physical model observer, and forbids any collapse rule outright. Within those unitary rules, a single definite outcome still emerges inside the observer's state. The result suggests classicality can be an outcome of the dynamics, not an added postulate.
arxiv-2509-12580:
Correlation energy, the part of an atom's energy that simple mean-field theory misses, can be split into pieces with distinct physical meanings. Ibrahim E. Awad and four co-authors compute those radial pieces in 2025 for every atom from helium to argon, using near-exact extrapolated configuration interaction wave functions.

Three components are separated: nucleus-electron potential, kinetic, and electron-electron potential correlation densities. Two standard atomic grids are graded for the job, with the finer one needed for kinetic effects and the coarser one accurate to about a kilojoule per mole elsewhere. The radial profiles show clear shell structure, and spin-up versus spin-down densities differ markedly in open-shell atoms.
arxiv-2509-12680:
Valence bond theory describes molecules in the language chemists think in. Its orbitals are not orthogonal, though. That makes the math costly. Quantum computers also lacked a matching encoding. Alessia Marruzzo and six co-authors fix the second gap in 2025. They extend the classic Jordan-Wigner mapping to nonorthogonal spin orbitals. The target is valence bond work.

Standard mappings assumed orthonormal orbitals. That left this chemically rich territory unmapped. The new mapping gives a route to simulate valence bond wavefunctions on quantum hardware. It does so efficiently. An opening theoretical analysis supports the encoding. A first test application supports it too. Larger and more complex molecules are the long-term prize.
arxiv-2509-12780:
Soumitra Daptari and Saurabh Dwivedi study in 2025 the state spaces of Banach spaces, the sets of peak maps that fix a unit point. Much of a space shape can be read from how large or tight those sets are.

They focus on spaces of summed functions and on sums where terms fade to zero. For summed functions, a tight state set in the strong sense forces the point to be smooth. For list sums they give exact tests for weak tightness in terms of each part and shrinking widths. The results add sharp tools for work on shape in broad function spaces.
arxiv-2509-12880:
Anna Deichler and 3 co-authors extend their work on pointing gestures toward context awareness in a 2025 paper. Most earlier research, though, taught machines to read a person's point. Far less of it taught a machine to make a point of its own. A good artificial point must also fit the moment: the style, the hand used, and where the target sits.

The team first built a data set from motion capture. Volunteers pointed in many styles, with either hand, toward targets scattered in space. The authors then trained policies by reinforcement learning, with imitation of the captured motion built in. The policies learn to copy how human pointing looks while also hitting the target as exactly as possible. In simulation, the method produced pointing that adapts to context. It balanced doing the task well against moving in a natural, human-like way.
arxiv-2509-12980:
Hemanth Chandravamsi, Dhanush Shenoy and Steven Frankel fix a start flaw in sine-based neural nets in 2025. Such nets store images, sound, and shapes as functions. Poor starts can leave them blind to parts of a signal.

When start range and signal range clash, output can fall near zero. The net then fails even on parts it could hold. Their WINNER start adds noise scaled by the signal core pitch. No new train weights are added. Tests show top sound fits and clear gains on images and shapes. The fix points to starts tuned to each target.
arxiv-2509-13580:
Jennifer Mead and nine co-authors ask how well metals mix in the early universe in a 2025 astrophysics paper. After the first stars, called Population III, explode, their metals spread into nearby gas that forms the next generation of stars. Models often assume that mixing is instant and perfectly even, and the team tests that assumption directly.

Using Aeos, a suite of star-by-star cosmological simulations, they compare gas and stellar abundances over space and time. Even mixing held only within a small region around a star-forming site and for a short time after the event. Farther away, the assumption breaks down until it does no better than a crude average, a warning for reading the chemistry of the oldest stars.
arxiv-2509-13980:
Sami Ul Haq and three co-authors present a shared task entry in a 2025 machine translation paper. It is their submission to the WMT25 task on automated translation quality evaluation. Judging a translation segment by segment misses context. Most quality estimation data still comes in short pieces. Reference translations, when available, give another anchor for judgment.

Built on the COMET framework, their systems predict error span annotation scores for whole passages. They manufactured long-context training data by joining human-annotated in-domain sentences. Their scores were averaged with weights. They also merged three human judgment collections, after normalizing their scales. Multilingual regression models then scored translations from source, hypothesis, and reference together. Long context improved agreement with human judgments over short-segment models by a clear margin.
arxiv-2509-14080:
JINHO CHA builds a framework for this inverse problem that moves in a solo 2025 paper. Inverse optimization reads a firm's observed spending decisions. It infers the priorities behind them. Real priorities drift gradually and jump after shocks, so a static inference goes stale. The aim is to recover time-varying preference parameters from a stream of decisions as they happen.

The framework pairs two pieces. An offline formulation fits a whole path with temporal smoothing. An online mirror-descent estimator handles streaming recovery. Cha proves conditions for local identifiability and existence. He gives regret bounds for the online estimator against fixed and moving baselines. A stability bound links data residuals to parameter error. Stylized experiments with drift, noise, and abrupt shocks act as finite-sample diagnostics. Temporal coupling softens the trade-off between sluggishness and jitter.
arxiv-2509-14180:
Akhil Theerthala builds training data for personal finance advisors in a solo 2025 paper. Good financial advice depends on a client's goals, constraints, risk tolerance, and local rules. Earlier language model work chased investor support tools or sprawling agent pipelines. Those cost heavily to maintain and returned a fraction of their expected value.

His framework weaves relevant financial context together with behavioral finance research. That research studies how people actually make money decisions. The result is synthesized reasoning chains that supervise an end-to-end advisor. From it he built a dataset of about nineteen thousand examples. He fine-tuned an eight-billion-parameter model. On held-out tests and a blind jury study run by other language models, the small model matched far larger systems. Accuracy, fluency, and personalization held up at a fifth of the cost.
arxiv-2509-14280:
Begum Gulsah Cakti, writing alone in 2025, studies Fermat type equations over quadratic number fields. Fermat style problems ask when power sums can balance exactly. Moving from whole numbers to fields with a square root added changes which tools work.

Cakti uses the modular approach to get explicit, computable bounds for such equations. She contrasts hurdles in fields that sit inside the real numbers with those in fields that do not. For a generalised Fermat equation over class number one fields, results extend earlier work by Freitas, Siksek and Turcas. For a listed set of fields, special solutions are ruled out past a bound. For two further fields, no nontrivial solutions of the type exist at all.
arxiv-2509-14380:
Seoyeon Choi and three co-authors propose CRAFT in 2025, where a foundation model coaches robot teams to coordinate. Multi robot learning is hard: joint actions are continuous and vast, rewards are tricky to design, and teammates change as they learn. Human athletes solve similar problems with coaches.

CRAFT gives the foundation model that coaching role for multi agent reinforcement learning. The coach designs staged curricula and gives detailed feedback as robots practise coordination tasks. Foundation models bring broad reasoning that a fixed reward script lacks. The authors argue a coach can steer exploration toward useful teamwork faster than trial and error alone. If the approach generalises, robot fleets could learn joint skills with far less hand tuned reward engineering.
arxiv-2509-15280:
Anthony Sisti, Ellen McCreedy, and Roee Gutman model compliance at two levels inside pragmatic cluster randomized trials in a 2025 biostatistics paper. In such trials, clinics rather than patients are randomized, and both providers and patients can drift from the assigned intervention. Standard analyses of the complier average causal effect track only individual compliance, ignoring how unevenly clusters implement the program.

Their Bayesian framework handles one-sided noncompliance at both levels: binary at the patient level, partial at the cluster level, where implementation is summarized by several continuous metrics. A latent mixture model captures heterogeneity in how clusters take up the intervention. The estimand then shows how treatment effects vary with both sources of compliance, information trialists need when rolling out programs that clinics adopt unevenly.
arxiv-2509-15380:
Vera Pavlova and Mohammed Makhlouf build a search tool for Islamic texts in many languages. Search across languages has grown in the lab, but real tools that people can use are rare. The pair use the Quran, which exists in many tongues, as their test ground. Their goal is one small model that serves users well in each language.

They train eleven search models in four ways, from single language training to a mixed plan that joins two methods. The mixed plan works best across their tests. They also study how each plan shapes the model's inner word space, and they weigh the cost of running one model in real service. Their work points to a cheap, shared design.
arxiv-2509-15480:
Yuliang Xu, Kaixuan Luo, and Li Ma build a tool for grouping gene access profiles. Their data come from DNase-seq tests, which show where the genome is open. Where a gene switch sits, the open pattern often dips in a telltale shape called a footprint. Those shapes stretch across far apart spots, so the grouping tool must track long range links.

Older grouping tools forced stiff rules on how profiles vary together, which hid the real groups. The trio propose a tree based kernel, a rule for how alike two profiles are, that bends to many patterns. It splits profiles step by step down a tree, with a sparse model for the split odds. A sampling method then fits groups to data.
arxiv-2509-15580:
C. A. S. Moltzer leads a team that explains odd pairs of stars that shed their outer layers. In these pairs, one star has just left a bright phase after losing most of its coat. A main sequence partner remains, and a dusty disk rings both stars. The pairs' orbits do not match what standard models predict.

The team focus on the dimmer group, whose stars left the red giant branch. They ask if steady mass flow between the stars can explain the orbit lengths. They fit the light of known pairs in our galaxy to get their brightness. They then run models of star pairs at two metal levels. The pairs fit the predicted links if their orbits stayed oval during the flow.
arxiv-2509-15780:
Natallia Kokash, Bernard de Bono, and Tom Gillespie build tools for mapping the body's wiring. Their infrastructure supports maps of the peripheral nervous system and other body systems, tied to the organs they serve. The nervous system is a web of nerves and hubs that coordinate signals body wide. Mapping it well takes shared terms and clear structure.

Their frame, ApiNATOMY, stands for maps of circuits across scales, in both shape and meaning. A knowledge model lets experts record how body parts interact. Management tools then turn high level sketches into detailed process models. Those models link with outside term sets and knowledge graphs. The work aids a large mapping program.
arxiv-2509-16180:
Picking the closest guess about a hidden distribution, while keeping each person's data private, usually takes many questions. Gautam Kamath and three co-authors cut that cost with a new method for private hypothesis choice. Their tool, a graph that maps how candidate distributions differ from each other, guides which questions to ask.

The method needs far fewer queries than the square of the candidate count that older methods required. It also asks all its questions in one round, with no back and forth. The graph idea may prove useful for other choice tasks under privacy rules, the authors note.
arxiv-2509-16280:
The faint radio glow from the early universe could reveal how the first stars reionized gas, but telescope flaws can warp that signal. Madhurima Choudhury and Jonathan C. Pober start a series on a learning pipeline that reads such radio images to infer early-universe traits. In this first study they test what happens when the modeled blur of the telescope is wrong.

They train a neural net on images from one antenna layout, then feed it images blurred as if the layout differed. The net's estimates of the neutral gas share drift, by amounts tied to the blur error. The work sets up ways to harden future surveys.
arxiv-2509-16480:
Finding the pitch of a voice in noise and echo is a small task with big stakes for speech tools. Anup Singh and Kris Demuynck build a pitch tracker that turns a difference signal into per-frame pitch odds, then sums odds across multiples of each candidate period and nearby frames. A path-finding step with a continuity rule picks the final pitch track.

Across noise levels, their method posted lower pitch and voicing errors than existing trackers, in both noisy and echoing rooms. Steady gains in harsh settings matter for hearing aids, voice assistants, and call tools alike.
arxiv-2509-16780:
Eason Chen and co-authors compare two ways to ground a tutor in a textbook in a 2025 paper. Plain retrieval fetches pages that match a question. A graph variant also uses links between ideas in the book. The team test both for page-level answers on an undergraduate math text.

The graph method gave a clear gain in answer quality. The gain matters most where budgets are tight, since graph methods can cost more to run. Knowing the trade-off helps schools pick a design. A tutor that cites the right page builds trust with students and teachers. The study gives builders hard numbers for that choice.
arxiv-2509-16880:
Tianhao He and Xintian Wu relate entropy measures across two spin chains in a 2025 physics paper. One chain is the XY chain, the other the quantum Ising chain. Entanglement entropy gauges how linked two parts of a chain are. Ends of the chain can be fixed in set directions or left free. The pair study exact links between the two chains under each end rule.

Three kinds of end rules are covered in the study. Ends can align the same way, oppose each other, or mix fixed and free. Exact relations let results from one chain transfer to the other. That saves work in a field where many quantities resist direct calculation.
arxiv-2509-17180:
David Arbour and five co-authors wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on a hidden risk in causal inference. Many standard tools predict by taking a weighted average of past outcomes. Some tools let weights go negative, which can fix imbalance in the data but leans hard on model assumptions and adds noise. Others ban negative weights and pay for safety with worse balance.

The team replaces the hard ban with a soft penalty on how far a tool reaches beyond its data. They bound the worst-case error from that reach and name a three-way trade-off among imbalance, model error, and noise. The trade-off bites hardest in high dimensions when overlap is poor. They give a method that tunes the bound while keeping balance low, plus a way to use it as a check on model trust. Tests on made-up and real data support the approach.
arxiv-2509-17580:
Zhenyu Du, Jinchang Liu, Elias X. Huber, Zi-Wen Liu, and Xiongfeng Ma show how to certify big quantum traits by measuring a small piece. Their 2025 arXiv paper attacks a cost problem: checking complex quantum systems usually grows pricey with size. Simple local measurements would be ideal, but it was unclear they could vouch for global properties.

The key is a phenomenon they name localizable quantumness. For most many-body states, core quantum traits survive inside small subsystems once the rest has been measured locally. Building on that, their protocols certify multipartite entanglement, circuit complexity, and quantum magic, with all three witnessed on one small, reachable subsystem. Randomizing the measurement bases extends the trick to state fidelity. The protocols use only local Pauli measurements, need a constant number of samples, and stay robust for almost all states.
arxiv-2509-17780: Nicolas Beike gives new group examples in a short 2025 maths note. The groups are p-groups, where group size is a power of a prime. He looks at groups whose chain of derived groups has length three, and he fixes the count of character sizes at three. Beike builds concrete cases that meet both traits at once, adding test cases for work on how group shape links to character sizes.
arxiv-2509-18180:
Yang Wang and Kai Li review how large language models are reshaping operations research. Their 2025 review covers a field that builds maths models for hard choices in transport, supply, and work plans. Classic methods lean on expert-built models and hand tuning, which strain at scale and in fast change.

Three paths for model use are sorted: build the maths model, aid the solver, or solve the task at once. Bench sets and field uses are surveyed for each path. Snags span shaky text-to-maths maps, weak spread to new tasks, and thin test sets. Paths to plant use close the review.
arxiv-2509-18280:
Thiago Landim proves an integral form of the Springer correspondence for reduced motives. His 2025 paper extends known results on reduced motives from plain schemes to quotient stacks. Those stacks are held to a finite count of orbits, which keeps the setup firm.

The work sits in a broad Springer setup set out by Eberhardt and Stroppel. That setup also serves quiver Hecke algebras, a sign of its reach. An integral form keeps whole-number traits that a field-based form can lose. Such care matters when torsion, the finite-order part of a group, drives the tale. The proof leans on the stack extension at each step.
arxiv-2509-18380:
Distant quasars are the bright cores of young galaxies, powered by black holes. John F. C. Wardle and six co-authors present sharp radio images of a full set of them in this 2025 paper. The set holds 113 radio-loud quasars with distances that place them early in cosmic time. All were picked by a clear brightness cutoff, so the sample has no gaps.

The team used the Very Large Array radio telescope at two frequencies to map each source. Their targets span the era from cosmic dawn to cosmic high noon, when galaxies and large structures grew fast. The paper shows images of the sources that spread out enough to map. It also lists the shape traits of all 113 sources. As the second paper in a series, it sets up the sample and the image analysis. Later work can mine it for how jets and cores changed over time.
arxiv-2509-18480:
Protein folding models usually stack custom parts built just for proteins. Yuyang Wang, Jiarui Lu, Navdeep Jaitly, Josh Susskind, and Miguel Angel Bautista ask whether plain parts can do the job. Their 2025 paper presents SimpleFold, a folding model built only from standard transformer blocks. It trains with a generative flow-matching goal plus a structural term.

The team scaled the model to three billion parameters. Training data mixed about nine million distilled structures with real experimental entries. On standard folding benchmarks, SimpleFold-3B matched top specialist models. It also did well at producing varied structure ensembles, a known weak spot for exact-fit models. Its plain design runs well on consumer hardware. The authors argue the field may not need bespoke protein blocks after all. Simpler designs could speed future progress.
arxiv-2509-18780:
Tracking many moving objects at once means juggling a probability spread over whole sets of trajectories. Thi Hong Thai Nguyen, Ba-Ngu Vo, and Ba-Tuong Vo present a tractable approximation for that spread in this 2025 paper. Exact posteriors for labeled multi-object models are usually out of reach. The spread is also very high-dimensional, so approximation is a must.

Their multi-scan approximation matches how the true posterior spreads over trajectory counts. They prove it also minimizes a standard divergence measure within its model class. A companion algorithm computes the approximation over finite time windows. Tests cover a simulated social force scene with weak observations and a real pedestrian data set. Both support the method. The work targets tracking systems that must label and follow many people or objects at once, with honest uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-18980:
Why did a system suggest that film or product? Maxime Manderlier and three co-authors test whether large language models can explain such suggestions in plain words. Their recommender is built on matrix factorization with tight constraints, so user types are stated openly. Predicted scores share the same scale as real ratings, which makes the model's inner workings easy to read in principle.

The team turns that inner structure into written explanations with carefully designed prompts. More than 300 people then rated the explanations for clarity, usefulness, power to persuade, trust, and overall satisfaction. All styles of explanation were received well, with modest gaps between them. Comments from users added detail on what each style did right or wrong, beyond what the scores alone could show.
arxiv-2509-19180:
Atomistic simulations lean on machine-learned potentials that predict energies and forces, but those models rarely say how unsure they are. Riccardo Farris and four co-authors compare two ways to attach uncertainty: Bayesian neural networks and deep ensembles. Knowing the uncertainty matters most when a model is used on structures unlike its training data, a common case in materials science. The team built a Bayesian network with variational inference inside a PyTorch-based framework.

Both approaches were trained on a dataset of about 7,800 titanium dioxide structures, once on the full set and once on a subset. The comparison shows how data coverage shapes both accuracy and the honesty of the uncertainty estimates. Each method has strengths and limits that the authors spell out. Their analysis offers practical guidance for building uncertainty-aware potentials that modelers can trust.
arxiv-2509-19280:
Hard combinatorial problems with constraints, like assigning jobs or packing knapsacks, strain the Ising machines built to solve them. Shunta Ide and two co-authors improve a trick called sample persistence variable reduction, which fixes some variables early based on repeated solutions. Constraints are usually enforced with penalty terms, whose strength is a delicate dial. Their extension gathers persistence across several penalty settings at once, rather than trusting one.

On benchmark assignment and knapsack problems, the multi-penalty version found feasible solutions more often than the classic method. Its solution quality matched or beat the classic as well. Studying low-energy states under weak penalties clarifies when feasibility breaks and how encoding choices shift the trade-off. The authors position the method as a practical tool for constrained problems on quantum-inspired hardware, and a foundation for systematic penalty tuning.
arxiv-2509-19680:
Rules for how language models should behave in mental health or law cannot be written by engineers alone. K. J. Kevin Feng and five co-authors built PolicyPad, a shared workspace for drafting such policies. Experts can edit a policy together while each tests how a model acts under it on sample scenarios. The design borrows from user-experience practice, such as storyboards and heuristic checks.

The system grew out of watching nineteen workshops with domain experts over fifteen weeks. Trials with twenty-two experts in mental health and law followed. Groups reported tighter feedback loops and better teamwork while drafting. Testing behavior beside the text surfaced gaps that prose alone hid. The authors offer policy prototyping as a practice, much like prototyping an interface before release.
arxiv-2509-19980:
Clinical diagnosis demands guideline-grade rigor, and Haolin Li with six co-authors argue that knowledge should be injected openly, not baked into weights. Their framework, RAD, retrieves disease-centered knowledge from several medical sources and refines it for the case at hand. A guideline-enhanced contrastive loss pulls multimodal features toward that knowledge in latent space. A dual transformer decoder then reasons over image and text together.

Retrieval keeps the knowledge current and auditable, unlike parametric memory. Task-specific guidance matters because downstream diagnostic tasks differ widely. Trust is the stated goal: outputs anchored to named guidelines are easier for clinicians to check. The design targets multimodal diagnosis, where scans and notes must be read jointly. External knowledge, refined per case, is the core bet.
arxiv-2509-20080:
Hannah Christie, Pauline Barmby, and Jason Young wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on faint galaxies. Low surface brightness galaxies look dim even though many hold large amounts of atomic hydrogen gas. They form stars slowly, which makes them a test for theories of how galaxies evolve. The authors compare their star formation with that of normal bright galaxies.

They built a matched sample of two hundred seventy-seven faint galaxies from two large catalogs. Standard trend lines link star formation rate with mass and gas content. On those trends, the faint galaxies look much like bright ones in gas share and star formation. Yet they turn gas into stars very slowly. A typical one would need about eighteen billion years to use up its gas. The authors link this to low gas density and a lack of dense molecular gas on small scales.
arxiv-2509-20180:
Alberto Bonollo, Michela Rigoselli, and five co-authors wrote this 2025 conference paper on gamma-ray astronomy. The LHAASO observatory has cataloged bright extended sources whose nature is still unknown. Some may be halos around pulsars, and others young massive star clusters. Their shapes look similar at current resolution, so telling them apart is hard.

The authors modeled the radial emission profiles of both source classes from real data. They derived classification methods from the profile features of known sources. Then they tested those methods on simulated views from two future telescopes, CTAO and the ASTRI Mini-Array. The targets were unidentified extended sources from the first LHAASO catalog. Results show future instruments should identify many of these sources and sharpen the search for extreme particle accelerators.
arxiv-2509-20380:
GPU programming with OpenACC directives still demands rare expertise. Samyak Jhaveri, Vanessa Klotzmann, and Crista Lopes fine-tune language models to write those directives in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their release, ACCeLLiuM, pairs two open models with the dataset that trained them. The data was mined from public code repositories.

The dataset holds more than four thousand pairs of loops and expert pragmas, split between training and testing. Base models failed to produce valid pragmas consistently on the held-out loops. The fine-tuned models produced the right directive type for eighty-seven percent of loops. Half of their outputs matched the expert pragma exactly, clause order included. Near misses often used sound clauses in a different order. The release aims to set a reproducible benchmark for automated GPU offloading.
arxiv-2509-20480:
A decades-old dispute over a quantum phase transition is revisited by Diego Subero and four co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. A Josephson junction in a resistive environment was predicted to switch between superconducting and insulating behavior. The switch should occur when the resistance crosses a quantum value set by fundamental constants. Experiments and theory have argued over that claim for years.

The team measured current-voltage curves at low frequency across a wide parameter range. Their resistor was a true metallic element placed on the same chip as the junction. The transition appeared where the original theory said it should, near six and a half kilohms for Cooper pairs. Modeling showed the finite temperature of the experiment does not undermine the conclusion. The crossover resistance matches the zero-temperature prediction.
arxiv-2509-20680:
Organizations want to fine-tune large language models together without pooling their private data. Wenkai Guo and five co-authors test whether federated learning really protects that data in a 2025 paper accepted to the Findings of EMNLP 2025. In federated learning, each client trains locally and shares only model updates.

The authors study attack methods that try to recover private training text from shared updates and from the merged global model. They then evaluate defenses meant to block such leaks. Their results show that privacy in this setting is weaker than many assume. The paper gives builders of shared training systems a clear map of the risks and of which defenses hold up.
arxiv-2509-21080:
When a language model writes an interview with people from another culture, it may cast itself as one of the insiders and them as outsiders. Yixin Wan, Xingrun Chen, and Kai-Wei Chang name and measure that pattern in a 2025 paper. They call it insider-outsider bias.

Their benchmark, InsideOut, holds four thousand generation prompts. The task places the model as a reporter interviewing local people across ten diverse cultures. Three metrics quantify how the model positions mainstream cultures as its own while externalizing less dominant ones. Empirical tests with current models confirm the bias appears in practice. The work gives fairness researchers a concrete instrument for a subtle cultural failure mode in generated stories and scripts.
arxiv-2509-21380:
A small, well chosen subset can stand in for a massive training set in biomedical image classification. Behind the work are Imran Ashraf and 3 co-authors. A coreset is a small subset that stands in for a full data set. Training on full sets is costly, and tuning settings needs many rounds. Biomedical image classification is a key target, where models aid diagnosis of complex diseases. Smaller training sets could cut that cost greatly.

The authors base selection on intra class diversity, the variety within each class. A good coreset must represent the full data well. Their method aims to keep that diversity while shrinking the set. Training and hyperparameter search can then run on the subset. The paper addresses both training from scratch and transfer learning, which both demand large compute on massive data sets.
arxiv-2509-21580:
Strong quasiconvexity is a weakened form of convexity with strong growth guarantees. Nicolas Hadjisavvas and Felipe Lara characterize such functions in a 2025 paper. Their results cover the nonsmooth case, where no derivative need exist. Necessary and sufficient conditions for strong quasiconvexity are provided. Conditions of this kind let users verify the property without checking every pair of points directly.

As a consequence, the authors give a proof for the differentiable case as well. They also improve the quadratic growth property for strongly quasiconvex functions. Quadratic growth bounds how fast the function rises away from its minimum. Sharper growth constants matter for optimization algorithms that rely on this function class.
