arxiv-2510-13480:
Quddus, Kirshenbaum, and Grier introduce a holographic assay that measures immunoglobulin A levels in biological samples. Their 2025 arXiv paper offers the first label-free, bead-free way to count protein clumps directly. The method uses Total Holographic Characterization, which reads particle size, refractive index, and count from holograms. A plant lectin called Jacalin triggers selective clumping of the target antibodies.

The team demonstrates a proof-of-concept assay measuring immunoglobulins in human serum. Jacalin binds the sugar galactose on IgA, forming measurable aggregates. The assay was calibrated across the healthy reference range in diluted sample fluid. That range runs from low to high IgA levels found in human serum. The assay clearly separated samples containing IgA from samples containing IgG. The authors present the platform as a base for monitoring other clumping proteins too.
arxiv-2510-13580:
Gurgurov, Van Genabith, and Ostermann improve low-resource language performance by fine-tuning only language-specific neurons. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses the uneven skill of large language models across languages. A measure called Language Activation Probability Entropy picks out neurons tied to one language. Only the weights of that sparse subnetwork are then updated on target-language data.

Trials on two open models covered twelve mid- and low-resource languages. The method beat full fine-tuning, feed-forward-only tuning, LoRA, and random-subset baselines. It did so while updating at most one percent of all parameters. The authors also report healthier training dynamics and better cross-lingual alignment of representations. They release neuron identifications for over one hundred languages, plus their adaptation pipeline. The package offers a cheap path for adapting strong models to neglected languages.
arxiv-2510-13780:
Tao and Yang link the global burden of four mental disorders to eighteen development indicators across twenty-seven regions. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses Global Burden of Disease 2021 data spanning 1990 to 2021. Disability burden is tracked by age group against economic, educational, social, and technology measures. Which macro factors move with mental illness, and on what delay, is the question.

The team applies correlation, mutual information, Granger causality, and related tools to hunt linear, nonlinear, and lagged links. Young adults aged twenty to thirty-nine show the sharpest regional and temporal variation. Couplings between development indicators and disorder burden run strongest in that age band. Overall, more education aligns with lower burden, while unemployment aligns with higher burden. Lag analysis splits the factors by speed: economic and technology effects arrive quickly. Education's influence unfolds over a much longer horizon.
arxiv-2510-13980:
Christopher S. Jackson develops a framework for quantum measurements that unfold over time rather than happening in an instant, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Basic values such as position, momentum, and spin direction escape the textbook picture of measurement as an abrupt projection. Ongoing measurements, which gather information over time, supply the missing theory.

Jackson groups the pieces of a time-dependent measuring instrument into an algebraic structure he calls the instrumental group. All the time change sits in a function, the Kraus-operator density. It obeys a standard Kolmogorov equation for how the density evolves. When measurements run in sequence, instruments combine by convolving these densities. This promotes the structure into a full algebra with its own operators, dubbed ultraoperators. He works out what generates the evolution for jump-like and diffusive processes. He also shows how his equation relates to the standard Lindblad master equation.
arxiv-2510-15080:
Luo, Zullo, Patel, and a synchrotron team report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, flat electronic bands that refuse to be fragile. Flat bands quench electrons' kinetic energy, amplifying correlations and hosting quantum phases. But the known routes, frustrated lattices, moiré superlattices, heavy fermions, trade robustness against tunability and orbital selectivity. The authors find an intrinsic mechanism in two layered materials, niobium and tantalum oxychloride.

Angle-resolved photoemission measurements show a momentum-independent flat band that survives from bulk crystal to a few layers, at room temperature. Density functional theory and Wannier analysis trace it to hybridization between chains of one niobium orbital and a Lieb-like sublattice of another. A Peierls dimerization reinforces the effect. Living in one orbital channel, the band is orbital-selective as well as robust. They offer the oxychlorides as a tunable platform for flat-band physics under ambient conditions, and the mechanism as a design principle.
arxiv-2510-15380:
Axel Flinth, Hubert Orlicki, Semira Einsele, and Gerhard Wunder harden a scheme that uses compressed sensing as encryption. Their 2025 arXiv paper explains the appeal first. A random measurement matrix can act like a one-time pad key, giving strong secrecy with low complexity, which suits tiny internet-of-things devices. The flaw is reuse, since a fixed key can be recovered once an attacker knows a few message and ciphertext pairs.

Their fix, bilinear compressive security, convolves the encoded message with a fresh random filter before sending. If both message and filter are sparse, the receiver can untangle them by blind deconvolution without knowing the filter. The team then studies a strong known-plaintext attack that hands the attacker extra advantages. Their main result shows recovering the key would demand a huge number of intercepted messages. In the sparsest case, with single-entry messages, recovery is impossible outright.
arxiv-2510-15780:
Alireza Moradi, Mathieu Tanneau, Reza Zandehshahvar, and Pascal Van Hentenryck wrote a 2025 paper on power forecasts. It gives wind and solar forecasts more honest uncertainty ranges. Grid operators need forecasts with probabilities attached. But the stated confidence bands are often off. Bands can be too wide or too narrow for the conditions.

The authors build on conformal prediction. That is a statistical wrapping method. Their calibration sets adapt to context. A new weighting scheme does this. Past errors from similar situations count more. Experiments used large data sets from several United States power systems. Forecast quality improved for single sites. It also improved for whole fleets of generators.
arxiv-2510-15980:
Dong Liu and Yanxuan Yu propose reading a deep model's effort the way psychologists read human cognitive load. Their Cognitive Load Traces are symbolic, time-varying functions that track how a model allocates internal resources while it works. The idea borrows the three-way split of Cognitive Load Theory into intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load.

Each load is measured through concrete proxies such as attention entropy, cache miss ratio, representation spread, and decoding stability. Symbolic formulas and pictures, including load curves and simplex diagrams, make the traces readable as accounts of reasoning dynamics. On reasoning and planning benchmarks, the traces predict where errors are about to start and reveal which strategy a model is following. Interventions guided by the loads improve reasoning efficiency by a solid margin while holding accuracy, the pair report.
arxiv-2510-16380:
Yu Ying Chiu leads a team of nineteen co-authors presenting MoReBench, a test of how language models reason about moral dilemmas. Final answers alone hide the quality of the thinking, and moral cases rarely have one right answer. Each of the benchmark's one thousand scenarios comes with expert rubric points a good reasoner should raise or avoid.

The set holds more than twenty-three thousand such criteria, spanning spotting moral stakes, weighing trade-offs, and giving workable advice. A companion set tests reasoning under five classic frameworks of normative ethics. Results show that skill at math, code, and science does not predict moral reasoning skill. Models also lean toward certain frameworks, like act utilitarianism and Kantian duty ethics, perhaps a side effect of training habits. The benchmarks push evaluation from outcomes toward the process of reasoning itself.
arxiv-2510-17280:
The CMS HGCAL collaboration reports leak currents in neutron-hit silicon sensors in this 2025 paper. The sensors will serve a new fine-grained calorimeter at the Large Hadron Collider. An upgrade will raise clash rates near tenfold in the next runs. Sensors must shrug off huge neutron doses and still read well.

Hexagonal pads on eight-inch wafers fill over six hundred square meters in total. The team blasted sensors with neutrons at a range of dose levels. Leak current acts were mapped by sensor type and dose. Heat shifts of the current were tracked as well. Split blasts were tested as a way to curb cure time in tests.
arxiv-2510-17380:
Running a smart power grid well means balancing supply, demand, and cost across many linked parts, a task where reinforcement learning is gaining ground. Julen Cestero and four co-authors note a practical snag: the learning agent must try actions again and again, and each trial on a costly grid simulator eats time. That sample hunger slows the search for a good control policy.

Cestero and his co-authors swap the costly simulator for a stand in model built with physics informed neural networks, which respect the basic equations of the system. Training against the cheaper stand in reached converging results in a fraction of the original time. The approach points to faster tuning of energy management for real grids.
arxiv-2510-17480:
Aurélien Bellet, with Edwige Cyffers and four co-authors, sharpens privacy accounting for shared learning in a 2025 arXiv paper. In shared learning, users train one model together without sending raw data away. Each user averages updates with neighbors on a network graph. Noise added for privacy, meaning formal limits on what others can infer, can protect users.

In practice, privacy often seems to cost more accuracy here than in central training. The authors show the accounting tools may be at fault, not the method itself. They adapt a matrix based accounting method from central training to the shared setting. Their new algorithm, with noise linked across users, beat prior methods on test graphs.
arxiv-2510-17580:
Kai Zhang, with Tao Xiao and two co-authors, studies error sources in plasma simulations in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their simulations track charged particles and must solve an electric potential equation on a grid. Accuracy often drops near odd shaped walls. Most past work blamed the equation's left side, which holds the unknown values. Zhang's team instead studies the right side, which holds charge data gathered near those walls.

Charge data gathered near walls often comes out too low. The authors show this error helps a simple solution scheme but harms a more refined one. Tests in one, two, and three dimensions confirmed the pattern. A simple fix to the charge data restored the refined scheme's accuracy. The findings guide how simulation codes should treat wall regions.
arxiv-2510-17780:
Simon Brendle, Raphael Tsiamis, and Yipeng Wang revisit a conjecture by Gromov about filling in manifolds. A fill-in extends a closed surface into a solid region. Here the region has spin structure and scalar curvature bounded below. Gromov linked its smallest boundary mean curvature to a spherical radius.

The authors show Gromov's claimed inequality follows from known results. One ingredient is an inequality by Hijazi, Montiel, and Roldán about Dirac eigenvalues. The other is a recent theorem by Bär. They also give a fresh proof of that eigenvalue inequality. Their proof builds on work by Bär and Ballmann.
arxiv-2510-18080:
Rukuang Huang and four co-authors present a foundation model for magnetoencephalography, the magnetic echo of brain activity. Modeling large-scale brain dynamics is hard, and classic methods miss much of the structure in such signals. MEG-GPT uses a transformer that attends over time and learns by predicting the next time point.

A new data-driven tokenizer keeps the fine time detail of continuous signals without lossy steps. Training used a large resting-state data set of several hundred people with eyes closed. The trained model generates data with realistic space and frequency traits, including brief events. Neuroscientists get a language-model-style tool for brain signals.
arxiv-2510-18180:
Vincent Cohen-Addad, David P Woodruff, Shenghao Xie, and Samson Zhou shrink graphs and hypergraphs on the fly as edges stream in. A sparsifier keeps a small stand-in that preserves the energy of every vector almost exactly. Their insertion-only streaming method reaches near-optimal space for hypergraphs, matching the best offline sampling up to small factors.

For plain graphs the space bound improves on the current record by log factors. A second efficient streaming method rounds out the results. Algorithms readers who face data too large to store get provably faithful sketches that fit in near-minimal memory.
arxiv-2510-18580:
P. Haerter and his four co-authors study how particles escape from a circular billiard, a toy system for chaos research. A uniform gravity field bends the motion inside the open circle, which has two symmetric holes in its boundary. By varying the particle's energy and the holes' size, the team tracks escape routes, escape times, and survival chances using basin maps and an entropy measure.

At low energies the system is fully chaotic, and particles escape in a simple exponential pattern. At higher energies, stable islands known as KAM islands appear and trap some orbits, making escape slower and survival decay follow a power-law pattern instead. Both the entropy measure and the average escape time react sharply to this change. At very high energy the motion becomes nearly orderly again, and the measured complexity falls, completing a full arc from chaos through mixture back toward regularity.
arxiv-2510-18680:
Philippe Formont and his seven co-authors propose a way to merge many specialized embedding models into one representation that serves any task. Embedding models turn complex inputs into lists of numbers, and different models capture different aspects depending on their design and training data. Combining several teachers into one student is called multi-teacher distillation, but existing versions are usually tailored to a single target task.

Their framework rests on a majority vote objective, which they show is bounded by the information shared between student and teacher embeddings. That connection yields a training loss needing no task labels or prior knowledge. Evaluations across text, vision, and molecular modeling showed the merged representations improved a wide range of later tasks, from classification to regression. The team also released new embedding models trained this way that set strong marks in several modalities.
arxiv-2510-18880:
Rory Sayres and twenty-three co-authors study how people use language models for health questions. A small design change improves those conversations a lot. Four mixed-methods studies were run. One hundred sixty-three participants took part in total. A clear theme stood out. Good health conversations need the system to seek context. Details a person may not volunteer must be drawn out.

Participants valued context-seeking even when it delayed the answer. Several turns of delay were acceptable. The team built a Wayfinding AI on that insight. It proactively asks for context before advising. A randomized, blinded study compared it with a baseline system. Participants rated it more helpful and more relevant. They rated it better tailored to their concerns too. The authors offer proactive context-seeking as a design pattern for sensitive domains.
arxiv-2510-19080:
The CMS Collaboration reports the first observation of a single top quark produced together with a W and a Z boson in proton-proton collisions. Data from the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, taken at two collision energies, were searched for events with three or four charged leptons, such as electrons or muons.

Better reconstruction and machine learning gave unmatched sensitivity to this rare process. The measured production rates at the two energies agree within their uncertainties, and the signal passes the level required to claim observation. Rare top processes like this test the Standard Model in regimes where new physics could hide.
arxiv-2510-19180:
Hanna Zbroszczyk reports recent results from the HADES experiment, which studies what happens when heavy atomic nuclei collide at modest energies. Gold and silver collisions at the reported energies create dense nuclear matter whose behavior helps physicists understand strong interaction physics and the insides of neutron stars.

Measurements cover both hadronic signals and dilepton pairs, which escape the collision zone carrying clean information about its hottest stage. Zbroszczyk also outlines the future experimental program. Together the results and plans show how HADES probes matter at densities reached in few other laboratory settings.
arxiv-2510-19280:
Qing Zhao and three co-authors show that pairs of nucleons inside atomic nuclei shrink at the nucleus surface in a universal way. Using microscopic calculations, they track two-neutron, two-proton, and deuteron pairs across six light nuclei with very different structures and binding strengths.

Surprisingly, every pair type compresses at the surface regardless of species or how tightly it is bound. The behavior connects to two known pairing styles, loose and tight, that new experimental methods can probe further. A universal pattern like this gives nuclear theorists a simple benchmark that detailed models must reproduce.
arxiv-2510-19380:
Marco Di Marco proves compactness and a Poincaré inequality for special functions of bounded variation in Carnot-Carathéodory spaces, a class of spaces with restricted directions of motion. Such results are the backbone of calculus in these rough geometries, where ordinary length and area must be replaced by intrinsic notions.

By introducing an intrinsic perimeter measure for intrinsic rectifiable sets, Di Marco works in equiregular spaces that satisfy one extra natural assumption. Bounded variation functions then behave well enough for the two cornerstone results to hold. The theory supports later work on minimal surfaces and partial differential equations in these spaces.
arxiv-2510-19480:
Iasonas Nikolaou, working with three co-authors, introduces an online version of two-stage submodular maximization, a selection problem used in tasks like influence maximization and data summarization. In the new version, the objective functions arrive one at a time rather than all at once. The goal stays the same: shrink the ground set so a randomly chosen objective still scores well on it.

The team designs an algorithm with sublinear regret guarantees under matroid constraints, covering both general matroids and uniform ones. The uniform-matroid result also improves the best known bound for the original offline problem. Experiments on real datasets confirm that the online method performs as the theory predicts.
arxiv-2510-19580:
Austin Christian and Tanushree Shah build a diagram-based method for studying symplectic fillings of three-dimensional contact manifolds. Their tool is the symplectic JSJ decomposition, which cuts a manifold into simpler pieces. Starting from a contact surgery diagram, their framework produces a finite collection of simpler contact manifolds, also given by diagrams.

The fillings of the original manifold are then determined by the fillings of those pieces. As checks, the method recovers known filling classifications for certain lens spaces and torus bundles. It also yields an algorithm for classifying exact and weak symplectic fillings for a large class of plumbed three-manifolds, a family built by gluing simple blocks together.
arxiv-2510-19780:
Adam Karczmarz, Wojciech Nadara, and Marek Sokołowski improve the parallel cost of the single-source shortest path problem in directed graphs with non-negative weights. Shortest paths are a bedrock task. The open challenge is to do much less total work while finishing in far fewer parallel steps. Running times should be polynomial in the input size, not in the weight values. Their main result reaches near-linear work bounds with sublinear depth.

For dense graphs, this is the first nearly work-efficient strongly polynomial parallel algorithm with sublinear depth. Gains flow at once to min-cost flow and the assignment problem. The result also yields the first non-trivial strongly polynomial dynamic algorithm for minimum mean cycle. The team also handles variants with huge edge weights in the word RAM model.
arxiv-2510-19880:
V. Apinyan and T. Kopeć investigate electron pairing in a pair of metallic wires placed in electric and magnetic fields. The two wires interact through the Hubbard interaction, and the authors consider both half-filled and partially filled lattices. Their focus is excitonic pairing, where an electron in one wire binds with a hole in the other.

They demonstrate that such pairing exists in this low-dimensional system and calculate its order parameter across interaction strengths, magnetic fields, and temperatures, including the effect of a Zeeman field. A second finding cuts the other way: the standard Hubbard repulsion localizes electrons strongly, which enhances local antiferromagnetic order. The paper maps the competition between pairing and magnetism in a geometry simple enough to model cleanly.
arxiv-2510-19980:
Renzhao Liang and six co-authors challenge a basic assumption of time series forecasting: that more history is always better. Through careful experiments they find that trimming the past window can, oddly, improve accuracy. Models absorb redundant features, noise and irrelevant fluctuations, during training. Their remedy, AMRC, is built on information bottleneck thinking.

One component masks the training loss adaptively, spotlighting the most discriminative time segments to guide learning. A second enforces a consistency rule, stabilizing how inputs, labels, and predictions map to one another. Together they suppress redundant feature learning and significantly improve forecast accuracy across tests. The work offers forecasting practice both a caution and a concrete fix.
arxiv-2510-20180:
Hans Guente Dosch, Guy F. de Teramond, and Stanley J. Brodsky review holographic light-front quantum chromodynamics, a framework that maps strong interaction physics onto a holographic model. A short review, the article lays out the key components of the approach and gives special attention to how the QCD confinement scale enters through a graded superconformal algebra.

The overview surveys applications in hadron spectroscopy, form factors, and parton distributions of hadrons. It also covers the link between entanglement entropy and high-energy scattering that the framework suggests. The authors note that many further applications exist in the literature but fall outside this concise summary of their latest work on the approach.
arxiv-2510-20480:
Václav Pritzl and four co-authors propose a cooperative localization method for robot teams working where satellite navigation signals are unavailable. Carrying every sensor type on one robot inflates size, weight, and power demands, so their design spreads sensors across several robots instead. The cost is a harder fusion problem, since the data arrive asynchronously from independently moving platforms with different sensing strengths.

A factor-graph formulation fuses visual-inertial odometry, LiDAR-inertial odometry, and three-dimensional detections of other robots in a loosely coupled way, with a new interpolation factor for unsynchronized measurements. Degradation is judged from the LiDAR scan-matching Hessian and from distances between consecutive visual outputs. A theoretical analysis covers the cooperative problem under sensory degradation conditions.
arxiv-2510-20580:
Miroslav Bulíček, Josef Málek, and Endre Süli analyze a coupled model for dilute polymer fluids where heat flow matters alongside motion and chain stretch. The model joins temperature dependent flow equations with a kinetic law for chain shapes and a heat balance law, built to respect energy storage and entropy growth.

Smooth solutions that obey uniform bounds are shown to settle toward a global weak solution that holds for all time and large data. Heat obeys a weaker variational form that still captures the physics, while flow and chain laws hold in the standard weak sense. The result proves weak sequential stability, meaning close starting data cannot drive the model toward wildly different long term behavior.
arxiv-2510-20780:
Runzhe Zhan and five co-authors test whether large reasoning models make good judges of translation quality, and how to improve them when they fall short. Reasoning models think aloud before answering, a habit that helps hard tasks but had not been checked for scoring translations.

Careful tests show the judges need tailored scoring materials, tend to overthink easy cases, and use score scales in ways that inflate grades. Training them on synthetic human like thinking traces cuts thinking length by a huge factor while raising agreement with human scores across model sizes. One mid sized model gains markedly in correlation, showing that brief guided thinking beats long free thinking for this job.
arxiv-2510-21380:
Bence Borda and Jean-Claude Cuenin bound the distance between two probability patterns on curved, closed spaces, using a transport cost known as the Wasserstein metric. Such bounds help judge how evenly points can be spread over a shape, a question arising in sampling and in physics.

Their estimates read the distance off the Fourier transforms of the two patterns, the fingerprints that describe each pattern as a sum of waves. The method works on tori, spheres, compact Lie groups, and other uniform spaces, and covers the full range of transport exponents for the first time. Tools include a comparison with a dual energy norm, transform estimates, and wave inequalities on manifolds. As a payoff, they show that spherical designs sit as close as possible to the uniform pattern on the sphere.
arxiv-2510-21680:
Quentin Nicolas and Geoffrey K. Vallis explain superrotation, the state where a planet's atmosphere races around faster than the surface below, across very different worlds. Gas giants, slow spinners like Venus, and planets locked to face their star all show the phenomenon, yet whether one mechanism or several drives it has stayed unsettled.

A deliberately simple two-level model, small enough to analyze by hand, holds the key machinery for both regimes. On tidally locked planets, a standing wave pattern organizes the eddies but cannot spin up superrotation alone. Sloping temperature fronts and friction near the ground are essential partners, and some thick, weakly dragged atmospheres instead subrotate. On evenly heated slow rotators, an instability coupling Rossby and Kelvin waves always does the job, and the same instability unexpectedly helps in some locked cases too.
arxiv-2510-21980:
Starlika Bauskar and seven co-authors, Jade Jiao, Narayanan Kannan, Alexander Kimm, Justin M. Baker, Matthew J. Tyler, Andrea L. Bertozzi, and Anne M. Andrews, rethink how to represent aptamers, short molecules selected for their grip on a target. Most machine learning tools freeze each molecule into its single lowest-energy shape, discarding the crowd of shapes it actually flickers between.

Their embedding instead treats a molecule as a weighted ensemble of interaction graphs, with weights set by thermodynamics, so common shapes count more and rare ones less. Tested on selection experiment data, where lab biases can make weak binders look abundant, the representation still grouped molecules sensibly and explained which substructures drove binding strength. The authors suggest it can surface overlooked low-abundance candidates worth testing in the lab.
arxiv-2510-22280:
Masaru Nagisa and Yasuo Watatani prove a law of large numbers for a kind of averaging that refuses to be linear. Their objects are non-linear traces of Choquet type on finite factors. Those factors are non-commutative analogues of the Choquet integral. Integration there runs against a monotone measure that need not add up in the usual way.

In this setting, averages need not converge at all. The authors bound the whole set of accumulation points instead. They estimate the limit supremum and limit infimum of the averages. Test sequences are modeled on coin tosses and on Powers' binary shifts. Some shifts unexpectedly satisfy a stronger uniform norm law. The work steps toward a probability theory that is non-linear and non-commutative at once. Matrix algebras and type-two-one factors are the arena.
arxiv-2510-22480:
Seonghoon Yu and three co-authors improve knowledge distillation, where a small student model learns from a large teacher. Varied teacher views help the student, but using many teacher networks costs too much. Their method attaches several branches to one teacher, creating many views from a single source at low cost.

Two losses shape the views by their angles, spreading them evenly around the original teacher output while staying close to it. The mixed knowledge then trains the student, and theory shows the spread views lower the expected loss bound. Experiments beat an earlier augmentation method and the approach plugs into other distillation setups.
arxiv-2510-22680:
Self driving cars can be dangerously confident when they meet scenes unlike their training data. Shireen Kudukkil Manchingal, with six co-authors, equips a 2025 autonomous vehicle system with explicit uncertainty awareness, using a classifier that reports how unsure its road layout prediction is.

Their Random-Set Neural Network predicts belief over sets of classes rather than one forced label. That design lets the vehicle flag novel or ambiguous scenes clearly. Tested inside a real autonomous racing vehicle stack, the system beat standard and Bayesian networks on accuracy and uncertainty calibration across road conditions. It runs within a common robot operating pipeline for vehicle control.
arxiv-2510-22780:
How do AI agents actually do human work, step by step? Zora Zhiruo Wang leads a team with five co-authors. In 2025 they give the first direct comparison of human and agent workflows. Skills covered include data analysis, engineering, and writing. Design and computation are also covered.

The team built a toolkit to extract workflows. It turns computer use logs into clear, structured steps. Agents often match human workflow shape. Yet agents lean hard on programmatic methods. Humans lean more on user interface actions. That gap holds even for open, visual tasks like design. Results also hint where agents fit best in mixed teams.
arxiv-2510-22880:
Federated learning trains one model across many private clients. Data can be multimodal, incomplete, and uneven. Duong M Nguyen leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they handle missing data in that setting. Each client may see a different modality subset. Features can also be missing within a modality.

Missing patterns misalign local representations. That weakens global model aggregation. Their frame adds learnable client side embedding controls. Controls encode each client's missing pattern. They act as reconfiguration signals for the global model. Similar clients can share aggregated controls. That boosts robustness of the adaptation signal. Tests on several federated benchmarks support the design.
arxiv-2510-22980:
Bhavya Vasudeva, Puneesh Deora, Yize Zhao, Vatsal Sharan, and Christos Thrampoulidis study why a matrix-based optimizer called Muon can generalize well. Such spectrum-aware optimizers are now widely used in deep learning, but when they beat rivals is not well understood. The authors use imbalanced data, where some classes appear far more often, as a clean test bed.

They reduce Muon-like updates to a canonical form based on singular value splits of the gradient. In that setting they trace how the spectral design handles rare classes. The analysis offers a clearer reason to pick these optimizers for skewed real-world data.
arxiv-2510-23080:
Joon-Hwi Kim derives field equations for massless particles from ambitwistor spaces, which serve as phase spaces for those particles. First and second order equations emerge in this frame. Strikingly, the second order equations of Yang-Mills theory and of general relativity take one unified form built from a doubled Poisson bracket.

That doubled structure comes from a one-loop diagram encoded in operator products along the particle worldlines. Kim conjectures that the kinematic algebra behind the double copy may simply be the Poisson algebra of ambitwistor space. The work offers a fresh geometric root for a link that has reshaped modern field theory.
arxiv-2510-23180:
A Armeni and six co-authors use high-resolution spectra to study the outflow of the young star RU Lup, which is spinning down. Magnetic winds carry away angular momentum, a key step in how young stars evolve. The ESPRESSO spectrograph let them resolve forbidden emission lines and blueshifted absorption in sodium and calcium lines.

They found three discrete absorption components at low, medium, and high speeds. A new method separates vertical and toroidal velocities in the outflow. The detailed split constrains the physics of the wind that brakes the star, informing models of early stellar rotation.
arxiv-2510-23580:
Eric M. Schmid, Fernando Tohmé, and William Chin gather, in one account, the links between sheaf theory and the representation theory of quivers. A quiver is a directed graph, and its representations assign vector spaces and maps to its arrows. The authors work with quivers that have no directed cycles, over an arbitrary field.

Their dictionary connects Grothendieck topologies on the quiver's path category with special subcategories of its representations. Every topology turns out to be rigid, so each sheaf category is just a presheaf category on some subset of the vertices. With linear coefficients, each topology cuts out a wide subcategory, described both as a perpendicular category and as the representations of a smaller reduced quiver. The authors record exactly when such a subcategory is a Serre subcategory. They also note that all results are known — the value here is a concrete, self-contained treatment of the quiver case.
arxiv-2510-23780:
Omran Abbas and three co-authors propose making stacked intelligent surfaces nonlinear, so a wireless surface can mimic a small neural network. These surfaces, layered sheets that steer radio waves by shifting their phase, promise better links at low power. Modeled the usual way, though, a surface can only perform linear operations, which caps what it can do for a signal.

The authors argue the idea is feasible and sketch a unit cell with a step-like response as the building block. In a case study, surfaces sit at both ends of a MIMO link and are tuned using only statistical channel knowledge to cut the symbol error rate. The nonlinear version beat the linear one: it paints more complex patterns across the surface, which add diversity against noise while the receiver can still read them. The paper closes with further uses for nonlinear surfaces in future wireless systems.
arxiv-2510-23880:
Hanke Chen and two co-authors present TRELLISWorld, a training-free way to generate 3D scenes from text by reusing object generators. Text-to-3D tools usually make single objects, need special training for scenes, or cannot be viewed from all sides. The authors instead treat a scene as a set of overlapping 3D tiles, each produced by a text-to-3D diffusion model meant for objects.

The tiles are denoised separately and then blended with weighted averaging where they overlap, so seams fade and the scene stays coherent. No scene-level dataset or retraining is required, and minimal heuristics glue the process together. Because the method borrows object-level priors wholesale, it inherits the ability to generalize to new prompts. The team shows layouts, efficient generation, and easy editing. They offer the approach as a foundation for language-driven scene building in prototyping, virtual reality, and simulation.
arxiv-2510-24080:
Johannes Hagel studies a family of nonlinear oscillators, systems whose motion is governed by an equation with a power term. He asks which cases in this family can be solved exactly, using invariants that are polynomial in position and speed. The usual energy does not serve here because the system changes with time.

Hagel shows that an invariant that is quadratic in speed exists exactly when a related function obeys a simple linear equation of third order. That condition gives a three parameter family of cases. For the squared power case, the result matches the known trigonometric form. The paper also maps the geometry behind the cases and finds a clear analytic border for stability.
arxiv-2510-24180:
Arpita Kundu and five co-authors introduce V-SAT, a tool that finds and fixes subtitle errors in video automatically. Streaming and social video have raised demand for accurate, accessible subtitles, but current methods based on speech or text recognition often misalign timing, garble text, break formatting, or set poor reading speeds. Fixing these faults by hand is slow.

V-SAT combines large language models and vision language models into one framework that detects and corrects a wide range of quality issues at once. It adapts to the changing audio and visual context of a scene, rather than treating each fault alone. The goal is to cut post editing work while raising subtitle quality.
arxiv-2510-24680:
Zishuo Wang, Joel Loo, and David Hsu want sight based robot guides that can bounce back from faults. Guides trained by copy can fail in odd new places, with no clear cause. Their frame, InFeR, adds fault sense and fix steps with no fault demos at all.

First, retraining shapes the inner code of the guide so odd cases stand out. Next, a heat map of the view points to the spot that most drove the fault call. A simple fix rule then acts on that clue. In real world tests, guides with this frame found and fixed faults on long runs.
arxiv-2510-24780:
Yuki Inoue, Daiki Tanabe, M Afif Ismail, Vivek Kumar, Mario Juvenal S Onglao, and Ta-Chun Yu lay out the light design for CHRONOS, a cold scope for low rate gravity waves. The scope forms a three side loop that reads speed, which helps keep quantum noise low at low rates. Twin bars that twist serve as its test weights.

With matrix math and a known light code, they show the loop modes stay stable and match well on entry. The tuned setup hits its goal sense level at one wave per second, set by quantum noise. Low rate noise is shaped most by one side loop's tune. A best read angle near that rate is also given.
arxiv-2510-24980:
Reza Saadati Fard leads a team with seven co-authors who sort bed sore grades with a chat model that checks its own work. Such sores run from stage one to four, and the right grade drives care. Fine sight gaps between stages make hand grades shift from staff to staff, while past nets gave scores with no clear grounds.

Their model, FT-ARM, was tuned from a large joint sight and text model. It rethinks its call in rounds, in the style of a doctor who rechecks a case. Sight traits and stored care facts both feed each round. On a public sore shot set, it hit a high right rate and beat past nets.
arxiv-2510-25180:
Utsab Saha, Jeffrey D'Andria, and Tyler Menezes ask how open source work on a student's record lines up with what bosses want in new hires. Schools add such work to classes more and more, in part as AI tools raise the bar for grads. Yet how bosses read that work was not well known.

The team spoke with hiring leads in the United States and built a pact list with each: traits they want, and how open work can show each trait. Leads vowed to grant talks to some grads who met the list. A poll of more than six hundred grads then tested if such know how lifts their drive to do open work.
arxiv-2510-25480:
Florian A Holzl, Daniel Rueckert, and Georgios Kaissis present Gradient-Weight Matching. Their 2025 paper seeks a train-time proxy for generalization. Robust validation metrics are needed in deep learning. They detect overfitting and poor generalization during training. Training changes also need monitoring for model quality. Supervised classification is their certain setting here.

Gradient-Weight Matching quantifies coherence between gradients and weights. Per-sample gradients are compared with current model weights. Effective learning corresponds to coherent matching, they show. Misalignment indicates deteriorating generalization in their tests. The metric is quickly computable during training runs. It reflects sample-certain contributions to learning changes. Dataset-wide learning patterns are also captured simultaneously. Extensive tests show it predicts optimal early stopping. Principled model comparisons are enabled by the metric. Influential training samples can be identified with it. No separate validation set is needed for study. That offers a useful tool for training monitoring.
arxiv-2510-25580:
Leticia Barchini, Nicolas Arancibia Robert, and Paul Mezo wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on a special family of symmetry groups. The groups are the real forms of G2, an exceptional group with a distinctive structure. Their topic is micro-packets, first proposed by Adams, Barbasch, and Vogan while studying Arthur's conjectures.

Each packet gathers a small number of basic representations, meaning symmetry descriptions that cannot be split further. Scholars build these groupings by studying characteristic cycles, which are geometric records tied to each representation. Barchini and her coauthors use moves from the Weyl group, a related symmetry group, on those cycles. By tracking those moves, they work out every packet for the G2 case. The full list gives other mathematicians a concrete reference for testing broader ideas about real groups.
arxiv-2510-25680:
Takato Tokuno investigates the rapid spin of Kepler-56. His 2025 astronomy paper studies a planet-hosting red giant. Asteroseismic analysis suggests a unique spin structure there. Core and envelope spin axes are misaligned. The envelope rotates about ten times faster than typical. Typical red giants rotate much more slowly. He asks what supplied that angular momentum.

Simplified calculations evolve angular momentum over time. Tidal interactions with known close-in planets are estimated. Kepler-56 b and c are those known planets. Unless tidal efficiency is extremely high, they fall short. Their supply cannot accelerate the star enough. Engulfment of a hot Jupiter could supply sufficient momentum. The engulfed planet mass is constrained by calculations. Orbital period between one and six days fits. Alternatively, the star may already spin rapidly before. Engulfment might still explain that early spin.
arxiv-2510-25980:
Brandon Massett and Walter Shmayda check whether a vacuum gauge still reads correctly after an accidental blast of high pressure. The device is the MKS 390 Micro-Ion Gauge, used to measure very low pressures. In some uses a gauge may face high pressure on purpose or by accident, which raises concern about later accuracy and about leaks.

Massett and Shmayda compare two gauges side by side, one exposed to ten thousand Torr and one kept below one thousand Torr. Torr is a unit of pressure tied to a millimeter of mercury. Differences between the readings stayed within the maker's stated uncertainty, which shows negligible harm from the exposure, and the exposed gauge kept its leak integrity.
arxiv-2510-26080:
Fan Yang, Renkai Ma, Yaxin Hu, Michael Rodgers, and Lingyao Li ask who should bear responsibility when a child robot companion is shut down. Social robots such as Moxie are built to form strong emotional bonds with children, so an abrupt end of service can cause real distress. The authors use the Moxie shutdown as a case study and survey seventy two United States participants in a qualitative study.

Yang and the team find that responsibility is seen as shared across the company, parents, developers, and government, though views split by political leaning and parental status. Opinions on whether service should continue are polarized, with supporters proposing technical, financial, or public paths and opponents citing business limits and risks of unhealthy dependence.
arxiv-2510-26480:
Sivajeet Chand, with four co-authors, tests whether open-source language models can clean up code on their own. Their task is the extract method refactoring, which moves a block of code into its own named method to make programs easier to read. Doing it by hand is slow, so automation would help, but the step needs care to keep code working.

Chand and the team compare five models, from three to eight billion parameters, on Python code. A loop of criticism and revision beat single-shot prompting on both test pass rates and quality. The best models passed most tests and cut method length from about twelve lines to about six. In a developer survey, over seventy percent accepted the machine-made changes, though the authors note that simple code metrics often clash with human judgement.
arxiv-2510-27080:
Arnabh Borah, Md Tanvirul Alam, and Nidhi Rastogi adapt large language models to fast-moving cybersecurity threats. Security teams increasingly use such models to detect threats, yet opaque reasoning limits trust and models lag behind new vulnerabilities. Retrieval-augmented generation, meaning fetching outside documents before answering, can supply fresh context, but its value for security work was little tested.

The team builds a retrieval framework that contextualizes security data for a Llama model and compares plain retrieval with an optimized hybrid approach. Metrics cover knowledge retention and temporal reasoning about incidents over time. Hybrid retrieval strengthens adaptability and reliability for security tasks in their tests. The work points toward assistants that keep pace with emerging attacks instead of freezing at training time.
arxiv-2510-27180:
Hao Jiao constrains how strongly axions could couple to light using the global twenty-one centimeter signal from the early universe. Axions are hypothetical light particles proposed for dark matter. When an oscillating axion field couples to electromagnetism, parametric resonance can excite a radiation field, a mechanism earlier work used to seed primordial magnetic fields and help form direct-collapse black holes.

Jiao tests that scenario against global twenty-one centimeter observations, which record ancient hydrogen absorption. The analysis finds viable parameter regions that satisfy observational limits while still meeting the physical needs of both the magnetic field and black hole formation stories. The result narrows where axion-photon coupling could hide and supports using cosmic dawn signals to probe new physics.
arxiv-2510-27280:
Zirui Zhu leads six co-authors in FOCUS, a keyframe picker that lets video models answer questions about hour-long footage within a tight token budget. Multimodal models turn frames into tokens, so long videos explode the budget. Pipelines either subsample uniformly or pre-filter with retrieval scoring, which can miss the most informative moments before selection even starts.

FOCUS treats short clips as bandit arms in a pure-exploration problem, using empirical means and a Bernstein confidence radius to find valuable regions while still exploring uncertain ones. A two-stage procedure first locates high-value regions, then picks top frames inside each. On two long-video benchmarks it improves accuracy substantially while processing under two percent of frames, with especially strong gains on videos over twenty minutes.
arxiv-2510-27380:
Johannes Schrotshamer, Bernd Kolar, and Markus Schöberl study a prized trait of control systems in this 2025 paper. The trait is flatness: a system is flat if all its states can be read off from a few chosen outputs. Flat systems are far easier to steer and to straighten out. The trio work with discrete-time systems, ones that step from tick to tick.

They treat two special kinds, forward-flat and backward-flat systems, within one general frame. Rank tests on parts of a key matrix tell which kind a system is. For systems with two inputs and a flat output of a common type, they derive a simple add-on. The add-on extends the system step by step until it can be linearized, rewritten in exact straight-line form.
arxiv-2510-27680:
Danyal Maqbool leads a team with thirteen co-authors who tackle auto-written reports for PET scans in 2025. PET, which maps tracer glow in the body, is vital in cancer care. Writing reports from whole-body 3D scans is hard: volumes are large, findings vary widely, and labeled data are scarce.

The team built PETARSeg-11K, the first large public set that pairs more than eleven thousand lesion notes with 3D lesion outlines. Their model, PETAR-4B, reads PET, CT, and lesion masks jointly, with a focal prompt that zooms on tiny lesions. Scores on auto gauges show strong gains over prior tools. Grounded reports could cut the time doctors spend drafting scan notes.
arxiv-2511-00180:
Nicky Pochinkov, Yulia Volkova, and Anna Vasileva ask what language model activations encode about future text, beyond the next token. Interpretability often tests single concepts or tokens, but long-horizon tasks need paragraph and document scale plans. Their framework of residual stream decoders probes activations for such longer plans, comparing several decoding methods.

Information equivalent to more than five tokens of future context can be decoded from activations in small models. Interpretability readers get groundwork for monitoring whether models form longer-term plans internally. Knowing a model encodes its future direction could support oversight of agents working over long horizons.
arxiv-2511-00380:
Xianghong Kong and six co-authors lay out a systematic way to build hyperbolic lattices with an added Z2 gauge structure inside the nearest-neighbor tight-binding framework. Hyperbolic lattices tile space with a curved geometry impossible in flat crystals, and gauge extensions enrich their symmetry in ways that can host exotic phases. The triangle group with parameters two, eight, eight serves as their worked example.

By computing a cohomology group, they classify all distinct symmetry extensions, each tied to a flux pattern, and build tight-binding models to verify each class. The extended lattices live on high-genus surfaces, as a classic formula predicts. Band calculations find fully flat dispersions along chosen directions and sharp spectral features linked to discrete energies, opening a route to symmetry fractionalization studies.
arxiv-2511-00480:
Weihao Bo, Yanpeng Sun, Yu Wang, Xinyu Zhang, and Zechao Li introduce FedMGP, a way to personalize federated learning for vision-language models. In federated prompt learning, each client keeps its data local and tunes small prompt vectors instead. One prompt set per client is too blunt, so FedMGP gives each client several paired text and visual prompt groups, each free to specialize.

A diversity loss pushes the groups toward distinct, complementary aspects of meaning. During communication rounds, clients compare their groups with the global prompts and sample which to share, guided by similarity, so shared knowledge flows while rare local patterns still surface. The total prompt budget stays fixed, giving the lowest communication cost among rivals, and experiments show consistent wins in personalization and domain generalization.
arxiv-2511-00680:
Yuntian Jiang, Chuwen Zhang, Bo Jiang, and Yinyu Ye attack a standing trade-off in second-order optimization for convex problems. Newton's method converges quadratically fast near a solution but can diverge from far away. Accelerated methods guarantee global progress yet crawl locally. The question is how much global acceleration is possible before the fast local finish is lost.

Their accelerated trust-region method uses Lagrange multiplier information, already present in the primal-dual structure, to detect when the search enters a local region. It achieves strong global complexity while keeping quadratic local convergence. Pushing further, an extragradient variant reaches still better global complexity but loses the quadratic finish, revealing a phase-transition-like boundary. Numerical experiments track the theory, mapping exactly where the trade-off turns.
arxiv-2511-00880:
Joonyoung Lim and Younghwan Yoo propose KFCPO, an algorithm for safe reinforcement learning, where an agent must earn reward while respecting cost limits. Second order methods can train such agents steadily, but the standard versions are slow, and clashes between reward and safety goals can destabilize learning.

KFCPO uses a Kronecker factored approximation to make natural gradient updates cheap and closed form, layer by layer. A margin aware rule blends the reward and cost gradients according to how close the agent sits to a safety boundary, avoiding harsh fixed thresholds. A rollback step keeps updates inside a trust region. On Safety Gymnasium tasks, returns rose ten to fifty percent over the best baseline that stayed within the safety limits.
arxiv-2511-00980:
Yiming Chen, Neil Fan, Rui Xiong, and Ming Yao build a new geometric home for bumpless pipe dreams, diagram objects used to compute Schubert polynomials in combinatorics. Starting from fragments of these diagrams, they define clan polynomials as the generating functions that collect the fragments' weights.

The payoff is geometric. Clan polynomials turn out to arise naturally in the equivariant geometry of certain group orbits on the flag variety. That flag variety is the space of nested subspaces. The orbits there are indexed by combinatorial objects called clans. The coefficients in the equivariant Schubert expansion of the orbit closures' fundamental classes are exactly these clan polynomials. That identity resolves an open problem posed by Wyser and Yong.
arxiv-2511-01380:
Wessel Poelman, Thomas Bauwens, and Miryam de Lhoneux warn that studies linking a language's morphology to how well language models handle it are riddled with confounds. Whether word structure matters for tokenization and model use has been argued both ways in past work, and they blame messy test setups for the contradiction.

They catalog the confounding factors. Then they reassess three claims about why agglutinative languages show higher perplexities than fusional ones. The three cover tokenization alignment, tokenization cost, and data set size. Confounds turn up in each conclusion. Instead they introduce token bigram metrics, which predict causal language modeling difficulty on their own and track morphological complexity as a gradient, with no expert labels needed. The paper ends with rules for answering the morphology question reliably.
arxiv-2511-01580:
Yevgeniya Korotinsky and Lior Arazi model the microscopic dose in Alpha DaRT, a cancer treatment that seeds tumors with sources diffusing alpha-particle emitters. Because alpha particles deposit their energy over tiny distances, predicting cell survival and tumor control requires tracking doses nucleus by nucleus, not averages over the tumor.

Part I of their study focuses on a detail with outsized effects: cell nuclei come in a broad range of sizes. Their model combines analytic hit statistics for alpha particles with Monte Carlo energy-deposition calculations, sampling nucleus radii from test distributions and from measured ones. Widening the size spread bends survival curves away from the simple exponential form. It also shrinks the survival gap between sensitive and resistant cells. Tumor control, meanwhile, turns out to hinge on the smallest nuclei included.
arxiv-2511-01680:
Jacob Carlson builds an automated pipeline for discovering findings in unstructured data, such as the free-text answers in surveys of economic beliefs. Traders of interpretation are the bottleneck: a researcher reading text chooses what to look for, which invites data snooping and missed angles.

The framework first uses AI interpretability methods to convert raw text into high-dimensional measurements of interpretable concepts. It then states concept-level hypotheses, tests them with algorithms backed by new high-dimensional multiple-testing results, and writes up the surviving discoveries in plain language, again automatically. With few researcher degrees of freedom, the method supports fast sensitivity checks and replication. Revisiting recent economics studies, Carlson's pipeline reproduced known discoveries, added nuance to others, and surfaced entirely new ones.
arxiv-2511-01980:
L. A. Harland-Lang gives the first complete treatment of incoherent photon-initiated production when heavy ions pass each other without colliding. In these collisions the ions' intense electric and magnetic fields act as photon beams. Production can be coherent, from the whole nucleus. Or it can be incoherent, from its parts. The paper covers dilepton and diphoton final states.

For dielectrons, the results match the ATLAS data very well. For diphotons, the incoherent part proves too small. It cannot explain the broad background seen under the coherent light-by-light scattering signal. A new quark emission topology might have dominated. It turns out suppressed by kinematics. Revisiting the QCD channel does not close the gap either. The origin of the enhanced diphoton background, notably larger than in the dilepton case, remains unexplained.
arxiv-2511-02080:
Daniel Glasscock, Andreas Koutsogiannis, Anh Le, Joel Moreira, Florian Richter, and Donald Robertson prove a structure theorem in topological dynamics, the study of systems that evolve without losing or gaining points. For a minimal system, they look at return-time sets: the times at which an orbit following polynomial patterns comes back near its start. The question is how much of that structure is captured by a simpler, algebraic shadow of the system.

Their theorem says return-time sets agree, apart from a thin exceptional set, with those of the system's maximal infinite-step pronilfactor. Applications include three new multiple recurrence results about linear and polynomial patterns along dynamically defined sets. The theorem also shows that two conjectures from different research groups, one by Glasner and collaborators and one by Leibman, are actually equivalent.
arxiv-2511-02280:
Fangxun Shu and eight co-authors train multimodal language models to think the right amount: neither coasting on hard problems nor overthinking easy ones. Outcome-only rewards can crown a correct answer reached by sloppy reasoning, and a single fixed thinking strategy wastes effort. Their reinforcement learning framework, SAIL-RL, grades the model with two rewards instead of one.

A thinking reward scores the reasoning itself for factual grounding, logical coherence, and consistency with the answer. A judging reward decides, case by case, whether deep reasoning is warranted or a direct answer is better. Applied to the SAIL-VL2 model family at two sizes, the training lifted reasoning and multimodal understanding on benchmarks, and reached performance competitive with a leading commercial closed model. It also substantially reduced hallucinations, according to the authors.
arxiv-2511-02680:
Figueras, Persson, and Viitasaari return to filtering on curved spaces in a companion 2025 paper. Here they ask a basic question: if the thing being watched stays still, does their extended Kalman filter settle on the right answer? The readings come with errors that live on a Stiefel manifold, a space of frames with perpendicular axes.

The authors prove that the filter does converge in that constant case. They then run simulations on a few chosen manifolds and measure how fast the estimates close in on the truth. The result gives users a firm footing: when the target is fixed and only the sensor noise moves, the method can be trusted to clean the signal over time.
arxiv-2511-02780:
Smart contracts hold real money, and a flaw can mean huge losses. Auditors prove a reported flaw is real by writing a small working exploit, which takes time under tight deadlines. Vivi Andersson, Sofia Bobadilla, Harald Hobbelhagen, and Martin Monperrus built PoCo to write those proofs on its own, described in a 2025 paper.

PoCo reads an auditor's plain-language report of a flaw, then works in a reason-act-observe loop with code tools. It outputs ready-to-run exploits in the Foundry testing format, fit for audit reports. On twenty-three real-world flaw reports, PoCo beat zero-shot and fixed workflow baselines, producing well-formed and logically correct proofs. The team argues such agents can cut audit effort without lowering quality.
arxiv-2511-03280:
Rob Romijnders and co-authors tackle the task of lining up many noisy copies of one signal that have each shifted in pose. That alignment task shows up in molecule imaging, vision, and wireless systems. Their probabilistic method treats the relative poses as extra unknowns to be averaged away, which strips out global symmetries that slow older solvers.

Splitting the job across copies avoids the steep cost growth of one central solver. Two algorithms built on the idea reach lower rebuild error across the test settings reported. The authors show gains for wireless setups with many senders and receivers as a leading use. Faster, truer alignment can lift performance wherever shifted repeats must be merged into one clean signal.
arxiv-2511-03580:
Jaden Thomas and colleagues prove that even the weakest mass-lowering flaw traps a vibrational mode in one- and two-dimensional crystal lattices. Their model is a grid of equal masses joined by nearest-neighbor springs, a clean stand-in for a monatomic crystal. Earlier results handled specific flaws, such as lightening a single mass, by explicit solution.

A simple variational argument now covers any localized change that cuts net mass. The trapped mode vibrates in place instead of spreading as a wave. Analogous results were known for light and electron equations, and phonons now join that list. Localized modes matter because they concentrate energy and can seed failure or, if harnessed, useful resonant behavior.
arxiv-2511-03680:
Marie Albenque, Laurent Menard, and Nicolas Tokka build a new counting bijection for two-colored planar maps with control over vertex degrees. Planar maps are networks drawn without crossings, and bijections turn counting them into counting trees, which is far easier. Their method grows from the blossoming-tree idea with a fresh family of arrow orientations on the maps.

That extension links an older Schaeffer-style bijection to a broader general scheme and covers several new map families at once. As a payoff, quartic maps carrying an Ising model gain a tidy rational parametrization with positive whole coefficients. Such formulas are the key that unlocks random sampling and limit studies of those maps.
arxiv-2511-03780:
Haider Alhazmi, Doojin Kim, Kyoungchul Kong, and Aishah Sumayli build a general framework for reading electron recoil signals caused by fast-moving dark matter. Such boosted particles could come from dark matter annihilation, decay, or acceleration by cosmic rays, and they leave signatures unlike slow, heavy candidates.

The framework handles relativistic motion and atomic effects through ionization form factors, giving cross-section predictions at low and high recoil energies. At high energies, atomic effects fade and a free-electron treatment becomes valid in stated regions. Low-threshold detectors and large neutrino observatories probe different parts of the range together. The result is a model-independent base for interpreting current and future searches.
arxiv-2511-04080:
Xiaolu Chen, Jie Bao, Haojie Wu, Zhen Chen, and Yong Liao propose Caption Injection, a method for improving how content ranks inside generative search engines. Such engines answer from many sources at once, shifting attention from ranked lists to how visible content feels inside a generated response, and earlier optimization work handled text only.

Their approach extracts captions from images and injects them into textual content, folding visual meaning into the text a system retrieves. That multimodal step aims to raise subjective visibility in generated answers. The work opens generative search optimization beyond words alone, reflecting how retrieval systems now blend text, images, audio, and video in one response.
arxiv-2511-04380:
Felipe Hernández wrote these lecture notes on quantum diffusion and random matrix theory. They grew out of joint work with Adam Black and Reuben Drogin. The lectures were given at a summer school on partial differential equations and probability at Sorbonne Université in June 2025.

The notes explain a new approach to the diffusive limit of the random Schrödinger equation. Ideas from random matrix theory supply the tools for that limit. Hernández presents the core argument in a self-contained and simplified form for students. Readers get a guided entry into how randomness spreads quantum waves over long times.
arxiv-2511-04480:
Huiyang Ma and two colleagues frame how to read critical field data in layered superconductors. Interest grew with findings in bilayer and multilayer graphene, some with added spin-orbit coupling. These materials can resist strong in-plane fields and even gain superconductivity from them.

The team builds its framework on a pairing model that stays solvable on paper. That model captures the normal-state behavior of the layered systems first. It then yields the relation for the upper critical in-plane field. A tractable yardstick like this helps experimental groups judge whether new graphene results are truly unconventional or fit known physics.
arxiv-2511-04580:
Gohar T. Khokhar leads five authors modeling and controlling solid-fuel ramjets. These compact engines suit long-range, high-speed flight, but thrust is hard to regulate. Fuel burn, combustion, and airflow couple strongly, and control authority is limited.

A fluid dynamics model with heat addition maps thrust response and the flight envelope. It also locates inlet unstart, where airflow breaks down at the intake. An adaptive controller, updated online by a retrospective cost method, then regulates thrust. Joining simulation with learning-based control aims at engines that hold thrust steady through changing flight conditions.
arxiv-2511-04880:
Yu Bai leads twelve authors with DMA, an online framework aligning retrieval systems with human feedback. Retrieval-augmented generation often freezes its ranking while user intent drifts. DMA keeps learning from feedback at three levels of detail.

Document, list, and response signals feed one coherent training pipeline. Supervised steps train pointwise and listwise rankers from the finer signals. Response-level preferences then drive policy optimization on top. Finally, distillation squeezes the result into a light scorer for fast serving. Memory here means the model's full visible context, and the dual-track evaluation checks alignment over time.
arxiv-2511-05080:
P. Bilha Githinji and co-authors compare how two language models simplify biomedical text for lay readers, set against human work. Public need for clear health facts is high, but models must gain ease of reading without losing meaning.

One model, Mistral, used a mild word-simplifying style that lifted ease of reading in a steady way. The other, QWen, used a distinct plan shaped by its reasoning tune. Their contrast shows that two strong models can trade accuracy for clarity in unlike ways, a choice that matters for safe health writing.
arxiv-2511-05280:
Xu'an Dou and co-authors study a simple Markov process that diffuses in one direction while it is carried sideways by a transport field. They ask how fast such a process mixes, even when the sideways field is rough or weak in spots.

Their bounds need only mild terms on that field, far from the smooth hypoelliptic case that past theory leans on. Quantitative rates tell how fast the process forgets its start. The result helps read models in fluids and plasmas where spread and drift act at right angles and the drift is far from tidy.
arxiv-2511-05580:
Bryce-Allen Bagley and Navin Khoshnan set out a math framework for psychodynamics, the study of how mental processes interact. Psychology leans on verbal theories more than most medical fields, partly because human cognition is so complex. A shared formal language, they argue, would let experts from many fields study the same phenomena with precision.

They build that language from process theory, a diagram-based framework, and spell out its key properties. Diagrams are then linked to core ideas in the analysis of thought. The authors discuss uses in psychotherapy, neurotechnology, and AI safety. Those uses include how AI agents represent people in talks and how human-like AI systems might be built.
arxiv-2511-05980:
Etienne Le Naour and co-authors run the first large study of foundation models built to fill gaps in time series. Filling missing values usually means retraining per data set. Two recent models index their input by time itself, which may let one model serve many series with no retraining, a zero-shot approach.

The team ran broad tests on thirty-three outside data sets, about one point three million imputation windows in all. They also checked whether extra side variables, fed in at run time, sharpen accuracy without fine-tuning. Their verdict: time-indexed foundation models are a strong, practical step toward general zero-shot imputation. The experiments map where the approach already works for real-world series and where covariates help.
arxiv-2511-06180:
Wenhui Ren and Liwei Zhang develop an algorithm for minimax quadratic programming problems with coupled inequality constraints. In a minimax problem, one side chooses variables to shrink a quadratic cost while the other side pushes it up. Constraints that link the two sides make such problems awkward for standard solvers.

Using a duality theorem, their dual method extends the classic dual active set approach into the minimax setting. The inequality problem becomes a chain of equality-constrained subproblems, and the authors prove the steps never repeat, so the method ends after finitely many rounds. Cholesky factorization and Givens rotations keep the computation stable, and tests on random problems confirm accuracy.
arxiv-2511-06380:
Chen He and colleagues diagnose a failure mode in how large language models reflect on their own reasoning. When tasks need deep domain knowledge rather than pure math, models often repeat earlier steps instead of thinking afresh, a habit the authors call echo reflection. Two defects drive it: unchecked flow of early thoughts and shallow use of internal knowledge.

Their reinforcement learning method, AEPO, attacks both defects directly. A filtration component measures information flow and blocks poor early reasoning from warping the final answer. An adaptive entropy component balances trying new paths against exploiting good ones at each stage. Across varied benchmarks, AEPO beat mainstream reinforcement learning baselines.
arxiv-2511-06480:
Alice Requier, Andrea Plati, Emmanuelle Rio, and Anniina Salonen shake foams and watch their bubbles merge far more than expected. Outside driving can give soft materials unusual behaviors. Here, mechanical vibration of nearly flat, quasi-two-dimensional foams triggered heavy coalescence, where neighboring bubbles pop into one another instead of keeping their walls.

A yield-stress continuous phase, the liquid that must be pushed past a threshold to flow, strengthened the effect further. Vibration strength and liquid fraction tune the contest between slow coarsening and outright merging, producing structural patterns rarely seen in still foams. A statistical model tracks the falling bubble count over time and matches the observations quantitatively.
arxiv-2511-06680:
Keunhyeung Park, Seunguk Yu, and Youngbin Kim steer language models toward genuine Korean local dialect instead of lightly edited standard speech. Translating into dialect is hard because models drift back to the standard form, and word-overlap metrics reward that copying while punishing real dialect. Evaluation itself was part of the problem.

Their DIA-REFINE framework loops translation, verification by dialect classifiers, and feedback until the output sounds faithful. Two new scores measure the linguistic shift achieved and the share of output truly in dialect, exposing fake successes where overlap looks high but dialect is absent. Across Korean dialects the loop improved fidelity over zero-shot and example-guided baselines, with responsiveness varying by model.
arxiv-2511-06880:
Giacomo Graziani presents a self-contained guide to one of algebraic geometry's cornerstone results, the Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch theorem, following Grothendieck's proof. The theorem connects algebraic data from sheaf cohomology with geometric data from intersection theory. Graziani starts from the classic versions for curves and surfaces before building the modern machinery needed for the general statement.

Two tools carry the proof: the Grothendieck group, which sorts sheaves so the Euler characteristic becomes natural, and the Chow ring, which organizes cycles for intersection theory. The Chern character and Todd class bridge these two worlds, and combining them yields the full Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch formula. Graziani closes by showing the general formula reproduces the familiar classic theorems for curves and surfaces, making the survey usable as an introduction.
arxiv-2511-07280:
Kevin Zielnicki and five co-authors measure what personalized recommendations are worth, using Netflix viewing data. Because recommendations are targeted, separating the value of the targeting from the value of the content itself is tricky. The team builds a discrete choice model with recommendation-induced utility, low-rank viewer heterogeneity, and flexible state dependence. It identifies its parts from idiosyncratic variation that the ranking algorithm itself introduces, cross-checked with model-free diversion ratios.

What-if tests put numbers on the stakes. Replacing the current system with matrix factorization would cut engagement by about four percent, and a popularity-based algorithm by about twelve percent, while also narrowing what people watch. Most of the gain comes from good targeting rather than mere exposure, and mid-popularity titles benefit most, not blockbusters or the deepest niches.
arxiv-2511-07380:
Pingjie Wang and seven co-authors mine plain general-domain data to teach language models specialized domains where training data is scarce. General chain-of-thought collections share question-answer formats and reasoning patterns with medical, financial, legal, and psychological tasks, and the team's initial tests showed such data helps adaptation even unselected. Their NTK-Selector method systematically picks the most beneficial general samples, guided by neural tangent kernel alignment of training dynamics.

Because exact neural tangent kernels are impractical for large pre-trained models, they introduce a Jacobian-free approximation and verify its stability during fine-tuning. Across the four domains, selected general data beat domain-only fine-tuning and other selection baselines: gains reached 8.7 points on Llama3-8B-Instruct and 5.1 on Qwen3-8B, against under one point from domain data alone. The result reframes domain adaptation as partly a data mining problem.
arxiv-2511-07480:
Shuyuan Liu and colleagues defend large language models against jailbreak prompts. Carefully crafted inputs can trick a model into unsafe or uncontrolled replies. Guards that are too strict hurt normal use, while weak guards leave holes.

Their framework, KG-DF, checks inputs against a knowledge graph without opening the model itself. Structured facts and semantic links help judge whether a request is benign or an attack in disguise. Because the defense sits outside the model, it can protect different systems the same way. Tests aim to keep helpful answers flowing while blocking manipulation. Safer deployment is the practical goal.
arxiv-2511-07680:
Sajad Salami bounds the arithmetic complexity of a family of algebraic curves. For curves shaped by a simple power equation, their Jacobian varieties carry a Mordell-Weil group whose rank counts independent rational points. Whether ranks stay bounded as the curve varies within the family was open.

Assuming a strong form of Lang conjecture on rational points, Salami proves uniform rank bounds across the family. The proof builds a parameter space for curves with chosen point patterns, extending Yamagishi geometric approach. Uniform bounds are prized in number theory because they promise whole families behave tamely, not just single examples checked one by one.
arxiv-2511-08080:
Ziyu Fan and co-authors propose HSPAG, a data efficient method for generating and editing molecules under property limits. Drug discovery needs molecules that meet several property goals at once, but structure property links are tangled and annotations are sparse. Note the arXiv title differs from the older evidence title for this record.

HSPAG aligns molecule structure and properties at atom, substructure, and whole molecule levels, treating SMILES strings and properties as paired views. Scaffold clustering picks representative training samples, while a variational model finds hard cases, cutting data needs. Masking based on property relevance and varied perturbations improve generation, and two real cases test editing.
arxiv-2511-08180:
Guido Masarotto presents a full algorithm for fitting generative models whose likelihoods and moments cannot be computed directly. Many realistic models can only be simulated, leaving standard inference tools unusable. His method needs only limited prior information about the parameters, aiming at a general solution rather than a model specific trick.

A global search first locates the promising region of parameter space. A local search then imitates a trust region form of Fisher scoring to produce a quasi likelihood estimate. Comparisons with rival methods show strong performance across cases. An R package on CRAN implements the algorithm for direct use by practitioners.
arxiv-2511-08380:
Bao-Jun Cai, Bao-An Li, and Yu-Gang Ma revisit whether a sharp first order phase transition can occur inside cold neutron stars, the densest visible matter in the universe. A hadron to quark transition would appear as a flat plateau in the equation of state, pressure against energy density. Many numerical studies accept such models because their mass radius curves look reasonable against observations.

The authors argue the plateau is intrinsically incompatible with regularity conditions required by the Tolman Oppenheimer Volkoff equations that govern star structure. Seemingly fine numerical integrations can hide that inconsistency.
