Zheng Fang and six co authors work on teaching language models to use tools well. Tool learning lets a model pick and combine external tools for complex real world tasks. With tools, a model goes beyond pure language and can act in specialized ways. The challenge is to make that skill generalize to new tools and tasks.

Their system is called MetaToolAgent, built on meta learning. Meta learning trains a model to adapt fast to fresh problems. Applied to tools, it should let a model learn new tools from few examples. Generalizable tool use is a key step toward agents that work in open settings. The work speaks to the fast growing agent research community.
arxiv-2601-13180:
Shreesha Rao D. S and co-authors take rare lab marks of a special glass fibre. The fibre is made of ZBLAN glass with a small oval core. It keeps the lean of light waves fixed as they pass. Such fibres draw work for light work in the mid infrared band.

Two marks are key to model fast pulse flow in them. One is group birefringence, the split in speed by wave lean. The other is group velocity dispersion, how pulse speed shifts with hue. Lab data for both marks were scarce. The team fills that gap. Their marks help staff who build supercontinuum sources and fast fibre lasers in that band plan with real numbers, not guesses.
arxiv-2601-13380:
Chaoxin Wang and co-authors give hands on guides to semi supervised object detection. The task trains a detector with few marked pics and many unmarked ones. That mix fits fields where marks cost a lot, such as scans or field pics.

Past work in the area grew fast, with many tricks that are hard to sort. The team shares what works in real use and where gains are thin. They weigh how pseudo marks for the unmarked set are made and kept clean. For vision teams with thin mark funds, sound guides can save weeks of blind tests. The piece is a field note set, not a new model claim.
arxiv-2601-13480:
Matthias Y. He and Eric B. Ford build one model to match two marks in the Kepler planet census. Kepler showed that planet sizes split in two crowds. A gap, called the radius valley, parts super Earths from sub Neptunes. Kepler also showed that worlds in one system tend to match in size, a peas in a pod mark.

A good growth model must yield both marks at once. Their model is a hybrid. It joins clumped multi planet forms with orbits set by a stability bound based on angular momentum deficit. By match of both marks, the model ties size growth to orbit calm in one tale.
arxiv-2601-13580:
Ahmad Al-Zuraiqi moves trained transformer layers as organs from one model to a next. His frame is called Neural Organ Transplantation. In stock fine tune, taught weights are tied tight to one model and its train data. They cannot be reused with ease in a next model.

His swap cuts a run of layers from a taught model as a donor organ. That run is taught on its own on field data. It is saved as a lone checkpoint file. It can then be set in a fit host model, with no need for the first train data. For teams that adapt models per field, reusable layer organs cut cost and time.
arxiv-2601-13780:
Antoine Siraudin and Christopher Morris build a faster way to generate new graphs with AI in 2026. Graph diffusion models make state-of-the-art graphs, from molecules to social nets. Their cost grows with the square of the node count. Much of that cost is spent modeling edges that are not there, in sparse graphs.

The pair compress graphs into a low-dimensional latent space first. Diffusion then runs in that small space, not on the full graph. Laplacian autoencoders do the compression and rebuild steps. Latent diffusion has cut costs in images, and may do the same for graphs.
arxiv-2601-13980:
Rishin Madan and co-authors study the geometry of flux surfaces with quasi-poloidal symmetry in 2026. Such magnetic fields aim to confine plasma in fusion devices. Quasi-poloidal fields bring prized traits: no radial drift of guiding centres, and zero Pfirsch-Schlüter current. They also damp poloidal flows less, which can cut anomalous transport.

Lower transport means heat stays in the plasma longer. Possible stability benefits add to the draw of this symmetry. The team examines the shape of the flux surfaces that carry it. Sound geometry is a base step toward stellarators with this design.
arxiv-2601-14180:
Yichao Liu, Zongru Shao, Yueyang Teng, and Junwen Guo denoise low-dose CT scans without paired clean data in 2026. Self-supervised learning has been increasingly investigated for low-dose CT denoising. Paired normal-dose data are often difficult to collect for training. Many blind-spot methods suffer training inefficiencies and suboptimal performance.

Restricted receptive fields limit what those methods can see in a scan. Their progressive J-invariant self-supervised learning targets those flaws. J-invariance keeps the model from cheating by peeking at the pixel it predicts. Cleaner low-dose scans could cut radiation exposure for patients.
arxiv-2601-14480:
Egemen Erbayat and five co-authors set shared ground rules for network design in this 2026 paper. Mobile networks are moving toward 5G and 6G architectures. Passive optical networks offer a critical solution for cost-effective fronthaul transport, the links that carry data from antennas inward. Many optimization strategies compete in this space.

The literature lacks standardized evaluation models, so objective comparison of those strategies is hard. The team proposes a unified benchmarking framework. It standardizes cost catalogs and deployment scenarios for PON-based fronthaul design. Readers get a common yardstick, so future design claims can be checked against the same facts.
arxiv-2601-15080:
Ka Kit Kelvin Ho, Vladislav Yu. Shishkov, and a large team report cooling a quantum fluid with light-like control. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with a Bose-Einstein condensate of exciton-polaritons. These hybrid light-matter particles form the condensate far from equilibrium.

The team observes stimulated cooling of that condensate. It falls from near room temperature all the way down to about 20 kelvin in the test. They map the condensate in energy and momentum space. Careful interferometric tests then set the true condensate apart from the hot particles that sit in excited states.
arxiv-2601-15180:
Pedro Ângelo, Atsushi Igarashi, Yuito Murase, and Vasco T. Vasconcelos add staged code generation to a language for message passing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with session types, which state the shape of a conversation between programs. Metaprogramming lets a program write code in stages.

The authors build on contextual modal type theory with multi-level contexts. Contextual values can close a term over a set of variables. Those values can be boxed and sent inside messages. The work shows how staged generation and session-typed messaging can live side by side in one language.
arxiv-2601-15280:
Chloe Qianhui Zhao, Jie Cao, Jionghao Lin, and Kenneth R. Koedinger let an AI tutor give feedback and compare it with a teacher's. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with feedback that is timely, targeted, and multimodal. Such feedback helps students fix errors fast and stay motivated.

Making that feedback at scale is the hard part. The authors build a real-time AI system for it. It joins written explanations with media: the most apt slide page, plus streaming AI audio narration. Their title reports the outcome: learning matched educator feedback, and student perceptions were better.
arxiv-2601-15380:
Elon Litman and Gabe Guo rethink the attention step inside transformer models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with how attention weighs the parts of an input. Seen through entropic optimal transport, standard attention solves a transport problem with a hidden assumption.

That assumption is an implicit uniform prior. The authors replace it with a learnable, continuous prior. Their mechanism is called Goat, short for a generalized optimal transport attention with trainable priors. It aims to encode each patch's context better. The design promises attention that adapts to the data instead of treating all routes alike.
arxiv-2601-15680:
M. P. Thejitha, James A. Sellers, and S. N. Fathima count colored partitions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their counting function tracks multicolored partitions of a number. Even parts and odd parts get different color allowances. Even parts may appear in one of r colors. Odd parts may appear in one of s colors. Both r and s are fixed, at least one each.

Parity restrictions drive the paper, per its title. Splitting parts by even and odd is a classic move in partition theory. Adding colors multiplies the structures to count. Such problems often yield generating functions with elegant forms. They also connect to q-series and modular forms. The authors work in that tradition, asking what arithmetic traits the counts display.
arxiv-2601-15780:
Pascal Benschop, Justin Dauwels, and Jan van Gemert test vision-language models on synthetic video in a 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial reasoning in these models stays fragile. It breaks when meaning hinges on subtle timing or geometry. The authors build a synthetic benchmark to probe two skills. One is situational awareness: telling a harmful interaction from a benign one. The other is spatial awareness: tracking who does what to whom.

Relative positions and motion also fall under the second skill. Synthetic video gives full control over those cues. Each factor can be varied while others stay fixed. That control exposes exactly where models fail. Real video cannot isolate causes so cleanly. For safety uses like monitoring, knowing a model's blind spots is essential.
arxiv-2601-15880:
Dennis Dobler, Alina Schenk, and Matthias Schmid build a regression method for comparing treatments in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their effect measure is the relative treatment effect. It compares outcome variables from two samples. It reads as a probability: how likely one sample's outcome beats the other's. It also links to the area under the ROC curve. The measure has been used for ordinal outcomes and for censored time-to-event data.

Their approach uses pseudo-observations in a two-sample regression. Pseudo-observations let standard regression tools handle the effect. That makes adjusting for covariates more straightforward. Clinicians like probability-scale effects because they are easy to explain. A method that puts such effects into regression form widens their use in trials and studies.
arxiv-2601-15980:
Martina Formichetti and four co-authors infer wall roughness from sparse data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Surface roughness shapes turbulent boundary layers. It acts mainly through the roughness function and the equivalent sand-grain height. Finding that height directly needs detailed velocity and wall-shear data. Such measurements are often impractical in real facilities. Roughness therefore often goes unmeasured where it matters.

The authors build a data-driven framework for the inference. Sparse experimental data go in; rough wall properties come out. The title calls the process assimilating rough features. Wind tunnels, pipelines, and aircraft surfaces all live with roughness effects. A tool that reads roughness from little data helps engineers predict drag and heat transfer without costly full surveys.
arxiv-2601-16680:
Zhenduo Wen and Amin Gohari study how to pack data with a kind of care. A pack tool is stable if small tweaks stay small. Change a few marks in the source, and the code should shift just a bit. Their 2026 preprint sets out this trait and tests known tools. A famed tool, random binning, fails the test flat.

In random binning, near twins can land in far bins. That leap breaks the care trait at once. The authors build the base math for stable packs. Such packs could guard streams where inputs shift by bits. They may also help codes that must shrug off small noise.
arxiv-2601-16880:
Bethan Evans and Jared Tanner work out the least nudge that flips a deep net's call. Small weight shifts can tilt a call in a set aim. Their 2026 preprint finds exact forms for that least shift. One-layer forms fall out in full. The team names what sets the shift's size.

They then set those forms next to broad multi-layer bounds. The two gauges land of the same rough size. That match says the broad bounds lose little truth. The work also feeds low-rank backdoor attack work. Such attacks flip calls with faint, cheap nudges. Sharp least-nudge math helps guard nets from such tricks.
arxiv-2601-17180:
Inés Gonzalez-Pepe and a team of four co-authors speed brain scan nets by use of junk marks. Scan nets grow vast, and their cost stays a pain. Much of their work runs on noise-drowned marks. Those marks sway the net's calls by next to nil. Their 2026 preprint sorts such marks in two grades. Safe junk can be skipped with no loss.

Bold junk skips trade a hair of truth for speed. The tool in view is the U-Net, a scan workhorse. Fast scans aid wards with long wait lists. Lean nets also cut the power bill of AI care.
arxiv-2601-17280:
David Condrey tests a claimed way to spot AI-written text. The claim rests on keystroke timing. A score from gaps between key presses is said to split human typing from AI text. Condrey shows that defense can be fooled in two plain ways. In one attack, a person just retypes AI text by hand.

That copy-type attack gives the timing signal a human shape. A second attack class forges timing in a like way. If both work, timing alone cannot prove who wrote a text. The study warns schools and firms not to trust such checks. False claims of AI use can harm real people, so proof must be strong.
arxiv-2601-17380:
Detelina Kamburova gives new tests for when a space is Hausdorff. Hausdorff spaces keep points apart with disjoint open sets. The paper works with first countable T1 spaces, a broad and common class. Kamburova defines two forms of contractive orbit for set-valued maps. One form uses the space's own topology. The other uses a generalized distance.

She ties those orbits to fixed point theorems. Fixed points are where a map sends a point to itself. Such theorems drive proofs across analysis and topology. New characterizations give topologists fresh ways to check a key trait. They also link separation traits to map behavior. That link can shorten proofs that now take long detours.
arxiv-2601-17480:
Marton Szep and five co-authors study a privacy leak in fine-tuned language models. Fine-tuning on sensitive data can make models memorize it. Names and other personal facts can then leak out. The team looks at a less studied path. They test facts that appear only in model inputs, not in the target outputs.

Input-only facts are easy to overlook in safety checks. If models store them, chat logs and forms are at risk. The study maps how bad that exposure can be. Its lessons guide data handling for health and legal tools. Teams learn what to strip before training starts. Privacy law sets a high bar here, and leaks can breach it.
arxiv-2601-17580:
Joshua Viszlai and four co-authors present PropHunt, a tool to optimize quantum syndrome measurement circuits. Fault-tolerant quantum computing rests on error correction codes. Codes run parity checks on data qubits again and again. Those checks are syndrome measurement circuits. Their design sets the code's logical error rate. Small design flaws cost dearly at scale.

PropHunt automates the search for better circuits. Hand design cannot scan the full space of layouts. Automated optimization can find leaner, safer checks. Each saved gate cuts noise in the full machine. The work targets a bottleneck in quantum scale-up. Better syndrome circuits bring useful quantum machines closer.
arxiv-2601-17680:
Shota Takashiro and four co-authors generalize Mixture of Experts to infinitely many experts. Standard MoE picks a few feed-forward networks per token. That gives a good trade of cost and quality. In standard designs, each expert stands alone. Experts combine in a discrete space. As expert counts grow, training each one well gets hard.

Their infinite form rethinks that structure. A continuous view of experts could scale more smoothly. Language models lean on MoE for cheap capacity growth. A better expert frame could cut training waste. The work asks what experts should be at the limit. It may reshape how large sparse models are built.
arxiv-2601-17780:
Andrea Medini works on a question in set theory about special kinds of filters. His 2026 preprint deals with P-filters that are non-meager, terms from the study of sets and size. Filters are rules for calling some sets large. The work also touches Miller measurability, a property tied to a classic forcing notion. A question posed by Hrušák frames part of the study.

The main result links a group of filters to a bound on a cardinal number. If a product of such filters has a strong sameness property, then the count of filters stays below a known cardinal. Each filter in the group must also be of the non-meager P kind. Results of this sort help map how set-theoretic claims hang together.
arxiv-2601-17880:
Muhammad Umar Salman, Mohammad Areeb Qazi, and Mohammed Talha Alam present Quran-MD, a data set of the Qur'an built for language and speech research. Their 2026 preprint describes the set at a fine grain. Each verse comes with its Arabic text, an English translation, and a phonetic rendering. The set also adds audio and language detail at both verse and word level.

Such layers let one resource serve many kinds of study. Text models, speech tools, and language teaching aids can all draw on it. Word-level links help where exact form matters, as it does in sacred text. The authors frame the set as broad and fine-grained at once. It fills a gap for multilingual, multimodal work on this text.
arxiv-2601-18580:
Vincenzo De Paola and three colleagues give a fresh twist to the way smart agents learn by trial. In the plain way, many twin agents run the same task to feed one learner fast. All twins act in the same style, so the learner sees a thin range of tries. That thin range can trap the learner in a poor style of play.

Their plan, named K-Myriad, runs a crowd of agents that are not twins. Each agent tries the task in its own style, with no training at that stage. The mix of styles gives the learner a wide first view of the task. A wide start could help the learner find strong styles that a thin start would miss. The trick may serve games, robots, and any task where the first tries shape all that comes next.
arxiv-2601-18680:
Marine Demarty and three colleagues build a fair test for when a noisy quantum tool could beat a plain one at a hard search. Such a win is the prize of the field, but it is hard to claim with care. A test must weigh the task, the way the tool is built, and the noise in the kit, all at once. One past test does weigh all three, and it gives a sharp read on where a win could lie.

Noise can be cut by tricks, but the tricks shift the test. The team fold the cost of those tricks into the test from the start. That way a claim of a win must clear the bar with its fix costs paid. A fair bar helps labs pick tasks where a real win is in reach. A fair bar also stops hype.
arxiv-2601-19280:
Kishan Panaganti and five co-authors train language models to reason well on every group, not just on average. Group distributionally robust optimization guards the worst off group in the data, rather than the mean case. The team drives reinforcement learning for reasoning with that guard in place.

Post training gains in reasoning often come from tweaking loss functions and alignment choices. A worst group lens asks whether those gains hold for the hardest slice of problems. Reasoning that stays strong on its weakest ground is the kind users can rely on when a hard query lands.
arxiv-2601-19580:
Cuong Le and five colleagues build vision systems that recover human motion in three dimensions. Filming a person and rebuilding their pose over time is a core task in computer vision. Frame-by-frame pose estimates often ignore how poses connect in time. The result is jittery motion that no real body could make.

The authors use quaternions, a compact way to represent rotations, to model motion between poses. Their kinematics-based approach estimates how each pose turns into the next. That focus on transitions enforces smoother, more plausible movement. Good motion capture feeds animation, sports analysis, and rehabilitation tools. The work aims for motion that looks right not just in stills, but as a moving sequence.
arxiv-2601-20180:
Ioannis Anagnostides and four colleagues study the computational hardness of performative prediction. In this setting, deploying a model changes the very data it predicts, since people react to the prediction. Simple retraining is known to settle down when the shift caused by the model is weak.

The authors tackle the strong-shift regime, where that earlier result no longer applies. They ask how hard prediction and retraining become when the model's effect on the data is large. The answer shapes what guarantees platforms can offer when their forecasts move markets, prices, or user behavior.
arxiv-2601-20280:
Daojun Liang and six colleagues argue that the future of time series forecasting lies after the forecast, in post-processing. Model design has long dominated the field, with recent gains from deep learning and hybrid methods. As accuracy gains from new architectures shrink, the authors see an overlooked chance in what is done to the output.

They frame post-processing as a distinct stage that can correct systematic errors of a forecaster. The shift matters for practice: firms already own working models, and improving their output may be cheaper than replacing them. The paper maps this stage as a research direction in its own right.
arxiv-2601-20480:
C. Vázquez-García and a team of colleagues link dementia to patterns in how the brain uses energy. Brain scans give a flood of data, and the links inside that data are curved and hard to pull apart with plain tools. The team uses a kind of network that squeezes each scan down to a small set of traits.

Those traits are picked to keep what marks the disease, and to drop the rest. The frame is built to be explainable, so a doctor can see what drove a read of a scan. A tool a doctor can question is worth more in a clinic than a black box. The work uses data from a large Alzheimer's disease study program.
arxiv-2601-20580:
Nurul Huda Mahmood and five colleagues write about what it takes for factory wireless links to be truly dependable. A dependable system keeps giving good service, safely and steadily, even when parts fail or trouble strikes from outside. In a plant, that is not a nice extra. It is a base need.

Fifth-generation networks brought very reliable, low-delay service, which covers part of the need. The authors say the move to sixth-generation systems must go further. Safety, security, and being up and running must be planned as one whole, not as add-ons. When a dropped link can halt a line or put staff at risk, that whole view is the point.
arxiv-2601-20680:
Ostap Vykhopen and three co-authors look at how software can track stories as they spread on social media. Their 2026 paper studies systems that watch news and posts as a live stream. Such systems group posts into clusters that stand for one theme or tale. The team asks if these groups can be formed on the fly.

The standard tool for this job works in batches, after the data has piled up. That batch method is HDBSCAN, and it does not scale well to an endless stream. The authors test online methods that add each new post to the groups at once. They run the test inside a real report-making pipeline. The paper shows what changes when a live feed is grouped step by step.
arxiv-2601-21280:
Dong Chen and seven co-authors work on matching antennas to the towers they belong to. Network crews now do this matching by climbing towers and checking by hand. That process is slow and easy to get wrong, and errors hurt network quality.

The team fuses three kinds of evidence: video of the site, the shape and position of each antenna, and cell identity signals. The job becomes a matching task across these sources. A measure based on token spread helps the model sort out hard cases. Automating the check could cut field work and fix records that guide repairs and upgrades.
arxiv-2601-21780:
Jun Qi and five co-authors propose a design principle for hybrid artificial intelligence, which mixes neural networks with variational quantum circuits. Each side brings different strengths, but many current hybrids are tightly coupled or built for one task only. That limits clarity, generality, and reuse across settings, the authors argue.

Their 2026 preprint names the principle Quantum LEGO Learning, after the building-block idea. The point is modular design: parts that can be combined, swapped, and understood on their own, rather than one fused block. A clear modular scheme could help researchers test which gains truly come from the quantum parts. And could let working pieces transfer to new learning problems instead of being rebuilt each time.
arxiv-2601-22280:
Mayia Vranas and a large team study a crystal where atoms of two metals share the layers. Their 2026 preprint looks at a mix of ruthenium and iridium in a lithium oxide. Such iridium crystals are prime hosts in the hunt for a strange state called a quantum spin liquid.

In that state, spins stay tangled and never settle into a fixed pattern. The team probe how the mix forms a spin glass with a clear sense of direction. Their work maps the line between glass-like freeze and liquid-like flow. That map can guide the search for true spin liquids. It also tests key claims about these crystals.
arxiv-2601-22480:
Seungu Han, Sungho Lee, and Kyogu Lee rethink how to blend the layers of a speech model to clean noisy speech. Speech models trained on their own learn rich sound cues. Their 2026 preprint notes that most cleaners merge those cues with a light add-on, yet the base models were not built to resist noise.

Noise can warp the very cues the cleaner trusts. The team use a phonetic yardstick — shared information with true speech sounds — to guide the blend. A better blend should keep meaning while cutting noise. The work aims at clearer calls and voice tools.
arxiv-2601-22680:
Rameen Abdal, James Burgess, Sergey Tulyakov, and Kuan-Chieh Jackson Wang set a Turing-style test for personalized visuals. Their 2026 preprint, VPTT, judges a model by likeness of feel, not by copying a face. A model passes if its output could pass as content that person might plausibly make.

A human or a tuned model judge makes the call. The test fits an age of feeds tuned to each user's taste. It gives creators a fair bar for personal media tools. The work reframes what good personalization means. Plausible, not identical, is the bar.
arxiv-2602-00080: Alexander Sheppert introduces the GT-Score, a composite objective meant to curb overfitting in data driven trading strategies. Models often learn false patterns in past prices and then fail on new data, worsened by data snooping and shaky inference when returns are not normal. The score joins performance, significance, consistency, and downside risk to steer tuning toward steadier strategies. Tests use 50 S and P 500 stocks from 2010 to 2024, with walk forward checks and a Monte Carlo study, lifting the generalization ratio sharply.
arxiv-2602-00180: Deepak Babu Piskala offers a practitioner guide to spec driven development, in which specifications, not code, form the primary artifact of software work. The approach inverts the usual workflow: specs are the source of truth, and code is a generated or verified secondary artifact. The paper sets out three rigor levels: spec first, spec anchored, and spec as source, with guidance on when each fits. Tool analysis runs from behavior driven frameworks to AI toolkits. Cases span API work, enterprise systems, and embedded software.
arxiv-2602-00280: Manuel González-Villa and team give an algorithm for the annihilator and Bernstein-Sato polynomial of a rational function. Rational functions are quotients of two polynomials, with a singularity theory studied for two decades. Takeuchi first defined this polynomial, yet only trivial examples were known. The new plan works out the annihilator from the pair made of the top and bottom of the quotient. Built in SINGULAR with Gröbner bases, it yields explicit non trivial examples and supports existing conjectures.
arxiv-2602-00480: Mohini Priya Kolluri and colleagues steer robot swarms with no messages between agents, taking cues from how a fluid moves through a volume. They give subsets of agents fluid-like traits, so the swarm flows under a pressure boundary rule while keeping its shape and coherence. The FISC scheme is tested in quadcopter simulations in a converging-diverging domain and set against computational fluid dynamics results. Checks show close match between swarm-derived and fluid fields, backing treatment of large swarms as continuum systems for scalable decentralised control.
arxiv-2602-00880: Ailin Liu and colleagues build a proactive system that predicts when survey takers need support from skin signals and mouse moves. Tough questions drain energy and hurt later scores, while users often miss when they need help or lack motivation to seek it. Tailored classifiers with rule-based thresholds trigger timely LLM clarifications and explanations. In a study of 32 people, aligned-adaptive timing beat misaligned and random controls. Aligned assistance improved accuracy by 21%, cut false negatives to 22.9%, and lifted perceived efficiency and dependability.
arxiv-2602-00980: Yichen Cai and colleagues steer robot swarms into complex shapes without a boss. Their method models a swarm as a mass spread over sample points, dodging the task of defining density functions for shapes. A decentralized meanshift rule nudges the swarm's spread to match the sample spread, using estimates fed back from the robots. Robots build these estimates without central control, and the authors show they converge to global values over time. Simulations and live trials confirm the method forms shapes and adapts as swarm size changes.
arxiv-2602-01080: Sam Adriaensen and co-authors hunt the smallest set skirting all q-ary n-tuples, where each tuple sits at full Hamming gap n from some picked point. That hunt is the total domination number of a graph whose nodes are all tuples and whose links join pairs at gap n. The team gives builds and bounds that pin the count to exponential growth in n, with base constants that shrink as q grows. Those constants can, for now, only be guessed at, not nailed down.
arxiv-2602-01280: Shuning Tan and co-authors probe wobbles in a 2D FFLO superfluid on light lattices, hunting Cooper-pair drift momentum. They run a spin-tilted Hubbard model on a square light grid under a Zeeman push, tracking density and spin wobble maps across the BCS-to-FFLO flip. In the FFLO phase, a low-energy bogolon wobble joins the density sound wobble in the spin lane. A roton dip near the corner point morphs from dot to ring, shifted by drift momentum, giving a roton-based drift read.
arxiv-2602-01680: Solovyev designs new ferromagnetic ferroelectricity by making orbital freedom active, since ferromagnetism alone cannot break inversion symmetry. Shifted orbitals along a bond, antiferro orbital order, favors ferromagnetic links and breaks inversion symmetry, making the bond ferroelectric as well. His rules require atoms away from inversion centers, as in a honeycomb lattice, and orbitals that adjust through intraatomic interactions behind Hund's second rule. Iodides with a d2 setup and weak d-p mixing lead for such compounds, a situation already seen in VI3, which he expects to be ferromagnetic ferroelectric.
arxiv-2602-01880: Giulio Antonio Abbo and colleagues test whether multimodal models can guide a vacuum robot, combining GPT-4o with a TurtleBot 4 in a home. The model watches the home through vision and judges whether starting cleaning fits now, reasoning about activities, social norms and user preferences. Decisions align with residents' values such as cleanliness, comfort and safety, and a home demo shows context and values inferred from limited visual input. The work shows promise for robotic autonomy and awareness, while flagging consistency, bias and real time performance as challenges.
arxiv-2602-02080: Aryan Alavi Razavi Ravari and colleagues study learning under a two-step contrastive oracle, where each queried example pairs with an opposite-label example. While earlier work assumes an idealized setting with the contrastive example at minimum distance, they introduce a non-decreasing noise function f perturbing the ideal. Perturbation is controlled by f of d, the distance to the boundary, yielding higher-quality examples near it. They study fixed and stochastic magnitudes. For one-dimensional thresholds and half-spaces under uniform distribution, they characterize active and passive complexity.
arxiv-2602-02280: Zeming Wei and others propose RACA, picture-aware coverage criteria for safety testing of language models. Jailbreak attacks pose severe safety risks, yet testing largely uses static data without systematic criteria for suite quality. RACA extracts safety pictures from hidden states using a small set of harmful calibration prompts. It measures test prompts against those directions, and computes coverage through six criteria spanning individual and compositional safety concepts. Experiments show RACA rewards quality jailbreak suites while ignoring redundant or invalid inputs, and applications include suite prioritization and prompt sampling.
arxiv-2602-02680:
Riccardo Zaccone's 2026 paper, with 3 co-authors, carves pretrained networks into nested pieces that can be switched on to fit any compute budget. Large models are usually monoliths with fixed cost, which blocks flexible deployment across devices. Training distinct models per budget costs far too much.

Their method, FlexRank, breaks weights into low-rank components ordered by importance. Nested merging extracts submodels of growing capability from a single pretrained network. A small budget switches on only the top components; a larger budget adds more, smoothly trading cost for performance. No retraining from scratch is needed for any tier. The authors frame the result as a train-once, deploy-everywhere model. One artifact serves a phone, a server, and everything between, advancing the practical rollout of large language and vision models.
arxiv-2602-02780:
Zihao Jing and 6 co-authors ground a language model's reasoning in the geometry of molecular and atomic structures, in a 2026 paper. Models reasoning over two- and 3D structures hallucinate when links compress geometry into fixed token budgets. Existing methods are also specific to one modality, blocking unified all-atom reasoning.

Their system, Cuttlefish, first applies scaling-aware patching. An instruction-conditioned gate makes variable-size patches over structural graphs, scaling the token budget with structural complexity. A geometry grounding adapter then refines those tokens through cross-attention to modality vectors and feeds them into the language model. Explicit geometric cues reach the reasoning process head-on. Across interdisciplinary all-atom benchmarks, Cuttlefish beat rivals at heterogeneous structure-grounded reasoning. Token budgets that breathe with the input, rather than fixed funnels, are the central design lesson.
arxiv-2602-03180:
A jet-free way to study how energy spreads in collisions is presented by Yazhen Lin, with 2 co-authors. Energy-energy correlators measure how energy is distributed at angles around a collision event at the Large Hadron Collider. Conventional measurements rely on reconstructing jets, which becomes unreliable at low transverse momentum, exactly where interesting shifts between perturbative and non-perturbative actions occur in quantum chromodynamics.

Their method uses the leading charged hadron as a reference axis instead. The azimuthal plane splits into toward and transverse regions, enabling robust background subtraction. Checking against jet-based results follows. The correlator's peak scales with the hard scale, suggesting the shift is captured. Quark and gluon initiated events differ clearly, reflecting their color charges. Heavy-flavor triggers show a suppressed, shifted pattern consistent with the dead-cone effect.
arxiv-2602-03380:
Multimodal models that reason step by step still invent details that are not in the image. Hao Fang and 6 co-authors tackle that hallucination problem in a 2026 paper. They trace the cause to reasoning chains that lean on language habits, carry few visual cues, and waste tokens on redundant text.

Their framework, called C3PO, first compresses the chain of thought by filtering out redundant thinking tokens. It then applies contrastive preference training, pairing good reasoning traces with deliberately induced bad ones so the model learns to prefer grounded answers. The authors give a theoretical argument for the design and report steady hallucination reductions across several multimodal reasoning models and benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-03680:
Fumihiko Ishiyama revisits a century-old assumption in signal analysis: Fourier methods quietly assume the signal repeats at the boundary. His 2026 paper replaces that periodic boundary condition with a linear extrapolation rule, removing the need for the signal to repeat. The change lifts what he calls the theory limit on time-frequency resolution.

The new instantaneous spectrum analysis applies to pulse series. Each pulse gets its own spectrum, and the spectra assemble into a full spectrogram. As a test case, Ishiyama analyzes two abnormal lung sounds, crackles and wheezing, alongside a normal recording. Crackles turn out to be a random pulse series. The method pictures the time-frequency structure of each recording pulse by pulse.
arxiv-2602-03880:
Approximate structure can still pin down exact structure, show Angshuman R. Goswami and 1 co-author. Their 2026 mathematics paper studies Hyers-Ulam stability for graphs, asking when a graph that almost has a property sits near one that has it exactly. They treat monotone, subadditive, and convex graphs.

For each class, they prove a matching exact graph exists on the same vertices and edges. The weight gap between the two graphs stays controlled by the original error. Results of this kind matter wherever networks are measured with noise, since they bound how far an imperfect graph can drift from an ideal one.
arxiv-2602-04380:
Why should KL divergence be the only leash on a learning policy? Rui Yuan and 2 co-authors generalize group-based policy optimization to flexible Bregman divergences in a 2026 paper. Methods like GRPO regularize with KL alone, leaving the divergence choice unexplored despite its grip on training behavior.

Their GBMPO framework admits hand-designed alternatives and mirror maps learned by neural networks. A probability-space L2 variant improved math reasoning accuracy notably over the baseline. Neural mirror maps led code generation results, with random initialization capturing most of the benefit. Meta-learned maps mainly reduced variance. Divergence, they show, is a design axis, not a default.
arxiv-2602-04680:
Haina Zhu and 7 co-authors add fine control to text-to-audio generation in a 2026 paper. Models can already synthesize high-quality sound from descriptions, but they rarely let users set loudness, pitch, or exactly which events occur and when.

Rather than retraining a model per control type, the team trains ControlNet-style add-ons on top of pretrained audio backbones. Their adapter design proved more efficient, reaching state-of-the-art scores with a modest number of extra parameters. The framework extends to editing as well. An editor variant removes or inserts audio events at time points specified by instructions. The authors plan to release models, code, and benchmarks for later research.
arxiv-2602-04780:
Emil Albrychiewicz, Andrés Franco Valiente, and Li-Ching Chen offer a theory for how multimodal diffusion models generate, dated 2026. These models synthesize high-dimensional data such as images and text together, yet the ways the modes are coordinated have stayed poorly understood.

Using coupled Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes as a tractable stand-in, the authors apply ideas from dynamical phase transitions. Making an output turns out to be governed by a ranking of interaction timescales, not by all parts settling at once. They predict a synchronization gap, a window where parts stabilize at varied rates, which explains common desynchronization flaws. Rules for mode splitting and collapse follow under varied coupling regimes. Controlled tests with image diffusion models backed the theory.
arxiv-2602-05280:
Cloud radio access networks cut costs by scaling capacity up and down on demand, but an adaptive controller that breaks a service agreement is a liability. Kim Hammar and 2 co-authors present COL in this 2026 networking paper. The method learns the network's safe operating region: the set of resource allocations and configurations under which its specification holds.

Learning runs online in two phases. First the method watches the running network passively and infers an initial safe region using causal inference and Gaussian process regression. Then it widens that region cautiously through interventional Bayesian learning, testing the edges rather than guessing them. The authors prove the learned region is safe with a chosen probability and converges to the complete safe region under standard conditions. On a live 5G testbed, COL learned quickly at low operational cost and needed up to ten times fewer samples than leading safe-learning methods.
arxiv-2602-05380:
Aligning image diffusion models with human taste usually demands enormous preference datasets or a separate reward model. Xiaoxuan He and 7 co-authors propose SAIL in this 2026 computer vision paper, a framework where the model teaches itself. Starting from a tiny seed of human-labeled preference pairs, the model generates samples, judges them by its own evolving understanding, and trains on the result, round after round.

A ranked preference mixup strategy keeps the loop honest, balancing exploration against loyalty to the original human examples so the model does not drift into self-confirming nonsense or forget its priors. Across multiple benchmarks, SAIL beat state-of-the-art alignment methods while using only about six percent of the preference data those methods consumed. The authors read this as evidence that diffusion models carry latent alignment ability that the right loop can unlock, replacing both mass annotation and external reward models.
arxiv-2602-05680:
Orbits that link two distinct periodic orbits, called heteroclinic connections, matter across physics, yet finding large ones from scratch is notoriously hard. Thomas Bridges, David Lloyd, Daniel Ratliff, and Patrick Sprenger use a codimension two singularity in a family of periodic orbits as an organizing center. From it, a normal form produces two finite amplitude periodic orbits with an explicit connection between them.

The team also builds connections far from the singularity by numerical continuation, using shooting and a core farfield split. A new quantity, the action of a connection, turns out to be invariant along the geometric structures involved and central to the normal form theory. Phase differences between the two ends matter as well. Applications include the Swift Hohenberg equation, a fourth order Schrödinger model, and coupled Boussinesq equations for water waves. All three test systems conserve energy and action.
arxiv-2602-06080:
One of the deepest open questions in math concerns the Riemann zeta function and where its partner function takes the value zero. Douglas F Watson compares that partner, the Xi-function, with a family of spectral formulas built from cycles. Those formulas have only real zeros, thanks to a symmetry property.

Watson's main tool is a rigidity result about functions on horizontal strips in the complex plane. Applied carefully, it shows a linking ratio between the two sides has no zeros at all on overlap strips. That means both sides share the exact same zeros there. Some checks behind the claim are promised in a follow-up paper.
arxiv-2602-06580:
Silicon-30 sits just two neutrons past silicon-28, yet its ground-state shape is far less settled. Y K Gupta and 19 co-authors probe both nuclei by scattering silicon beams off a zirconium target near the Coulomb barrier. Coupled-channels calculations scanned a wide space of quadrupole and hexadecapole deformations for each nucleus.

Silicon-28 proved uniquely oblate, flattened like a disc, in its ground state. For silicon-30, oblate, prolate, and spherical descriptions all fit the measurements equally well. Shell-model calculations then revealed a sudden structural change between the two isotopes. The combined evidence indicates silicon-30 has no well-defined intrinsic shape, making it a candidate for ground-state shape fluctuations.
arxiv-2602-07080:
Yicheng He and five co-authors ask if a language model's code can be judged right or wrong from inside alone. Today's checks lean on outside tools: running unit tests, or asking another model to judge. Those routes cost labor, or they inherit the judge model's own limits. The paper poses a fresh question: do a model's neural dynamics carry signals, readable from inside, that predict logical validity as code is generated?

The team turns code checks into a diagnostic task, mapping the model's algorithmic path into graphs that attribute each line. By breaking down complex residual flows, they hunt for structural signatures that mark sound reasoning apart from logical failure within the model's circuits. Tests across Python, C++, and Java show those intrinsic correctness signals hold across diverse syntaxes. Graph topology features predict correctness better than surface heuristics, and they enable targeted causal interventions to repair faulty logic.
arxiv-2602-07380:
A spontaneously broken discrete symmetry in the early universe would fill space with domain walls that could dominate cosmic energy, a classic problem usually patched with ad hoc symmetry-breaking terms.  Debasish Borah and two co-authors show those terms can arise naturally if the same symmetry generates light Dirac neutrino masses.

Radiative effects from the neutrino-mass particles supply the bias term, which scales inversely with the cube of the Dirac neutrino mass. That produces a gravitational wave spectrum proportional to the sixth power of that mass.  The result links the Dirac seesaw scale to a potentially observable signal.  Particle cosmologists get a connection between neutrino mass and gravitational waves with no extra patching.
arxiv-2602-08080:
Soldiers' health and safety depend on timely body information, yet wearable trackers must be secure, long-lived, and power-lean. Luciano Bozzi and 17 co-authors describe CAPSARII, a Eu project building a wearable system and Web of Field Things method for tracking soldiers' real and mental status.

The system tracks body, motion, and outdoor readings, supports field choices with AI models on edge nodes, and feeds cloud data work for compare studies. Smart fabrics improve comfort, hardware and software tuning stretch battery life, and lean coding plus strong login checks address security. Defense builders gain a blueprint for health tracking that weighs awareness, life, and cyber safety.
arxiv-2602-08380:
Millimeter-wave links need precisely aimed beams, and finding the right beam among many takes time. Akanksha Sneh and three co-authors speed the search by letting the base station's radar help the communication system. Their arXiv paper builds on bandit algorithms, which balance trying new beams against reusing good ones.

Because radar and communication share the same field of view, radar detections of users as targets prune the candidate beam list sharply. Radar data also help estimate when realignment is needed in near-stationary scenes. The team implemented the algorithms on a system-on-chip and showed a 35 percent cut in exploration time plus 1.4 times higher throughput. Readers get a practical fusion of sensing and communication.
arxiv-2602-08680:
Fast and slow fluid motions interact in complex ways when the fast part is shaken by random noise. Eliseo Luongo and Francesco Triggiano study a coupled system of two- and three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations with a fast component driven by fractional Brownian motion. Their arXiv paper uses rough path theory to find the slow limit.

The limit depends sharply on the Hurst parameter. Below one half, the slow flow converges to a Navier-Stokes system with an extra Itô-Stokes drift. Between one half and one, the limit instead carries only transport noise driven by a rough path. Readers get a clean split: the same system yields two very different slow laws on either side of one half.
arxiv-2602-08880:
Antonin Sulc reframes quantum circuit design as a logic puzzle that can be solved with gradients. Instead of fixed circuit templates or hand-written compiler rules, his neuro-symbolic framework treats a scaffold of candidate gates as learnable switches, each a number between zero and one. Gradient descent tunes those switches to satisfy user-set logical rules for correctness, simplicity, and robustness.

The method bridges continuous logic and unitary evolution while dodging the barren-plateau trap through biased starting points. It rediscovers a four-qubit quantum Fourier transform from 21 candidate gates and adapts on the 156-qubit IBM Fez chip, beating static baselines after both slow noise drift and sudden hardware failure.
arxiv-2602-08980:
Neural ordinary differential equations can learn dynamics from time series, but do they survive when the graph underneath changes size or shape? Moritz Laber and two co-authors train such models, with Barabási-Barzel-style vector fields, on five synthetic dynamical systems over graphs from the S-one model, which tunes realistic structure. They then test generalization to new graphs.

Degree heterogeneity and the type of dynamics matter most for success, including capturing fixed points and coping with missing data. Average clustering plays a secondary role. The findings mark neural ODEs as powerful for complex systems, while warning that uneven node degrees and clustering in real graphs pose genuine challenges.
arxiv-2602-09380:
A weak value is a curious quantum number, defined as a ratio of a matrix element to an overlap of two state vectors. It was first tied to gentle measurements plus post-selection in papers from the late 1980s. Since then, weak values have yielded practical tools for signal amplification and state tomography. Jacob A. Barandes sets those spin-offs aside in his single-author 2026 paper, turning instead to the bolder claims made on weak values' behalf.

The paper challenges attempts to give weak values a transparent meaning for single systems, and the exotic claims about individual particles sometimes drawn from them. Barandes argues those interpretations rest on several forms of fallacious reasoning, not on what the mathematics or the experiments actually license. The work is a critique of interpretation, not of the techniques: the measurement methods stand, while the stories told about single systems do not.
arxiv-2602-09580:
Fine-tuning dexterous robot policies in the real world is hard: interaction budgets are small and action distributions are highly multimodal. Chenyu Yang and five co-authors present SERNF, a 2026 sample-efficient off-policy fine-tuning framework built on normalizing flows. Diffusion policies cannot support conservative likelihood-based updates since their action odds are intractable, while Gaussian policies collapse under multimodality, especially for chunked actions.

A normalizing flow policy yields exact likelihoods for multimodal action chunks, enabling stable updates through likelihood regularization. An action-chunked critic scores whole action sequences, aligning value estimates with the policy's temporal structure for better long-horizon credit assignment. Tested on cutting tape with scissors from a case and rotating a cube in hand palm-down, the framework adapts stably and efficiently where standard methods struggle.
arxiv-2602-09980:
Physics-informed neural networks learn solutions that obey known equations, but sharp regime changes, such as bifurcations, can make them blur distinct behaviors together. A 2026 paper led by Enzo Nicolas Spotorno, with two co-authors, proposes a topology-aware variant called TAPINN. It organizes the latent space so different regimes stay metrically apart.

A phase-based alternating schedule balances the metric and physics goals during training. On the Duffing oscillator, the method cuts the physics residual to about half the standard level, with lower gradient variance than a Sobolev-error baseline. It also uses about a fifth as many parameters as a hypernetwork alternative, avoiding memorization that violates physics.
arxiv-2602-10280:
Linear logic with fixed points poses deep questions for infinitary proof theory, where branching rules run over transfinite ordinals. A 2026 paper by Anupam Das and Tikhon Pshenitsyn investigates infinitary well-founded systems for fixed-point linear logic, with branching rules over transfinite ordinals indexed by a closure ordinal for fixed points. The main result places provability in that system for some computable ordinal at a high level of the hyperarithmetical hierarchy, complete for that level.

Proof-theoretic foundations come first: cut elimination and focusing results control both upper and lower bound analysis. Arguments use a finely tuned notion of formula rank, working out a tight cap on cut-free proof search height. The work advances both proof theory and complexity for fixed-point linear logic.
arxiv-2602-10380:
Breaking complex claims into sub-claims is often proposed as a verification fix, yet results have been inconsistent. A 2026 paper led by Mahmud Elahi Akhter, with four co-authors, blames two overlooked bottlenecks: poor evidence alignment and sub-claim error patterns. They build a dataset of real-world complex claims with temporally bounded evidence. Annotated spans link each sub-claim to its evidence. They test two setups: sub-claim aligned evidence, giving each sub-claim its own evidence, and repeated claim-level evidence, reusing the whole claim's evidence throughout.

Decomposition helps substantially only with fine-grained evidence tied to each sub-claim. Standard setups reusing claim-level evidence fail to improve and often degrade performance. The pattern holds across PHEMEPlus, MMM-Fact, and COVID-Fact. When sub-claim labels are noisy, the authors show, the error's nature shapes downstream robustness. Pipelines must therefore mind both alignment and label quality.
arxiv-2602-10480:
Hongyu Zhao and four co-authors combine neural and symbolic models to build better world models in a 2026 paper. Language models reason flexibly but hallucinate when asked to follow strict deterministic rules, mainly in corner cases. Symbolic models follow rules exactly but lack meaning range. Each covers the other's weakness.

Their system, NeSyS, alternates training between the two models on paths the other explains poorly. The symbolic side scores candidate transitions through log-linear reranking, without forcing the language model to read rule text. Rule-guided sampling focuses effort on transitions symbolic rules cover weakly. The result, the authors report, is a world model with both expressivity and the logical consistency that planning demands.
arxiv-2602-10580:
Quang Dinh Thien Nguyen and three co-authors extend random approximation theory to heavy-tailed noise in a 2026 paper. Older settling results assume square-integrable noise, under which any non-summable but square-summable step size suffices. Many machine learning and work problems violate that assumption, with noise of endless spread.

The authors study settling to a fixed point under a negative drift setting and a general noise sequence with only a finite moment above one. They portray which step-size strings promise almost sure settling in this broader setting. They also show where older step-size guidance becomes too conservative when stronger noise settings hold. The results give builders settling promises matched to the noise they face.
arxiv-2602-10680:
Vicente Conde Mendes and six co-authors construct a model where uneven autoencoders beat linear methods provably in a 2026 paper. Real datasets often hide structure that linear links cannot see: latent factors may act in concert while remaining invisible to covariance. Neural networks routinely extract such structure, but rigorous minimal models of the advantage have been missing.

Their tractable large spiked model carries two latent factors: one visible to covariance, one statistically dependent yet uncorrelated, appearing only in higher-order moments. Principal part analysis and linear autoencoders fail to recover the second factor, while a minimal uneven autoencoder provably extracts both. The model also reveals a mismatch: test loss can misalign with transfer, warning builders not to trust loss alone.
arxiv-2602-10880:
Minggui He and seven co-authors improve chart-to-code making with structural supervision in a 2026 paper. Vision-language models can generate plotting code from chart images, yet structural fidelity lags. Supervised fine-tuning encourages token imitation rather than faithful modeling of chart structure, producing hallucinated or inconsistent outputs.

Their chart specification is an ordered intermediate model that shifts training from text imitation to meaning-based supervision. It filters syntactic noise to build a structurally even training set and supports a spec-align reward giving fine-grained, verifiable feedback on structural correctness. Reward-based learning then enforces consistent plotting logic. Tests on three public benchmarks show consistent gains over prior methods.
arxiv-2602-10980:
Robot brains trained in simulation often stumble in real rooms. Yuhao Chen and thirteen co-authors offer RADAR, a benchmark that tests vision-language-action models under real-world change. It targets three gaps: shifting scenes, weak spatial tests, and costly human judging.

RADAR pairs a suite of physical changes, such as moved objects, new starts, light shifts, and sensor noise, with tasks that probe shape and space sense. Judging runs on its own, using 3D scores rather than flat ones or human raters. Audits of leading models show sharp falls under mild change, with one score dropping steeply under noise and spatial sense proving thin. The benchmark aims to make real-world robot claims harder to fake.
arxiv-2602-11080:
Fitting Gaussian models without a prior calls for a other kind of inference. Hank Flury and two co-authors build a fiducial Markov chain Monte Carlo method for parametric Gaussian models. A Cayley transform splits the covariance matrix, yielding a general recipe for generating Gaussian data.

Constrained generalized fiducial inference then shapes an MCMC sampler that needs little model-specific effort and targets the correct fiducial spread, as proved in the paper. No independence or identical spread need be assumed, which suits time series and spatial data. Simulations on moving-average and Matérn models perform well, showing the method's broad reach.
arxiv-2602-11180:
Language models decide in ways no one can yet read. Usman Naseem, writing alone, surveys inner clarity for matching, from circuit discovery and trait visualization to signal steering and causal move. He asks how those tools have shaped matching methods like feedback tuning, constitutional AI, and scalable oversight.

Key obstacles include overlap, polysemantic neurons, and emergent conduct in large models. The survey proposes automated clarity, cross-model circuit transfer, and matching techniques driven by clarity itself. It serves readers who want one map of a fast field, and a case for building matching on grasp rather than on scores alone.
arxiv-2602-11380:
Nanomachines that swim and signal at once face a coupled design problem. Shaojie Zhang and Ozgur B. Akan offer a chemo-hydrodynamic transceiver model for catalytic Janus particles, where optical control drives both molecule emission and self-propulsion. Most abstractions decouple mobility from communication, missing their contact.

Their random channel model shows actuation-induced distance jitter can dominate received-signal variance. Stronger actuation boosts emission but can sharply cut trust through motion-induced fading, giving a unimodal trust profile with a key actuation level. The optimal control level scales roughly linearly with link distance. Ignoring active motility noise can understate bit error by orders of magnitude, a warning for bio-nano network design.
arxiv-2602-11480:
Two hyperon resonances may hide other inner structures. Yuan Gao and two co-authors study production of Lambda(1405) and Lambda(1520) in pion-proton spread with an effective Lagrangian approach including Regge paths. Parts from two exchange channels are fitted globally to total and differential cross sections.

Fits agree well with test data. One channel dominates Lambda(1405) production, while the other dominates Lambda(1520), and their differential shapes differ distinctly, reflecting other mechanisms. Constituent counting suggests Lambda(1520) fits a usual three-quark picture, while Lambda(1405) deviates clearly, hinting at a more exotic structure. Reconstruction through a three-body final state proves experimentally feasible, guiding future high-precision measurements.
arxiv-2602-11680:
Recommending a bundle of items together is hard when new bundles appear constantly, since most models learn only from observed user-bundle interactions and treat each bundle as an isolated case. Yihang Li and two co-authors propose EpicCBR, a multi-view contrastive framework for cold-start bundle recommendation that mines item relations to build user profiles and spot likely bundle users. A popularity-based method characterizes new bundles from historical bundle information and user preferences.

A multi-view graph contrastive design then fuses cold-start and warm-start scenarios into one framework, aiming for generalization across both. On three popular benchmarks the method beats the state of the art by a large margin, up to 387 percent, in the cold-start setting. For shops that constantly assemble new bundles, that gap suggests relations between items carry far more signal than bundle histories alone.
arxiv-2602-11980:
Diffusion models paint beautiful images yet often fumble spatial reasoning, and existing fixes either cost heavily in joint training or lose spatial detail through text-only prompts. Wei Chen and eleven co-authors propose Spatial Chain-of-Thought, a plug-and-play framework bridging multimodal language model reasoning with diffusion generation. First, the diffusion model gains layout awareness by training on an interleaved text-coordinate instruction format.

Then state-of-the-art multimodal models act as planners, producing comprehensive layout plans whose spatial planning transfers directly into generation. Experiments show state-of-the-art results on image generation benchmarks and large gains over baselines on complex reasoning tasks, with strong performance in image editing as well. By separating planning from painting, the framework gives diffusion models spatial sense without retraining them jointly.
arxiv-2602-12080:
Soccer event data still depends on labor-heavy manual annotation, and ball tracking is too costly to scale beyond top leagues. Hyunsung Kim and five co-authors propose PathCRF, spotting on-ball soccer events from player trajectories alone, without ball data. Player paths form a fully connected dynamic graph, and event detection becomes choosing exactly one edge, the current possession state, at each timestep.

A conditional random field forbids bad transitions between consecutive edges, with emission and transition scores computed live from edge codes of a socio-time backbone. Viterbi decoding yields the most probable edge sequence, and events like ball controls or passes are detected whenever the chosen edge changes between timesteps. Experiments show accurate, sound control paths, enabling reliable downstream analysis while greatly reducing manual work.
arxiv-2602-12180:
Aligning a language model usually means learning from ranked pairs of answers while staying near a reference model. Yurong Chen led this work with three co-authors, asking how the choice of samples and reference shapes what is learned. Using Identity Preference Optimization as the lens, they show that well-chosen, case-dependent sampling can sharpen ranking, while skewed sampling can over-concentrate answers.

They then trace what happens when a trained model feeds its own samples and references into the next round, as often happens in practice. For some settings, that loop swings without settling or collapses toward narrow outputs, and the paper maps the settings that stay stable. Tests on real preference data back the theory, which also carries over to Direct Preference Optimization.
arxiv-2602-12280:
Visual illusions usually play with space, but a sketch can also change meaning over time as strokes are added. Huai-Hsun Cheng led this work with two co-authors, introducing progressive semantic illusions in vector sketching. Their system, Stroke of Surprise, tunes vector strokes so one sketch reads as one object early on, then as a second object once more strokes arrive.

The dual constraint is strict: early strokes must form a coherent first object, such as a duck, while also forming the base for a second, such as a sheep. A sequence-aware joint optimisation, driven by a dual-branch score distillation method, adjusts early strokes rather than freezing them, and an overlay loss keeps parts complementary rather than occluding. Tests beat top baselines on recognisability and illusion strength.
arxiv-2602-13080:
Turing patterns arise when diffusion destabilises a uniform state, but most network models use scalar edge weights, sometimes with uniform cross-diffusion. Anna Gallo and two co-authors study pattern formation on matrix-weighted networks, where each edge carries a matrix weight. Aiming at tidy networks, they describe coherence through node-linked orthonormal matrices, so link transformations become relative rotations between nodes.

That picture handles tidy networks of any size and supports a change of variables reducing matrix-weighted diffusion to ordinary scalar-weighted diffusion. The standard Turing analysis then extends to matrix-weighted networks, yielding rules for a even equilibrium to lose calm. Network topology, scalar weights, and transformations between nodes jointly shape patterns, giving a constructive system for analysing and designing Turing patterns on richer networked systems.
arxiv-2602-13280:
Simulated students could help train tutoring systems and test teaching ideas, but real student data is private and costly to gather over time. Language models offer a shortcut with a flaw: they aim for slick correctness, unlike novices who struggle, stall, and err in messy ways. BEAGLE corrects that bias with a neuro-symbolic design grounded in self-regulated learning theory, timing mental moves with a semi-Markov model and injecting real knowledge gaps through Bayesian knowledge tracing.

A split design also keeps strategy apart from code writing, so the model cannot quietly fix its own planned mistakes. On Python tasks, BEAGLE beat leading baselines at mimicking real learning paths, and in a human test with 71 judges, its traces were told apart from real student work at chance level. Hanchen David Wang leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13580:
Cold atomic and molecular gas appears in galactic winds, yet how cool clouds survive inside hot winds and where they come from is poorly understood. This paper models cool clouds in the Milky Way's nuclear wind over time, clouds whose molecular-to-atomic hydrogen ratios match neither disc values nor chemical equilibrium predictions. Gas in equilibrium cannot produce the observed carbon monoxide and atomic hydrogen emission, the authors confirm.

Instead, a molecule-dominated cloud stripped of its atomic envelope, not yet settled into a new equilibrium, can match observations. Such clouds hold large molecular reservoirs and anomalously large CO-to-H2 conversion factors, implying observed cloud masses may exceed earlier disc-based estimates, and that the nuclear outflow may be more mass-loaded than thought. Karlie A. Noon leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14080:
Nitay Calderon and four co-authors argue in a 2026 arXiv paper that recall, not missing knowledge, is the main bottleneck for factual language models. Standard tests lump all errors together, hiding whether a fact was never stored or merely could not be fetched. The team profiles facts by whether they are encoded and how easily they can be recalled.

Their WikiProfile benchmark, built with web-grounded model prompts, underpins 4 million responses from 13 models. Frontier models encoded 95 to 98% of facts, yet recall failures were common, hitting long-tail facts and reverse questions hardest. Extra thinking time at inference recovered many failures, suggesting future gains may come from better use of stored knowledge, not just larger models.
arxiv-2602-14180:
Prashant Singh and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv trapping problem with a Sokoban twist. A random walker moves through a disordered field of obstacles and can push some blockers out of its path. In one dimension, the walker may push up to Np obstacles at once, a setting where trapping theory meets active escape.

For large Np, survival odds cross from exponential decay at mid times to stretched-exponential decay at long times, with exponent 1/3 regardless of Np. That long-time exponent matches Balagurov-Vaks-Donsker-Varadhan theory, while the mid-time decay departs from Rosenstock theory. In two dimensions, simulations give stretched-exponential relaxation with exponent 1/2, again matching BVDV theory, for both the base and generalized models.
arxiv-2602-14280:
Nick Polson and one co-author present a 2026 arXiv optimizer for losses with a variance-mean scale-mixture form. Under that form, each EM step becomes a weighted least-squares update, with latent variables setting observation and parameter weights. Those weights play roles like Adam's second-moment scaling and AdamW's weight decay, but they arise from the model itself.

The resulting Scale Mixture EM needs no user-set learning-rate or momentum schedules. On ill-conditioned logistic regression benchmarks with 20 to 500 parameters, the Nesterov-accelerated version reached up to 13 times lower final loss than grid-searched Adam. Sharing sufficient statistics across a 40-point regularization path cut runtime tenfold versus the same Adam protocol, though Nesterov extrapolation trades EM monotonicity for speed.
arxiv-2602-14480:
Meixia Lin and two co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv penalized setup for fits on space-time matrix data. Such data show up widely, yet fitting is hard due to tangled, size-tied ties. The model uses a fused penalty to grasp smooth time change and a graph-led penalty to push space likeness, widening to multi-task settings for joint guessing across tied tasks.

Theory study proves stats steadiness of the guessers, while compute uses a deft solver based on the Halpern Peaceman-Rachford method for the joined convex tune problem. The method hits a fast global non-ergodic order 1 over k settling rate with low per-round cost. Wide number tests weigh the setup, showing its worth for space-time fits where time and space mix.
arxiv-2602-14680:
Maps between triangulated shapes have a measure of how hard they are to deform. Nilay Ekiz Yazici, with Nursultan Kuanyshov and Ayse Borat as co-authors, builds the m-contiguity distance as a staged ladder toward that measure. Each rung gives a coarser gauge that sits below the full one.

The new gauge stays the same under strong shape sameness and meets the full gauge when the source has dimension m. Its traits under splits, chains, and products are set out in full. As spin-offs, the authors define the m-simplicial Lusternik-Schnirelmann category and the m-discrete topological complexity as cases of the same gauge. The frame gives a step path to full shape complexity.
arxiv-2602-14980:
Maisenbacher and colleagues put the Standard Model through its sharpest test yet with atomic hydrogen. Quantum electrodynamics predicts hydrogen energy levels to many digits, so constants drawn from different transitions must agree if the theory holds. Recent atomic hydrogen values for the proton charge radius partly disagreed with each other and with a sharper muonic hydrogen value, blocking a test at full experimental precision.

The team measures the 2S-6P transition precisely enough to tell the discrepant values apart. Their proton radius, about 0.84 femtometres, is more than twice as precise as prior atomic hydrogen values and matches the muonic value well. The measured frequency agrees with the Standard Model prediction to less than one part per trillion, testing bound-state quantum electrodynamics corrections to about half a part per million.
arxiv-2602-15080:
AlMasri explores the geometry of quantum logic gates inside the holomorphic picture of quantum mechanics. The physical qubit space is embedded into a space of functions homogeneous of degree one in each Schwinger boson pair. Within that setting, the paper derives closed-form rules for a universal gate set. The set includes Pauli, Hadamard, CNOT, CZ, and SWAP. All of them preserve the physical space exactly.

Restricting to unit-magnitude variables reveals a toroidal space. On it, gates act as canonical transforms. Pauli gates drive Hamiltonian flows. Hadamard induces a nonlinear automorphism. Entangling gates yield correlated diffeomorphisms coupling distinct factors of that space. Beyond the torus, the full Segal-Bargmann space carries a natural Kahler form ruling amplitude dynamics. Entanglement is read through the Segre embedding into complex projective space. Topological protection follows from the fiber bundle structure of the Jordan-Schwinger constraint.
arxiv-2602-15280:
Reinders and colleagues present a multi-mode data use design combining chat AI with refreshable tactile displays for people who are blind or have low vision. To support labs and builders building open charts with touch screens, the team offers the design and a sample build. Their system is the first to combine touch input with a chat agent on a touch screen. It enables questions fusing touch context with voice words, such as asking about the trend between two points.

The design tackles key hurdles: touch feeling on screens, visual-to-touch coding, joining touch context with chat AI, and syncing multi-mode results. The work gives two things: a design joining screen gear, outside touch feeling, and chat AI; and a sample build showing promise. This work provides a base for later study in multi-mode open charting.
arxiv-2602-15480:
Tomar and Rani build a new kind of normal space, which they call meekly SC-star normal. In topology, normal spaces are those where closed sets can be kept apart by open sets, and the authors widen that old idea in two ways at once. Their frame takes in SC-star normal spaces and other known forms of normality, so several separate lines of work sit under one roof.

The chapter works out the basic traits of these spaces, gives matching ways to spot them, and maps how they relate to kindred normal-type spaces. It also ties the new frame to work on broad kinds of closed sets and on separation rules. For readers of pure topology, it offers both a tidier map of known results and fresh paths for next steps.
arxiv-2602-15780:
Henao Arbeláez and colleagues build an AI model of the point spread function, or PSF. It beats the current best approach, PIFF. PIFF is used in weak-lensing surveys including DES, HSC, and Rubin LSST. The PSF describes how a point source such as a star is imaged after light crosses air and optics. It is the blurred fingerprint of the whole imaging system.

Accurate PSF modelling matters. Biases in PSF estimation feed straight into cosmic shear measures, a main probe of cosmic expansion and structure growth for dark energy studies. PIFF builds models per CCD alone, losing coherence across the focal plane. The new hybrid model trains an autoencoder on HSC star images and pairs it with a Gaussian process to fill in the PSF across the full field. It reaches a rebuild error of 3.4 times ten to the minus six against PIFF 3.7, laying groundwork for LSST pipelines.
arxiv-2602-15880:
Bian and colleagues join Newton-type thresholding with ReLU methods for sparse signal recovery with no negative values. Such recovery has wide uses and a long research history. Recent work has used rectified linear units to boost older recovery methods.

The team offers two methods. The first is Newton-Direction-Based ReLU-Thresholding, or NDRT. The second is its stronger form, Newton-Direction-Based ReLU-Thresholding Pursuit, or NDRTP. Theory shows both can recover such signals exactly when the measure matrix meets a set condition. Tests show NDRTP matching top rivals in both noisy and noiseless cases.
arxiv-2602-16580:
Fabian Faulstich and co-authors extend algebro-geometric results for coupled cluster theory. They study the doubles truncation variety for four electrons, the first genuinely nonlinear doubles regime. This variety differs from earlier studied ones. The paper opens a systematic study of its basic invariants, mixing theory with numerical evidence. For four electrons on enough orbitals, the variety is a complete intersection of a stated degree. A Pfaffian structure lies behind its quadratic relations.

An exact tensor product factorization holds in a limit of disconnected doubles. The structural results are tied to a small but hard test case. That case is beryllium insertion into molecular hydrogen, where multiconfigurational effects run strong. Quantum chemists and algebraic geometers get new exact structure for a workhorse approximation method.
arxiv-2602-17180:
Alexander Setescak led an eleven-author team turning a hard magnetic imaging problem into a tractable one. Rebuilding magnetization textures from nitrogen-vacancy stray-field data is ill-posed at heart, and the sensor-to-sample gap is usually unknown. The paper builds a micromagnetic energy term directly into the inversion, filtering out unphysical high-energy layouts.

Fourier-space upward continuation of the stray field then lets the gap be fitted at the same time. Applied to the van der Waals ferromagnet iron gallium telluride, the method found a plausible gap size and low-energy layouts matching the observed field. More broadly, building physics into rebuilding makes magnetic inverse problems clear and interpretable, with uses well beyond nitrogen-vacancy magnetometry.
arxiv-2602-17280:
Arshia Dutta led a two-author study of how refugees and asylum seekers in the UK experience border control and the wider immigration system, and how those encounters shape later life.
