They define fractional bandlimited signals, prove a sampling and perfect-reconstruction result, and design several sampling strategies around cutoff frequency, error, and localized bases. A fast selection method built on a joint vertex-and-spectrum localization operator rounds out the theory. Tests show it beats graph Fourier methods on reconstruction error and speed.
arxiv-2605-26280: Olga Soloveva and three colleagues' 2026 trigger uses a convolutional network to spot quark-gluon plasma events live, as reconstructed collisions stream in. Events become compact histograms of particle species, momentum size, and angular data. The concept is tested first in the Parton-Hadron-String Dynamics framework, where true plasma labels exist, then validated on UrQMD simulations. For gold-gold collisions at 30 GeV per nucleon, accuracy falls from ninety-five point one percent at generator level to eighty-three point seven percent after reconstruction, while keeping practical separation power.
arxiv-2605-26380: Jingru Chen and seven colleagues' 2026 benchmark, VisualNeedle, tests whether multimodal models genuinely search images or lean on shortcuts. Three shortcuts inflate scores elsewhere: linguistic priors in questions, coarse semantics bypassing local detail, and tool images whose corruption barely changes answers. VisualNeedle hides critical evidence in minute regions of dense scenes, and a crop-black ablation swaps tool crops for black images. Text-only accuracy stays below ten percent, tool-free accuracy below twenty percent, and the best tool model reaches fifty-six percent, trailing human accuracy of sixty-three percent.
arxiv-2605-26480: Jing-Juan Qi and five colleagues split CP asymmetry in heavy-meson decays into interference and non-interference parts. Observables integrated over phase space miss higher wave-expansion terms in the squared amplitude and drop interference facts. The team partitions phase space at Legendre-polynomial zeros with sign weighting, defining an asymmetry observable and its CP counterpart. In B-meson decay to three pions near the rho-1450 resonance, LHCb data show odd schemes isolate interference well, while even schemes favor non-interference terms. The scheme should extend to other decays.
arxiv-2605-26580: Taekyun Lee and three others present CIDER, a learned decoder for shared-codebook random access where many senders transmit at once. The receiver must untangle slot evidence into distinct codewords under parity rules. CIDER mixes masked-diffusion refinement, cross-row demixing, and parity-aware message passing on the code graph, re-decoding shaky rows at high load. On GF(64) LDPC codes it beats two belief-propagation rivals on error rates and runs 8.2 to 167 times faster in decoder-only timing.
arxiv-2605-26680: Peng Zhang and twelve others present DynFrame, a video-understanding frame that learns both where to look and how densely to sample. Existing thinking-with-video systems fix frame rates per window and credit looking and answering with one shared score, forcing repeated retrievals. DynFrame emits window and density as tokens in one pass. It then splits credit at the retrieval boundary so sampling and answering earn separate rewards. Its 4B model rivals 7B to 8B rivals on six benches, and its 8B model sets new bests on most metrics.
arxiv-2605-27280: Sumana Hatui and Poonam Nayak describe the cocycles giving faithful projective representations of finite groups. A p-group admits a faithful irreducible projective representation exactly when its class avoids the inflation image for every nontrivial central subgroup. They then define a group's projective embedding degree as the smallest n with a faithful complex projective representation. The second half of the work studies these degrees across group families.
arxiv-2605-27480: Tianyao Shi and Yi Ding measure the biodiversity cost of serving large language models. Their BIRDS framework defines request-level units, counts operational and embodied ecological damage, and adds a quality-normalized impact metric joining damage to response quality. Across workloads, models, hardware, and regions, impact grows with scale and exposes quality-aware serving tradeoffs.
arxiv-2605-28680: Kuntal Ghosh, Marc Hassenzahl, and Shadan Sadeghian examine how AI affects perceived job decency and meaningfulness at work. Through interviews with 24 employees across IT, service, and healthcare sectors, they study satisfaction now and in the future. Anticipated overall satisfaction varies by occupation, with IT and healthcare expecting better decency such as working hours but worse meaningfulness such as social image, fearing misconceptions that AI handles most tasks. Service workers instead foresee no better hours but higher social standing from the status boost of working with AI.
arxiv-2605-28780: Thomas Vitry, Kieran Edgeworth, Stefan Wermter, and Jae Hee Lee present a label-free method for finding spurious concepts in frozen models. Per target class they gather patches from inputs of that class and factor activations into interpretable concept vectors. Candidate concepts rank by an estimator from backpropagated gradients on misclassified cases: bias concepts fire correcting false negatives and quiet correcting false positives. On Colored MNIST and Waterbirds it recovers the spurious cue, and suppressing concepts at inference lifts worst-group accuracy by up to 17.9 points on Waterbirds without retraining.
arxiv-2605-28880: Dennis Thumm, Ruben Wiedemann, and Ying Chen build a test for causal models. Stretching Prior-data Fitted Networks to flow time invites a random change rule. But stepping once per viewing gap leaves a grid Markov model. Their test demands path laws stay fixed across viewing schedules, with a three-tier ladder of discrete, naive grid, and fine-grid runs with split viewing. Fine-grid runs beat naive on eight cells. The gap grows as grids refine. The encoder axis is null with fine runs.
arxiv-2605-29080: Béla Csaba proves that a bounded-degree tree on n vertices embeds in a non-extremal n-vertex graph when minimum degree falls below half of n by a linear term. The proof avoids the Regularity lemma, using instead the author's vertex decomposition theorem that needs no tower-type lower bound on n. The result gives a stability theorem for spanning-tree embedding: graphs just below the degree threshold still contain every bounded-degree spanning tree, unless extremal. The argument trades heavy regularity machinery for a leaner decomposition approach.
arxiv-2605-29180: Yicheng Mao and Rob Deardon replace costly Monte Carlo runs for spatial epidemic models with neural posterior estimation. The new method trains a conditional flow on simulated data to gauge the posterior, with no likelihood sums. Designs compared: a convolutional network on incidence curves, and a graph network on individual infection and location data. Both reach coverage near the target level, with the graph giving lower error and narrower intervals. In the 2001 UK foot-and-mouth outbreak on 1,177 farms, both recover the reproduction number, with the graph narrower but shifted.
arxiv-2605-29280: Hua Zheng proposes LoopFM, which opens a wider transfer channel from foundation models to compact vertical models. Standard distillation transfers only a single scalar prediction, so much improvement is lost. LoopFM instead uses intermediate embeddings as input features for downstream models, without live model runs or design coupling. The authors provide a theory with a gain split and transfer-ratio analysis. On three public benchmarks, LoopFM shows strong gains and added transfer, and on large-scale systems it about doubles the transfer ratio.
arxiv-2605-29380: Hesam Asadollahzadeh and colleagues develop TRACER, for many-mode tuning with control. Standard tuning methods degrade out of distribution strength, known as catastrophic forgetting. The authors develop a tool for contrast tuning, yielding closed form answers and a split. Analysis shows self teaching is better than control methods at keeping pretrained knowledge. It also reveals a flaw: moving average teachers suffer from collapse. They prove a weighted teacher maintains a lasting control force and yields clean settling in the subspace. Experiments on CLIP tuning show out of distribution gains.
arxiv-2605-29480: Moirangthem Tiken Singh proposes a dual-stream network for forecasting outcomes in mixed-motive negotiations, where spoken words and hard limits like budgets both shape the result. One stream reads dialogue with transformer encoders while a graph stream tracks economic states, and a gated fusion step shifts weight between language and strategy as the task demands. A fairness-aware loss penalizes gaps between predicted and true utility differences, cutting measured inequality discrepancy by 43.8% in high-disparity settings with little accuracy loss.
arxiv-2605-29580: Daniel Dold and four colleagues ask whether low-loss valleys link separate optima in low-rank adaptation space, where discrete ensembles help little. They introduce LoRA-Curve, a Bézier curve in segmented free and anchored forms, the latter joining separately tuned optima. They prove continuity and Lipschitz regularity of loss along the curve. Tests show straight-line blends hit loss barriers, while anchored curves join optima through low-loss valleys. With flat-minima tweaks plus a divergence regularizer, the method raises predictive mutual information without losing performance.
arxiv-2605-29780: José M. Amigó and Roberto Dale survey transcript-based tools for coupled time series through algebra. Algebraic representations code series symbols as group elements, with ordinal patterns from permutations as the prototype. Transcripts, mapping one group element to another, suit coupling studies since they involve two elements at once. The paper covers entropic tools like divergence, statistical complexity, and mutual information, plus algebraic tools like order classes and Cayley-Kendall distances. A similarity distance, a mean Kendall distance, is tested on generalized synchronization detection and beats the others tried.
arxiv-2605-29980: Muhammed Furkan Dasdelen and five colleagues line up single white blood cell images with karyotypes and gene-panel mutations for blood-cancer diagnosis. Training runs in two stages: vision-only pretraining of a transformer aggregator on over fifteen hundred patients, then genetic lining up on acute myeloid leukemia patients. The lined patient encoder beats slide-level histopathology models on blood diagnosis tasks. It also offers retrieval for diseases and genetic changes. Folding genetic data into patient encoders lifts quality and matches clinical workflow, opening the way to blood-specific AI.
arxiv-2605-30080: Thang Dang, Akira Nakagawa, Kenichi Kobayashi and Koichi Shirahata propose Adaptive Targeted Dynamic Chunking for tokenization-free models that read raw bytes, not preset vocabularies. Byte models dodge vocabulary design and unknown-word errors, but their quality hinges on chunk compression ratios. Their method raises compression gradually during training through curriculum learning, and links the target ratio to bytes per innermost chunk. On FineWeb-Edu 100B, chunked models match byte- and token-level baselines on bits per byte, with steadier training and stronger downstream scores.
arxiv-2605-30180: Han Gao and four co-authors compute thermal dilepton emission and polarization in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. Their setup joins virtual photon spectra complete at next order in the strong coupling with fluid simulations. Dilepton polarization responds to in-medium traits of the quark-gluon plasma. For lead collisions at LHC runs, they track how strong polarization is across frames and how early gluon abundance affects it. They derive a direct mapping between dielectron and dimuon polarization.
arxiv-2605-30380: Surendar Devasundaram, Banafsheh Saber Latibari and Abhijit Mahalanobis propose SURGE, a way to teach a small ship-spotting model from a big teacher model for SAR images. It passes shape links from teacher to student with an InfoNCE goal in a shared space. The method works with two-stage, one-stage, and transformer models, with no change to how they run. Tests on the SSDD and HRSID sets show big gains for two-stage models, up to about six mAP points and eight AP75 points over the base student.
arxiv-2605-30580: Paudel and colleagues test speculative decoding, drafting tokens with a small model for a large one to check, across eleven languages. The speedup, well studied in English, largely evaporates for low-resource languages whose small draft models lack multilingual skill. Distilling the large model into the draft model generalized poorly across tasks in the same language, suggesting a fully representative task-agnostic dataset is infeasible there. Weaker n-gram draft models, by contrast, delivered moderate speedups simply because they cost almost nothing to run.
arxiv-2605-30680: Wang and colleagues recast mechanism design as program synthesis. Current benchmarks freeze provider response, so they cannot judge mechanisms by their equilibrium. Their typed rule programs run through Medi-Sim, a simulator with five channels: coding, selection, delay, effort, and triage. An incentive sweep recovers findings as regimes, including up-coding and selection of easy cases under profit pressure, and Goodhart-style drift. Closing the coding channel more than doubles selection of easy cases, while search synthesizes a program that eliminates up-coding, halves rejection, and keeps funds.
arxiv-2605-30880: Bai and colleagues learn world models for text agents from trajectories, without a latent state or transition model. Their PatchWorld turns offline trajectories into executable Python world models through code repair. Instead of black-box next prediction, it induces symbolic programs whose updates can be inspected, replayed, and patched. Across seven environments, the simple version scores highest among code methods, matching or beating language-model lookahead with no language-model calls inside prediction. A memory bias improves fidelity but weakens decision utility, revealing a fidelity-action trade-off.
arxiv-2605-30980: Lei offers DREAM, a strategy for Bayesian calibration of costly nuclear models. Missing exact gradients in legacy codes has blocked full fitting. DREAM samples the system offline, shrinks it by singular value factors, and rebuilds it online. Gradients then follow at the cost of one extra run per Monte Carlo step. Applied to coupled-channels deuteron-nickel elastic scattering with eighteen optical values, sampling settles on a single graphics chip in under ten minutes, yielding a posterior.
arxiv-2605-31180: Nimr and colleagues study focused beams sent from groups of satellites that work together. When timing is perfect, a method called maximum-ratio transmission makes the received power grow with the square of the satellite count. But small errors in timing, motion and position eat away that joint gain until the beams add up without coherence. Group shape also governs pointing and separation. Strong side lobes limit how finely space can be split, so the authors call for joint beam and precoding design.
arxiv-2605-31280: Martin Contreras and colleagues study the thermal response of the rho meson in an isospectral family of the soft-wall AdS/QCD model. Working out spectra at finite temperature and chemical potential, they isolate how the ground-state decay constant shapes the melting point. The melting point rises slowly with that constant, backing its role as a key scale for quarkonium dissociation. Fixing the constant to its known value gives a melting point of 157 MeV and a smooth shift from confinement to deconfinement.
arxiv-2605-31480: Evelo, Fowlie, and Paperno test whether language models truly grasp reference in a compositional way. They use a task about people and their relations. One part asks what a phrase like Amber's parent's friend points to in the world. The other asks for its sense as a nested formula. People do better on the first part, and models on the second. The authors read this split as a sign that missing real-world grounding in model training blocks human-like understanding.
arxiv-2606-00180:
Chen and co-authors tackle a hard snag in brain-based tests for deep sadness. Brain wave tests for this ill health need large data sets. Small sets are the norm in clinics. Fake added data can blur the line that tests must draw, and it costs much to make.

Their frame, SGC, makes no fake cases at all. A self-taught net grades how odd each brain trace looks. That grade acts as a clue drawn from ill health signs. The clue is smoothed, then fused with deep traits from the trace. A cross-channel part adapts the tool to rigs with varied wire counts. Tests on two data sets show strong scores with no fake data at all.
arxiv-2606-00280:
Maloney and co-authors chase a faint sky drift that should mark our own motion. The solar system moves against the glow left from the big bang. That move should shift far galaxy spots in one shared lean. The lean is tiny, and no team has caught it yet.

The team pairs two Gaia sky maps with range lists for near galaxies. Their full-sky set holds more than 67,000 galaxies. No firm drift shows in the data. Still, they set the tightest cap yet on that drift. For far parts, doubt is ten times the size of the sought mark. For near parts, doubt sits just past the mark's size. Next Gaia drops may cross the line to a true catch.
arxiv-2606-00380:
Andreou and co-authors share a frame to test image unlearning tools in a fair, firm way. Unlearning strips the mark of set data from a trained model. It spares a full retrain from scratch. A fair test must loop train, strip, and grade rounds across many seeds.

That loop costs vast chip time on one chip alone. Their frame, SUPREME, spreads those rounds across many chips. A list-based build lets teams add new tools, marks, and scenes with ease. It takes more than one chip type and math grade. A face-set demo runs full-class and part-strip cases on two net types. Ten seeds run in that demo to show the frame at work.
arxiv-2606-00680:
Lin, Wang, and Zheng work on learning from fixed data in this 2026 paper. In offline reinforcement learning, an agent must learn a good policy from old logs, with no new trials. The hard part is doubt: the logs cover few cases, and the true dynamics stay unclear from finite data.

The team puts both kinds of doubt in one Bayesian frame, where the dynamics count as a random draw. Their method, PhyB, rewrites a hard average as a weighted mix over a small set of dynamics models. They prove the error from this shortcut stays bounded. On top of it they build a training loop with a penalty term. The loop is shown to improve step by step till it settles. The authors report top scores on several standard tests.
arxiv-2606-00780:
Qian and co-authors help software agents adapt to new tasks in this 2026 paper. Their field is offline meta-reinforcement learning. Agents learn from fixed datasets, then must cope with environments they have never seen. Shifts in context and in past behavior policy can trap them in stale patterns. Sparse rewards make the trap worse.

Their frame joins two parts. One part learns task features that stay the same no matter which behavior policy made the data. This cuts the harm from context shift. The second part is a Transformer-based world model that dreams up rollouts of future play. A cautious value penalty stops the policy from exploiting flaws in that model. In broad tests, the authors report, the method beats top prior work. It stays stable and adapts well under out-of-distribution tests and sparse rewards. The work targets agents that must generalize from logs alone.
arxiv-2606-00880:
Seth and co-authors ask how task variety shapes agents that keep learning in this 2026 paper. Continual RL aims at agents that never stop adapting. Training on many diverse tasks is known to build strong zero-shot skill. But past work froze the agent's weights before testing.

Their domain, Banyan, runs on GPUs and varies three axes of a task. Map layouts, target objects, and subgoal chains can each be dialed up or down. More diversity gives systematic transfer: agents start each new task near their last score. This holds even when the best policy changes shape. But too much diversity hurts, they find. Learners plateau on new tasks while still improving on old ones, with no fresh play on them. The result is a trade-off at the heart of lifelong learning. Variety builds a springboard and a ceiling.
arxiv-2606-01080:
Saini and Pandey move the gains of slow thinking into a fast model's weights in this 2026 paper. Thinking models solve hard tasks by writing a reasoning trace first. That trace costs time, tokens, and serving complexity. Their procedure, ThinkSwitch, co-trains a paired instruct and thinking checkpoint in a loop.

Each round, the thinking model answers task prompts. The trace is stripped, and the answer only pairs are distilled into the instruct model with QLoRA. Spherical weight interpolation then rebuilds a fresh thinking model. Only the prompts are human supplied. On 30 AIME questions, the instruct model climbs from 10 to 20 correct, they report. The thinking model rises from 14 to 22. A PubMedQA subset shows like gains. The whole run uses 15 prompts per domain and costs under three dollars on one cloud card.
arxiv-2606-01280:
Capogrosso, Bonazzi, and Magno review event-based vision for use in space. Earth observation is shifting with new sensor types. Frame cameras blur, draw power, and repeat data in orbit. Event cameras report only local light changes. They give microsecond timing and huge dynamic range. They also sip power compared with frame cameras. Yet writing on their space use stays scattered.

Their survey sorts the field into four domains. These cover air and high-speed observation first. Next come environment checks and change detection. Onboard support and processing form the third group. Geospatial modeling and forecasts form the fourth. They argue this is a paradigm shift, not a minor add-on.
arxiv-2606-01480:
Roohi asks if a correct heat-flux field certifies a closure state. In rarefied cavities, heat can flow from cold to hot. That anti-Fourier flow signals Fourier-law failure. He studies a two-dimensional monatomic flow in such cavities. The heat-flux hierarchy sees only a composite tensor's divergence. It does not see the fourth-order anisotropy and scalar excess apart. Hidden states can thus shift those parts invisibly. DSMC data for argon lid-driven cavities ground the study.

The anti-Fourier region shrinks as lid speed doubles. It grows when the Knudsen number doubles instead. Shifted states pass key scalar and positivity checks. Yet they change closure parts by order-one amounts. The flux stays below statistical resolution, or exactly unchanged. Agreement is a target, not a certificate.
arxiv-2606-01580:
Hao computes the spin of primordial black holes from phase transitions. First-order phase transitions in the early cosmos nucleate bubbles at random. Start times vary across different Hubble volumes. Regions with delayed transitions gain non-Gaussian density perturbations. Black holes can form from nonspherical collapse in such regions. Hao studies their spin angular momentum in that setting. A nucleation history integration method drives the calculation. No Gaussian distribution is assumed for the perturbations.

He derives mean values and variances for the semi-axis lengths. Overdense ellipsoidal regions supply those lengths. Velocity shear statistics complete the inputs to the spin. The Kerr parameter grows with latent heat strength. It falls as the transition rate rises. Typical values reach about ten to the minus three.
arxiv-2606-01680:
Chen and co-authors keep AllReduce fast when a few network links fail. Network failures are frequent hardware faults in large GPU clusters. They are a leading cause of training-job interruptions. Libraries like NCCL reroute traffic through surviving NICs on a server. Training continues, but the degraded server stays on the critical path. The whole collective slows to its pace. They prove a first information-theoretic lower bound for this setting. It covers AllReduce time under asymmetric bandwidth.

When the straggler keeps half its bandwidth, overhead is tiny. OptCC is their four-stage pipelined algorithm that nears that bound. SimAI experiments confirm it closes the gap of prior schemes. With up to 50 percent bandwidth loss, it runs within 2 to 6 percent of fault-free speed.
arxiv-2606-01780:
Korsky proves new bounds on hitting all long runs in a row of numbers. Take the numbers from zero up to a bound. A set hits a run if it shares a point with it. The runs here are arithmetic progressions. Each run has a fixed step and many terms. The aim is the least set that hits all such runs.

Korsky sharpens a past bound due to Truss. He also sharpens a bound due to Xu for prime cases. The new bounds sit near the square-root scale. They show how small a hitting set can be. The work is pure math with exact growth rates.
arxiv-2606-01880:
Kumar and co-authors study layered Janus materials for flexible electronics. Normal two-dimensional materials shift band gaps under strain. That shift can turn a direct gap indirect. It harms use in bendable nanoelectronic devices. Janus layers break mirror symmetry by design. They carry built-in out-of-plane dipoles as well.

The team studies MoSSe and WSSe paired bilayers. They use first-principles methods for the tests. Interface chemistry shapes how the layers couple. It also drives charge shifts and dipole interplay. Built-in fields plus interface effects suppress gap shifts. Strain resilience thus improves for these stacks. The results point to paths for flexible piezotronics.
arxiv-2606-01980:
Jiang and Zhang compute quantum field energy near a traversable wormhole throat. A static wormhole needs exotic matter to stay open. Morris-Thorne conditions state what that matter must do. Quantum stress-energy tensors are a leading candidate source. No prior calculation covered thermal states at the throat.

The field is a massive scalar in a thermal state. It sits on a zero-tidal-force wormhole background. Dimensionless temperature and mass are varied in the study. Conditions hold only for a bounded mass interval. Each mass in that interval has a critical temperature. Below that threshold, the conditions are fulfilled. Above it, they fail for that mass. The bounds give concrete limits for wormhole models.
arxiv-2606-02080:
Johanns and co-authors build an AI agent for biological microscopy analysis. Image analysis in biology spans many tools and settings. Few researchers command all of them at once. Their Agentic-J assistant is containerised and multi-agent. It focuses mainly on ImageJ and Fiji workflows.

Biologists state analysis tasks in natural language. Tasks range from nuclei segmentation to cell tracking. Multi-condition quantification is also covered by the agent. It writes executable scripts in a documented project layout. Every analysis decision stays traceable that way. Workflows can be reproduced or shared with others. Specialised sub-agents handle plugins, code, and debugging. Quality assurance and statistical reporting have their own agents. Real microscopy workflows demonstrate the system in action.
arxiv-2606-02480:
Perminov reports new fast matrix multiplication schemes for small formats. The work joins two tools: the meta flip graph framework and the serendipitous product construction. The framework now covers all 680 rectangular formats up to 16 by 16 by 16. Ranks improve for 207 formats against the prior best.

Ternary schemes appear for 84 formats where only integer or rational coefficients were known. Twenty-three new schemes beat the exponent log base 2 of 7. That brings the total of such schemes to 52. Across all formats, coefficient types split into 375 ternary, 18 integer, and 287 rational. All code and schemes are open source. The work pushes the frontier for small-format multiplication. It also gives a complete public record of the new schemes.
arxiv-2606-02780:
He and co-authors ask whether deep attention layers need context to build their value vectors. Attention layers normally read the residual stream. Query, key, and value vectors all become context-dependent. The team finds a surprise. Performance improves when deeper layers learn a context-free value vector. That vector preserves the original token information. Adding the context-dependent part back gives little extra benefit on aggregate benchmarks.

Context-free values can be stored as sparse parameters. No recompute or persistent cache is needed for them. Ablations map the key design choices. The result is Bank of Values, a lookup table of token-specific value vectors. It covers the last third of layers. On 135M and 780M models, BoV improves validation loss over standard attention. At 780M, it matches the previous best method's average across 21 benchmarks. It does so with less compute and memory.
arxiv-2606-02980:
Yin and Zhao build TFPARN, a network that spots fake speech in speaker checks. Fake and warped speech can fool such checks. The test is the closed track of ASVspoof 5. Plain cross-entropy training can slight the hard cases, and it does not match the rank-based scores used to grade.

TFPARN takes log-Mel traits from speech and codes them with a transformer. Attention pooling turns them into one vector per clip. Training mixes a focal loss with a pair rank loss. RawBoost noise helps in training, and test-time boosts help at test. Against new builds of AASIST and RawNet2 on the same rules, TFPARN scored best. Its minDCF was 0.2430 and its equal error rate was 12.52 percent. Ablation tests showed each loss and the pooling step helped. It used the least run memory, 1.4 GB, and ran at about 0.79 ms per clip.
arxiv-2606-03280:
Zhang and Xin report a negative result on sending hidden states between language models. Recent work shows models can pass traits through hidden signals in training data. The team asks about a direct channel: can one model hand a useful mid-reasoning state to another at run time? A learned linear bridge would translate activations between the two models, with no text relay.

The test pairs a Pythia-160M sender with a Pythia-410M receiver on multi-hop reasoning. The bridge learned a strong map: cosine similarity near 0.97 across seeds in normalized space. Yet injected activations did not help the receiver answer. Weak additive injection stayed near the no-injection baseline. Replacement injection hurt in every case. Rescaling the vectors to the receiver's norm did not rescue the effect. Offline alignment of representations, at least here, is not enough for causal talk inside the receiver.
arxiv-2606-04080:
Samson Abramsky and Radha Jagadeesan build a framework in 2026 for higher-order quantum computing. Here, quantum operations can themselves be passed as inputs to other operations.

The core tension is unitarity, the rule that quantum steps must be reversible. The authors meet it with a trick from category theory: forms that track which states are set apart. They also import Shock's boundary condition, which keeps time evolution from leaking out of the modeled space. The result is a setting where reversible higher-order computation has a clean mathematical home. Known constructions, including open quantum registers with coherent control, fall out as special cases. The authors present it as a base for future programming languages.
arxiv-2606-04180:
Youqi Wu, Mohammad Jalali, and Farzan Farnia propose a way in 2026 to measure when a vision-language model's words and images pull apart. Such models join a text side and an image side. A quiet gap can open between what the text says and what the image shows.

Their method compares the model's internal maps for paired text and image inputs. It looks for spots where the two maps disagree in a stable, patterned way. Across standard vision-language tests, the method found clear gap patterns tied to groups of samples. It also flagged cases where the two sides interacted badly. From these, the team built concrete subsets that expose the mismatch. The tool gives builders a way to audit cross-modal drift before it ships.
arxiv-2606-04280:
Justinas Zaliaduonis and co-authors clarify in 2026 when contrastive learning truly recovers the hidden shape of data. This self-supervised method pulls matching pairs together and pushes other pairs apart.

The answer hinges on how the positive pairs are sampled. The pairs must cover the latent space richly enough. When they do, the best models recover the true shape up to a rotation. When sampling is narrow, warped maps can score better than the true one. Their corrected loss restores the chance of exact recovery, though not its uniqueness. Tests on synthetic and image data backed the theory. Model design mattered most when the sampling was thin.
arxiv-2606-04580:
Nakano, Koide, and Chiba build a system that turns scattered social media chatter into early-warning cyber threat intelligence, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Threat signals fragment across platforms. Their system, TIBlender, monitors four platforms: X, Reddit, Telegram, and Discord. It uses role-specialized language model agents. They investigate from multiple perspectives. They trace chains of evidence to uncover related indicators of compromise, the fingerprints of an attack.

In a real-world deployment, TIBlender detected emerging threats across all four threat categories ahead of public feeds. It flagged exploitation in the wild before public vulnerability registries listed it. Most of its indicators were absent from each evaluated feed. Each platform contributed unique threat information. Removing any one platform caused substantial losses in specific categories. Given only a single platform, its extraction matched or beat baselines. The full pipeline surfaced substantially more indicators, most absent from every single-platform baseline.
arxiv-2606-04880:
Park and colleagues unify image selection so editors can grab materials, by text or by click, in a 2026 arXiv graphics paper. Selection is a core editing operation, but vision-language selection methods are object-centric and usually accept only one style. Their system, MAOAM, couples a vision-language model that interprets selection intent with a head that decodes the model's output token into a mask.

Because no dataset pairs material masks with text annotations, they build a data pipeline: real and synthetic images with material masks. Training uses a multi-task objective over click-based and text-based selection plus an auxiliary task from those descriptions. Although trained with single-modality prompts, the model improves when text and clicks are combined at inference. Experiments show accurate selections across diverse objects and scenarios.
arxiv-2606-05080:
Zhangchen Xu and a large team introduce AutoLab in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark asking whether frontier AI models can handle long-horizon research and engineering work. Real progress is iterative: propose a change, run an experiment, measure the outcome, and refine again over many cycles. Existing benchmarks mostly test single answers or short agent runs, missing that sustained loop.

AutoLab holds 36 expert-curated tasks in four domains: system optimization, puzzles and challenges, model development, and CUDA kernel optimization. Each task starts from a correct but suboptimal baseline, and agents must improve it within a strict wall-clock budget. Evaluating 17 leading models, the team found the dominant predictor of success was not the quality of the first attempt but persistence: repeatedly benchmarking, editing, and absorbing feedback. One model, claude-opus-4.6, showed strong long-horizon ability, while many others quit early or burned their budgets with minimal progress.
arxiv-2606-05180:
Ivo Bueno and colleagues compare two ways of explaining automated teaching quality scores in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scoring models increasingly assign rubric-based ratings to classroom transcripts, but they rarely show why a score was given, which matters when teachers must trust or contest the judgment. The authors propose a general framework for sentence-level interpretability of such scoring.

The framework pairs model-agnostic Shapley attributions, which assign credit to individual sentences, with rationales generated by large language models. The testbed is the Quality of Feedback dimension of the CLASS framework, with the NCTE corpus of about 6,000 transcript segments. Fine-tuned models beat prompted language models on accuracy but compressed their scores toward the middle. Deletion tests showed SHAP picks sentences that reliably drive predictions, producing larger, more coherent shifts than the rationales. SHAP attributions transferred robustly across architectures, while the rationales influenced other models only weakly.
arxiv-2606-05280:
Rafael Álvarez-García and Fabian Ruehle study how kaleidoscope-like symmetries constrain the prepotential of compactifications in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is type IIA string theory on Calabi-Yau threefolds, where the prepotential controls gauge and Yukawa couplings. Isomorphic flops generate Coxeter symmetries acting on the moduli space, so the prepotential must assemble from Coxeter-invariant functions.

The authors construct a database of Coxeter symmetries arising from isomorphic flops in Kähler-favorable intersection Calabi-Yau manifolds. The action preserves a bilinear form, which they interpret as a metric and use to build its Laplace-Beltrami operator. They argue these functions solve the Helmholtz equation for that Laplacian, so it is resummed as a decomposition into eigenfunctions. Orbit sums over worldsheet instanton contributions and the resummed expressions converge in separate regions, with the new form settling onto its few terms inside moduli space.
arxiv-2606-05380:
Christian Coester, Alexa Tudose, and Alexander Turoczy give learning-augmented algorithms for online minimization driven by dual predictions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Online problems force irrevocable decisions as requests arrive, and learning-augmented algorithms try to exploit predictions without losing worst-case guarantees when the predictions are bad. The prediction used here is unusual: an optimal solution of the dual linear program rather than of the problem itself.

Optimal primal solutions can change drastically under tiny perturbations of the instance, making them nearly impossible to predict well. Optimal dual solutions are far more stable, so good learnable predictions exist for families of similar instances. The authors build such algorithms for two classes, metrical task systems and laminar set cover, with improved guarantees. Dual predictions had been used only in offline settings and for online maximization, making this the first demonstration that they can power online minimization.
arxiv-2606-05480:
Malik Ali and colleagues introduce CAPE in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework for benchmarking racing controllers under learned vehicle dynamics models. CAPE provides joint evaluation of controllers and the physics models they plan with.

The authors propose an enhanced physics model learned from data and compare it against two state-of-the-art learned dynamics models across five closed-loop control architectures. Their model achieved the best average lap times across all combinations. Paired with an adaptive nonlinear model-predictive controller it lapped in 5.82 seconds against 12.99 and 8.80 for the rival models under identical settings, with lower tracking errors. A disturbance-aware simulation adding sensor noise, process disturbances, actuator delay, and parameter uncertainty confirmed the advantage. The enhanced model cut longitudinal and lateral tracking errors by a quarter to a third against one rival while driving faster.
arxiv-2606-05780:
Tully, Kourkchi, and Neill weigh the stars of the nearby universe in infrared light in a 2026 arXiv paper. Faint galaxies glow too weakly for ground telescopes at these wavelengths, so space data from the WISE survey do the work. The team assembled brightness measures for a complete sample within ten megaparsecs. Only galaxies above a set infrared brightness entered the census. Precise distances, from the red giant branch tip method, anchor the sample.

Stellar masses follow from the mid-infrared flux and those distances. The census confirms a stark split in the local volume. Most galaxies in the sample are dwarfs, small and dim. Most of the stellar mass, though, sits in a small number of giant galaxies. The inventory gives a firm baseline for studies of how mass gathers near the Milky Way. It also sharpens the target list for deeper surveys of faint neighbors.
arxiv-2606-06080:
Shota Takashiro and colleagues fix a subtle centering flaw in the score estimates used to train reasoning models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Max-at-K objectives reward the best of K sampled answers, matching how models are judged at inference. Existing estimators for these objectives differ in signals and baselines, confusing comparisons. The team dissects a leading method's estimator and proves a split verdict.

It is unbiased as a policy gradient, yet its realized advantages are not centered within a batch. Their Leave-Two-Out baseline repairs exactly that while staying unbiased. The resulting method, MaxPO, runs in quadratic time and slots into group-based post-training. A single finite-batch advantage formula unifies the earlier estimators in one view. Experiments confirmed the baseline cuts gradient variance. It also outperformed the non-centered alternatives head-to-head. Small bookkeeping changes in scoring, the paper shows, buy real training stability.
arxiv-2606-06280:
Wutao Si, Hamza Ennaji, and Jalal Fadili study dynamics that solve a class of equilibrium problems in this 2026 arXiv paper on optimization. A monotone inclusion asks for a point where the sum of two operators vanishes. The setup captures performative prediction, where a model's decisions reshape the very data distribution it was trained on, closing the loop. The authors design a continuous time, second order splitting dynamic for this closed loop setting.

The motion is driven by a forward backward splitting operator evaluated against the shifting distribution itself. Under uniform monotonicity, they prove an equilibrium exists and is unique. With damping that fades over time, trajectories converge strongly to it, at fast velocity rates. When the regularizing operator is strongly monotone, constant Polyak style damping upgrades this to global exponential convergence.
arxiv-2606-06380:
Zengqing Wu and Chuan Xiao propose a new route toward studying machine consciousness in this 2026 arXiv paper. Current approaches either grade systems against theory checklists or bolt on theory inspired modules. Both risk finding only what human language already planted. Their alternative is generative: let agents invent their own communication from scratch, under task pressure alone, and watch what structures appear.

In their setup, learning agents start with no language, no concept of self, and minimal exposure to human text. Any pattern that emerges can then be credited to the task, not to inherited priors. As a proof of concept in a minimal environment, the agents developed self referential communication. They even built an echo mismatch detection circuit, for noticing when a returned signal differs from their own. Neither the task design nor the architecture predicted it. The authors argue richer environments are the next test.
arxiv-2606-06580:
Moon Moon Devi prepares three detectors for a once in a generation measurement in this 2026 arXiv paper. When the next nearby star explodes, its neutrino burst could settle the neutrino mass ordering. Devi studies two early signals. The neutronization burst is a sharp electron neutrino spike in the first tens of milliseconds. Flavor change makes it appear or vanish depending on the ordering. One event could settle a basic question.

Simulating a supernova in our own galaxy, she computes event rates for DUNE, Hyper Kamiokande, and JUNO. The burst proves robust across explosion models. DUNE reaches above six sigma separation between the orderings, and Hyper Kamiokande above four sigma. A second signal, the rise time of electron anti neutrinos, also separates the orderings but is muddied by the progenitor star. Combining the two signals, and all three detectors, protects the measurement. No single site carries the claim alone.
arxiv-2606-06780:
Stack two atom thin crystals with a slight twist, and a moire pattern appears. Wakabayashi studies the light these stacks emit in this 2026 arXiv paper. The materials are transition metal dichalcogenides, layered semiconductors with strong light matter coupling. Their glow comes from excitons, bound pairs of electrons and holes.

Maps of the glow show patterns at many scales at once. Wakabayashi explains them with nine simple spectral descriptors. Each descriptor is a summary number taken from a spectrum, with no peak fitting needed. Different descriptors filter the underlying disorder differently. Some average over the light spot and see only smooth variation. Others react to tiny traps switching inside the spot. This filtering yields a clear hierarchy of correlation lengths. One descriptor always varies over longer distances than another. The theory also explains the measured links between descriptors, including one near perfect anti-correlation.
arxiv-2606-06880:
Search agents no longer just read ranked documents; they can poke at whole collections with shell tools. Zhuang and co-authors argue that freedom does not scale in this 2026 arXiv paper. Every broad command scans the full corpus. Latency balloons as collections grow toward millions of documents.

Their proposal reframes the retriever's job. Retrieval should build an interaction space, a bounded slice of the corpus. The agent can then explore that slice freely with tools. Documents inside are prepared at indexing time for shell style navigation. Their proof of concept, RISE, uses the classic BM25 ranker to draw the boundary. On a browsing benchmark, RISE matched the pure shell baseline at seventy eight percent accuracy. It cost about a quarter as much per query. At one million documents, it held eighty one percent accuracy. The unbounded rival fell to sixty percent, with many timed out runs.
arxiv-2606-06980:
An electric field might one day switch a magnet without any current at all. Ghosh, Heinze, and Paul compute how fields tune magnetic couplings in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their systems are trilayers: an iron sheet sandwiched between other transition metals. Partners include ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, and iridium layers.

Density functional theory maps the energy of spin spirals in each stack. Fields up to one volt per angstrom were applied. The spiral patterns barely changed, and the magnetic ground state stayed put. Fitted exchange constants, though, drifted in telling ways. Nearest neighbor coupling moved by only a few percent. Longer range and higher order couplings shifted by up to tens of percent. All changes ran nearly linear at small fields. Their signs never flipped. The overlayer's identity set the sensitivity. Spin dependent screening explains much of the pattern.
arxiv-2606-07080:
Text to speech systems now face a harder bar than mere intelligibility: they must sound human over minutes. The dots.tts team presents its foundation model in this 2026 technical report, hosted as a 2026 arXiv paper. The model holds two billion parameters. Unusually, it generates speech in a continuous latent space, not discrete sound tokens.

Three ideas carry the design. A specially trained audio encoder builds a tidy, predictable speech space. The generation head conditions on the full history, curbing long range drift. A reward free self corrective step then polishes robustness and sound quality. On a standard evaluation suite, the model posted the best average scores. Word error rates fell under one percent on its Chinese test set. A distilled fast version streams its first sound packet in tens of milliseconds. Code and model checkpoints are released openly under the Apache license.
arxiv-2606-07180:
Heat maps that explain an image classifier often look plausible while proving nothing. Hoarau, Zhu, and Nguyen demand proofs in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their OPTIMUS-Prime framework explains predictions with concepts borrowed from logic. A prime implicant is a smallest set of facts that already forces a conclusion.

Translated to vision, the highlighted concepts must satisfy two properties. Sufficiency means they provably guarantee the classifier's prediction. Minimality means removing any one of them breaks that guarantee. The resulting heat maps are therefore both tight and readable. Tests on a visual classification benchmark showed the explanations surfacing genuinely decision relevant concepts. The guarantees rest on assumptions the authors state openly. The explained layer must be linear, and earlier activations must stay bounded. Tangled neurons can also blur the meanings. Even so, the work moves saliency from suggestive art toward auditable evidence.
arxiv-2606-07380:
Chou and Yu discover a kind of multicritical point driven by topology in this 2026 arXiv letter. A multicritical point is where several phase transition lines meet, and its character is usually set by critical exponents for how quantities diverge. Recent work showed it can enrich transition classes. The authors construct 1D fermionic systems with chiral symmetry, relating left- and right-moving particles, where neighboring critical lines differ topologically rather than in exponents.

Where those lines meet, the multicriticality is enforced by topology alone, a mechanism distinct from previously known ones. These points can host degeneracies, meaning protected ground states that share the same energy. They also exhibit a breakdown of the Li-Haldane bulk-boundary correspondence, the rule linking a material's interior to its edge states. The authors explain the breakdown with a physical picture. The results extend how quantum phase changes are classified beyond the exponent-based view.
arxiv-2606-08280:
Almeida derives exact results for how sharply a quantum ground state responds to a threaded magnetic flux, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The system is a two-dimensional massive Dirac fermion, a particle obeying the Dirac equation with a mass, subject to Aharonov-Bohm flux, a magnetic influence felt even where the field itself vanishes. The response is measured by the fidelity susceptibility, also called the Bures metric.

By projecting the full operator onto an effective two-level system, Almeida obtains a closed-form expression for the ground-state metric. It takes a universal Lorentzian profile, a bell-shaped curve, centered at integer flux with width set by the mass. The peak grows like the inverse square of the mass and diverges as the mass vanishes, mirroring how susceptibilities diverge near critical points.
arxiv-2606-08480:
Kewei Xu and colleagues make reinforcement learning for recommendation robust to untrustworthy rewards, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning can improve generative recommendation beyond supervised imitation by using reward signals to guide policy improvement. In production systems the reward model is usually an existing ranker trained on exposure-biased logs, so its scores carry inaccuracies that violate the assumption that rewards are reliable. Their stratified analysis uncovers a consistent pattern in when reward guidance actually helps.

Reward guidance benefits most when the policy is uncertain about its choice and the ranker can discriminate the true item from the negatives the policy rolled out. On other samples the reward signal is negligible or actively detrimental, teaching the policy the ranker's biases. The authors respond with adaptive loss balancing for a group-relative policy optimization method, weighting the reinforcement loss per sample by how trustworthy the reward is there.
arxiv-2606-08580:
Yike Wang and colleagues clean up noisy speech without needing a clean sample of the speaker, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speaker embeddings, compact voice fingerprints, can strengthen speech enhancement when used as conditioning. But most methods either require clean enrollment audio or extract embeddings from the noisy speech itself, which are fragile under noise and domain shift. Their framework, G-MaP-SE, builds a clean-speech embedding prior using a Gaussian mixture model. It refines each noisy conditioning embedding by matching it to that prior.

The matched prior embedding is injected into a time-frequency enhancement backbone through a lightweight gated fusion module. Experiments on two standard noisy-speech datasets show the prior matching consistently outperforms conditioning on the noisy embedding directly. It also substantially narrows the gap to an oracle upper bound that uses the true clean embedding, while requiring no enrollment audio at inference time.
arxiv-2606-08680:
Xiangzhong Liu adapts a 3D object detector to the warped images of fisheye cameras in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fisheye cameras are widely deployed in autonomous driving for their low cost and wide field of view. But severe radial distortion challenges most bird's-eye-view detectors. Liu's detector, DAPETR, is projection-free and tailored for mixed suites of pinhole and fisheye cameras. It builds on the PETR architecture, which reasons about three-dimensional positions from image features.

Two learned-adaptive modules do the work. A unified distortion-aware positional embedding aligns encodings with fisheye geometry, so the network knows where each distorted pixel truly points. A bidirectional co-modulation module lets image features and positional embeddings adapt each other. On a converted benchmark, both approaches improve over the baseline, but the learned modules perform better in the reported comparisons.
arxiv-2606-08980:
Zhu and colleagues label 3D scenes from multi-view photos in one pass, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Panoptic segmentation assigns every point a category, like chair, and an instance identity, separating one chair from another. Open-vocabulary means the categories are not fixed. Earlier pipelines stitched together 2D models and preprocessing, accumulating errors, and labels disagreed across viewpoints. EPS3D learns end-to-end, distilling across 3D scenes to predict semantic and instance features consistent in three dimensions.

A mutual enhancement module cross-checks the two feature kinds. Semantics align within each instance, and instance features refine under semantic guidance, so the two views correct one another. On two benchmarks EPS3D beat prior systems, improving accuracy by 13 percent in mean intersection-over-union on Replica. It processes a scene in about 1 second. The authors point to robotic manipulation and 3D scene editing as uses, and release the code.
arxiv-2606-09680:
Haripada Sau pins down when a derived kernel carries a strong interpolation trait in this 2026 arXiv paper. The objects are reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, function spaces where point values are read off by inner products. From a base kernel and a contractive multiplier, one builds a de Branges-Rovnyak kernel. The trait in question is a complete Pick factor, a mark of how freely values can be fit.

Sau asks for the exact traits a general such kernel needs to hold the factor. The answer covers a broad class of base kernels, both Pick and non-Pick types, like the Szegő kernel on the polydisk. One form of the answer uses operator-valued holomorphic functions that meet a fit condition. A second form is neat: the factor exists just when a built helper kernel is itself a complete Pick kernel.
arxiv-2606-09780:
Björn Jónsson and his co-authors let evolution roam for fresh sounds that no one asked for by name in this 2026 arXiv paper. Composers often want a sound they cannot state in advance. A quality-diversity search breeds many variants, keeps the best of each kind, and prizes spread as much as score. Their system pairs that search with a trained classifier, in the spirit of an innovation engine.

Two builders make the sounds: pattern networks that draw control curves, and signal chains that shape the audio. A fresh twist uses split networks for split pitch bands, which kept quality with simpler nets. An archive method, MAP-Elites, stores the champion of each niche. Lineage checks showed winners reached their spots by odd detours, like goal switches between music and noise classes. The sound pool spread across lengths as well, with niches split by span.
arxiv-2606-09880:
Yaqian Zhan and co-authors let a network model tune its own knobs while it learns in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model class is latent factorization of tensors, a low-rank lens for dynamic weighted directed networks, graphs whose links swell, shrink, and flip with time. Its skill leans hard on three regularization weights. Hand picks and grid hunts for those weights burn time and compute.

Their DE-LFT frame folds differential evolution into the training run. The evolution breeds weight sets, keeps the fittest, and breeds on, all while the factors learn. The model thus adapts its own settings to the data at hand. On four real sets, the tuned model posted lower mean absolute and root-mean-square errors than hand-set rivals. It also spared the team the long grid hunt.
arxiv-2606-10080:
Yu and Olson audit protein design models for hidden hazardous capabilities, in a 2026 arXiv paper on AI safety and interpretability. Their method, VFUSE, trains sparse autoencoders on the activations of diffusion-transformer protein models to surface hazard-aware features. They apply it to RoseTTAFold3 and RFDiffusion3, two popular open-weight models for protein folding and synthesis.

In certain blocks, simple linear probes detected hazardous designs significantly better when fitted in the autoencoder's latent space than on the model's raw representations, improving interpretability without hurting performance. They also found monosemantic features, individual units with a single clear meaning, that fire only on hazardous designs, reaching strong discrimination scores. The authors describe VFUSE as the first sparse autoencoder trained on an all-atom diffusion model. It is also the first feature-level virulence audit of a protein design model, pointing toward safer, more transparent protein engineering.
arxiv-2606-10480:
Filippo and Mazza analyse a tool for modelling spread on networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tool is a regularized fractional Laplacian, an operator that lets influence jump beyond nearest neighbours on a graph. The plain fractional version breaks compatibility with the network's own structure. A recent fix blends it with the standard Laplacian, and this paper studies the blend closely.

The authors prove the regularized operator always produces superdiffusion, spread faster than ordinary diffusion, whether the graph is weighted or unweighted. Other non-local variants lack that guarantee. They also give an efficient construction with the same cost as the fractional Laplacian itself. Tests on synthetic and real networks confirm the theory: it is the only operator tested that stays superdiffusive in every configuration.
arxiv-2606-10680:
Torrente-Lujan recasts a black hole phase transition in topological language in this 2026 arXiv paper on gravitation. The Hawking-Page transition marks where large black holes in anti-de Sitter space beat empty space. Using a thermodynamic vector field, the author assigns winding numbers, topological charges, to the Davies point, where heat capacity diverges, and to the Hawking-Page point. The charges are minus one and plus one, so the pair cancels yet forms a dipole with nonzero separation.

Normalising by the Davies scales gives universal ratios: in four dimensions the entropy ratio is exactly two, the temperature ratio two over root three minus one. The construction checks out for plain, charged, and rotating cases, and the same geometry yields a barrier of one third in four dimensions. The paper closes by proposing a defect-resolved version for exotic categorical symmetry sectors.
arxiv-2606-11080:
Hoffmann and Mahadevan ask how a growing biological filament stays straight in a 2026 arXiv paper. Random growth fluctuations should bend it over time, yet plant shoots and spines grow reproducibly straight. The authors build a minimal model of a noisy, growing elastic filament. Growth responds to strain, curvature, and orientation through feedback laws, local or nonlocal.

Linear stability analysis, checking whether small bends shrink or grow, separates the feedback rules that work from those that fail. With noise, purely local feedback needs orientation sensing to suppress long-wavelength instabilities, the broad slow bends ruining straightness. Nonlocal feedback can manage with proprioceptive sensing alone, meaning curvature sensing, the filament feeling its own shape. Coupling to an elastic substrate suppresses large-scale fluctuations further, and nonlocal orientation sensing alone is always unstable. Measuring angle fluctuations, they suggest, can reveal which feedback a real tissue uses.
arxiv-2606-11180:
Cho and nine co-authors present Lip Forcing in a 2026 arXiv paper, for real-time lip synchronization in video. Lip sync rewrites a speaker's mouth movements to match new audio. Diffusion models do it beautifully but slowly, over many denoising steps. Lip Forcing distills a fourteen-billion-parameter bidirectional teacher into causal students generating video chunk by chunk, looking only backward.

Each chunk takes just two denoising steps, with no classifier-free guidance at inference. A teacher-trajectory analysis found a fidelity-sync trade-off, answered by three components: Sync-Window DMD distillation, a two-step schedule, and a SyncNet-based reward. The 1.3-billion-parameter student streams at thirty-one frames per second, 17.6 times faster than its same-scale bidirectional counterpart. The full fourteen-billion student runs 39.8 times faster than its teacher at comparable fidelity. Time to first frame stays under a millisecond at both scales.
arxiv-2606-11480:
Arockiaraj, Parikh, Adivarahan, Kannan, and Prasanna pursue accurate, resource-efficient federated continual learning in a 2026 arXiv paper, whose hosted text carries placeholder conference metadata. It must learn from distributed task streams under limited communication, memory, and labels. Existing methods rely on local training, replay, and full labels. Analytic options avoid training loops and replay, but wide random features need the Gram matrix, whose communication cost grows quadratically.

The authors build an analytic learner designed to keep accuracy while cutting those costs. It targets the Gram matrix choke point, the quadratic burden that makes such methods expensive at scale. The work extends analytic, replay-free continual learning to the federated setting, where clients learn task streams without sharing raw data.
arxiv-2606-11580:
Eric Yocam and five co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on superspace concentration, from quantum theory, which studies matter and energy at very small scales. They define a focus measure, one number showing how strongly a quantum state piles its information into a preferred corner of a larger space. It is the largest eigenvalue, roughly the biggest weight, of a reduced state.

Simulations on graphics processors test five claims about this measure. Predictions for decoherence, the loss of quantum behaviour through noise, match formulas to machine precision across five space sizes. The measure never rises under four allowed noise channels, with zero violations across 120,000 state and channel pairs. Focused states resist deliberate attacks far better than fidelity, a standard accuracy score, suggests. The authors link the measure to Grover's search method and show a capacity gap growing with the logarithm of the space size.
arxiv-2606-11980:
Niklas Elmqvist, Panagiotis D Ritsos and Peter W S Butcher set a research agenda for analytics beyond the desktop in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ubiquitous analytics means using many distributed, networked devices, from headsets to smartglasses, to make sense of data anywhere. Three spatial operating systems now ship with scene understanding built in, and AI agents share the same physical spaces as users.

The authors read the field's history as a genealogy, organised into seven clusters: cognition, context, interaction, platforms, visualisation, collaboration and evaluation. Crossing every cluster with every other yields forty-two future research challenges, each scoped as a tractable project. Their positions are stated falsifiably, and the crossing matrix doubles as a map of what the field studies and what it neglects. The warning running through the agenda is timely: proprietary platforms are settling design conventions right now, and without evidence-based alternatives those conventions will calcify.
arxiv-2606-12180:
Huang and co-authors show that stretching a carbon nanotube steers its quantum behavior precisely, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A nanotube is a rolled graphene sheet one atom thick, and a quantum dot is an island confining electrons one by one. The field, called quantum transport straintronics, uses mechanical strain, a controlled stretch, to tune how electrons flow. The team built suspended nanotube transistors with channels about 30 nanometers long, stretched by moving gold clamps.

Across three devices, strain was tuned reversibly from zero to about 3 percent while current maps were recorded. The data show a large mechanical gating effect that repeats precisely and matches theory, proving elastic stretching without slipping. Careful checks rule out capacitive effects as the cause. Instead, strain shifts the band structure, the allowed electron energies, changing doping and the bandgap as theory predicts quantitatively. Such control could serve future qubits and molecular transistors.
arxiv-2606-12380:
Kelman and co-authors solve a forbidden-pattern problem for matrices, extending a theorem of combinatorics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem says the largest families of sets sharing a common core are the plain ones: everything containing a fixed subset. This paper asks the matrix analogue. A family of matrices is forbidden-intersection-free if no two differ by a matrix whose kernel has a specified dimension. The expected champions are umvirates: all matrices agreeing on a subspace, and their duals.

The authors prove umvirates and duals are the maximal such families whenever the forbidden dimension stays below a fixed fraction of the matrix size. Earlier work needed the size to tower over the dimension; the new result needs only a constant-factor gap. Constructions in the Frankl-Rödl style show the range is best possible, since behavior changes beyond half the size.
arxiv-2606-12480:
Amraoui and Toffano redraw quantum gates as geometry, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum gates are usually written as matrices, which hide what they do to space. Working in complex geometric algebra, where vectors, planes, and volumes are objects called blades, the authors reformulate the Pauli and Clifford groups. The Pauli group turns out to be the group of blades, up to a phase. Pauli operators thus become oriented directions and planes, and their commutation rules become statements about geometric compatibility.

Clifford operators, the gate set behind stabilizer codes and error correction, are generated by quarter-turn Pauli rotors, rotations built from Pauli elements. A greedy algorithm decomposes any Clifford operator into such rotors, and empirically the decompositions come out unexpectedly compact. Adding the T gate, the standard route to universal quantum computing, corresponds geometrically to eighth-turn rotors. The framework gives circuit designers a picture where algebra and shape coincide.
arxiv-2606-12780:
Ma and colleagues present ProPlay, a procedural world model that lets language-model agents rehearse future task paths before acting, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Self-evolving agents should improve on their own, without external supervision, but in partially observable environments they must explore actively, learn from sparse feedback, and judge when past experience is trustworthy.

ProPlay abstracts paths into procedures, reusable task stages such as boiling water or verifying a result, and keeps them in a procedure graph whose edges capture causal transitions between stages. Each transition carries a reliability record rating its contribution to past successes on similar tasks. Before each episode, the agent performs preplay, simulating a path over the graph and injecting it as soft guidance rather than a hard constraint. On the ScienceWorld, tau-Bench, and PlanCraft benchmarks, ProPlay improves understanding and self-evolution capability over baselines.
arxiv-2606-12880:
Ku studies a monochromatic variant of the k-in-a-row game, in which all players place stones of the same colour and whoever completes a k-in-a-row wins, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Creating a line with exactly 1 empty position, a near k-in-a-row, lets the opponent complete it and win. Rational play therefore avoids such patterns.

Ku investigates the infinite grid and the d-dimensional hypercube with side k. For the grid, he establishes nearly tight bounds on the maximum density. He shows it equals 1 minus 2 over k whenever k is not divisible by 3. He also determines both the maximum and minimum densities exactly for k equals 3. For hypercubes, he derives asymptotic bounds on the maximum density up to order k to the minus 2 and obtains the exact value of the minimum density.
arxiv-2606-13180:
Kurada and Baruah present JiRAIYA, a decentralised hierarchical federated learning framework built on Web3 tech, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Federated learning trains a shared model across members who keep their data local. But systems suffer from opaque aggregation: it is unclear which model updates are accepted or discarded, and outside validators add computing and communication overhead.

The design is hierarchical: delegated managers run training within their own federations. Model updates are encoded, encrypted, and broadcast to all managers, who check them on their own; only updates approved by consensus enter the model, so raw updates are never exposed. Defence against adversarial and poisoning attacks joins statistical novelty detection with the consensus check, spotting anomalous updates without iterative verification. A reputation-score-based backup ensures the model keeps training if managers fail. The design cuts smart contract calls and on-chain data footprint to keep gas costs practical.
arxiv-2606-13480:
Serry presents a biomechanical model of the vocal folds in this 2026 arXiv paper. Voice production depends on how laryngeal muscles posture the vocal folds during vibration. Abnormal settings are linked to inefficient phonation and voice disorders, and clinicians observe varied glottal closure patterns. Yet how muscle activation, fold posture, and the sound connect remains not fully understood. Models that include the intrinsic muscles are expensive to run, which blocks wide sweeps. Serry's model is inexpensive: the fold body is treated as a layered beam and the cover layer as a coupled membrane.

Muscle activation in the model positions the arytenoid cartilages and cricothyroid joint, changing fold tension and shape, and thereby the glottal shape during vibration. Because the model runs cheaply, researchers can sweep many postures and compare what each posture does to the voice. The aim is a tool for exploring how posturing produces voices.
arxiv-2606-13580:
Kai and colleagues present EvTexture++ in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that uses event cameras to sharpen video. Video super-resolution reconstructs high-resolution frames from low-resolution input. Event sensors record brightness changes with extremely fine timing and wide range, and earlier work used them to improve motion estimation and frame alignment. This paper instead aims the event stream at texture: the fine detail in events is exactly what upscaling algorithms struggle to invent. A texture branch exploits it directly.

An iterative texture enhancement module refines texture regions across repeated passes, yielding sharper, more detailed output. The framework also addresses large motions, which can hurt consistency between frames, so textures do not flicker. Event cameras are moving from labs into consumer devices, and this work shows their signals can repair the weakest part of video upscaling. The result is a clean division of labour between frames and events.
arxiv-2606-13780:
Araz and Spannowsky give machine-learned anomaly detection a rigorous foundation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Anomaly detection is reshaping searches for new physics at colliders, but its statistics lag behind. A raw anomaly score has no calibrated meaning. Scanning many regions inflates the look-elsewhere effect, where chance fluctuations somewhere become likely, and standard formulas are blind to the background mismodelling that anomaly detectors are prone to. The authors propose a calibration layer built on conformal prediction, a method giving distribution-free, finite-sample guarantees.

The layer converts any anomaly score into valid local significance values. Weighted and grouped variants repair the symmetry failures that resonant searches suffer, and a trials-factor step produces a look-elsewhere-aware global value. The layer exposes bad calibration the pipeline cannot see and corrects it, without retraining the detector. Tests on public collider benchmark data show the approach working.
arxiv-2606-14680:
Garvan and Sarma prove congruence patterns for two kinds of integer partitions in a 2026 arXiv paper. A partition writes a number as a sum of parts. Overpartitions allow the first occurrence of each part size to be overlined. The authors track sums of certain non-overlined parts, sorted by parity.

They obtain several Ramanujan-type congruences. These are divisibility patterns repeating modulo five and modulo seven. They apply to those part sums. The same treatment covers partitions without repeated odd parts, again classified by parity. Their proofs are elementary. They depend only on classical theta function identities. Theta functions are the standard generating-function machinery of partition theory. Such congruences reveal hidden arithmetic regularity in counting functions that otherwise look irregular.
arxiv-2606-14980:
Song and coauthors compute shape information for the a0(1450) meson and apply it to B meson decays in a 2026 study. The structure of light scalar mesons remains disputed, with a quark-antiquark picture favored in B decays. The key object is the leading-twist light-cone distribution amplitude, which describes how momentum is shared inside it. Its moments can be extracted with QCD sum rules.

Working in background field theory, the team calculates the first five odd moments with condensates kept to dimension six. They build the amplitude two ways: a light-cone harmonic oscillator model and a Gegenbauer polynomial expansion. Light-cone sum rules give the transition form factors for the anti-B decay into a0(1450). Extrapolating across the kinematic range yields decay widths and branching ratios for the semileptonic channel. The authors report angular observables, including forward-backward and lepton polarization asymmetries, for comparison with experiment.
arxiv-2606-15080:
Ki and coauthors teach reasoning models to think in the language of the question in a 2026 study. Large reasoning models often default to English reasoning even for non-English queries, a failure called language collapse. Simple fixes add a binary reward for language match, but trade away accuracy and tokens. Models also slip between languages mid-trace under those rewards.

Their recipe, AdaMame, runs in two stages for multilingual math reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning on natural reasoning traces in five languages builds basic multilingual skill. A reinforcement stage then uses a modified group-relative optimizer whose alignment factor grows over training. The model first explores many reasoning languages, then settles into the query language. Across two benchmarks, two base models, and twelve languages, the recipe reaches the best balance of accuracy, language fidelity, and token use. Gains are strongest on lower-resource, out-of-domain languages.
arxiv-2606-15180:
Zheng and coauthors propose a spectroscopy scheme to pin down five thorium-229 nuclear parameters at once, in a 2026 physics paper. Thorium-229 has an unusually low-energy excited nuclear state, ideal for a nuclear optical clock. Building that clock needs precise values for several nuclear quantities, now known only loosely. The scheme uses two highly charged thorium ions whose electrons sit far above the nuclear transition. That arrangement mixes the nuclear states with the electronic ground state.

Precision measurements on both ions feed one unified analysis. The analysis extracts both magnetic dipole moments, the bare transition energy, and the charge-radius difference. It also yields the transition matrix element governing the isomer's lifetime. No outside nuclear inputs are needed, removing a major error source. Estimated uncertainties shrink about threefold for the transition energy and twofold for the radius difference. The scheme could benchmark nuclear theory and advance the nuclear clock.
arxiv-2606-15480:
Diemert and coauthor model how much work it takes to apply quantitative confidence methods to assurance cases, in a 2026 safety engineering paper. An assurance case is a structured argument, backed by evidence, that a critical system meets its goals. Confidence methods attach numbers to how strongly the argument should be believed, but practitioners cite the extra effort as a barrier. The authors define decision complexity, the count of judgments a user must supply, and how it scales with argument size.

The model compares three methods: a Bayesian belief network approach, a Dempster-Shafer approach, and the mixed method Certus. Certus carries the highest worst-case decision count, thanks to its flexible belief propagation, yet in the average case its effort falls below the Bayesian method and to roughly half the Dempster-Shafer method. Designers can now quote scalability up front instead of leaving adopters to discover the cost.
arxiv-2606-15780:
Das and Sarkar solve coefficient problems in 2026 for the apple-like convex subclass of univalent functions. The class is defined by a subordination condition involving e to the z times the square root of one plus z. Coefficient bounds describe how large the Taylor coefficients of such functions and their inverses can be. Sharp bounds are the exact extremes, attained by specific extremal functions.

They find sharp bounds for the first three inverse logarithmic coefficients and for the difference of the second and first moduli.
