Antibodies from survivors are candidates for preventive and therapeutic drugs, and they reveal which parts of the virus vaccines should imitate.

A high-throughput pipeline screened antibodies that bind the spike protein, which the virus uses to enter cells through ACE2. Most antibodies bound outside the receptor binding domain, but the domain binders were more often neutralizing, the strongest at a site overlapping the ACE2 contact point. Two selected antibodies protected Syrian hamsters against SARS-CoV-2 infection. The work shows survivor antibodies can be found fast and turned toward treatment and vaccine design.
europmc-pmc7316580:
Shadmi and co-authors pull together world views on health equity in the COVID-19 pandemic. Their article shows the virus hits the poor, minorities, and other at-risk groups hardest. It spreads fast where homes are dense, long-term ills are common, and good care is hard to reach. Shutdowns and job losses add harm that falls on the same groups.

To show what states and local groups did, the team built 13 country case studies. The set runs from China and Brazil to India, Israel, Australia, Colombia, and Belgium, plus more. The set is not meant to stand for the whole world. It is a call for hard, careful study of pandemic unfairness, so the next response rests on proof and not on guesswork.
europmc-pmc7401880:
Nakra and co-authors review multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children, MIS-C, in the journal Children. The syndrome follows SARS-CoV-2 infection and presents with fever, severe illness, and failure across two or more organ systems, alongside lab evidence of inflammation. Some features echo Kawasaki disease, toxic shock, and macrophage activation syndromes.

The timing after infection suggests a post-infectious immune dysregulation rather than direct viral damage. Because children can deteriorate fast, the authors advise management in pediatric intensive care where possible. Immunomodulatory treatment choices depend on how the case presents. An open question closes the review: how vaccine-driven immune responses might relate to the syndrome. Clinicians get an early synthesis of a frightening new condition.
europmc-pmc7407580:
Aldinucci and co-authors review the CCL5/CCR5 signaling axis in cancer in Cancers. Chemokines are the body's cell-traffic signals, and tumors hijack them. The signal CCL5 and its receptor CCR5 show abnormal levels in blood cancers and solid tumors alike.

The axis feeds cancer on many fronts: direct growth signals, matrix remodeling, cell migration, stem cell expansion, DNA repair, metabolic rewiring, and new blood vessels. The review then goes tumor by tumor through the preclinical evidence. Blocking the receptor is already testable in patients, because maraviroc, a CCR5 blocker used against HIV, can be repurposed. Trials of that drug and of antibodies fill the closing section. A borrowed AIDS drug may get a second career.
europmc-pmc7408280:
Pajares and co-authors review inflammation in Parkinson's disease in Cells. Parkinson's is defined by the death of dopamine neurons projecting from the substantia nigra, the brain's movement control hub. Its molecular triggers stay ill-defined, but human samples and animal models strongly implicate inflammation in starting or advancing the disease.

The review works cell by cell through the mediators: microglia, astroglia, and blood vessel lining cells. It also covers the genetic and transcriptional control of inflammation, and the surprising immune roles of dopamine itself and of reactive oxygen species. A final section sorts preclinical and clinical attempts to treat Parkinson's by calming neuroinflammation. Readers get a systematic case for inflammation as a therapeutic front.
europmc-pmc7460980:
Ruwizhi and Aderibigbe review cinnamic acid derivatives and their healing power. Cinnamic acid comes from cinnamon bark. Its ring and double bond can be reshaped into many new compounds.

Changed forms show action against cancer, bacterial infection, diabetes, and nerve disorders. The groups added to the base shape decide if power rises or falls. Some forms beat standard drugs in lab tests. Named compounds showed strong anti-tuberculosis, antibacterial, and antimalarial action. Others hit cancer cells hard or blocked enzymes tied to memory loss. The review collects recent gains in this family. It makes the case for these derivatives as promising leads for new drugs.
europmc-pmc7461480:
Popkin and co-authors review global evidence on obesity and COVID-19, from infection risk to death. The link had been disputed and lacked a full review. The team searched Chinese and English sources and built pooled analyses.

They used 75 studies across the full course of illness. People with obesity faced higher risk at each step. Hospital admission risk more than doubled, with a 113% higher rate in pooled results. Intensive care admission rose by 74%, and deaths rose by 48% in the pooled analysis figures. The review also maps body pathways that may explain the pattern. Immune strain, lung strain, and other obesity-linked changes all play a part. The authors warn that vaccines may work less well in this group.
europmc-pmc7551780:
Radujkovic and co-authors study vitamin D status and COVID-19 outcomes. No causal treatment existed at that time. Modifiable risk factors could help improve patient outcomes.

The team studied 185 patients treated at their center. Vitamin D status was checked at first presentation. Deficiency meant a level below 12 ng/mL. A total of 41 patients met that threshold. That was 22% of the cohort. Deficiency linked to higher risk of severe disease. Adjusted risk for ventilation or death was 6.12 times higher. The authors call for trials of vitamin D supplements. Inpatient results showed a similar pattern of risk.
europmc-pmc7554980:
Xu, Yang, Li and Zhang review the mRNA vaccine platform and its prospects. mRNA drugs have shown promise in immune therapy. Vaccines of this type are now common in trials.

Advantages include high efficacy and mild side effects. Production costs can also be relatively low. Past barriers included weak delivery into cells. Translation of the mRNA message was also limited. New technology has eased both problems. Immune response strength can now be tuned. The review covers uses in infection and cancer. It also looks at bacterial targets such as tuberculosis. Storage and safety questions for future work are discussed.
europmc-pmc7605980:
Snoswell and co-authors ask whether telehealth can cut health system costs. Their scoping review focuses on the Australian setting. Telehealth may raise access and cut travel for patients.

Evidence showed savings when funded travel was prevented. Savings also came when telehealth avoided pricey specialist follow-up. An expert group named four possible saving areas. They were productivity gains and less secondary care. Alternate funding models and telementoring completed the list. Productivity gains may not save cash under current funding. Running and monitoring costs offset savings in many studies. Cases where users pay direct showed clearer savings. Telementoring showed little economic evidence so far.
europmc-pmc7775580:
Polykovskiy and co-authors build a benchmark for AI models that invent new molecules. Generative models learn from known compounds and propose fresh structures. Such structures can feed drug screens. But with many models on offer, no shared test existed to rank them fairly. Their platform, MOSES, fills that gap.

MOSES gives standard training and test sets for molecule generation. Its metrics score both quality and diversity of the output. The team ran several known models through the suite. Their scores serve as reference points for new work. The platform and its code are free online for any lab to use and extend.
europmc-pmc7839780:
Corp and co-authors compare treatment advice for neck and low back pain in European guidelines. Care for this pain varies across countries. The team gathered clinical practice guidelines from across Europe. They searched thirteen databases for them.

The authors pulled out each guideline's treatment options. They checked which options carry solid evidence. Shared advice across countries was mapped. Points of disagreement were flagged as well. Drug and non-drug options both appear in the set. The goal is a shared base for care across Europe. Wide gaps in advice show where research or consensus is still thin.
europmc-pmc7844180:
Hawes and co-authors track depression and anxiety changes in teens and young adults during COVID-19. The pandemic brought sweeping life changes and stress. This age group felt them hard. Early reports hinted at worse symptoms. None had tracked change inside the same people.

The team followed the same youths over time. Each person's symptoms were compared with their own baseline. That within-person view filters out fixed traits. Scores for depression rose during the pandemic months. Anxiety scores rose as well. The authors place the shift in the setting of school and social upheaval. Their results argue for support aimed at young people during long crises.
europmc-pmc7847680:
Liang and co-authors review how exosomes can be engineered for targeted drug delivery. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that cells release. They ferry materials between cells in the body. Drugs can be loaded into them. Small molecules and nucleic acid drugs both fit.

Targeting sends more drug to the right tissue. That raises local dose and trims side effects. Genetic tricks can add homing parts to the vesicle coat. Chemical tweaks offer a second route. The authors sort methods by how they build and load the vesicles. Exosomes bring low toxicity and low immune reaction. The field is young, but cell-free therapy is the prize.
europmc-pmc7885480:
Li and co-authors present a review of drug resistance in cancer, with a focus on cancer stem cells. Tumours often learn to withstand the drugs used against them. The surviving cells can be fitter and more aggressive. The review explains the main routes to that resistance.

Some resistance is present from the start, and some is gained during treatment. The authors cover drug efflux pumps, changes that dodge cell death, and DNA damage responses. Cancer stem cells sit at the centre of their account. These self-renewing cells resist standard treatment and adapt to shifts around them. The review ends with strategies to wipe out such cells. It frames combination treatment as the most likely way past resistance.
europmc-pmc7922180:
Dehelean and co-authors present a review of plant-derived compounds in cancer drug discovery. Nature remains the main source of active molecules for medicine. Plant compounds hold a large share of current drugs. In cancer care, they offer an answer to the harsh side effects and drug resistance of standard chemotherapy.

The review first revisits classic natural agents such as taxol, vincristine, and doxorubicin. Their ways of killing cancer cells are shown in three-dimensional detail. It then follows newer candidates such as resveratrol, curcumin, and betulinic acid. Each is traced step by step from lab tests toward clinical use. Their action as killers, preventers, and sensitisers of tumours is weighed. Delivery platforms that wrap the compounds and aim them at tumours close the account. The authors argue natural products still have much to give oncology.
europmc-pmc7940280:
Catrina and Zheng present a review of low oxygen and its control factors in diabetes and its complications. Hypoxia-inducible factors, or HIFs, are the key switches that help cells adapt to low oxygen. In diabetes, many tissues run short of oxygen. Yet the adaptive response is blunted. High blood sugar and raised fatty acids block the stability and action of HIF-1α, the main switch.

The review sums up how HIF signalling is regulated in diabetes. It then traces the harm that faulty signalling does as the disease and its complications develop. Eye, kidney, nerve, and vessel damage all enter the account. The authors close with the treatment angle. Drugs that restore HIF signalling might prevent or ease these outcomes. The review weighs that hope against the current evidence.
europmc-pmc7994380:
Bonsergent and co-authors report a laboratory study measuring how cells take up extracellular vesicles and release their cargo. These tiny sacs ferry material between cells. Whether their contents truly reach the inside of a receiving cell was debated, and no one had counted it well. The team built a cell assay with tagged cargo to watch the process in numbers.

Uptake proved to be a low-yield process, at about 1% within an hour. Of the vesicles taken up, about 30% spilled their cargo into the cell's main body. That release needed the acid conditions found in endosomes. A drug that blocks acid build-up stopped it. So did proteins that block virus entry and fusion. The results suggest the vesicle membrane fuses to free its load. The study gives the field hard rates to design around.
europmc-pmc8012680:
Damase and co-authors survey the fast-growing field of RNA therapeutics. Advances in making, purifying, and delivering RNA have opened a new class of drugs. These medicines are cheap to produce and quick to design. They can reach targets once called undruggable. Some have already won regulatory approval, and many more sit in clinical trials.

The review walks through the main drug classes one by one. Antisense oligonucleotides, aptamers, small interfering RNAs, microRNAs, and messenger RNA each get treatment. The authors weigh delivery as the central challenge and compare current approaches. They close with a new idea: hospital-based RNA platforms. Their own experience building one at Houston Methodist Hospital grounds the proposal.
europmc-pmc8053180:
Elliott-Sale and co-authors lay out standards for sport and exercise research with women participants. Most high-quality data in the field come from studies of men. Known sex differences, above all in reproductive hormones, limit how far those data stretch. Specialist knowledge of female physiology is scarce in the field. Designs rarely adapt to the menstrual cycle or menopause.

The guide addresses participant selection across the female lifespan. Oestrogen swings fivefold across a cycle, and progesterone over 50-fold. Hormonal contraception, pregnancy, and menopause each need design answers. The authors give gold-standard techniques for tracking these states. Terminology gets aligned as well. The statement aims at two gains: more women in studies, and better-run studies when they join. Female exercisers deserve guidance built on their own data.
europmc-pmc8053280:
Swanson and co-authors report a phase 2b trial of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease. Lecanemab is an antibody that targets soluble aggregated amyloid beta. The trial used a Bayesian design with response-adaptive randomization. It tested three doses across two regimens against placebo. A total of 854 subjects were treated: 609 on lecanemab and 245 on placebo.

At 12 months, the best dose showed only a 64% probability of beating placebo by 25%. That missed the 80% bar for the primary endpoint. At 18 months, the picture improved markedly. Brain amyloid fell by 0.306 SUVr units on the top dose. Clinical decline slowed across several scales at once. Spinal fluid markers supported a real treatment effect. Brain swelling side effects hit 9.9% at the biweekly dose. A phase 3 trial was already underway.
europmc-pmc8058480:
Chen and co-authors review the vaginal microbiome in health and in bacterial vaginosis. The mix of microbes shifts across the month and across a woman's life. In health, Lactobacillus species rule the space. They release compounds that hold other microbes back. Bacterial vaginosis flips that balance. Lactobacillus counts crash while anaerobic microbes surge.

The review describes Gardnerella vaginalis, the microbe found most often in the disorder. It anchors mixed biofilms that shield other bacteria from the host. The disorder links to pelvic inflammation and preterm birth. It also raises the risk of infections caught through sex. The authors then cover how diagnosis has sharpened in recent years. Treatment choices, old and new, get the same survey. Better handling of this common disorder is the practical prize.
europmc-pmc8352980:
Lopez-Leon and co-authors review and pool the long-term effects of COVID-19. Effects can linger for weeks or months after recovery. The team searched LitCOVID and Embase for original data.

They screened 18,251 publications dated before January 1, 2021. Studies needed at least 100 patients to enter. Fifteen studies met the bar. The prevalence of 55 long-term effects was estimated. Twenty-one effects drew on two or more studies for pooling. Fatigue and other symptoms fill the list. The work gave long COVID an early, numbered shape. Random-effects pooling handled the spread between studies.
europmc-pmc8478580:
Michelen and co-authors run a living systematic review to characterize long COVID. Lasting effects after acute COVID-19 were clear, but their nature and rate stayed poorly defined. A review that keeps updating can guide care and rehab plans as evidence grows.

The search ran to March 17, 2021, across major databases. Studies needed at least 100 people seen 12 weeks or more after onset. In all, 39 studies covered 10,951 people in 12 countries. Most people studied had been in hospital. Over 60 physical and mental features were reported. Bias risk was high or moderate in most studies. No study came from a low-income country.
europmc-pmc8532080:
Asano and co-authors link rare TLR7 gene faults to life-threatening COVID-19 in men. Errors in type I interferon immunity were known to underlie some critical cases. TLR7 sits on the X chromosome, so faults hit males hardest. The team hunted such variants in men with unexplained critical pneumonia.

They found harmful TLR7 variants in 16 unrelated men from a cohort of 1202 patients. No such variants showed in 331 men with silent or mild infection. Blood cells from patients failed to answer TLR7 stimulation in tests. Family cases showed the same gene link. The authors place this fault behind about 1 percent of critical cases in men under 60 years.
europmc-pmc8710080:
Witwer and co-authors report on the planned update of MISEV, the minimal standards for studies of extracellular vesicles. These standards are a field-wide rigor effort led by the field's international society. The 2018 version drew input from more than 400 scientists. It covered naming, sample handling, separation, and reporting.

The society board asked past authors and members for views on the next update. This piece shares what that canvass found. It sets out themes for how the standards should evolve. Other rigor and standardization efforts in the society are also covered. The goal is work that other labs can check and repeat.
europmc-pmc8748880:
Kundu and co-authors test whether cross-reactive memory T cells protect household contacts of COVID-19 patients from infection. Such cells, left by past common cold coronaviruses, had been seen in earlier cohorts. The team studied 52 household contacts right after exposure. Blood tests counted T cells that react to several SARS-CoV-2 proteins.

Contacts who stayed PCR-negative held more cross-reactive memory T cells. The gap was clear for cells that secrete interleukin-2. Nucleocapsid-specific cells also ran higher in that group. Spike responses did not differ between groups. The authors back adding non-spike parts to next-generation vaccines.
europmc-pmc8810380:
Monroe and co-authors show that mutation bias in the plant Arabidopsis thaliana reflects natural selection. Classic theory holds that mutations strike at random with respect to their effects. Large surveys of brand-new mutations in this plant told a different story. Mutations landed less often in the genome's most constrained parts.

Mutation rates fell by half inside gene bodies. In essential genes, they fell by two-thirds. Genome features explained over 90 percent of the pattern. Natural variant patterns in wild plants matched the bias closely, with a correlation of 0.96. Genes under stronger selection had lower mutation rates. The authors say this challenges the view of mutation as directionless.
europmc-pmc8828480:
Lange and co-authors present CellRank, a method that maps where single cells are heading. Cells change state during growth, repair, and disease. Single-cell RNA data capture those states but lose their order. Older trajectory methods need the direction of change in advance. That limits them to known growth paths. CellRank works without that prior knowledge.

The method joins trajectory inference with RNA velocity data. It treats fate choices as gradual and partly random. It also accounts for shaky velocity estimates. On pancreas data, it found start, middle, and end cell groups on its own. It recovered known outcomes in reprogramming data. In injured lung, it predicted a new dedifferentiation path. Lab tests confirmed that path, the authors report.
europmc-pmc8951280:
Lahlali and co-authors review biological control of plant diseases from a global view. Chemical fungicides carry health and environmental costs. Consumers increasingly resist them. Helpful microbes offer an alternative shield for crops. Many candidate agents have been screened. Bacillus, Trichoderma, and Pseudomonas species lead the lists. Some products already fight leaf, root, and storage diseases. Yet few screened agents reach the market. That gap is the review's central puzzle.

The authors present the rhizosphere as a reservoir of biopesticides. Modes of action get a detailed section. Competition, antibiosis, and induced plant resistance all feature. A reality-check section follows. Field success depends on many shifting factors. Formulation, climate, and farm practice all count. Legislation slows products in many regions. The authors end with the sector's bottlenecks. Efficacy proof and approval rules are the chief ones.
europmc-pmc9090780:
Engeland sets out how the p53-p21-RB path controls the cell cycle. The proteins p53 and RB both act as tumor suppressors. They are often switched off in tumors. When p53 is turned on, it raises levels of p21. In turn, p21 helps RB lock onto gene targets and shut down genes that drive cell division.

The account shows how this chain leads to cell cycle arrest after DNA damage. It also compares this path with the closely linked p53-p21-DREAM path. The two paths share many target genes but differ in key ways. Engeland notes open questions about how cells choose between them. Readers get a precise map of a core brake on cell growth.
europmc-pmc9133880:
K and Rout comprehensively review conducting polymers, plastics that can carry electric current. These polymers offer tunable electric traits, good optical and mechanical traits, and easy making. In pure form they have limits, but blends with other materials can overcome them. Such blends serve energy, sensing, and medical fields.

The review explains the models that describe how charge moves in these materials. It covers main synthesis routes and key physical traits in depth. Carbon materials, metal oxides, and other partners in composites get close attention. Recent uses include energy storage, photocatalysis, anti-corrosion coatings, and sensors. Readers get a full picture of a material class that bridges plastics and electronics.
europmc-pmc9575280:
Tiwari, Trivedi, and Lin ask whether the tumor microenvironment is a barrier or an opening for cancer therapy. Tumors build a custom ecosystem from host parts. That setting helps tumors grow and spread. Its makeup varies a lot from patient to patient.

That spread helps explain uneven immunotherapy results. Some patients respond while others gain nothing. The review sorts the setting into niches and parts. Hypoxic and acidic zones get their own accounts. Stromal cells and the matrix between cells follow. Immune parts from macrophages to T cells are detailed. Therapy routes that strike the setting are surveyed next. Checkpoint blockers and cell therapies lead that list. The last part covers tools for study. Three-dimensional models and profiling software now read the setting in fine detail.
europmc-pmc9605880:
GBD 2019 LRI Collaborators assess age and sex gaps in the global burden of lower respiratory infections. Burden in children under five has been studied in depth. Older children and adults lacked the same full coverage. The study spans 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2019.

In 2019 there were an estimated 257 million infection episodes in males. Females had an estimated 232 million episodes that year. Deaths came to 1.30 million in males and 1.20 million in females. Standardized rates ran higher in males on both counts. Trends split sharply by age across the decades. Episodes and deaths fell in children under 15 years. Both rose in every adult age group over the same span. Men aged 70 years and older saw the largest rises. Top risk factors shifted with age and sex.
europmc-pmc9916680:
Chelakkot and co-authors explore how changing glycolysis could improve cancer therapy. Cancer cells shift to a glycolysis-dominant profile to gain energy and building blocks. This shift is known as the Warburg effect. It also makes the tumor setting more pro-cancer and raises drug and radiation resistance.

Immune cells in tumors make a like shift, so both cell types compete for nutrients. Blocking high glycolysis may leave cancer cells open to other treatments. Options include chemotherapy, radiotherapy, hormone therapy, immunotherapy, and photodynamic therapy. Many targeting tactics sit in preclinical or clinical testing. Few yet hit cancer glycolysis with enough precision. The review weighs what is known and what still blocks progress.
europmc-pmc9931580:
Karimi and co-authors chart single-cell spatial immune landscapes in primary and metastatic brain tumors. Tumor immunity depends on cell relationships inside the tumor setting. Many single-cell studies lose that spatial context by breaking tissue apart. The team used imaging mass cytometry to keep it.

They studied 139 high-grade glioma tumors and 46 brain metastasis tumors. Analysis covered more than 1.1 million cells in 389 images. Immune layouts differed between primary tumors and metastases from varied cancers. Cell neighborhoods linked to survival in glioblastoma patients. One group, myeloperoxidase-positive macrophages, marked long-term survival. The findings show why spatial detail matters in tumor studies. They also offer new clues on brain tumor biology.
europmc-pmc9952180:
Michaelis and Grohmann examine how antibiotic resistance genes spread by horizontal gene transfer in biofilms. Most bacteria live attached to surfaces inside a shared matrix. Biofilms in clinics hinder infection treatment by easing resistance gene uptake. Environmental biofilms can act as hotspots for spreading those genes.

Resistance genes often sit on mobile elements such as plasmids. Transfer runs faster in biofilms than in free-floating cultures. The review sums up biofilm study methods and tools that visualize transfer. It covers the three main routes: transformation, transduction, and conjugation. Fluorescence microscopy features among the imaging tools. The authors frame biofilm models as key tools for tracking resistance spread. The work links lab models to real-world risk.
frus-1861-d180:
Writing on 18 September 1861, William H. Seward sent a letter to Carl Schurz in Madrid. It is document 180 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Enclosed papers gave an envoy proof and text to lay before a court. Schurz could use such matter in talks at Madrid the same week. The letter with its pack of papers shows diplomacy supplied like a brief for a case at law. Papers sent with a letter often held the texts of laws or notes for the envoy's use. A brief fit for a case at law is a fair image of the envoy's whole craft.
frus-1861-d280:
4 July 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from Mr. Haldeman. The printed record keeps it as Document 280 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d80:
On 10 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote a second letter to Charles Francis Adams. It is document 80 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The habit of paired letters served a clerical end: one point per paper. It also served a human one, since Adams could act on each at its own speed. The pair shows the Secretary's office at its most neat under wartime strain. The clerks who kept these files gave the record the clean order it still has. A clear order to the record serves readers a century and a half later.
frus-1862-d180:
Two Seward dispatches to London are dated 3 November 1862, and the first of them is Document 180 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain.

Early November brought the British cabinet to its choice on the French truce plan. London was close to saying no, which would leave France to act alone or drop the scheme. Seward's mail in these days armed Adams for the final round of talks. This letter is one strand of the pressure and patience that kept Britain neutral. The State Department printed the London mail in full for Congress, enclosures and all.
frus-1862-d280:
On 22 May 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 280 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris, reporting on his post.

Late May found the war's focus on Richmond, where McClellan's advance had slowed to a siege pace. In Paris, the question of the hour was whether France would act with Britain on the American war or wait. Dayton's reports tracked that question through court and ministry talk. This one belongs to the quiet weeks before the summer's storms. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock.
frus-1862-d380:
Cassius Clay, the American minister in Russia, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 January 1862, opening the Russian file in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume as Document 380.

Russia was the great power most friendly to the Union in these years, and the St. Petersburg post carried a warmth the London and Paris files lack. Clay, a Kentucky abolitionist serving as envoy, reported from a court that wished the Union well. His early 1862 letters set the tone for the volume's calmest channel. Prince Gorchakov, Russia's foreign minister, made his government's sympathy for the Union plain. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d480:
On 16 September 1862 James E. Harvey wrote from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 480 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Harvey wrote the day before Antietam, though no word of the battle could reach him for weeks. His subject was Portugal: its court's temper, its port rules, and its place in the Atlantic war of cruisers and blockaders. Reports written in such ignorance of home events have their own honesty; they show what a post knew and feared on its own evidence. Seward read them all before shaping his autumn answers to Europe. The letter keeps the Portuguese thread of that story intact.
frus-1862-d580:
On 7 September 1862 James Watson Webb sent this report from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 580 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the annual message.

Webb wrote ten days before Antietam, in a hemisphere where the battle could not be known for many weeks. His subject was Brazil as he found it: its court's policy, its ports' practice, and the Union's standing there. Reports written in that isolation had to stand on the minister's own judgment, which in Webb's case was never in short supply. Seward read them for the southern facts of his global brief, and the September letter supplied them for the autumn file.
frus-1862-d680:
On 25 September 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to a Mr. Blatchford. The letter is document 680 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, set between the China file and the Egypt papers. Unlike most letters in the volume, it was not sent to an envoy posted abroad.

Seward's desk work ranged far past the great powers. Letters to men outside the legations still formed part of the State Department's record, and this one was kept and printed with the rest. It gives a glimpse of the smaller business that crossed a secretary's desk in wartime, next to the fate of nations.
frus-1862-d80:
Dated 13 June 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 80 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d180:
Reports like this one carried London news to Washington. This one went from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 May 1863, and it is document 180 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d280:
On 4 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 280 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d380:
Washington's business with Britain on 31 January 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 380 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Britain had claimed neutral rights at sea, while the Union navy stopped British ships suspected of aiding the South. The friction from those seizures runs through this whole exchange. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d480:
W. Hunter, chief clerk of the State Department directed a letter to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington on 27 April 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d580:
Document 580, dated 30 June 1863, records a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to William H. Seward, Secretary of State. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d680:
On 5 December 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent fresh word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The dispatch is document 680 in Foreign Relations of the United States, the printed record of Civil War era talks with other nations.

December brought the close of a hard year. Gettysburg and Vicksburg had raised Union hopes, yet British choices still mattered a great deal. Seward's job was to keep Britain neutral and to guard American trade and rights at sea. This letter is one link in that chain. It lets readers watch policy move in real time, not in a later summary.
frus-1863p1-d80:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 13 February 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 80 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The same date also drew a letter from Seward's side of the file, so the pens crossed that day on the Atlantic. Adams's third sheet rounds out his 13 February set. His winter mail kept a steady theme: Britain calm, the South's friends busy, the Union's cause held by care and facts. This letter is the last word of that day from London, filed with the rest.
frus-1880:
The 1880 volume opens with Hayes celebrating peace and prosperity. Its country files then run from Argentina to Venezuela. China takes the longest single run. Mexico and Germany follow at a distance. Legation correspondence from Washington doubles many sections. A special block stands apart from the country order. It prints the Fortune Bay affair in full. American fishermen, London says, suffered an outrage in Newfoundland.

Morocco supplies the mid-volume flavor. Evarts names Fairchild, the minister at Madrid, as American delegate. A conference on Morocco is gathering under Spanish invitation. Tangier negotiations supply his briefing papers. Turkey splits into Turkey, Egypt, and Tunis. The volume shows the series in its mature form. Every post reports; a few files flare into disputes.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d180: The Secret Protocol of the Moscow Conference, dated November 1, 1943, is Document 180 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Protocols fixed in binding words what the ministers had agreed behind the public declarations, and this one was kept from print at the time. Its signing closed the first three-power foreign ministers' meeting of the war. The text, once secret, is printed in the Foreign Relations series, where readers can weigh what the allies promised each other in private.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d280:
The United States Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 404 at Cairo on 22 November 1943, the proposed American agenda for the Sextant Conference. It is the detailed counterpart to the shorter British agenda printed next in the volume, and it lays out five heads of business.

After procedure and the overall objective, the European and Mediterranean head calls for enemy estimates, bomber offensive and anti-U-boat reports, the Azores facilities, and readiness reports on Overlord, Rankin, and Jupiter. The Japan head asks for a 1944 enemy estimate, a short-term plan for Japan's defeat, and reports on Southeast Asia, China, and the Pacific. A final head weighs resources against plans, asking whether the forces exist to carry out everything proposed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d380: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume covers the Tehran dinner meeting of 1 December 1943, which lasted, by the President's Log, until half past ten at night. No official minutes of the conversation appear to have been prepared at the time. A memorandum written by Charles Bohlen a few days later indicates two things. The Declaration on Iran and the conference communiqué were discussed at the dinner. They were also put into final form there. The editors print this note in place of a contemporary record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d480:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull wrote to President Roosevelt on December 4, 1943, the day the Second Cairo Conference opened. Hull remained in Washington while Roosevelt met Churchill at Cairo, fresh from Tehran. The cable appears in the State Department's published Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Hull's cables were the department's way of sitting at a conference it had not attended in person. They brought Washington's news and views to the President at the moment decisions were being made abroad. For the reader, this message is part of the long-distance conversation that tied the traveling summit to the home government throughout December 1943.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d80: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 31, 1943, and another Churchill note of the same date stands beside it in the volume. This one is Document 80 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Halloween found the alliance counting Moscow's gains and drafting the November meetings. The catalog record gives the date and the two names and no subject. The message is part of the Foreign Relations series' dense autumn run.
frus-1944-quebec-d180:
An editors' note prints Harry Dexter White's memorandum of Roosevelt's talk with Morgenthau on September 13, 1944. White was not present; he summarized what the Treasury secretary told him. Roosevelt had summoned Morgenthau to Quebec to talk with Lord Cherwell, and over tea he went through the Treasury's book of memoranda on Germany item by item, setting limits on the discussion.

Morgenthau could discuss internationalizing the Ruhr and the Saar, including the Kiel Canal, Roosevelt said. He could even mention giving Holland a piece of western Germany for land the Germans had inundated. But occupation zones were a military question, and partitioning a political one; both were off limits. Eden was being sent for. "Don't worry about Churchill," the president added. "He is going to be tough too."
frus-1944-quebec-d280:
Amphibious craft, above all LSTs, are the subject of C.C.S. 687, proposed by the United States Chiefs on September 16, 1944. Accelerated operations in the Pacific and prospective plans for Southeast Asia required the earliest practicable withdrawal of landing craft from the European theater. The Combined Chiefs approved sending the message to Eisenhower, and it went out as Facs 81.

Eisenhower was asked to review the situation carefully with the object of an early release of craft from Overlord. Regard was to be had for his build-up needs until adequate port facilities became available, and for the weather limits on using such craft in the near future. An early report on the matter was desired.
frus-1944-quebec-d80:
Riddleberger wrote to Secretary of State Hull on September 4, 1944. He headed the Division of Central European Affairs at the department. His letter appears in the pre-conference papers of the Quebec 1944 volume. The conference in Canada opened eight days later.

A division chief reported upward as summit planning quickened. Central Europe faced occupation, new borders, and great human need. Hull needed his experts' judgment before advising the President. For readers, the letter shows the State Department's own chain at work. Regional specialists briefed their secretary while the Quebec agenda took shape.
frus-1945-50-intel-d180:
On 24 December 1946, the Chairman (Eddy) sent a memorandum to the Members of the Advisory Committee on Intelligence. It stands as document 180 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d280: The title "Memorandum of Meeting" heads a text dated 28 May 1948. It is document 280 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA was in its first year, and the Council was taking up covert action for the first time. After key talks, an aide would write up what was said for the file.
frus-1945-50-intel-d380:
On 7 April 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 37th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 380, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Reform talk filled the files that year, as the government weighed the Dulles team's harsh grades for the CIA.

A memcon lets later readers sit in on a talk they could not attend: who spoke, what was asked, what was left open. So the talk could guide later work, each point is set down while its weight is still clear. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d80:
McCormack wrote to Under Secretary Acheson on 27 October 1945. The intelligence chief carried his office's case to the department's second-ranking man. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Acheson was the officer who most shaped the State Department's daily work, and his ear was worth more than most men's votes. McCormack's memorandum shows the intelligence office pleading its needs, staff, standing, or scope, at that level. Readers following the State thread should mark the Acheson papers: his support raised the office. His later doubts about its fit inside the department helped end its season at the center of American intelligence.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d180:
“Principal Yugoslav Problems” gives the bleakest reading of Tito's rise in the briefing book. Prepared on 27 January 1945 for the President's trip, the paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary pulls no punches about who holds Yugoslavia.

The Partisan movement, it says, in fact controls the freed parts of the country. Its armed strength, the Soviet armies present under a formal deal with Tito, and months of British and Soviet support have built a powerful political machine. Rival groups, from Mihailovic's nationalists to the Croatian Peasant Party, sit in sullen impotence. All signs point to a firmly totalitarian regime to come. The Tito–Subasic agreement would hand real power to Tito's organization, with just enough exile faces to win foreign recognition.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d280:
Richard Law initialled the shipping agreement with a caveat, and explained it to Harry Hopkins on 14 January 1945. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, concerns clause 10 of the American-British memorandum on supplies for freed Europe. Law was the British minister of state who signed for London.

Clause 10, as Law reads it, is a “no prejudice” clause. It leaves the present way of deciding shipping space exactly as it stands. Nothing in the paper settles, or even touches, what those procedures are or should be. He is sure it cannot fairly be read as changing them at all. Present practice, he notes, gives the military no veto over civilian shipping allotments. It does ensure the fullest exchange of information and consultation between the shipping authorities and the chiefs of staff.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d380:
Hold off. Secretary Stettinius's top secret cable to Ambassador Winant in London, sent February 7, 1945, orders a pause on France. In view of talks at Yalta, Winant was to take no action on the American position about France in German affairs. The cable repeats "no" for stress. He must wait for further instructions.

The freeze mattered because Winant had called a meeting of the European Advisory Commission for February 9. There he meant to announce American acceptance of France's request. Stettinius's wire stopped the announcement while the leaders settled France's zone and status. A copy went to Grew in Washington for his information.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d480:
A solemn warning to Germany is the subject of Grew's cable of February 6, 1945. The French Embassy had presented a formal note in Washington on February 3. France intended to warn the German government against maltreatment of, or reprisals against, French prisoners of war and deportees. Such acts would violate international law.

The French believed the warning would carry more weight, and might save thousands of lives, if issued by the United Nations as a whole. Paris sought clarification on one point: would the warning cover all United Nations nationals, not only French ones? Grew sent the matter on in case it rose at the conference. Left there, he would take it up in Washington.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d80:
Harriman was told to carry the President's words to Stalin in person. Secretary of State Stettinius sent the instruction on 5 December 1944, marked for the ambassador's urgent and personal attention. The cable, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, opens the final push to settle Security Council voting.

Roosevelt's message says the Big Three meeting is still unsettled, so the voting question cannot wait. Agreement on it must come before a general United Nations conference can be called. Harriman is to discuss the matter with Stalin on the President's behalf, and the same approach is being made to Churchill. The cable then quotes the draft voting provision itself, beginning with one vote for each Council member.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d180:
Under Secretary Grew forwarded the revised British agenda to the President in a memorandum dated July 3, 1945. The short covering memo is document 180 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It follows the trail of the original British list, sent May 30, and the Department's comments of June 14.

The British Embassy has now handed over a revised list of suggested topics, with comments, drawn up in a form fit to be shown to the Soviet government. Many problems on the first list have since been solved, as the Department expected. The new list runs mostly parallel to the Department's own draft agenda. The principal difference, Grew notes, is that it contains no topic on the Far East, an omission the Department pointed out to the embassy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d280:
Ambassador Kirk reported a standstill over the British move into Styria in a telegram from Caserta on July 3, 1945. The message is document 280 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Allied headquarters had directed the British Eighth Army to arrange with the local Soviet commander for a withdrawal from southern Austria.

On July 1 the British Fifth Corps commander met the Russians at Soviet Fourth Army headquarters and delivered the Eighth Army's letter. The Soviet commander said he had received no orders to withdraw and would hold his position until he did. A written reply the next day was cordial: the letter would go promptly to Marshal Koniev, but Soviet forces in Styria could not move without his orders. The episode mirrors the delays the Americans met over Berlin and Austria alike.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d380:
American and British reparations men met at Babelsberg on July 15, 1945, and a delegation memorandum records the session. Sir Walter Monckton led the British group; Pauley, Clayton, and others spoke for the United States. Clayton read the American paper's sections on war booty, labor services, restitution, and territorial cessions.

On war booty the British agreed in principle, but counseled against pressing the point. An agreed definition, they argued, would bind the West while not restricting the Russians. Pauley disagreed, saying the negotiations would drag on without end unless agreement was reached. The memo captures allied tactics, not just allied aims, on the eve of Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d480:
British second thoughts on Allied Force Headquarters come in a memorandum by the British Chiefs of Staff representatives dated July 12, 1945. London has given further thought, it reports, to the dissolution of the headquarters and the organization that would follow it. The supreme commander, Mediterranean, and the commanders-in-chief, Middle East, have sent in their comments on the original proposals.

When those comments are considered, the British chiefs will put forward further draft proposals for the American chiefs. Meanwhile they agree to dispatching the message enclosed with the American paper, with one amendment. A substituted paragraph promises that the Combined Chiefs will send direction for the headquarters' future following the Terminal conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d580:
Japan's foreign minister, Shigenori Togo, wired his ambassador in Moscow, Naotake Sato, on July 11, 1945. The very secret cable, read here in translation, is document 580 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. U.S. officials held a copy within days of its sending.

Togo says Japan's state at home and abroad is very grave. Even ending the war, he admits, is now weighed in private. Tokyo's talks with Moscow aim not just at closer ties, but at sounding out Soviet help to end the war. He hints Japan could give up fishing rights won in 1905 to please the Soviets. He orders Sato to see Molotov at once and learn Soviet thinking. Yet Sato must not let Moscow sense that Japan hopes to use it to end the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d680:
A top secret briefing paper on the Montreux Convention was dated June 27, 1945. It is document 680 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The 1936 pact set the rules for warships and trade ships passing the Turkish Straits.

The paper notes that Moscow aired its discontent at Yalta without stating its wishes. The Big Three agreed Russia would present them later for talks among foreign ministers. Washington has since told London it stands ready to discuss the Straits at the heads-of-government meeting. The paper remarks on an oddity in that stance. The United States never signed the Montreux Convention, yet Britain and Russia have drawn it fully into the question. Turkey, the state most affected, has not been consulted at all. U.S. interests are named as free commerce and a Straits regime that best promotes peace.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d80:
General John Deane, head of the U.S. military mission in Moscow, reported a Soviet refusal to Eisenhower on June 20, 1945. His urgent telegram is document 80 in the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Americans wanted General Parks's survey party admitted to Berlin at once; Soviet General Antonov would not move the date.

Antonov told Deane the question was being decided between the two governments, and he could not change his earlier decision to hold the survey until Zhukov returned around June 28 or 29. Deane notes that Harriman had raised the matter with the Foreign Office twice already, on June 15 and again the night before. They would keep trying. The exchange is an early taste of the slow Soviet bargaining style that marked the conference itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1080:
Foy Kohler, an assistant chief of Near Eastern affairs, recorded this conversation in Washington on July 25, 1945. The Greek ambassador had called to read a telegram from Athens. It quotes a Yugoslav note of July 23 demanding an end to terror against people of Yugoslav origin in Aegean Macedonia. Property was to be restored and reparations paid.

Athens calls the note a planned blow at Greek security and refuses to answer it. Greece has never recognized a Yugoslav minority, the telegram insists, and foreign meddling cannot be admitted. The refugees in Yugoslavia are branded collaborators or fugitive ELAS men. Greece will take no action, the ambassador adds, until it hears the American and British views.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1180:
The Secretary of State wrote to the President on 30 June 1945, more than two weeks before Potsdam opened. Papers from the run-up set the agenda and framed the choices Truman would face in Germany. The war in Europe had been over for less than two months.

Pre-summit messages did quiet, vital work. They sorted the questions, marked the hard ones, and lined up the facts the president would need. This letter belongs to that groundwork. It shows the peace being planned while the guns in Europe were barely cold. The summit's story starts here, not at the opening gavel.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1280:
General Deane, who commanded the United States Military Mission to the Soviet Union, wrote this memorandum on 24 July 1945. Deane's mission in Moscow was the American army's post inside the Soviet capital. He dealt with Soviet officers daily and knew their ways at first hand.

His memoranda carried that hard-won knowledge to the summit's staff. Few Americans had watched Soviet conduct as closely, or with as much friction, as Deane. A paper from his hand gave the team the Moscow mission's view. It is the soldier-envoy's voice in the record, blunt from experience.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1380:
W. Averell Brown, a special assistant to the secretary of state, wrote to both President Truman and Secretary Byrnes on 2 August 1945. That was the day the Potsdam Conference issued its closing papers. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A paper addressed to the president and the secretary together sits high in the pile. Brown wrote as the talks ended, when the results had to be summed up and carried home. Readers can place his memorandum at the hinge between the conference and what followed. First came the return to Washington and the reports to Congress and the press. Then came the hard work of making the Potsdam choices stick, in a world still at war with Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-80:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 23, 1945, compress the day's foreign ministers' report into a page. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov read the report aloud, and Cohen tracked its points in order.

The economic subcommittee was told to study the Soviet reparations plans. On German economic principles, Russia withdrew her amendment to paragraph 13. She asked instead that paragraph 18 be deleted for further study by the Control Council, and no agreement was reached. The Council of Foreign Ministers proposal was approved with wording changes. On trusteeships, the Italian colonies' disposition was assigned to that council. Tangier produced a clean decision amid the disputes. It would return to its international status, with a four-power conference, France included, to meet in the near future.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d780:
Erhardt reported again on Austrian affairs on July 23, 1945, in document 780. The political adviser wrote to the Acting Secretary of State from his post among the occupiers. Austria's zones and its future government were live questions. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Follow-up reports show a problem refusing to sit still. Erhardt updated Washington as facts on the ground changed. Readers see occupation politics at working level: parties, officers, and rumors. The document adds ground truth to the summit's air. It reminds us that Potsdam's lines on maps had to be walked by men like Erhardt.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d880:
Willard Thorp, deputy to the Assistant Secretary of State for economic affairs, cabled William Clayton at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. Thorp reports a Washington meeting with British officials on German supply problems. The talks backed a zonal approach to buying and financing imports for occupied Germany.

Thorp quotes the British telegram that reported the American plan. Zone needs would be coordinated through CRAB, a joint supply body, using shared standards for food and industry. Shortfalls in one zone would be met from surpluses in others where possible. Import programs would go to the Combined Boards together, with equal priority for each zone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d980:
Edwin Pauley and Isador Lubin sent this report on German reparations to the President on September 20, 1945. The printed text is an extract. It reviews their work from February to September 1945. Part V, shown here, covers the tripartite conference at Berlin, from July 16 to August 2.

Pauley reached Berlin from Moscow on July 14 with his senior staff. Talks with William Clayton's team shaped how to lay the reparations problem before the Big Three. The American proposals went into an annex on reparations. It held the seven agreed principles, the disputed first charge clause, and the agreed division of shares. It also offered definitions of restitution, war booty, and reparations.
gaius-institutes-muirhead-1880:
James Muirhead published his translation of The Institutes of Gaius in 1880. Gaius, a Roman law teacher, wrote the Institutes around 160 CE as a textbook for students. The text was lost for centuries and recovered in 1816 from a scraped parchment in Verona.

Gaius sorted all law under persons, things, and actions, a scheme that law teaching used for a thousand years. His plain style and clear order made Roman law learnable, and Justinian's own Institutes copied his plan. Muirhead, a Scottish professor of law, added notes for English students. The translation gives modern readers the Roman law school's own starting point, in the form that taught lawyers for a millennium.
gao-gaoreports-b-295780:
GAO ruled in file B-295780 on March 28, 2005, in the protest brought by AVL Books.Com, Inc. The Naval Supply Systems Command had sought medical journal subscriptions. The firm's quotation was judged in part on an ability to process claims online. The firm said that term was added by word of mouth, without proper notice to it. GAO denied the protest. The digest holds that the oral notice fairly advised firms of the added requirement.

An amendment need not take any set form to count. What matters is that offerors learn of the new term in time to meet it. On this record, they did.
gao-gaoreports-b-297280:
Alluviam protested the rejection of its bid for guard gear in GAO decision B-297280, dated December 15, 2005. The buyer was the Army. The gear would help stop and meet terror threats. The firm's gear was not yet on the federal supply schedule. Its place there was in the works. The call said gear had to be on the list at bid time.

GAO denied the protest. A place in the works is not a place on the list. The call set bid time as the test date. The gear missed that test. The cut was thus proper. Firms must meet list terms at the date the call sets.
gao-gaoreports-b-299880:
Kemron Environmental Services protested an Environmental Protection Agency award to WRS Infrastructure & Environment. The contract covers superfund emergency and rapid response services. Crews remove hazardous substances at spill sites. GAO decided B-299880 on September 7, 2007.

The agency had let slip some of the firm's price facts. Those facts reached the winning rival mid-contest. The firm sought a fresh buy or an award to itself. GAO found the slip was narrow in scope. The record did not show real harm to the firm's fair chance. A leak without shown harm does not force so harsh a cure. The award could stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310780:
An acting chief's long service is cleared in this GAO opinion, B-310780, dated June 13, 2008. Steven G. Bradbury served as top aide in the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel. The post needs a nod from the Senate to fill for good. Three senators asked if his stint broke the Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998. That act caps most acting stints at 210 days.

GAO held that it did not. The act lets an aide stay on once a pick is sent to the Senate. It gives fresh spans when a pick is sent back. Bradbury's spans fit those paths. The post was not held past the act's clock.
gao-gaoreports-b-310980:
Fedcar Company, Ltd. won its protest. That ruling is B-310980, dated March 25, 2008. The case turns on a lease pick by the General Services Administration. The winner bid high in price and score. Fedcar bid low in both, by a slim gap. The file on the pick praised the winner's plus points in full. It said naught of flaws on that side or merits on Fedcar's.

GAO sustained the protest. The cost math in the pick was wrong in fact. A one-sided file can not back a trade of price for worth. One more point hit the lease act. A take with new terms is a counter-bid, not a deal.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-380:
Technology Assessment, GAO-05-380 of April 26, 2005, gathers what tech and craft can save homes from wild fire, and let crews talk as they fight. Since 1984, wild fires have burned a mean of more than 850 homes a year. More folks move to the wild edge each year, so the count at risk grows. Fire loss was 2 percent of all vast loss claims from 1983 through 2002.

Home care rests with owners and town rule, not the federal state. GAO lists the steps that shield a home, from roof stuff to clear yards. It names what stops folks from use of them. It weighs new radio paths for crews.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-480:
Three programs that move new defense technology from lab to field are assessed in GAO-05-480, a report released on June 17, 2005. Both Congress and the Defense Department agree new ideas move too slowly into use. The Technology Transition Initiative speeds lab work into purchases. The Defense Acquisition Challenge Program brings in cost-saving ideas from inside and outside. The Quick Reaction Fund tests prototypes fast.

All three were well aimed at a real problem, GAO said. Each used its own tests, letting the department try varied approaches. But it was too soon to judge results. Of 68 projects funded in fiscal years 2003 and 2004, only 11 were done. 4 gave users full capability. The programs had few ways to measure success or return on spending. Early gains included faster fielding and one small drone that can sniff out chemical and biological agents. The report urges stronger selection and tracking.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-380:
Infant formula is a big cost in a food program for mothers and young children. GAO decided GAO-06-380 on March 28, 2006. The program is the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children, known as WIC. It serves close to 8 million low-income women, infants, and young children each year. Rebate savings from formula makers help serve about a quarter of them.

The Food and Nutrition Service runs WIC. GAO studied what drives formula spending and how rebate savings have changed. It also reviewed steps taken to contain state formula costs. GAO said the service could take more steps. Readers get the cost drivers and savings trade-offs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-580:
A new trade processing system must speed cargo and strengthen the border at once. Report GAO-06-580, issued May 31, 2006, reviews the Automated Commercial Environment system. The Homeland Security Department is building the system over many years at multibillion-dollar cost. By law, spending plans for it must meet set conditions, including GAO review. This study addresses the fiscal year 2006 plan. It asks whether the plan satisfies those conditions.

GAO also describes progress on its prior recommendations for the program. It gives observations on the plan and on program management. Progress has been made, GAO found. Long-standing management challenges and new risks remain. Readers get a plan check and a risk list.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-780:
Health gains from cleaner air are weighed in GAO-06-780. GAO issued the report on July 17, 2006. Tiny airborne particles, called particulate matter, are linked to asthma and early death. The Environmental Protection Agency sets national air quality standards for them under the Clean Air Act. Cost-benefit studies of those rules rest on estimates of health benefits. The National Academies had urged the agency to improve those estimates, and GAO checked the response.

GAO found that the agency had started to act on the advice. It was assessing uncertainty more rigorously and showing its math with more openness. It also analyzed exposure in more detail and weighed each regulatory option. Even so, GAO said more progress was needed. Better benefit estimates, GAO argued, lead to better air rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-80:
Aging workers and the labor market are studied in GAO report GAO-06-80, issued on December 5, 2005. As baby boomers near retirement age, their exit could drain skills and slow growth. Many older Americans also face less secure retirements, due to health costs and pension changes. GAO examined where older workers are employed. GAO also judged how the Labor Department can help employers and workers plan ahead.

GAO found that workers aged 55 to 74 appear in every part of the labor market. Almost 80 percent of them work in professional, management, service, office, and sales jobs. Those fields make up about 76 percent of the total workforce aged 25 to 74. The aging wave thus touches nearly every employer. GAO urged the department to spread planning tools for phased retirement and skill retention.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-880:
Medicare hospital pay, and a new way to set it, is the matter in GAO-06-880, a report dated July 28, 2006. Hospitals get fixed pay per stay under groups based on diagnosis and care given. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or CMS, had used charge-based weights to update that pay.

A 2003 law told GAO to study pay against true cost. GAO tested whether CMS's cost-based method, used for outpatient pay, could weight inpatient groups too. It used cost reports and claims for thousands of hospitals. GAO judged the planned approach promising, and weighed where it beat the older method.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-980:
Claimed savings from a defense travel system are doubted in GAO report GAO-06-980, dated September 26, 2006. The Defense Travel System, begun in 1995, aims to be the one travel tool for the whole Defense Department. A January 2006 GAO report had flagged build problems.

For this follow-up, GAO tested two key claims in a September 2003 cost study. It asked if the department pushes full use of the system, and tracks that use. It checked if past flaws in flight data were fixed. Reported savings look shaky, GAO found, and build hurdles remain. The report shows why big office systems need proof, not pledges.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-280:
Do the elderly drain their savings to qualify for Medicaid nursing home care? GAO measured the practice in GAO-07-280, issued March 26, 2007. Medicaid paid nearly half of U.S. long-term care costs in 2004. Giving assets away cheaply can trigger a coverage penalty. GAO studied national survey data on nursing home residents. It also read 540 application files in three states.

Most residents entered care with modest means, GAO found. About 90 percent had yearly incomes of $20,000 or less. The median savings of Medicaid-covered residents was just $48. That compares with $36,123 for residents not on Medicaid. In the file review, about 10 percent of approved applicants had given assets away cheaply. That was 47 of 465 approved files. Their penalties had mostly expired before they applied. A 2005 law tightened the rules, but its effect stays unclear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-380:
The Army handed a contractor a partner's seat in running its biggest weapons program, and oversight blurred. GAO examined the arrangement in GAO-07-380, issued June 6, 2007. The Future Combat Systems program began in 2003. Its integrator firm helps define the systems it builds. The Army said it lacked staff and network skills to run the program alone. The schedule allowed about 5 and a half years. GAO reviewed the contract's fees and incentives.

The defense oversight office largely accepted Army framing, GAO found. It approved the program in 2003 despite immature technology. It skipped a planned recheck 18 months later. Budget requests used the Army's cost figures, not higher independent ones. The integrator manages work across old program lines. That reach exceeds a normal contractor's role. Fees aim to reward development effort. GAO urged tighter links between fees and proven results. The department agreed with the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-480:
Guarding sewage plants costs each site a different sum, and GAO-07-480, a GAO report issued March 30, 2007, gathers the range. Big wastewater plants face a terror and accident risk from chlorine gas. The Clean Air Act forces plants that hold set amounts of the gas to write risk management plans. Many plants had also run voluntary security checks and switched to safer disinfection methods.

GAO phoned plants it had surveyed for a 2006 report. It asked what the security checks and risk plans cost to prepare. It also priced the switch away from chlorine gas to other methods. Answers varied widely by plant size and method chosen. The Environmental Protection Agency agreed with the report and offered small fixes. For towns weighing a switch, the study gives real-world cost bands instead of guesses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-680:
Unemployment Insurance claimants who may run out of benefits are the focus of GAO-07-680, issued June 14, 2007. The program paid about $30 billion in benefits in 2006. Since 1993, states must spot claimants who are most likely to exhaust their benefits. States then refer those claimants to job help services. This effort is called the Worker Profiling and Reemployment Services initiative. GAO studied how states pick claimants and what help they get.

Most states use math models to rank claimants by risk. Forty-five of 53 states and territories use such models. Yet 30 states had not updated their models since the mid-1990s. Six of seven states GAO visited gave less job help than the Department of Labor advised. Little proof exists that the program speeds a return to work. GAO urged Labor to guide states more and to test the program's impact. Labor largely agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-780:
Deployment pace data for troops are faulted in GAO-07-780, dated July 17, 2007. Law requires the Defense Department to report each year on personnel tempo. That term means time service members spend away from home. Congress asked GAO to check how policy shifts affected reserve forces. It also asked how well the Army and Marine Corps track tempo data. GAO read the department's tempo databases. It spoke with officials across the services.

In January 2007, the Defense chief scrapped a 24-month cap on involuntary reserve call-ups. Nearly all reserve members became open to repeat call-ups with no total limit. Tours will in general run 12 months at a time. The shift greatly widened the pool for war duty. GAO found the tempo data themselves unreliable, though. The Army and Marine Corps lacked checks to validate the figures. GAO urged quality controls for the data. The department agreed with that call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-80:
Phone and data lines for big users are studied in GAO-07-80, dated November 29, 2006. Dedicated access services link offices that need heavy voice and data capacity. They earned major phone firms about $16 billion in 2005. The Federal Communications Commission once set their prices by rule. Since 2001, it has let prices float where it sees rivalry. GAO tested whether rivals truly serve those areas. It tracked price shifts and the agency's monitoring.

Rivals served less than 6 percent of buildings with basic demand in 16 big metro areas. For buildings with the highest demand, the share rose to about 24 percent. The agency's triggers for judging rivalry did not match building-level facts well. Some areas saw rival presence shrink over time. Prices under flexible rules raised concern for government buyers. GAO urged the agency to define effective competition better. It also urged more data to track the market. The agency disagreed with both calls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-180:
First responders' tools for chemical and nuclear hazards are tested in GAO report GAO-08-180, dated June 27, 2008. City crews must answer both terror attacks and accidents that release such agents. Two tools guide them. Detectors name the agent in the air. Plume models chart where it will drift and whom it may harm.

GAO found that both tools fall well short in city settings. Detection gear has clear limits, and its testing and standards are thin. Plume models track spread poorly among tall buildings. Data on how exposure harms city crowds are also scarce. The title states the result in plain terms: the ability is significantly limited.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-280:
Computer security at the market watchdog is graded in GAO report GAO-08-280 (February 29, 2008). The Securities and Exchange Commission leans on computer systems to police the markets. Layers of controls must guard its financial and sensitive data. The review grew from GAO's audit of the agency's fiscal year 2007 statements. It checked old flaws and live defenses alike.

GAO tested whether past security weaknesses have been corrected. It also judged how well current controls keep data private, sound, and available. Plans, policies, and hands-on tests inform the findings. The verdict sits in the title: the agency needs to keep improving its program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-380:
School improvement funds under the No Child Left Behind Act are tracked in GAO report GAO-08-380, released February 29, 2008. Over 10,000 schools were flagged for improvement in the 2006-2007 school year. States must set aside 4 percent of their Title I funds to help those schools.

A hold-harmless rule kept 22 states from setting aside the full 4 percent since 2002, since it guards district funding levels first. States still aimed most funds at the lowest-performing schools, though 4 states broke some targeting rules and 4 could not list which schools got funds. The Department of Education had not spotted the targeting issue in its monitoring. GAO recommended tighter monitoring and clear guidance on listing funded schools. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-480:
Funding choices for the global AIDS program are studied in GAO report GAO-08-480, dated April 2, 2008.
