Martin Ouma and co-authors tested whether extracts of a traditional African plant can protect male fertility against oxidative stress. Carissa spinarum is used traditionally for male infertility, but its chemistry and effects were unproven. Their 2026 study profiled root and leaf extracts, then fed root extract to rats whose fertility was damaged by a stress-inducing drug.

Leaves carried more protective chemicals and stronger antioxidant activity than roots in the test tube. In rats, a mid-level root dose raised sperm count, normal sperm shape, and testis weight. Antioxidant defences in the testes rose while a damage marker fell. Two doses visibly repaired drug-damaged testis tissue. Ouma and colleagues say the results support the traditional use, within animal limits.
plos-pone-0355480:
Fayssal Mekaret and seven colleagues compare ways of modeling a tricky electrical contact in silicon carbide, a material prized for high-power electronics. Where metal meets this semiconductor, the energy barrier that controls current flow is not uniform; it varies from spot to spot. Engineers use different mathematical models to describe that unevenness, and choosing among them is not obvious.

Working with computer simulations across three forms of silicon carbide, the team tested three established approaches. One stresses surface states that pin the energy level, another treats the barrier height as spread out statistically, and the third focuses on small low-barrier patches that carry most of the current. Each revealed a different mechanism, yet all showed current rising with heat in the expected way. The comparison gives device designers clearer guidance for building better contacts.
plos-pone-0355680:
Connor T Panter and colleagues tracked 103 red kites through 180 winters using satellite tags. Red kites are elegant raptors of European farmland. The team asked how much of the birds' winter ground sits inside protected areas. Their 2026 study modeled overlap with Europe's Natura 2000 reserves and other bird areas. It also looked for what predicted a well-protected winter.

Only about a quarter of the kites' core and home ranges overlapped protected land. Birds wintering amid heavy agriculture were worst covered. Birds in Iberia and the Pyrenees fared worse than central European birds. Yet Spain hosts the world's largest wintering population. It also lists the species as endangered nationally. The authors urge new designations aimed at traditional farmland, where legal protection currently thins out.
plos-pone-0355780:
Shaheer Khan, Gautam Talukdar, and Bilal Habib map safe ground for one of the world's rarest large birds in India's Deccan region, in this 2026 conservation study. The Great Indian Bustard, a heavy grassland bird once spread across India and southern Pakistan, now numbers perhaps one hundred to one hundred fifty individuals. Combining landscape surveys with species distribution modeling across an enormous study area, the team estimated where suitable habitat remains.

Only about six to seven percent of the Deccan landscape qualified as suitable. Sixteen critical sites, together about eighteen thousand square kilometers, were named as conservation priorities, forming a mosaic of grassland and farmland. The authors stress that these areas' futures hinge on reviving traditional low-intensity farming and protecting remnant grassland patches. They recommend habitat restoration there as the species' best remaining chance in the south of its range.
plos-pone-0356180:
Koki Nambu and colleagues describe a planned trial of a fibre supplement for a chronic mouth inflammation called oral lichen planus. The condition has no cure, and the team's earlier work found disturbed gut microbes in patients, with too few bacteria that make a calming chemical. Their 2026 protocol sets out a double-blind trial across several centres.

Eighty patients will receive either inulin fibre or a look-alike placebo daily for four weeks, alongside usual care. The main measure is change in the share of the target gut bacteria by week six. Immune markers and wider microbe shifts are secondary measures. No results exist yet; the paper's contribution is a careful, registered test of a gut-directed idea.
plos-pone-0356280:
Ning Shi and three colleagues develop a faster way to judge whether a landslide dam might collapse, in this 2026 study. Such dams form when a slope dumps debris into a river, and their failure can flood downstream towns with little warning. The team used the huge Tangjiashan dam, created by the 2008 Wenchuan earthquake, as their test case, building computer models that treat the debris strength as variable rather than fixed.

Their full model scattered strength values randomly across the dam and ran many simulations to estimate the odds of failure. A leaner local version, which weakens only the most stressed zones, matched the full model's answers while running far more cheaply. The authors offer the method as a practical tool for emergency teams who must judge a new dam's stability within hours, not weeks.
plos-pone-0356380:
Kritika Roka and five colleagues survey mothers in Biratnagar, Nepal, about how they fed their babies, in this 2026 study. Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is among the cheapest ways to protect infant health, yet rates lag in many countries. Interviewers spoke with just over two hundred mothers of children aged six to twenty-three months about feeding since birth and what they knew of the guidance.

Only about thirty-eight percent had breastfed exclusively, for a median of four months, and barely a fifth had adequate knowledge of the recommendation. Many babies received water or formula early, most often because mothers believed their milk was insufficient, or because of work. Mothers in joint families, mothers without schooling, and especially mothers who had no breastfeeding problems were more likely to manage exclusive feeding. The authors call for counseling built into routine mother-and-baby visits.
plos-pone-0356480:
Vera Logan leads a team of seven testing a checklist against the quiet harm of repeat prescriptions, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Older patients on many medicines accumulate side effects nobody is assigned to notice. The intervention is a structured symptom profile patients complete. A practice pharmacist reviews it and acts. Six practices in South West Wales were randomized as clusters. They recruited sixty patients over sixty-five, each on more than four long term medicines, living at home.

The trial paired numbers with a process evaluation. Records before and after were modeled for problems and prescribing changes, adjusting for age, deprivation, and comorbidity. Symptoms on first and second profiles were compared to see what resolved. Patients and staff described the work involved. Harm from unmonitored prescriptions has been documented for decades and prevented by almost nothing. This trial asks whether structured patient reporting can move it.
plos-pone-0356880:
Chia-En Hsieh and colleagues surveyed 345 clinical nurses at a Taiwanese medical center to trace how workplace stress erodes commitment to the profession, and what psychological steps carry the damage. Their 2026 cross-sectional study measured stress, resilience, coping style, and professional commitment, then tested a chain model in which stress works through resilience and then coping.

Stress was indeed linked to weaker commitment, and the chain held: nurses with depleted resilience coped less adaptively, and commitment suffered further, though a direct stress effect remained. Because the design captures one moment, the authors avoid causal claims. Still, the pathway suggests hospitals wanting to keep nurses should invest in resilience training and coping support, not merely exhort loyalty.
plos-pone-0357180:
Bianca Cristina dos Santos led a team of eight researchers studying sickle cell anemia in mice, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. In this disease, misshapen red cells break apart and spill free hemoglobin into the blood, where it does harm. The team tested haptoglobin, a protein the body already uses to mop up that free hemoglobin.

Dos Santos and her colleagues asked whether giving extra haptoglobin could work as a treatment in a mouse model of the disease. Their results point to real promise for that approach. If the effect holds up in later work, boosting a natural cleanup protein could become one way to limit the damage sickle cell disease does to organs over time.
plos-pone-0357380:
Wanjie Kang and Youshun Pan presented a method for hiding messages inside images, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Steganography conceals data within a picture so its very presence stays secret. The hidden data must survive routine handling, such as compression or cropping, or the message is lost or exposed.

Kang and Pan aimed for a method that is both lightweight and robust. Their technique keeps the payload secret and intact even when the image is squeezed or edited along the way. Lightweight design matters for phones and small devices that lack computing power. Secure communication tools benefit when hiding power does not demand heavy software that few people can run.
plos-pone-0357780:
Lingmei Wu and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an improved detector for weeds in cotton fields, called YOLO-CCG. The setting is complex fields, where weeds hide among crop plants with similar color and shape. The model builds on the YOLO family of fast image detectors.

Reliable weed spotting is the first step toward targeted spraying, which cuts chemical use by treating only where weeds grow. Cotton fields are a hard test because young weeds and cotton seedlings look alike. Agricultural engineers developing spraying robots and drone scouting are the audience for a detector tuned to this crop.
plos-pone-0358080:
Emily R. Spencer and coauthors published a 2026 analysis in PLOS ONE on menopause, human papillomavirus, and cervical disease among middle-aged women in Senegal. Cervical cancer is a leading cancer killer in West Africa, and hormone and immune changes at menopause might affect whether the virus is detected. The team reanalyzed three earlier Dakar studies of women aged forty to sixty, comparing those past menopause with those who were not.

After menopause, women had notably higher odds of a positive HPV test, for both high-risk and low-risk virus types. Odds of cervical cell changes were also higher, though that result was not statistically firm and weakened in checks limited to women with known HIV status. The authors read the pattern as a hint that menopause may help the virus persist or reappear. They argue screening programs in the region should not assume risk ends at midlife.
plos-pone-0358180:
Chunxiao Liu and coauthors published a 2026 gene analysis in PLOS ONE on liposarcoma, a common cancer of fatty soft tissue whose molecular drivers remain unclear. They compared gene activity in tumor and normal fat tissue, mapped how the differing genes interact, and checked key candidates with laboratory tests on real samples. They also estimated which immune cells were present inside the tumors.

Several genes tied to cell division stood out: tumors expressing high levels of a set of seven of them were linked to shorter survival, and a further group predicted earlier relapse. Another ten genes emerged as possible diagnostic markers. The immune analysis found resting mast cells more common in tumor tissue than in normal fat, hinting they may play a role in how the cancer develops. The mast cell finding needs experimental confirmation, but the gene lists give treatment researchers concrete targets.
plos-pone-0358480: Ahmad and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in mathematics on fixed point methods. A fixed point is a value that a function leaves unchanged, and finding one solves many equations. The team built a shared approach for enriched paired mappings. They applied it to Volterra systems, which carry memory of the past, and to chaos in fractional-order systems. One method that covers many cases saves later researchers work.
plos-pone-0358580:
Ruba Malkawi, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2026, turns fish waste into a drug delivery trick. Baicalein, a plant flavonoid with antioxidant and medicinal promise, barely dissolves in water, which keeps it from being absorbed when swallowed. Malkawi extracted oil from salmon viscera, normally discarded. It became the liquid core of a liquisolid compact. That tablet form spreads a drug through oil on a powder carrier, to speed dissolving.

Laboratory checks found no chemical clash between the drug and its new partners. Heat and X-ray analysis showed the baicalein's stubborn crystal structure largely broken down inside the formulation, the change that lets such drugs dissolve faster. Dissolution tests in a standard apparatus and an antioxidant assay completed the evaluation. The study pairs two sustainability stories: a waste stream becomes a pharmaceutical ingredient, and a hard to deliver natural compound gets a greener vehicle.
plos-pone-0358780:
Jin Chen and three colleagues study why a stubborn breast inflammation returns after treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Granulomatous lobular mastitis mostly strikes young women and often recurs, frustrating patients and doctors. The team reviewed five hundred twenty confirmed cases from a provincial hospital registry spanning 2017 to 2024. They asked whether tiny abscesses seen under the microscope predict relapse. They also asked whether treatment choice changes that risk.

Just over half the patients showed microabscesses in their tissue samples. Statistical models that adjust for other factors singled out microabscess, the side of the affected breast, and white blood cell counts among the independent predictors of recurrence. The authors then compared one year relapse rates across treatment paths, including a class of antibiotics and surgical removal, split by microabscess status. Their stratified results aim at matching treatment intensity to each woman's actual relapse risk.
plos-pone-0358880:
Michelle Beattie, Lesley Campbell, Bev Fraser, and Anna Terje wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on emergency care. It evaluates the Trigger Checklist, a prompt tool, paired with assertive outreach, active follow-up rather than waiting. The aim is to reduce drug-related harm among people arriving at the Emergency Department.

The method is a realist evaluation, which asks what works, for whom, and in what circumstances, instead of chasing one average effect. Emergency departments see drug harm at its sharpest but rarely control what happens after discharge. Hospital teams designing harm reduction links from the emergency door are the readers.
plos-pone-0358980:
Aijie Yu and co-authors investigated in 2026 how the glaciers of the Karakoram have gained or lost mass over the past twenty-five years. The Karakoram range, between Pakistan, India, and China, holds some of the largest glaciers outside the polar regions, and they have behaved unusually compared with shrinking glaciers elsewhere. The team combined observations from several sources to build a fuller picture than any single method allows.

Glacier mass balance decides how much meltwater flows to the rivers that hundreds of millions of people depend on. Tracking it carefully over decades separates real change from year to year weather noise. The study refines the account of a region sometimes called the Karakoram anomaly, where glaciers have resisted the global pattern of loss.
plos-pone-0359280: Lin and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study in abstract mathematics. Their topic is bornological stabilization families, a way to describe how sets settle down in spaces with a built-in notion of bounded parts. They also study how sequences of closed sets swing or converge. Such work builds the basic language that other branches of analysis and topology rely on.
plos-pone-0359580:
Bira Belay and Alamiya Abdo published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study, based in the community, of adolescents in urban Dire Dawa, in eastern Ethiopia. The subject is the daily purchase of unhealthy food by teenagers, and the factors associated with that habit.

Daily buying matters more than occasional treats, because routine purchases of sugary or fatty snacks shape diet and health over years. Surveying a whole community, not just school pupils, catches adolescents who might otherwise be missed. City health officers and school program planners in Ethiopia can use the linked factors to target the shops, prices, and habits behind teen diets.
plos-pone-0360080:
Rodrigo Martinez Alcala and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns early-stage classic Hodgkin lymphoma, a cancer of the lymph system. The team tested whether staining tumor tissue for three markers, CD68, c-MET, and HLA class II, could help predict how patients would do.

The data come from the H9 trial run jointly by EORTC and GELA, a large randomised treatment study across several countries. As the title states, the marker tests did not show prognostic value in these patients. A clear negative answer like this still helps doctors, because it rules out tests that would add cost and effort without guiding care.
plos-pone-0360380:
Zihan Dong and colleagues unraveled in 2026 how a Burkholderia bacterium frees potassium from biotite, a common mineral in soils. Potassium is one of the three main nutrients crops need, and most of it in soil is locked inside minerals that plants cannot use directly. Certain bacteria can weather those minerals and release the nutrient, acting as living fertilizer.

The authors work out the biochemical steps and the speed of the process, its kinetics, for their strain working on biotite. Knowing the mechanism, rather than only the outcome, helps scientists breed or select better strains and predict how they behave in real fields. The study supports the wider search for biological replacements for mined potash fertilizer.
plos-pone-0360480:
Amanuel Yoseph, Lakew Mussie, Mehretu Belayneh, and Francisco Guillen-Grima wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It reports a trial in Southern Ethiopia on food during pregnancy. The food is amaranth flatbread, made from a grain rich in nutrients, and the outcome measured is maternal anthropometry, body measurements of the mothers.

The trial is cluster-randomized and controlled, meaning whole groups rather than single women were assigned by chance to receive the bread or not. Testing a local, affordable food matters where undernutrition in pregnancy is common. Nutrition programs in similar settings can judge from this design whether amaranth deserves a place in maternal diets.
pmc-10654680:
Xijing Yan and co-authors test a pair of drugs against liver cancer, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Single-drug care works poorly for this cancer, above all when it is advanced. The pair joins a common pain and fever drug with a targeted cancer drug.

In cell tests and in mice, the pair shrank tumors more than either drug alone. No grave side effects showed in the mouse tests. Gene work found the pair hits many cancer-linked genes and cell pathways at once. The team calls the pair a hopeful option to test further for patients with this cancer.
pmc-10655880:
Kamran Abbasi and a large group of journal editors called on health workers to press for cuts in nuclear war risk, in an editorial published in 2023. The Doomsday Clock stands at ninety seconds to midnight, its worst mark. The UN chief has warned of danger not seen since the height of the Cold War. Arms agreements lag, and the last big review meeting closed with no joint statement.

Even a small war, they write, could kill more than a hundred million at once and starve billions in the cold aftermath. A full war between the United States and Russia could kill billions more and risk the survival of humankind. New fast missiles shrink the time to tell a true strike from a false alarm. The editors urge health voices to push leaders to scrap the bombs.
pmc-10669580:
Francesca Brutti and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-three comparing two AI approaches for judging skin lesions. Melanoma rates have risen fast, and early diagnosis improves survival. The team asked whether a classic image-analysis pipeline or a deep learning network better separates harmless moles from malignant ones in magnified skin images.

Both models trained on the same large public set of more than twenty-five thousand images. On a separate test set of two hundred images, the deep learning method reached higher accuracy and specificity than the classic ensemble method. The authors note both did well in validation, but the network generalized better to unseen images. They suggest such tools could speed population screening when joined with clinic devices.
pmc-10691380:
Shuai Wang and seven co-authors mapped a research field where knee arthritis meets cell aging in a 2023 bibliometric study. Aging cells are thought to drive knee osteoarthritis, and the authors charted who publishes what on the pair. They analyzed 1,074 papers from 1992 to 2023 in a major citation database.

Output grew about 30 percent a year. The United States led in papers and citations, and one journal dominated influence. The most productive author had 31 papers, yet collaboration between authors was weak. Sixty percent of the 1,556 institutions sat in one country group the analysis highlights. The study offers newcomers a map of the field's leaders, journals, and hot topics.
pmc-10691680:
Ibarra-Sanchez, Abelsen, Chen, and Wisløff track in twenty twenty-three how schooling levels pattern weight and health habits over time in northern Norway. Unequal weight, smoking, inactivity, and heavy drinking help explain social gaps in chronic disease, but how they move together across life was unclear. The team used two waves of a big regional survey, nearly nine thousand adults, spaced about eight years apart.

Most people stayed in the same weight and habit groups at follow-up. Healthy patterns, and shifts toward them, clustered among the most educated. Less educated groups more often kept or gained risky patterns. The authors say measuring such uneven exposures can help set policy priorities to close health gaps.
pmc-10692880:
Jinqing Yang, Zhifeng Liu, Qicong Wang, and Na Lu published a 2023 study of what makes a health post on a question-and-answer site attract good answers, and what makes it popular. Such sites are now a first stop for health information. The team collected all health posts from Metafilter, a well-known site of this kind.

Their collection ran to more than eighteen thousand posts. Statistical models then measured what influenced two scores: how many favorite marks a post won, and how many comments it drew. What a post said influenced both, most of all its tone. A warm tone won more favorites but drew fewer comments. How actively and how widely the poster took part on the site also influenced the scores, in opposite ways. The topic area of a post influenced popularity more than answers. The study maps which posts fly and which sink.
pmc-10694280:
Mwesige and co-authors report a newborn repair done with few resources. The baby had esophageal atresia with a fistula to the airway. Such defects block feeding and threaten life without prompt surgery. The term infant weighed 3 kg at birth. Signs included choking, spit-up after feeds, and a swollen belly.

Scans showed the blocked esophagus and the abnormal link. A heart scan found a moderate ductus that had not yet closed. The team did an open repair on day six of life. The repair worked, and the child survived. The authors stress sharp suspicion, teamwork, and skill in low-resource care.
pmc-10694380:
Yakun Luo, Qing Shi, Lu Wang, and two colleagues write a research letter on a transcription factor that helps kidney cancer cells multiply, published in two thousand twenty-three. The cancer is clear cell renal cell carcinoma, whose advanced cases resist surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, and often outlast targeted drugs too.

The factor, TCF19, had already shown prognostic value: its levels predict patient survival. What it actually does in these cells was unstudied. The authors set out to dissect the mechanism behind its effect on proliferation. Their title names the axis they uncover: TCF19 epigenetically regulates FOXM1 and AURKB, two drivers of cell division. Understanding such circuits is how new drug targets and biomarkers are found. The letter reports the analysis of TCF19 expression in tumor tissue and the experiments that follow. It addresses clinicians and researchers hunting better options for a stubborn cancer.
pmc-10694580:
Chen-Chan Hsieh and colleagues give a step-by-step protocol for turning human stem cells into cartilage cells without the usual growth factor, in this methods paper from twenty twenty-three. Mesenchymal stem cells can become cartilage, bone, or fat. The standard cartilage recipe uses TGF-beta, but it can overshoot, pushing cells toward bone-like hypertrophy and other fates.

Their route blocks the Wnt signal instead, which steers the cells to cartilage more cleanly. The protocol details each step: forming the cell pellets, applying the Wnt blockade, and refreshing the medium on schedule. It also details the tests used to prove the cells became cartilage. The authors offer the method to labs building cartilage therapies that need efficient, on-target differentiation, and point to their earlier study for the full evidence behind it.
pmc-10694880:
Jenner and four co-authors review eye-tracking as a way to study social thinking in people with intellectual disability. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-three. Classic tasks lean hard on language and general thinking, which can mask the social skills they aim to measure.

Eye-tracking watches where people look, offering a gentler probe. The team searched four databases and kept forty-nine sound studies across many disability groups. A pooled analysis of twelve studies linked gaze on social parts of images with autism traits on clinical scales. The technology measured several kinds of social attention. The authors judge it a useful tool for this group, including for understanding how autism overlaps with intellectual disability.
pmc-10701980:
Han, Xie, Shao, Li, and Du study how ventilator use injures lungs in mice in twenty twenty-three. Mechanical ventilation can harm lungs in patients with severe respiratory failure. The injury involves inflammation driven by immune cells and their signals. The team focused on macrophages that live in the air sacs of the lung.

Mice were ventilated with high tidal volumes to model the injury. Removing the macrophages eased the lung injury and lowered levels of an enzyme they release. Blocking that enzyme had a like effect. The enzyme switched on a pathway in airway lining cells that disturbed mitochondria, the energy centres of the cell. Cell experiments matched the animal findings. The authors say the pathway may be a target for prevention or treatment.
pmc-10708280:
Siegfried Reipert and co-authors speed up a preservation method that lets electron microscopes see lichens in near-living detail. Standard chemical fixation is slow and creates artifacts, while freezing methods lock living structure in place but took far too long to adopt. Their automated protocol adds constant agitation to freeze substitution, the step where frozen water is swapped for solvent.

Applied to three lichen species, the method preserved the native state of the algal and fungal partners and their shared outer matrix. The images reveal varied fungal threads, the matrix itself, and crystallized metabolite deposits, plus algal pockets crowded with mitochondria. The authors expect the faster protocol to spread cryo-preparation through lichen research.
pmc-10708680:
Liu and co-authors propose a way to pack more data channels into free-space light links. Light beams that carry orbital angular momentum can multiply channels and raise capacity. In practice, imperfect beam making and sorting limit how many states get used. Their scheme uses a multi-ring perfect vortex beam. A checkerboard method encodes both brightness and phase into a single hologram. The beam's four rings act as separate channels in one spot.

Each ring carries its own angular momentum beam independently. That layout raises both total capacity and capacity per unit of space. The scheme needs only a small range of momentum states. The authors frame it as a path to denser optical links.
pmc-10709880:
Mihyeon Seong, Dajung Ryu, and Sohyune Sok published a 2023 study of nursing students in South Korea. They explored how students view disaster safety. Thirty students sorted statements about disasters into a grid. The method reveals shared viewpoints, not just averages. Better understanding can shape disaster training.

Four viewpoints emerged from the sorting patterns. One stressed national responsibility for safety. Another stressed personal responsibility. A third focused on being prepared in advance. The fourth emphasized education. Each type implies a different teaching strategy. Nursing schools can match lessons to how students actually think.
pmc-10709980:
Yongbing Sun and colleagues ask how social support eases anxiety and depression in people living with HIV, in this study from China, published in twenty twenty-three. Support from family and friends is known to help, but the path from support to calm was unclear. The team proposed that resilience, the skill of bouncing back, carries the effect.

One hundred sixty-one patients at one hospital filled in scales for support, resilience, anxiety, and depression. Both anxiety and depression ran lower where support and resilience ran higher. Statistical tests then showed the chain: support predicted resilience, and resilience predicted lower distress. Once resilience was counted, support's direct link to distress faded away, meaning resilience fully carried it. The authors advise care teams to widen patients' support networks precisely because support builds the inner strength that holds distress down.
pmc-10713580:
Six researchers led by Eli Worth studied how to slow the stiff fiber growth that harms red blood cells in sickle cell disease. The disease stems from a fault in one hemoglobin chain. The fetal form of hemoglobin blocks fiber growth, so most work tries to switch that form back on or mimic it.

The team instead changed a single site on the other chain, the alpha chain. That change slowed fiber growth as well as fetal hemoglobin did. Because it works on its own path, it could pair with other treatments to boost their effect. The authors present it as a new tool in the search for stronger sickle cell therapies.
pmc-10713680:
Emma Parkins and seven co-authors study a tiny RNA that shapes memory circuits in this two thousand twenty-three paper. MicroRNAs fine-tune gene activity after genes are read, and they act fast at synapses. One of them, miR-324-5p, is known to raise seizure risk. The team removed its gene in mice and also blocked it with a drug-like molecule. Both moves thinned the small spines where excitatory synapses sit in the hippocampus.

Knockout mice also shifted spine shapes away from thin, unstable forms. Measures of key proteins and messages changed as well. The electrical strengthening tied to learning was impaired. The work links one small RNA to the physical basis of memory. Neuroscientists studying plasticity are the readers.
pmc-10714480:
Jiayan Chen, Yimeng Chen, Guanghao Qin, and fifteen colleagues lay out a head-to-head eye drop trial in this two thousand twenty-three protocol paper. Diabetes is rising, and about seventy percent of diabetic people have dry eye disease, which damages the corneal surface and nerves while tear production falls. Anti-inflammatory treatments exist, but two drops, three percent diquafosol and zero point one percent hyaluronic acid, had never been rigorously compared in diabetic dry eye.

The planned single-center, triple-blind randomized trial assigns two hundred two patients equally to either drop, one drop six times daily for eight weeks. Outcomes span the tear film, corneal staining and sensitivity, tear inflammation markers, meibomian gland function, corneal nerves, and symptom questionnaires, measured at baseline and weeks four and eight. The protocol promises a standardized verdict on which drop better serves diabetic patients, whose dry eye is common but understudied.
pmc-10714880:
Opare-Asamoah and co-authors catalog the bacteria behind newborn sepsis at a large hospital in northern Ghana. Sepsis in newborns is an emergency that demands fast, accurate lab work. The team took blood samples from 275 babies judged to have sepsis. Samples came from a single vein draw under sterile care. Lab staff identified each germ and tested which antibiotics still worked. A standard disk method measured drug sensitivity.

Most babies, about 79%, arrived with early-onset illness. The profile of germs and drug responses guides local prescribing. Knowing which drugs fail locally can save lives where time is short. The study gives the unit a current map of its sepsis threat.
pmc-10714980:
Yuanyuan Luo and Xiaojie Ma present a 2023 study on predicting the return of cervical cancer after radiotherapy. They studied patients with intermediate and advanced cancer treated at one hospital between June 2017 and January 2023. The goal was a simple chart, called a nomogram, that estimates each patient's risk of recurrence.

Records for 114 patients were analyzed with regression methods. Two blood markers stood out as independent predictors: an enzyme called thymidine kinase 1 and a standard tumor antigen. The chart built from them scored well on accuracy tests. It beat both stage-based prediction and either marker used alone. Check curves showed the risk estimates matched real outcomes closely, which could help doctors plan follow-up care.
pmc-10715980:
Kyazimzade and co-authors present a case of heart failure shock during pregnancy, a rare but deadly event. Shock in pregnancy threatens both mother and fetus, and fast action matters. Care works best when heart, pregnancy, and critical care teams act together. The case covers shock that arose before delivery in one patient.

Doctors used a mechanical support device to keep blood moving. The device served as a bridge, buying time until the pregnancy could safely continue to viability. The report walks through how the team judged timing and risk. It offers a template for centers that may face the same rare crisis. Early recognition is the central lesson.
pmc-10718480:
Lee and four co-authors scope phone and web tools that aid lung cure stick in this twenty twenty-three review. The lung cure runs months, and missed doses breed drug-proof germs. Tech aids could keep sick folks on plan with less ward strain.

Inside, five years of banks gave the team near thirty fit works. Text pings, dose bells, and web watch care led the aid types found. Most aids sped self-care for sick folks and eased staff work as well. Two-way tools, with pings back and forth, sat rare in the pool. The team backs talk-both-ways builds as the next step for the field.
pmc-10722880:
Keogh, Thompson, Crouse, and Narayan test whether moose hooves can record reproductive history, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Hormones stored in keratin tissues like hair and hooves preserve a timeline of stress and reproduction. The team collected hoof tissue from immobilized moose. They validated immunoassays for cortisol and progesterone in hoof and hair.

Both hormones were measurable and varied among samples and animals. Pregnant females showed about twice the progesterone of non-pregnant moose in post-breeding hoof locations. Front hooves grew faster than rear ones, with growth peaking in summer. Adult female hooves held roughly two years of growth, spanning up to two reproductive cycles. The method even detected previous pregnancies in postmortem samples. Hair progesterone, by contrast, did not track reproductive state.
pmc-10729180:
Lin Ang and co-authors lay out a protocol for mapping every systematic review of traditional medicine, a project commissioned by the World Health Organization. Traditional medicine is a mainstay or complement of care worldwide, and thousands of reviews have already synthesized its trials, but no one has charted the whole landscape. The team will search seventeen databases for reviews from 2018 to 2022. Pairs of reviewers will screen, extract data, and grade quality with a standard tool.

Results will be drawn as interactive maps sorted by disease and by type of traditional intervention. The point is to show where evidence piles up and where it is absent, so future trials can be aimed at the gaps. No ethics approval is needed, since only published work is used. The document is a plan, registered in advance, meant to keep the mapping honest and reproducible.
pmc-10736580:
Yan-Jhu Su, Janelle Fassi, and Christine Fruhauf introduce a symposium on using technology in education for older adults, from twenty twenty-three. Online learning for life has grown common, but tech changes faster than many older people can follow. That gap between age groups is known as the digital divide.

Five talks make up the session. One covers an online program mixing age groups that tackled age bias. Others cover design rules for tech support for older learners, cases from other countries, and a campus program where students coach seniors. The last talk weighs the gains and strains of tech for older learners in Taiwan. The aim throughout is learning that includes all ages.
pmc-10736780:
Shevaun Neupert and Yuval Palgi present a symposium report from 2023 on how aging feels in daily life. How old a person feels can affect mood, memory, health, and even length of life. Most past work drew on rich Western samples, which leaves other cultures out.

A global group was formed to gather daily diary data in five countries. The talks cover the United States, Turkey, Germany, the United Kingdom, and Israel. Daily stress made people feel older in several samples. Good daily events and absorbing tasks made people feel younger. One talk compares Jews and Arabs inside Israel, and Israel with the United States. The group says culture shapes how daily life and felt age connect.
pmc-10736980:
Nicole Richards, Zexi Zhou, and Karen Fingerman study gratitude, close ties, and life satisfaction in late life. Their work from two thousand twenty-three draws on a study of daily life and well-being. More than three hundred adults, from sixty-five to ninety-two years old, took part and named their closest social partners.

Adults with more gratitude felt more satisfied with life, the team found. Warmth from close partners also tracked with higher satisfaction, while conflict alone did not. Gratitude seemed to guard satisfaction when warmth from partners was low. In high conflict ties, though, satisfaction fell for all, gratitude or not. The authors call the links between gratitude and well-being complex.
pmc-10739280:
Sumiyyah Zimami, Hala Darwish, and Deanna Marriott study what shapes the experiences of dementia caregivers. Their paper appeared in 2023. They reanalyzed survey data from two national caregiver groups, covering 927 caregivers, most of them women aged 50 to 74. Caregivers rated their experience from fully negative to fully positive. The team tested two factors: whether the caregiver chose the role, and how well they knew dementia's symptoms.

Both factors mattered. Caregivers who had chosen to provide care were more likely to report positive experiences. Those who recognized dementia symptoms were more than twice as likely to do so. The analysis adjusted for disease stage, kinship, mental health, and attitude. The authors argue that teaching symptom knowledge and honoring choice could ease the load on families.
pmc-10742680:
Katarína Kušíková and a team of co-authors studied a rare muscle disease in a 2023 paper. X-linked myotubular myopathy weakens muscles from birth and often kills in infancy, though some patients live to adulthood. The disease stems from faults in the MTM1 gene, and patients also share a distinct facial look.

The team compared gene faults with disease severity in 414 patients, including three new variants. Faults that break the gene's message went with severe illness, while gentler missense changes went with milder cases. A face-reading app also separated patients from controls with a clear gap. The authors say gene type can guide prognosis for most patients, within limits.
pmc-10744180:
Ezzat and colleagues studied blood markers in twenty twenty-three that might flag kidney damage in people with type 2 diabetes. Kidney decline is a common and serious turn of this disease, and catching it early shapes how doctors treat it.

The team compared one hundred twenty-eight healthy people with one hundred twenty-nine diabetic patients, some with early urine protein, some with heavy protein, and some with failing kidneys. A small RNA molecule and two inflammation signals ran high in diabetes but fell as kidney damage advanced. Zinc and magnesium ran low, while copper ran high. One gene variant of a calcium-sensing enzyme appeared more often in the diabetic and kidney groups. The authors say the pattern of markers, read together with the gene test, could sharpen diagnosis and care planning.
pmc-10744380:
Aleksei Shefer, Oleg Tutanov, Maxim Belenikin, Yuri Tsentalovich, and Svetlana Tamkovich compare proteins riding on DNA in the blood. They contrast healthy women with breast cancer patients. Their liquid biopsy paper showed up in two thousand twenty-three. Cell-free DNA is usually studied alone, its protein partners ignored.

The team pulled nucleoprotein complexes from blood and listed their cargo by mass spectrometry: about one hundred seventy proteins in each group. Cancer patients' complexes carried more proteins tied to invasion, migration, and the epithelial-mesenchymal switch. A five-protein set split patients from healthy donors with perfect sensitivity and eighty percent specificity. The authors argue DNA-protein complexes take an active part in how cells talk to each other.
pmc-10746480:
Jingsha Zhao and co-authors report treating a blocked airway under heart-lung support in a case report from two thousand twenty-three. A lung cancer had narrowed the main airway, risking suffocation. Placing a metal stent can open it, but the procedure itself can block the last air path.

The team ran veno-venous ECMO, a machine that oxygenates blood outside the body, with only a low dose of heparin blood thinner. Standard doses raise bleeding risk during surgery. With low-dose support, bleeding during the operation fell and the work went faster. The machine came off soon after, and the patient recovered. The authors present the approach as a safer way to stent such airways.
pmc-10747880:
Erofeev, Antifeev, Vinokurov, Bezprozvanny, and Vlasova present a wireless brain recording system for rodents in twenty twenty-three. Studying complex brain interactions often needs animals that move freely. Wired systems restrict that movement during experiments. The team earlier built an open source wireless system to solve this.

The first version had flaws: a heavy module, redundant parts, and short battery life. The new version is lighter and simpler, with better sampling. It records neural activity in vivo and transmits the data in real time. Tests confirm it works during live recordings in rodent brains. The authors offer it as a low cost, capable tool for brain research. Full designs are open source for other labs.
pmc-10748280:
Six researchers led by Arantza Vega-Castro asked which stinging insects show up around human food in Spain. Knowing this helps doctors pin down which venom caused a sting near food, so the right protective treatment can be chosen. The team gathered photos of wasps, bees, and kin taken where people were eating, and an insect expert named each one.

Of seventy-one insects, most were common wasps, found in nearly four of five cases. Almost all photos came from summer and early autumn, mostly on outdoor terraces. Meat and seafood drew the most insects. Where protein food was present, the insect was a common wasp in nine of ten cases.
pmc-10754480:
Sirry Alang, Chelsey Carter, and Oni Blackstock argued that colonial roots still shape Black health in the United States. Their paper, from twenty twenty-three, ties the harm to health care run as a good for sale. That trade frame, they say, exploits staff and hits the most pushed out worst, much like colonial rule. Four moves are put forth to tear those roots out.

Spend on gene mark reads of how stress gets in the flesh. Put Black voice and Black ways of knowing at the core of school, care, and law. Back Black staff who call out set flaws. Widen care that stops ills early. Readers in health justice get a past is prologue call to act.
pmc-10754580:
Na Li, Yue Tian, Xin Liu, Ciming Pan, and Jian Xue present a 2023 study on the KRAS gene in lung adenocarcinoma. KRAS is a notorious cancer gene tied to tumor growth and drug resistance. What it does to the immune cells inside lung tumors, and to patient survival, was less clear.

Using public expression databases and survival tools, the team linked KRAS levels to outcome. Higher KRAS expression went with better prognosis in this analysis, alongside effects on tumor progression. Its level also tracked with markers of several immune cell types that infiltrate tumors. Pathway checks connected KRAS to a web of other cancer genes. The authors frame KRAS as both a prognostic signal and a shaper of the tumor immune landscape.
pmc-10758680:
Abbas Ghazanfar and colleagues sort kidney transplant patients by who fared worst with COVID-19, to sharpen follow-up care, in this study from twenty twenty-three. Transplant patients take immune-damping drugs, so infection risk runs high. The team reviewed its follow-up program's patients through the pandemic's first year.

Of five hundred five recipients in the program, twenty-nine caught the virus and eight of them died, a death toll of more than a quarter among the infected. Survival fell with age over sixty-eight, male sex, and non-Caucasian background. Diabetes was present in nearly all who died. Routine blood values also warned: low kidney function, low albumin, low hemoglobin, and low calcium each marked higher risk. The authors argue these everyday numbers, already collected at every visit, should trigger earlier, closer care for the patients they flag.
pmc-10764180:
Qingyuan Qian and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-three, how low-pressure, low-oxygen conditions affect blood gases and red blood cells in rats. The team simulated an altitude of six thousand five hundred meters in small and large chambers. Blood from the abdominal aorta was sampled for gas measures, red cell counts, and hemoglobin. They varied exposure length, hypoxia mode, recovery at normal oxygen, and repeat exposure after preconditioning. A drug, acetazolamide, was also tested.

Hypoxia disturbed acid-base balance, worse with longer exposure. Red cell counts and hemoglobin rose with exposure time too. Reoxygenation effects on acid-base balance were stronger for rats in the small chamber. The drug eased reoxygenation effects. Hypoxia mode and the drug had little effect on red cell counts or hemoglobin.
pmc-10787080:
Grant Borne and ten colleagues review Palforzia, the first approved oral immunotherapy for peanut allergy. Peanut allergy can kill, and avoidance was long the only strategy. Palforzia feeds patients carefully escalating peanut protein doses to retrain the immune response. The narrative review summarizes the clinical trials behind approval. It explains the dosing mechanism and how the therapy is used in real practice.

Current research concentrates on age groups that respond best. Other studies pair oral immunotherapy with additional immune modulators to deepen tolerance. Many optimization questions remain open, including who benefits most and how durable protection is. The twenty twenty-three update frames Palforzia as both a treatment and a research platform: proof that food allergy can be modified, not merely managed by vigilance.
pmc-10801180:
Philip Manfield and four co-authors report early evidence for a rapid trauma therapy technique in a 2024 paper. The flash technique aims to shrink the sting of a disturbing memory with little distress during treatment. Four similar studies, run during trainings in the United States, Australia, and Uganda, each gave volunteers a single fifteen minute group session.

Over six hundred fifty people rated a disturbing memory's intensity before and after. Average disturbance fell by more than two thirds in every study, a large and significant effect. Only two of over eight hundred sessions saw slight increases, and both eased in a repeat session. Follow up at four weeks suggested gains held. The authors call the technique acceptable and safe, pending stronger trials.
pmc-10826880:
Guang-Zhao Cao and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study of the traditional formula Pien Tze Huang applied to diabetic wounds. Diabetic ulcers heal slowly and cause much disability. Existing treatments fall short, prompting interest in this established remedy.

Diabetic rats with full-thickness wounds received the formula at two doses or a growth-factor drug. Treated wounds closed faster with richer collagen. Gene sequencing and network analysis traced the biological routes involved, backed by protein tests. The work gives a molecular account of how an old formula speeds repair, supporting controlled clinical evaluation.
pmc-10844580:
Chen-Shuan Chung and co-authors show that throat cancer patients live longer when the esophagus is screened in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Head and neck cancers often seed a second cancer in the esophagus. A magnified scope with special light can spot it early.

The team reviewed two hundred sixty-one patients with hypopharyngeal cancer at one hospital. About a quarter grew a second primary tumor, most often in the esophagus. Patients screened within six months of diagnosis and kept on regular watch had markedly better survival in adjusted models. Late stage still worsened odds. The authors back early screening plus steady surveillance for these patients.
pmc-10909080:
Priyanka Ravi and colleagues interview users of tobacco tooth powder about why they trust a harmful habit, in this qualitative study from twenty twenty-three. The product, a smokeless tobacco rubbed on teeth and gums, comes in forms such as mishri and gul. Smokeless tobacco is tied to cancers of the mouth, throat, and pancreas, yet this form is sold as dental care.

Thirty users at a dental hospital spoke in depth. Family, friends, easy access, and curiosity started most of them. Many believed the powder helps teeth, gums, and even digestion, and most rated it gentler than other tobacco. Some knew the harms and had tried to stop, but none had sought professional help to quit. The authors call for plain awareness drives and stronger health warnings on these products, since myth, not ignorance alone, keeps the habit alive.
pmc-11225480:
Ruth Ketty Kisuza and nine co-authors survey how Ugandan university students suffered and coped during a COVID-19 lockdown. Their study was published in twenty twenty-three, set at Makerere University during the country's second lockdown.

Three hundred and one undergraduates answered a semi-structured questionnaire. The median age was twenty-three, and most were male and single. Nearly half worried about COVID-19. The top harms were disruption of studies, named by over nine in ten, and money problems, named by six in ten. Listening to music led the coping list. The team also hunted factors tied to worry. The portrait can help universities plan support for the next campus closure.
pmc-11271080:
Rupsa Mallik, Eszter Kismodi, and Sundari Ravindran report on a roundtable about the money behind advocacy for sexual and reproductive health and rights, in an article published in 2023. The meeting, held in September 2022, brought funders and advocates together to ask whether current funding helps or hinders the movement. Two groups, a journal and a grant-making fund, hosted the talks.

Participants mapped how grants are given today and how success gets measured, since those measures steer future funding. Many worried that present patterns may blunt the bold advocacy needed to counter rollbacks of rights. The article shares early ideas for a way forward and calls for a shared set of values, principles, and strategies. The aim, the authors say, is not just more funding but better funding, centered on people and movements.
pmc-11531880:
Cao and co-authors census large and mid-sized mammals in Xishuangbanna over a decade. Camera traps ran from 2012 to 2022 across nine sites. The team set 784 traps in eight reserves and one state forest farm. Records found 43 species in six orders and 37 genera. Nine species from old records did not appear.

Small, split reserves lacked big predators and big grazers. Most common species also showed lower counts in those sites. The less guarded forest farm held rich mammal diversity. Mix of species varied a lot by site, most for rare species. The authors warn that large, rare mammals face the most risk.
pmc-11532480: Andreas Mischok, a solo author, surveys a display technology in a 2024 commentary. Exciton-polaritons are hybrid particles, part light and part matter excitation, long studied for lasers, chemistry, and quantum optics. Recent work, he reports, shows their striking promise for screens: very efficient, very bright, and with the purest colors in principle. The short piece argues that this fundamental physics topic is ready to move toward future display products, where color purity and efficiency are prized.
pmc-11536780:
Martine Myhre and three co-authors counted pre-hospital care for young children in central Norway, in a study published in 2024. Calls involving children are rare, so crews get little practice with them. The team read five years of call logs for one county with about 43,000 children under twelve. They added helicopter crew files for the most serious cases.

Of about 109,000 calls, six in a hundred were for young children. Half of those led to a ground or air crew being sent out. Breathing distress, altered awareness, and injury topped the list of causes. Of 309 helicopter cases, more than four in ten received advanced treatment from the flight doctor, with breathing help the most common. The authors say the rarity itself is the risk, and they point training toward the gaps they found.
pmc-11538280:
Xin He and eight co-authors use a genetics method to test whether gut microbes and blood chemicals actually cause acne. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Acne is a common skin disease of the young that carries heavy money, body, and mood costs.

Links between the gut, blood, and skin are often proposed, but plain observation cannot prove cause. The team used gene variants as natural instruments for four hundred and twelve gut microbes and two hundred and forty-nine blood compounds. They ran the test in both directions and added a mediation step to trace chains from microbe to chemical to acne. Some factors looked protective and others harmful. The results give drug and diet research firmer targets than simple association studies.
pmc-11542480:
Iris Xiaoxue Yin and five co-authors engineer a nanomaterial that sticks to teeth, kills cavity bacteria, and rebuilds mineral at the same time. Silver nanoparticles fight Streptococcus mutans but can stain teeth and wander off. Anchoring silver to graphene quantum dots functionalized with alendronate, a bone-seeking drug fragment, aims the particles at tooth mineral.

The composite was characterized by electron microscopy and spectroscopy, then tested for toxicity against gum fibroblasts and tooth stem cells. Binding to hydroxyapatite was measured directly. Antibacterial power against the cavity bacterium was checked by imaging and colony counts. Finally, mineral regrowth on human dentine was assessed by micro-CT and microscopy. The work targets prevention that stays where it is painted.
pmc-11545580:
Jaroń, Grajek, and Kobza survey what drives good doctor patient talks about patient rights during the pandemic in twenty twenty-four. Patients have a right to clear facts about their health and care, and to ask questions. The team surveyed two hundred three adults face to face at a rehab clinic in twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two. Patients split into active talkers and passive ones.

A third of patients asked questions or had the chance to do so. That active group got far more facts about their state, tests, and outlook. They also rated talks with doctors far higher on trust, clarity, and warmth. The authors say the heart of a good visit is full facts plus room for questions.
pmc-11546580:
Pedro Forte and co-authors test a long exercise plan for older adults, in work from 2024. The eight-month plan mixed many forms of training. Twenty-four adults were split into a training group and a control group. Body makeup, fitness tests, and a sleep survey were taken at the start and the end.

The training group curled more, stood from a chair faster, and stepped far more in two minutes. Body fat fell by a tenth, though flexibility dropped. Sleep quality jumped by near half in the training group and fell in controls. Better sleep tied to leaner bodies and stronger fitness after the plan.
pmc-11570880:
Chris Acquah and eight co-authors study two light-activated compounds that could treat cancer, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Such drugs, called photosensitizers, wake under light and harm tumor cells. Newer versions swap oxygen atoms for sulfur to avoid heavy atoms, shifting the light they absorb and boosting their active states. How they relax after absorbing light was still murky.

The pair studied were thio-coumarin and thio-acridone. The team fired ultra-short light pulses and tracked changes from trillionths of a second out to millionths. Computer chemistry backed the readings. The path they mapped explains how the compounds settle into long-lived, reactive states. Those states do the work in light therapy, so the map helps design better drugs.
pmc-11586780:
Jennifer Petkovic and a large team of co-authors review guidance on involving interest-holders in health guideline work in two thousand twenty-four. Guidelines shape care, so the people affected by them should have a voice in their making. Those voices range from patients and payers to policy makers and the public.

A major checklist sorts guideline work into eighteen topics, one of which covers engagement. That topic, though, does not say how to engage, and input could be sought at every stage. The review maps what guidance exists across the full process. It is one of four linked reviews that will feed new guidance on engagement by many groups at once.
pmc-11587780:
Ouyang and six co-authors study citrus canker tolerance at the gene level, in work from twenty twenty-four. Citrus bacterial canker is a major disease that threatens the citrus industry. A resistant bud mutant of a common sweet orange offers a natural comparison.

The team compared leaf traits and gene activity between the susceptible Newhall cultivar and its resistant mutant Longhuitian. Transcript profiling revealed distinct regulatory patterns tied to tolerance. Such gene maps can guide breeding or editing for canker resistant citrus, reducing spray use and crop loss in groves worldwide.
pmc-11591880:
Junbiao Wang and co-authors tested compounds from the chaga mushroom against breast cancer cells in 2024. Chaga, a fungus used in traditional Chinese medicine as a tea, contains triterpenoids with noted anticancer traits. To mimic drinking it, the team digested a chaga water extract in vitro, then identified its parts with high-resolution mass spectrometry. Four triterpenoids, including inotodiol and betulin, stood out as the main active parts.

The extract reduced viability of breast cancer cell lines representing HER2-positive and triple-negative subtypes, and disturbed their cell cycles. A key process emerged: the triterpenoids inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, an enzyme cancer cells need to copy DNA. That is the same target as some established chemotherapy drugs. The title reports the compounds also act synergistically with standard treatments. Mushroom chemistry rarely yields such a certain process, making this a lead worth following.
pmc-11595580:
So Yeon Yoon and co-authors build a rainwater filter from palm waste carbon in a 2024 study. Rainwater can carry heavy metals, organic pollutants, and gut germs, so it needs cleaning before use. Their cartridge stacks three forms of activated carbon made from palm shells: plain carbon, carbon doped with magnesium and silicon, and carbon doped with silver.

The magnesium-silicon layer added surface area and binding sites, which lifted heavy metal capture. In column tests that mimic a working filter, the full cartridge beat plain carbon and a commercial carbon. It removed one and a half to two times more Escherichia coli germs, and more metals and organics as well. The silver layer added disinfection. The authors present the system as a single pass answer for rainwater with mixed pollution.
pmc-11599580:
Andreia Penso Pereira and three colleagues ask whether the social networks of people with diabetes predict who shows up for eye screening. Diabetic retinopathy screening prevents blindness, but attendance varies. Using records of nearly seventy-six thousand patients grouped under twenty Portuguese primary care clusters, they built a social network for each cluster and computed its structure.

Paradoxically, the least connected networks, split into many small communities, had the highest screening adherence. Non-adherence concentrated in a small group of highly connected individuals, and node-level metrics pinpointed where the problem is worst. The authors offer network analysis as a planning tool for targeting screening interventions.
pmc-11603480:
Andrew Sagalov and seven colleagues compare heart risks in cardiac amyloidosis against other stiff-heart diseases, in a twenty twenty-four study. In amyloidosis, stray proteins clog the heart muscle. Other stiff-heart causes include iron overload and sarcoid. The team drew on a national hospital database for twenty sixteen to twenty nineteen, covering more than thirteen thousand patients.

Amyloidosis patients faced near four times the stroke risk of the other group. They also had double the rate of a dangerous fast heart rhythm. Yet their risk of the common flutter rhythm was lower. Death rates in hospital were alike in both groups. The authors argue screening should weigh these rhythm and stroke gaps.
pmc-11607080:
Elham Farokh Gisour, Fatemeh Jahanimoghadam, and Pouya Karimipour compare three materials for saving the pulp of baby molars, in a clinical trial from 2024. The procedure, pulpotomy, removes the diseased top of the pulp and seals the rest. The standard agent, formocresol, has long raised safety questions, so rivals are wanted.

Ninety-six children aged three to nine each had one molar treated with formocresol, Portland cement, or NeoMTA Plus. Clinical success at six and twelve months was total in all three groups. X-ray success ran a few points lower, with NeoMTA Plus on top at 96.9 percent at one year. Gaps between groups were too small to count as real. The authors name both rivals as sound stand-ins.
pmc-11608480:
Pyo and coauthors ask if blood pressure shapes heart valve infection risk in diabetes. The infection is grave and can kill if missed. Diabetes already raises infection risk for many patients. The team used a national health database in Korea.

The full set held more than 2.6 million people. Groups split by normal, raised, and high blood pressure. Low body weight was checked as an added risk too. Follow-up ran for about seven years on average. Just over 1,700 new infections arose in that span. High pressure tracked with the top infection rates.
pmc-11611180:
Soonok An, Jisoo Youn, Qihao Zhan, and Soo-Jung Byoun gauged partner violence among young adults in South Korea. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with intimate partner violence. Such harm peaks in young adults, yet proof on Korean youth and on care fit to their culture is scarce. An online survey of six hundred young adults, drawn by a simple random pick, read both harm done and harm faced.

Life long rates for both sides sat near three in ten. More than a fifth told of each in the past year. Stats models tied a set of traits to each side. Readers who build prevention for Korean youth get base rates and a trait map to aim at.
pmc-11612380:
Gülden Gök, Şevket Tulun, and Hakan Çelebi map, in a 2024 study, heavy metal pollution in the soil of a Turkish university campus, treating it as a miniature city. They sampled nine points across the grounds and measured contamination with standard indices. The soil ran alkaline, which tends to lock metals in place.

Lead stood out. It concentrated where students circulate and gather. By a combined pollution index, three quarters of the campus rated moderately to highly polluted, and the rest clean. Statistical source tracking split the blame: natural background supplied about 57 percent, industry and traffic about 21, farming about 13, and other sources the remainder. Lead tied mainly to the traffic and industry mix. The authors urge continuous soil monitoring to keep the long-term buildup in view.
pmc-11612580:
A team of co-authors presents a study from two thousand twenty-four on whether social media buzz tracked with doctors' prescribing during COVID-19. The drug in question is hydroxychloroquine, an old malaria drug promoted early in the pandemic on thin evidence. Social platforms spread health claims fast, with little checking, which can push practice ahead of proof.

The team gathered the drug's use in forty-eight United States hospitals across two thousand twenty. They set that beside posts on X, formerly Twitter, that mentioned the drug or its brand name, sorted by whether the tone was positive, negative, or neutral. The design tests for a population-level link between chatter and prescribing.
pmc-11613380:
Peiyang Lin and five colleagues test whether the available oocytes rate predicts pregnancy in assisted reproduction, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Ovarian stimulation and embryo culture can affect how oocytes mature. The rate summarizes what share of retrieved eggs are usable. The team reviewed nearly eight thousand treatment cycles at a Fujian hospital.

Analysis linked several factors to clinical pregnancy, including hormone levels, endometrial thickness, and follicle counts. The available oocytes rate itself contributed independently. A cutoff near thirty-four percent separated outcome groups in the analysis. Matched comparisons below and above that threshold showed significantly different stimulation drug doses. The authors argue the rate helps evaluate stimulation quality. It may also guide clinicians adjusting protocols for better oocyte development.
pmc-11613780:
Nozomu Motono and co-authors describe a hard case of trauma-induced clotting failure after a fall from a roof. Their case report appeared in 2024. The patient, a 68-year-old man with epilepsy, broke ribs, his collarbone, an elbow, and his pelvis, and bled into his right chest. Emergency surgery five hours after the fall stabilized him. Blood tests, though, showed the trauma itself had wrecked his clotting: hemoglobin and platelets stayed low and clotting time stayed long despite transfusions and clot-protecting medicine.

On the second evening the chest bleeding worsened and surgeons reopened it, finding slow oozing from the many rib fractures. The authors walk through the management choices, arguing the case shows why trauma teams must treat the clotting disorder itself, not just the holes it springs from.
pmc-11614480:
Ryan Antar and co-authors report a rare benign tumor deep in a child's palm, in work from twenty twenty-four. The tumor type, calcifying aponeurotic fibroma, usually sits near tendons in the hand or foot. Deep palm involvement is exceptionally rare and hard to diagnose.

The patient was a nine year old girl with a slowly growing mass on the inner side of her left palm. Scans showed an ill defined growth with fatty streaks across two finger bone spaces, raising fears of an aggressive tumor. Surgeons removed it at the margins while sparing tendons, bone, and nerves. The quiet spot and lack of symptoms had let it grow unusually large. One year on, no return was seen.
pmc-11616180:
Hiroki Hirano and Keiko Ishii published a 2024 study on childhood hardship and adult well-being. They surveyed adults in the United States and Japan. Participants reported hardships from their childhood homes. They also rated happiness, loneliness, trust, and emotional expression.

The authors asked whether trust and expression explain lasting effects. People who express positive feelings may recover better. People who trust others may feel less lonely. Comparing two cultures tests whether these paths hold broadly. Findings like these can guide support for adults with difficult childhoods. The study treats emotional habits as possible bridges to better health.
pmc-11616880:
Li, Zhang, Montag, and Hisham link communication overload to information overload and videoconference fatigue, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Videoconferencing surged with remote work and study, bringing fatigue as a side effect. A limited capacity model of message processing frames the investigation. Two studies test the model in education and work contexts.

Study one surveys four hundred eighty-nine students in educational settings. Study two covers professionals in Singapore and Germany with large samples. More frequent meetings consistently predict higher communication overload. Perceived overload in turn predicts information overload and fatigue. Findings hold across students and professionals and across countries. Design and norms should curb verbal overload in meetings.
pmc-11619280:
Chenglong Yao and co-authors asked whether a simple blood-based score can flag heart rhythm trouble in patients with acute coronary syndrome. The score, called the TyG index, combines blood fats and sugar and stands in for insulin resistance, a known risk factor for atrial fibrillation. The team reviewed six hundred thirteen patients treated in Tianjin between twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-four.

A feature-picking method narrowed the risk list to heart disease, valve disease, the TyG score, age, and one blood pressure measure. Higher scores tracked a steadily higher risk of the rhythm problem, with no bend in the line. The score alone predicted cases fairly, and a model built from all five factors did better. The authors say the cheap score could help spot patients who need closer watching.
pmc-11623480:
Patricia Gita Naully and a team of co-authors design a vaccine candidate for chronic hepatitis B on the computer, in two thousand twenty-four. Chronic infection persists because the immune system fails to clear a small hidden form of the virus. Two viral proteins help control that hidden form and make good targets.

The team gathered protein data from ten virus types and picked shared pieces that immune cells can recognize. They joined those pieces with helper parts into one candidate design. Computer checks predicted the design would be safe, stable, and able to cover nearly all people worldwide. Simulations showed it binding immune receptors and stirring antibody and cell responses.
pmc-11623880:
Wang and seven colleagues assess a temple incision face lift in Chinese patients in twenty twenty-four. The method lifts a deep facial tissue layer called the SMAS. Surgeons anchor that flap high to raise sagging cheek fat. The aim is a younger midface and softer nose to mouth folds.

Ninety-five patients had the operation between twenty nineteen and twenty twenty-three. Sixty-one completed follow up from six months to two years. Most reported satisfaction with the aesthetic results. No lasting facial nerve injury or other major complication occurred. The flap reached from above the eye corner down past the cheek bone. The authors say success demands deep knowledge of facial anatomy. The working space is small, so the technique is demanding.
pmc-11624680:
Youcef Bagdad and Maria A Miteva review how artificial intelligence is being used to find new antibacterial drugs. Their 2024 review starts from drug resistance, a global threat that weakens standard treatments for many infections. AI has emerged as a tool to speed the hunt for fresh candidates.

The review sums up methods that found small molecules and peptides able to kill bacteria, including strains that resist current drugs. It walks through case studies where AI-guided picks proved active in tests. The authors also weigh the challenges and openings in this use of AI, from data quality to validation. With resistance rising faster than the drug pipeline, they argue AI progress matters for keeping infections treatable.
pmc-11629580:
Jiani Liu and co-authors chart the aroma styles of Ningxia Chardonnay wines in a 2024 study. The wines come from the eastern foothills of the Helan Mountain in China. Twenty-nine wines were tasted and sorted with two sensory methods. Two styles emerged: lively wines with citrus and floral notes from two sub-regions, and implicit wines with truffle and kerosene notes from a third.

Chemical analysis found one hundred ninety-one aroma compounds in the wines. A handful of them formed the likely core of each style. The team also measured twenty-six phenolic compounds, which shape taste and color. The implicit-style region's wines looked more yellow, matching their higher flavanol content. The authors say the maps of aroma and color can guide growers and winemakers. They may also help shoppers pick wines by style.
pmc-11629780:
Hein Rune Skjoldal and colleagues compare two plankton samplers for measuring zooplankton biomass in the Barents Sea. Their 2024 study draws on decades of monitoring from an annual autumn survey.

The dataset covered hundreds of MOCNESS stations and thousands of WP-2 stations with size-fractioned dry-weight biomass. MOCNESS consistently collected more large-fraction biomass and less small-fraction biomass than the WP-2. The authors interpret this as less avoidance by large plankton and more extrusion of small plankton. Three research vessels collected the data, with no clear effect from towing speed differences. The comparison supports consistent calculation methods across the long time series.
pmc-11633180:
Lucía Guggeri and co-authors published a 2024 study on a protein that helps fat tissue form, studied in zebrafish. Obesity has tangled causes, and rare genetic diseases can reveal its pathways. One clue came from a syndrome where tiny hair-like sensors on cells, called cilia, fail. Cell studies had linked a protein, Fstl1, to both cilia and fat cell formation. The team tested that link in living fish.

Zebrafish carry two versions of the gene. Knocking down one version reduced cilia in early embryos and slowed fat tissue formation in larvae. The second version partly covered for the loss. A new mutant fish line confirmed the effects. On a high-fat diet, fish lacking the first version showed changed activity in fat cell markers. The results support the protein as a regulator of fat tissue development. The authors say pinning down such proteins helps explain how obesity begins.
pmc-11635280:
Yusheng Wang and co-authors compare two ways of removing a small piece of lung for early cancer, inside a day surgery model where patients aim to go home within forty-eight hours. One group had robot-assisted surgery; the other had camera-guided keyhole surgery. The records covered 204 patients treated in Changzhou between 2021 and 2023.

The robot group fared better on most short-term measures: shorter operations, less blood loss, less drainage, and drains removed sooner. Their pain scores were lower and they needed less pain medicine. Far fewer robot patients missed the forty-eight-hour discharge, eleven against thirty-nine. Complications also ran lower overall. A side analysis tied delayed discharge to pain medicine use in the first day, operation length, bleeding, and a history of tumors. The authors favor the robot route for this setting.
pmc-11636080:
Davide Potrich and co-authors published a 2024 study on whether zebrafish can do a simple kind of counting. Zebrafish are small fish often used in brain research. They like to swim with groups of their own kind. The team used that shoaling habit to test whether a male fish tracks how many females he has seen.

In the tests, females were shown one at a time and then hidden behind one of two panels. The male could swim toward either panel. With one female against two, he chose the panel hiding the larger group. With two against three, or two against four, he did not. As long as the total stayed at three or fewer, the fish seemed to handle adding and taking away. They even acted as if they grasped an empty set, the idea of zero. Speed and timing of the display also shaped their choices.
pmc-11637480:
Berner and six colleagues compare drug options for early frozen shoulder in twenty twenty-four. The stiff, sore shoulder eases best when treated in its early pain phase. The team pooled thirty-one studies, most of them trials. A network method ranked injections and pills against physical therapy.

Steroid shots into the joint eased pain and raised function by twelve weeks. Platelet rich plasma shots did the same, and alone improved range of motion. Common pain pills and one gel like shot showed no gain. Bias and mixed study traits temper the verdict. The authors urge early care and cleaner trials.
pmc-11638480:
Ilaria Arduino and colleagues wrap drug-carrying fat bubbles in tumor membrane so the brain tumor welcomes its own poison, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Glioblastoma hides behind the blood-brain barrier and sheds drugs quickly. Their liposomes wear fragments of glioma cell membrane, a disguise meant to fool guards and to home on the same tumor type.

The hybrids were made in microfluidic chips, themselves simplified by 3D printing, which kept quality high and costs down. Loaded with two standard chemotherapy drugs, the bubbles crossed a model blood-brain barrier, sought out their matching glioma cells, and kept the drugs' killing power. The authors pitch membrane-cloaked liposomes as a practical way to smuggle proven drugs into a cancer that defeats them at the gate.
pmc-11639780:
Huseyin Yonder and co-authors propose a new score in a 2024 study to predict death from Fournier's gangrene, a fast and deadly flesh-eating infection of the genital and perineal area. Doctors already use several scores to judge risk in this emergency. The team wanted a tool built for this disease alone.

They looked back at patients treated at three hospitals in one Turkish province between 2014 and 2024. The group covered twenty patients who died and a much larger group who survived.
