Their new index combines a set of measures taken at intake. They test how well the index splits those who died from those who lived, and compare it with older scores. A surer early warning could speed up surgery and intensive care.
pmc-11643280:
Leclercq reviewed colloidal tectonics in this paper from twenty twenty-four. The concept treats small building blocks, called tectons, that assemble themselves into particles and larger structures. Living systems inspired the idea, and chemists now design their own versions. Each assembled system shows traits such as two-sided solubility, predictability, or reversibility.

The review walks from natural examples to lab-made systems. Uses include stabilizing emulsions for catalysis and carrying drugs. Precise control of each block's traits lets new behaviors emerge at the assembled scale. Theory for designing fresh systems closes the survey. Leclercq frames the field as engineering at the nano and micro scales with bioinspired rules.
pmc-11643880:
Zixuan Wang and co-authors grow faceted gold crystals with no seeds or soaps for a flour safety sensor, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. A charged form of hydrazine both shrinks the gold and caps its growth. The crystals come out even, with rare high-index faces.

Those faces shrug off alcohol yet attack peroxides with vigor. A coated electrode then sniffed out a banned flour whitener by its current. The test proved keen and picky in the team's hands. Wider use in catalysis and light tools is forecast. Readers get a simpler path to fancy gold shapes, plus a food guard.
pmc-11644080:
Amina Bramki and co-authors study the leaves of a bramble plant gathered in Algeria in a 2024 paper. The plant, Rubus ulmifolius, is a wild blackberry relative. The team made an extract from its leaves with a solvent and tested what the extract contains and what it can do in lab tests and computer models.

Screening found the leaves rich in plant compounds such as flavonoids and tannins, and measures of key groups ran high. A gas-based analysis named the main small compounds, among them gallic acid and caffeic acid. Tests showed a strong power to block oxygen-driven damage, a trait tied to many health claims for plant extracts. The computer work adds guesses about how the compounds might act in the body.
pmc-11647580:
Fabela-Hardy, Moreno-Ruiz, Necoechea-Osuna, and Conde-García present a case in twenty twenty-four of back pain caused by a rare birth defect of the aorta, the main artery. A man in his fifties had six months of back pain that common pain drugs did not ease. His heart tests were mostly normal, but a chest X-ray showed a widened central chest area.

Detailed scans found a pouch on the aorta pressing on his windpipe, plus an artery branch in the wrong place. Surgeons removed the pouch and rebuilt the branch, and after rehab he had no symptoms. The authors stress that lasting back pain can hide a vessel defect. Good scans can reveal it before the pouch tears, a far more deadly event.
pmc-11647880:
Jonathan Raybin and co-authors show that an electron beam can push tiny particles around on a liquid surface, and pull them back. Their twenty twenty-four article studies silica nanoparticles pinned to the surface of ionic liquid droplets. Beam-driven assembly could shape materials at scales where other fields lose their grip, but its mechanisms were murky.

A scanning electron microscope both watched and drove the particles. By tuning the beam voltage, the team flipped the force: low voltage repelled particles, high voltage drew them in. Patterns formed and dissolved on command. Tracking single particles showed the cause is a flow in the liquid, born from trace chemical damage by the beam. Uses in photonics and catalysis are proposed.
pmc-11649580:
Helal and colleagues studied how gut germs change in people with anorexia nervosa after hospital care. Their work mixed a broad review of past studies with close tracking of a few patients. A short correction notice from twenty twenty-four fixes part of that work.

The notice says three chart notes were placed under the wrong charts, so each note must move. It then prints the notes in the right places. Those notes describe charts for three patients at set time points. They cover germ groups, how mixed the germs were, and a ratio of two large germ groups. Readers get the right labels, so the charts can be read as meant.
pmc-11650080:
Krista Oei and colleagues piloted a food photo app for teenagers in two thousand twenty-four. The app estimates meal nutrition from pictures. Teenagers with obesity often avoid written food logging. Photo logging feels easier and faster. The app also supports personal nutrition goals. Clinicians view the data through a separate portal. Displays for teens minimize calorie counting focus.

Usability testing ran through several improvement cycles. Teen clinic patients tried tasks and gave interviews. A randomized pilot phase followed the refinement. Feasibility in a real obesity clinic was the core question. Digital tools must fit teen habits to work. This phased approach models careful health app testing.
pmc-11654980:
Smaragdi Marinaki and co-authors follow adults in Greece with a kidney disease that scars the filters inside the kidney, in work published in 2024. The disease is a common cause of heavy protein loss in urine. The team used a national registry to track who reached kidney failure and what shaped that risk.

The study covered 579 patients seen over nearly four decades, with a mean age of 46 years. Two factors stood out in the analysis. Higher kidney function at the start meant better survival of the kidneys. Patients whose disease went into full or partial remission fared far better than those with no remission. Patients who got immune-suppressing drugs reached full remission more often, but also relapsed more. The work guides how doctors weigh treatment for this disease.
pmc-11655180:
Margo Goldfarb and co-authors present a 2024 study on how plants make beta-alanine, a small building block with many jobs. In plants it helps answer stresses such as drought, heat, and flooding. It also feeds into making vitamin B5 and coenzyme A, two vital molecules.

Plants can build beta-alanine from several starting materials, unlike bacteria, which use one route. Working with a model plant, the team fed labeled forms of isoleucine and propionate to cells. Tracking the labels showed both feed into beta-alanine through a shared middle step. They then found three enzymes, all aminotransferases, that can run the final step of that route. The work links amino acid breakdown to a wider stress and vitamin network.
pmc-11656380:
Ryota Uchimura and co-authors build a cell-entering peptide that kills blood cancer cells without the usual death pathway. Many leukemias resist treatment by blocking apoptosis, the tidy cell death route. Their peptide joins a NOTCH1 fragment to a viral entry tag. It slips into leukemia cells through a gulping route called macropinocytosis.

Inside, NOTCH target genes switch down, and death follows fast. Membranes burst, spilling cell contents, with no caspase alarm fired. Normal blood cells and solid tumor lines stayed unharmed in the tests. Four greasy building blocks in the fragment proved vital to the kill. The agent offers a spare route against stubborn leukemias and lymphomas.
pmc-11658680:
Shaftoe and Gillis issued a correction in twenty twenty-four to their review of how load reshapes the heart in fish and mammals. The review compared hearts across species to learn how hearts adapt. The correction fixes how one older study on a turtle heart was read.

The older study showed more collagen, a tough fibre, in one heart layer after cold exposure. It did not show that the layer grew thicker, as the review first said. So a line in one figure and one cell in a table were removed. Both the web text and the PDF were updated, and the authors say sorry for the errors.
pmc-11659880:
Sun and five co-authors test if a twin gene's loss deepens a worm nerve fault in this twenty twenty-four study. The main gene guides link growth and wire ends in worm nerves. Its near twin sits close by and shares most of its code.

Inside, gene cuts made worms that lacked both genes at once. Their link and wire faults matched the main-gene lone loss band. A tagged prey protein rose by the same span in both bands. Past plant-in tests also failed to save the main loss with the twin. The team reads the twin as a by-stand gene in this work.
pmc-11661880:
Saskia Locke, James Doonan, and Bryn Jones survey recent advances in caring for fragility fractures, the breaks that occur when osteoporotic bone meets minor trauma. British guidance stresses prompt, coordinated multidisciplinary care and early mobilization. Medical therapy now includes the bone-building drug romosozumab for patients at imminent fracture risk.

Regional nerve blocks are replacing opioids for many, with less delirium. Surgeons have gained polyaxial and far cortical locking systems that let osteoporotic bone heal by controlled motion, plus cement-augmented screws for grip in weak bone. Minimally invasive approaches preserve blood supply and shorten recovery. The authors expect future gains in vertebral and pelvic fracture care aimed at independence.
pmc-11662680:
Chelsea Blankenchip and Kevin Corbett show how a bacterial repressor senses loose DNA strands to switch on immune defenses, in a study from 2024. Bacteria carry immune systems against the viruses that hunt them. Those systems must stay off until truly needed, or they harm their host. The repressor, CapW, holds one such system quiet by gripping double-stranded DNA.

When damage frees single strands, CapW grabs them with a special domain. That grab changes its shape and frees the genes it guards. In a test bacterium, this switch proved key to fighting off a dormant virus. The authors map the full chain from sensing to gene release. Their work explains a whole family of like repressors. It also shows how bacteria balance defense against self-harm.
pmc-11663480:
Sinian Li and co-authors report a case where tuberculosis passed from mother to fetus before birth, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The mother conceived through lab-assisted fertilization, a path that raises tuberculosis risk. Both mother and her three-month-old baby were found with spread tuberculosis, including a brain lesion in the baby.

Gene sequencing proved the same drug-resistant strain in both. Drug care began fast and worked well for both patients. The baby's plan had to change several times due to liver harm and acid buildup from the drugs. The authors urge vigilance in such pregnancies.
pmc-11664280:
Mohammad Keshavarzi, Moein Ghasemi, Mohammad Amin Manavi, Ahmad Reza Dehpour, and Hamed Shafaroodi test how a common drug calms seizures in mice, and whether nitric oxide carries the effect. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. A third of epilepsy patients still seize despite modern drugs, so fresh angles are needed.

Seizures were triggered three ways: a slow vein infusion, a belly injection of a convulsant, and a maximal electric shock. The drug, pentoxifylline, was dosed alone and with a nitric oxide building block or with blockers of its making enzymes. Thresholds, delays, and deaths were scored. The design separates which enzyme branch, if any, the drug leans on. The work probes a cheap, approved drug as a possible seizure add-on.
pmc-11667280:
Neumann, Subah, and van der Westhuizen study how Liberia made community health workers into paid professionals. These workers are central to fair care, yet few nations formally employ or pay them. Health policy forms inside power struggles among funders and governments.

The case follows Liberia's Community Health Assistant program at national scale. Using Lukes' theory of power, the authors credit strong government will for the win. Liberia pushed back on funder resistance to paying workers and reclaimed decision control. Agreement across ministries strengthened that hand. Local proof framed around workers' rights helped proactive talks with funders.
pmc-11668980:
Klemens Höfer and co-authors present a 2024 protocol for a study of health apps in German mental health care. Mental illness touches about 28 percent of German adults each year. Since 2020, some apps can be prescribed and paid for by public insurance, and many target mental health. Yet doctors prescribe them with clear reluctance, a sign that fit problems persist.

The project will map current app use, weigh ways to weave apps into talk therapy, and name the blocks. Methods mix a scoping review, focus groups, expert talks, and insurance claims data. The end goal is policy advice for smoother use of the apps in outpatient care. Funded by a federal innovation fund, the work speaks to payers, doctors, and patients alike.
pmc-11669880:
Emilie Bryne, Kathrine Høyvik Bergum, and William Gilje Gjedrem set out a trial protocol for improving prisoners' oral health, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. Prisoners suffer poor oral health from limited care access, poverty, and low prioritization. A pilot using motivational interviewing showed promise.

Four prisons in Norway's Rogaland County recruited toward three hundred twenty inmates. Participants are randomized to oral hygiene packages with or without motivational interviewing, a thirty-minute counseling session among the intervention components. The trial is multicenter and double-blinded by design. Protocols published in advance lock methods before results arrive. If counseling plus supplies beat supplies alone, prison health services gain an inexpensive, scalable intervention.
pmc-11669980:
Ling-Yu Bai, Ming Zhao, and Kui-Ying Ma report a heart rhythm case and review the drug behind it, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. A seventy-five-year-old woman came in with chest tightness, breath loss, and one faint. Her dangerous ventricular rhythm kept returning in hospital.

Standard drugs and electric shocks failed to settle it. Once nicorandil was added, the rhythm stopped. The drug opens potassium channels, which steadies the heart's electrical timing. The authors pair the case with a literature review and pitch nicorandil as a strong option when usual care fails.
pmc-11672680:
Van Leuven and co-authors ask whether antibiotic use in hospital wards feeds drug resistance in the slimy biofilms inside sink drains. Such films can shelter dangerous bacteria. The team sampled drains in four wards of a German hospital and matched the findings to each ward's prescribing records.

Every ward's drains held medically relevant species. A resistance marker gene grew more common as ward antibiotic use rose. Visible drug resistance in the bacteria, though, showed no matching trend. Lab-grown films shifted their makeup depending on the starting community and the drug added. The authors conclude there is no single general effect of low-dose antibiotics on drain films.
pmc-11675080:
Liping Wang, Xuming Hu, Chenyue Tao, Jacob Xiang, and Hengmi Cui identified a natural antisense RNA that appears to restrain liver cancer, in this 2024 study. The RNA, called NRAS-AS, is the mirror-strand partner of a known cancer gene, NRAS. The team found it by sequencing liver cancer cells and then tested what it does.

Raising the antisense RNA in two liver cancer cell lines slowed their growth and spread, pushed them toward cell death, and reshaped their division cycle. Silencing it did the opposite. Mice given cells with extra antisense RNA grew smaller tumors. In patient samples, the antisense ran low where the cancer gene ran high, and its protein fell when the antisense rose. The authors propose it as a possible drug target and test marker.
pmc-11675480:
Dejun Xiong and co-authors study a gene called ISCA1 across many cancers in a 2024 paper. The gene helps build iron-sulfur clusters, small parts that many proteins need to move energy and do their work. The team asks how the gene links to a form of cell death driven by iron, and to the immune cells around a tumor.

Using large cancer data sets, the authors track the gene's level, its changes, and patient outcomes in many tumor types. They also test drug ideas with computer docking models. The gene stands out most in thyroid cancer, where it may serve as a marker for outlook and for response to immune therapy. It also works with distinct partner genes in distinct cell types. The team sees it as a lead for new drugs.
pmc-11676180:
Maitane Serrano and nine co-authors feed male mice an omega-3-rich diet and trace changes in the brain's cannabinoid system and behavior, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Omega-3 fats support brain membranes and plasticity, and they interact with the endocannabinoid system, but effects in a healthy brain were unclear.

Hippocampal synapse preparations from fed mice showed more of the main cannabinoid receptor and several partner proteins, and less of others, including a key postsynaptic scaffold. A form of synaptic strengthening in the fed mice depended on that receptor system and its lipid messenger. Behavior shifted too: less exploration, better object discrimination, and signs of lower anxiety in a maze test. The authors say omega-3 works partly through the cannabinoid system.
pmc-11676380:
Frank Strnad and co-authors read how growth curb in the womb shapes mouse brain cells and guard cells past birth. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Such babes bear high risk of learn and mind loss. A mouse model of womb flow lack was used. At one month past birth, nerve cells of the mind gate zone were lit and drawn, and guard cells read by stain.

Curbed pups kept main branch spans but lost branch nets and bulk. Guard cells grew in count and size. Brain call parts split by sex. First-born cells grow awry on their own, the team say.
pmc-11677080:
Bin Tang and nine co-authors offer a narrative review from two thousand twenty-four on psoriasis and extracellular vesicles. Psoriasis is a long-term skin disease that also harms joints and raises care costs. Vesicles are tiny sacs with a lipid skin that cells release into the body.

The review explains how these vesicles help cells talk to each other and carry cargo such as miRNA. Through that cargo they can shape immune response, cell growth, and cell change, and thus help drive the disease. The authors also weigh vesicles as treatment tools in their own right. They discuss using them to carry drugs straight to target tissue.
pmc-11677380:
Boyne and co-authors study whether sitting time links to prescription drug use in adults. Past work tied physical activity to lower medication use, but sedentary time itself was rarely tested. Sitting is linked to chronic disease and death risk even after activity levels are counted, so its own role matters.

The pilot study measured sedentary time with devices rather than self-reports, which are often inaccurate. Adults also reported their own prescription medication use for comparison. The team examined total sitting and sitting patterns apart from exercise. Results may show if cutting sitting could ease medication burden.
pmc-11679380:
Liuxu Ding and three co-authors build a way to fix font and line lean for scene text reads. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Scene text comes in bent shapes, odd fonts, and with parts hid, which makes machine reads hard. A set true font was built to right odd text, with a trait align and fuse block to match it back to the raw read path.

A two-heed block set tween path steps sharp heed on text grain to fight the hid parts. A fresh Chinese set was made for split light states. Marks hit past ninety percent on that set and a high mark in whole.
pmc-11679680:
Matteo Riccò and co-authors produced a consensus document for an international group of infection experts, setting out new ways to prevent respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV. The virus is a leading cause of chest infections, hitting young infants, older adults, and people with other health problems hardest. For years, care meant support alone, plus one antibody drug that needed repeated doses.

The group reports a wider toolkit now. A long-acting antibody gives infants season-long protection from a single dose and cut hospital stays and intensive care use. New vaccines protect older adults, and shots given in pregnancy may pass protection to newborns. The document also weighs the global burden of the virus, its costs, and the problems of rolling these options out in different health systems.
pmc-11679980:
Joel Oliveira and seven colleagues published a modelling study in two thousand twenty-four on making fibre-reinforced plastic parts. In liquid moulding, resin is pushed into a closed mould packed with fibres. Most models assume the resin flows in a straight line and ignore resin soaking into the fibres.

The authors built a maths model for resin spreading outward in a circle from the injection point. Their model includes the soaking effect of the fibres. It predicts where the flow front sits over time, plus speed and pressure inside the mould. They then tested how resin thickness, fibre traits, and injection settings change the flow. The work aims at better mould design and fewer wasted parts.
pmc-11682780:
Elsobky and eleven co-authors map bird flu spread in farm birds across Egypt in this twenty twenty-four study. The harsh H5N1 strain has sat in Egypt for near two decades and hits both farms and folks. Past control plans have not held the spread in check.

Inside, the team tracked waves of the disease at the sub-district scale and marked the hot zones. Risk rose first near the north edge, then faded through later waves of spread. Hot zones sat most in farm towns and small villages, not in dense city zones. Zones with high risk in one wave tended to host the next wave's core too. The authors urge plans shaped per zone, not one plan for all.
pmc-11689580:
Mo-kyung Sin and four co-authors link late-life blood pressure to brain signs of Alzheimer's disease. Their twenty twenty-four study uses a large national data set. It covers more than five thousand people who had four blood pressure checks before death. Brain scores after death came from two rating systems that grade plaques and tangles, the clumps tied to the disease.

Higher late-life pressure linked to worse scores on one system, but not the other. The link held when drugs and a known gene risk were counted. The authors say keeping blood pressure in check late in life may slow the brain changes of the disease. The effect they found was small.
pmc-11690780:
Ana Quiñones, David Dorr, and Arlene Bierman led a symposium in 2024 on person-centered care planning for people living with multiple chronic conditions. Providing such care well is a critical challenge. Health systems are often fragmented, which adds cost, duplicates work, and leaves families and caregivers to share information and coordinate care between providers.

The symposium shared early findings from a collaborative, multidisciplinary initiative funded by a federal research agency. One talk summarized the care planning models that exist now. A second shared barriers, facilitators, and solutions raised by frontline providers, health care leaders, and policy makers. A third covered what health systems need to make such planning a routine part of care. The goal is care that is equitable, coordinated, and shaped by each person's own goals, values, and preferences.
pmc-11691380:
Caroline Stephens and seven co-authors published a study in 2024 on the family characteristics of nursing home residents in Utah at the end of life, comparing rural and urban homes. Families play a critical role in end-of-life care, yet how family size and characteristics affect the care residents use had not been examined by place.

The researchers linked nursing home decedents from 1998 to 2016 to their first-degree relatives in the state. Urban homes accounted for far more of the deaths than rural homes. Rural decedents were slightly more likely to have no close family in the state. Having a spouse was associated with higher rates of hospitalization in both groups. Having a child was associated with more hospitalizations in urban homes, but not in rural ones. The study aims to sharpen understanding of the family role at the end of life.
pmc-11692080:
Rinanda Shaleha, Nelson Roque, and Erin Harrell study what keeps older adults using brain training technology in a 2024 paper. One hundred eighteen adults aged sixty five and over took part in a tech based cognitive training program. Prior work found that how the program was framed mattered little, so the authors tested personal motivation instead.

Motivation was measured from game performance, with steady success and low failure marking high motivation. Statistical models showed a strong link: each step up in motivation came with a clear rise in how faithfully participants stuck with training. Model comparisons confirmed motivation improved prediction a lot. The authors suggest game design that feeds motivation can raise adherence in such programs.
pmc-11692180:
Alex Speers and Amala Soumyanath lay out a stepwise plan for testing herbal supplements properly in older adults. Their overview appeared in twenty twenty-four. Supplement use is rising among seniors, yet good proof of benefit is scarce, product quality varies, and mixing herbs with many medicines adds risk.

Their center in Oregon studies two herbs tied to brain and body resilience in aging: gotu kola and ashwagandha. The pipeline starts with checking what is actually in each product. It then tests how the herbs act in cells and animals, and how to measure their compounds in blood. Human safety and dosing studies follow. The aim is the solid groundwork that fair, optimized trials in older adults require.
pmc-11692480:
Eduardo Silveyra and Soham Al Snih wrote a study in two thousand twenty-four on multiple chronic conditions and disability in older Mexican American adults. Longer lives mean more people live with several diseases at once. The authors asked whether the link between disease count and trouble with daily tasks differs for women and men.

They followed nearly one thousand adults aged seventy-five and older who began the study without disability, over twelve years. Women with three conditions had higher odds of later disability than women with at most one. Both sexes with four or more conditions faced higher odds, but the pattern was clear and significant only in women. The authors call for programs that account for these sex differences.
pmc-11693380:
Shuna Khoo, Zhihao Ma, and Lile Jia map how well-being hangs together for adults with different schooling in Singapore in a 2024 study. Singapore's older adults today had far less schooling than the cohort now aging, so support programs must serve both profiles. The team surveyed a representative community sample of more than five thousand adults.

Using network analysis, they mapped links among the elements of well-being for each education group. The patterns differed sharply. For residents with less schooling, well-being centered on present conditions such as illness, eating habits, and quality of life. For the highly schooled, it centered on balance, harmony, and expected quality of life ten years ahead. The authors say programs can be judged by whether they move the central factors for each group.
pmc-11696780:
Hao Zhu, Xuan Yin, and six co-authors study brain bleeds found in unborn babies by MRI scans. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, reviews cases from two large hospitals over near ten years. The bleeds were first spotted on ultrasound. MRI then gave a clearer look before birth.

The set holds one hundred twenty-six cases, most of them single babies. The most common added problem was swelling of the brain's fluid spaces. About a third of cases showed that trait. Other cases showed missing or extra fluid pockets in the head. The size of the bleed did not match the count of added problems. The team links scan traits to how the babies fared at birth.
pmc-11702980:
Jian Wu and eleven co-authors published a 2024 paper on making oilseed rape fragrant using gene editing. Oilseed rape is a major oil crop, and scent strongly affects the value of farm products. In rice, fragrance comes from a broken gene that lets a scent compound build up.

The team asked whether the same trick works in rape, which carries several copies of the related gene. Using CRISPR editing, they knocked out two copies of one gene that do the same job. Edited plants accumulated 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the compound behind the scent in fragrant rice. The result opens a path to fragrant rape lines with added market value. It also shows a known fragrance pathway can transfer across crops.
pmc-11709480:
Lise Colmant and eight co-authors report a study of wayfinding in older adults, published in twenty twenty-five. The work asks if errors in tracking one's own path link to early signs of Alzheimer's disease. The team used a game where people moved in a virtual space and then tried to return to the start point.

Ninety adults took part, some with mild memory loss and some with none. Brain scans checked for amyloid and tau, two proteins tied to the disease. People with early disease signs but no symptoms did worse when no landmark was present. Turn errors linked most to tau in key brain areas. The authors say such tests may spot change before memory fails.
pmc-11710280:
Chunyu Wang, Jian Liu, Lianchun Wang, Dylan Mah, and Fuming Zhang review evidence, published in 2025, that a rare sugar coating on cell surfaces may matter in Alzheimer disease. The coating is heparan sulfate, and it binds many proteins. A rare form of it, marked by a chemical change called 3-O sulfation, has been tied to disease risk by large gene studies. The gene behind it is named Hs3st1.

Using lab methods that track how molecules bind, the team showed that tau sticks to this rare form. Tau is the protein that builds the tangles seen in Alzheimer brains. ApoE, a protein whose forms strongly change disease risk, also binds it, and the riskiest form binds tightest. A new test found much more of this sugar form in Alzheimer brains than in healthy ones. They argue it could serve both as a drug target and as a sign of disease.
pmc-11715480:
Jessie Yan and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on how often United States doctors used tests to diagnose memory loss and dementia. Scans, spinal fluid tests, and blood tests can make an Alzheimer's diagnosis earlier and more exact.

The team used full Medicare records for more than six hundred fifty thousand people aged sixty-seven or older, newly diagnosed between twenty fifteen and twenty twenty. In the year before diagnosis, most had a blood test and about half had a brain scan. CT scans were common, while PET scans and spinal fluid tests were rare. Test use crept up a bit across the six years. The authors say the sharp tests needed for new disease-changing drugs were barely used in that span.
pmc-11772480:
Marina Zaychikova and a large team of co-authors report the isolation of a new bacteria-infecting virus in Russia, in this study published in 2024. The virus, named Vic9, attacks Mycobacterium species, the group that includes the tuberculosis germ. Such viruses are studied both for what they show about virus diversity and as possible tools against drug-resistant infections.

The team grew Vic9 on a harmless host species and placed it in the B2 subcluster of its virus family, the first of that group found in Russia. They measured how fast it sticks to cells, how long it hides inside them, and how many copies burst out. Its genome holds eighty-nine genes, with one odd stretch in a gene cluster that stands out even among close relatives. Vic9 could also kill the tuberculosis strain, though weakly.
pmc-11783280:
Mark Edward Gonzales and three co-authors built a tool to guess which host a phage infects from its protein shapes. Their paper deals with phage-host interaction calls. Past tools lean on gene text reads from language models. Those reads miss shape facts, though shape sets whom a phage can dock. Their tool, PHIStruct, feeds shape aware protein codes into a small neural net.

The codes come from a shape tuned protein model, run on the phage's dock proteins. It calls the host genus from a set of hard to treat kinds. Next to fresh tools it held the best blend of precision and recall, with the top F1 across trust marks. Readers get host calls that hold even when gene texts drift far apart.
pmc-11789180:
Eder and Weil report two new cadmium tellurium oxide crystals. Both crystals grew as single forms in hot water under pressure. One form stacks in flat layers like sheets. The next form builds a full three-axis frame.

The first form holds five cadmium atoms per unit set. Its cadmium centers bind six or seven oxygen atoms each. Bond lengths span a narrow range in that form. The second form holds four cadmium and five tellurium atoms. Both forms share one growth bath yet take distinct shapes. Full bond maps are given for each crystal type.
pmc-11871880:
Morris Muriuki, Sherry Oluchina, and Bernard Mbithi study strain on family caregivers of cancer patients in a 2024 study at a national referral hospital in Kenya. Cancer care runs over a long course, much of it as outpatient visits. Around the world, families carry most of that daily care, yet little was known about their strain in Africa.

The team surveyed two hundred fifty-five family caregivers at the hospital's outpatient cancer clinic in early 2020. They gathered both counted answers and open accounts. They looked for caregiver traits, such as age, income, and relation to the patient, that line up with strain in the role. Naming those factors is a first step toward support plans that ease the load on families who hold up long-term care.
pmc-12082680:
Okon and co-authors probe drug-proof germs in lung illness among people with HIV in Uyo, Nigeria, in work from 2024. They took sputum from sixty-one people with signs of chest infection who were on standard HIV therapy. Lab tools named the germs grown, and gene tests searched the germs for traits that block drugs.

Germs grew in about four in ten samples. One staph type was most common, and proof was strong against two common drugs. Four proof genes turned up, and one of them sat in every germ that blocked many drugs. The team urges close watch and firm action in this at-risk group.
pmc-12118280:
Yang and co-authors review single glowing probes that watch two cell organelles at once in two thousand twenty-four. Organelles are the cell's work zones, and they trade signals to keep the cell running. Faults in their network feed many diseases, yet their fast interplay is hard to see.

Glow imaging suits the task since it is gentle and can track change live. The review sorts probes that target two organelles and shine in two colors, by how they aim and how they glow. Uses in biology and medicine are covered for each class. The authors close with current limits and where probe design should go next, to guide fresh work in the field.
pmc-12259280:
Birhan Assega and co-authors hunted soda lakes in Ethiopia for bacteria that make the enzyme L-arginase, a candidate cancer drug. The enzyme starves cancer cells by breaking down an amino acid they need. From thirty-one water samples the team grew 102 colonies and screened them for enzyme output. The best producer, a strain of Alcaligenes aquatilis from Lake Chitu, was identified by gene sequencing. Tuning eight growth conditions nearly doubled its output.

The work, published in 2024, shows that extreme soda-lake microbes can supply a medically interesting enzyme at useful levels. Bacterial production matters because the enzyme must be made cheaply and in bulk to be a practical therapy. The authors present the strain and its tuned recipe as a starting point for development. Further steps would test the enzyme's purity, safety, and real anticancer effect, none of which this screening study attempts.
pmc-12660980:
Wan-Feng Zhang and his eight co-authors, publishing in 2025, untangle a dating problem in a common volcanic rock. The argon-argon method dates basic rocks by measuring argon trapped in minerals. Stray extra argon hides in some samples and scrambles the ages. The team studied a diabase whose whole-rock ages formed a telltale saddle shape, a classic sign of contamination.

Their feldspar, measured separately, gave one clean age: about 48.7 million years. Chemical and mineral mapping then fingered the culprit. Altered amphibole, a mineral reshaped by later heating, held most of the stray argon. The authors advise dating teams to avoid separates containing that mineral in basic rocks. Their combined approach, chemistry plus imaging plus the dating itself, offers a template for spotting the same trap elsewhere.
pmc-12662880:
Yang Zhang, Yanyan Jiang, and Zeng Xu test refined intensive care nursing for severe pancreas swelling in a trial of eighty-four patients, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. The refined plan adds a trained team, custom care plans, tight organ watch, teaching media, mind support, and staged feeding. Usual care alone formed the control.

Refined care cleared symptoms faster and cut hospital stays. Harm events ran near seven percent versus about twenty-four with usual care. Mood scores eased and life quality rose across all domains. Satisfaction topped ninety-five percent in the refined group. Readmission rates did not differ. Readers get a care bundle with broad gains for a deadly illness.
pmc-12663580:
Maryna Zhylina and co-authors trace how the structure of biochar develops when barley waste pellets are slowly heated without oxygen. Their 2025 study joins a push to turn farm waste into useful products instead of burning it. Biochar can serve as a sorbent that soaks up pollutants.

The team first found a durable pellet mix of mostly barley straw with some bran. Pellets were heated at three temperatures and held for one to three hours. The resulting chars were compared on yield, carbon and nitrogen content, surface area, and pore spread. Higher temperature and longer holding raised surface area and widened the pores. Those traits decide how well a char can adsorb, so the recipe map helps producers tune char for water or soil uses.
pmc-12664280:
Liu and seven co-authors mapped skin peptides in twenty twenty-five in a frog whose skin makes many guard compounds. Finding those peptides is hard in kinds with no genome map. Their pipe joins gene reads with mass reads of the skin wash to catch more of them.

A fix for start-site slips lifted find rates by more than three fifths. They found more than one hundred such peptides, most of them new for this frog. One family held the bulk, with wide spread between frogs of one group. Most of the peptides tie to defense work, the gene maps show.
pmc-12666080:
Prabhdeep Kaur and a team of co-authors report treatment outcomes from a hypertension control program scaled across fifteen Indian states, in two thousand twenty-five. More than a million people with high blood pressure were enrolled at public facilities in eighty-nine districts. Records covered care from two thousand eighteen into two thousand twenty-two.

About forty-four percent of those still in care had their pressure controlled. Control ranged widely, from top states above half to others below a quarter. It also fell when two readings, rather than one, defined control. Younger patients, men, and people with diabetes faced a higher risk of uncontrolled pressure. Higher-level facilities also lagged. The authors call for focused strategies for those groups.
pmc-12696080:
Perrine Lardellier and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five comparison of lab methods for checking messenger RNA quality. Products built on messenger RNA power new vaccines and medicines, but the molecules break down easily. Broken strands cannot make the right protein, so makers must measure damage reliably.

Three methods were tested on raw and finished material. Two used gel separation in fine tubes with different light detection. The third used a pairing chromatography method. All three tracked integrity and purity, while chromatography separated stray forms more sharply. The study also flagged functional joined molecules that routine methods might miss or misread.
pmc-12702780:
Beilei Ye and co-authors sort thinking profiles in older adults with type two diabetes, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Over five hundred patients at a large hospital took a standard thinking test. The team grouped scores into hidden profiles and weighed factors tied to each group.

Three profiles emerged: full, partial, and at-risk thinking loss. The partial group held over half the patients. Sex, schooling, years with diabetes, and blood sugar control each shaped profile membership. D varied mental activity and good nutrition also mattered. The authors urge early steps on sugar control, mental variety, and social support.
pmc-12706980:
Valter Cordeiro Barbosa Filho and colleagues describe how stakeholders co-created the logic model for a health-promoting school program in socially vulnerable areas of a Brazilian capital. The World Health Organization backs health-promoting schools as a core strategy. Yet school programs based on implementation science are still rare, above all in vulnerable areas. Building it with others should help it win support and last.

The co-creation went in three stages: planning, doing and checking, and final check. The logic model was built on a framework for such research, with determinants, strategies, mechanisms, and outcomes. Planning drew on facts from theory, evidence, and practice, through five strategies. Stakeholders were researchers, teachers, managers, health workers, students, and recent school graduates.
pmc-12707780:
Volkan Selmi and five co-authors test two simple ways to ease prostate biopsy in a 2025 trial. The biopsy, guided by ultrasound through the rectum, is the standard check for prostate cancer, but it can hurt and cause strong anxiety. The team compared music, conversation, and no extra support during the procedure.

Ninety patients at a university hospital in Türkiye were split evenly into the three groups. Pain and anxiety were scored before and after. Talk with the staff cut both pain and anxiety by clear margins. Music, by contrast, scored about the same as the control group. The authors suggest that engaging the patient in conversation is a cheap, drug-free way to make the test easier.
pmc-12709680:
Feng-Juan Gao and nine co-authors widen the known mutation spectrum of gyrate atrophy, a rare inherited eye disease, in patients from Yunnan province. The condition, caused by faults in the OAT gene, progressively destroys the choroid and retina. Multi-ethnic Chinese populations had been little studied.

Eight patients from five families shared high myopia, early vision loss, and raised blood ornithine. Atrophy around the optic disc appeared in most eyes and tracked with worse vision and longer eyes. Four mutations were new to science, including the first pathogenic variant found in the gene's five-prime untranslated region. A minigene test proved that variant disrupts splicing. The authors stress population-specific profiles for diagnosis.
pmc-12714080:
Carlos Valladares and four co-authors sum what is known on droxidopa, a blood-press drug, used off-label in intensive care. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-five. Long drip drugs to hold blood press bring harm, and droxidopa is cleared for a nerve-based press drop on standing. The team swept four bases through April twenty twenty-five for real patient data on its ICU use to wean drips.

Seven small past-look works held one hundred sixty-one patients in all. Time to drip stop ran from one day to five. ICU stay ran long where told. The team call the proof thin and mixed, and urge more and stricter work.
pmc-12715080:
Yi Zhou and co-authors investigated in 2025 how an immune drug called pomalidomide makes built T cell treatment work better against blood cancers. CAR-T treatment, where a patient's own T cells are fitted with a synthetic receptor, makes high remission rates in lymphoid malignancies. But too many responses fade as the cells exhaust and disappear. Clinicians had noticed pomalidomide synergizing with the treatment without knowing why, so the team attacked the process from three directions.

In lab assays, pomalidomide boosted CAR-T cell proliferation and killing in a manner that depended on the cells being activated. Raised their output of key effector molecules and cell-recruiting chemokines, favored long-lived central memory cells. And reprogrammed their metabolism. Mouse xenograft models tested the mix in a living system, and single-cell sequencing of blood from a lymphoma patient treated with both mapped how the wider immune setting was remodeled.
pmc-12718580:
Astrid Dauchez and ten co-authors test whether bone health can be screened from scans that prostate cancer patients already receive. Their study came out in 2025. Hormone therapy for this cancer thins bones and raises fracture risk, yet bone density is rarely checked at baseline.

The team measured bone attenuation, a density signal, in the lower spine on both a combined PET and CT scan and a stand-alone CT scan. The two methods agreed well at all three vertebrae measured. Longer hormone therapy went with lower attenuation values. About one in five patients had a spinal fracture, and those patients had clearly lower attenuation. The authors conclude that routine scans can flag osteoporosis risk without extra appointments or radiation.
pmc-12719880:
Svetlana O Kushch and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five chemistry study of competing ring-forming reactions that build fused drug-like scaffolds. A two-headed starting alcohol can react through nitrogen or oxygen first. That choice decides which ring system forms.

Three ingredients combined in one pot: the diamine alcohol, a fluorinated building block, and varied methyl ketones. The ketone's tail steered which product dominated. Dual acid-base catalysis sharpened selectivity for simple ketones. Products carried up to three handed centers, giving several mirror forms. Structures were proven with magnetic resonance and X-ray methods.
pmc-12722780:
Hansoo Song and co-authors published a study in 2025 on how to judge workplace health systems in large firms. A good system protects worker health, but firms need fair rules to rate how well their system works. The team set out to build such a set of rules.

The team first drafted rules from past writing on the topic. Then twenty experts in work medicine and hygiene rated the rules in two survey rounds. Rules that scored too low on expert agreement were cut or revised. Talks with firm health managers also shaped the final list. The end result was twenty-eight rules in four areas. The authors say firm health chiefs can use the list to track and improve their systems over time.
pmc-12723080:
Five authors report a hospital study from two thousand twenty-five on a blood disease in which the body attacks its own red blood cells. The disease is primary warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. They ask what a positive indirect antiglobulin test, a lab screen for antibodies in the blood, means when a patient is first diagnosed.

The team looked back at records for eighty adults treated at one Jordanian hospital. About two thirds had a positive test at the start. Those patients had higher levels of a marker of cell damage and more relapses after steroid doses were lowered. Response to steroids was also lower in that group.
pmc-12727880:
Yangxiu Wu and a large team of co-authors built a resource on how cancer cells keep their chromosome ends alive in a 2025 paper. Immortal growth is a hallmark of cancer, granted by telomere maintenance, yet drugs barely exploit it. The team measured telomere biology across 976 cancer cell lines.

They added fresh protein data for most lines and merged it with gene, drug response, and gene-knockout data. Telomere states proved far more varied than the classic two-mechanism picture. The team derived protein and gene-activity signatures that predict which mechanism a line uses. They also found weak points tied to the alternative lengthening route and drug sensitivities tied to telomerase levels. The resource aims to speed telomere-directed drugs and matching tests.
pmc-12728580:
Ting Zhang and five co-authors traced how brain structure before COVID predicted fear during the pandemic and strain a year later, in a study published in 2025. A total of 115 students in Chengdu had brain scans before the outbreak. At its peak they scored their fear. A year later the team scored stress and broad distress markers.

Two deep zones, the insulae, stood out: more volume there meant more fear at the peak. The link held with sex, age, and whole brain size held constant. Fear then carried the brain link onward: it bridged the insula tie to later stress and distress scores. The authors say such scans could flag who needs early help in the next outbreak. Fear is the path to treat.
pmc-12729680:
Subarna Barua and co-authors published this methods study in 2025. Bats make up nearly a fifth of all mammal species and matter for pollination, pest control, and disease tracking. Naming a species correctly is harder than it looks. Looks and calls overlap between species, and the standard DNA barcode gene varies too much in places. The team built a simpler test around a short stretch of another gene, the mitochondrial 12S rRNA.

Using sequences from 232 species, they designed one primer pair that copies a fragment of about two hundred letters. That fragment separated every species analyzed. The test worked on all 241 real samples tried. Its identifications agreed with expert naming in 97.2 percent of cases. Two samples hinted at an undescribed species. Ten species from six genera turned up in the set. The authors offer the assay as a sturdy tool for conservation work.
pmc-12729880:
Anxin Li, Yanan Meng, and Martin Drapeau test group therapy for students in psychological subhealth. Their exploratory study from twenty twenty-five sorts students by core predicament. Subhealth means struggling without a formal diagnosis. Trauma, study pressure, and family dysfunction form separate groups.

Sixty students split evenly across the three predicament types. Half received eight weeks of group intervention. The programme blends thinking skills with social support ideas. Overall mental health and depression improved with treatment. Trauma students gained most on sensitivity and anxiety measures. Different struggles responded differently to the same programme. Matching support to predicament type may raise student wellbeing faster.
pmc-12730380:
Sofia Kasradze and co-authors locate where seizures start in the brain using scalp recordings in a 2025 study. Finding the seizure onset zone guides surgery for patients whose epilepsy resists drugs. The usual method needs electrodes placed inside the skull. The team instead tracked information flow in scalp signals with a causality method built on a new factorization algorithm.

They studied six patients who were being assessed for surgery, across pairs of brain regions and short time windows. The method found the start zones and the paths seizures took from them. Its answers matched the good surgical outcomes seen in all six cases, each reaching the best outcome class. The authors see promise for safer planning and for wider studies of brain information flow.
pmc-12730480:
Solafah Abdalla and colleagues review preclinical gene therapy for Crohn's disease and its path toward patients, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Progress has been constrained by several challenges. Optimal gene targets are hard to identify. Therapy-resistant cells in chronically inflamed tissue, especially the gut's nervous system, are hard to reach. Animal models mostly rely on toxin-induced colitis, unlike human disease.

The review synthesizes major preclinical studies in Crohn's and related bowel diseases. Vector platforms are compared by type, promoter, and administration route. Biodistribution data from rodent and primate gut tissue are critically assessed. Strategies targeting the enteric nervous system get special attention. Possible aims include calming intestinal inflammation directly. Local gene delivery during surgery might also prevent postoperative recurrence. The authors frame the field's foundations for translational research.
pmc-12730580:
Li and colleagues sequence the full mitochondrial genome of a small fish found only in southwest China in twenty twenty-five. The fish belongs to a carp subfamily whose family tree is unsettled. Its full ring of mitochondrial DNA was read and charted gene by gene. The team then rebuilt the subfamily tree from thirteen protein coding genes.

The genome held the usual fish gene set plus a control region. One transfer RNA broke the classic cloverleaf shape. The tree split the subfamily into two big limbs, not one clean branch. The study fish landed in the more derived limb, apart from its named kin. The genome adds a firm data point for carp taxonomy.
pmc-12732380:
Yan Liang and colleagues published a 2025 food study comparing ways to dry orange slices. The oranges came from Gannan, a major growing region. Fresh fruit processing options there are limited. Two drying methods were tested side by side. Freeze-drying used vacuum and cold. Hot-air drying used heated airflow.

Freeze-dried slices looked whiter and brighter. They kept more vitamin C as well. Hot-air slices held more protective plant compounds. Aroma chemicals shifted under both methods. Tasters scored the sensory qualities of each batch. Neither method won on every measure. Producers can choose based on cost and target quality.
pmc-12732780:
Sarah Moncado and co-authors check how often inherited variants spotted in tumor testing are confirmed by true germline testing. Their 2025 study covers adults with solid tumors at two United States community cancer centers. Tumor profiling often turns up variants that may be inherited, with implications for the patient and their family.

The team reviewed patients who had both tumor profiling and dedicated germline sequencing. They measured the agreement rate between the two, checked whether confirmed variants matched the patient's tumor type, and analyzed how strongly each variant appeared in the tumor data. Community centers handle most cancer care, so rates measured there matter more than academic-center figures. Confirming a variant can change treatment and trigger screening for relatives.
pmc-12732980:
Meizhu Dang and co-authors test, in twenty twenty-five, a natural antifreeze peptide from grass carp on wet gluten protein. Gluten is the elastic protein network in wheat dough. Freeze-thaw cycles damage it in frozen foods. The peptide, GCAFP, may serve as a natural cryoprotectant. The team measured freezing behavior, water states, flow traits, and microstructure with calorimetry, magnetic resonance, rheology, and electron microscopy. Adding half a percent of the peptide lowered the freezing point clearly.

It also widened the melting range, a sign of better freezing stability. After five weeks frozen, ice crystal growth in the treated gluten was less than in controls. After five freeze-thaw cycles, freezable water fell. The peptide curbed water migration and ice recrystallization.
pmc-12742080:
Xiaoyi Ji and a large team published a study protocol in twenty twenty-five for putting a prostate biopsy AI through unusually strict validation. Grading prostate biopsies is subjective, and pathologists disagree enough to sway treatment. AI systems can match experts in their home laboratory yet stumble elsewhere, a generalizability problem recent reviews keep flagging.

The protocol pre-registers a retrospective test on an independent cohort, scoring the system on grade, cancer volume, and pattern detection against independent pathologists. Bias risks that plagued earlier studies are designed against from the start. Publishing the protocol before results exist is itself part of the rigor. The study aims to produce the kind of external evidence regulators and clinics actually need.
pmc-12743480:
Joanna Koort and three co-authors surveyed online case tools for veterinary students in a 2025 paper. The University of Helsinki built two web tools: one with interactive cases in animal disease patterns, the other in bacteriology. The team asked whether working through the cases measurably improved students' skills.

Students filled in tests before and after the cases across several school years, 104 for the disease tool and 191 for the bacteriology one. Both tools raised thinking skills and broader academic skills by a small but firm margin. Reasoning tests and graded written answers both improved. The authors present the cases as a working model for digital teaching in veterinary schools.
pmc-12743680:
Jérémy Mercier and co-authors review in 2025 how to watch for prostate cancer return after a focused ultrasound treatment. The treatment, called HIFU, blasts the tumor with sound waves while sparing healthy tissue. Afterward, standard blood tests and scans can miss a return, since treatment changes the gland's shape.

The review gathered eight studies from major databases. Standard MRI scans remain the norm but read the treated zone poorly. A newer scan, PSMA-PET, hunts a marker found on prostate cancer cells. It caught hidden returns with high accuracy, even when blood tests were low and other scans had failed. The authors call it a strong partner to standard checks, pending larger trials.
pmc-12749080:
Wu and seven colleagues coax a ring shaped molecule out of naphthalene by breaking its aromatic calm in twenty twenty-five. Naphthalene is a fused double ring that resists change. Adding an oxygen bridge across one ring makes a useful but fragile epoxide. A manganese catalyst modeled on enzymes did the job with a mild oxidant.

Electron poor rings gave epoxides where rich ones gave hydroxyl products instead. The swap hinged on the ring's substitution pattern. Math modeling traced the split to two distinct paths. One runs through a radical route, the other through a charged one. Such epoxides are rare catches, the team notes.
pmc-12749780:
Atefeh Tahmasebzadeh leads a team that teaches a net to read eye tumor response. Their study from twenty twenty-five deals with uveal melanoma after plaque therapy. Response falls into shrink, grow, stable, or other types.

Sound images from diagnosis were labeled by eye doctors. Labels used the response seen after the plaque care. Two deep nets were trained and scored on the task. One net beat the other on a mean score across classes. It also led on each response class in the checks. Early response guesses could shape follow up care.
pmc-12750580:
Catherine Giroux and co-authors validate a questionnaire on learning health systems in a study from two thousand twenty-five. A learning health system joins care, data, and research so practice improves continuously. Organizations need a way to judge their readiness before adopting the approach.

Experts from Canada and abroad rated draft items over three Delphi rounds, checking importance, relevance, and clarity. The final tool holds sixty-eight items in four domains, covering the path from performance data to knowledge and back to performance, plus core values. Many items were revised or dropped along the way. The authors say the measure can gauge readiness, and they call for tests of its measurement quality.
pmc-12753780:
Qingshan Li and four co-authors screen for key genes tied to a fresh cell death form in psoriasis. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Psoriasis drives skin cell overgrowth, and the death form, called disulfidptosis, may play a part. Gene web tools sifted a past data set for gene groups tied to the ill.

One gene group tied to the ill most, and six hub genes were named. Three of them ran high in sick skin and stood as driver genes. One, SLC7A11, steered free sulfur marks and a flare path in lab tests. Skin stain, blot, and gene checks backed the finds. The team flags the three as marks for tests and cures.
pmc-12764880:
Salniccia and five co-authors test nerve gliding therapy after brain injury, in work from twenty twenty-five. Acquired brain injury can stiffen and weaken an arm, limiting daily tasks. Neurodynamics, gentle nerve movement methods, help muscles and nerves in other groups, so benefit was plausible here.

Twenty-four patients were split evenly in a blinded randomized trial. One group got one session of median nerve neurodynamics. The other got a placebo session. Tests right after measured grip strength, spasticity, pain, joint range, and muscle electrical activity. A single session design shows instant effects only, a first step before longer programs are tested.
pmc-12767380:
Tianyue Zhang and co-authors probe how failing cell power plants and immune cells drive diabetic kidney disease. The disease is a grave side effect of diabetes, shaped by many forces. Which forces cause it, rather than just track it, was unclear. The team used a gene-based method that mimics a trial, plus single-cell gene reads from kidney tissue. They also checked blood cells from patients for changed genes.

Some power plant genes raised the risk of the disease, while others lowered it. Certain immune cell traits carried part of the harm from weak power plants to the kidney. In sick kidneys, key genes fell in filter and tube cells, and immune cells moved in. Blood cells showed raised genes tied to swelling. The named genes and cell paths offer new drug targets.
pmc-12768680:
Aléxia Vieira and four co-authors report a study coded OP66, published in twenty twenty-five. They looked at how well reports in Brazil say that patients and the public took part. The reports came from CONITEC, the national group that decides which new health tools public care will pay for. The years covered were twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-four.

The team read the reports again and checked them with a short guide called GRIPP2-SF. That guide has five items and is meant to lift the quality of such reporting. Patient input is valued more and more around the world, but it stays hard to do well in Brazil. Readers learn how the reports were sorted and what the checks can show.
pmc-12770480:
Sayantan Mondal, Agustín Mangiarotti, Rumiana Dimova, and Qiang Cui study how protein droplets reshape cell-like membranes in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Disordered proteins can condense into droplets that stick to membranes and bend them. The details of that touching interface were incomplete.

Using microscopy, light-based chemistry probes, and two simulation styles, the team watched a simple droplet pair meet artificial membranes. Stickiness could be tuned by the membrane's charged lipid share, and a contact angle measured it in both lab and computer. The membrane under the droplet flowed about half as fast, because lipids crowded there and packed tighter. Local lipid sorting also appeared where droplet met membrane. The framework joins experiment and simulation cleanly.
pmc-12776180:
Amanda Herrmann, Christopher Grant, and Lyudmila Bazhenova review targeted treatment for a lung cancer gene pathway in a 2025 article. Changes in the MET gene can drive non small cell lung cancer on their own or help it resist other drugs. The review covers the last decade of work on this pathway.

Four kinds of MET change are covered: a skipped gene segment, extra gene copies, excess protein, and gene fusions. For each, the authors sum up how it is detected and classified. Treatment options include blocking drugs, antibodies, dual target antibodies, and drug carrying antibodies. Approved options remain limited, and the authors map key challenges and future directions for the field.
pmc-12785080:
Deo Ruhagazi and eight co-authors track cranes returned to the wild in Rwanda, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. The grey crowned crane is endangered, hurt by habitat loss, disturbance, and illegal capture. An amnesty freed hundreds of pet cranes, and many were healed and released into Akagera National Park.

The team fitted twenty-one cranes with satellite trackers, mixing released birds with wild ones. Released cranes wandered far less than wild cranes. Few left the release area, and those that did left much later. Their home ranges and longest trips were far smaller. The authors link this to feeding by keepers and long years in cages. Staying put may aid short-term survival, but the team urges long-term checks on survival and breeding.
pmc-12785180:
Mengyi Jiang and Meixiang Zhou build a simple model to forecast survival for patients with pancreatic cancer. The cancer is known for poor outcomes, so a cheap and accessible forecast tool has real value. The team reviewed blood measures and survival for 500 patients at their center. They tested cutoffs two ways, then screened the strongest factors into a final model.

Several blood values and ratios carried independent weight, including neutrophils, lymphocytes, two tumor markers, and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio, alongside cancer stage. The final model combines sex, age, treatment, stage, tumor grade, two markers, and that ratio. Its discrimination score, a C-index of 0.73, shows fair predictive power. The authors plotted risk diagrams and calibration curves to check the model against real outcomes. They offer it as a bedside aid built from tests a hospital already runs, rather than from costly new assays.
pmc-12786280:
Di Liang, Hongyu Su, and Xian Ju dissect how the pesticide carbofuran damages ovaries, combining computer toxicology with metabolic profiling in mice. Female mice dosed daily for forty-five days showed harm that grew with dose: low follicle reserves, more dying follicles, abnormal hormone levels, and ovarian tissue in disarray.

Network analysis named thirty-eight shared toxicity targets, with four core proteins showing strong binding. Metabolomics found upset amino-acid pathways. The joint picture points to hormone disruption, oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolic systems out of balance acting together. The authors offer the joint approach as a template for judging risks from chemicals around us to breeding health.
pmc-12788080:
Benjamas Klaykruayat and her team grow zinc oxide nanoparticles on hemp cloth itself, with soy protein as aid. Their study from twenty twenty-five seeks a green finish for cloth. The grains add a UV shield and germ-killing acts. Standard cloth work wastes fuel and scatters the grains in patches.

A soy protein pre-wash held the grains steady on the cloth threads. Infrared heat formed them fast and with less fuel. Close views showed round grains for the most part, with scant clumps. Beam checks showed the due zinc oxide build in the grains. Cloth so treated hit the top UV shield class. Plain hemp scored far lower. Green paths can still give cloth a strong finish.
pmc-12795680:
Willian das Neves and four co-authors study late wasting in head and neck cancer survivors in a 2026 paper. Most of these cancers are of one cell type, and survivors often suffer long term treatment side effects even when cured. The team checked one hundred twenty patients who had chemotherapy plus radiation with curative intent and no sign of disease for at least two years.

Using two standard definitions, wasting was found in about a fifth of patients by one rule and about a tenth by the other. Wasted patients had smaller arm muscle size, and most had swallowing trouble. Under the stricter rule they also had weaker grip. The authors say late wasting is common and missed.
pmc-12812980:
Chen and co-authors study how nutrient overload reshapes life in the Han River Basin in China. The basin is a key water source for the South-to-North Water Diversion Project. Human activity drives rising eutrophication, where excess nutrients fuel algal growth and strain the whole ecosystem.

The team tracked phytoplankton and bacterial communities along eutrophication gradients. These tiny organisms form the base of the river food web and signal water quality early. Their responses show which species thrive or fade as nutrients climb. The findings guide protection of a river that supplies drinking water far beyond its banks.
pmc-12813080:
Nana Cui, Haochen Yang, and Naholo Malakia Mwetuhafifa studied bus stops in Windhoek, Namibia. Their study appeared in 2025; the catalog lists it under 2026. It tests a planning idea that links homes and jobs close to transit. Most past work on the idea comes from Asia and the Americas, not from African cities without rail lines.

The team scored 135 bus stops with a model that rates both transit access and land use nearby. Most stops had stronger land use than transit access. Stops near the city center worked better as a pair, while outer stops lagged on access. The authors say the city still has time to plan ahead. No stop showed the worst strain pattern, so action now can prevent future gaps.
pmc-12816180:
Zhao and Huang asked whether regular exercise goes along with less smoking, using a large national survey of China, in work published in twenty twenty-five. Knowing why the two habits might link could help public health programs do double duty.

The study drew on the twenty twenty-one China General Social Survey and kept two thousand three hundred seventy-three valid cases. People who exercised more tended to smoke less, and the link survived several different statistical checks. It was strongest for middle-aged adults and somewhat larger for men than for women. Better mental health and stronger social support each explained part of the connection. Higher income made the link stronger still. Because the data capture one moment in time, the authors are careful to call the pattern a correlation, not proof of cause.
pmc-12818380:
Joana Rodrigues Ferreira and co-authors report a rare case of bowel blockage caused by a gallstone in a 2025 article. The stone slips from the gallbladder into the gut through an abnormal channel and lodges in the narrow small bowel. The condition mostly strikes older women with other illnesses, and its vague symptoms often delay diagnosis.

The patient was an eighty-four-year-old man with four days of vomiting, stomach pain, and inability to eat. Scans guided by suspicion confirmed the blockage, and he was stabilized in intensive care. When drug treatment failed, surgeons cut the bowel and removed the stone, and a scope later broke up remaining material. He recovered well, with no new episodes over six months. The case favors gentler approaches for frail patients.
pmc-12821180:
Zhoumeng Ying and a large team predict which children with mycoplasma pneumonia gain from bronchoscopy. Their two-centre study from twenty twenty-five uses causal machine learning. The scope procedure helps some children with stubborn lung collapse. Others recover without it, so selection matters greatly.

Scan scores were measured by an AI system automatically. Clinical and lab data joined the scan features. A causal forest estimated each child benefit from the procedure. One cohort built the model and another validated it. Benefit varied substantially between children with similar illness labels. Feature rankings show what drives the predicted benefit. Doctors could aim an invasive procedure at likely responders.
pmc-12821580:
Kieran Sandhu and co-authors chart 24 years of kidney biopsy trends in Australia. Small kidney masses turn up more and more often, and many prove benign or slow-growing. A needle biopsy can clarify the diagnosis before major surgery, yet it was long reserved for other uses. About 31,870 biopsies take place over the period. Rates climb steadily, adding about 4.9 procedures per 100,000 people overall. Men receive biopsies more often than women. New South Wales posts the largest rise, while South Australia, Tasmania, and the capital territory fall. Rates peak in the 55 to 74 and over-75 age groups. The ratio of biopsies to kidney removals also grows, matching the consensus that biopsy should guide care of small masses.
pmc-12827180:
Nancy Uriegas and three co-authors ask women athletes at historically Black colleges about food access, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Campus food settings can be thin, and athletes need fuel to train. The team explored how these students eat, shop, and cope.

Ten athletes living in dorms took part in long interviews, after a survey on energy needs. Half were food secure and half were not. Four themes emerged: dorm life, personal factors, convenience, and nutrition awareness. Students described few ways to cook, cafeteria food that varied in quality, and tight schedules that drove quick choices. Food existed on and off campus, yet many felt the options fell short for sport. The study gives schools a view from the athletes' side.
pmc-12828680:
Yipu Li and colleagues compare a radioactive brachytherapy stent with conventional plastic stents for malignant blockage of the ureter. Their 2026 initial experience report covers patients treated over five years.

Thirty patients received the new stent loaded with radioactive seeds, while forty-one received standard stents. Technical success was complete in both groups, and complication rates did not differ significantly. Local disease response at eight weeks was far higher with the brachytherapy stent. Control of visible blood in urine was also much better in that group. Overall survival was longer with the new stent. The authors call it safe and effective while noting longer follow-up is needed.
pmc-12830880:
Hyesoo Wang and co-authors examine, in a 2025 study, tiny parcels released by a friendly gut bacterium and put to work outside the cell. The parcels, called extracellular vesicles, came from Lactobacillus rhamnosus, a well-known probiotic strain. Both types looked round under the microscope, but their protein cargo differed. A heat-shock protein marked only the natural set. Across more than thirteen hundred proteins found, the natural vesicles leaned toward signaling and transport roles, while the cell-made ones leaned toward growth machinery. In lab assays the natural vesicles also fought oxidation and calmed inflammation more strongly. The authors back them as the better base for probiotic products, with skin health named as one aim.
pmc-12843980:
Jie Yu and co-authors published a 2025 study of dihydromyricetin, a compound from a vine, fed to dairy cows, and what it did to their gut microbes and metabolite profiles. High-yielding cows carry a heavy metabolic load. It wears down their defenses and sets them up for farm diseases. The team fed the compound to half of fourteen mid-lactation cows for sixty days, at a small share of the diet. Blood tests showed a rise in one antioxidant defense score. Gut microbe readings showed more of the beneficial kinds: fiber digesters and friendly commensals rose. Metabolite readings in feces and blood shifted too, with a set of named compounds on the rise. The team reads the compound as a support for the health of the cows.
pmc-12849180:
Zareen Kiran and five colleagues compared two diabetes drugs for safety during Ramadan fasting at a single center. Fasting from dawn to dusk destabilizes blood sugar, and sulfonylurea drugs are notorious for causing dangerous lows. The prospective cohort ran from March to June twenty twenty-two. Patients on stable empagliflozin or sulfonylurea regimens, alongside other standard drugs, were followed through the fast. Hospital admissions for hypoglycemia and blood sugar control were the outcomes.

The empagliflozin group reported slightly fewer hypoglycemic episodes, about twenty-seven versus thirty-one percent. Both groups improved their long-term glucose marker significantly and similarly. Women made up sixty percent of the empagliflozin group. For the hundreds of millions who fast with diabetes, even small safety margins matter. This twenty twenty-five study supports preferring the newer drug class when lows are the chief fear.
pmc-12877180:
Wanghong Shi and a team of co-authors show how lost DNA methylation wakes silent RNAs in a model plant, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Long non-coding RNAs from between genes stir when the methylation guard drops. The team used nanopore reads of both RNA and DNA in mutant Arabidopsis.

They found 340 lincRNAs switched on and 209 held steady against methylation loss. The same patterns appeared in wild plant populations. Fifty data features trained six machine learning models to sort the woken RNAs. The best model scored near-perfect precision, with methylation and jumping genes as top clues.
pmc-12888680:
Yasmine Khan and co-authors model what delayed breast cancer diagnosis in the first COVID wave may cost Belgium over five years, split by tumor subtype. pmc-12907180:

The team thus posits a flesh root for those signs in hosts.

Lime floods then harm those power bits in the chain tale. Thin pump work also drains flesh skin charge in the tale. Low charge dulls spark spread and force in hosts there.
pmc-12913580:
Hadida Yasmin and co-authors studied a complement protein at the meeting point of mother and fetus in preeclampsia, in work published in twenty twenty-five. The protein, properdin, is the only known booster of one arm of the complement immune system. Too much complement activity at that interface can harm the placenta. In blood and vesicles, though, properdin ran lower than in healthy pregnancies. Staining showed it spread through the affected placenta, pooled near knots of dying nuclei. The authors say properdin may help drive complement damage in the placenta and could be part of how this severe condition takes hold.
pmc-13085680:
Satoshi Yamada and co-authors forge a joint score to forecast relapse in a wart-like airway disease, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Records of one hundred twenty-five patients from sixteen Japanese centers split into check and test sets. Virus stains on tissue fed a new tissue score.

Three stain marks, each worth one point, formed the tissue score. Both it and the older clinic score forecast return on their own. Joined, they sorted patients into mild, middle, and severe bands with clear gaps in relapse-free time. Mild cases rarely came back, and severity eased with repeat surgery. Virus grains were seen where one stain lit up. Readers get a sharper forecast for an unruly disease.
pmc-13130180:
Daria Turculet, Shurui Miao, Kieran Agg, and Susan Perkin study carbonate chemistry in water films squeezed between mica sheets, in work from twenty twenty-six. Carbonate balance in open water is well known and drives ocean and rock processes. In tiny gaps, surface charge and fields may tilt that balance in new ways.

The team measured the force between two mica sheets across thin carbonate films tied to a bulk pool. Fits to a charge aware model showed extra push in the gap versus plain salt water. The mica held more negative charge, and screening length shifted with fluid acid level as theory predicts. Below two nanometres, water layer forces showed fine steps. The work informs mineral weathering and shell growth in tight spaces.
pmc-13137480:
Simon Flügel and co-authors present, in a 2026 paper, a sharper set of definitions for peptides inside a large chemistry database called ChEBI.
