The team built sixty-seven classes for peptides, with plain-language definitions made more precise than the old ones. Each definition also has a formal logic form that a computer can check. A method turns those forms into an automatic sorter for new compounds. Tests against the current sorting exposed clashes and gaps, and experts rated the new wording in a survey.
pmc-13138080:

The authors frame the yeast as fixing a known microbial shortfall in celiac disease. They call for clinical trials, above all for patients who stay ill on a gluten-free diet.
pmc-13146580:
Nicoletta Brunelli and nine colleagues studied a blood cell condition that may shape stroke risk and damage. The condition, shortened to CHIP, arises when blood stem cells gain mutations with age. It linked most with the stroke type caused by clots from the heart. One gene's mutations appeared only in that group. Larger mutation shares went with larger areas of brain damage. The authors say CHIP deserves a place in stroke workups and future risk studies.
pmc-13152980:
Andreas Krieg, Sarah Krieg, and Karel Kostev ask whether developing an incisional hernia raises a person's risk of depression, in a two thousand twenty-six population study. Hernias after abdominal surgery are usually treated as purely structural problems.

Using a German primary care database, the authors matched about ten thousand hernia patients one-to-one with controls on age, sex, and health history. Over five years, depression was diagnosed in 18.4 percent of hernia patients versus 16.5 percent of controls. The adjusted hazard ratio was 1.12, a slight increase, stronger in women and in people without earlier depression. The authors suggest modest awareness of psychological comorbidity in hernia care.
pmc-13156280:

The team also checked the models on real hardware. Their results suggest learning tools can tune Li-Fi links well. That could make light-based networks cheaper to run and more reliable.
pmc-13157380:
Lidia Urbina-Treviño and five co-authors asked whether raising levels of the P2X7 receptor changes anxious behavior in mice, and found it did not, in this 2026 study. The authors caution that sheer receptor amount may not equal the boosted activity seen with the human variant. Under quiet home-cage conditions, they conclude, more of this receptor alone does not drive anxiety.
pmc-13157480:

The array covers a wide band, tuned for the slice the radar uses, where it wastes very little power and keeps cross-talk low. Two extra layers on top sharpen the beam, lift the gain, and shield the board from heat, shaking, damp, and knocks in harsh settings. A built copy matched the simulations well, supporting use in tough field conditions.
pmc-13158280:
Tuwani Rasengane and co-authors compare mental health in parents and non-parents at universities across sub-Saharan Africa, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. A web survey drew near twelve hundred staff and students from twenty-two universities in four countries. Standard scales scored depression, anxiety, and stress, with social factors weighed.

Readers get a counter to the guess that parenthood always strains campus minds.
pmc-13159580:

Three scenarios combine different fertility and preterm-rate assumptions. Recent years saw roughly twenty-one to twenty-seven thousand preterm births annually. Under the baseline scenario the number stabilizes near thirty to thirty-three thousand by twenty fifty. The authors urge long-term planning of maternal and newborn services.
pmc-13161980:

At age three, her gap passed 3 cm and she moved to a bone ward. By age eight, the gap hit 5.6 cm and her walk was off. Cuts from age eight to past 14 used rods, pins, and bone trims. Three-part walk scans guided the work, and the gap shrank to under 1 cm.
pmc-13163080:

After full adjustment, tissue fat itself, rather than the metabolic label, kept the survival link. The benefit was clearest in patients without cirrhosis. Masld patients also died less from liver causes. The authors advise factoring fat and scarring into risk plans.
pmc-13175880:
Ying Yang, Yan Zhu, Dongmei Feng, and Xiaoqun Wang study a blood ratio and a diabetes-linked eye ill. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The ill, diabetic macular edema, swells the centre of the retina and can harm sight. Body-wide swelling and immune imbalance may play a part in its growth.

Their ratio joins a count of lymphocytes to the level of a good cholesterol carrier. In past cases at one hospital, those with the eye ill had a lower ratio than those without. The link held after other factors were held in check. Those in the lowest ratio group had the eye ill far more often than those in the highest.
pmc-13178980:

One writer, KMT2F, lays most of the mark there, they find. It also grips the parts of the RNA make machine in tests. Loss of the mark sours the gene land and halts the reads. The writer helps the start kit form, they show.
pmc-13184180:
Chelouati and thirteen co-authors profile a juniper shrub long used in folk medicine, testing leaf and fruit extracts in dishes, animals, and computer models. Lab chemistry found both extracts rich in plant phenols, with ferulic acid on top. Safety tests in rodents showed no clear harm at the doses used.

The leaf extract eased inflammation nearly as well as a standard drug, at 94 percent against diclofenac's 97. Pain relief reached about three quarters of a reference drug's effect. The extracts also fought oxidation and slowed bacteria and fungi in dishes. Docking simulations showed the compounds binding stably to enzyme targets.
pmc-13189080:
Fanjing Wang and co-authors review targets for therapy, how drugs work, and ways to bring drugs to the body, for diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Their 2026 review covers a state that is common in diabetes, and that leaves people weak and in pain.

Standard drugs most of all ease the signs of the disease. First-line drugs for pain give a gain that is no more than moderate. Natural products such as resveratrol and ginkgo show power to fight oxidation and swelling. But the proof for them is, for the most part, from work done before trials in people. The team also surveys new therapies aimed at set targets, and delivery systems based on nanocarriers. Those may lift how much of a drug the body can use. They stress two gaps: no treatments change the course of the disease, and proof from trials of high quality is thin.
pmc-13190580:
Brown, McGovern, Schickle, Sharp, and Apprill studied coral microbes in this paper from twenty twenty-six. A temperate coral off the United States East Coast sleeps through winter each year. Its microbe community is thought to help manage that dormancy. The team chilled corals in the lab to trigger the sleep state.

Two coral populations were tracked through dormancy and the days of waking. Microbe shifts followed a consistent, predictable pattern in both groups. The pattern held during the sleep and through recovery. One bacterial genus, also key in tropical corals, seemed to help early rebuilding of the community. The authors suggest the tidy cycle can inform work on stressed tropical reefs.
pmc-13192180:
Nikolai Malorny and co-authors published this neuroscience study in 2026. It examines how two immune signal molecules, TNF-alpha and interferon-gamma, harm brain circuits. The team applied the signals for three days to living slices of rat hippocampus, a memory region, and watched the resident immune cells, the microglia, along with the neurons. They focused on gamma oscillations, the fast brain rhythms that support perception, attention, and memory.

The signals multiplied microglia and switched on genes for inflammation and oxidative stress. Fewer slices then produced gamma rhythms, and some tissue fired in abnormal bursts instead. Brief exposure did nothing; the damage needed time. Adding the second signal amplified the attack. Blocking nitric oxide production, mopping up oxidative stress, removing microglia, or cutting the main TNF receptor all softened the harm. The authors say the pathway helps explain brain damage in diseases from sepsis to Alzheimer's.
pmc-13193780:
Six authors present a data paper dated two thousand twenty-six supporting water modeling in Canada's permafrost country. Over half of Canada sits on permanently frozen ground, and the Arctic there warms more than three times faster than the global average. Thaw reshapes the water cycle, yet big water models often leave permafrost out.

Their dataset covers the Carcajou watershed in the Northwest Territories, a transition zone between continuous and patchy permafrost. It bundles three-dimensional geology, land cover, terrain, and surface flows, refined from national maps with local data. Modelers can build a groundwater-only or a fully combined water model from it.
pmc-13195080: Qian-Mei Deng, Jun-Hao Zeng, Feng-Jun Li, and Zi-Lan Deng wrote up a low light way to read tiny shifts, in a short note from twenty twenty-six. Fine shift reads drive chip print tools. Old light ways burn many photons, which slows in place checks. A recent team joined a polarization slope surface with two photon quantum play. Like truth came with near three in a hundred of the photons a classic way needs.
pmc-13197280:
Juan Federico Bennett and colleagues compared drone and boat lake sampling in a 2026 study. Lake checks track water health, but boats are slow and hard to use in remote spots. The team tested whether drones match boat results on three small, shallow lakes in Ireland.

Both methods sampled key measures such as phosphorus, oxygen, and acidity over three months. Results matched on nine of ten measures. Drones cost more at first but proved faster and cheaper over the medium and long term. They also reach spots boats cannot and lower risk for staff. The authors judge drones a sound swap for routine lake checks, with care on setup costs.
pmc-13200280:
Narendra Prasad Bhatta and colleagues tested antibiotic residues in chicken meat in Nepal in a 2026 study. Heavy farm antibiotic use leaves residues that feed drug resistance. Data from border districts with busy poultry trade were scarce, so the team sampled shops in one municipality of Rupandehi District.

They gathered eighty-two samples of breast meat and liver and ran one hundred sixty-four tests for two drugs. About fifty-nine percent of tests came back positive. Mean levels for both drugs stayed within the national limit. Liver held more residue than breast meat. Colistin levels ran high, hinting at ongoing illegal use despite a ban since 2019. The authors urge stronger enforcement and non-drug alternatives.
pmc-13200380:
Ayana Baidya and colleagues studied how hepatitis B virus dims a key immune protein in a 2026 paper. The complement system is a blood defense cascade, and its hub protein C3 tags germs for removal. Chronic hepatitis B infection lasts for years, yet how the virus tunes C3 was unclear.

Blood and liver samples from patients held far less C3 than healthy controls. Cell work showed a viral protein, HBx, silences the C3 gene by chemical locks on its switch region. A surface viral protein blocked the activator's needed modification too. With C3 low, cells failed to clear viral proteins through self-digestion. Antiviral therapy effects on C3 were also tracked. The silencing may help the virus persist.
pmc-13200680:
Faisal Aljahdali and a team of co-authors compared lens power formulas for cataract surgery in warped corneas. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, deals with keratoconus, a state where the cornea bulges and bends. That bend skews the math for the lens that replaces the cloudy one. Plain formulas, built for normal eyes, often miss. The team searched three databases for studies that test formula truth in such eyes.

Seven studies fit the screen. They weighed mean error, mean absolute error, and the share of eyes that land near the target. Readers who do eye surgery get a network based rank of formulas for these hard eyes. The work guides a choice that can cut blur after surgery.
pmc-13201780:
Offshore bucket footings must be leveled as they sink into the seabed, and a 2026 engineering study authored by Kunpeng Gao improves the models used to plan that process. The research article develops a simulation method for penetration-leveling of multi-bucket footings, which support structures such as wind turbines and drilling platforms.

Large soil deformation defeats conventional simulation, so the authors used a coupled Eulerian-Lagrangian approach with a temperature analogy to represent water flow in soil. Their model matched a physical experiment on a four-bucket footing and reproduced its displacement closely. The method also revealed seepage patterns during leveling that experiments cannot easily observe, aiding safer installation plans.
pmc-13202480:
María Núñez and six colleagues made new analogs of brassinosteroids, the plant hormones that steer growth. The new compounds carry a benzoate group at a key carbon, decorated with added groups of differing size and electronegativity. Activity was tested two ways: bending of rice leaf segments, a classic hormone assay, and root growth inhibition in Arabidopsis. Buildup of a signaling protein measured pathway activation inside cells.

Set against earlier series, the tests isolated the effect of one ring's chemistry. A two-hydroxy setup beat carbonyl or single-hydroxy variants. Docking math linked binding strength to the measured responses. The team could thus follow structure from first binding, through a signaling step, to whole plant response. Such maps help design growth regulators that work at lower doses in agriculture.
pmc-13203080:
Haozhen Li, Mengyu Shi, and Qiuhan Zhu follow three hundred fifty-six Chinese university faculty across six months to test whether after-hours exercise calms anxiety, and for whom it backfires. Academic work mixes challenge stressors, which can motivate, with hindrance stressors, which only obstruct. Three survey waves spanned the academic calendar's pressure points.

Earlier leisure exercise predicted lower emotional exhaustion at the next wave, and exhaustion in turn predicted later anxiety symptoms, forming a full indirect pathway. The two stressor types then moderated that chain in opposite directions, as the title's question anticipates. The cross-lagged design separates the exercise-to-calm direction from its reverse better than a snapshot could.
pmc-13203880:
Attila Nemes, Nóra Ambrus, and Csaba Lengyel read the shape of the ring at the heart's great valve in top sports folk. Their study, from two thousand twenty-six, uses a fine three-way sound scan.

Long training swells and reshapes the heart, from the pull of more blood and force. The group held just past fifty elite sports folk. They were split three ways by the still part of their sport, from low to high, all with a high swift part. The team read the ring's size and its shifts in play. They asked if those reads part by how still the sport is.
pmc-13205180:
Alma Hernández-Arias and colleagues load a hydrogel with plasma-activated water for killing microbes. Their study from twenty twenty-six builds a controlled oxidant delivery platform. Antibiotic resistance demands new ways to deliver oxidising agents. Plasma-treated water carries reactive oxygen but fades fast in liquid form.

The gel sponge-like structure traps those reactive species. It held ozone and peroxide fully for over an hour. Useful peroxide levels persisted beyond forty-five hours in the gel. Bacteria tests confirmed strong killing in the lab. The gel architecture works like a chemical reservoir. Wound care could use such slow-release antimicrobial dressings. Stability is the advance over plain activated water.
pmc-13206280:
Two laparoscopic operations for severe pelvic organ prolapse are compared in a 2026 retrospective study authored by Guanghua Chu. Both approaches were paired with the same posterior repair: the standard sacrocolpopexy, which anchors tissue to the spine, and lateral abdominal wall suspension, which fixes it sideways instead.

Records covered 132 women with advanced, multi-compartment prolapse treated between 2019 and 2021. The lateral suspension took less operating time and caused less blood loss, with no surgical failures in its group during the study. Anatomical results and quality-of-life gains matched the standard operation, and bowel emptying problems were rarer after lateral suspension at three years.
pmc-13207080:
A urine measure may predict who gains from a kidney-protecting diet, in a 2026 retrospective study headed by Ewelina Jędrych. The article follows thirty-eight patients with advanced chronic kidney disease who spent six months on a low-protein diet plus amino acid ketoanalogues under a Polish national program.

Average kidney filtration did not change significantly over the six months of treatment. Half the patients improved and half declined, and the split tracked with starting protein intake and how much phosphate they excreted in urine. High initial phosphate excretion independently flagged the improvers in the analysis, which the authors say needs testing in larger groups before clinical use.
pmc-13207880:
Depression and endometriosis travel as a pair, and a 2026 study led by Yuru Wang asks which one drives the other. Combining gene studies with cell tests, the article tests which way cause runs between several mental conditions and the estrogen-driven pelvic disease using Mendelian randomization.

Genetic risk for depression raised endometriosis risk in the forward analysis, while anxiety, insomnia, bipolar illness, and schizophrenia showed no robust causal signal. The reverse check found no evidence that endometriosis risk causes mental illness in these data. In the lab, stress-system nerve cells let out more norepinephrine and sped growth of endometriotic cells, giving the genetic result a plausible living echo.
pmc-13208080:
Tenreiro and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a broad review of NRF2, a protein that guards cells against stress. NRF2 has long been seen as the master switch for antioxidant defense. New evidence casts it as a wider integrator of cell balance. It links redox state, metabolism, protein quality, and inflammation. The pathway arose early in animal evolution as oxygen rose. The review traces that history and its modern roles in human tissue.

The authors stress that NRF2 acts like a dial, not a simple switch. Mild activation through lifestyle or environment can build resilience. They discuss its two-sided role in health and disease, including cancer. Regulation differs by species, tissue, age, and sex, they note. The review frames NRF2 as a target for extending healthy years.
pmc-13211680:
Xiaoli Wu, Xinyue Zhang, and Zengliang Ruan tested whether a chemical in cooking oil fumes can harm developing eyes, in this 2026 study. The chemical is the main aldehyde in such fumes and a common air pollutant. Its effects on eye development had barely been studied, so the team used zebrafish larvae and human retinal cells.

Larvae injected in the eye with the chemical showed dose-linked harm: smaller eyes, less vessel growth inside the eye, and tangled retinal layers. Cell death in the eye rose with dose. Human retinal vessel cells in dishes also died back when exposed. The authors warn that early-life exposure to this fume chemical may pose a real risk to eye development.
pmc-13212680:
Andrew P. Loehrer and a large team map in 2026 where new cancer cases and late-stage diagnoses cluster across Indiana. Knowing whether hotspots for different cancers overlap would help planners aim screening and outreach money.

The study placed more than 130,000 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2019 onto fine-grained maps for breast, colorectal, and lung cancers. Hotspots for new cases barely overlapped with hotspots for late diagnosis within each cancer type. Late-stage hotspots overlapped somewhat more across cancer types, and incidence hotspots for breast and colorectal cancer overlapped most. The patchwork pattern argues for place-based strategies tailored to each cancer and outcome.
pmc-13213080:
Samhitha Munugoti and co-authors recount in 2026 an extreme case of autoimmune insulin resistance in a 24-year-old man. Antibodies attacked his insulin receptors, and at the peak he needed staggering daily insulin doses while also developing newly discovered lupus.

Standard immune treatments followed one after another, including steroids, several antibody drugs, blood plasma exchange, and immune globulin, yet resistance persisted because long-lived plasma cells kept making the harmful antibodies. A drug aimed at those plasma cells finally turned the course. Insulin needs fell steadily, and seventeen months after he arrived he stopped insulin altogether with normal blood sugar control. The case argues for plasma-cell targeting when usual therapy fails.
pmc-13213580:
Syeda Sumayya Tariq, Muhammad Salman Haleem, and Reaz Uddin use in 2026 a type of AI that writes new drug shapes the way chat tools write text. Their foe is a germ enzyme that breaks carbapenem drugs, among the last strong antibiotics doctors hold in reserve.

They trained the tool on millions of known compounds. All of the shapes it wrote were sound, most passed the usual rules for drug-like traits, and few raised harm flags. The team then docked the best shapes into the enzyme on a computer and ran long motion sims. Four shapes held firm and gripped the enzyme about as well as a drug now in use. The same path could hunt drugs for other germ enzymes.
pmc-13215180:
Congcong Gai and colleagues reconstruct in 2026 how the Southern Hemisphere's great westerly winds have shifted their balance over twenty million years. These winds steer moisture, temperature, and ocean circulation, and past warm periods may preview their future behaviour.

Chemical and magnetic fingerprints in South Pacific seafloor sediment reveal where wind-blown dust came from. Until about eight million years ago the dust flew mainly from central South America, helped by a strong subtropical jet in the middle Miocene. Afterwards Australia took over as the dominant source. Climate simulations support the shift. In warm states, the authors suggest, the westerlies grow more lopsided between ocean basins, a feature future projections should capture.
pmc-13215880:
Ignas Juodžbalis and co-authors report a 2026 astronomy study that weighs a black hole directly in a distant 'little red dot' galaxy. Such compact red objects are common among early galaxies, and their black hole masses were previously estimated only by indirect formulas.

Gravitational lensing magnified the galaxy, which sits at redshift 7.04, and deep spectroscopy from the James Webb Space Telescope mapped gas motion around its centre. The rotation pattern fits a point mass of about fifty million suns and rules out a dense star cluster as the explanation. Almost no room remains for stars in the host, which suggests a massive black hole seed caught near the start of its growth.
pmc-13216280:
Sandip Mallikarjun Kale and a large team present a 2026 genomics study of hop, the plant that gives beer its bitterness. Most modern cultivars mix European and North American ancestry, yet how each lineage contributes the prized bitter acids was unclear.

The team built chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies of the hybrid cultivar Apollo and painted European or North American ancestry along each chromosome. Some chromosomes showed suppressed mixing between the two origins. Comparing chemistry and genes exposed diversity in the bittering pathways of the two lineages, and beneficial alleles from both sides added up to raise bitter acid content. The authors offer the reference as groundwork for genome-guided hop breeding.
pmc-13217180:
Pongsakornkullachart and colleagues present two case reports where Duchenne muscular dystrophy appeared together with a chromosomal condition. Duchenne dystrophy is an X-linked muscle disease caused by faults in the dystrophin gene. Down syndrome and Turner syndrome are far better known, and each rarely coincides with a single-gene disorder of this kind.

The two cases show how one diagnosis can hide or mimic parts of another. Muscle weakness, growth, and development must be read against both conditions at once. For clinicians, the reports argue for full genetic workups when a child's picture does not fit one label. For families, they show why care plans need both lenses.
pmc-13220580:
Marcus F. Johansson and colleagues interview Swedish spouses who care for partners with dementia about life and unmet needs in a 2026 study. Most people with dementia live at home, and a spouse is the one holding their life together, at a cost to the carer's well-being. Services built without hearing carers risk missing what would help.

Twenty-four spouses took part in interviews, analyzed thematically. Two themes organize the findings. The first, being consumed by caring, describes the slide from partner to carer and the feeling of confinement. The second, longing to be seen and feel supported, captures what carers ask for: acknowledgment of their situation as people in their own right, and care good enough for their partner. The couple's needs are inseparably tangled. The authors recommend professionals protect the spouse's sense of self and treat the couple, not the patient alone, as the unit of care.
pmc-13222580:
Cheng-Wei Lu and Kuo-Chen Chang write a 2026 letter raising unaddressed biases in a study of anticoagulant prevention in trauma patients. Their central concern is uneven imaging: patients given anticoagulation received far more leg ultrasounds and chest CT rechecks than the comparison group. Finding more clots in the more-scanned group may reflect looking harder, not treatment failure.

Selection bias compounds the problem, since clinicians gave the drug to older, longer-staying, higher-risk patients by judgment rather than chance. Standard regression cannot fully undo that sorting, Lu and Chang argue, suggesting matching or weighting methods instead. Blinded outcome checks and complete-imaging subgroups would also help. The letter urges readers to discount the reported event gap accordingly.
pmc-13222980:
Fabian M. Wedmann and colleagues studied heat and mental health care in Bolzano, Italy, in 2026. Heatwaves are growing more frequent and intense across Europe. Long heat exposure may worsen psychiatric symptoms. It may also raise demand for urgent mental health care. The team gathered daily emergency psychiatric consultations for three separate years. They added daily admissions to acute psychiatric wards. Weather records came from the provincial environment agency. Time-series models tested several heat measures.

Models with weekday patterns fit the data best. Adding a cumulative heatwave measure improved fit in every year. Single-day high or low temperatures did not help. Heatwave duration beat isolated heat peaks as a predictor. No yearly seasonal pattern explained the effect. The authors read heat as an independent driver of demand. They urge mental health services to plan for climate change. Early warning systems should trigger extra readiness, they say.
pmc-13226780:
Prabha M. Kumarage, Sachini Gunasekara, and Mirka Saarela describe a 2026 dataset of Reddit discussions about generative AI in education, gathered between September 2022 and October 2025. The window brackets the public launch of ChatGPT, letting researchers watch debate evolve. Posts came from 320 education-related communities, then were cleaned to strip names and details.

The release holds 984 original posts and 8,346 comments, each labelled by stakeholder group: students, educators, or parents. Each item carries details of community, time, and response counts. Because the material is openly shared with privacy care, other teams can reproduce or extend studies of how teaching, learning, and assessment are being renegotiated in public conversation.
pmc-13226880:
Thandazile Sibindi, Jennifer-Anne Chipps, and Talitha Crowley survey a 2026 study of primary-care nurses in South Africa's Western Cape on climate change and health. Nurses stand on the front line for heat, drought, and storm-related illness, yet evidence from lower-income settings is scarce. An adapted questionnaire reached 128 professional nurses across thirty-eight facilities.

About three quarters knew about climate change, mainly through television and social media. Two thirds had personally lived through extreme weather, and three quarters had treated climate-sensitive illness, especially respiratory problems. Concern and motivation ran high, but climate-friendly habits were far commoner at home than at work, and very few nurses spoke with policy makers. The authors call for stronger institutional backing.
pmc-13227080:
Israa A Serhal, Reem Al Makari, Ali Kallas, and Ghenwa K El Dakdoukii describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of a toe cancer disguised as infection. A seventy-eight-year-old farmer had a persistent sore between her toes. Imaging suggested deep infection and possible bone involvement.

Surgeons amputated with wide cleaning, expecting infection. Microscopy instead revealed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma reaching toward, but not into, bone. Margins were clear. Virus typing detected human papillomavirus type six, usually classed low-risk. Stubborn toe lesions in older patients deserve biopsy before assumptions harden, the authors warn.
pmc-13227280:
Akram Khezri and colleagues test a 2026 plant-based stand-in for gelatin in dairy desserts, made by treating potato starch with ozone. Ozone is a clean oxidising agent, and the team combined it with preheating and tuned starch levels to minimise weeping and maximise firmness. The optimised starch then fully replaced gelatin alongside carrageenan in a semi-solid dessert at several ratios.

The best blend used the highest starch level with the lower carrageenan level. Its hardness and gel strength closely matched the gelatin control, and weeping fell to control-like levels as starch rose. Tasters rated flavour on par with the original, with only small texture and colour differences. Firmness measurements showed a slightly stronger, still elastic gel, supporting the swap.
pmc-13229280:
Daniel P. Groom and colleagues resolve a 2026 atomic-scale picture of a human enzyme, hsART1, that attaches a chemical tag from the energy molecule NAD onto arginine building blocks of other proteins. In lung cancer, excess tagging by this enzyme marks immune cells for death, helping tumours evade attack. Knowing the fleeting shape the enzyme and its target adopt mid-reaction is the key to designing blockers.

The team combined kinetic isotope effects, which track atomic motion during the reaction, with computational chemistry to reconstruct that transition state. The resulting structure explains the enzyme's chemistry step by step. It also supplies the blueprint for transition-state analogues, molecules shaped like the fleeting form that should bind tightly and shut the enzyme down.
pmc-13229380:
Yan Zheng and ten colleagues found a hidden gene inside one of the most guarded genes of a mouse virus. Deep scans of infected cells had hinted at hundreds of new viral products. One, called m54.5, sits inside the gene for the virus's DNA-copying enzyme, a stretch few expected to hold a second gene. Its protein moves to the cell nucleus. There it binds the cell's own protein-disposal machine and a partner enzyme.

Adding the protein on its own froze cells at the first growth stage and piled up the disposal machine's targets. A virus stripped of the gene grew at normal speed in dishes, but fared a bit worse in mouse lungs two weeks after infection. The twenty twenty-six study shows that even a virus's most basic gene can hide a second tool, one that bends the host cell cycle to the virus's ends.
pmc-13230280:
Pedro Henrique Furst Leite and colleagues test in 2026 whether one hormone injection can replace two before radioiodine treatment for thyroid cancer. The standard plan gives two daily shots of lab-made thyroid stimulating hormone so leftover thyroid tissue absorbs the treatment. Because the drug is costly, the team tried a single shot in eighty-eight patients.

Every patient reached the target hormone level needed for treatment after the single dose. Age and body weight each helped predict how high the level rose the next day. Patients could keep taking their usual thyroid hormone pills, avoiding the strain of stopping them. Trials that follow cancer outcomes over time are still needed before the cheaper plan becomes routine.
pmc-13231280:
Cheng Zhang and colleagues build in 2026 a gene control network in blood that may help explain rheumatoid arthritis. Circular RNAs, micro RNAs, control factors, and standard genes can sponge and tune each other, shaping immune activity. Public datasets for each layer were pulled together and filtered for changes seen in patients.

Hundreds of changed molecules in each layer narrowed to a small starting network after cross-checking several databases. Lab tests in arthritic rats checked the shortlisted parts in blood, and most matched the dataset patterns. One micro RNA did not hold up and its branch was cut, leaving a tighter final network. The map nominates a focused biomarker set for follow-up, without proving that the sponge effects cause disease.
pmc-13232280:
Yiming Wang and colleagues test in 2026 how the brain keeps vision steady across the quick eye jumps called saccades. Before each jump, some vision cells shift their sensing zones toward where the eyes will land. Uneven zone sizes across the visual field raised a puzzle about how updating stays uniform everywhere.

Their circuit model predicted that true uniform updating in visual space would leave zone sizes unchanged during the shift. Updating measured in brain space instead would stretch or shrink the zones. Recordings from two brain areas matched the first pattern, with shift sizes alike for cells at varied positions. Checks confirmed zone sizes held steady during remapping, supporting a circuit that protects stable sight across every jump.
pmc-13232780:
Dimitrios Zikos and colleagues comment in 2026 on a hybrid method for mapping huge, messy literatures such as social media health studies. Classic mapping tools match exact keywords, which splits one idea across many synonyms and leans on hand-set cutoffs. The study under discussion replaces word matching with meaning vectors from biomedical language models.

Citation-aware and medical text models place papers in a meaning space, then clustering groups true neighbors without forced borders. Statistical checks come first, with large language models used later for reading and synthesis. Time patterns in the map could help judge public health campaigns after the fact. The price is a computing skill bar that many health teams do not yet clear.
pmc-13233580:
Bjørnar Berg and colleagues published a 2026 prediction study on recovery after surgery for lumbar spinal stenosis, a narrowing of the spinal canal that is a leading reason for spine operations. Results vary widely between patients, so the team built models forecasting disability and pain twelve months after surgery. Development used Norway's spine registry, with more than thirty thousand patients.

The finished models were then tested in Swedish and Danish registries covering tens of thousands more patients. Simple linear regression predicted the main disability score with average errors around twelve to thirteen points, and fancier machine learning brought no clear gain. Because the models held up across three countries, the authors offer them for shared decision-making conversations before surgery.
pmc-13233980:
Jared D W Price and colleagues published a 2026 cancer study hunting for weaknesses that appear only when a cancer switches its telomerase enzyme back on. Nearly all cancers reactivate telomerase to keep their chromosome ends intact, yet blocking the enzyme itself has disappointed. The team used a dosage-lethality screen with CRISPR and gene silencing across matched cell pairs that differed only in telomerase expression, then checked the hits in animals and patient-derived mini-organs.

One gene, FTSJ3, stood out. It chemically decorates the telomeric RNA called TERRA, keeping that RNA stable. Removing FTSJ3 unraveled the protective wrapping at chromosome ends, causing genome instability and death in telomerase-positive cancer cells while sparing normal ones. The authors nominate this RNA-editing step as a drug target.
pmc-13234080:
Danielle R Lavage and colleagues published a 2026 letter reporting a study of simpler machine learning for sepsis, the life-threatening reaction to infection. Clinicians increasingly use complex models to sort sepsis patients into subtypes, yet black-box tools sit awkwardly at the bedside. The team asked whether regression models built on Boolean logic, simple and/or combinations of yes-no conditions, could match heavier machine learning.

Their target was the delta subtype, the SENECA grouping tied to the worst outcomes and distinct treatment responses. Models trained on more than twenty thousand health records from twelve Pittsburgh hospitals. They then faced a later test set of over forty-three thousand records, plus an outside cohort of about a thousand patients. The letter frames parsimony as the prize: a subtype rule a clinician can actually hold in mind.
pmc-13234980:
Zhuangyue Lu and co-authors grew in 2026 pine seedlings in soils representing worsening rocky desertification of karst land in southwest China. Such land has shallow, nutrient-poor soil that limits plant recovery. Yunnan pine is a native tree widely planted to restore these sites. One-year-old seedlings spent sixty days in control soil or in soil from lightly, moderately, or severely degraded sites.

Growth held up under light degradation but fell progressively as conditions worsened. Under light stress, seedlings stored more soluble sugar relative to starch, a shift that may aid flexibility. Nutrient ratios differed sharply between roots, stems, and needles, pointing to nitrogen shortage overall. Severe stress lowered potassium and sodium while some other minerals accumulated in stems and needles. The authors describe a coordinated carbon, nutrient, and ion response that fails as degradation deepens.
pmc-13235380:
Jahidul Haque Chaudhuri and Dhiman Chatterjee studied in 2026 a water treatment reactor that uses collapsing bubbles to break down pollutants. Hydrodynamic cavitation forces water through a shaped opening, creating vapour bubbles whose collapse releases intense local energy. Computer simulations first optimized the opening shape for strong collapse at low energy cost. Experiments then filmed bubble behaviour and tracked removal of a blue dye.

A cloud cavitation pattern, with bubbles shedding and collapsing in cycles, gave the greatest treatment potential. Pressure swings in the flow matched closely with how much dye lost its colour. That link offers a cheap, fast way to predict reactor performance without chemical sampling every time. Energy use per litre compared favourably with published reactors at similar dye removal. The authors present the design as a strong candidate for scaling up wastewater treatment.
pmc-13236680:
Donghai Wang and co-authors studied in 2026 children in southwest China with a long-lasting bacterial chest disease that causes chronic wet cough. Lung wash samples from one hundred thirty-eight children were cultured to identify the responsible bacteria. Statistical models and a decision tree searched for factors tied to needing more than four weeks of antibiotics. Most earlier research on this condition came from wealthy countries, the authors note.

Two bacteria dominated the cultures, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae, sometimes appearing together. Pneumococcal disease independently lengthened the antibiotic course children needed in the regression analysis. A simple three-part rule predicted prolonged treatment with accuracy near eighty-eight percent in their data. The rule combined pneumococcal disease, a very high share of one white cell type in lung fluid, and prior inhaled steroid use. The authors call for more research in lower-income settings.
pmc-13237380:
Macdonald and colleagues uncover a synaptic mechanism by which the brain learns that an action made things safe. Acting well means letting the right signals reach the circuits that steer behaviour. The thalamus, a relay deep in the brain, has long been cast as the gatekeeper of outside information flowing to higher centres.

What was unclear is whether it also tracks goals the animal sets itself. The team shows a pathway that encodes the learned value of safety earned through one's own actions. That is a distinct lesson from safety that merely happens. Knowing its wiring helps explain how animals learn to repeat what protected them, a core of adaptive behaviour.
pmc-13239280:
Mario Arturo González Mariño mined the American vaccine safety reporting system in 2026 for Guillain-Barré syndrome cases after the nine-valent HPV vaccine. Reports from 2016 to mid-2024 covered people aged six to twenty-nine. He counted eleven serious cases among more than fourteen thousand adverse event reports for this vaccine and compared reporting proportions against all other vaccines.

No disproportionality signal appeared: Guillain-Barré was not reported more often after this vaccine than after others, and the statistical ratio sat below the signal threshold. Most cases occurred ten to thirty days after vaccination, more in females, and none died. Mariño stresses the limits of passive reporting: eleven cases cannot establish incidence or rule out causality questions. The result is about reporting patterns, and it is reassuring within them.

pmc-13251080:
