Twenty-nine hospice and palliative patients completed questionnaires pairing that fatigue scale with a quality-of-life instrument.

Overall quality of life correlated with total fatigue and, among the three strands, with physical fatigue. Emotional fatigue showed no correlation, and cognitive fatigue fell short of significance despite a moderate coefficient. Median scores placed quality of life at the scale's midpoint, while physical fatigue formed the largest component. The authors conclude that physical exhaustion may be the strand that matters most for how these patients rate their lives. They caution that the answer depends on which scale a clinician chooses.
pmc-13281880:
Surawach Piyawannarat and colleagues compared two kidney stone surgeries in a 2026 study. Both thread a small scope through the back into the kidney to break stones. The newer form adds suction to control pressure inside the kidney. High pressure can wash germs into the blood and spark a body-wide swelling response. The team read records of one hundred thirty-six patients at a referral center from 2021 to 2025. Seventy-eight had the standard form and fifty-eight the suction form.

The swelling response struck about nine in one hundred suction patients. It struck about twenty-two in one hundred standard patients. Suction cases also ran shorter and left hospital sooner. Stone clearing matched between the groups. Germs in urine before surgery raised the risk on their own. The authors say suction adds safety without costing success. They note the records-based design calls for a confirming trial.
pmc-13282380:
Yixi Chen and co-authors present a 2026 study identifying a new drug target in a hard-to-treat pancreatic cancer driven by a mutated gene called KRASG12D. Drugs blocking that mutation are in clinical testing, but cancers often adapt and resist them. The team found a protein, WFS1, that rises when the mutation is active and may help tumours grow and spread. In resistant tumours, WFS1 rose further, regardless of the mutation's state.

Blocking WFS1 partly restored the blocking drug's effect in resistant tumours. It did so by overloading the cell's protein-folding stress response, which then triggered cell death. The team traced resistance to loss of a protein that normally tags WFS1 for disposal, letting WFS1 build up. The authors propose WFS1 as an adaptive shield for these cancers. Targeting it alongside the mutation blocker could, they argue, extend treatment benefit.
pmc-13282480:
Sam P B van Beljouw and Li Yuping wrote a 2026 review on jumbo bacteriophages, giant viruses that infect bacteria. Their DNA genomes exceed two hundred thousand letters, far above typical phages, and their particles are exceptionally large. Some carry traits resembling those of complex cells. The review examines their diversity, evolutionary origins, shapes, and life cycles, plus how they interact with bacterial hosts.

One family, the Chimalliviridae, gets special focus for its elaborate biology. Jumbo phages challenge the notion that phages are simple, minimal parasites. Their expansive gene sets include many genes of unknown function, a frontier for discovery. The authors also weigh uses in biotechnology and in phage therapy, where viruses are deployed against drug-resistant infections. Understanding how these giants build internal structures and outwit bacterial defences could unlock new tools. The review maps a field still young relative to the diversity it has uncovered.
pmc-13282680:
Yadi Li and co-authors report a 2026 genetic study of severe short-sightedness starting in childhood in a Chinese family across generations. Early-onset high myopia is strongly inherited. Faults in a gene called ARR3, which makes a cone-cell protein in the eye, were known to cause a form affecting only females. The team sequenced the family's genes and checked how a candidate variant behaved in lab cells.

They found a new frameshift variant, a slip in the DNA code that truncates the protein. It tracked with the disease in the family and was absent from public databases. Notably, affected males carried it too, challenging the female-only pattern. In eye cells, the mutant gene produced far less message and protein signal than the normal version, supporting a loss-of-function effect. The authors class it as likely disease-causing.
pmc-13282880:
Late care seeking among older tuberculosis patients in Ningbo is measured across nine years in a 2026 analysis by Haiyan Tian's group. Delays can worsen illness and spread infection. The team looked for traits and periods linked to late care seeking.

Data covered 7,821 patients aged 60 years and older from 2015 to 2023. The median delay was 17 days, and just over half of patients delayed care. Farmers and people from poorer areas faced higher risk. Risk fell in 2020 to 2023 and was lower in men than women. Patients found by health checks had lower risk than referred patients. Targeted outreach is the main lesson.
pmc-13282980:
Iranian women recovering from partner violence joined a small 2026 trial of group support, organized by Mahdieh Khodadadi's team. Lasting harm from abuse can weaken a sense of control and worth. The trial tests whether group sessions can rebuild that sense of power.

A total of 28 women were split at random into program and control groups. The program held eight group sessions of 90 minutes each on thought skills and inner strengths. Scores for skill, impact, meaning, trust, and self-rule all rose more in the program group. Gains held at a 50-day follow-up with no clear drop. Small group size limits how far the results can be stretched.
pmc-13283380:
A glowing peptide that seeks an immune brake lets researchers watch radiation reshape liver tumors, Qingyun Lu's team demonstrates in 2026. The marker is LAG-3, a brake on immune cells found at high levels in these tumors. Focused radiation may change LAG-3 and help immune therapy work better.

The team built a peptide probe that binds LAG-3 and glows in near-infrared light. Probe glow in tumors peaked one hour after vein injection in mice. A mid-level radiation dose worked best for cell killing in lab tests. Radiation lowered LAG-3 and shifted killer T cell levels in tumors. Glow imaging plus MRI tracked tumor growth after treatment over time.
pmc-13283880:
Junfeng Ma and colleagues told in 2026 of a lung cancer patient whose treatment path changed after an immune drug flared his arthritis. The 41-year-old man had active rheumatoid arthritis and stage IVA lung adenocarcinoma with a rare EGFR mutation and high PD-L1 levels. His first regimen paired chemotherapy with an immune checkpoint drug, but one cycle triggered a bad arthritis flare, so the immune drug stopped for good.

Steroids and a slow taper calmed the flare. Care switched to chemotherapy plus bevacizumab, a vessel-blocking drug, for six cycles, and scans showed the tumour and chest deposits shrinking, then clearing on metabolic imaging. After a six-week washout, surgeons removed the lung lobe, and lab checks confirmed strong tumour regression. Maintenance therapy followed, and he stayed disease-free at twenty months.
pmc-13284080:
Beatriz Revuelta and Raynier Hernández compared public policies for Paralympic sport in 2026 across ten Latin American countries with strong recent medal records, from Brazil and Colombia to Peru and Ecuador. Reading the region through a social view of disability, they examined laws, programmes, and plans for how disability sport enters official frameworks and what support tools exist.

Most countries have formally recognised the right to sport for disabled people and built support tools, mainly scholarships and prizes for high performance. Those tools reward results already won more than they fix unequal access. The weakest points were talent spotting, clear pathways for athlete development, and attention to gender and territory. The authors urge stable systems for training and continuity over prize-led policy.
pmc-13284480:
Xuanyu Wang and colleagues report a 2026 mouse and cell study on how broken body clocks harm tooth enamel in offspring. Enamel growth follows a daily rhythm, and melatonin helps set that rhythm, yet its role in enamel mineral growth was unclear. The team disrupted light cycles in pregnant mice and tested whether melatonin could protect pups enamel.

Disruption thinned enamel, lowered its density, and left rough, disordered prisms. Melatonin partly restored those traits. Cell work tied the harm to loss of the clock gene Bmal1, weaker mitochondria, and excess JNK3 activity, which melatonin reversed. The authors name a BMAL1 and JNK3 pathway that may guide future steps to prevent enamel defects.
pmc-13284580:
Chang Seok Bang and Eun Jeong Gong reviewed in 2026 the tightrope of treating peptic ulcers in patients who take blood-thinning drugs. Antithrombotic agents prevent dangerous clots yet raise gut bleeding risk, and ulcer disease has shifted from mostly infection-driven to often drug-driven. The review blends Korean and international guidance into practical steps for acute care and long-term prevention.

Core advice includes weighing each patient's bleeding risk against clot risk, restarting blood thinners promptly once bleeding is stopped, and pairing them with acid-blocking protection in high-risk patients. The authors stress team-based decisions across gut and heart specialties. Done well, they argue, management can cut both gut and cardiovascular complications rather than trading one for the other.
pmc-13284880:
Vipin Kataria and Nitin Kumar presented in 2026 a toolkit that lets business users question company data lakes in plain English. Analysts often lack SQL skills, and earlier language-to-SQL tools suffered security holes, missed data-lake features such as time travel, and used inconsistent metric definitions. Their LangChain Iceberg Toolkit wraps the Apache Iceberg lake format with a conversational agent.

A plain-language question is interpreted by a language model and matched to business terms through a semantic layer. It then runs through a hybrid engine. That engine uses a type-safe interface for simple queries and a fast SQL engine for complex ones. Across one hundred test questions the system answered every one correctly, beating a schema-aware baseline by thirty-three points, with no successful injection attacks. Average answers took about 2.6 seconds over fifteen million records.
pmc-13285280:
Ana Cláudia Figueiredo Frizzo and co-authors study hearing brain responses and language growth in a 2026 article on children with small heads from Zika virus. Brazil faced a Zika outbreak from 2015, and infection in pregnancy caused severe nerve harm before and after birth. Hearing checks must go beyond the ear, since sound decoding shapes speech.

Cortical auditory evoked responses let the team study how the hearing pathway works in the brain. Paired with brainstem tests, they give hard data on early steps toward language in children who cannot yet report what they hear. The authors stress that intact hearing alone does not ensure language growth, so brain-level checks should guide early support.
pmc-13285380:
Dead fingers in a man on a long-used blood drug anchor a 2026 case report and case review by Angela Misic and co-authors. Hydroxyurea is a front-line pill for some blood growth disorders, and skin ulcers are a known late snag, but finger gangrene is rare. The 72-year-old had well-held polycythemia vera and took the drug for over ten years.

His right index and middle fingers dried and died without pain, yet vessel scans showed no major block or clot source, and other cause hunts came up clean. Stopping the drug held the damage steady with no surgery. Three past cases, all in legs, shared the same arc. The authors name a slow vessel harm from the drug.
pmc-13286080:
Asheley R Landrum, Nitin Verma, and Amanda Kehrberg test trust in health advice from people versus chatbots in a 2026 preregistered survey experiment. Patients now meet answers from smart systems inside the same portals where nurses write, and labels alone may not drive belief. The experiment varied who seemed to give the advice, how risky the topic was, and whether the advice felt obvious or surprising.

A national sample of 1,502 adults judged advice said to come from a human nurse, a health-tuned system, or a general chatbot. The nurse's advice won the most trust, though both smart sources still read as able and fair-minded. Advice that matched common sense beat surprising advice by as much as the source itself mattered, and the gap grew on risky topics. People wary of doctors rated the health-tuned system as more able, which suggests trust shifts rather than simply fading.
pmc-13286180:
Mesafint Amare Kebede leads a 2026 study of kidney harm after major blood vessel surgery at a large hospital in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Weak kidneys after such operations stretch stays and can end in dialysis or death, yet local proof from Ethiopia had been thin. Charts for patients treated between 2018 and 2024 were graded by standard kidney injury stages.

The review covered 377 adults, and close to one in four left surgery with some kidney dysfunction. Most cases were mild, though a small share reached the severe stage by the grading scale. Age over sixty, prior kidney disease, and diabetes each raised the odds, as did heavy bleeding during surgery and low urine flow. The authors press for sharper risk checks before surgery and tight watch on blood loss and urine during the case.
pmc-13286580:
Giuseppe Alexandre Romito and colleagues report four-year results for implants set in rebuilt jaw ridges in a 2026 follow-up study. Shrunk ridges need bone blocks before implants can anchor, and the patient's own bone has long been the gold standard despite harvest pain. Twenty patients from an earlier randomized trial, eleven grafted with animal-derived collagenated blocks and nine with their own bone, were rechecked four years on.

Only one implant failed late, in the own-bone group, and survival and success rates matched between grafts. Gum health around the implants looked equally sound on every clinical measure. The own-bone group edged ahead on two pink-esthetic details, tissue level and contour, while patient satisfaction questionnaires tied. The authors call the manufactured blocks a workable substitute, with the small headcount demanding cautious reading.
pmc-13286980:
Haoran Peng and a large team show that a family of jumping genes in wheat can still move, given the right conditions. Published in 2026, the study concerns Helitrons, DNA elements that copy themselves around genomes through a rolling-circle trick. Direct evidence of their movement in plants has been rare because cells keep them chemically silenced.

When the silencing marks were reduced and plants faced heat stress, the Xuan-Feng family woke up. The team saw fresh gene activity, circular DNA copies, and brand-new insertions in the genome. Crossbreeding and reconstruction experiments pinned the activity on one element, Feng8, as the family's driver. Active Helitrons, the authors note, could become tools for crop breeding as well as subjects of genome research.
pmc-13287280:
Dinie Qurratuaini Zulkifly and co-authors compared repair methods in 2026 for lower premolar teeth that had root canal treatment, using 76 extracted teeth loaded until they cracked. Groups covered untouched teeth, a layered sandwich repair, a deep composite core method, and a partly pre-made composite cap.

Untouched teeth resisted most force. Among repairs, the sandwich method held up best, followed by the core method, with the cap design weakest. Only some gaps between groups passed statistical checks. Work was done on teeth with careful, narrow access and intact side ridges. The authors therefore limit their preference for the sandwich method to similar low-damage cases.
pmc-13287380:
Maya Albin and colleagues review speech-language therapy for autistic children in a scoping review published in 2026. The review asks how social communication programs use the strengths of autistic children and include family views. The team searched four large databases plus gray literature sources such as professional guidance documents. They sorted the material with a standard framework for scoping reviews.

The review kept 26 articles for close analysis. Most studies spoke only about deficits linked to autism and said little about strengths. Parents' views on goals and activities appeared often, yet children's own views rarely appeared. Guidance documents, by contrast, often advised strength-based and family-centered care. The authors urge clinicians to share decisions with children and families rather than set goals for them.
pmc-13288380:
Prosun Santra and co-authors compute whether single-atom metal chains can form inside two-dimensional crystals, in a 2026 study. Mirror twin boundaries are line defects where a crystal's pattern flips. Experiments have grown chains of metal atoms along such lines in molybdenum disulfide. The team used first-principles calculations to test similar chains in related molybdenum and tungsten compounds.

For metal atoms with different electron counts from the host, settling into a chain beat scattering as lone impurities. That result suggests the chains can likely be made in the lab. Many of the predicted chains show half-metal behavior, passing current of only one spin type. A slight lattice distortion accompanies that property, which suits spin-based electronics. Some chains also split hydrogen from water in models as well as a platinum surface does. The findings widen a route toward atomic-scale devices and catalysts.
pmc-13288480:
Sixing Liu and colleagues survey nursing interns in China on engagement, confidence, and career benefits in 2026. Nursing interns are students in clinical placements who will soon join a strained workforce. The study asked whether psychological capital, a bundle of hope, confidence, optimism, and resilience, carries part of engagement's effect. Surveys went to 363 interns at six top-tier hospitals in Hainan Province.

All three measures moved together in the survey data. Interns with higher work engagement reported stronger inner strength and greater perceived benefits from the profession. A structural model found that psychological capital carried about 36 percent of the link between engagement and perceived benefits. In other words, engaged interns felt more benefit partly because engagement built their inner resources. The authors advise managers to grow both engagement and that strength. That pairing may help interns choose to stay in nursing.
pmc-13288880:
Lu Wang and colleagues lay out a 2026 protocol for a heart surgery trial. The trial will run at many centers. Silent strokes after surgery are common. Thinking woes after surgery are common too. No standard prevention bundle exists. In all, 912 people will be split by chance.

The guarded arm holds tight targets. Blood pressure and brain oxygen stay in range. Anesthesia depth and rewarming speed also count. Routine care forms the other arm. New silent brain injury leads the outcomes. Scans at seven days will read it. Thinking woes at thirty days come next. Delirium, stroke, and costs run to one year.
pmc-13288980:
Koichiro Hamada and colleagues unveil a 2026 trial plan in Japan. The trial tests a portable heart sound device at home. The device uses AI to read heart sounds. It aims to spot heart failure flares early. Home patients often lack scans and X-rays.

Two clinics in Nagasaki will host the trial. Patients will be 65 or older with heart failure. Half will get device checks on home visits. Half will get standard home care. The team will track how well the plan runs. Safety events will also be logged. The study tests fit, not final proof of benefit.
pmc-13289080:
Andreas Wagenknecht and colleagues study a new care path for belly pain in 2026. The path is called the Abdominal Pain Unit. It aims to sort acute belly pain in ERs. The team spoke with ER doctors. Talks probed what helped and what blocked the path.

In all, 36 doctors from ten ERs took part. Seven themes came out of the talks. Most doctors saw the path as a plus. It made work more ordered and standard. Junior doctors gained the most, they said. The app felt easy to use. But links to old IT systems lagged. Fears of over-testing and lost freedom slowed uptake.
pmc-13289180:
Sarah Campbell and colleagues lay out a 2026 trial plan on HIV drugs for rare tumors. The RETREAT trial deals with NF2-related growths. No licensed drug treatment exists for this disease. Two HIV drugs slowed such cells in lab tests. Their safety record is already well known.

The trial will enroll up to 16 patients. Treatment will last 30 days. A 30-day follow-up will come next. Skin tumors will be biopsied for study. Blood samples will also be taken. The main check is a drop in tumor signals. Such a drop must be clear in biopsy tissue. The phase 0 design gives a fast read.
pmc-13289480:
Asmaa AbdulHak and coauthors report a 2026 study on a drug resistance gene, blaNDM-1, in Pseudomonas aeruginosa from blood infections in Egyptian cancer patients. This germ resists carbapenems, a last-line antibiotic family, making care in very sick patients hard. The team checked how common the gene is and which high-risk clones carry it in this setting.

Fifty isolates underwent drug testing, resistance gene checks, biofilm assays, and typing, with two isolates fully sequenced. All isolates resisted many drugs, and 80 percent resisted carbapenems in testing. The target gene appeared in 64 percent of isolates and in most carbapenem-resistant ones as reported. Strong biofilm growth tied to gene carriage, and typing found two global high-risk clones.
pmc-13289780:
Qianfei Liu headed a 2026 validation study on a simple blood ratio for predicting intensive care death in septic shock with heart failure. The ratio divides platelet count by white cell count. Prior links to bad outcomes existed, but outside proof in this combined condition was weak, so a large database plus a local cohort were used together.

Discovery data held 934 patients from public intensive care databases, and validation held 124 patients from a hospital in Enshi, China, from August 2023 to June 2025. The ratio linked to death in a straight-line pattern, split into thirds for analysis. The highest third had lower death risk than the lowest after full adjustment. The same cutoff separated risk in validation.
pmc-13290080:
Peter S. Nyasulu headed a 2026 scoping review mapping vaccinology courses worldwide, with special focus on Africa. Strong vaccination programs need trained workforces, yet course supply and content had never been mapped globally. The review compared full programs and short professional trainings across continents to expose gaps in topics, delivery, cost, and hands-on practice for curriculum reform.

Eight courses were found in Africa, spread across nine named countries from Morocco to Zimbabwe in the listing. Module shares differed sharply between Africa and other continents across core topics, from immunology basics to cold chain management and advocacy. Target groups, goals, duration, teaching mode, practical sessions, and funding all varied widely. Constraints in funding recurred as a barrier.
pmc-13290280:
Federica Zanotti and colleagues review how tiny cell vesicles steer the bone marrow in health and cancer, in 2026. Extracellular vesicles are bubble-like packets that cells release with proteins and RNA pieces inside. In the marrow, they help stem cells balance self-renewal, rest, and maturation into blood cells. Signals from support cells reach stem cells partly through these packets. The review maps cargo changes as blood cancers develop.

Healthy stem cell vesicles can prompt neighbors to make growth factors that sustain the niche. Support-cell vesicles nudge stem cell fate through immune pathways and RNA transfer. Leukemia cells load their vesicles with suppressive and drug-resistance cargo instead. Those packets quiet stem cells, bend immune cells toward tolerance, and reshape the niche for tumor growth. Because cancer and healthy vesicles carry distinct marks, they may serve as blood markers and drug targets.
pmc-13290680:
Correcting for multiple tests should depend on the question being asked, not on habit, Gudrun Schappacher-Tilp and Markus Tilp argue in a 2026 opinion article for exercise physiology and sport science. Blanket adjustment has become a default badge of rigor, yet the authors say it often hides real findings.

They sort studies into three modes. If the question is whether any effect exists, an omnibus test answers it and follow-up comparisons stay descriptive. If a few directed hypotheses were fixed in advance, no blanket correction is owed. Only when researchers hunt across many contrasts for where an effect sits does explicit error control become necessary, applied through false discovery rates or stricter familywise control. Related outcomes measuring one process deserve latent-structure thinking instead of count-based penalties. The piece offers guiding questions to match method to aim.
pmc-13290880:
Laser treatment for hemorrhoids delivered gentle recoveries in a two-year cohort, Osama Elhardello and colleagues report in a chart review from 2026. The laser method shrinks hemorrhoidal tissue from inside, and the team reviewed outcomes for 77 patients, most with advanced grade III or IV disease.

Over follow-up stretching to two years, more than 90% of patients kept full symptom relief through the first year, and recurrence reached only 9.1%. Pain after surgery stayed low with little opioid use, most patients went home in a day and resumed normal activities within a week. Patients were pleased: 81% were highly satisfied and 90% rated outcomes as good. One complication occurred, an abscess under the mucosa needing surgery. Elhardello and colleagues call the laser approach a promising low-trauma option for advanced disease.
pmc-13291280:
A protein shield helps brain tumors resist drug treatment. Yue Shi leads a 2026 study of glioblastoma, a fast and deadly brain cancer. Tumors rich in two proteins, MET and YANK2, fared worse. The team traced how one protects the other.

MET adds a phosphate tag to YANK2 at one spot. That tag blocks a cleanup mark on YANK2. The protein thus lasts longer and drives growth. Removing the tag weakened tumor cell growth. A plant compound called rutin binds YANK2 directly. It curbed growth in high-YANK2 cells. Paired with the standard drug, effects grew stronger. A new drug target takes shape here.
pmc-13291780:
Dong Liu and co-authors present a 2026 meta-synthesis of qualitative research on eye injections used to treat age-related macular degeneration. These anti-VEGF injections are given into the eye over long periods. The reviewers searched five databases in May 2025 and combined studies appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools.

Thirteen studies from 11 countries, published between 2010 and 2023, fed into four themes. Patients described barriers to care and sources of anxiety, ways of coping, reasons they kept or missed appointments, and the weight of contact with their doctors. The authors conclude that psychological support, structured teaching, and smoother treatment pathways could help patients stay with therapy despite heavy burdens.
pmc-13292180:
Shira Gabizon-Peretz and Harriet M Kluger review progress in cancer immunotherapy for solid tumors in a 2026 article. Checkpoint blockers against CTLA-4 and the PD-1 pathway remain the field's backbone. Responses still vary widely, side effects bite, and tumors find escape routes. The review ranges over what is coming next, from new checkpoints to biomarker-guided approvals. Antibody platforms that both target tumors and wake immune cells get special attention.

Adoptive cell therapies, where patients receive engineered immune cells, feature alongside next-generation cytokine drugs. Cancer vaccines aimed at sharpening tumor-specific responses round out the tour. The authors dwell on open problems in resistance biology and in ordering treatments well. Dose and sequence choices can decide whether combinations help or harm. Trial design must keep pace with the platforms, they argue. The overall direction is broader effect with less collateral damage, matched to each patient's tumor.
pmc-13292380:
Liying Han and co-authors build a 2026 process for pulling high-purity flavonoids from persimmon leaves and test whether the extract guards the heart. Leaves are a farm by-product rich in these compounds. Their method pairs ultrasound-assisted extraction with resin purification, then profiles the product with advanced chromatography and mass spectrometry before cell and rat testing.

The polished extract beat crude reflux extract on content and purity, reaching a total flavonoid mass fraction of 87.78 percent in the reported analysis. Four named compounds, including hyperoside and astragalin, acted in synergy. In rats with heart ischemia-reperfusion injury, the extract eased infarction and oxidative damage by tuning oxidation-related proteins. The authors say efficient preparation plus stronger activity makes the leaf resource worth developing.
pmc-13292580:
Ying Zhou and co-authors feed a 2026 remedy to broiler chickens breathing dirty air: rosmarinic acid, a plant polyphenol, against lung damage from fine particulate matter. One hundred forty-four male Arbor Acres broilers, starting at 21 days old, split into clean-air controls, PM2.5-exposed birds, and exposed birds eating 200 milligrams of the acid per kilogram of feed for 21 days.

The supplement visibly eased lung inflammation, restoring tissue structure and trimming IL-6, IL-10, TNF-alpha, and interferon-gamma output. It also throttled the TLR4/MyD88/NF-kappaB cascade driving the reaction. Lung microbes grew richer and more even, with helpful genera such as Turicibacter gaining ground. Metabolite screening found 66 shifted compounds across tryptophan, energy, and membrane lipid pathways. The authors back the additive for poultry houses battling particulate pollution.
pmc-13292680:
Vincent Jean-Pierre and co-authors profile a 2026 biofilm study of Achromobacter xylosoxidans, an opportunistic bacterium haunting cystic fibrosis and other patients alike. Fifty-seven clinical isolates faced three lenses: a ring test for early sticking, colony counts for mature biofilm mass, and a flow system mimicking body currents. Five standard antibiotics were then tried at low and high doses.

Isolates from non-CF patients stuck faster at first, yet mature biofilm mass ended equal between origins, and early grip did not predict final bulk. Under flow, coverage matched the static mature readings. Weak antibiotic doses mostly failed to stop adhesion; three drugs actually fattened biofilms, one did nothing, and cefiderocol shrank them. On mature biofilm at tenfold inhibitory strength, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and cefiderocol cleared most. The authors offer the map for treating this stubborn, drug-resistant newcomer.
pmc-13292780:
Thays Herbst Carvalho and colleagues describe, in a 2026 letter, skin rashes seen after dengue vaccination in Brazil. The cases followed use of Butantan-DV, a single-dose live vaccine made by the Butantan Institute and rolled out in pilot towns.

Eleven patients in Botucatu developed a delayed, flat and spotty red rash that the authors class as benign. Large trials had already listed rash among common reactions, with rash in 22.5% of vaccine recipients in the first 21 days. Clear case detail helps doctors tell a harmless vaccine rash from dengue or other illness, and helps counsel patients. Real-world reports like this one remain scarce.
pmc-13293580:
Yifeng Chen and colleagues update, in a 2026 review, evidence on oral bacterial lysates as add-on care for childhood asthma. These products aim to tune the immune system, yet their value alongside standard asthma therapy needed a fresh pooling of trials.

Twenty-eight randomized trials with 2,893 children were combined, comparing standard care plus lysates against standard care or placebo. Children on lysates had fewer wheezing bouts and chest infections, faster relief, and better lung measures. Immune markers also shifted in favorable ways, while side effects did not rise clearly. Benefit looked steady across ages and follow-up lengths, with inhaled steroids possibly shaping the effect.
pmc-13293780:
John R. Talburt and colleagues present, in a 2026 paper, a metric system for comparing results of entity resolution, the task of deciding which records name the same person or thing. When the true links are unknown, standard accuracy scores cannot judge two system runs.

Their system, called CCMS, sorts every cluster from a first run into four fates under a second run: unchanged, merged, split, or overlapping. Summary counts and per-cluster detail show whether changes mean over-linking, under-linking, or deeper reshuffling. Tests on made-up people data and an industrial materials set showed the tool can track shifts from tuning or system swaps.
pmc-13293980:
Anca F Savulescu joins Renate Weizbauer, Marion Hogg, and Kif Liakath-Ali to introduce a 2026 special issue editorial on RNA detection tools. RNA does far more than carry protein recipes: it regulates genes and helps hold chromosome structure. Tracking where RNAs sit and what they bind needs sharp spatial and timing methods.

Highlighted work covers live-cell aptamer imaging, peptide-linked probes with brighter signals, and combined RNA plus protein staining in marrow and brain. A flow method reads RNA and protein in single spleen cells, while a split-guide Cas12a test finds RNA without amplification. Data analysis tools for sequencing and structure prediction round out the set.
pmc-13294280:
Yanan Wang and coauthors compare two blood microRNAs as warning signs for thinking decline in brain small vessel disease for a 2026 study. Three hundred patients were split by glucose testing into 151 with impaired regulation and 149 with normal metabolism, then grouped by Montreal Cognitive Assessment scores. Plasma levels of miR-34a-5p, tied to cell aging, and miR-126-3p, tied to vessel lining health, were measured.

Levels moved opposite ways as cognition worsened: the aging-linked marker rose while the vessel marker fell step by step. Only miR-34a-5p carried a clear mediating link from glucose trouble to cognitive trouble. At 2-year follow-up its accuracy area reached 0.803, beating its baseline showing.
pmc-13294380:
Mohammed Magdy Hamed and colleagues model future wind power in Egypt as the climate warms for a 2026 study. Big state spending on wind makes long-range output risk a key planning need. The team graded 23 world climate models against past data and kept the best three. Outputs were bias-fixed across four shared future paths. Nine turbine types were then scored.

Two turbine types led in past data by a wide margin. By 2100 the region warms and mean wind speed drops in the model runs. The worst path gave the highest heat and the lowest wind. Ras Ghareb and the south still gain under one mid-range path. Site and turbine picks can guard output.
pmc-13294480:
AbdElAziz A. Nayl and coauthors craft a phosphate-dressed hydrogel that grabs blue dye from water in a 2026 study. The base gel joined acrylic acid and acrylamide chains, then hot phosphate treatment added sticky groups. Microscopy, spectra, heat, and element checks confirmed the makeover, and batch soaks varied time, dose, acidity, salt, and heat to map uptake of methylene blue.

The dressed gel hit balance in 15 minutes, twice as fast as the plain gel, and swelled to 5590% of dry weight within 3 minutes in the reported peak. Uptake kinetics fit a second-order pattern closely. Selective, fast, and hugely swelling gels could polish dye wastewater cheaply.
pmc-13294880:
Jazia Awassa and colleagues test whether ultraviolet light boosts the germ-killing power of zinc-based nanoparticles in a 2026 study. The layered particles can harm bacteria by contact, by releasing zinc ions, or by making reactive oxygen species under light. Which route matters most was still unclear.

Staphylococcus aureus bacteria were exposed to the particles with and without four hours of UVA light. Killing rose clearly under light, and adding histidine, which mops up reactive oxygen, weakened the effect. Infrared readings and microscope images showed damaged, roughened, and deformed cells, worst under light, supporting a combined attack by particles and reactive oxygen together.
pmc-13295380:
Yao Chen, Xueli Yang, and Junfeng Mao test sleep loss on short-sight development in guinea pigs in a 2026 study. Poor sleep tracks with myopia in teenagers, but the biology behind the link is murky. Animals wearing a blurring lens were kept awake for long daily stretches.

Sleep loss alone did not create myopia in normal eyes, yet it sped lens-driven worsening clearly. Eyes grew longer, focus shifted further, and a retinal chemical balance tipped while a receptor called Sigma-1 rose. Blocking that receptor with a drug partly undid the extra worsening and steadied retinal chemistry, marking a possible treatment lead for myopia control.
pmc-13295780:
Benjamin Lond and colleagues pilot a nurse support tool for trial talks in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Only about five percent of lung cancer patients join trials, and nurses often feel unready to raise the topic. A leaflet for patients plus a poster for nurses, called Lung I-ACT, was tested for six months.

Seven hospital sites took part, four using the tool and three as comparisons, with 34 nurses answering surveys. Trial discussions grew more frequent at tool sites, and nurse knowledge, awareness, and confidence rose in step. Interviews with nurses and patients filled five themes covering format, use, and the ward conditions that help or hinder talks.
pmc-13295880:
Rahima Aftab and colleagues compare drug pairings for people newly told they have type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 study from Pakistan. Rising case loads push care beyond one drug alone. One hundred twenty patients were split into three groups of forty: an SGLT2 inhibitor alone, that drug plus metformin, or metformin alone. All were followed for six months with checks at three set points.

The paired group improved most on body measures, above all waist and hip size. Metformin alone led on blood sugar and blood fat gains, and its insulin resistance score fell fastest early on. Insulin levels barely parted among groups, while glucagon fell in all three, most in the paired group. The authors weigh the trade-offs of pairing drugs from the start.
pmc-13295980:
Yusuff Adebayo Adebisi and co-authors lay out a 2026 protocol linking disability, household set-up and COVID-19 outcomes in Scotland. Disabled people faced higher risks in the pandemic, but how living arrangements shaped those gaps at national scale is little studied.

The study will link 2011 census records to health data for everyone aged sixteen or over in March 2020. Disability type, home type and household size will be set against infection, hospital admission and death through April 2022. The team aim to show whether communal living or larger households sharpened disability-related inequalities.
pmc-13296080:
Marryam Riaz Farooqui and colleagues test wound checks by smartphone after keyhole surgery in a low-resource setting, in a 2026 study from Pakistan. Follow-up trips burden patients who live far from hospital. At a public teaching hospital, 113 adults who had elective keyhole operations sent wound photos and questions to their surgeon within two weeks of going home, through an encrypted chat service.

About one in five needed to come back in person. Of those handled from afar, just over half needed only reassurance, and the rest got a drug change or new prescription. Satisfaction scores ran high across operation types. The authors find phone-based wound checks workable and welcome where resources are thin, with most worries settled without a trip.
pmc-13296980:
Youmin Son and Yeonhak Jung track blood flow at the front of the brain while young adults move, then test their focus, in a 2026 study. Twenty-four healthy young adults each did a jogging session and a pickleball-style game on separate days. A light sensor read oxygen levels in the front brain region during each session. A flanker task, which tests focus amid distractions, was given before and after.

Effort matched between the two sessions. People whose brain oxygen rose more while they moved gained more on the focus task afterward. The game gave higher oxygen readings than jogging, yet the task gains did not differ. Each person's brain response may help explain why the mental boost from exercise varies so much between people.
pmc-13297080:
Rania H. H. Ahmed and colleagues load curcumin, a plant compound from turmeric, into tiny soft capsules aimed at sore joints in a 2026 study. Curcumin calms swelling in principle, but it barely dissolves in water and reaches tissues poorly. Six base materials were made, and the best match was formed into capsules by a mixing method.

The chosen capsules were small and even in size, and they trapped nearly all the curcumin offered. Checks covered shape, make-up, heat response, and slow release in the lab. The mix stayed stable over three months in storage and did not harm cultured cells. Gene tests backed an anti-swelling effect. Tests in animals are the stated next step.
pmc-13297580:
Shipping living heart organoids at room temperature beat freezing them, found a 2026 study headed by Cynthia Van Rompay. The team tested a commercial transport medium meant to keep human cardiac organoids alive for up to seven days, against standard slow freezing in a cryopreservation solution.

Organoids grew in size, energy content, and beating strength as they matured. Freezing shrank them, cut proliferation and ATP, disturbed beating, and raised cell death. Organoids kept at room temperature instead held stable viability and function after recovery. The authors present ambient transport as a practical option for short-term storage and shipping of three-dimensional cardiac models, with uses on Earth and possibly beyond it.
pmc-13298280:
Malnourished ovarian cancer patients fare worse after surgery, shows a 2026 database study by Lina Salman and colleagues. Using the American College of Surgeons NSQIP registry, they compared postoperative outcomes for patients undergoing ovarian cancer operations by nutritional status.

Malnutrition tracked with more complications within thirty days, including infections, heart problems, and venous blood clots, and with higher postoperative death rates as well. The authors argue that checking nutrition should become routine before these operations. They note the study cannot prove that feeding patients beforehand would change outcomes, and they call for trials of nutritional intervention in this group.
pmc-13298380:
Andreea Onofrei (Popa) and co-authors review how to spot cervical neuroendocrine carcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer, in a 2026 practical survey. Tumours can resemble other poorly differentiated growths, small biopsies may show crush damage, and standard neuroendocrine markers vary. The review integrates tissue appearance, staining markers, gene-level findings, and clinical context.

Useful stains span cytokeratins, several neuroendocrine markers, p16, and a proliferation index, picked case by case. Human papillomavirus links, most often type 18, and recurring pathway changes are summarised, though gene test results cannot yet guide outlook or therapy in routine care. A stepwise multimodal approach is recommended for consistency.
pmc-13298880:
A contrast enema both fixed a telescoped colon temporarily and uncovered the cancer behind it, describe Sumra Irum and colleagues in a 2026 case report. A 75-year-old woman arrived with two weeks of right-sided abdominal pain first treated as a urinary infection; CT showed colonic intussusception but no clear cause.

Because she was stable, doctors tried a CT-guided water-soluble contrast enema instead of rushing to surgery. The procedure undid the intussusception and exposed a caecal mass the first scan had missed, later confirmed as adenocarcinoma and removed in planned surgery. The authors present enema reduction as a selective diagnostic bridge in stable adults, not a substitute for resection.
pmc-13300680:
H Swartz and co-authors track tricuspid valve leakage after leadless Micra pacemaker implantation in a 2026 single-center study. Because no wire crosses the valve, these devices should spare it, yet long-term valve data are limited. The retrospective review covered fifty-one patients implanted between 2016 and 2025, with ultrasound follow-up at least three months later and clinical events recorded alongside.

Nearly half the patients had at least one cardiac hospitalization during follow-up, seven died, and three needed a tricuspid intervention. Valve leakage grades mostly held steady or improved: about forty-three percent were stable, and two improvement bands covered much of the rest. A minority, about fourteen percent, worsened by two grades or more. Averaged across the group, leakage did not significantly deteriorate. The authors read this as support for the valve-sparing promise of leadless pacing, pending larger prospective confirmation.
pmc-13300780:
F Klein and colleagues compare two resynchronization strategies on the electromechanical window, a timing marker whose negativity signals arrhythmia risk, in a 2026 study. Left bundle branch area pacing had been linked with lower arrhythmia risk than biventricular pacing, so the team asked whether it also repairs this marker more strongly. The cohort held 129 recipients, sixty-three paced through the bundle area and sixty-six biventricularly, assessed before implant and six to twelve months later.

Measurements were feasible in about two thirds of patients. Among those starting with a negative window, both strategies raised it significantly, and the gains did not differ between groups. Pumping function improved and chamber volume shrank similarly under both approaches. In adjusted analysis, only a negative starting window predicted improvement, not the amount of structural remodeling. The authors conclude the two strategies restore electromechanical timing to a comparable degree.
pmc-13301280:
A seaweed sugar proved gentle in a first human test, Shohei Mizuno and colleagues report in a 2026 randomized pilot trial. Twelve healthy adults took ascophyllan, a sulfated polysaccharide from brown seaweed, or a placebo daily for twenty-eight days, six per arm. Blood counts, chemistry, immune profiles, antioxidant capacity, and gut microbes were followed in this double-blind study.

No adverse events appeared, and laboratory values stayed steady throughout. Natural killer cell markers drifted in suggestive directions, and gut microbe families shifted modestly, but nothing survived correction for multiple comparisons. Antioxidant capacity wobbled between individuals. The authors frame safety as the solid finding and call for larger trials to test the hints.
pmc-13302280:
Teaching STEM with artificial intelligence lifts student results by a solid margin, Yunus Doğan and colleagues calculate in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Thirty-five experimental and quasi-experimental studies from 2005 to 2025 met their criteria across five databases. Effects were pooled with a random-effects model and probed by school level, subject, and program length.

The overall effect size came to g = 0.67, a moderately strong gain favoring AI-supported lessons. High school students benefited most, while science and mathematics edged other subjects without a decisive gap. Programs running one to two months posted the largest effects, and longer was not automatically better. Bias checks suggested the headline finding stands on firm ground.
pmc-13302780:
Two metals bonded into one plate promise strength plus rust resistance, Ziheng Ding and colleagues review in a 2026 survey of bimetallic steels. A corrosion-proof cladding metallurgically fused to a tough, cheaper base already serves marine, petrochemical, and energy equipment. The review organizes the field by how the plates are made, how they behave, and how finished components perform under load.

Explosive welding and roll bonding headline the fabrication routes, each leaving its mark on bond quality. Welding behavior, mechanical properties, and corrosion performance get their own appraisals, followed by failure mechanisms in real parts. The authors flag long-term service prediction, extreme environments, and smarter manufacturing as the open frontiers.
pmc-13305480:
Jothi Murali-Larson and four co-authors present a technique video for fixing ankle fibula fractures with a nail inside the bone instead of a plate on its surface. Their paper appears in two thousand twenty-six as a surgical technique report. Intramedullary nails promise smaller incisions, less prominent hardware, and earlier weightbearing.

Indications span open, displaced, and unstable fractures needing anatomic reduction. The walkthrough covers clamp reduction through stab incisions, guidewire and reamer placement from the fibular tip, talon deployment, interlocking screws, and syndesmosis fixation when needed. Good outcomes run near ninety percent, with driving braking normal by about nine weeks. Cortex size limits and reduction quality gate the technique.
pmc-13305980:
Yaa Yeboaa Asare and colleagues look beyond the main Buruli ulcer bacterium in a 2026 study of lesions from two endemic areas of Ghana. Secondary bacteria in these wounds may cause pain, slow healing, and resist standard ulcer drugs. Swabs from 67 samples were tested with gene-based checks, metagenomic sequencing, and culture.

Only eleven samples confirmed Buruli ulcer, while sequencing found up to forty-four bacterial genera across the set. Staphylococcus aureus was the most common cultured isolate. Almost all secondary isolates resisted rifampicin, clarithromycin, and the other ulcer treatment drugs tested. Earlier beliefs that the main toxin clears other bacteria from lesions do not hold, the authors show. Their results argue for treating wound care and drug resistance as separate problems in Buruli ulcer.
pmc-13306080:
José Márcio Fernandes da Silva and co-authors test in 2026 whether packing parthenolide into lipid nanoparticles makes it work against schistosomiasis in living animals. Parthenolide, from feverfew, kills the parasite in dishes but dissolves poorly and breaks down easily. Mice infected with Schistosoma mansoni received the free compound or the nanoparticle form.

Nanoparticles were small, uniform, and released the drug slowly, with high packing efficiency. Free parthenolide did not reduce worm numbers, while the packed form cut adult worms by roughly seventy-eight percent and lowered egg output. Empty carriers had no effect, so the benefit came from delivery rather than the shell. The authors argue that formulation can rescue promising natural compounds that fail when given plain.
pmc-13306180:
Inam Vulindlela made tin sulfide dots from three start salts for solar cells in a 2026 study. Each salt gave a named batch, and the team checked how start choice shaped dot size, light gap and cell yield.

All three batches shared one crystal form in the reported checks. Dot sizes ran from about six to nine small units, and light gaps ran from 2.2 to 2.8 in the given scale. Cell yield was best in the third batch at 7.63% in reported tests, well clear of the first two. Two side light added little gain.
pmc-13306580:
Weihao Lin built a salt sensor from a tapered fibre loop inside a ring laser in a 2026 optics study. Salt changes the fibre's polarisation behaviour and shifts the interference colour, which the laser sharpens for easier reading.

A 20-cm fibre thinned to 10.86 μm gave sensitivity near 97 pm per salinity unit across 0 to 30 parts per thousand in reported tests, close to a plain light source result. Laser action lifted signal clarity from 22 dB to about 54 dB in the given figures, and a regression model cut reading error further. The gain in clarity should help long term watch of sea and lake salt shifts.
pmc-13306880:
Ren Li embedded elevator physics inside a neural network for early wear warnings in a 2026 study. Fixed thresholds miss slow decline and wobble under changing loads and noisy readings, so the model learns hidden physical parameters while fitting sensor data.

Multi-sensor streams are time-aligned and rebuilt into features, with a dual-path method steadying acceleration estimates. Electrical and motion residual signs describe health from two angles, then a risk score grows with fault size and staying time. Tests showed stable parameter settling and useful condition grading for maintenance teams.
pmc-13307180:
Goodluck Cleophas Mushi surveyed dairy care and antibiotic use among small farms in Korogwe District, Tanzania, in a 2026 study. A total of 82 farmers and nine other stakeholders answered structured questionnaires on housing, disease and drug habits.

About 55% kept cattle under intensive or semi-intensive systems, with good husbandry, vaccination and tick sprays as main defences in reported shares. Nine diseases appeared, led by trypanosomiasis at 59% and tick-borne illness at 49% in farmer reports. Every farmer used antimicrobials, most dosing animals themselves, raising public health concern. The team urges rules on drug sale and use to curb harm to herds and to public health.
pmc-13307380:
Jianlan Hu and co-authors build in 2026 a machine learning tool that flags the risk of acute kidney injury in very ill patients with primary peritonitis. They drew one group of 329 patients from a hospital in Hengyang and a second group of 367 patients from the MIMIC-IV database.

From 15 traits, the team kept nine in a final index and tested many model pairings to find the best fit. The index scored an area under the curve of 0.976 in the first group and 0.901 in the second group, both strong marks. A free web calculator shares the tool for use at the bedside.
pmc-13307680:
Christopher Gaffney and co-authors write a 2026 editorial on prehabilitation, the planned build up of body, food, and mind before cancer care begins. Surgery and drug care place heavy strain on patients whose strength is already low, so the window before care offers a chance to build reserve.

Proof so far hints that training and food plans can cut problems and shorten hospital stays, yet sureness stays low and access stays uneven. A survey found such care offered to all patients in only 21 percent of centres, with lack of funds as the chief block. The editorial invites new work on who gains most, what dose works, and fair delivery.
pmc-13308580:
Akın Akbulut and co-authors report in 2026 anaesthetic and bleeding care for a girl aged 15 years with Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome who needed scoliosis surgery. The rare inherited state brings pale skin and eyes, faulty platelets, and a strong bleed risk, plus low white cells and heart quirks in her case.

Joint planning across blood, lung, and anaesthesia teams set the plan before surgery day for this high risk case. During surgery, a hormone drug, a clot aiding drug, and matched blood goods held a major bleed in check. She then needed intensive care and left hospital with no further snags. Early spotting and a tailored plan guard such patients best.
pmc-13309280:
Stéphanie M Swarbreck and co-authors test in 2026 how 15 named wheat varieties cope with low nitrogen on a fresh field platform, across six feed levels and two seasons of unlike weather. Yield and grain protein both rose with feed, though protein kept rising past the point where yield levelled off in their trials.

Gap in nitrogen use skill, yield per unit of feed on hand, ran widest at zero feed, which exposed inborn grit in some lines. Extra spikes, not heavier spikes, drove most yield gains as feed rose in the plots. Two Danish lines won high yield by rival routes, one via light spikes and one via heavy ones. Late feed uptake past flowering set the protein edge.
pmc-13309580:
Wubing Feng and Weiyang He build a bladder cancer outlook model in 2026 from genes involved in glycosylation, the sugar-tagging of proteins. Cancer atlas data and gene set collections supplied the material, and a shrinkage regression distilled a signature of nine sugar-related messages. Survival separation between risk groups was the test.

The signature split patients into groups with clearly different overall survival and stayed predictive beside ordinary clinical factors. One gene, ALG3, sat at the signature's centre, ran higher in tumours, and drove cancer cell growth in laboratory checks. Sugar tagging touches growth, invasion, and immune escape across cancers, yet bladder studies had largely ignored it. The authors propose ALG3 as both a marker and a drug target. Their framework gives clinicians a molecular reading to place beside staging, which alone predicts individual outcomes poorly.
pmc-13309680:
Bin Liu and co-authors sort childhood vessel inflammation into low-oxygen subtypes in a 2026 data study. Vasculitis inflames blood vessels and differs widely between patients. How low oxygen shapes the disease in children, and how child cases differ from adult ones, stayed poorly defined.

Gene activity data from public banks were grouped by low-oxygen gene patterns, yielding two child subtypes with distinct profiles. The high-oxygen-stress group showed higher activity in several immune brake genes and differed in cell-death and RNA-tag gene sets. Gene contrasts between child and adult cases were mapped to body functions. The authors suggest subtype-aware study of treatment targets, while noting the work rests on public data alone.
pmc-13310580:
Katsuhiko Shibata and co-authors report a fatal tumor breakdown crisis after a new immune drug in a 2026 case article. Tumor lysis syndrome strikes when cancer cells burst en masse and flood the blood with their contents. It is rare in solid tumors but can hit small cell lung cancer with heavy spread.

A 61-year-old woman whose lung cancer had returned with extensive liver spread received a first 1 mg step-up dose of tarlatamab as second-line care. Mild cytokine release on day two eased with steroids. On day six she abruptly developed breathing failure and clouded consciousness, and blood tests showed the classic lysis pattern with kidney injury; she died that day. The authors urge close watching and prevention in high-burden patients.
pmc-13310680:
Songbai Xu and co-authors review circular RNAs as dual regulators of iron-driven cell death and anti-tumor immunity in a 2026 article. Circular RNAs are looped RNA molecules prized for stability and tissue-specific patterns. Ferroptosis, a death route driven by iron and fat oxidation, interacts tightly with the tumor immune setting.

Loops can sponge small RNAs, scaffold proteins, and even encode small peptides, letting one loop touch both death and immunity nodes at once, a pattern the authors name dual regulation. Three major crosstalk routes are mapped in detail, with inflammatory signals passing both ways. The review weighs how loop-based drugs might force tumor death while waking immune attack, and what blocks that plan today.
pmc-13310780:
Yuanhong Liu led a 2026 study that builds a risk chart for skin cancer return after surgery in China. Cutaneous squamous cell cancer can grow back at the cut site, mostly within three years. Tools built for Asian patients are scarce, so the team searched past cases for clear warning signs.

Records covered 603 patients at four centers, split into build and test groups. Seventy seven returns were seen in follow up. Age, tumor size and depth, cell grade, and cancer stage each raised risk on their own. A chart sums those signs into one, two, and three year return odds and sorts patients into three risk bands.
pmc-13310980:
Ying Li and co-authors compare resting brain activity between men and women with Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Brain changes in the disease are well mapped, yet sex splits in inner brain function are little known. Resting scans from a large marker study were used to compare signal strength in key deep areas and the whole brain.

Women showed stronger signals in the right substantia nigra and in both premotor areas than men. The nigra split grew clear in a matched subgroup test. Right premotor strength also trended with better space skill scores in women alone. Sex split scan studies may sharpen brain profiling.
pmc-13311080:
Claudia Vaiana led a 2026 genome study of drug resistant Klebsiella in blood infections. Strains that make the KPC enzyme resist key drugs, and loss of response to a newer pairing has emerged. Pore proteins in the cell coat were suspected as drivers, so isolates and patient records were joined.

Sixteen resistant blood cases from 2022 to 2025 were reviewed, and illness was severe with high early death rates. Most patients carried the germ in the gut and had prior dosing with the failing drug, which hints at pressure driven change. Gene work flagged two pore proteins as central, plus high risk clones. Last line options were already narrowed.
pmc-13311280:
Dae Hyun Lee and colleagues report their 2026 study on whether placenta stem cells can protect ovaries harmed by fat buildup. The hormone adiponectin, acting through its two receptors, sits at the center of the work.

Rats with metabolic harm and ovary fat overload received the stem cells through a vein, and lab dishes paired the cells with ovary cells. Treated rats showed better insulin response, cleaner blood fats, and partly restored liver and ovary structure. Blocking either receptor in the dish work weakened the benefit. The findings support a fat-burning path that guards eggs and hormone balance.
pmc-13311680:
Kazuki Kagami and co-authors set out the PERSEUS-HF trial protocol in 2026, testing a full medication management program for heart failure patients juggling many drugs. Too many pills can crowd out the drugs that matter most.

The multicenter trial will enroll 300 patients taking at least five regular oral drugs and split them evenly between the program and standard care. The program reviews the whole drug list, trims needless items, and supports steady use of guideline therapy. The main check is drug adherence at six months. The design targets a real-world snag in heart failure care for older patients.
pmc-13311780:
Yi Chen and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how gut microbes may drive type 2 diabetes through inflammation and faulty insulin signaling. In the diabetic gut, bacteria that make butyrate, a fuel for the gut lining, decline, while harmful Gram-negative bacteria grow. A leakier gut wall then lets bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide slip into the body and switch on inflammatory pathways.

The review traces several linked chains: inflammatory signals that block insulin's message inside cells, inflammasome activation that harms insulin-producing beta cells, and falling short-chain fatty acid levels that disturb gut hormone release. Altered bile acid handling and amino acid metabolism add further pressure on the liver and muscles. By laying these routes side by side, the authors present the microbiota as a connected set of treatment targets rather than a bystander in diabetes.
pmc-13311980:
Holan Liang and co-authors, in 2026, present a study on autism among young people and children showing functional tic-like behaviors at a London tic service. These sudden, complex tics usually start in the teen years.

The study reviewed 63 patients seen from August 2020 to May 2022. Autism was diagnosed in 69.8 percent, and Tourette syndrome in 37 percent, both far above general rates in this clinic group. Patients with autism had more ADHD and specific learning disorders, while overall impairment scores matched those without autism. A standard assessment tool performed poorly at spotting autism here, warning clinics to assess directly.
pmc-13312080:
Tasuku Takadera and co-authors describe, in a 2026 paper, a simulation-based curriculum teaching ultrasound pulse checks during pediatric cardiac arrest. Feeling for a pulse in a child is often unreliable. Guidelines cap the check at ten seconds to protect chest compressions. Their Res-US protocol structures how point-of-care ultrasound joins the resuscitation sequence. The curriculum trains teams to use it before real arrests demand it.

Training ran in simulation, the natural setting for a rare, high-stakes event. Judging by the authors' summary of the evaluation, the curriculum improved how accurately and efficiently learners detected pulses in simulated resuscitation. Crucially, ultrasound pulse checks did not stretch the pauses in compressions. The paper offers resuscitation educators a ready framework for adding ultrasound to pediatric arrest drills. It does so without trading away the compression time that keeps children alive.
pmc-13313280:
Jill Maxwell and co-workers show in a 2026 study that a strong vaccine adjuvant can rescue weak vaccine responses in old animals. Aging dulls the immune system, a change called immunosenescence, and older people often gain less from shots even though they need them most.

The team compared vaccine types in aged mice and then in monkeys, setting each against young animals. The chief age mark was lower antibody output after shots given into the body. Adding a proven immune-boosting adjuvant, one with a record of working in people, reversed that low output in both animal types. The result offers a clear path to better shots for older adults: pair the vaccine with a strong helper rather than accept weak responses as fixed.
pmc-13314080:
Nelyta Mulyati, Ronny Rachman Noor, and Jakaria report a preliminary study from two thousand twenty-six on gene variation in Bali cattle bulls. The gene, CYP26B1, controls breakdown of retinoic acid, a signal tied to reproduction and development in cattle. Mapping its variation gives a baseline for breeding and conservation work.

The team sampled blood from ten bulls at an insemination center in East Java, Indonesia, and sequenced the gene's coding region. Six single-letter variants turned up in the roughly fifteen-hundred-letter stretch. Most were rare, with one common split; all were silent, changing no amino acid. None departed from expected population proportions. The authors conclude the gene shows low-to-moderate variation in these bulls and call the data groundwork for larger surveys.
pmc-13314580:
Oscar A. Garcia Valencia and colleagues study slow graft start after kidney transplant and its long shadow, in a paper from 2026. Delayed graft function is a frequent snag after deceased-donor transplant, yet its long-term weight was muddied by mixed cohorts and short follow-up.

The team used a national registry of transplant recipients from 2005 to 2024 and found 103,678 dialysis-dependent recipients kept on standard drugs, as counted in the report. Delayed start hit a share of 30.1 percent of them, as given, and tied to higher graft failure, with ratios such as 1.40 kept mid-sentence as reported. A mate-kidney check, pairing kidneys from the same donor with unlike starts, let them strip out donor traits. The design gives the cleanest proof yet that a slow start costs graft years.
pmc-13315180:
Ravinder S Saini and co-authors present a computer-based study from 2026 on peptides that might stop denture-related yeast infection. Instead of killing Candida albicans, the work targets how the fungus sticks to denture surfaces and builds biofilms, using two proteins tied to attachment and biofilm support.

Peptides were ranked with docking, 100-nanosecond motion simulations, and energy calculations. One peptide, tachystatin, held the largest share of the attachment surfaces on both targets, kept its hydrogen bonds, and showed steady favorable binding driven mainly by van der Waals forces. The authors suggest it could block attachment by covering key sites, though lab testing is still needed.
pmc-13315980:
Ary Serpa Neto reviews in 2026 the long debate over sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis in critically ill patients. The acid buildup links with organ failure, kidney injury, dependence on blood pressure drugs, and death, and correcting blood pH sounds logical, yet patient outcomes have stayed uncertain.

A large multicenter, double-blind randomized trial, SODa-BIC, tested protocol bicarbonate against placebo in intensive care patients on vasopressors. An earlier pilot showed the treatment fixed acidity fast. The commentary weighs whether that chemical correction turns into real clinical gain, a question that decides routine use at the bedside.
pmc-13316080:
Nathan Farner and colleagues compared in 2026 augmented reality guided knee replacement with standard manual surgery in one surgeon's consecutive series. The AR system gives live alignment guidance during the operation without the cost and workflow load of a robot, yet head-to-head outcome data were scarce.

Records covered 586 primary knee replacements from 2022 and 2023, with 570 patients in the final cohort, manual work in the first year and AR work in the second. AR cases took slightly longer, by a mean of 3.54 minutes. Thirty-day readmissions were eight after manual surgery and four after AR surgery, a difference that was not significant.
pmc-13316280:
Viktoria Menzel and a very large team report the German ProKontinenz trial in 2026 on knowledge gaps in men leaking urine after prostate removal. Most affected men do not know their surgical options, the headline message states, and missing information from doctors and partners plus symptom severity shape what men know.

This large multicenter study names information deficits as the main barrier to surgical treatment, since how bad symptoms are, on its own, does not explain why most men stay untreated. Structured, guideline-based patient information could close the gap and connect men with care that might restore continence.
pmc-13316380:
Christian P Subbe, Anne Kinderlerer, and Yogini H Jani wrote a 2026 narrative review on digital records in acute medicine, the hospital specialty covering the first 72 hours of a stay. They ask what front-line doctors actually need from electronic systems, and whether heavy spending has paid off.

Evidence for better outcomes, savings, or happier users stays modest, with gains mostly in neater notes and safer prescribing. Systems designed around imagined work, rather than real ward work, feed burnout and slow uptake. Still, good examples show change is possible. The authors call for human-factors science, tough usability testing, and design that gives the right facts at the right moment, first time.
pmc-13316580:
Axel Fenwick and colleagues, in 2026, describe a new way to study how insect muscle switches on and off, using the jump muscle of the fruit fly Drosophila. Whole fly muscle fibres respond too slowly for precise timing because calcium spreads slowly to the fibre core. Much thinner myofibrils, the contractile strands inside fibres, solve that problem.

Earlier attempts with flight muscle produced no measurable force. The team instead isolated myofibrils from jump muscle with brief gentle sonication. The strands produced active tension and showed the two-phase relaxation seen in vertebrates. Expressing a larval myosin variant raised tension and slowed activation without changing relaxation. The preparation lets researchers combine fly genetics with direct mechanical tests of sarcomere proteins.
pmc-13316780:
Martin R Fischer wrote a 2026 editorial on the uneasy marriage of research and teaching in medical schools, opening with a tennis saying that great players rarely make great coaches. Universities assume fine researchers teach well, and he asks how solid that belief really is.

Medicine adds patient care as a third pull, forming a triangle that shapes daily work in clinics and wards. Students learn at bedsides as much as in seminar rooms, so teaching quality rides on real care conditions. Education research, he argues, must study how learning succeeds inside that pressured setting while guarding safety. Keeping research, teaching, and care in balance is presented as a moving target, not a fixed state.
pmc-13316880:
Tony Vieira Faria, Luiz Gonzaga Gandini, and Lucas Arrais Campos translated and checked, in a 2026 study, a questionnaire on catastrophizing. The habit of expecting the worst was their target, in Brazilian adults in orthodontic care. Spotting the trait early, before braces go on, could tailor how clinicians talk and plan.

Factor testing gave a sound fit, and consistency scores were strong, though one shared-variance measure fell a bit under its target line. pmc-13317780:
Qingkai Wang and colleagues built, in a 2026 two-hospital study, a blood-test model that flags esophageal cancer risk before any scope is passed. Routine blood markers are cheap and painless, making them ideal for a first sieve.

The study enrolled 454 people, 198 with cancer and 256 without, between March 2021 and June 2025, splitting them into training and validation sets. Nine markers survived feature selection, and seven algorithms competed. A random forest won clearly in validation, with an AUC of 0.973 and accuracy of 0.926 in the reported scores. Low creatinine and high inflammation index pushed risk up most. The authors stress the tool guides referrals, not diagnosis, and needs prospective proof.
pmc-13318380:
Paresh C Dey and his team compare, in 2026, two keyhole techniques for degenerative spine disease such as disc herniation and spinal narrowing. Biportal surgery uses two separate openings for camera and tools, giving a wide field and freedom of movement. The Destandau method uses one port with a rigid scope, and is simpler with a shorter learning curve.

Complication rates were low and similar. Biportal operations can take longer while surgeons learn, whereas the single-port method suits simple decompression. The authors frame the choice around patient needs, case complexity and surgeon experience.
pmc-13318580:
Özge Özer and colleagues ask, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, whether a simple dry skin score might flag people with type 2 diabetes who are more likely to have eye damage. One hundred patients at a single centre had skin dryness graded on the forearm and lower leg, and complications were taken from their records.

After adjustment, only age and retinopathy stayed independently tied to the total score, with retinopathy showing a clear link in the analysis. The authors suggest the score as a cheap extra check, pending larger prospective studies.
pmc-13318680:
Lijuan Xu and Li Li report a 2026 survey study of Chinese vocational college students. They examine how negative life events relate to mobile phone addiction. Two middle factors interest them: perceived stress and psychological resilience. The work claims the first full test of their chain effect.

It did not differ by gender or home origin. Bad life events linked directly to heavier phone addiction. They also linked through stress alone, resilience alone, and a stress-then-resilience chain. The authors offer the model as a base for college support programmes.
pmc-13318880:
Zhaohui Jia, Zongzong Sun, and Hairui Zhou review, in 2026, the signalling cross-talk inside irreversible pulpitis, the painful inflammation of tooth pulp. The pulp sits in a rigid dentine chamber with little room to swell. Inflammation there easily tips into tissue death. Several molecular pathways fight or cooperate in that space.

Repair pathways, Wnt and TGF-β, try to rebuild dentine but are often suppressed. The authors assess targeted plant chemicals, gene regulators, and resolving mediators such as Resolvin E1. Smart materials that respond to pulp conditions also feature in their plan for precise vital pulp therapy.
pmc-13318980:
Junjie Xie and colleagues report a 2026 field trial of a new phosphorus fertiliser in Moso bamboo forest. Acidic soils lock phosphorus away quickly, starving the bamboo. The trial ran 24 months in a subtropical forest. It compared standard fertiliser, a biochar-based version, and one coupled with nano-zeolite.

It held less phosphorus in the hard-to-use acid-extractable pool. Microbe-held phosphorus, enzyme activity, and a key phosphorus gene all rose. Leaf phosphorus concentration also improved under that treatment. The authors credit combined chemical and biological routes for the sustained supply.
pmc-13319580:
Janis Fernandes and co-authors wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 raising doubts about a trial of blood thinning during scope care for liver vein bleeds. The trial, by He and co-authors, reported that steady thinning beat on and off dosing. It found fewer rebleeds and better survival at 12 months in people with liver scarring and a fresh vein clot.
