Main goals shifted over time with no clear public record of the change, and no prior plan for this slice was shown. Such limits make the claims early hints at best, not firm proof for care.
pmc-13319680:
Benedetta Ruzzenente and co-authors report a gene fault case in a 2026 study of a child with slow growth of skills, floppy muscles, and infant seizure spasms. The fault sits in both copies of a gene that trims proteins once they enter the cell power houses. Past cases of faults in this gene often caused heart harm and early death, so a milder course stood out.

Skin cells from the child showed low levels of the trimming protein and poor trimming of three known target proteins. Adding the healthy gene back fixed those faults, which proves the new variant caused the illness. The case widens the known range of this rare disease, from severe early cases to milder nerve led forms.
pmc-13319880:
Chisung Yuh and co-authors map links among sleep, stress, and mood in Korean dentists in a 2026 network study. Dentists face high work strain and poor sleep, yet past work lumped sleep into one score and hid which parts matter most. A web of pairwise links was drawn instead to find the hubs that tie sleep to mood and strain.

Survey answers came from 229 dentists and covered six sleep parts plus mood, worry, and job stress scales. Low mood sat at the center of the web with the tightest links, and its tie to worry was the strongest single link. Poor daytime function and slow drift into sleep bridged sleep to the rest. Fixing those two parts may ease wider strain.
pmc-13320280:
Zhi-heng Yang and co-authors pair two natural compounds into a light armed gel for drug proof eye infection in a 2026 study. A stubborn staph germ that resists key drugs causes hard corneal infections, guarded by a golden pigment shield and by the cornea wall itself. Their carrier free mix joins a light active plant dye with a root extract that slips through membranes.

Under blue light the mix bleaches the golden shield away and floods the germ with harmful oxygen forms at the same time, leaving it wide open to kill. The root part also calms the infected tissue and nudges repair cells into healing mode. In mice the light paired gel cleared germs fast and sped corneal rebuild.
pmc-13320380:
Albra Kamal and colleagues study, in 2026, reconstruction of acquired scrotal defects in a Sudanese multicentre cohort. Such defects usually follow infection or trauma and pose complex reconstructive problems. The team set out to identify causes, describe techniques and compare outcomes between flap types.

Forty-two patients, averaging about 37 years, were treated at two hospitals during 2024 and 2025. Infection caused three quarters of defects, and diabetes, present in over two fifths of patients, was strongly tied to infection-related cases. Most defects were bilateral and moderate or large. Surgeons used scrotal advancement, thigh-based flaps and skin grafts in varied combinations. Complications affected nearly half of patients, most often partial flap death and wound opening, and type of complication varied by flap choice.
pmc-13320480:
Silvia Bonardi and colleagues describe a 2026 study of cattle germs that can cause severe gut illness in people. At an Italian slaughter site, the team swabbed hides and carcasses from 150 dairy cows to find Shiga toxin producing E. coli and judge how risky each strain was.

The germ turned up on 6.7 percent of hides and 4.0 percent of carcasses, with no case where the same cow carried it in both places. Gene reading placed most of the 20 strains in higher risk groups tied to bloody diarrhoea and kidney harm. Few strains resisted drug treatment, and all higher risk strains stayed open to one drug used to slow severe illness.
pmc-13320680:
A 2026 correction notice updates a 2009 study by Daxing Xie and colleagues on a protein called DAB2IP and cell survival. The original study, in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, held that DAB2IP links two pathways, PI3K-Akt and ASK1, that guide whether cells live or die. During figure assembly, wrong Western blot images were placed in Figure 4 panels B and D and in a supplement figure, as loading controls for two proteins. Figure 4 and the supplement figure have now been updated using the original data. The corrected captions restate that DAB2IP lowered PI3K and Akt activity in treated 293 cells.
pmc-13321380:
Bin Liu and co-authors report severe pneumonia from a bird virus in a 2026 case study. Avian paramyxovirus type 1, also called Newcastle disease virus, is a major poultry germ that rarely infects people and usually causes mild illness. A 65-year-old man with severe pneumonia had handled sick backyard feeder chickens.

Gene sequencing of his samples found the virus at high share, and its gene code matched poultry strains of class I genotype 1.1.2 1b in the report. Virus was also abundant in the chickens and their surroundings, and his blood held high antibody levels. The authors warn that this bird germ can cross to people with normal immunity and urge stronger surveillance.
pmc-13322080:
Alejandra Samano and a large student team hunt the gene faults behind classic fruit fly traits in a 2026 study. Structural variants, large DNA rearrangements, form much trait variation but hide from short read sequencing. Long read assemblies for 11 Drosophila melanogaster strains were joined into a pangenome graph with fine maps of those variants.

The team traced 50 classic visible traits and found new candidate faults for 15 of them. A wing vein trait linked to a 1.5 kilobase partial gene duplication, and the century old Curved wing trait linked to a 7.5 kilobase retrotransposon breaking a muscle gene. Harmful visible traits proved rich in structural variants.
pmc-13322180:
Matia Haïm Muller and colleagues analyse, in 2026, regional differences in survival and first breeding age for white storks across Germany. These long-lived birds are ringed and resighted nationwide, giving rare large-scale demographic data. Western populations are growing while eastern ones decline slightly, for reasons that were unclear.

Records for more than ninety-two thousand birds from 2000 to 2023 were fitted with spatial capture and recovery models, using federal states as units. A model structured by migration flyway performed best. Survival was higher at every age in the west, and birds bred younger there, matching the population trends. Young birds showed the most spatial variation, and their survival rose and fell in step across regions, unlike older birds. The work ties geography to population change.
pmc-13322980:
Pamela C Guruciaga and co-authors show that boundary shape steers defects that seed fluid spaces in embryos, in a 2026 study joining theory with mouse experiments. Three-dimensional polar defects were thought to lack a clear biological role, unlike their flat counterparts.

A change between defect layouts, driven purely by boundary geometry, kept total charge fixed and did not depend on material values in their model. In mouse embryos, those defect sites matched where fluid-filled lumina first form, a step needed for later development. Pushing embryo shape past the predicted switch point created extra lumen sites near the forecast spots. The authors expect the same control idea to apply across ordered soft materials.
pmc-13323180:
Chowdhury and colleagues review the links between fruit bats, Nipah virus, and drug resistant bacteria in this 2026 paper. The bat Pteropus medius carries Nipah virus, which causes repeated fatal brain inflammation outbreaks in Bangladesh. People are usually infected by drinking raw date palm sap fouled by bat waste. The review also treats bat droppings and gut microbes as a source of resistance to antibiotics.

Searching five databases for studies from 2006 to 2025, the authors found resistant Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Staphylococcus in these bat populations. Roosts near farms, wastewater, and settlements may pass resistance genes between wildlife, livestock, and people. Habitat damage, urban growth, and farm expansion drive both virus spillover and resistance spread. Chowdhury calls for joint surveillance across human, animal, and environmental health.
pmc-13323580:
Dongzhe Li and co-authors review ECMO use between heart surgery stages in babies born with a single ventricle, in a 2026 systematic review. The first-stage Norwood operation carries high risk of heart failure, often needing this life-support circuit before the next stage.

Searching four databases for work from 1990 to March 2026, they kept 15 studies with 4,030 patients. Pooled ECMO use after Norwood surgery reached 18.1 percent of cases in their estimate, and hospital survival for supported babies ranged widely with no clear gain over time. Low birth weight, long bypass, valve leakage and complex anatomy raised ECMO risk. Longer runs and complications such as brain injury, kidney failure and bleeding worsened outcomes.
pmc-13323680:
Xiao-Chen Wei, Ming-Feng Zhao, Hai-Rong Lyu and Xia Xiao model antifungal dosing by blood albumin level, in a 2026 simulation study of isavuconazole against Aspergillus. The drug binds strongly to plasma protein, so low albumin, common in critical illness, can leave standard doses too weak.

Using a published population model, the team simulated four daily doses across albumin levels with Monte Carlo methods, judging success by exposure targets for immune-competent and immune-compromised patients. Low doses failed almost everywhere in low-albumin settings. Their results support 300 mg daily for immune-competent adults with low albumin and 400 mg daily for immune-compromised peers, giving prescribers a level-based starting rule to test in practice.
pmc-13324480:
Wenliang Liu and co-authors describe a new snail species from the East China Sea in a 2026 taxonomic paper. The animal was collected near Zhoushan in Zhejiang Province during a survey of local marine life.

Placed in the genus Pseudomphala, the species shows a shell with a thread below the suture and a covered umbilicus. Its penis lacks a papilla. Its central radular teeth carry 4 to 5 pairs of strong side cusps. Its outer marginal teeth bear 6 to 7 large cusps with a thin flap. DNA checks with COI sequences, run under Bayesian and likelihood methods, backed the placement. Only two other Pseudomphala species were known from the northwest Pacific.
pmc-13324680:
Reza Yousefi, Niloufar Darbandi, and Majid komijani test a probiotic against memory loss in rats in a 2026 animal study. Two insults, streptozotocin and aluminum chloride, damage thinking through metabolic and metal-related routes.

Object and avoidance tests showed both insults impaired memory and raised oxidative stress and inflammation. Probiotic feeding restored memory scores, lowered lipid damage and inflammatory markers, and boosted antioxidant defenses. Treated rats also held less aluminum in tissue and kept more healthy hippocampus neurons. The authors float probiotics as a guard against varied toxic insults.
pmc-13324880:
Ayça Seyfettin, Serap Gültekin, and Mecit Kantarcı review breast cancer imaging in women aged 80 and older in a 2026 single-center study. Data on this age group stay scarce even though cases are common.

Records covered 23 patients diagnosed between January 2021 and January 2026. About 30.4 percent were found by screening and 69.6 percent after symptoms appeared. Tumors in the symptom group were larger, with a median of 24.5 mm against 14.5 mm for screen finds. Spread to distant sites occurred only in the symptom group, at 31.3 percent of those cases. Most tumors were grade 2, and BI-RADS 5 was the top imaging class. Screening may still catch disease earlier in fit older women.
pmc-13325080:
Qianru Lei and co-authors model why boreholes collapse in soft coal seams in a 2026 study of coal-bed methane drilling. Wall failure hampers sealing and cuts gas extraction, yet the chain of causes was not fully laid out.

A coupled model joined stress, methane flow, and coal strength fields around the hole. Damage in the stress zone boosted methane movement by over 3 orders of magnitude, and sharp pressure gradients formed within 0.12 m of the wall. Plastic damage also trimmed coal tensile strength by about 14.86 percent near the hole. Once gas pressure beat that strength, slabs of coal split away. Stress drives the damage, gas drives the split, and strength resists it.
pmc-13325480:
Rafael Santamaria and team argue that chronic kidney disease itself drives polypharmacy, beyond the effect of age alone. Their 2026 letter reports a look-back watching study of 70,385 adults, in which medication burden rose with age, worse kidney function, and higher albuminuria. The striking finding was that younger adults with weak kidney function carried drug lists like older adults with good kidney function.

It mattered most in advanced disease, and they urge prevention and lifestyle change to slow progression, plus structured drug review and deprescribing in older patients to cut adverse events and improve adherence. Coordinated care among nephrologists, pharmacists, and primary care providers, they conclude, is essential to improve drug management in later-stage kidney disease.
pmc-13325580:

After matching, seven hundred fifty-six patients form the comparison set. Infections within four weeks occur more often with added cryobiopsy. Rates are near five percent versus under two percent for standard sampling alone. That gap means one extra infection per thirty-three added procedures. Weighting checks confirm the pattern. pmc-13325780:
Yi-Ju Tsai, Hsin-I Shih, Kai-Chia Cheng, and Hsiang-Chin Hsu compare body function in ambulance technicians with strong and weak movement patterns. Their cross-sectional study was published in twenty twenty-six. The job demands lifting, balance, and quick moves, often under strain.

Strength and flexibility were checked with handheld devices and clinic tests; balance and agility had their own trials. The average movement score was modest, and nearly half the group scored in the higher band. Technicians with impaired patterns showed poorer dynamic balance and less flexible muscles. The authors suggest movement screening could flag staff who need targeted training to cut injury risk.
pmc-13326180:
Fadhel Nabil Hamidani and colleagues report the late embolization of a patent foramen ovale closure device, retrieved without surgery. pmc-13326480:
Ren He and colleagues test how copper and cadmium in farm soil shape antibiotic resistance genes in a 2026 study. Metals can co-select for drug resistance in soil microbes, a risk for food chains.

Network analysis named Pseudomonadota, Actinobacteriota, and Acidobacteriota as the likely gene hosts. Path modeling gave cadmium the stronger hand over gene abundance. pmc-13328680:
Jia-Jie Chen and co-authors published this study in 2026. It names a possible drug target in pancreatic cancer, a protein called PRRG1. A low dose of warfarin, the blood thinner, cut the protein's levels and blunted its tumor drive, even in living tumors. Single-cell reads placed the protein in the cancer cells themselves. The authors propose PRRG1 as both target and marker for new therapy.
pmc-13328780:
Yun-Jeong Boo, Yeong-Mi Jo, and Da-Jung Kim review Korean studies in 2026 on combined programs that aim to improve daily habits in older primary school children with obesity. Rather than focus only on weight, the review looks at food, movement, and behaviour together. It covers work in Korean journals from 2005 to 2025.

Most programs joined food teaching, active play or exercise, and behaviour support. Children often gained confidence and showed better eating and activity habits after taking part. The reviewers judge the combined approach as helpful for health behaviour. They call for tighter program design and broader checks of results, so gains last longer and can be compared fairly across schools.
pmc-13329380:
Antoine Gekière and colleagues share a 2026 dataset on farm chemicals and metals found in food stores of wild bees. Wild bees are falling in number, and sprays plus metals are among the suspected causes. Most past exposure work used honeybee material, which may not match how wild bees forage and store food.

Bee hotels numbering 79 were spread over varied land uses in four countries of West Europe. They screened pollen stores and nearby soils for 501 pesticides and seven trace metals. In total, 92 pesticides plus all seven metals were found and measured. More kinds appeared in soil than in pollen stores. The dataset gives field-based levels to guide lab tests and to probe links between soil and bee food.
pmc-13331180:
André Luiz Girotto and team reported spontaneous regression of DISH-linked retro-odontoid pannus after occipitocervical fusion. Their 2026 case paper presents an 85-year-old man with diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis and wide cervical ankylosis, severe occipital neck pain. Imaging showed a soft-tissue mass behind the peg that lit up with gadolinium at the edges, causing brainstem compression. Over two decades, back stabilization alone emerged as the favored first-line approach, bringing spontaneous regression by stopping motion. After occipitocervical decompression and fusion from C0 to C2, imaging six months later showed shrinkage on its own. The team concludes posterior stabilization at the skull base fixes worn retro-odontoid pannus from DISH and may melt away after fusion.
pmc-13331980:
Francesca Greco and a large physics and clinical team tested a way to check radiation dose during total body irradiation of children in a 2026 study. They reviewed 40 children treated under two dose schemes and read the dose from portal images captured during each arc. Agreement scores were highest for the head at a mean of 99.3 percent and chest at 99.0 percent, and lower for the lower back at 96.5 percent and pelvis at 94.3 percent. Simulated belly swelling of 1.5 cm or more cut target coverage, while weight loss and bowel gas mattered little. Dummy tests confirmed the method catches meaningful body changes between sessions.
pmc-13332380:

The assembly spans 777.39 megabases, with 99.89 percent of it arranged into 12 chromosome-scale pieces. The team also assembled two mitochondrial sequences of 380.47 and 15.0 kilobases and a plastid genome of 161.2 kilobases. Annotation on Ensembl found 25,805 protein-coding genes. The background notes describe a deciduous tree reaching 40 m, native from France to Türkiye, widely planted in Britain and Ireland, quick to seed itself, and tolerant of drought. It is also known to hybridize with cork oak.
pmc-13333280:

Open datasets for elder care are scarce and synthetic ones are welcome, but the letter writers found the released file could mislead machine learning benchmarks.

Checking the original CSV row by row, they found 612 rows but only 36 unique ones: each row repeated exactly 17 times, matching the claimed 17 synthetic subjects. The original authors agreed an intermediate file had been released by mistake, skipping the step that varies data per subject, and published a corrected Version 2 in May 2026. pmc-13333480:
Jiao Jiang and colleagues trial light therapy as an add-on for a childhood eye allergy in a 2026 clinical study. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis inflames the cornea and conjunctiva of mostly under-tens, returning season after season with itching, discharge, and swelling that drops control only partly.

They were split by treatment choice: 27 added intense pulsed light sessions to conventional drugs, and 35 stayed on drugs alone. No adverse reactions appeared in either group. pmc-13334080:
Hao Tang and co-authors built a portable test for the SFTS bunyavirus in a 2026 methods study, joining CRISPR/Cas12a detection with simple test strips. Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome kills a notable share of patients, and labs in low-resource settings struggle to diagnose it.

Tested on 40 clinical serum samples, the method matched PCR completely, with 100 percent sensitivity and specificity in this set and a detection limit of 2.5 copies per microliter. No cross-reaction with other common pathogens appeared, and results arrive within 80 minutes, readable by eye.
pmc-13334480:

The team grew self-assembled skin substitutes at air-liquid interface with varying linoleic acid levels and measured lipid makeup, bioactive lipid mediators, and enzyme gene expression. High linoleic acid clearly improved barrier function, cutting testosterone passage, and boosted the fatty acid's entry into phospholipids and other lipid classes. Surprisingly, one ceramide family fell, matching reduced activity of enzymes that build those barrier lipids. The trade-offs give skin model makers concrete guidance on feeding their cultures.
pmc-13334880:

Other factors are advanced age, female sex, estrogen use, severe respiratory failure, and severe acid reflux disease.

The patient was a 33-year-old woman diagnosed with tracheal narrowing on scope exam nine years after initial short-term windpipe tube placement. They should also keep a low threshold for fiber-optic scope exam in patients with respiratory symptoms after tube placement, even years later.
pmc-13335680:
Yi-Chin Lu and co-authors translated and checked a learning styles questionnaire for traditional Chinese medicine residents in Taiwan in a 2026 schooling study. Taiwan's TCM training is shifting from apprenticeship to standardized residency, and these trainees straddle two medical systems.

A one-time survey gathered 217 TCM residents across the Chang Gung Memorial Hospital system. Confirmatory factor analysis of the Traditional Chinese Index of Learning Styles gave mixed support for its four-factor structure. One fit index looked fine while others showed substantial misfit, echoing earlier reports with this instrument. Joint reliability was acceptable for some dimensions. The team also profiled how learning styles distribute among residents and where subgroups differ, giving program directors a cautious tool for shaping teaching.
pmc-13336080:

Notably, extra SHM1 not only restored leaf width in the nlss3 mutant but also greatly increased grain yield and salt toughness in wild-type plants.
pmc-13336380:

Menstrual distress covers the cluster of painful and mood symptoms tied to the cycle, and it weighs on quality of life. Nurses work long shifts with chemical, physical, and emotional hazards, so the team asked whether the job itself feeds the distress.

The case-control study used standard tools: a menstrual distress questionnaire, anxiety scales, a sleep quality index, and a worksheet of workplace hazards. Data was gathered in 2024. A structural model then sorted how background traits, anxiety, sleep, and hazards connect to distress. Findings of this kind can shape shift planning and support for a mostly female workforce whose own health is often last in line.
pmc-13375780:
Tzu-Hsing Lin, Yi-hao Cheng, and Chih-Hui Lin published a fungus study in two thousand twenty-six on pigment making in red mold rice production. The mold Monascus purpureus yields valued yellow pigments, monascin and ankaflavin. A colourless albino variant appeared spontaneously, the first such report in this genus.

The albino strain grew faster but made far less yellow pigment, a threat to stable industrial cultures. Gene activity comparisons across conditions pointed to a mitochondrial carrier in the malate-citrate shuttle as a key player. Its activity correlated with pigment output and two other genes. The authors suggest tuning this pathway to raise yields. The variant also offers a window into pigment regulation.
pmc-13376080:
Haoke Li leads a large team in tracing how a fat in obese cartilage speeds joint wear. The paper is from two thousand twenty-six. Obesity-linked osteoarthritis wears joints down with metabolic upset in train, but the key molecules were unclear. Mice on a high-fat diet show faster cartilage decay.

A calcium-led kinase, CaMK2, is switched on by the fat and drives that disposal. A drug that blocks the kinase undoes the harm in tests. The chain names a fresh target for care.

Qi Zhang and co-authors published this transplant outcomes study in 2026. Safety-net hospitals serve many low-income and uninsured patients, but their results for stem cell transplants were unclear. Using a national readmissions database, the team compared hospitals by the share of Medicaid patients they treated. The study covered about 131,000 transplant patients. Roughly 31,000 were treated at safety-net hospitals and about 100,000 elsewhere.

Complications during the hospital stay were more common at safety-net hospitals. For both main transplant types, deaths in hospital and returns within thirty days ran modestly higher there. Among self-donor transplants, in-hospital mortality was 2.7 percent against 2.3 percent. Among donor transplants it was 6.5 percent against 5.1 percent. The authors stress that the gaps are small. They also note that this kind of data cannot show whether patient factors or hospital factors drive the difference.
pmc-13377080:
Ronghui Zhu and co-authors watch a catalyst's lattice breathe in real time under electric and heat drive. Tracking bond changes while a reaction runs has long been a blind spot. A fast X-ray scattering setup now resolves the shifts in milliseconds. Manganese dioxide on nickel foam served as the test catalyst for low-temperature oxidation.

With the field on, one lattice spacing shrank; with it off, the spacing recovered. Absorption spectra and theory runs explain the dance. Current reshuffles the electrons on manganese and oxygen, loosening their bond. Looser bonds wake the lattice oxygen for reaction duty. The work links field control of bonds to stronger catalysis.
pmc-13377180:
Chris Ke Bai and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on how a chemical tag on DNA packaging shapes skin formation. The tag, called H3K9me3, silences stray genes and repeats in early embryos. Its role in building organs later in development was less clear.

The team removed the tag's three writer enzymes from the embryonic mouse skin layer. Skin cells then failed to mature, the barrier never formed, and hair follicles and touch cells did not appear. pmc-13377480:
H. Mark Kenney and Francisco Tausk tell of skin ills that share one map in a 2026 case report and review. The two ills, scaly red plaques and white skin loss, are known mates since 1890. Most tales mix split and shared spots on the body.

The new case is rare: fresh plaques grew just in old white-loss zones, and in no next spot. That strict share has a name in skin craft and is a rare bird. pmc-13377580:
Athina Tousia and co-authors summed up deaths on bikes and e-scooters in a 2026 review. Two-wheel deaths take a large share of road deaths, most of all in poor and mid lands. The search spanned three data banks from 2014 to April 2026.

Watch work of three types was pooled: group, match, and snapshot. Logs held hat use, drink and drug use, wound maps, and folk facts. Finds split too much for one pooled sum, so the team laid them in tale form. Hat laws and drink laws exist, yet deaths stay high, which makes the driver list of use to road leads.
pmc-13377880:
Benhui Pang and co-authors dress glass strands to firm cold-land clay in a 2026 study. Freeze and thaw rounds crack and sap clay beds under roads in cold zones. Glass strands were coated in two steps, the next with a dust of white paint ore, to grip the clay more hard.

pmc-13378380:
Kayhan Alvandipour and co-authors describe a 2026 method for mapping the many shapes and states of human microglia, the immune cells of the brain. Microglia shift between states that affect brain health, but capturing that variety across many cells is hard. The team grew microglia from human stem cells in the lab.

They photographed the cells with two staining methods and measured each cell in two ways, by hand-designed features and by features learned by a computer. A grouping method then assigned each cell a probability of belonging to each state, which captures cells in transition. The learned features from one staining method proved most informative and matched well with signs of inflammation inside the cells.
pmc-13379680:
Arantxa A Corona Bacelis and co-authors describe a 2026 case of bowel cancer that first showed up as swollen glands in the neck. Bowel cancer usually spreads to the liver or lungs, so glands in the neck as the first sign is extremely rare. Their patient was a 68-year-old woman with no other major illness.

She had lost weight, and a blood marker for bowel cancer was markedly raised. Tissue from a neck gland confirmed cancer that had spread, and a camera examination of the bowel found the source in the transverse colon. Chemotherapy combined with a drug that blocks blood vessel growth shrank the disease steadily. Over follow-up she reached a complete clinical response.
pmc-13382180:
Zhiyang Xie and colleagues wrote a 2026 narrative review of jaw angle surgery in Asian patients who seek a slimmer lower face. Many designs for cutting the jaw angle exist, plus newer supporting technologies. Practical guidance on matching technique to each patient's jaw shape and goals has been limited.

The review, based on literature searched to the end of 2025, explains how techniques differ in where the cut starts, ends, and runs. A long curved cut remains common for prominent angles, while other designs suit different bone and soft-tissue features. The authors stress that endpoints should include appearance and function, not bone removal alone, and they discuss complications and long-term bone remodelling.
pmc-13382580:
Kalvis Brangulis published a 2026 study of the machinery that builds the outer membrane of the Lyme disease bacterium. Gram-negative bacteria insert barrel-shaped proteins into their outer membrane using an assembly machine. In the well-studied gut bacterium that machine has five parts, but in this spirochete it is simpler, with only three.

Modelling predicted how the three parts fit together into a closed ring shape unlike the arrangement in other bacteria, and measurements confirmed which parts bind and where. Crystal structures of pieces of the main component showed its flexibility. A partner system appears fused with the main machine here. The map helps explain how this pathogen builds its surface.
pmc-13383080:
Gutierrez and colleagues study how Lake Baikal's sculpin fishes lightened their skeletons to leave the floor for water, in 2026 evolutionary morphology research. Sculpins lack swim bladders, so buoyancy must come from the body. Two Baikal genera independently became mid-water swimmers. Using micro-CT scanning and shape analysis across ten species, six bottom-dwelling, two intermediate, and two pelagic, the team measured bone mineral density, porosity, and thickness. They compared body shapes between habitat groups.

Reductions in skeletal density evolved independently in the pelagic and intermediate lineages, with mineral density showing the most consistent drops. Reductions spread through the skull, and the jaws, though the densest bones, showed the greatest change: a 56.86 percent decrease in mineral percentage and a 21.39 percent increase in porosity in pelagic species. Bodies shifted toward elongation, smaller eyes, and higher fin placement. Gutierrez reads the pattern as predictable evolution under the physics of floating.
pmc-13383480:
Jingyu Yan's team built a cell-powerhouse-targeted gel to regrow bone in diabetes-linked gum disease, in a 2026 study. Diabetes-linked gum disease mixes metabolic disorder with chronic swelling, failing mitochondria, excess reactive oxygen species, and weak bone metabolism. The team combined antioxidant, mitochondria-targeting, and regenerative functions in one injectable system.

A manganese-zinc-tannic acid enzyme mimic carrying the SS31 peptide was set in a heat-sensitive PLGA-PEG-PLGA gel. The mimic acts like superoxide dismutase and catalase to clear reactive oxygen, while SS31 guides it into mitochondria to restore energy production. In animals, the gel curbed jaw bone loss, grew new bone, and shifted immune cells toward repair.
pmc-13385880:
Rui Yan and co-authors build a chart that predicts heart-related death in young Hodgkin lymphoma patients. As cure rates rise, heart disease has become a top cause of later death in this group. Data came from a national cancer registry, split into training and check sets. A competing risk model weighed heart death against death from the cancer itself.

Risk rose with Black race, male sex, older age, early diagnosis years, and radiation care. The chart scores fifteen and twenty-five year risk from six inputs, adding stage to that list. Checks showed strong sorting power and sound calibration of the scores. Use tests backed its worth for clinic choices. The authors offer it as a guide for long-term heart watch.
pmc-13389880:
Mao and colleagues test whether the ITIH cluster, a schizophrenia-associated region on chromosome 3, also confers risk in Japanese patients, in 2026 genetics research. Schizophrenia affects 1 percent of people, with heritability estimated at 60 to 85 percent. Genome-wide studies in Europeans implicate these inter-alpha-trypsin inhibitor genes, which surface in bipolar illness. The team ran a case-control study and haplotype analysis of variants, then resequenced the ITIH1 gene hunting damaging changes and modeled their effects on the protein.

A difference in frequencies appeared for a window combining rs2710322 and rs1042779. Resequencing found 4 harmful variants in ITIH1 whose predicted effects could destabilize the protein. Effects were modest, as expected, and the authors frame the result as supportive rather than decisive. Mao suggests ITIH1 may contribute in Japanese patients, extending a European signal across groups, and nominates the gene for functional follow-up.
pmc-13391480:
Zhilin Zhang and a large team build, in 2026, a tough hydrogel that can both move heavy loads and sense its own motion. Soft gels usually force a trade-off between strength and response speed, limiting their use as artificial muscles.

A cascade polymerisation strategy toughens the multiphase gel so it can bear loads while still actuating quickly. The team also derived a coding law linking mass and deformation. The gel can thus encode binary information through its movement. They built logic-gate units too. Those units close a loop from light trigger to signal, processing, and robotic action. Soft robotics engineers gain a material that unites muscle, sensor, and simple logic in one body.
pmc-13392180:
Edel Ryan's team used a three-round Delphi study with twenty-two global experts to create best-practice guidance for including children with autism in local body play sessions. Children with autism are less active than peers, and barriers are well shown, but methods to overcome them needed a shared view.

Sixteen shared-view statements, agreed at sixty-seven percent or higher, formed the STARTS guidance covering skill growth, coach and volunteer training, session aims, resources, bridging-to-mainstream moves, and welcome supports. Clubs can use STARTS when setting up or adapting sessions so children with autism join in fully.
pmc-13393480:
Muayad Saud Albadrani reviews research on climate change and women's reproductive and sexual health in a 2026 systematic review. Rising heat, disasters, and shifting environments have been linked in prior studies to fertility, ovarian reserve, menopause timing, and mother and child health, and reproductive choices.

Following PRISMA guidance and a registered PROSPERO protocol, the review gathers and weighs studies across those outcomes. It pulls the scattered literature into one framework for researchers, clinicians, and educators. Policy readers can use it to see where the findings are firm, where it is thin, and what health planning should watch next.
pmc-13393780:
Gong and colleagues report a 2026 randomized controlled trial on preventing perioperative hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature during surgery under general anesthesia. At a single hospital, 206 patients scheduled for operations lasting four to eight hours received either passive insulation with cotton quilts or a multimodal strategy. The strategy combined pre-warming, forced-air blankets, warmed fluids, a warmer room, and medication. Core temperature was tracked throughout surgery and afterward.

By the end of surgery, hypothermia struck 69.2 percent of the passive group but only 27.5 percent of the multimodal group, a wide gap. At discharge from the operating room, the rates were 72 percent against 28 percent in favor of active warming. Postoperative cardiac adverse events occurred in 3.85 percent of control patients and none of the warmed patients. The authors urge hospitals to make proactive, layered warming standard care for long operations.
pmc-13393880:
Seda Serhatlioğlu and others record breast feeding under war among Palestinian women in a 2026 interview study. War writing has stressed feeding rates and food value, while mothers' own lived tales went largely unheard.

Lack of food, forced flight, unsafe shelter, and deep trauma wore feeding down at a structural level, yet mothers still used feeding for food, calm, closeness, mood steadiness, and mother-baby bond. The writers hold that guarding breast feeding in war is a duty no aid plan may skip, not an optional extra. Aid chiefs gain a stark, human brief on feeding under siege.
pmc-13394080:
Hong Zhang and others review paper-strip gene tests for bedside diagnosis in a 2026 paper. Fast, true gene reads are key to early care, yet lab gene tests are slow, dear, and fiddly.

Paper strips offer a cheap swap, but gene spotting and signal boost inside paper strands have been hard. New strips build 3D nooks from porous strands and treated mats, lifting base reads and ease of use. The review maps signal boost and noise hush tricks from sample in to read out. Field clinics gain a guide to gene tests that fit in a pocket, not a lab.
pmc-13394480:
Yangsong Wang and colleagues describe, in 2026, how tumours borrow the thymus to shield themselves. The thymus trains T cells and deletes those that attack the body. Two kinds of plasmacytoid dendritic cells gather there in mice with tumours, the team found. One kind carries tumour parts into the thymus and prompts deletion of tumour-fighting T cells.

The second kind slows the making of fresh T cells and releases type I interferon. A signal named CCR9 guides both kinds into the thymus. Mice that lacked CCR9 kept stronger anti-tumour defence and grew smaller tumours. The authors call this a hidden route to immune tolerance.
pmc-13395980:
Manoj Kumar and colleagues review brown algae as a farm input that can lift crop growth and help plants withstand stress, in a 2026 article. Extracts of these seaweeds are rich in natural sugars such as alginates, fucoidans, and laminarins, plus vitamins, minerals, and polyphenols.

With climate pressure and heavy chemical use straining food production, interest in gentler inputs has grown. The review pulls together earlier work on how seaweed extracts act on plants, from growth signals to stronger defenses against disease, drought, and salt. The authors present brown algae as a practical, lower-impact tool for modern farming, while sorting proven effects from claims that still rest on thin proof.
pmc-13396080:
Lingzhi Luo and co-authors built a light-based processor that can update its own settings while it works, and describe it in a 2026 paper. Most computer chips, including earlier light-based ones, run with fixed settings, so they cope poorly when incoming data changes character mid-task.

Their temporally plastic photonic processor pairs two kinds of light circuits. A slow, reconfigurable part holds stable long-term processing, while a fast part adjusts on the fly, and a loop of optical delay acts as short-term memory. The design targets real-time jobs such as signal handling and control, where retraining a fixed chip is too slow and electronic memory limits bite.
pmc-13396180:
Min Wu and others test whether brain waves for known names foretell coma fate in a 2026 forward group study. Coma fate in intensive care steers weighty choices yet stays hard to guess, and task brain wave tests may bare hidden awareness.

Across five intensive care wards, 461 acute brain harm patients were screened and 81 made the final set, with one ward's patients kept for outside check. Brain waves for known versus strange names were weighed as fate signs. Doctors gain a bedside wave sign that may sharpen coma fate calls without new invasive tests.
pmc-13396280:
Hong Seok Oh and co-authors revisit a 17th-century writer's idea of melancholy in a 2026 study of how depressive symptoms hang together in Asian patients. Richard Baxter, an English churchman, treated guilt as central to melancholy, and the authors test whether guilt still shapes the pattern of modern depression.

Data came from a prescription-pattern study spanning 11 Asian countries. Patients were split by whether strong guilt appeared among their symptoms, based on one survey item about feeling bad about oneself. Network analysis mapped which symptoms link most tightly in each group and which sit at the center, showing whether guilt-rich depression forms a distinct web.
pmc-13396380:
Bhattacharjee and co-authors present, in 2026, FORGE, a framework that predicts which cancer patients will benefit from targeted drugs, grounded in gene essentiality. Targeted inhibitors work by blocking proteins a cancer cell cannot live without, yet most sensitivity models ignore that mechanism. FORGE jointly factorizes two data types, drug response measured by IC50, the dose halving cell growth, and gene dependency scores from knockout screens, learning shared embeddings for both.

From those embeddings the team derived a Benefit Score, an index for predicting prognosis under targeted therapies. The design contrasts with expression-only predictors such as DeepHE and XGEP, which report 94 to 96 percent accuracy at the narrower task of calling gene essentiality. By forcing drug response and gene dependency into one model, FORGE ties its predictions to the drug's actual target biology. The authors offer the score as a stratification tool for matching patients to targeted treatments.
pmc-13396480:
Maria Zimmermann and others use signed tales to test brain tale ladders shared by all tongues in a 2026 brain-scan study. Spoken tales engage a brain time ladder from words to plots, but whether signs share that ladder was untested.

Twenty born signers watched a Polish Sign tale from Poe plus scrambled cuts during brain scans. Signed tales synced layered brain nets, with front-temple zones tracking sentence build and the default net tracking plot, as in speech. Top-side wall zones showed a sign-only long-time mark. The paper proves tale shape in the brain crosses tongue mode.
pmc-13396680:
Jiang and colleagues improve, in 2026, thermal de-icing by engineering the type of ice that forms against a surface under airflow. Ice on aircraft wings costs lift and safety, and electric heating is the incumbent fix. Wisdom held that flow conditions alone dictate ice type, but their non-wetting microstructured surfaces grow a porous rime layer under flow, changing how the ice lets go when heated.

The microstructures fragment pre-frozen droplets with help from the airflow, shrinking the ice crystals. Smaller crystals block heat pathways differently, thickening the rime layer, which melts free as direct solid-ice contact rather than through an energy-wasting water film. The effect cut thermal de-icing energy consumption by roughly 56 percent without extra energy input in their experiments. Earlier work shows porous rime alone can trim melting time by 27.2 percent, context the authors build into a surface-design strategy.
pmc-13396880:
Ali Gohar and co-authors present a patient in whom two autoimmune diseases overlap, a combination called Reynolds syndrome, in a 2026 case report. pmc-13397680:
Mohammad Mehdi Rajabi and others probe generational gaps in ageism among Iranian nurses in a 2026 study. Ageism in health care can thin care quality and worsen outcomes for older patients, and generational upbringing may shape nurses' views.

Two hundred and ten nurses from two Tehran referral hospitals, picked by stratified random sampling, were grouped as Generation X, Y, and Z and scored with a proven ageism scale. The study compares views across cohorts shaped by different lives and cultural settings. Nurse educators gain proof for generation-aware anti-ageism training.
pmc-13397780:
Vitaliy Voznyy and a large team reviewed trials of a nerve block used after lung surgery to see if it eases pain and cuts opioid use. Their 2026 review covers the erector spinae plane block, an injection near the spine that numbs chest wall nerves, compared with usual care without the block. Lung surgery often brings strong pain, heavy opioid use, and nausea, so safer pain control is a pressing clinical goal.

The review pooled 20 randomized trials with 1,391 patients and tracked pain at rest and on movement at 6, 12, and 24 hours. Patients given the block reported lower pain at each time point and used less opioid in the first day, with fewer cases of nausea and vomiting. The authors present the block as a useful addition to lung surgery pain plans. Readers should note that trial methods and block techniques varied, so the size of benefit may differ by setting.
pmc-13399280:
Christopher David Chapman, Myles Hyla Edward Dakin, and Richard Aspinall investigated a defined hypochlorite solution in 2026, asking whether the antiseptic does more than kill germs. Hypochlorite is a long-used disinfectant. Its use on severe burns improved survival after infections in ways germ killing alone seemed unable to explain. The team suspected the solution also reshapes the wound's inflammatory signals.

Lab tests confirmed that a concentration of 7 millimoles per liter wiped out both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. The same strength attacked two signaling proteins unevenly. IL-6, which drives inflammation, lost its function about three times faster than IL-10, which calms inflammation, after only five minutes of exposure. Tests on skin cells checked how much direct exposure the tissue could tolerate. The authors argue that trimming IL-6 while sparing IL-10 could quiet wound inflammation, reduce scarring, and help explain the survival benefit seen in burn care.
pmc-13399380:
Marcia Maria Gimenez and team tested ankle nerve stimulation for overactive bladder after ischemic stroke in women. Their 2026 prospective case series addresses neurogenic overactive bladder, where stroke damage disrupts bladder control and harms quality of life. Transcutaneous tibial nerve stimulation sends mild pulses through skin near the ankle to calm bladder nerves.

Thirty-one women completed twice-weekly, 30-minute sessions for six weeks, with follow-up at six months. Daytime voiding fell from about 12 to 7 times per day. Urgency episodes dropped from about 13 to 1, urge incontinence fell sharply, and nighttime voiding also improved, with gains largely holding at follow-up. The work supports the therapy as a noninvasive option, while its small, uncontrolled design calls for randomized trials.
pmc-13399480:
Junhui Wu, Zerui Dai, and Dawit Dibekulu revisit how the English future expression be going to became grammar, in a 2026 corpus linguistics study. The phrase began as literal motion toward a place. It was then reanalyzed so that to marked intention and future time instead of direction. Drawing on three large text collections, EEBO, Google Books, and the modern COCA corpus, they measured the expression's frequency across centuries. They date the critical window to 110 years, from 1580 to 1690, with a synchronic intensity of 0.81 occurrences per million words at the threshold, as their calculations report. The authors present the case as confirmation that a measurable threshold exists. They offer it as a template for quantifying other grammaticalization stories.
pmc-13400580:
Ken Watanabe and colleagues analyze, in 2026, which patients with thyroid cancer spread to the lungs respond to radioactive iodine therapy. The team reviewed 186 patients treated between 2010 and 2024, grading response by scans, imaging of iodine uptake and a blood marker. Overall disease control, counting complete, partial and stable outcomes, was under a quarter of cases. Patients younger than 55 and those whose lung spread was found at the time of thyroid surgery fared better. A lung uptake score also tracked outcome strongly, while the starting dose made no clear difference.
pmc-13400680:
Jingcheng Zhang and colleagues examine, in 2026, pancreatic cancer surgery where a major vein must be removed along with the tumor. Among 117 patients operated on after initial therapy, 65 had vein resection and 52 did not. Complications and deaths around surgery were similar, as were overall and disease-free survival times. Within the resection group, however, finding true cancer invasion in the removed vein wall under the microscope marked much shorter survival. The vein invasion, not the resection, carried the grim signal.
pmc-13401380:
Lili Shao, Ruyi Zhang, Yinqing Huang, and Xiaochun Dai published a 2026 study building a prediction model for mild cognitive impairment in older adults who live with several chronic conditions at once. Early screening matters because impairment can hide inside multimorbidity.

The cross-sectional study enrolled 238 older inpatients at a Wenzhou Medical University hospital between April 2022 and February 2025, testing cognition with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment Basic scale. About 27 percent had mild cognitive impairment. Risk rose with age at or above 80 years, hearing impairment, and emotional disorders, each roughly tripling or quadrupling the odds. Higher education, frequent exercise, and frequent social activity were protective. The authors turned these factors into a nomogram chart and validated it in a separate group of 68 patients.
pmc-13401580:
Hirakawa and colleagues test, in 2026, whether blood levels of VEGF-A isoforms predict how EGFR-mutated lung cancer responds to targeted inhibitor drugs. Above a cutoff of 339.3 picograms per milliliter, response rate dropped to 64.9 percent from 96.3 percent below it, and progression-free survival shortened to 6.2 months from 14.4 months in the comparison. The authors propose serum VEGF121 as a pre-treatment stratification marker.
pmc-13401680:
Setayesh Sindarreh and co-authors conducted a 2026 observational study of influenza in patients with blood cancers, hunting for factors tied to death. People with hematologic malignancies are among the most vulnerable to severe flu results, yet risk details are sparse.

The cross-sectional study included 90 patients with confirmed influenza and a blood cancer. It collected demographics, cancer type and status, flu type, symptoms, and lab and imaging findings. Hospital stay length, intensive care admissions, and deaths were also recorded. The mean age was about 34 years, with patients ranging from toddlers to a 91-year-old. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia was most common at about 46 percent, followed by acute myeloid leukemia at about 22 percent, lymphomas, myeloma, and rarer types. Analysis focused on which features, from cancer type to intensive care need, separated survivors from those who died.
pmc-13401880:
Meng Chen and Chengcheng Che developed a machine learning model to sort clinical nurses in China by their risk of compassion fatigue, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Feature selection combined the Boruta algorithm with LASSO regression, and eight machine learning algorithms were trained and compared on discrimination, accuracy, recall, and F1 score. The winning model was interpreted with SHAP analysis, which shows how much each factor pushes a prediction up or down, keeping the tool explainable rather than a black box.
pmc-13402680:

Using fiber photometry to watch the cells and optogenetics to steer them, the team ran mice through a touchscreen working memory test at varied difficulty.

The cells raised their activity, and proved necessary, only under high-demand conditions; easy versions of the task ran fine without their extra push. That demand split, the authors suggest, explains the clash in earlier literature: studies using light tasks would miss the cells role entirely, while heavy tasks expose it. The result frames working memory support as a reserve system the prefrontal cortex calls in when load climbs.
pmc-13402880:
Deepak Kumar Singhal leads a team surveying dental students on tobacco habits, a pointed choice since dentists are often the first to spot tobacco damage in the mouth. Tobacco kills more than 8 million people a year worldwide, most in poorer countries, and India ranks among the largest producers and consumers, with cheap products everywhere. Use typically starts between ages 14 and 25, making campuses prime ground for prevention.

Their cross-sectional questionnaire maps how common smoking and smokeless habits are among future dentists, and in what patterns. The stakes are double: students own health, and their credibility as counselors, since health workers are urged under the WHO tobacco framework to advise quitting at every chance. Findings on stains, halitosis, and precancerous lesions tie the survey back to the clinic, where dental teams can catch early harm.
pmc-13403280:
Alexandre Lahens and team pinned down medical factors that skew kidney function guesses in a large French group. Formulas use age and sex, but medical states can skew results and mislead dosing.
