The team engineered zebrafish carrying the Notch3 p.C680S fault and tracked vessels, brain size, thinking and protein deposits as the fish aged.

Mutant fish reproduced key age-linked features, including vessel dysfunction, forebrain shrinkage, cognitive impairment and granular deposits typical of the disease. Gene and protein studies showed lower type IV collagen signals, confirmed by staining around brain vessels, and structural modelling classed the fault as nonconventional. The fish model thus gives researchers a faster vertebrate system for testing whether falling collagen helps drive CADASIL.
pmc-13456580:
Daniel M. Zeitler and four colleagues report, in a 2026 post-market study, outcomes of cochlear implants for adults deaf in one ear. Thirty adults with profound one-sided loss and a healthy other ear received implants at five referral centers. The study tracked speech understanding, hearing with both ears, ringing in the ears, and quality of life over twelve months.

Speech scores in quiet and in noise rose significantly by the one-year mark. Tasks that separate the target voice from a masker improved on both the head-shadow and the two-ear squelch measures. Patients also reported less tinnitus, less listening fatigue, better spatial hearing, and higher quality of life. No comparison group was used, since the design follows real-world approval practice. The authors conclude that implantation is an excellent option for single-sided deafness, with benefits reaching well past test scores.
pmc-13456880:
Fei, Li, and Li examine weekend catch-up sleep and stroke in this 2026 analysis of United States survey data. Many adults sleep less on workdays and repay the debt on weekends, and whether that habit relates to stroke was unclear. The team used national health survey cycles from 2017 to 2023, covering 11,134 adults aged 20 and over who reported weekday and weekend sleep and any stroke history.

Adults who slept longer on weekends than weekdays had lower odds of reporting a stroke. Those who did not catch up had higher odds. The adjusted odds ratio was about 0.78 in the fully adjusted model they fitted. The clearest benefit sat in the two-to-three-hour catch-up group, where odds were roughly forty percent lower. The association was strongest in women, in adults aged 36 to 64, and in people who drank alcohol.
pmc-13457080:
Vegar Rangul and colleagues profile device-measured movement and sleep in Norway's long-running HUNT study in a 2026 data resource paper. Self-reported activity and sleep mislead research, while wrist and body sensors capture the full day, including unplanned movement. The Trøndelag Health Study began in 1984 to 1986 and now holds data on about 230,000 people, with its fourth round running in 2017 to 2019.

In that round, 38,756 participants agreed to wear thigh and lower-back sensors for up to seven days, and 32,644 gave at least one valid day, including 27,329 adults and 5,315 adolescents. Validated machine-learning models turn the signals into walking, running, cycling, posture and sleep duration, with methods and training data public. Linked to national registries, the resource supports long-term studies of disease, prescriptions and care use, subject to ethics approval and a Norwegian partner.
pmc-13457380:
Shawn Eagle and a multi-center team lay out the protocol for EDI for TBI, a trial testing whether a bedside blood test for brain injury can be woven into busy emergency departments. Roughly five million Americans are checked for traumatic brain injury each year, most receive a head CT scan, and fewer than one in ten scans shows damage. The 2026 protocol describes a hybrid effectiveness-implementation study across three academic Level 1 trauma centers.

The whole-blood test measures two brain-injury biomarkers from a standard blood draw. Researchers will enroll 280 patients with Glasgow Coma Scale scores of 13 to 15, the mild range. An initial phase enrolls 140 to map what helps or blocks routine use, then 140 more join while an implementation blueprint is piloted per site. Success means fewer needless scans and radiation exposure, shorter emergency stays, and a playbook other trauma centers can copy. The trial is registered as NCT07373509.
pmc-13457880:
Do-Sung Kim and colleagues test a double-layered nano-liposomal curcumin for absorption in a 2026 trial. Curcumin from turmeric shows anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective promise, yet poor solubility, fast metabolism and weak gut permeability keep blood levels low. Eighteen healthy men in a randomised, double-blind trial took either 400 mg of BNT-C060, a chitosan and alginate coated nano-liposome, or 2,000 mg of free curcumin while fasting. Blood and urine were tracked for 24 hours.

Dose-normalised blood exposure rose 23.2-fold and peak concentration 53-fold with BNT-C060, urinary exposure rose 35.3-fold, and peak arrived earlier at 0.86 versus 3.3 hours, with no significant safety signals at the tested dose. The trial is small, single-dose and male-only, so it proves absorption, not treatment benefit, but it gives a strong rationale for testing the formulation in patients with inflammatory or brain conditions.
pmc-13458080:
Justine Renaud and colleagues listen to how long-term high blood sugar changes rat calls in a 2026 study. Diabetes links with mood disorders in people, and rats signal emotion through ultrasonic vocalisations, offering a window on that link. Male diabetic hyperglycaemic rats and controls were paired with a matched partner to elicit calls, scoring counts and sound traits for appetitive 50-kHz calls and aversive 22-kHz calls.

Diabetic pairs emitted more 50-kHz calls than controls, with differences in duration, frequency range and call shape across total, flat and frequency-modulated calls. Thirty percent of diabetic pairs, and no control pairs, also emitted aversive 22-kHz calls. The authors present ultrasonic calling as an informative marker of emotional change under chronic hyperglycaemia in rats, while translation to human mood remains indirect.
pmc-13458580:
Cinja Koller and co-authors tested whether a smartphone photograph of the back of a hand could reveal swollen finger joints in inflammatory arthritis. Their 2026 study built a measure called the Finger Fold Index, which compares a joint's width with the surface area of the skin folds over it, since swelling stretches those folds flatter. Machine learning software measured 1,275 finger joint images from 124 patients with rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, plus hands from 53 healthy people.

The index tracked clinician swelling scores moderately well, with a correlation of 0.443 across the arthritis patients. It separated swollen from unswollen joints with middling accuracy, and its ability to rule out swelling was notably weak. Values above the healthy cut-offs were clearly linked with swelling, most strongly for the most swollen joints. The tool is not accurate enough for clinic use yet, the authors say.
pmc-13459280:
Elham Babadi and co-authors describe a 21 year old Iranian woman with an unusually large odontoma, a benign lump made of disorganized tooth tissues like enamel and dentin, in her lower jaw. Odontomas are the most common tumors of tooth forming tissue and usually stay small and silent. This complex type stretched from her first molar back to the jaw's ramus and was associated with her second and third molars trapped beneath it. Their 2026 case report describes removing the mass through an incision inside the mouth.

Despite the lesion's size, the surgeons completed the removal intraorally without breaking the jaw or needing any fixation plates or screws. Healing proceeded without complications afterward. At the four month follow up visit, she showed no sign of the lesion returning. Even large mandibular odontomas can be managed through the mouth, the authors argue, sparing patients external incisions.
pmc-13459380:
Yasuhiro Mitani and co-authors surveyed adolescent wind players about playing related pain in the neck, shoulders, and lower back, and how instrument and posture contribute. Their 2026 study questioned 120 members of a high school brass band about pain occurrence, severity, and duration while playing. The team then compared pain patterns between light and heavy instruments. It also compared symmetrical and asymmetrical playing postures, the twisted positions some instruments force on the body during long rehearsals.

Pain was widespread: 82 students, 68.3 percent, reported neck and shoulder pain, and 53 students, 44.2 percent, reported low back pain while playing. Surprisingly, players of light instruments reported low back pain more often than heavy instrument players, possibly because light instruments demand sustained unsupported postures. Students with asymmetrical posture were more likely to report moderate to severe back pain lasting at least three months. Posture coaching may matter more than instrument weight alone, the authors suggest.
pmc-13459780:
Ding Hu and co-authors mapped how the signaling protein NOTCH3 turns ordinary bladder fibroblasts into the muscle like supporters that drive bladder cancer growth. Cancer linked fibroblasts of the myofibroblastic type lay down matrix and contract tissue, sheltering tumors. In their 2026 study, the team combined patient derived fibroblasts with bulk, single cell, and spatial gene expression data from bladder tumors. It then silenced NOTCH3 to watch what the fibroblasts lost, tracing the pathway step by step from the initial growth factor signal downward.

NOTCH3 was markedly enriched in tumor fibroblasts across every dataset examined. Silencing it cut matrix deposition, contractile strength, internal oxidant build up, and the fibroblasts' ability to support tumor growth. The chain runs through TGF beta switching the gene on, after which NOTCH3 helps destroy the P62 protein. That disables an antioxidant defense and lets reactive oxygen species build up to lock in the aggressive state.
pmc-13460080:
Binaya Krushna Sahu and co-authors review in 2026 the case for probiotics in keeping the vaginal microbiome healthy. A healthy community is dominated by Lactobacillus species, which hold acidity high and crowd out pathogens. When that balance slips, bacterial vaginosis, yeast infections, and urinary infections become more likely, and pregnancy complications such as preterm labor can follow.

Trial evidence supports certain strains for cutting recurrence of those infections, working through acid production, surface competition, and immune effects. Early work extends to gestational diabetes and anemia in pregnancy. Safety in people with weak immune systems needs care, and strains beyond Lactobacillus are gaining interest. The authors stress that strain, dose, and delivery route must be standardized before routine practice.
pmc-13460680:
Yael Applbaum and six co-authors chart twenty-five years of children's intensive care in Israel in a 2026 paper. They linked national hospital records with bed capacity and population data. Their aim was to track use, outcomes, repeat hospital stays, and regional spread of resources for patients up to age seventeen.

The share of hospital stays involving intensive care nearly doubled over the period. Deaths in hospital fell by almost half, and deaths within a year of discharge also fell. Yet nearly half of intensive care survivors were back in hospital within a year, far above other patients. Bed capacity grew, but regional ratios still varied widely. The authors urge structured follow-up after discharge.
pmc-13461480:
Kennedy Diema Konlan leads a Ghanaian team that studied in 2026 why older adults in Sokode, a peri-urban town near Ho, do or do not take their blood pressure medicines reliably. Their community survey covered 202 adults aged sixty and above with hypertension, scoring knowledge on a graded scale and adherence from six behavior questions, alongside personal, medical, and barrier details.

Knowledge was not the problem: four fifths understood their condition and its management well. Adherence still failed for about sixty-one percent. Forgetting, stopping when feeling better, and cultural or religious beliefs each explained roughly half the lapses. Income, very advanced age, and living with the diagnosis for more than a decade each tied significantly to adherence patterns, which the authors use to target support.
pmc-13461580:
Fabiani and colleagues tested in 2026 whether digestate, the leftover slurry from biogas production, can fertilise lettuce without harming the bacteria living on its leaves. Digestate returns nutrients to soil in a circular system, but its effects on leaf microbes and resistance genes were little known. Lettuce grew in a greenhouse under several digestate plans, and the team checked growth, leaf nutrients, faecal bacteria, salmonella, and resistance gene levels.

Fabiani found that splitting the digestate dose across the season gave growth and leaf nutrient levels matching chemical fertiliser. This happened without raising resistance gene counts or faecal indicator bacteria and salmonella on the leaves, even though the starting digestate held some. The fertiliser plan did shift which bacteria lived on the leaves, while total bacterial counts stayed steady. The authors see digestate as workable for lettuce with limited leaf-community impact.
pmc-13461980:
Laura Mickes and co-authors tested whether an eyewitness's confidence means anything in a live showup, the quick one person identification police run when a suspect is caught near a crime scene. Most research uses photographs, where confidence predicts accuracy weakly. In their 2026 work, a laboratory study of 229 participants and a field study of 153 real showup cases from two American jurisdictions both examined live identifications. Response speed in the lab and an evidence strength scale in the field served as checks on correctness.

Confident and fast identifications were more likely correct in the laboratory, and high confidence rejections pointed to innocence. The field cases agreed: witness confidence again tracked accuracy when scored against independent evidence strength. Live showups, long feared as suggestive and unreliable, produced confidence that carried real information in both settings. Run with bias reducing safeguards, the authors argue, showups yield evidence solid enough to keep using.
pmc-13462080:
Disha Mittal and colleagues measure the psychosocial toll of stress urinary incontinence in young college women in a 2026 study. Leakage during exertion is increasingly recognised in young women, yet its effects on stress, sleep and quality of life in students were understudied. A cross-sectional study surveyed 233 nulligravid female students, mean age 21.1 years, at an Indian university with validated incontinence, stress, sleep and quality-of-life instruments.

High incontinence impact tracked higher perceived stress and poorer sleep, and markedly lower quality of life, with incontinence impact, stress and poor sleep independently explaining 46.2 percent of quality-of-life variance. Stress mediated 17.8 percent of the incontinence-to-quality-of-life link, though cross-sectional data cannot prove causation. Campus health services gain a case for pelvic floor therapy plus psychological support.
pmc-13462380:
Lee and La studied in 2026 hikikomori, severe social withdrawal, among young adults in South Korea, and its links to narcissistic vulnerability, a fragile self-image that craves approval. Their survey covered 352 adults aged 19 to 34 years. They measured withdrawal, depression, and the gap between how people experience relationships online versus offline, along two axes: control and affiliation, meaning warmth and closeness.

Lee found depression partly carried the effect: vulnerable narcissism linked to withdrawal in part through raised depression. The strength of that path depended on the online-offline gap in both axes, with the control gap mattering more. In other words, withdrawal tied less to screen time itself than to how different relationships feel across the two worlds. The authors suggest support should target that relational mismatch, not just digital habits, for withdrawn young adults.
pmc-13462580:
Amidu Alhassan leads a 2026 comparative study of sexual violence before age eighteen among women in Ghana, drawing on national health surveys from 2008 and 2022. Laws and policies, including a 2007 domestic violence act, aimed to cut such harm, yet gaps between groups were poorly charted. The team used a World Health Organization equity toolkit to compare rates by age cohort and marital status, .

The national rate fell from over eight percent in 2008 to about six percent in 2022. Never-married women carried the highest rate in both years. Women aged 20 to 24 held the highest estimate in 2008, then fell by 2022. Rates rose in two older groups, women in their late thirties and early forties, hinting at a cohort pattern in who reports harm. Age-based inequality shifted markedly across the period, while marital status gaps stayed modest. The authors call for prevention aimed at the groups still carrying a heavy share.
pmc-13463480:
Al-Essawe and colleagues investigate in this 2026 study why some stallions' semen survives freezing far better than others, a persistent headache for horse breeding. Their suspect is seminal plasma, the fluid surrounding sperm, and specifically whether plasma from good-freezing stallions protects sperm while plasma from poor freezers damages it.

The team cleaned sperm using a single-layer centrifugation technique, then froze samples with no plasma, with their own plasma, or with swapped plasma from the opposite type of stallion. Plasma-free samples kept more intact acrosomes, the cap structure sperm need to fertilize an egg, than samples frozen in their own plasma. Adding plasma from bad freezers pushed more sperm into premature acrosome reactions, while plasma from good freezers preserved the caps. The authors suggest tailoring freezing protocols to each stallion's plasma profile.
pmc-13463880:
Shuailin Li and five co-authors chart the gene activity of two eye surface tissues in healthy people. The team lifted cells gently with impression cytology, a press-on collection method, and read both gene messages and their microRNA regulators.

Corneal cells leaned toward barrier strength, tight sealing, and defense against viruses. Conjunctival cells leaned toward immune watch, fluid release, clearing of stray chemicals, and repair. Paired microRNA and gene networks helped explain how each tissue keeps its own role. The map gives eye researchers a healthy baseline for spotting disease changes and new drug targets.
pmc-13463980:
Jiagui Zhong and eight co-authors probe the triangle of depression, poor sleep, and epilepsy in United States adults. The team mined a national health survey from 2013 to 2020, covering 8,223 adults. Depression is common in people with epilepsy, and the pair are known to feed each other.

Adults with depression showed a clearly higher rate of epilepsy in weighted models. Poor sleep carried a large share of that link, accounting for close to half of the total effect in mediation tests. The strength of the link shifted with schooling level and with heart or vessel disease. The authors argue that mood care and sleep care deserve a place in epilepsy prevention plans.
pmc-13464580:
Daniil Spector and colleagues reviewed platinum(IV) nanocarriers in 2026, a next step for platinum chemotherapy that leads treatment for many tumours. Platinum prodrugs kill cancer well, yet they break down fast in blood and reach tumours poorly. Tiny carriers aim to fix both faults through targeted delivery, triggered release, and combined therapy.

The review covers designs from 2022 to 2025 that steer drug to tumours, spark immune cell death, and stir native and adaptive immunity to block recurrence. Theranostic versions add light-based imaging and heat or light therapy, letting doctors watch delivery live. Photocontrolled chemo plus immune and light treatments holds strong combined promise, though clinic translation still needs safety and scale proof.
pmc-13464880:
Karaja and colleagues reported in 2026 a three-year-old Syrian girl whose bulging left eye came from a large arachnoid cyst inside the eye socket. Only 18 such cases had ever been published, just five of them in children. The team reviewed them all alongside their patient. She also had a drooping eyelid from birth.

CT and MRI scans together pinned down the diagnosis and excluded look-alike conditions. Surgeons removed the cyst, and the protrusion resolved completely. Follow-up imaging showed no return. The authors argue a large, symptomatic cyst deserves surgery even when eyesight is intact. Pressure can quietly damage the optic nerve.
pmc-13464980:
Şahin Doğan and colleagues report a 2026 study making silver nanoparticles with the leaf extract of Lotus sanguineus, an endemic plant. Plant extracts can reduce silver into nanoparticles without harsh chemicals, a greener synthesis. The particles were tested for breaking down dye pollutants under light, killing bacteria, and stopping biofilms, with computer docking against bacterial quorum-sensing proteins, the signals bacteria use to coordinate.

The particles showed strong dye degradation and clear antibacterial and antibiofilm action in the tests. Docking suggested plausible binding to the coordination proteins that biofilms depend on, a mechanistic hint for the lab results.  A plant-based route that keeps performance while cutting chemical waste speaks to both water treatment and medical uses, pending safety checks on the particles themselves.
pmc-13465280:
Jai-Sing Yang and five co-authors show how a small RNA, microRNA-34a, drives fat buildup in liver cells by muting a master switch. Fatty liver disease tied to metabolism is now the world's commonest chronic liver problem. In liver cells flooded with fatty acids, the small RNA climbed sharply.

The authors frame the RNA-to-switch axis as one lever among several in liver fat control.
pmc-13465480:
Ancuta Elena Tupu leads a team that reviews nighttime screen use in teens as a driver of lost blood pressure dipping, under a proposed frame they call digital chronotoxicity. Suppressed melatonin, revved stress systems, oxidative strain, and metabolic drift form the proposed links. Round-the-clock pressure monitoring stands as the reference test for catching the flat pattern and masked hypertension. Early damage markers across heart, vessels, kidneys, and brain get a full survey. Wearables and AI screening close the piece, with a pathway that adds screen and sleep history to every teen workup.
pmc-13467080:
Beata Krasińska and a large team measure fatty signal molecules that fan or calm inflammation in patients with chronic coronary syndrome, across body types and ages, in a 2026 study. Eighty-three patients hospitalized with stable chest pain gave blood for five mediators, spanning attack signals and the specialized molecules that resolve inflammation. Comparisons split by sex, age, and weight class.

Women, older patients, and those with obesity carried higher levels of both an attack signal and two resolving ones, a mixed picture. A third resolving mediator ran higher in men, younger patients, and leaner patients instead. One classic inflammatory lipid showed no group differences. Uneven resolution chemistry may help explain why the same artery disease behaves differently across people.
pmc-13467580:
Buket Karalar, Merve Nur Yılmaz, and Merve Pelin Dur Sarıgüzel compare in 2026 how well modern dental filling resins blend with natural tooth color, including under ultraviolet light. Five fillings were single-shade products, with the rest being simplified, multi-shade, or group-shade systems for comparison. Color blending was measured with a spectrophotometer and with cross-polarized photographs, while fluorescence matching used photographs under ultraviolet illumination. Checking both light conditions matters because a filling that vanishes in daylight can still stand out under the ultraviolet light found in clubs and some clinics. The authors report how the methods and materials compared across those tests.
pmc-13468180:
Angelo Santoro and co-authors examine in 2026 the restless structures of GLP-1 analogues, the peptide drugs now central to diabetes and obesity care. These peptides do not sit in one shape. Salt levels, temperature, and even manufacturing steps act as perturbations that can disturb structural integrity. The authors argue predictive models must treat folding and aggregation as one coupled problem.
pmc-13468380:
Agnieszka Piegat, Agata Goszczyńska, and Agata Niemczyk argue in a 2026 perspective that modified chitosan is failing to reach the clinic for practical rather than biological reasons. Their subject is a chitosan variant whose chains carry water-hating groups, a much-studied biomaterial from crustacean shells. The material carries both water-loving and water-hating parts, so it self-assembles into carriers for drugs, antimicrobials, and tissue scaffolds, with plenty of promising lab results. Yet very few products have advanced toward real medical use.

The authors trace the bottleneck to results others cannot repeat, loose structure checks, and scant care for process design and factory scale-up. Their piece follows the material from chemical modification through self-assembly to formulation, showing where design and process choices decide reliability. They urge standard checks and shared write-up rules, the plain fixes they say translation actually needs.
pmc-13468480:
Georgia Lagodonti and colleagues investigate in 2026 whether the antioxidant capacity of a man seminal plasma tracks with his sperm quality and with how many antioxidants he eats. Seminal plasma was tested with two antioxidant assays, one based on iron reduction and one on radical scavenging. Dietary antioxidant intake came from a validated food frequency questionnaire, and smoking, alcohol, exercise, and supplement habits were recorded for adjustment. Correlations and regression models then linked antioxidant indices with semen parameters. A clear verdict would tell fertility clinics whether diet and seminal antioxidant screening deserve a routine place in male infertility workups.
pmc-13468580:
Anna Łupińska and colleagues assess bone health in 2026 in children whose autoimmune gut diseases put their skeletons at risk. Vitamin D blood levels, density values, and texture scores were compared across the groups. Judging whether the texture score flags fragile bones earlier than density alone is the clinical point. pmc-13468880:
Luoqi Cui and colleagues read hand gestures from forearm muscle signals in 2026 with a three-branch neural network that respects how the sensors are physically arranged. The temporal and spectral branches use compact residual blocks, keeping the whole model modest despite the added topology branch. Prosthetic hands and rehabilitation devices live or die on gesture accuracy for new users, where the transfer result matters most.
pmc-13469280:

Reconstructing the years 2015 through 2024, they estimate plant transpiration supplied roughly 36 to 40 percent of recycled precipitation, forming coherent belts over vegetated ground. Years with weaker incoming airflow showed expanded plant contributions, while strong moisture inflow shifted the balance toward outside sources. Transpiration fractions also tracked independent vegetation greenness and water-flux indicators.
pmc-13469580:
Li and a large team built a machine learning model in this 2026 study to predict how irritating a tobacco leaf feels when smoked, using chemistry instead of human tasters. They measured 78 chemical components in 353 leaf samples and paired each sample with sensory scores that split leaves into high-irritation and low-irritation groups.

After cleaning outliers and narrowing the data to 33 core features, their random forest model with 60 decision trees classified an independent test set with 84.38 percent accuracy, beating support vector machine and nearest-neighbor models in the same comparison. Eight chemicals mattered most, including total nitrogen, total alkaloids, and reducing sugar. Higher nitrogen compounds tracked with stronger irritation, while sugars and certain organic acids tracked with milder leaves, giving growers targets for breeding and blending.
pmc-13470180:
He and colleagues review how often ankle pump exercises should be done to keep blood moving in the legs, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The exercise, repeatedly flexing the ankle up and down, helps immobilized patients avoid dangerous clots. The team searched six databases up to March 2026. They compared blood flow speed in the main thigh vein across exercise frequencies, from slow cycles to faster ones, in healthy people and patients with limited mobility.

Eight studies with 546 participants met the inclusion rules, and only one was a randomized controlled trial. Vein blood flow velocity rose from baseline at every frequency tested. Gains were smallest at 3 cycles per minute and generally stronger at 10 cycles per minute or higher, where the pooled increase reached 15.16 centimeters per second. He cautions that the evidence is thin and mostly non-randomized, so the frequency guidance stays provisional until stronger trials confirm it.
pmc-13470580:
Fadi El-Jardali and a multinational team report in 2026 a readiness check of One Health systems in Croatia, Ghana, and Nigeria. Their tool walks national teams through a facilitated self assessment in two phases. The first reviews documents, maps stakeholders, and builds consensus across five components, from system foundations to how evidence informs policy. The second turns the findings into strength and weakness profiles for each country. Those profiles then set strategic priorities for policy and spending. The authors present the pilot as a route from diagnosis to an agreed action list.
pmc-13471080:
Madhuri Akella and a large team report a case series, published in 2026. It evaluates an eye-stroke protocol in an emergency department. The series was prospective. Blocked retinal arteries cause sudden vision loss. They are often diagnosed too late. The department used camera and scan imaging. The imaging does not need pupil dilation. Eye specialists read the images remotely.

One hundred affected eyes were seen. All arrived within a week of vision loss. Imaging was done quickly. The median was under half an hour for the earliest arrivals. Yet only sixteen percent arrived early enough for clot-busting treatment. Stroke workup found a major cause in nearly three quarters. The authors blame transfer delays. They urge wider use of remote imaging.
pmc-13471180:
Long and a multicenter team built an MRI-based scoring tool in 2026 to predict breast cancer recurrence and, more pointedly, who actually gains from radiation after surgery. Radiomics extracts hundreds of texture numbers from scans that eyes cannot see. The study enrolled 771 patients from a Chinese cancer hospital and a Duke University dataset abroad. A signature distilled the scan numbers into one risk score. Survival models then tested radiation benefit within risk groups.

The score split patients cleanly. High-risk patients relapsed significantly sooner in both the home and external datasets. A combined model adding clinical factors predicted recurrence with an accuracy score of 0.75, where 1.0 is perfect. The radiation finding inverted expectations. High-risk patients gained nothing measurable from radiation in either dataset. Low-risk patients gained significantly, with fewer relapses after treatment. The authors propose the score as a way to personalize radiation decisions rather than treating risk uniformly.
pmc-13471280:
Ma and colleagues built self-propelled nanomotors in 2026 that carry ferroptosis therapy deep into tumors. Inside, they raised reactive oxygen species and switched off glutathione peroxidase 4, letting lipid peroxides accumulate into immunogenic ferroptosis. Meanwhile the anchored cyclodextrin drained cholesterol, so tumor cells stiffened and T cells killed them more effectively. In mice bearing liver tumors, the treatment caused marked regression and lasting immune memory, and the mice lived for two months.
pmc-13471480:
Villaverde and co-authors describe building bedside ultrasound training into the full medical degree at the University of Global Health Equity in Rwanda. Their 2026 report covers the longitudinal curriculum launched in 2022, woven into the school's 6.5-year program with handheld scanners, hands-on practice, and online materials.

Knowledge scores jumped after the introductory session, rising from 68.8% correct to 90.0% correct on testing. Students who received the full preclinical curriculum reported significantly higher confidence than peers with clinical-only training at the same stage. Of 30 graduating students, 27 sat the final certification exam and 96% of them passed, while 68% of interns reported using ultrasound in real patient care.
pmc-13471680:
Zheng and co-authors synthesize a vicious-cycle theory of heart failure in which ferroptosis, iron-driven cell death, keeps inflammation burning by overwhelming the heart's cleanup crews. Their 2026 review lays out how dying heart muscle cells spill alarm signals and oxidized fats that reprogram macrophages, the immune cells meant to clear debris and calm tissue.

The bottleneck is efferocytosis, the macrophage job of eating dead cells. In failing hearts, sheer death burden, redox imbalance, and metabolic stress cripple that capacity, so debris piles up and drives more inflammation and scarring. The authors evaluate escape routes including iron modulation, targeted antioxidants, and metabolic reprogramming of macrophages. They frame the axis as a hypothesis for patient stratification, not yet a proven treatment target.
pmc-13472280:
Michael P Zimmerman leads a team linking in 2026 weak behavioral inhibition in a fragile X mouse model to fading theta brain rhythms in the visual cortex. Fragile X syndrome brings sensory and learning problems, and familiar sights normally evoke steady theta oscillations in visual areas and the hippocampus. Electrode arrays recorded three brain regions while the mice performed a visual go and no go task, licking for one image and withholding for another.

Theta power ran low in the visual cortex and hippocampus of the model mice, and it vanished on no go trials, exactly where the mice licked wrongly most. In healthy mice, strong visual theta predicted correct answers. Prefrontal cue responses also ran weak in the model, suggesting failed top down control. The circuit picture ties a rhythm loss to a behavior loss.
pmc-13472780:
Tian and colleagues present a 2026 study of music and creative activities as paths to learning and well-being in adolescents, using PISA 2018 data from four Chinese regions. The study measures opportunity rather than participation: whether schools offer bands, orchestras, or choirs, and whether homes hold instruments and art books. Outcomes were school achievement and subjective well-being.

The team tested whether self-regulation and school climate statistically carry the link between these opportunities and the outcomes.  If climate and self-regulation mediate the association, then music provision works partly by changing how school feels and how students manage themselves, not by notes alone. That would argue for protecting creative programs as infrastructure for learning, not decoration.
pmc-13472980: Hou and colleagues published an author correction in 2026 to their 2024 Nature Aging article on bone marrow macrophages and aging. Two images in one figure were picked by mistake from another figure's raw data. The team found the correct images and source data and updated the figure. Files for two other figures held a wrong replicate and a stray protein entry, plus near duplicate fractions from compiling errors. The journal checked the originals, fixed the source data, and the authors state the conclusions stand.
pmc-13473080:
Huanhuan Zhao and two colleagues surveyed 2,103 medical students in 2026 to test how a sense of calling in medicine relates to academic burnout. A career calling means feeling drawn to medicine as a purpose rather than merely a job, and burnout here covers exhaustion and disengagement from study. The team asked whether two middle factors, feeling connected to nature and feeling supported by others, carry part of that link, either alone or in a chain.

Using validated scales and a mediation analysis with 5,000 resampled estimates, they found that a stronger calling predicted lower burnout. Both nature connection and perceived social support each carried part of the effect on their own. A chain also ran from calling through nature connection and then social support to lower burnout. The practical hint is that schools might ease burnout by building time outdoors and genuine peer support into training.
pmc-13473280:
Wang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how gut microbe imbalance drives chronic kidney disease progression. The result is a build-up of uremic toxins, poisons normally cleared by kidneys, and a loss of protective gut products such as short-chain fatty acids. The review maps the pathways involved and compares several kidney disease types.

Toxins and missing protectors jointly trigger kidney inflammation and scarring through many signalling routes, including oxidative stress and inflammasome activation. The same gut-kidney axis appears in diabetic kidney disease, lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, and others, with disease-specific twists. The authors organise these shared and unique mechanisms into one framework. Such a map, they argue, points to shared drug targets across kidney diseases. It also supports gut-directed treatments, such as diet, probiotics, or toxin binders, as adjuncts to kidney care.
pmc-13473980:
Sunyoung Moon and co-authors test a belly wall nerve block in 2026 for pain after robot-assisted gynecologic surgery done through one small cut. Sixty patients were split evenly between the block and standard care. The block group got numbing drug placed by ultrasound on both sides of the belly after sleep anesthesia began. Pain was scored at six time points across two days.

Pain scores at zero, one, and six hours were lower in the block group. Rescue pain drug use right after surgery was also much lower in that group. Gains showed most for ovary surgery and fibroid removal, less for womb removal. A simple block done in minutes can ease the first hours after this surgery.
pmc-13474480:
Sgobbi and fellow Brazilian specialists set out in 2026 their shared view on genetic testing for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a disease that kills the nerve cells that control muscles. Most cases appear without family history, yet genes play a large part through single-gene and combined routes. About one in ten cases runs in families, though the gene often stays unknown.

The experts argue that gene testing should now be a standard, early part of care rather than an extra. A result can shape counseling for the patient and family, flag relatives at risk before symptoms start, and forecast how the disease may unfold. Testing also decides who can receive gene-targeted drugs, such as tofersen for cases tied to the SOD1 gene. The group writes from long clinic experience in Brazil.
pmc-13474580:
Hashida and colleagues argue in a 2026 perspective that MCL-1 should be seen as a survival hub. The protein blocks cell death and links bile duct cancer cells to their surroundings. Cholangiocarcinoma is a lethal cancer with dense scar-like tissue and poor responses to standard therapy.

The authors gather evidence that MCL-1 helps tumor cells resist a death signal called TRAIL and shields them from chemotherapy. Inflammatory signals in the tumor, including interleukin-6, reinforce this protection through growth pathways. In a commercial tissue sample set, MCL-1 appeared in 40 of 54 tumors, about three quarters of cases. Its presence also showed an early link with tumor stage. The authors suggest treatments should disrupt these supportive circuits, not only attack cancer cells directly.
pmc-13474780:
Jin and co-authors tracked varicella, the illness better known as chickenpox, across Xuzhou in China from 2015 to 2024 using national disease reporting systems. Their 2026 surveillance study counted cases by year, season, age, and place, and it also reviewed outbreak events reported by schools and other group settings. The team compared city and countryside rates to see where the illness hit hardest over the decade.

Yearly incidence climbed to a peak of about 65 cases per 100,000 people in 2019, fell in 2020, then eased downward through 2024 in the data. Children under 15 made up about 83 percent of all cases, with the highest rate in children aged five to nine years old. Cases clustered in winter, and every reported outbreak event happened at a school site, with primary schools and kindergartens accounting for roughly nine in ten events.
pmc-13474880:
Kurtz and co-authors reviewed healthy ageing programs in 2026 to see whether studies check who benefits and who gets left behind. They used the PROGRESS framework, which lists eight equity factors from place of residence and race to education and social capital. The team searched three databases for measured evaluations of programs meant to help people age well.

Of 5,892 studies screened, 66 qualified, most published after 2018 with participants averaging 71.4 years of age across the included trials. Every study reported gender, 74 percent reported education, and 58 percent reported race or ethnicity, yet 38 percent never analyzed outcomes by any equity factor. Among 254 outcome results pulled from the studies, about 39 percent suggested shrinking inequity, while about 4 percent suggested programs actually widened gaps between groups.
pmc-13476780:
Zahra Chakeri and co-authors set out a trial plan in 2026 testing pelvic physiotherapy for blood flow to the womb in repeated implantation failure. Women with at least two failed transfers and weak womb flow by ultrasound index may join. Care blends electrical therapy, hands-on work, exercise, and a heat-based device method. A pilot at one hospital in Tabriz plans twenty-two members.

Primary checks cover womb blood flow, lining thickness, and lining pattern. Secondary checks span sexual function, mood, life quality, and pregnancy up to twelve weeks. At submission, the pilot was planned but not yet run, so no outcome data exist. The protocol fixes methods before results can sway them.
pmc-13477380:
Francesco Bax and colleagues report a 2026 prospective study on why stress-related high blood sugar worsens recovery after a minor stroke. The team recruited patients at five stroke centers in Italy and the United Kingdom between 2022 and 2023. All had mild strokes, little prior disability, and no large blocked vessel.

Among 1,316 patients, higher stress sugar ratios were linked to worse function at three months and to more bleeding inside the damaged brain area. Statistical mediation analysis credited that bleeding with about 15 percent of the sugar effect on poor outcome. The bleeding pathway mattered most in patients near age 60, those without diabetes, and those with higher inflammation markers. The authors say these patterns could guide patient selection for future treatment trials.
pmc-13477480:
Rye feeds people and livestock and shrugs off cold and pests, but its huge, repeat-filled genome long resisted a clean read. Erwang Chen led a large team that built a fresh, chromosome-scale assembly of the inbred rye line Lo7. They combined several sequencing and mapping methods to span six point seven six billion DNA letters, with long unbroken stretches and all seven centromeres, the chromosome hubs, fully assembled.

Inside those hubs they traced jumping DNA elements called retrotransposons. Two families proved both plentiful and recently active in rye, unlike in wheat. Clusters of rye-only repeat DNA were assembled whole and confirmed by microscope tests. The team offers the genome as a sharper base for rye and cereal research.
pmc-13477580:
Zexuan Wang and colleagues present a 2026 methods paper on shrinking complex biomedical data into maps that people can inspect. Standard mapping tools ignore known labels, such as cell type or patient status, so maps can miss the structure that matters. Supervised tools use labels but often pull groups too far apart and distort the true shape of the data.

Their framework, DG-UMAP, first trains a classifier in the original high-dimensional space. It then uses the geometry near the classifier's decision boundaries to gently stretch the space along informative directions. A parametric mapping step follows, so the final picture should separate classes while staying faithful to the underlying layout. The authors frame the method for single-cell, clinical, and other health datasets where labels carry real biological meaning.
pmc-13477780:
Aiswarya and a lab team in India set in 2026 two ways of testing semen side by side, and tried a fresh marker for male infertility. Hand counts under a lens are cheap but swing with the eye of the tester. A computer rig, called CASA, reads count, swim speed, and shape the same way each run. The team ran both ways on 200 samples from men in couples who could not conceive. They also gauged calprotectin, a swelling linked protein, in the fluid.

The two ways tracked each other tight on main scores, above all total sperm count and strength of swim. The marker told a weak tale: more calprotectin went with slightly worse counts, swim, and shape, but the links were faint. Smoking showed faint harm links as well. The authors back the rig for fair, firm reads, and ask for bigger studies on the marker.
pmc-13478580:
Shinji Takasugi and three colleagues tested in 2026 smaller one-hot encodings for QUBO problems solved by quantum and simulated annealing. One-hot rules force exactly one variable to be true, and their encoding size drives how large a problem the solver can handle.

They compared encodings borrowed from Boolean satisfiability problems with newly invented ones, judging each on problem size and solution quality. Their new reduced commander encoding gave one of the best trade-offs between compact size and good solutions on the benchmark studied. The result offers solver users a leaner way to state exactly-one rules without giving up answer quality.
pmc-13479580:
Yi-Xi Zhang and two colleagues proposed in 2026 epineuronal space as a hidden layer between neurons and mind. Mapping single cells to whole minds stalls because one element can yield many outcomes and one outcome can arise from many elements.

Borrowing from embryo biology, where epigenotype bridges genes and traits at tissue scale, they describe a level above single neurons built from neural assemblies, rhythms, and their joint patterns and working states. New probes such as Neuropixels let researchers build this space and test the frame, joining system-level and cell-level views. The proposal turns a mapping snag into a testable hierarchy rather than a mystery of emergence.
pmc-13479980:
Fatemeh Mahmoudi and colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of violence faced by nurses in hospitals in poorer countries. The team searched four large databases for work from 2003 to 2024 and kept 74 studies for close review. Their aim was to map why attacks and abuse occur and what steps might cut the risk.

Causes fell into groups tied to patients and families, to nurses under strain, to crowded wards, to low public awareness, and to wider politics. Suggested steps were grouped by timing: steps before an event, steps during an event such as calling security, and steps after an event such as filing a report. The review shows that no single fix will work and that ward design, policy, and public outreach all matter.
pmc-13480280:
Soichiro Kobayashi and co-authors report a heart artery link that grew into a septal defect closure device over eight years, in work from twenty twenty-six. The patient, a seventy year old man, had a device placed to close a hole between the heart's upper chambers. A check angiogram years later found the odd vessel.

No artery narrowing was seen. Instead, a branch of a heart artery had enlarged and stretched into the device over time. CT scans showed dye inside the device and a left to right leak, which hints the device surface never fully sealed. The authors think a prior vessel link grew with the device in place. Such growth may add to late device problems and needs watch.
pmc-13480580:
Tomoya Yamamoto and co-authors describe a 2026 glow probe that watches protein droplets harden inside cells. Proteins often gather into liquid droplets that slowly stiffen into fibres tied to disease, yet the standard check bleaches one droplet at a time. The team built coumarin dyes that shine in two colours at once, with a twisted shape set by a five-atom ring that carries varied atoms.

Swapping ring atoms tuned both the two-colour balance and brightness. Glued to a test protein, the dye reported droplet stiffening as a colour ratio that microscopes could read across many droplets at once. A light-tag trick then let the team compare droplet interiors inside living cells. Screening drugs that slow fibre growth gains a faster, parallel readout from the probe.
pmc-13481480:
Roger S. McIntyre and seven colleagues published this 2026 review on add-on drug treatments for major depression in patients who also have anxiety symptoms. Anxiety alongside depression signals heavier illness, more suicide risk and worse daily function, yet guidelines say little that is specific to this group. The authors first examine the monoamine theory, which blames disturbed brain chemicals, then survey trial evidence for add-on medicines.

The treatments reviewed include several antipsychotic drugs, bupropion, ketamine and esketamine, lithium and others. Aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, quetiapine XR and ketamine or esketamine showed improvement in depression or anxiety in this subgroup, though mostly in short-term analyses of trials not designed for anxiety. For olanzapine, risperidone and several others, data in anxious depression were scarce or absent. The authors call for trials built around anxiety outcomes from the start, rather than afterthoughts to depression trials.
pmc-13482280:
Nakano and colleagues test whether two sperm proteins are essential for fertilisation in rats. Their 2026 paper examines DCST1 and DCST2, sperm membrane proteins known to matter in mice and zebrafish. Their exact step differed between species: binding in fish, fusion in mice. The team created rats lacking both proteins.

Double-knockout males were completely infertile in mating tests, matching the mouse and fish results. Their sperm swam normally and completed the acrosome reaction, the preparatory change for fertilisation, at normal rates. The sperm crossed into the space around the egg and attached to its membrane but could not fuse with it. Since the human proteins resemble the rodent versions more than the fish ones, the authors conclude the fusion role is widely conserved in mammals.
pmc-13482580:
Kei Jokura and Gáspár Jékely offer a 2026 review that rethinks nerve nets, the loose mesh wiring found in jellyfish, comb jellies, and many other animals. Old theory casts such nets as crude leftovers on the road to brains. Fresh tools, from gene-tagged animals to volume electron microscopy, now reveal fine wiring that classical anatomy missed.

Signals can spread widely through the mesh, and chemical broadcast without direct contacts adds layered control that drives rich behaviour. Comb jellies even fuse their net cells into one shared web that runs the body as a distributed system. The authors argue the net is no rough draft but a lasting design with real strengths for whole-body coordination. Evolution courses that file nets under primitive need a rewrite in light of the new maps.
pmc-13483580:
Kathryn Berzins and colleagues describe building a primary care intervention for people whose mental distress is rooted in poverty. Published in 2026, the Destress II project responds to rising antidepressant prescribing in low-income areas of the United Kingdom, where short visits and long therapy waits push clinicians toward medication. General practitioners and community members shaped the program together using the Behaviour Change Wheel.

An early in-person version ran in 53 practices, then a refined web-based version was tested in 30 more. Participants valued the content, the chance for whole-team discussion, and a length that fit existing training meetings. Many said the program reinforced holistic habits rather than teaching wholly new ideas. The work offers a practical template for time-pressed practices.
pmc-13484480:
Mustika and colleagues explored whether butterfly pea flower extract could calm the immune pathways that drive psoriasis, a chronic scaly skin disease. Current injected drugs targeting those pathways work well but cost much and carry safety concerns. Their 2026 study profiled the extract's chemistry, predicted effects by computer, docked candidate compounds against two key immune signals, and ran antioxidant tests in dishes.

Chemical profiling found fourteen major compounds, mostly flavonoids, the pigment family common in edible flowers. Five candidates passed safety and activity screens, and two bound the target signals more strongly in docking than a standard steroid drug used for comparison. The extract showed moderate radical-scavenging power in laboratory antioxidant assays. Cell tests in an inflammation model supported a calming effect. Mustika positions the flower as a functional food candidate, not a drug replacement.
pmc-13486680:
Han Wu tackles a coal mine roadway squeezed between two already-mined faces, where rock deforms unevenly and support keeps failing. Published in 2026, the study of the Xiegou mine's isolated face combines field measurement, calculation, and simulation across digging and mining phases. Stress mapping shows a fractured, highly stressed ring at the face edges with calmer rock in the middle.

Shallow rock fails by pulling apart while deep rock fails by shearing under the high-low-high stress pattern. Early even sagging of roof, floor, and walls later turns lopsided, with walls and roof sinking faster on one side. Ahead of the advancing face, peak stress swings toward the working side at about seven meters out. Differentiated support, stronger where the asymmetry bites, follows from the mapped pattern.
pmc-13487380:
Perpetuini and colleagues in Italy took neck tests on the road in 2026, tracking fifteen adults on a fourteen day Himalayan trek. Long walks with a pack can strain the neck, and thin air adds stress. The team gauged neck movement range at low camp, at the top stay near five thousand meters, and back down low. The men also wore sensors for muscle signals and heat based skin scans. Packs stayed light, under a tenth of body weight.

Forward and back neck bend range grew by the end of the trek. Muscle sensors showed uneven change: the right side worked harder in turns, the left in side bends. Skin heat over the worked muscles fell during side bends. The authors read this as lopsided tuning of neck muscles to the trek. They also see proof that this test mix can work in harsh field sites.
pmc-13488180:
Auda Nadira and co-authors pool studies on fat tissue hormones and later heart events after a heart attack in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The hormones adiponectin and visfatin come from body fat and may signal risk beyond body weight alone. Five cohort studies with 707 patients from four countries, followed for periods from two months to nearly four years, met the review rules.

Patients who went on to suffer major heart events had lower adiponectin and higher visfatin levels than those who stayed event-free in pooled results. Body mass index did not separate the groups usefully. Results varied a lot between studies for adiponectin, which tempers confidence. The authors suggest the pair could refine risk checks after a heart attack.
pmc-13488280:
Caroline Jensen and colleagues run a farm pilot on magnesium feed supplements and tail biting in young pigs in a 2026 study in Denmark. Tail biting harms welfare and farm income, and routine tail docking is banned in the European Union, so alternatives matter. The trial covered 381 pigs with intact tails across two batches. It compared magnesium oxide, magnesium aspartate, and no supplement. Blood magnesium, stress hormone, and tail and ear lesions were tracked to nine weeks of life.

Blood magnesium fell in all groups after three weeks, just as tail lesions rose, including in the oxide group. The aspartate form held blood levels somewhat higher, yet neither form reliably cut lesions or stress markers in this age group. Baseline oddities cloud reading, and the authors call for deeper work on magnesium in young pigs.
pmc-13489780:
Barbara Burtness and others report pivotal results for amivantamab in recurrent or spread head and neck cancer after checkpoint immune care and chemo. In 2026, the phase Ib/II OrigAMI-4 cohort gives under the skin amivantamab every three weeks to 102 people with HPV-negative disease, excluding prior anti-EGFR therapy. The drug blocks both EGFR and MET, targets overexpressed in most such tumours.

Independent review found a response rate of forty-two percent, with fifteen percent complete responses and over half of responses lasting at least six months. Median progression-free lives was about seven months and overall lives about twelve and a half months at a median follow-up near one year. Side effects matched prior experience, with low treatment-related discontinuation, beating historical results for paclitaxel or cetuximab.
pmc-13490280:
Rueter and co-workers in Australia reviewed in 2026 how anaphylaxis, a severe allergic shock, shows up in babies and toddlers. They read emergency ward records for 243 children aged two years and under, drawn from two five year spans. Cases in this age group had more than doubled between the spans. The team charted symptoms, food and drug triggers, care given, and which children had a second wave of illness after the first one eased.

Hives were the top sign, seen in most cases, while pale skin and floppy tone marked the youngest group in a way not seen in older kids. A second wave hit a small share of cases, always after food triggers, and struck between about one and five and a half hours later. Low blood pressure, pale and floppy signs, need for fluids, and a severe first wave each raised the risk of a return.
pmc-13490480:
Palone and a large team exposed newborn mice to 5G millimeter waves for their first three weeks of life and examined their skin, where such waves mostly stop. Public concern about 5G focuses on skin because penetration is shallow. Their 2026 study exposed two mouse strains around the clock in cycles at two power levels, comparing them with sham-exposed controls on tissue structure, gene activity, and immune cell behavior.

Skin structure stayed visibly normal at both exposure levels, with no overt tissue damage under the microscope. Gene activity shifted modestly in inflammation pathways, with three signaling genes acting as hubs across all groups. Mast cells, the skin's allergy sentries, released their granules more readily after exposure. One change appeared only in normal mice, a mild immune activation pattern. Palone stresses the effects were molecular and mild, not disease.
pmc-13491680:
Prabin Upadhyaya reviews in 2026 how epigenetic machinery, the systems that switch genes on and off without changing DNA, shapes diseases of heart muscle called cardiomyopathies. Mutations explain only part of why patients with the same genetic change fare so differently. The review covers the main disease types, from dilated to hypertrophic, and the protein complexes that remodel chromatin, the packaging of DNA.

Complexes such as SWI/SNF, NuRD, and Polycomb work with chemical marks on DNA and its packaging proteins to drive harmful gene programs. Because these changes can in principle be reversed, they offer treatment angles that fixed mutations do not. Drugs that block certain mark-removing enzymes helped in early models, and gene editing tools aimed at single loci are proposed for the future.
pmc-13491980:
Grace Mamibel Lassio and nine colleagues describe in 2026 the face of mpox in Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, across 2024 and 2025. The viral disease has shifted from rural spillovers toward sustained city transmission since 2022. The team combined treatment center records with national laboratory data for confirmed cases with complete files.

Nearly every health zone in the city reported cases, with the densest incidence in five urban districts. Young adults aged fifteen to thirty-four made up well over half of patients, and hospitalization typically lasted about two weeks. Fever, itching, swollen glands, and skin ulcers were frequent complaints. Two viral subclades circulated side by side, one commoner in men and the other in women within the hardest-hit age group, a split the authors say surveillance must track.
pmc-13492380:
Francesca Bonato leads a twenty-one-author team probing in 2026 why the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel damages nerves. Their focus is how the drug physically reshapes microtubules, the cell's internal rails. Paclitaxel locks those rails steady against cancer, yet the same treatment often causes peripheral neuropathy, nerve damage in hands and feet. The team designed chemical cousins of the drug to separate its rail-locking action from its lattice-warping side effect.

One analogue, called 1b, held microtubules just as steady while leaving their lattice in a near-natural state. Cells treated with the original drug showed expanded lattices, disrupted cargo transport by motor proteins, and frozen behavior of the stabilizing protein Tau. The gentler analogue preserved healthier Tau dynamics and transport. Rail locking and lattice damage, the authors conclude, are separable, opening a path to kinder taxane drugs.
pmc-13494080:
Erland Östberg and colleagues report a 2026 lab study on whether low blood pressure during general anesthesia helps cause atelectasis, the collapse of tiny air sacs in the lung. Collapsed areas are common under anesthesia and can lead to lung problems after surgery. The team tested the idea in pigs, since known causes do not fully explain how much collapse still occurs.

Twelve anesthetized pigs on breathing machines went through both a normal-pressure phase and a phase of deep low pressure brought on with a drug, in random order. Scans showed more collapsed lung volume when pressure was low, in eleven of the twelve animals. Blood flow also shifted toward the back of the lung, and the blood there carried less oxygen. The authors suggest that keeping pressure up at the start of anesthesia may limit collapse.
pmc-13495080:
Breydan Wright and six co-authors weighed the costs and gains of longer antibiotic cover after joint replacement in twenty twenty-six. They drew on same-day hip and knee replacements at one surgery center, where some patients got extra oral antibiotics after the operation and some did not. The main outcome was joint infection within ninety days, judged with Bayesian methods and cost models.

For knees, infection rates were point one three percent with extra cover and point two six percent without. That small gain was one the models found likely to pay off at the stated costs. For hips, rates were close either way and no gain was found. Gains in patient-rated outcomes were alike in both groups. The authors back a selective, risk-based use of longer cover, in line with care not to overuse antibiotics.
pmc-13495180:
Karl Valerdi and colleagues trace, in a 2026 animal study, how Nipah virus attacks the brain in hamsters. Nipah, found across South-East Asia and the western Pacific, kills a large share of those it infects and leaves survivors with disability. No drug or vaccine exists, and how the virus wrecks the brain stayed unclear, so the team used a hamster model that mirrors illness.

The virus reached brain areas, among them the cortex and the hippocampus, a memory center. It infected neurons, their support cells, and cells of the blood-brain barrier, the wall that guards the brain. Support cells switched into an active, inflamed state, and vessels and neurons suffered harm, leaving patches of damaged tissue. The authors describe a pull toward the central nervous system as the driver of the damage and death seen in this model, a picture that may guide the hunt for treatments.
pmc-13495280:
Aylin Yılmaz and Didar Kurt compare, in a 2026 study, blood inflammation markers in women with eclampsia and in healthy pregnant women. Eclampsia, marked by seizures in pregnancy, is a grave cause of mother death and harm, and cheap blood markers that flag it would help. The team computed eight combined markers from blood counts taken before delivery in 31 patients and 51 matched controls.

Most markers did not differ between the groups. Two, built from platelet counts, ran lower in the eclampsia group. The patients also delivered earlier, had smaller babies, and faced far more cesarean births, intensive care stays, and complications. The authors say the two lower markers might one day serve as negative signs, ruling risk down rather than up, but their diagnostic weight stays limited and larger forward-looking studies are needed.
pmc-13495480:
Xuyi Tang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two rootstocks of Camellia oleifera, China's main woody oil crop, under phosphorus shortage. Acid soils across the south starve the crop of phosphorus, and grafting onto tough roots can help, yet how rootstocks confer tolerance was murky. The team set a tolerant line, Ganwu 1, against a sensitive one, Ganwu 2, and read roots, chemistry, and genes.

Under low phosphorus the tolerant line rebuilt its roots, growing far more root mass and fine root volume than its rival. It gathered several times more phosphorus into roots and used each unit better, while feeding potassium to shoots. The sensitive line wasted effort on sprawling roots, lost protein, and took more cell damage. Gene switches for phosphorus hunting fired earlier and stronger in the tolerant line. The authors name it a prime rootstock for poor acid soils.
pmc-13499480:
Tae-Hwan Park and colleagues study in 2026 how a variant in a gene called USP15, linked to autism spectrum disorder, changes early brain development in lab-grown tissue. The gene helps recycle proteins, and rare damaging variants turn up in some autistic people, yet their effect on growing brains was unknown. The team grew miniature brain tissues, called organoids, from human stem cells carrying the variant and profiled single cells gene by gene.

Effects depended on dose. Organoids with one altered copy shifted progenitor cells, the early builders of the cortex, toward later states, with altered deep-layer nerve cell maturation and wiring organisation. Cells with two altered copies showed broader disruption, including slowed cell division, misplaced body-pattern genes, and stress responses. Mutant signatures overlapped known autism risk genes, offering a human model for tracing how one rare variant steers development.
pmc-13500080:
Jacques Balayla proposes in 2026 a new way to read fetal heart tracings during labour, testing the idea in simulation before any patient data are touched. Standard tracing review suffers from poor reader agreement and weak specificity for fetal oxygen failure. His framework, named FETAL, compares the frequency spectrum of a heart-rate signal, meaning how its rhythm energy distributes across speeds, against a reference template built from normal-like signals. The score is the distance between spectra.

Twelve rounds covered five scenarios, from no true difference through weak, moderate, and strong spectral shifts, plus a moderate shift corrupted by artefacts such as signal gaps and maternal heart-rate contamination. The spectral score stayed at chance where no difference existed and rose steadily with shift strength. It dipped under artefact stress, while two standard summary measures stayed near chance throughout. Validation against cord blood gases is the decisive next step.
pmc-13500980:
Hiroshi Sonobe leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 case of pleural deciduoid mesothelioma, a rare form of a cancer that grows on the lining of the chest. The patient was a 75-year-old man with past asbestos exposure. CT imaging showed multiple nodules in the left pleura plus fluid around the lung, and fluid cytology found large, highly atypical epithelioid tumour cells. Biopsy tissue formed sheets of large cells resembling decidual tissue, which gives this variant its name.

Staining showed the cells carried mesothelial markers calretinin, Wilms tumor 1, and podoplanin, while three tumour-related proteins, BAP1, MTAP, and merlin, were lost. A fluorescence test found frequent homozygous deletions of the CDKN2A gene, and electron microscopy showed sheets of large cells packed with intermediate filaments but no surface microvilli. The man received immune checkpoint inhibitors combined with chemotherapy, and no disease progression was seen seven months into treatment.
pmc-13501580:
Bokyoung Choi leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 project to build a survey for tracking working conditions and health among formal care workers in South Korea. The country became a super-aged society in 2024, and aides in hospitals and long-term care facilities carry much of the elder care load, yet no dedicated cohort study of this workforce existed. Development ran in phases: reviewing labour and care surveys, interviewing facility workers, drafting and merging items, checking content validity with experts, and pilot testing.

The finished framework has three major domains covering sociodemographic characteristics, the care work environment, and health. Those domains split into 11 subdomains and 79 survey variables in total. Items span employment status, workload, occupational safety, organizational and social support, working hours, income, and physical and mental health. The authors present the instrument as a foundation for long-term monitoring and policy evaluation in ageing societies.
pmc-13501680:
Jingjia He leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 study linking daily movement patterns to depressive symptom risk in Chinese adolescents. Data came from a city-wide school physical examination covering 11,152 adolescents, about half of them boys, with a mean age of 14.3 years. Questionnaires captured sedentary time, walking, moderate-to-vigorous activity, sleep, and depressive symptoms. An isotemporal substitution model then estimated what happens when thirty minutes of one behaviour replaces another.

Overall, about 38 percent of participants screened at risk for depressive symptoms, with girls at 44 percent against 32 percent for boys in that flagged share. Swapping thirty minutes of sitting for sleep lowered the odds of risk, with odds ratios near 0.9 in both boys and girls. Among adolescents missing the one-hour activity target, swapping sitting for vigorous activity helped boys clearly, with an odds ratio of 0.67, while the girls' estimate was inconclusive.
pmc-13502480:
Melih E Ceyhan leads a five-author team with a 2026 case where tuberculosis of the abdominal lining impersonated widespread cancer. A 47-year-old woman arrived with three months of abdominal pain, appetite loss, night sweats, and about six kilograms of weight loss. CT imaging showed free fluid, infiltrated fat, and many nodules studding the peritoneum and omentum. Her CA-125 tumour marker was markedly high at 758.3 units per millilitre, and a specialist review found no cancer, leaving the picture genuinely unclear.

Endoscopies added incidental findings, so the team proceeded to laparoscopy and biopsied both tissues. Under the microscope the tissue showed granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid cells and Langhans-type giant cells, the signature architecture of the disease, and her QuantiFERON blood test came back positive. Anti-tuberculosis therapy began at once and ran seven months without adverse events. The authors warn that peritoneal tuberculosis copies carcinomatosis feature for feature, marker included.
pmc-13503880:
Zhen Wu and four colleagues build a detector for tiny flaws on silicon wafers, in a 2026 paper. Such flaws are faint, sparse in detail, and packed close on noisy backgrounds, so standard image tools miss them. Missed flaws lower chip yield and can harm device life.

Their detector, Wafer-DETR, sharpens detail by mixing wave-based and edge cues early in the network. A fusion step weighs traits across scales and adapts to noise. A rebuild step keeps edges crisp so close flaws do not merge into one blob. On factory data from a real line, scores beat a strong rival detector by a few points. The authors say the steadier reads suit automated checks on live production lines.
pmc-13504780:
I. M. Sambade leads a team mapping the genetics of Manila clam resistance to a deadly parasite, in a 2026 study. The clam is a top farmed shellfish, and the parasite Perkinsus olseni causes mass die-offs on clam beds. Breeding resistant stock could cut those losses.

The team raised over six hundred young clams from 32 families and exposed them to the parasite in tanks. A new gene chip read nearly fifty thousand markers per clam. About half the spread in parasite load traced to additive gene effects, a moderate-high heritability that favors selective breeding. Several genome zones linked to resistance, spread across seven chromosomes. One zone on chromosome 18 stood out, also within the largest family. The authors back gene-guided breeding for hardier clams.
pmc-13505180:
Ying-xiang Chen and colleagues gathered qualitative research on how stigma around opioids affects cancer pain care. Guidelines support opioids for moderate to severe cancer pain, yet undertreatment stays common amid tight regulation. The team searched eight databases through March 2026 and combined twenty studies using thematic synthesis, gathering 145 findings.

Four broad themes emerged from the combined findings. Cultural stories and hospital routines built the stigma, and patients often absorbed it as shame or fear, speaking less about pain and asking less for help. Clinicians felt pulled between relieving pain and managing risk, and many prescribed cautiously. During visits, patients felt forced to prove their pain was real while clinicians answered defensively. The authors call for action at several levels to ease stigma and support shared decisions about pain treatment.
pmc-13506980:
Evelien Hoevenaars and a team of co-authors compare two non-surgical care paths for adults with spinal deformity. Their twenty twenty-six cohort study deals with patients who have scoliosis and chronic low back pain but no case for surgery. One group got a biopsychosocial program, which treats pain as a mix of body, mind, and social factors.

The other group got usual care, focused on the body alone. Each group held ninety-five patients, matched on set rules, and all were tracked for one year. The program group improved far more in function, the main measure. About half hit a meaningful gain, against about a quarter under usual care. Pain and quality of life moved the same way.
pmc-13507080:
Parker T Bassett leads a 2026 team that imaged heart amyloid fibrils from a patient with light chain amyloidosis, a disease where faulty antibody parts fold wrong and clog organs. Using cryo-electron microscopy, a method that freezes samples for detailed imaging, they solved fibrils built from the IGLV6-57 gene segment. The fibrils came in two forms, with single and double strands.

Each form showed a fold not seen before in this disease. Side-by-side checks with known fibrils found shared motifs despite local shifts from sequence changes. Shared folding steps may drive fibril growth across patients. Mapping those steps could guide drugs that block harmful buildup in heart and kidney tissue.
pmc-13507380:
Andrews and Kanekiyo reviewed what is known about the antibody repertoire humans deploy against influenza, in a 2026 survey of the field. Flu has co-evolved with people for centuries. Across people antibodies repeatedly converge on the same solutions, gripping conserved weak spots on the virus's two surface proteins that the virus cannot change without crippling itself. Many of these shared antibodies are written directly into inherited immune genes.

Andrews describes these recurring multi-donor antibody classes aimed at supersites on hemagglutinin, the attachment protein, and neuraminidase, the release enzyme. The review explains how single-cell methods, structural biology, and computation are now revealing previously uncharted parts of the repertoire. Because such antibodies arise reliably in person after person, vaccine designers hope to aim new vaccines squarely at the conserved sites they target. That would shift the long arms race with this shape-shifting virus in humanity's favor.
pmc-13508280:
Ruth Pérez Gallego and others uncover new genomic insights into long-chain sea-fat making in the marine alga Gephyrocapsa huxleyi. In 2026, the study cleans and builds genomes of two extra non-axenic strains, CCMP1742 and CCMP2758, adding to the single on-hand guide genome of strain CCMP1516. Long-chain sea-fats, lipids with thirty-five to forty-two carbon chains, serve as widely used old-heat clues.

A chain-building synthase in CCMP1516 emerges as a possible source of sea-fat making, with close look-alike makers switched on at varied levels across heats and time in the new strains. A limited set of bond-adders may add the third and fourth double bonds. Mapping this pathway lifts grasp of sea-fat control and strengthens old-heat rebuilds.
pmc-13508380:
Benjamin Clarkson leads a ten-author team asking whether inflamed human neurons can show their own proteins to killer immune cells, in 2026 work. In multiple sclerosis, brain lesions swarm with CD8 killer T cells in an inflammation-rich setting, and neurons may be targets. The team grew neuron clusters from human stem cells and dosed them with an inflammatory signal, IFNγ. Protein display machinery on the neurons was then pulled down and read with sensitive instruments.

The signal switched the display system on, letting the team recover a normal-looking set of short protein fragments. Neurons fitted with a test protein string showed those pieces and provoked matching T cells, which damaged the nerve fibers. Comparing four donors, the neuron display differed from skin cell controls and shared recurring pieces from a nerve fiber protein. The platform opens a route to naming the exact targets in this disease.
pmc-13509180:
Magdalena Maj and Leszek Czupryniak track five years of germ changes in diabetic foot infections at a large Polish outpatient center, in 2026 work. These infections drive most non-trauma leg amputations, and starter antibiotic choices must match local germs. The team re-read every culture from infected diabetic foot wounds from 2021 to 2025. In total, 274 cultures grew 443 germs, most wounds holding more than one kind.
