The classic skin germ Staphylococcus aureus stayed most common, yet its share fell from over half to under two fifths of cultures. Gut-family germs climbed to nearly half of all isolates. Drug resistance milestones arrived in 2025: the first resistant staph cases on renewed testing, the first germ fully resisting a last-line drug class, and two more with reduced sensitivity. The authors urge starter regimens for serious infections to cover gut germs and resistant staph by default.
pmc-13509880:
Shakeel Shahzad, Mark D. P. Willcox, Bushra Jamil, Binod Rayamajhee, and Muhammad Yasir test how hospital strains of a hard-to-treat bacterium respond to last-line antibiotics and to related germ-killing chemicals, in 2026 work. The panel held clinical strains from Australia, Pakistan, and Switzerland plus standard lab strains, including a few already resistant to the last-line drugs called polymyxins. Because these drugs, common disinfectants, and natural peptide defenses all attack the cell outer coat, the team checked whether resistance to one meant resistance to others.

Most strains stayed sensitive to the polymyxins, while a small set showed strong resistance. One disinfectant worked best among its kind, and one natural peptide gave the lowest and steadiest blocking levels. Strains resistant to polymyxins unexpectedly needed less of two disinfectants to be stopped. The authors call the work exploratory and say cross-resistance fears need testing strain by strain.
pmc-13510280:
Felix A. Wolters, Anna Eichler, and Oliver Kratz set out a 2026 study protocol for testing a German version of a clinical interview that rates limited prosocial emotions in young people. Such emotions cover a lack of guilt, shallow feeling, and low concern for others, and they mark a subgroup within disruptive behavior disorders. The planned study will recruit children and teenagers aged eight to eighteen with that diagnosis, across several centers in Germany, together with their main caregivers.

The semi-structured interview will be checked against other measures to judge whether it captures the trait soundly. A planned side analysis will sort high-trait young people into two variants. One shows low anxiety and less abuse history, and the other shows high anxiety and more abuse history. The team hopes a proven German tool will let clinics tailor treatment to each variant. The protocol was registered before the work began.
pmc-13510580:
Isabella Martins and five co-authors show that a simple chain molecule found in all cells can switch down a key enzyme, in 2026 work. The chain, called inorganic polyphosphate, attaches loosely to lysine-rich stretches of proteins. The enzyme studied here tags other proteins with a fatty anchor so they can sit in cell membranes and pass signals. It was already flagged as a possible chain target.

Lab tests showed the chain lowered enzyme activity in a dose-linked way, with longer chains blocking more strongly than medium ones. In living cells, added or internally raised chain levels cut signaling from a membrane protein that depends on the enzyme. Cells loaded with extra enzyme lost viability as chain dose rose. A short lysine-rich peptide reversed the binding signs, confirming a specific, reversible grip. The authors name the enzyme as a true functional target.
pmc-13511080:
Xiaoyue Zheng, Hao Li, Shu Wang, Huiyan Cheng, and Huien Zhao build a lab system for growing and genetically altering a wild chrysanthemum relative prized for toughness, in 2026 work. The plant, Ajania achilleoides, adapts well to harsh settings, which makes its genes valuable for study and breeding. No efficient way to regrow whole plants from tissue or to insert genes had existed for this species.

Starting from leaf pieces, one hormone mix coaxed shoots to form in nearly every case, and a halved nutrient mix with a rooting hormone rooted every shoot. The team set the doses of a selection drug that separate altered tissue from plain tissue, then tuned infection timing and strength for gene delivery by a soil bacterium. Gene tests confirmed insertion in three lines. The system gives breeders a working platform for gene studies in this wild relative.
pmc-13515680:
Yeon Soo Kim and four colleagues report, in a 2026 cohort study with meta-analysis, a safer way to perform surgical tracheostomy. A tube that slips out by accident can kill a patient within minutes. Their hospital reviewed 1,485 open tracheostomies done between 2011 and early 2026. In 2015 the hospital adopted a bundle built on a downward-based flap of tracheal wall, the Björk flap, plus standardised care before and after surgery.

Before the bundle, such emergencies struck once or twice a year, with at least one death. Afterward, a single event occurred in twelve years, with no deaths. In a closely tracked subset, accidental tube loss hit about five percent with the classic vertical cut against under one percent with the flap. Pooling published studies pointed the same way for infection, blockage, bleeding, and other harms, though certainty stays low. The authors present the flap-plus-bundle package as promising, not proven.
pmc-13518180:
Nourah Almansour and colleagues test two small antimicrobial proteins as blood flags for sepsis and pneumonia, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Sepsis is deadly and hard to spot early, and it overlaps confusingly with pneumonia. The candidate markers, human beta-defensins 3 and 6, are part of the body's first-line defenses.

One hundred ninety adults were sorted into sepsis, pneumonia, both, and healthy groups. Both defensins, as gene activity and as protein, ran clearly higher in every patient group than in controls. Their accuracy profile was lopsided: sensitive, catching most cases, but only modestly specific. Defensin 6 stood out for sepsis with or without pneumonia. The authors present the pair as candidate diagnostic markers, promising but not clinic-ready, and call for bigger studies to sharpen their reliability.
pmc-13518980:
Abdulganiyu Sanusi and six colleagues test in 2026 whether eggshell powder can replace part of Portland cement in construction. Cement making drives about 8 percent of global emissions, while eggshells are a calcium-rich farm waste, over 80 percent calcium carbonate. The team swapped powder into two cement types and checked physical, strength, and chemical behavior against British and Indian standards.

Workability and setting times stayed within acceptable limits across mixes. Most samples beat the required strength benchmark, though two 10-percent mixes lost ground. Microscope and X-ray analyses confirmed the high carbonate content. Sanusi and co-authors recommend capping eggshell powder at 5 percent by weight to protect performance while cutting waste and emissions.
pmc-13520180:
Hirofumi Inoue, Yasumasa Tsuda, Yoshiko Nawata, and Kiyoshi Ichihara examine in 2026 why a bacterial-infection marker rises in toddlers with roseola, a mild viral illness caused by human herpesvirus 6. Procalcitonin usually flags severe bacterial disease and has been proposed as an early warning for brain complications, so stray elevations confuse clinicians. Their hospital cohort covered 188 febrile children under five who received the test.

Thirty children with confirmed first HHV-6 infection showed a higher median procalcitonin than 53 children with other confirmed viral illnesses. The roseola group also had lower white cell and platelet counts and higher liver enzymes. Every roseola patient recovered without brain complications. The authors link the elevation to virus-driven blood changes, urging cautious interpretation.
pmc-13520280:
Shulan Lin leads an eight-author cell study in 2026 on how dental pulp stem cells learn to act like pericytes, the contractile cells that wrap and stabilize new blood vessels. A signaling pair called EphB4 and EphrinB2 was suspected of steering this transformation, which matters for growing vessels in engineered tissue.

Dialing EphB4 down stripped the stem cells of contractile marker proteins and weakened their squeeze in gel assays, while dialing it up strengthened both. Gene profiling pointed to the transcription factor SRF as the relay: silencing SRF erased EphB4's gains. In three-dimensional sprouting cultures, impaired stem cells failed to restrain vessel outgrowth. Lin and colleagues map a three-step signaling axis for vessel maturation.
pmc-13520380:
Thomas B. Swinburn and colleagues study in 2026 written accounts from gay and bisexual men in Aotearoa New Zealand, plus other men who have sex with men. The accounts describe poor care talks about sexuality with family doctors. Fear of harsh judgement can delay testing for HIV and other infections.

The accounts came from 422 men in a large 2022 national survey. About one in five men in that survey reported a bad care talk. Themes covered judgement, disrespect and bias. Poor skills among doctors also came up often. Lasting harm included changing doctors and skipping care. One man said bad care put him off testing for years.
pmc-13521080:
Younus A Bhat and colleagues dissect in 2026 how two chromatin marks interact on yeast gene control units, where one mark tags histone H2B while a remodeler inserts a variant histone H2A.Z nearby. Yeast missing both systems cannot survive, hinting at a shared essential job.

Bench tests with rebuilt control units showed the H2B tag strongly blocks variant insertion by the remodeler. Genome-wide maps in normal growth barely changed without the tag, which surprised the team. Under replication stress, however, the tag proved necessary for moving the variant from promoters into gene bodies. Stress-specific teamwork reframes how the two marks cooperate.
pmc-13521780:
Huixia Wang and colleagues look for blood clues that forecast IVF success in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Ninety-two women at one Chinese hospital went through their first IVF cycle with embryo transfer. The team compared those who conceived with those who did not, across hormone, metabolic, and treatment measures.

The successful group was younger, needed less stimulating drug, and yielded more eggs. Its hormone pattern was calmer and its metabolism cleaner: lower blood sugar, insulin, and fats. Four measures independently tracked lower success odds: the LH-to-FSH ratio, a free testosterone index, the muscle hormone irisin, and total drug dose. Each offered moderate predictive power on its own. The authors suggest these everyday numbers can help counsel patients and tune cycles, while larger studies test firmer combinations.
pmc-13522580:
Mengyu Gan and collaborators create a tough smart hydrogel using an ionic weaving approach in a 2026 materials study. Hydrogels are water-rich soft materials prized for sensing and soft robotics, yet most are weak and swell underwater or freeze in the cold. Polymer chains were first arranged by controlled drying, then metal ions were added to form a network of reversible bonds.

Breaking many bonds at once absorbs energy, giving the gel high strength, stiffness, and toughness. Tight network constraints also resisted swelling and freezing and allowed reactivation after drying. The gel sensed reliably underwater, combined movement with sensing under solvent stimulation, and could be printed into shapes with programmed motion. The work points toward durable soft devices that act and sense together.
pmc-13523280:
Martina Ollosu leads a team comparing drugs added to spinal anesthesia for leg orthopedic surgery in a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis. One hundred eighty-three randomized trials covering more than fourteen thousand patients and twenty-seven interventions were pooled. The main outcome was how long effective pain relief lasted before the first extra painkiller was needed.

Combinations involving morphine ranked highest for prolonging relief, and morphine alone also lowered pain at twelve hours and reduced later opioid use without lengthening leg weakness. One alternative reduced pain yet markedly prolonged motor block and slowed heart rate more often. Nausea, vomiting, and itching were more frequent with some options. The authors rate the certainty of evidence as low to very low, so choices should weigh side effects alongside duration of relief.
pmc-13523380:
Golazin Garousi and co-authors test how a hormone signal suppresses feeding in newborn chicks in a 2026 animal study. Adropin, a peptide made mainly in liver and brain, was injected into the brain ventricles of broiler chicks across six experiments. Food intake was measured over two hours, and blockers of several appetite-related receptors were combined with adropin to find which pathways carry its effect.

Adropin reduced food intake more at higher doses. Blocking one neuropeptide Y receptor strengthened the effect, while blocking related receptors of another type had no effect. Blocking melanocortin receptors wiped out the effect entirely. The authors conclude that specific neuropeptide and melanocortin receptors contribute to how adropin curbs appetite in chicks, clarifying its brain signaling route.
pmc-13523480:
Mahboubeh Sadat Yousefi and colleagues compare, in a 2026 randomized trial, flipped classroom teaching with traditional lectures for nursing students learning fluid and electrolyte content. Students often struggle with this detailed, fast-moving topic. In a flipped model, students study material before class and use class time actively.

Fifty-eight students at Qom University of Medical Sciences in Iran were randomized evenly during the 2019-2020 academic year. Knowledge was measured with a 20-item multiple-choice test, and views of the classroom environment came from a standard inventory. Groups started alike on knowledge. After adjustment for starting scores, the flipped group scored markedly higher on the post-test, and classroom environment ratings also favored the flipped approach. The authors support wider use of the method for difficult nursing content.
pmc-13524080:
Thomas, writing solo in 2026, explains why a newly phased genome matters for the Kyoho grape. The article concerns polyploid plants, which carry more than two sets of chromosomes. Kyoho is a widely grown table grape whose extra chromosome sets came from a tangled ancestry that older genome assemblies could not separate.

Thomas describes how phasing splits the genome into haplotypes, the variant sets inherited together from each parent. That separation lets researchers ask which genome regions came from which ancestor and whether the ancestral genomes stayed distinct or mixed. Because haplotypes often track traits that matter to growers, the author argues a phased Kyoho reference enables precise haplotype-aware breeding. The piece also notes that many real polyploids blur the textbook split between duplication within one species and hybrid origins.
pmc-13524480:
Humberto de Araújo Brito Filho leads a large team in a 2026 feeding trial testing extracts from fruit residue as replacements for antibiotic growth promoters in European quail. Poultry producers seek natural additives that support growth and gut health. Extracts from pineapple, acerola, and cajá, all agro-industrial leftovers, were compared with an antibiotic control and an unsupplemented control.

Two hundred fifty day-old birds were randomized to five diets for 35 days. Pineapple and acerola groups matched controls on final weight and showed taller intestinal villi and better villus-to-crypt ratios in the ileum. The cajá group grew less, ate less in the later phase, had poorer ileal structure, and showed lower blood glucose, phosphorus, and protein measures. The authors conclude pineapple and acerola extracts look more promising than cajá for this purpose.
pmc-13525480:
Sramko and colleagues trial an intensive heart-rate strategy for a dangerous rhythm problem in failing hearts. Their 2026 LARISA trial enrols 40 patients with acute heart failure caused by atrial fibrillation, with heart rates above 130 and weakened pumping function. One group received protocolised rate control with landiolol, a fast, short-acting intravenous drug, plus digoxin; the other received standard therapy.

Rate control came faster with the intensive approach, at a median of one and a half hours against four hours. By two hours, heart rate had fallen 40 percent in the intensive group against 23 percent with standard care. The target was reached in 80 percent of intensive patients versus 20 percent of the rest. Breathlessness and lung congestion also eased more, without extra low blood pressure or adverse events. By 24 hours the groups had converged, so the benefit is speed.
pmc-13526080:
Kerim Şeker and colleagues assess, in a 2026 retrospective study, how well FDG PET and CT scan measures predict spread to armpit lymph nodes. Their focus is Luminal A breast cancer, a slower-growing hormone-sensitive subtype. Knowing nodal status before surgery shapes treatment. The team compared expert visual reading with quantitative uptake measures from the tumor and the armpit.

The cohort held 279 untreated women staged between January 2012 and December 2025, and nodal spread was confirmed in 152, over half. Every quantitative measure ran higher in the metastatic group. Armpit uptake outperformed visual reading alone, and a combined model integrating both reached the best accuracy. Adding numbers correctly reclassified nearly a third of metastatic patients whom visual reading had missed, and decision analysis favored the combined approach.
pmc-13526480:
Dundi and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare liver tumor presentation in a twelve-year-old boy with neurofibromatosis type 1, a common inherited disorder that grows benign nerve tumors. Plexiform neurofibromas, a sprawling subtype, usually arise under the skin of the back or limbs, almost never in the liver. The boy was brought in with vague abdominal pain, and ultrasound showed an infiltrating nodular growth along the porta hepatis, the liver's entry gate for vessels and ducts.

Liver MRI supported a plexiform neurofibroma diagnosis without the need for tissue sampling. The authors stress such lesions belong on the list when a patient with the disorder shows a liver mass, since plexiform tumors carry a small risk of turning malignant and need watching. The case adds a documented example to a literature that counts only a handful of children with this presentation.
pmc-13527080:
Neelam Rawat and colleagues turn curry plant seeds, a kitchen waste, into activated carbon for supercapacitor electrodes in a 2026 materials study. Sustainable energy storage needs cheap, high-surface carbon, and biomass precursors fit that goal. Ferrous chloride served as the activating agent before heating to nine hundred degrees under inert gas.

Multiple characterization methods confirmed a partially graphitized, hierarchically porous carbon with a surface area near 1,606 square meters per gram. Symmetric test cells using a polymer gel electrolyte delivered a specific capacitance above 220 farads per gram at low current, with modest energy density. After ten thousand charge cycles the device kept about eighty-eight percent of its capacitance with similar efficiency. The authors present the route as green, economical waste valorization.
pmc-13527980:
Chun-Chieh Yeh and three colleagues report a 2026 case of a hidden burn injury found after knee ligament surgery. The patient had revision arthroscopic repair of the anterior cruciate ligament under general anesthesia. A tourniquet stayed on for 120 minutes. Warming was applied to the upper body only. After transfer to the ward, staff found a deep partial-thickness injury on the top of the foot. It measured about eight by four centimeters.

The wound healed slowly with conservative care over roughly three months. A temporary contracture limited ankle movement and slowed rehab. By nine months the skin had closed and motion was nearly normal. The authors blame a mix of pressure, trapped heat under drapes, and poor heat escape during tourniquet use. They urge padding, care with drapes, and routine skin checks after surgery.
pmc-13528080:
Shuroug A. Alowais and six colleagues present flu-related heart inflammation cases from Saudi Arabia in a 2026 paper. Four adults were treated in Riyadh between late 2024 and mid-2025. Ages ran from 37 to 79, and three were women. Flu was confirmed by PCR testing. Heart involvement was judged by expert consensus criteria.

Illness ranged from mild inflammation with stable circulation to collapse needing heart-lung machines. All patients got the antiviral oseltamivir. Some also got anti-inflammatory or immune-calming drugs. Three recovered with normal heart function. The most severe patient died despite full support. A review of twenty-four published cases showed a similar split. About four in five recovered fully, while one in five died. The authors urge quick recognition and ready access to circulatory support.
pmc-13529080:
Suthar and colleagues tested whether ultrasound measurement of diaphragm strength before major abdominal surgery predicts which older patients will need a breathing machine afterward. Their 2026 prospective study enrolled ninety patients over fifty at one center. It measured the diaphragm thickening fraction before surgery and again before tube removal. That fraction shows how much the main breathing muscle thickens during a maximal breath.

Suthar found that patients whose preoperative thickening fell below the study threshold needed mechanical ventilation about one in four times, compared with roughly one in thirteen among stronger patients. About half the group already had diaphragmatic weakness before surgery. Preoperative thickening was the only independent predictor of later diaphragm function in adjusted analysis. A lower cutoff predicted intensive care stay with a strong ability to rule out risk when values were good. Better nutrition tracked with stronger diaphragms, suggesting a modifiable factor worth testing.
pmc-13529680:
Mola and colleagues investigated in 2026 whether antifungal medicines used in pregnancy, many sold without prescription, disturb the unborn child's hormone making. Some drugs act like endocrine disruptors, chemicals that interfere with hormones. The team joined a prospective mother-child cohort of 589 pairs with lab cultures of human fetal adrenal glands and rat pregnancy experiments to trace effects across species.

Timing decided the direction. Exposure early in pregnancy went with lower steroid hormone levels in babies and signs of weaker androgen action, including narrower penile width in infancy. Exposure from mid-pregnancy went with higher hormone levels and longer anogenital distance, a hormone-sensitive measure, in girls and boys. In the lab, clotrimazole cut progesterone output in human fetal adrenal cultures and in exposed rats, while miconazole lengthened anogenital distance in rats. The authors say the safety of topical antifungal use in pregnancy deserves a fresh look.
pmc-13530180:
Theng-Jia Law and colleagues tackle 2026 prediction of where public complaints will arise in a Malaysian city. Urban data mix numbers, places, and categories in ways that plain text models handle poorly. Their answer converts each record into a layered picture-like format that a language model can read directly.

Records covered 48,103 complaints from Seberang Perai plus landmarks, weather, population, and income data. A customized model pairing sentence embeddings with the picture format reached the top accuracy and trained far faster than fully retrained baselines. The approach gives councils a quicker way to aim inspections and repairs.
pmc-13530880:
Annahita Ghaedrahmati and Mohammad Zandi reviewed 3D culture systems for eggs, follicles, and embryos. Published in 2026, the narrative review covers tiny fluid devices, dynamic culture, ball-shaped cell models, and co-cultures with support cells. Flat cultures limit embryo production, with low blastocyst rates, weaker embryo quality, and worrying epigenetic shifts.

3D systems better mimic the body's inner setting, preserving tissue shape and restoring cell contacts and food and gas exchange. Evidence shows gains in egg maturation, embryo strength, and fertilization outcomes. Hurdles remain: tuning per species, scale-up, cost, and clinical standards. Future paths include smart responsive gels, AI links, and organ-on-a-chip platforms. Readers get a roadmap for a basic shift in reproductive science.
pmc-13530980:
Gabriela Riscuta and co-authors report on a 2024 National Institutes of Health workshop about the oral microbiome. Their 2026 commentary argues the mouth's microbes were long treated as a dental matter only. Evidence now links imbalance among them to wider diseases, including cancer and heart disease.

The authors frame the mouth as a gateway into the body's broader networks. They propose a care model that joins oral and whole-body health instead of splitting them between separate clinics. Research gaps and clinical priorities are laid out, with stress on cancer-related markers and chances to intervene early. If mouth microbes signal or drive disease elsewhere, then dentists and physicians share one patient, not two.
pmc-13531080:
Mohit Bandla and co-authors trace in 2026 a breathing problem to a lung vein narrowed shut after earlier heart surgery. A 77-year-old woman grew steadily breathless after valve replacement that had used that vein for venting, plus later repairs. Pressure readings varied by lung region, pointing to a blocked vein.

Dye imaging confirmed the right upper lung vein was fully closed. Two drug-coated balloon widenings followed, then a stent once tiny channels allowed passage. Flow finally normalized. The authors urge checking lung veins when breathlessness persists after procedures near them.
pmc-13531780:
Sileshi Belew and colleagues pool in 2026 published data on essential medicine availability in African regions torn by armed conflict. Searches gathered studies from 1985 onward, ending with data from 1,581 facilities and 989 medicines across eight countries. Standard quality checks and random-effects pooling handled the wide spread between studies.

Average availability came to about 55 percent, with the Central African Republic highest and Nigeria lowest among country estimates. Availability fell over time, from about 76 percent in the first decade to 46 percent after 2020. No publication bias appeared. The decline frames medicine supply as a worsening casualty of war.
pmc-13532580:
Rudong Li and colleagues report in 2026 that brains of people with alcohol use disorder keep more introns, the parts of a gene message that are normally cut out. Kept introns can form double-stranded RNA, a shape that can trigger immune sensors and swelling in tissue. The team studied 142 people and 320 brain samples from four regions.

Total kept introns ran higher in the disorder group, with larger rises in females. Checks in rats that prefer alcohol confirmed more double-stranded RNA, and cell data showed active immune paths. Readers see a new link between alcohol, gene splicing, and brain harm.
pmc-13533780:
Huesa-Carballo and co-authors tested cow colostrum particles against cancer in this study from twenty twenty-six. Colostrum, the first milk after birth, is rich in tiny vesicles that carry proteins between cells. The team extracted those vesicles and applied them to gut cancer models. Both cell lines and patient-grown mini-tumors were used.

The vesicles slowed cancer cell growth without killing the cells outright. Instead they threw the cells' gene-reading machinery into disarray. Chromatin packed tighter, the nucleus reshaped, and the cell skeleton remodeled. The arrest lifted once the vesicles were withdrawn. The vesicles also made standard chemotherapy bite harder. The authors propose them as gentle partners to existing cancer drugs.
pmc-13534580:
Yasemin Torlak and colleagues make in 2026 a lithium-bearing catalyst of the Dawson type for clean hydrogen release from a boron fuel in methanol. Hydrogen storage and release need catalysts that work well yet stay gentle on nature. Many checks confirmed the frame and rough surface of the new solid.

Tests varied heat, catalyst dose, and fuel strength to map how fast gas formed. The catalyst beat similar systems reported before, with a low energy barrier from rate analysis. Its kept frame and rough surface likely help reactants meet and react, marking it as a strong pick for green hydrogen work.
pmc-13536780:
Lisa Novianti and colleagues build a self-check score for early birth risk suited to low-resource clinics in a 2026 study from Jakarta. Early birth drives much newborn death and illness, yet many clinics lack tools for early screening. Cases and controls at a major hospital between 2021 and 2022 supplied data on social background, nutrition, lifestyle, pregnancy history, and maternal health. A scoring formula was derived and tested for accuracy.

Five factors predicted early birth on their own, covering income level, clinic visit pattern, prior early birth, high blood pressure history, and weight gain in pregnancy. A cutoff score separated risk groups with solid sensitivity and specificity, and overall accuracy was good. The authors offer the simple score as a fast, low-cost screen where equipment is scarce.
pmc-13536880:
Julie Christina Grew and co-authors test whether a gaming-based wellbeing program for teens facing social challenges is ready for larger study in a 2026 Danish feasibility project. The program uses interest in gaming to draw teens into shared physical and social activity plus healthy living lessons. A working group first built a theory and evaluation plan, then piloted both with thirteen teens aged 13 to 16 years meeting weekly for twenty-five weeks.

The evaluation plan proved usable, though several measures and collection steps need adjustment. A standard five-item wellbeing scale was judged fit as the main future outcome, and early wellbeing shifts appeared. Teens found the program format workable and acceptable, with recruitment and retention tracked through the pilot. The authors conclude that larger evaluation can proceed after refinements.
pmc-13538080:
Noor Mohammad and co-authors build a cheap phone-based test for HIV, in work published in 2026. Most people with HIV in poor regions stay untested for lack of cheap, gear-free tools. Their test pairs a copying step that works on the long viral genome with a CRISPR step that reads the copies without labels.

The test sensed the virus at very low levels in samples drawn from patients. A small phone-run gel box let users run the full test with no lab gear. The same setup also caught a cancer-linked gene flaw. The authors frame it as a robust path to wide testing for many diseases.
pmc-13538280:
Samantha Mombelli and colleagues test a new theory of idiopathic hypersomnia: that patients sleep too well, not too little. The disorder causes too much daytime sleepiness, yet sleep at night appears intact, challenging models based on sleep loss or fragmentation. The authors hypothesized that sleepiness reflects a sleep state held too stable, fitting dysfunctional thalamocortical control.

They analyzed overnight recordings from sixty-two patients and eighty-one matched healthy controls, using sleep bout lengths, stage shift dynamics, and automated spindle detection. Composite indices captured stability in non-REM and REM sleep. Patients showed fewer shifts from deep sleep toward lighter stages and wakefulness. Their REM sleep lasted longer with fewer awakenings. Spindle amplitude was reduced while spindle density was preserved, and smaller amplitudes tracked shorter sleep latencies on daytime testing. The problem, on this evidence, is a sleep state that will not let go.
pmc-13538680:
Mohd Izzuddin Hairol and colleagues create and validate Malay sentences for a standardized reading chart in a 2026 study. Reading charts exist in many European languages but not Malay, spoken by hundreds of millions in Southeast Asia. Forty candidate sentences matched for word count, length, difficulty, and structure were read by 120 young adults while timing, speed, and errors were recorded. Statistical screening kept only tightly matched sentences.

Twenty-four sentences passed the matching window with near identical reading speeds and times and very few errors. Their speeds correlated strongly with a standard Malay reading passage, and internal consistency ran very high. The selected sentences now form the Malay edition of the chart for measuring reading sharpness and speed in visually normal young adults.
pmc-13539380:
Abeer Abdulaziz H. Bukhari and a team of co-authors graft a drug-like molecule onto a zirconium framework to sniff cadmium in water. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-six. Cadmium is a quiet poison in drinking supplies, and field tests need to be cheap and sure.

The base is a porous metal-organic crystal, UiO-66, studded with amino groups. Post-synthesis chemistry anchored a sulfadoxine-based dye inside its pores. Cadmium binding chokes the dye's glow and shifts its absorption, giving two independent readouts. Absorbance stayed linear up to zero point one two parts per million, with detection down near zero point zero one eight. Fifteen rival metal ions barely disturbed the signal. Spiked water samples returned honest recoveries.
pmc-13539880:
Duogang Xu, Ruotian Wang, and Jing Tan review, in a 2026 article, the role of web-like structures that white blood cells called neutrophils cast out into surrounding tissue in colorectal cancer. These traps were first described as germ catchers, yet evidence now links them to tumor growth and spread.

The review follows the traps through inflamed bowel tissue, the primary tumor, and the liver, where colorectal cancer often spreads. Effects seem to depend on disease stage, body site, and treatment, with some trap responses accompanying tumor control rather than harm. Weak detection methods and thin human data limit certainty, the authors caution, so blanket claims about blocking the traps are premature.
pmc-13540780:
Héctor Aceituno and ten colleagues review brain surgery for mental illness that resists all other care, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The review covers obsessive-compulsive disorder, stubborn depression, and pathological aggression. It spans older lesion methods, such as targeted cuts and focused ultrasound, and deep brain stimulation with implanted electrodes. Studies came from three databases plus a web search.

For obsessive-compulsive disorder, two methods reached response rates of about half to three fifths of patients. For depression, open follow-ups showed fair gains, but blinded trials mostly found no edge over sham. Proof for aggression rests on case series only. The authors frame these as last-resort options needing careful ethics.
pmc-13541180:
Patrick Addo-Fordjour and six co-authors measure forest loss across Ghana in this twenty twenty-six study. Past counts of lost forest in Ghana varied a lot and covered only single reserves or small areas. That left the true scale and causes in doubt.

Using space images from three points across a decade, the team mapped land cover for the whole country and tracked change. Farm growth and mining drove most of the clearing, even as the yearly rate of loss fell. A national picture with named causes can help Ghana aim its forest policy and guard what remains.
pmc-13541780:
Elsa Davidson presents an ethnographic study dated 2026 on parenting neurodivergent children in the United States. The study follows middle-class families and asks how daily care practices shape parents' ethics and understanding. One mother and her neurodivergent child form the central case.

Video interviews and field material show care built on bodily and emotional attunement. Shared touch and close attention let the mother feel with her child, not just observe him. Over time her framing shifted: what she first called sensory issues became anxiety, a state made and eased together. Davidson reads this shift as an ethical change in the parent herself. Care, in this account, is a gift that transforms the giver.
pmc-13542080:
Hariprasad Thangavel and colleagues showed fat-cell parcels can drive spread in triple-negative breast cancer. Published in 2026, the study pulled large adipomes, tiny fat-cell parcels, from patient blood and mouse tumor fat. Triple-negative disease lacks hormone and HER2 targets, leaving chemo as the main option, and it returns early with distant spread.

Blood parcels from spread-stage patients pushed healthy breast cells toward a mobile, stem-like state and spurred foot-like prongs. Mouse tumor-fat parcels, rich in phospholipids, rewired mouse cancer cells in gene and protein work. Both routes switched on stress MAPK signals and builders for cell frames, energy, and protein making, all feeding prongs and matrix breakdown. The authors name fat parcels as potent spread drivers and a fresh drug target.
pmc-13542180:
Anil Ahmed and four colleagues tackle, in a 2026 study, judging whether two Urdu sentences mean the same thing, a task starved of labelled examples in this low-resource language. Their framework learns partly from unlabelled text it labels itself, but only when it is confident.

Back-translation and word masking manufactured extra training variety. A twin graph network blending two graph methods compared sentence structures, sharpened by an attention encoder that resists the blurring graph networks suffer. Triple filtering by probability, meaning match, and uncertainty kept pseudo-labels clean. Across six benchmark sets the system beat strong rivals, with one dataset showing an eight-point accuracy gain over the best baseline.
pmc-13543480:
Jorge Beltrán's team screened antimicrobial peptides in 2026 against Piscirickettsia salmonis, the bacterium behind a septicemia that drives heavy antibiotic use in Chilean salmon farming. Thirteen compounds were tested on the standard strain in the cold over seven days: eleven natural-style peptides plus florfenicol and chlorhexidine as controls. The two strongest peptides then went into molecular dynamics simulations against a membrane built on its unusual makeup.

Two beta-hairpin peptides, folded shapes locked by tight bonds, beat all else. Tachyplesin I halted most growth at just 2 micrograms per millilitre, while Protegrin-1 needed higher levels. The best straight-chain peptides needed far more. In simulations both leaders stuck to the membrane surface but behaved in unlike ways once there, warning that binding readings alone do not predict killing power. Hairpin peptides stand out as leads for new drugs.
pmc-13545180:
Sreemoyee Mitra and co-authors (2026) review whether bacteria-eating viruses can deliver genes into liver cancer cells. Hepatocellular carcinoma kills many patients because drugs work briefly and the cancer returns. Gene therapy could strike more precisely, but it needs a carrier that finds the tumor. Bacteriophages are easy to engineer and decorate with targeting molecules. The review covers phage display for homing, gene delivery into cells, a death-signal gene, TRAIL, and CRISPR-based strategies.

The authors are candid about the obstacles. Phages get trapped and digested inside cells before their cargo can act. The immune system clears them, and making them at scale under drug rules is unproven. Still, the targeting tricks are flexible and cheap compared with viral carriers. The reviewers conclude phages are a promising platform for liver cancer gene delivery. They ask for deeper mechanism work and animal studies before clinical claims.
pmc-13546680:
Shasha Liao, Shaoling Qiu, Na Li, Yunyuan Liu, and Xiuneng Tang report a newborn infected in blood and brain by a hardy hospital germ. Their case report was published in twenty twenty-six. The germ, Elizabethkingia meningoseptica, preys on the weak, above all early babies and people with low immunity.

The baby was born at thirty-three weeks and fell ill at one month with fever and poor feeding. Blood and spinal fluid cultures grew the germ, which answered several antibiotics. Three drug pairings were tried in sequence over an eighty-five-day hospital course. The infection swelled the brain's fluid spaces, a lasting complication. The case shows how stubborn this germ can be and why drug choice must follow lab sensitivity closely.
pmc-13547580:
Vincent Rothweiler and ten co-authors pool phase three trials of PD-1 blocker cures as first care for spread throat cancer of one type. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Immune block care changed first care for this cancer, but gain size across trials needs a clean sum. Six trials from four bases fit the brief.

More than four thousand patients were in the source trials. Blocker care plus chemo beat chemo alone on life span by a clear span, with like gains across trials. Gains ran larger where a tumor mark was high, but low-mark gain stays unsure. Grave side harms were common in both arms, and immune harms need close watch.
pmc-13548580:
Karolina Soroczynska and colleagues grow placenta-derived healing cells in stirred bioreactors and test the tiny parcels those cells release, in a 2026 study of lung inflammation models. Such parcels, called extracellular vesicles, are hoped to work as cell-free medicines. The team compared standard flat cultures with three-dimensional bioreactor growth, then applied cells or vesicles to laboratory airway models mimicking cystic fibrosis and acute respiratory distress.

Bioreactor growth produced far more vesicles without hurting quality. Effects varied strongly by donor, however, and vesicles behaved differently from their parent cells across airway and immune compartments. One consistent trend was a rise in calming signals IL-10 and Arginase-1 inside macrophages. The authors warn that donor choice and disease setting will decide whether these products help, so screening matters before clinical use.
pmc-13548880:
Shanyue Li and colleagues work out how self-trapping light-like waves, called solitons, arise in lattices with one-way, nonreciprocal behavior, in a 2026 theoretical physics paper. In systems showing the non-Hermitian skin effect, waves pile up at the boundary, and adding nonlinearity gradually turns those boundary modes into solitons. What was missing was a rule for when each kind of soliton forms.

Building a simplified effective model projected onto localized states, the team shows that soliton birth depends on how boundary localization and band one-wayness each fight or feed wave spreading. Two families emerge: solitons helped by skin modes, and solitons dressed by nonreciprocity. In a stacked test lattice, stronger nonreciprocity lowers the threshold for the first family and raises it for the second. The authors extend the scheme to richer lattices and higher dimensions as an engineering guide.
pmc-13550080:
Röh and colleagues wrote in 2026, in German, about whether vitamin D supplements make sense for people with depression. Vitamin D is made in the skin under sunlight, and in central Europe the light in autumn and winter is too weak to keep blood levels up. Low levels are common then, and they have been linked with mental illness as well as poorer mood, energy, in people already depressed.

Röh weighs practice against the evidence and the German guideline for depression care. Supplements must not push aside proven treatments, the guideline warns, since they are not a replacement therapy. But targeted vitamin D can still help as an added measure when a shortage is found or likely. The authors call for testing-based, individual care, diet support for at-risk groups, and closer agreement between guidelines and nutrition experts so gaps in care for these patients close.
pmc-13550580:
S Nakul, together with six colleagues, reported in 2026 on three new uranyl complexes, compounds built around uranium and oxygen, held by salen ligands. The team made the ligands and complexes, then checked their makeup with infrared, ultraviolet-visible, and nuclear magnetic resonance methods. X-ray work on two complexes showed a distorted seven-sided shape around the uranium center.

The complexes glowed blue, with sharp emission peaks near 450 nanometers, and the authors measured how long that glow lasted. Computer calculations helped explain the light absorption and emission. All three complexes, plus plain uranyl acetate, were tried as catalysts for turning a diol into hexene, and the plain acetate actually performed best under the tuned conditions reported.
pmc-13550880:
Ziyi Wang leads a team that screens for mind decline in Parkinson's disease. Their study from twenty twenty-six joins blood tests with sleep surveys. Mind decline is a common non motor problem in the disease.

Patients were split by a standard mind test cut off. One group showed decline, the other did not. Data split into training and test sets by design. A strict no leak pipeline guarded the model build. Twenty candidate inputs were screened down to ten. Nested models then tested how well they classify. Cheap routine inputs are the appeal of the route.
pmc-13551680:
Haotian Jin, Yinan Zhang, Yi Sun, and Yan Shao published a 2026 network meta-analysis comparing exercise types and doses for anxiety in older adults. Exercise helps anxiety without drugs, yet the best form and amount were unclear. The team searched five databases to January 2025 for randomized trials in people aged 60 or older, extracting dose in metabolic equivalent minutes per week.

Twenty-three trials with 2,093 participants entered the analysis. Tai Chi ranked most effective against control, followed by resistance training, yoga, qigong, and aerobic exercise, while mixed exercise showed no significant effect. Dose modeling put Tai Chi's best effect near 500 metabolic equivalent minutes weekly, with significant benefit starting lower, giving practitioners a concrete target for prescription.
pmc-13551780:
Nikita Hensen, leading a large international team, published a 2026 protocol for the PIECES study, which evaluates support for adapting cancer prevention programs to local settings. Programs that work in trials often falter in routine practice because contexts differ. The project co-developed a toolkit with practitioners and researchers to guide adapting, tailoring, and evaluating primary cancer prevention programs, aiming to build implementation skills through structured planning and shared learning.

The evaluation uses a multi-site pre-post comparative case study with mixed methods across eleven sites in Europe and Australia. Sites vary in organization, resources, and culture, letting the team test the toolkit's usability, feasibility, and mechanisms of impact. The authors present the design as practical guidance where earlier frameworks stayed abstract.
pmc-13551980:
Han-Ying Lin, with eight colleagues, published a 2026 study of MRI signs in soft tissue sarcoma. Sarcoma is a cancer of muscle, fat, and other soft tissues. The study focused on tumors driven by gene fusions, a group past series underplayed. Adults scanned before treatment at one center from 2008 to 2024 were included. Two radiologists, blind to outcomes, scored thirteen set image features.

The cohort held 158 patients. About forty percent of classed tumors were fusion-driven. Uneven dye uptake in the tumor predicted shorter survival. Swelling around the tumor also predicted shorter survival and local return. A panel of all thirteen signs barely split the top grade. The team concludes two simple signs beat grade and tumor class here.
pmc-13552080:
Vishal Kundnani and co-authors test a three-part drug mix as add-on therapy for spinal cord injury in a 2026 trial. Spinal cord injury leaves lasting loss of movement and feeling, and few drugs help recovery. The mix combines three compounds, each with protective effects on nerve cells, aimed at several damage pathways at once.

One hundred twenty patients with recent but not immediate injuries were split into two groups for six months. One group got standard care alone, the other standard care plus the mix. By six months the mix group had gained more in movement scores, independence measures, and quality of life. Feeling scores did not differ. Side effects were few and mild. The authors call for larger multi-center trials to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13554180:
Mojgan Esparvarinha leads an eight-author team silencing a placenta-linked protein in mouse bowel cancer in a 2026 study. The protein, PLAC1, shows up more in human bowel tumours, yet its job there stays unclear. Short RNA strands switched the protein off in mouse cancer cells. Those cells were then planted in mice, and tumours plus immune cells were tracked.

Silencing shrank tumours and lengthened mouse survival. Suppressor T cells, which shield tumours from attack, grew rarer in both tumour and spleen. Helper T cells rose in the spleen, and killer T cells rose inside tumours. The shift points to a less sheltered tumour setting. The team backs more work on PLAC1 as a drug target for immune therapy.
pmc-13554280:
Kuldeep Dutta leads a five-author team tracing how two days of extreme rain in the Eastern Himalaya set off a chain of disasters in a 2026 study. In September 2020, heavy rain in Arunachal Pradesh triggered landslides that later flooded Assam plains. Satellite images mapped slides, debris flows, and flood extent. Rainfall records reaching back to 1996 set the event in context.

Slides briefly dammed streams, then the dams burst, sending sediment-laden water over a wide floodplain. Earlier wet spells had soaked the slopes before the peak daily rain hit. Total rainfall tracked storm length far better than peak intensity did. The authors argue that judging rain by both traits matters for warning systems in mountain-to-plain hazard chains.
pmc-13554480:
Fukushima and coauthors find a gene switch that responds to muscle work. Muscle adapts to exercise by fast shifts in gene use. Which switches link contraction to those shifts was unclear. One small switch rose after acute exercise in two species.

The switch rose in human and mouse muscle after workouts. It rose just in muscles the workout style recruited. In lab muscle cells, electric pulses also raised it. Cells that lack the switch fused poorly as they grew. Gene scans showed wide shifts in those weak cells. Muscle form genes fell, while immune genes rose.
pmc-13555880:
Mirela Marinova-Takorova and Zornitsa Mihaylova survey students and staff on dental teaching in Sofia, Bulgaria, in a 2026 study. Their 576 respondents included Bulgarian students, foreign students, and fifty-seven teachers. Two questionnaires probed lecture attendance, drive to learn, personal support, hands-on training, and whether exams match course aims. The survey ran through the 2024/2025 school year.

About half the students attended every lecture, drawn mainly by exam preparation and clearer grasp of the work. Teachers instead prized well-ordered delivery and class talk. More than half the students felt teaching was not tailored to them, a view staff did not share. Bulgarian students favoured oral exams, while foreign students preferred hands-on and written tests. Staff leaned toward written tests as well.
pmc-13555980:
Anila Cake and four colleagues reported in 2026 on anxiety among nurses and midwives in Albania after the COVID-19 emergency phase had passed. Their survey covered 1,201 staff in public hospitals, chosen through stratified random sampling between March 2024 and May 2025. Each person completed a questionnaire that included standard scales for state anxiety, trait anxiety, and discomfort with uncertainty.

Average scores sat in the moderate range for all three measures. People who disliked uncertainty more tended to report higher trait anxiety, and staff living with chronic health conditions scored higher than colleagues without such conditions. Less work experience also linked to higher trait anxiety, and the authors argue that support for this workforce should continue well beyond the crisis itself.
pmc-13556080:
Wang and colleagues reviewed in 2026 why cancer immunotherapy so often stops working. Checkpoint drugs free the immune system to attack tumours, yet many tumours learn to resist. The authors treat the tumour and its surroundings as one ecosystem: cancer cells, immune cells, vessels, and fuel supply act together to shut immunity down.

Treatments they discuss include calming suppressor immune cells, reshaping tumour tissue and vessels, and restoring lymph drainage. They also cover cytokine drugs, metabolism-based treatments, virus therapies, vaccines, and engineered cells. Failed trials teach a lesson, they argue: sound ideas flop when the main block is not found first, or when drug order ignores tumour layout. They propose matching drug mixes to each tumour's ecosystem, guided by tissue markers and checks during treatment.
pmc-13556380:
Earley and colleagues pooled two large trials of the drug lumateperone added to antidepressant care for major depression. Depression varies a lot between patients, and traits like age can shape how well a drug works. Lumateperone is already approved for schizophrenia and bipolar depression. The question was whether its benefit holds across patient groups.

The pooled group held nine hundred fifty adults whose depression had not eased on one or two antidepressants. Half got lumateperone plus their antidepressant for six weeks, and half got a placebo instead. The team checked symptom scores across age, sex, and clinical subgroups, and tracked side effects. Such pooling shows whether a treatment's effect is steady or limited to a narrow slice of patients.
pmc-13557480:
Vilaplana and colleagues described SEHOP-PENCIL, a 2026 national program bringing tailored genomic medicine to children, teenagers, and young adults with cancer across Spain. Spain earlier had no national program of this kind. A survey by the team found hospitals had gained access to targeted gene panels while advanced tests such as whole-genome sequencing and methylation profiling stayed scarce and hard to get.

Vilaplana explains that the program runs ten expert genomic centers serving 45 hospitals through one central entry system, with shared rules for who qualifies, testing workflows, and reading results. A national molecular tumor board, a panel that matches tumor gene findings to treatments, helps every site decide. The framework aims to give every young patient a gene-based diagnosis and access to new therapies no matter their hometown, while building one shared dataset to improve children's cancer research.
pmc-13558480:
Jing Zeng and five colleagues tracked in 2026 survival trends for primary ocular adnexal lymphoma, the most common cancer around the eye, using a large United States registry. They calculated five-year relative survival for patients diagnosed in three periods spanning 2005 to 2019 and used model-based period analysis to project the years 2020 to 2024. Results were broken down by age, sex, race, tumour site, and subtype.

Five-year relative survival climbed from about ninety-six percent to about ninety-nine percent across the observed periods. Survival dipped with age yet improved in every age band, and the projection puts younger patients near one hundred percent. Women did slightly better than men, and conjunctival disease and two slower subtypes fared best. The authors say the steady gains give clinicians and patients a firmer basis for counselling.
pmc-13558580:
Rima Solianik and three colleagues measured in 2026 what six days without food does to strength, jumping, and the nerve control of muscle in healthy men. Fourteen inactive, non-obese men fasted for six days, then returned to their normal diet for a week. Testing covered mood, fine hand skills, reflex arcs in the calf muscles, involuntary and voluntary force, the brain's drive to the muscle, and drop jump performance.

Jumping, fine motor skill, and maximum voluntary force survived the fast intact, even though the men felt more fatigued. Neural measures shifted: reflex ratios fell by day four, and the brain's activation of the muscle dipped by day six, showing adaptation at both spine and brain levels. After refeeding, the neural changes reversed, mood lifted beyond baseline, and fine motor performance improved. Survival capacity, the authors note, is well defended.
pmc-13559680:
Yurui Liu and four colleagues build a prognostic model for liver cancer from genes tied to kynurenine metabolism, a pathway that helps tumors dampen immune attack. Their 2026 study draws transcriptomic and clinical data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and an international genome consortium cohort. Penalized regression distilled the pathway's genes into a risk score.

Seven genes formed the final signature. Patients scored high risk died markedly sooner than those scored low. Genes active in the high-risk group clustered around spliceosome assembly and the building of ribonucleoprotein complexes. A nomogram blending the score with clinical features predicted outcomes with moderate accuracy. The team also singled out ALDH8A1 as a favorable marker, since it slowed tumor cell migration in their cell line test. The authors offer the model for risk stratification and further therapeutic study.
pmc-13560180:
Mohammad Shah Jalal and eight colleagues pool the world's studies, published in 2026, on how many seizure patients owe their epilepsy to a parasite. The cause is neurocysticercosis, the larval stage of a tapeworm lodged in the brain. The team searched twenty databases for studies from 1990 to 2023 that confirmed the infection by imaging, biopsy, or autopsy. Seventy-seven studies passed the quality screens. In the thirty-five studies with clear definitions for both conditions, the pooled share came out near one in four.

Shares did not differ by sex or age group. Studies with loose definitions reported much lower shares, a warning about mislabeling. Across Africa, the Americas, and Southeast Asia, the share fell between the earlier and later periods studied. The authors caution that studies vary a lot by setting, so the pooled figure is a guide, not a universal constant.
pmc-13560680: Tanmoy Mukherjee, Ricardo Delgado Santander, and Youfu Zhao publish full genomes of eight orchard germs that may fight apple blight, in a note from two thousand twenty-six. The eight came from sick apple tissue in Washington groves. Their complete gene sets are offered as a base for tracing how they guard trees, mix with kin, and fit orchard life.
pmc-13561080:
Dan Bez Golanski and co-authors track parrotfish behavior through a dozen marine heatwaves, in a study from 2026. Heatwaves at sea are growing longer, stronger, and more frequent. Their toll on fish groups is known, but how single fish act during one was not. The team tagged thirty-two large male parrotfish in the northern Red Sea.

Sound tags logged each fish's activity, depth, and daily travel. The span covered years that included a mass die-off of parrotfish during one fast warming. Yet the tagged fish barely changed how they behaved, during or after each heatwave. The result held no matter how a heatwave was defined. The authors read this two ways. Either the fish cope through body changes, not behavior, or only harsher heatwaves move them.
pmc-13562080:
Tonghui Li and colleagues report a pepper line, Capsicum annuum TC48, that both resists and tolerates cucumber mosaic virus, in a 2026 research letter. The virus attacks over twelve hundred plant species, yellowing leaves, stunting plants, and spoiling fruit, and no chemical targets it directly. Breeding resistant cultivars is the sustainable route, yet commercial pepper resistance remains inadequate.

The letter frames the plant's two defense strategies: resistance, which limits the pathogen's spread, and tolerance, which preserves growth despite infection. Immune layers from pattern recognition to RNA interference are reviewed as backdrop for the line's behavior. A pepper that keeps yielding while infected, and slows the virus besides, offers breeders a double asset. The authors present TC48 as a genetic resource for pepper improvement and a tool for dissecting how resistance and tolerance combine against this virus.
pmc-13562280:
Jieyun Li and colleagues map twelve years of myelodysplastic syndromes research with scientometric tools, mining the Web of Science for articles and reviews from 2014 to 2025. Their 2026 analysis of 6,822 publications charts annual output, leading countries and institutions, collaboration networks, and thematic hotspots for this family of blood stem cell disorders.

Global output peaked in 2021. The United States supplied 2,838 papers, far ahead of China's 1,169 and Germany's 717 in the counted totals, and the top institutions and authors were mostly American. Networks showed a core-and-edge pattern, with strong transatlantic ties and growing Asian participation. Hot topics ranged from specific chromosomal lesions and TP53 mutation to newer drugs, immunotherapy, and artificial intelligence. The authors see the field tilting toward precision medicine, and they call for multi-ethnic cohorts and stronger multidisciplinary collaboration.
pmc-13562580:
Eunice Oluwakemi Ogunmodede and seven colleagues measure how common sexual abuse is among school pupils in Ogun State, in southwest Nigeria, and what raises or lowers the risk. Evidence from that region has been scarce. The 2026 survey questioned 353 pupils aged 10 to 19 at three secondary schools in Abeokuta South, chosen through staged sampling. Pupils answered a structured questionnaire in private, and abuse meant any unwanted sexual experience they reported. Analysis sorted influences into personal, family, and wider social levels.

About one pupil in three, 34.3 percent, reported abuse, and schoolmates were the most common perpetrators named. Girls reported more than boys. Living with both parents lowered the odds sharply, while family type and religion also shifted risk in the adjusted model. Age alone did not. The authors call for stronger school safeguarding and family support structures, arguing that protection must work at every level the data implicates.
pmc-13563180:
Sofya Ilmer, Vivienne Lopez-Cabreza, and Parissa Salemi tell in 2026 of three babies whose thyroids faltered because of their mothers' soup. Seaweed soup is a daily tradition for Korean mothers around birth, and it can push iodine intake far above safe levels. Too much iodine can switch a newborn's thyroid off for a while.

One baby recovered fast once the mother stopped the soup, and thyroid medicine ended by six months. A second needed dose changes and proved temporary only at age three and a half. A third was treated for six years as a lifelong case, until the diet history revealed the cause and treatment stopped. The authors urge diet questions and a fresh look at age three.
pmc-13563680:
Yonghyun Yoon and four colleagues describe a man whose shoulder blade winged outward and chest wall ached for months after a chest drain for a blood-and-air leak. Long thoracic nerve injury after drain placement is known, but this case also trapped a second nerve, the skin branch of an intercostal nerve, a pairing rarely reported. Ultrasound scanning found both nerves caught where they crossed scar tissue at the drain site, and pressing them with the probe reproduced his pain.

Hydrodissection, fluid injected under ultrasound guidance, freed each nerve from scar. About 20 millilitres of 5 percent dextrose water went around each nerve. Pain fell at once from 9 to 2 on a ten-point scale. Five sessions over ten weeks restored full strength, erased the winging, and cut disability scores steeply. Gains held at one year. The authors commend ultrasound for finding such double entrapments and guiding their release.
pmc-13563780:
Weishuyi Ruan and eleven colleagues point a light-based brain scanner at people with functional constipation, looking for the brain's role in a disorder. The condition involves the nervous system as well as the bowel, touching feeling and emotion. Their 2026 case-control study recruited 64 patients meeting criteria at Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital and 64 neighbours. Sensors tracked blood oxygen across forehead regions while participants rested, imagined emptying their bowels, mimicked the act, and squeezed the anal sphincter.

Headline differences refused to appear: connectivity and activation gaps between groups stayed short of significance. The patterns underneath told a story. Healthy brains tuned their response to each task, quieting one speech area for the squeeze task. Patient brains ramped in a straight line across tasks, as if failing to modulate. The authors call this first-of-its-kind scan a map of targets for brain-stimulation therapies, labelled trend-level evidence.
pmc-13563980:
Min-Ji Kim, Ji-Young Seo, Utkarsh Mangal, and Sung-Hwan Choi test, in a 2026 laboratory study, a braces glue containing zinc-doped phosphate glass meant to stop cavity-causing biofilms. Glues with plain glass, zinc glass, or no glass were compared against Streptococcus mutans alone and against mixed mouth bacteria grown in the lab.

The zinc version released zinc steadily and cut survival of the cavity bacterium by about thirty percent compared with plain glue. Mixed biofilms grew thinner and less dense on the zinc glue over the seven-day test. Orthodontists get early, lab-only evidence for a glue that fights the white spots and decay that often form around braces.
pmc-13564080:
Mohamed Shamseldin and ten co-authors hunted for bacterial parts that protective immune cells recognize in whooping cough, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Cases are rising worldwide despite wide vaccine use. A key class of immune cells is known to be vital for lasting protection, but the targets they aim at were poorly mapped.

The team used protein scanning, computer prediction, and cell tests to find strong target pieces from lab and clinical strains. A vaccine built from two of the found proteins nearly cleared the germ from mouse lungs and cut it sharply in the nose. Removing the immune cells in question erased the protection. The authors propose adding these targets to future vaccines.
pmc-13564680:
Faisal Abed and co-authors published this review in 2026. It asks how parents in the Middle East feel about behavior methods in children's dentistry. Basic methods guide a child with words and presence. Advanced ones include general anesthesia and physical restraint. The team searched five databases for studies from 2015 to early 2026. Eleven studies from seven countries qualified.

One basic method, tell-show-do, won the highest acceptance everywhere, at 88 to 98 percent. General anesthesia and restraint were the least liked. Pooled results confirmed the gap with strong statistical support. Parents clearly favor gentle guidance first. The authors suggest dentists lead with basic methods and explain advanced ones with care. The review also notes the thin evidence base: eleven studies for a whole region.
pmc-13564880:
Samrat Basak, Kaushik Inamdar, and seven co-authors rescue a powerful microscope label from a blinking failure. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, concerns single-molecule localization microscopy. The method builds sharp images from dyes that blink on and off. Tiny antibody fragments called nanobodies give precise labels, but the standard dye falters on them.

A self-blinking dye, JF635b, keeps blinking steadily once attached to nanobodies. It needs no special chemical buffers to switch. The team images with it across three advanced modes. Precision reaches from fifteen nanometers down to below one. Samples also keep well over time. The dye even blinks in pure water, easing gentle imaging.
pmc-13565980:
Aleksandra Kosikowska and seven co-authors study infections picked up in hospital after bleeding from a burst brain aneurysm, in a two thousand twenty-six paper. Such infections often make care harder in neurocritical care units. The team looked back at one hundred six adults treated at one center from two thousand nineteen to two thousand twenty-four. They tracked the time to a first infection and what it meant for how patients fared.

Infections hit forty-four percent of patients, at a median of ten days. Lung infections from ventilators were most common, followed by urinary and spinal fluid infections. One highly resistant bacterium dominated the severe resistant isolates. Higher severity grades at admission were tied to a first infection. An infection was tied to slower live discharge, but not clearly to death in hospital. The team took timing into account when they weighed those links.
pmc-13567280:
Danliang Zhang, Peiran Li, Sihan Liu, Qing Ye, and Ying Chen present a 2026 study of flat chromium sulfide sheets grown in a guided vapor process. Such non-layered sheets draw eyes for their magnet and light traits. The team grew clean sheets on mica at open air pressure. The sheets double light frequency strongly, a trick called second-harmonic generation. The glow grew with sheet thickness and swung with the light's angle.

Cooling past the sheet's magnet flip point near 120 kelvin made the glow jump, as magnet order added its own share. Round-turned light came out near fully round below that point. Light thus reads the magnet state without wires. Flat magnets gain a contact-free probe for their inner turns.
pmc-13568180:
Sophie Harris and colleagues review tubeless anaesthesia for throat and voice-box surgery, publishing the clinical review in 2026. Endoscopic pharyngolaryngeal operations need a clear view of the tongue base, pharynx, larynx, and upper gullet, so the anaesthetist must oxygenate without a tube blocking the field. High-flow nasal oxygen during apnoea has spread widely over the past decade, yet it suits neither every patient nor every lesion.

The review explains the physiology behind apnoeic oxygenation, weighs its benefits against limits such as carbon-dioxide build-up and fire risk, and compares open and closed airway strategies. It stresses team-based case selection and a rescue oxygenation plan ready at all times. Surgeons, nurses, and anaesthetists get a practical guide to using the technique safely and knowing when to abandon it.
pmc-13568380:
Hanmin Park and Hansang Kim build an automated computational workflow that screens rubber O-rings for high-pressure hydrogen service. Hydrogen transport and cyclic loading together complicate seal assessment, so the workflow chains three analyses in sequence. A mass diffusion simulation in Abaqus computes absorbed hydrogen; the concentration field transfers one-way into a nonlinear structural and contact analysis with prescribed swelling; fatigue post-processing then estimates service life.

Two EPDM compounds, a softer and a harder grade, were evaluated across sampled pressures and installation stretches, with radial squeeze fixed. The fatigue-life outputs fell dramatically as pressure rose, collapsing between the mid-range pressures tested. At the highest pressure the outputs dropped below a single repeat, which the authors stress are screening indicators only. The outputs support only input-conditional comparisons between designs. The workflow gives engineers a fast comparative screen for seals whose failure could leak flammable gas.
pmc-13570780:
Wang and co-authors flag a lung guard clan that drives grave breath ill. Grave breath ill is a long flare ill with stiff drug hold. Steroid drugs oft fail to tame it in grave hosts. Guard cells in the lung steer much of that flare. One clan, the gap guards, had stayed dim in past reads. The team read lone-cell genes and flow counts in a mouse set.

Two hits set off the grave state in the mice. Lung bits from a house dust mite and a salt mix did it. Grave care wiped the home sac guards from the lungs. New sac guards tied to weave fix took their place. A gap clan with low Lyve1 and high MHCII rose to lead. That clan bore high CCR2 and CCR5 marks in its reads. A dual block drug then tests that clan's worth.
pmc-13570880:
Bo Chen and Xiangyi Li combine, in a 2026 cohort study of a Chinese aging survey, a blood-fat marker of artery disease and a frailty index into one combined score. The index counts health deficits. They then ask whether the score predicts new arthritis. More than four thousand adults aged forty-five and older without arthritis at entry were followed from 2011 to 2020.

About a third developed arthritis over ten years. Each step up in the combined score raised risk slightly. The highest third of scores carried about fifty-five percent more risk than the lowest third, in a curved rather than straight-line pattern. Blending metabolic and frailty information may flag older adults who deserve earlier joint monitoring, pending outside confirmation.
pmc-13572380:
Sanika Kulkarni, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 review of whether blood pressure drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system relate to depression. Two drug classes are in focus: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers. Lab work hints these drugs might lift mood, but human data have been mixed.

The team searched five databases for studies of adults, up to November 2024, and kept 15 studies with more than 7 million people in all. Eight studies linked the drugs to lower rates of depression, six found no clear link, and one found a small rise in major depression. Gains showed most in large registry studies that used doctor-coded diagnoses. The authors say varied methods and leftover bias bar firm claims, and they call for cleaner future studies.
pmc-13572480:
Isabel Pinheiro and colleagues released a multi-modal dataset for mapping kiwifruit growth stages automatically, publishing the data paper in 2026. Hand counting of buds, flowers, and fruit takes about ten minutes per square metre, making orchard-wide monitoring impractical and yield forecasts imprecise. The dataset pairs 1,665 annotated images from bud to fruit set with georeferenced videos carrying manual ground-truth counts.

An adapted 17-class growth-stage system merges visually similar stages, drops troublesome categories, and adds structural classes, organised across plant parts, genders, and stages. The images train computer-vision models while the videos validate automated counting at plant level. The resource should advance precision kiwifruit farming, from pollination timing to yield prediction.
pmc-13572580:
Taguchi and co-authors test preventive coiling of side branches during aneurysm repair in this 2026 study. Endovascular repair seals a weak aortic bulge from inside, but blood leaking back through branches can regrow the sac. Their low-volume center applied a fixed anatomy-based rule for who gets preventive embolization.

Of 132 elective patients, 30 received coils and 102 did not. The coiled group actually started with riskier anatomy, including wider feeder arteries. Yet at 24 months none of the coiled patients showed sac growth. Five-year re-intervention was 0 percent with coils against 10.8 percent without. The authors say a standardized rule makes results reproducible even at small centers.
pmc-13573380:
Xianyao Li, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of microbes that live on tea tree bark and in the soil below. Tea is a major crop in Yunnan, China, and its microbes shape plant health. The team asked where bark microbes come from and what steers their mix across regions.

Samples came from Pu'er, Lincang, and Xishuangbanna, the main tea zones. Source tracking showed soil acts as the reservoir for bark: in Pu'er it held all bark bacteria and about two thirds of bark fungi, with little flow back. Soil held wider variety, while bark picked a narrower set. Plant type shaped bark bacteria most, and place shaped soil mixes. Nitrogen and organic matter in soil drove change in both niches. Soil microbes leaned to nutrient cycling, bark microbes to carbon fixing and stress defence.
pmc-13573680:
Tang and seven co-authors show the enzyme USP10 restrains esophageal cancer by stabilizing a NOTCH pathway fragment, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Oxidative stress imbalance is a major factor in this cancer. USP10 removes ubiquitin tags from the NICD1 protein fragment. That stabilization shapes antioxidant gene activity.

Losing USP10 destabilizes NICD1 and speeds cancer development in models. Extra USP10 gene therapy slows tumor formation in animals. Low USP10 levels link to worse patient prognosis. The enzyme responds to oxidative stress by protecting NICD1. USP10 emerges as a candidate therapeutic target.
pmc-13573980:
Jethwa and colleagues examined in 2026 what happens after new mothers screen positive for depression at the six-week checkup. They followed records from more than eight thousand patients at one center. Screening with a standard questionnaire is routine, but whether a positive screen turns into care was poorly charted. The team tracked referrals to social work and psychiatry for a year after birth.

About one patient in eight received a new mental health referral after the screening visit. Positive screens drew far more referrals than negative ones, roughly thirty-seven versus five in a hundred for social work. Still, most positive-screen patients were never referred, a gap the authors call critical. Referrals after positive screens also came faster, mostly within two months. The authors back screening across the whole perinatal period, not once.
pmc-13574780:
Yunchong Guo, with six colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of gene-mark shifts in men whose low testosterone stems from severe obesity. This hormone drop is common in very heavy men and can persist after surgery. The team asked whether the weight-loss drug semaglutide leaves marks on gene control tags.

Samples came from two healthy controls, seven men with the condition, and four men checked again after drug use. The team read chemical tags on DNA and small RNA switches that tune genes. Six RNA switches differed, and eighty genes carried altered DNA tags, most on the X chromosome. One switch governed many of the tagged genes. Four well-linked hub genes surfaced, all tied to fat and sugar handling. The authors stress the read is early and needs larger checks.
pmc-13574880:
Guangzhi Wan, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 study of frailty before cancer and survival after it in older adults. Frailty, a worn-down state of low reserve, is known to worsen odds once cancer is present. Its weight when measured years before any diagnosis was far less clear.

The team drew on a large United States ageing survey, taking its 2006 wave as the start line. Adults aged fifty-two and up who were free of cancer at entry had their frailty scored then. Records ran through the end of 2020, so later cancers and deaths could be tracked against that early score. A long view like this separates frailty's own drag from the shock of diagnosis. The authors aim to show whether an early frailty check can flag patients who will need extra support.
pmc-13575180:
A Benmakhlouf leads a 2026 computing study of two rare-earth gold compounds under pressure. The compounds, ErAu and TmAu, mix a rare earth metal with gold in a simple cubic form. Such materials blend traits of metals and ceramics, and pressure can stiffen or destabilise them.

Calculations from first principles tracked structure, stiffness, sound speeds, and electronic states up to 20 gigapascals of pressure.
